contentBlocks.title: What goes into an accounting firm website

children.text: Why accounting firm websites all look the same

Because a large share of them come from a handful of vendors who build sites for the profession by the hundred. The result is the same structure, the same stock photograph of a handshake, and the same sentence: «we provide tax, audit and advisory services to businesses of all sizes». It is not laziness on the firm's part — it is what the product delivers, and it is cheap for a reason.

The cost shows up in the one moment that matters. A prospect comparing three firms in three browser tabs sees three pages that say the same thing, so the decision falls back to whichever answered the phone first or quoted lowest. A site that names the client's situation in its heading does not enter that comparison on price.
Web design for accounting firms: structure decided before decoration

The design question in this profession is not which shade of blue. It is what a visitor sees in the first screen: a slogan about trusted partnership, or the sentence that tells them you handle exactly their case. Everything else in the design follows from that choice — the navigation, the length of the pages, where the fee goes, and whether the team photographs come before or after the services.

What design decides here, concretely: how a client type is chosen from the first screen; whether the fee is above or below the fold; how a long regulatory explanation is made readable rather than skipped; and how the site looks to someone opening it on a phone between meetings, which is where most of these pages are actually opened.
Accounting firm website design that survives contact with the content

A design shown as three pretty screens usually falls apart when the real material arrives: a service list with twenty items, a bio that runs to two paragraphs, a fee table with footnotes, and a disclaimer the firm is obliged to carry. So the design is built against the real content — your service list, your bios, your fee structure — rather than against placeholder text. That is also why I ask for the material before drawing anything.
A page per client type, as pages rather than a list

Accounting is bought by segment. An e-commerce seller with inventory across states, a construction firm with progress billing and retainage, a dental practice with equipment leases, a freelancer who has just crossed a registration threshold — different questions, different software, different anxieties. One page listing all of them answers none of them.
the segment named in the heading, not in the third paragraph;
the specific problems that segment brings, in its own words;
the software you work in, because the segment asks about it first;
what the engagement includes and what it costs;
and no page for work you would rather not take — the site is also a filter.
Publishing fees on an accounting firm website

The most common complaint from visitors to these sites is that no figure appears anywhere. «Contact us for a quote» reads as «expensive, and awkward to ask about», and the enquiries it does produce are the hardest to qualify, because everyone arrives without any idea of the range.

Going as far as you are willing is enough: a monthly fee for a defined scope, a fixed price for an annual return at a stated revenue level, or a range with what moves it. Firms that publish a floor get fewer enquiries and close more of them, which is the trade most practices actually want.
Document exchange without building a portal

Clients will send tax documents through whatever channel is easiest, and if the site offers a plain upload form, that is where sensitive material will land — on your web hosting, outside whatever system your practice actually runs on. That is a liability, not a feature.

The right answer is almost always a link, not a build: practice software such as TaxDome, Karbon or Canopy already has a client portal with the access controls and the audit trail, so the site's job is to route people into it clearly and explain what to send. Building a second upload path on the website costs money and creates a copy of the data nobody is watching.
Making credentials and the signing accountant visible

In a profession where the buyer is assessing risk, the page that converts is often the team page. What belongs on it: who holds which licence or membership, who would actually handle the visitor's segment, and who signs off the work. What does not: a wall of certification logos with no names attached, which reads as decoration.
A site for a solo bookkeeping practice

A solo practice sells a recurring operational service rather than an annual engagement, and the buyer compares monthly price, the software and how fast you answer. So the site is shorter and sharper: the software named on the first screen, the monthly fee stated, what is and is not included, and how handover works. A five-page site does this job; a twenty-page firm site does not suit it.
What an accounting firm website costs and what moves the price

A full site with client-type pages, fees, document routing and an editable CMS starts at €2,000. A landing page for one segment is €700–1,400. Moving off a vendor template while keeping the rankings starts at €1,000. What moves the price: how many client segments get their own page, how many offices and team members, whether the fee structure is ready or has to be worked out, and whether the content exists. Design is included and never quoted separately. The full list is on the
pricing page
How long an accounting firm website takes to build

A landing page two to three weeks, a full site four to six. The code is rarely what stretches it: it is the segment decisions, the fee structure and who inside the firm signs off the professional wording. Projects that finish on time are the ones where one partner can decide without a meeting.
Getting the site found once it is built

A site built like this can be found; being found is separate work. Segment pages have to earn positions, the Google Business Profile has to match the site, and in this profession the content has to be published before the busy season rather than during it. That is
SEO for accounting firms
— a separate job with a separate price, and I will say if the site has to be rebuilt before any of it is worth doing.

children.text: Adult SEO is search engine optimization for legal 18+ businesses — membership and video sites, adult shops, studios and platforms, OnlyFans management agencies and independent creators — and it is the service on this page. The work is mine from research to reports. Paid search barely helps in this niche: Google Ads restricts sexual content and refuses adult offers in many countries, and most social networks limit what you may promote. Organic search, AI answers and your own list therefore carry more of the load than in almost any other industry.
Adult SEO services from one consultant instead of an adult SEO agency

People who search for an adult SEO agency or an adult SEO company usually find agencies with long service menus and link sellers who promise first place within weeks. My offer has a different shape. You deal with a single specialist who can also code, so whoever reads your server logs also rewrites the category pages and fixes the templates. There are no ranking guarantees and no link networks, because those put an adult domain at more risk than a mainstream one.

My clients are lawful businesses whose performers have all been verified as adults. Checking their age and keeping the records — US 18 U.S.C. 2257 paperwork, UK Online Safety Act age assurance and similar rules — remain the operator’s legal responsibility; check with your lawyer which rules apply to you. Work for adult clients is kept private and never appears among my public case studies.
Google SafeSearch and SEO for adult websites

SafeSearch hides explicit results for a large share of searchers: signed-in teenagers, many work, school and public networks, and everyone who leaves the default setting on. Google classifies pages by their content, and a whole site can be treated as explicit if SFW and explicit pages are mixed without structure. Three rules help:
explicit material lives in its own section or subdomain, marked with the adult rating meta tag Google recommends
SFW pages — about, guides, agency services, product categories without explicit images — are kept clean, so they can appear in filtered results too
titles and descriptions describe the page in neutral words; explicit phrasing in a title does not help ranking and narrows who sees it
SFW pages and a blog in adult website SEO

Most business demand in this niche is not explicit at all: how to start as a creator, how payouts work, which agency terms are fair, how to protect paid content, gift ideas from a legal adult shop. These queries are visible without SafeSearch getting in the way, and they bring visitors who later subscribe, buy or apply. A blog with guides written by real people, pages that answer one question each and internal links into the gated areas give an adult site reach it would never get from explicit keywords alone.

Trust matters here as it does for health or money topics. A registered company name, an address, an editorial policy, named authors and clear refund and privacy terms make both readers and quality raters more willing to treat the site as a real business.
Link building for adult websites without link schemes

Link building is the hardest part of SEO for adult websites. Many publishers refuse adult links outright, guest-post marketplaces filter the niche out, and what remains is often private blog networks and paid link packages that Google treats as link schemes. Those can work for a while and then take the domain down with them. Cleaner sources are slower but last:
industry press, review sites and forums that cover adult business openly
partners you already work with: processors, platforms, affiliate programs, event organizers
data and guides others cite — payout surveys, safety checklists, legal overviews
interviews and podcasts for founders and agency owners
Every outbound paid or affiliate link on your own pages carries the sponsored attribute.
Technical SEO for large adult sites: crawl budget, duplicate thumbnails and pagination

Tube sites, clip stores and big membership catalogs often have hundreds of thousands of URLs, and most of them are near-duplicates: the same video under five tags, the same thumbnail at four sizes, sorting and filter parameters, endless pagination. Googlebot spends its time on those instead of the pages that matter. The fixes are known but need care:
tag and category pages kept only where there is real search demand and enough unique items; the rest set to noindex or merged
filter and sort parameters canonicalized or blocked from crawling
pagination with clean links and no infinite scroll without fallback URLs
server log analysis to see where the crawler actually goes
Image and video SEO for adult websites: what structured data can do

Video is the core content of many adult sites, and search engines index it through a crawlable page per video, a stable thumbnail, a sitemap with video entries and VideoObject markup with title, description, duration and upload date. Rich results for explicit pages are limited and filtered by SafeSearch, so markup on gated pages helps understanding more than display. On shops and SFW pages, Product, Organization and Breadcrumb markup work as on any other site. Images need descriptive file names and alt text in neutral language.
SEO for OnlyFans management agencies: ranking for creators’ searches

“onlyfans management agency” is the largest business search in this niche, and the people typing it are creators looking for help. An agency that ranks for it, and for variants with a country such as the UK or the US, receives applications without paying for each one. The pages that rank answer what creators ask before signing: services, commission, contract length, payout reports, the team, how to leave. Location and language pages target creators in other markets, a careers section ranks for management jobs, and reviews on independent sites build the trust these searchers check for.
SEO for adult content creators: owning your name in search

Fans search for a creator by name. Without a site of your own, the first results are leak sites, fan wikis and aggregators that profit from your name. An own domain with an SFW page, a consistent name across platforms, Person markup and links from your official profiles gives Google one clear official source. DMCA notices then remove the worst results, and the official page takes their place.
Adult SEO in Bing and other languages

In this niche Bing usually brings a larger share of visits than in mainstream search, partly because its filters behave differently. It gets a verified webmaster account and a sitemap. Language versions open markets where competition is lower than in English; each gets pages written for local searches, not machine translation, and hreflang so every searcher lands on the right version.
Adult SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Assistants refuse explicit queries, but business ones get full answers: “best OnlyFans management agencies in the UK”, “is it legal to be an OnlyFans manager”, “which payment processors accept adult sites”. Work on those answers is called GEO (generative engine optimization) or AEO (answer engine optimization). For an adult business it means facts on SFW pages in plain text, an About page with the legal entity, consistent descriptions across directories and review sites, and AI crawlers allowed in robots.txt for public sections.
A fixed set of business questions goes to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google at the start and again a few months later, so you see which brands they name and whether yours joins them. More on this in

Appliance repair searches: by appliance, by brand and by symptom
People describe a broken appliance in three ways, and each needs a different kind of page:
by appliance and place — “refrigerator repair near me”, “dryer repair [town]”, “dishwasher repair service”
by brand — “Samsung refrigerator repair”, “LG washer repair”, “Sub-Zero repair [city]”
by symptom or code — “fridge not cooling but freezer works”, “washer won’t spin”, “oven F3 error”

The first two groups are close to a booking. The third mixes do-it-yourselfers with people who will call once they understand the problem is not a five-minute fix. A good site catches all three and moves the last group toward the phone.
Appliance pages for appliance repair SEO: refrigerators, washers, dryers, dishwashers, ovens

Each appliance you repair deserves its own page, because each has its own searches, faults and parts. A refrigerator page covers cooling problems, ice makers, water leaks and compressors; a laundry page covers drains, bearings, belts and heating elements; a cooking page separates gas ranges, electric cooktops, wall ovens and microwaves. Write about the faults you see every week, what a typical repair involves and how long it takes. If you repair gas appliances, say what you do with gas lines and what you leave to a licensed gas fitter where your state requires one.
Brand pages for appliance repair: Samsung, LG, Whirlpool, GE and high-end brands

Brand searches are some of the best searches in this trade: the person knows exactly what they own and wants someone who knows it too. A brand page lists the appliance types you service for that brand, common problems on its models and whether you stock its parts. High-end built-in brands — Sub-Zero, Wolf, Thermador, Viking, Miele — bring fewer calls but larger tickets, and owners of these appliances search for specialists by name.

Be careful with the word “authorized”. Use it only for brands where you hold factory authorization, and say “we repair Samsung appliances” elsewhere. Brand names in domains, profile names or fake “brand service center” listings can bring trademark complaints and suspended profiles; plain, accurate brand pages bring the same searches without that risk.

The service call fee is the first objection in appliance repair. Customers want to know what they pay for the visit, what it includes and what happens if the repair is not worth doing. Put it on one clear page and in short form on each appliance page: the fee, what the technician checks, whether it is applied to the repair, how a written estimate is given before any work starts.

The other question behind most calls is whether an old appliance is worth fixing. A short guide by appliance — typical lifespan, repairs that usually make sense, repairs that rarely do — builds trust and keeps the reader on your site instead of a national cost guide.

Many repair companies fill their schedule with warranty work: manufacturer warranty repairs for brands that authorize them, extended warranty claims and dispatches from home warranty companies. children.text: A visual profession judged on load time

There's an awkward paradox in architecture websites. The work is visual, so the instinct is to present it at full quality — large renders, high-resolution photography, generous galleries. And that instinct, followed without technical discipline, produces a site where the work is never seen. A visitor on a phone gives a slow page a few seconds; if the first image hasn't appeared, they leave with no impression of the studio at all.

Solving this isn't about compromising on quality. Modern image formats, sizes generated per device, and a loading strategy that prioritises what's on screen let a portfolio stay visually uncompromised and still appear immediately. This is straightforward engineering work, and it's the single highest-impact decision on an architecture site. On a client project in another visual field — a workshop with an extensive gallery of work — the same approach moved the mobile performance score from around 50 to 92 without reducing the number or quality of the photographs.

The second decision is structural. Most studio sites treat projects as gallery items: a thumbnail, a lightbox, perhaps a caption. Search engines find nothing there to read, which means the studio's strongest asset contributes nothing to being found. Giving each project its own page — with the brief, the constraints, the decisions taken and the materials used — changes that twice over. It creates something indexable, and it answers the question a serious client is actually asking, which is not what you build but how you think.

Segmentation follows from this. A family commissioning a house, a developer planning apartments and a company fitting out an office are three different clients searching three different ways. A portfolio that separates project types lets each of them find the work that matters to them, rather than scrolling past everything else.
And then there's the process. Clients who haven't commissioned design before don't know the stages, what each produces, how long they take or what determines cost. Studios that explain this plainly
remove the uncertainty that quietly ends a lot of enquiries
— and, incidentally, create the content that answers what people search for long before they're ready to choose a studio. This is what

Project filters by typology, location and status: the information architecture of an architect’s site

A studio with forty projects needs a way to show the right five. Filters by typology — houses, housing, offices, education, interiors, landscape — by location and by status — built, in progress, competition — let a developer see only commercial work and a homeowner only houses. The chosen filter stays in the page address, so a link to “built houses in Colorado” can be sent in an email.

This is the part of the job that “website architecture design” refers to in the web sense: the structure behind the pages. On an architect’s site it decides how fast the right project is found, so it is agreed before any visual design starts.
Typography, whitespace and grids in website design for architects
Architects notice type and spacing, and their clients judge the site with the same eye. Choices I make together with the studio:
one or two typefaces, often a neutral sans serif for text with a more distinctive face for headings
a grid that respects the proportions of the photography rather than cropping every image to a square
generous whitespace around images, and text set at a comfortable line length
a restrained palette taken from the studio’s identity, with one color kept for buttons
body text large enough to read on a phone without zooming
Minimal does not have to mean hard to use. Menus stay visible, labels stay readable, and buttons look like buttons.
Team, process and studio pages in architecture firm website design

Clients hire people. A team page with real portraits, roles, registration details and the projects each architect led works better than a grid of black-and-white faces without names. A process page walks through the stages — first meeting, feasibility, concept, permit drawings, technical design, construction — with what the client receives at each and roughly how long it takes. A studio page can show the office, physical models and sketches: work in progress says more about method than a mission statement.
Awards, publications and press on an architecture website
Awards and features in architecture media are proof that clients understand. The design gives them a place without turning the site into a trophy shelf:
a short line on the project page naming the award or publication and the year, linked to the source
a press page listing each publication, the date and the article, as text
publication logos only beside the matching text, never as an unexplained strip
Website design for residential, commercial, interior and landscape architects
Residential architecture websites

Homeowners compare houses, not concepts. Interior photography, before-and-after views, a plain description of the process and a first-meeting form that asks about the plot, the budget and the timeline.
Commercial and public-sector practices
Developers and public clients look for experience by sector and scale. Sector pages, project facts in tables, team credentials, and the frameworks or tenders you can name.
Architecture and interior design websites
Studios that do both need projects tagged by service, so a client who wants only an interior is not lost among buildings. Materials, furniture and supplier credits interest this audience.
Landscape architecture websites
Gardens and public spaces change with the seasons and the years. Pages that show the same place over time, planting plans and maps for large sites tell that story.
Architecture website design templates or a custom design

Architecture website design templates on Squarespace, Webflow, WordPress or Format are popular because their demos use beautiful photography and six neat projects. For a young studio they are a sensible start: low cost, quick launch, easy editing.

Limits appear as the portfolio grows: filters that cannot combine typology and location, project pages without room for drawings or facts, galleries that get heavier with every project, one language, little control over structured data. A custom design pays off when the studio has dozens of projects, works in several sectors or countries, or wants commissions from search. Leaving a template later means building again, so the choice is worth making early.
Best architecture website design: patterns behind sites that bring clients

Collections of the best architecture websites and architecture website design inspiration on Pinterest, Archello or Webflow show striking home pages. Behind the ones that bring clients, the same patterns repeat:
a first screen that says what the studio designs and where
project thumbnails with the type and place written under each
filters by typology and location
project pages that combine images, drawings and a short text
a contact button that stays in reach without covering the photography
the same quality on a phone as on a large monitor
When you collect ideas, open a project page and the contact page on your phone, not only the home page on a desktop.
An architecture website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews for an architect who designs a certain type of building in a certain place, the answer comes from text the assistant can read. A site where projects exist only as images, services sit in a PDF and the address appears only on an embedded map gives assistants nothing to repeat. The design keeps services, project types, places, team and awards as page text, with structured data for the practice and each project.

children.text: Artist website design is what this page offers: I plan, design and build portfolio websites for painters, printmakers, sculptors and illustrators, and I do the work myself from first sketch to launch. The site is a quiet room for your work — images large, text short, nothing competing with the art — with clear paths for the three people who matter: a collector who wants to buy, a curator who wants your CV, and a client who wants to commission.
Artist website design: what a collector, curator or gallerist checks first
Most visitors already saw a piece at a fair, in a group show or on Instagram, and they arrive with one question each. The first screen and the menu answer all three without a scroll:
the work — one strong image or a short row from the current series, not a logo on a blank page
who you are — your name, medium and city in one line, such as “Painter working in oil and cold wax, Santa Fe”
where to go — Works, Available, Commissions, CV and Contact, in words rather than icons
An artist statement belongs one click away. Opening the site with three paragraphs of theory asks a buyer to read before they have seen anything.
An artist portfolio website with large images that load fast

Art is judged on detail, and detail means large files. Uploaded unchanged, a dozen high-resolution photos make a portfolio stall on a phone, and the visitor leaves after the first one. The build handles that for you:
each image saved in several widths and in WebP or AVIF, so a phone gets a light file and a 27-inch monitor a sharp one
color profiles kept, so your blues stay the blues you painted
the first image shows immediately, and the others load only when the visitor scrolls to them
a full-screen view with zoom on details such as brushwork or surface texture
Good photographs matter as much as code. Shoot paintings straight on, in even light and without the frame; for sculpture, three or four angles and one shot that shows scale in a room.
Artwork pages with medium, dimensions, year and price or “enquire”
Every work has its own page and address, so you can send a collector a direct link instead of a screenshot. The page lists, as text:
title, year and medium — “Oil and graphite on panel”
dimensions in inches and centimeters, with framed size if it ships framed
status: available, sold, on loan or in an exhibition, with the gallery named
price, a price range, or an “Enquire about this work” button that sends the title with the message
a few lines about the work and two or three related pieces from the same series
Sold works stay on the site. They show your range and your market, and a sold label often prompts a commission request for something similar.
Series and collections on an artist website

Most artists work in bodies of work, and a long grid mixes them into noise. Grouping by series gives each body its own page with a short text — what started it, the materials, where it was shown — and lets a curator see how your practice has moved over the years. Filters by medium, size and availability help a buyer who has a specific wall in mind. Older series move to an archive section rather than disappearing.
Artist CV, exhibitions and artist statement pages

Curators, juries and grant panels expect a CV in a familiar order, and gallerists check it before a studio visit. The CV page is HTML text rather than a PDF so it can be read on a phone and found by search engines, with a PDF version to download:
education and residencies
solo and group exhibitions, newest first, with venue and city
awards, grants, public and private collections
press and publications with links where they exist

Upcoming shows sit on a separate page with dates, the venue and opening hours. The statement and a short bio, written in the third person for press use, get their own page next to downloadable portrait photos.
A commissions page for portraits, murals and custom work
Commissions need more explanation than a finished work, because the client is buying something that does not exist yet. A dedicated page lays it out:
what you take on: pet or family portraits, large paintings for a particular room, murals, illustration
examples of past commissions, with the client’s permission
the steps: brief, sketch, approval, painting, delivery, and how many revisions are included
timeline, deposit and a starting price or price per size, if you choose to publish them
a form that asks for size, subject, reference photos, deadline and budget range
Selling prints and original art from your website

Originals and prints are different purchases. An original usually starts a conversation — about shipping, framing, a studio visit — so an enquiry button often works better than a cart. Prints are impulse buys and sell best with a checkout.
A print shop on your own site

Limited editions show the edition size, paper, printing method and whether each print is signed and numbered. Checkout runs through Stripe or a Shopify store connected to the site, with shipping zones and costs you set. Print-on-demand services such as Fine Art America or Printful can handle production, linked from your print pages.
Links to marketplaces and galleries

If you already sell through Saatchi Art, Etsy or a gallery’s online viewing room, the artwork page links to the listing so prices stay in one place. Photographers who sell prints have different needs; they are covered under
photographer website design
Protecting images on an artist website: what works in practice

No setting fully prevents copying: anything that appears on a screen can be screenshotted. What reduces misuse in practice is publishing images at web size, about 2,000 pixels on the long side, never your print files; adding your name and a copyright line to the image metadata and under every work; and using a reverse image search now and then to find copies. A subtle watermark is an option for new work you share widely. Blocking the right-click menu mostly annoys real buyers and does little else.
Artist website examples: Squarespace, Format, Artlogic or a custom design

Look through any list of the top 10 artist websites and the pattern is the same: few words, generous white space, fast images, simple menus. Beautiful artist websites are quiet; the art supplies the color.
When a template is enough
Squarespace, Wix, Format, Pixpa or Artlogic’s artist sites are a sensible start for an early career, a small body of work, or an artist who enjoys updating pages personally.
When a custom artist website pays off

Custom design pays off once you manage hundreds of works with status and pricing, sell prints and originals in different ways, show in several countries and need a second language, or want a site that does not look like the same template other artists in your scene use.
Instagram or your own artist website

Instagram is where many collectors discover new work, and it is worth keeping active. It is still a feed: posts sink within days, sizes and order belong to the platform, and the reach of your next post is decided by an algorithm. Your website is the permanent record — every series, every price, your full CV — and the link in your bio leads to the current series or the available works page rather than the home page.
An artist website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Buyers and curators increasingly ask AI assistants things like “abstract landscape painters in New Mexico” or “artists who paint large commissions for hotel lobbies”. An assistant can only recommend an artist whose site it can read. Your name, medium, themes, city, galleries and exhibitions are written as text, and structured data describes you, each artwork with medium, size and year, and each exhibition with its venue and dates.

children.text: Author website design is the service: I plan, design and build websites for novelists and nonfiction writers, so the same person draws your book pages, codes them and puts the site live. Retailers show one title at a time next to other people’s books. Your site shows your whole shelf, tells a new reader where to begin and asks them to stay in touch when they finish.
Author website design starts with the reader who just finished your book

The typical visitor read your last page five minutes ago, often in an ebook app, and tapped a link in the back matter or searched your name on a phone. They want to know three things before their interest fades:
what kind of books you write — one line such as “Gothic mysteries set on the Maine coast”, placed above everything else
what comes next — the newest or upcoming book, with its cover and a buy button
how to hear about the next one — a sign-up form, not a social media icon row

Covers are the heaviest images on the page, so each one is stored in several sizes and modern formats: a phone on a slow connection gets a light file in a fraction of a second, a large screen gets a sharp one. A home page that opens with a long biography or a slider of reviews makes this reader scroll past what they came for.
Book pages with retailer links for every store and country
Every book gets its own address that you can put in back matter, ads, podcast notes and email signatures. On that page:
the cover, the blurb as real text and a short hook line
each format — ebook, paperback, hardcover, audiobook — with page count, narrator, publisher and ISBN
a sample chapter readers can open on the page
review lines and award mentions with their source
content notes and age range where your readers expect them

A reader in Melbourne who taps a link to the US Kindle store lands in a store where they cannot buy. Retailer buttons point to the right regional store, or to a universal book link from a service such as Books2Read, next to Bookshop.org, Barnes & Noble, Kobo, Apple Books, Google Play and the audiobook stores. Links live in one place in the editor, so a changed store link is fixed once and updates on the book page, the series page and the home page.
Series reading order page on an author website

“Where do I start?” and “What order do these go in?” are the questions readers email authors most. A series page settles them: the books numbered, novellas and short stories placed where they belong in the story, and a short note when the publishing order differs from the reading order. Every book page then carries a “Next in the series” block, so the reader who finishes book two late at night goes straight to book three.

Authors with several series, or with pen names in different genres, get a separate hub for each. A reader of your sweet small-town romances should not land on your dark thrillers without warning, and the menus keep the two apart.
Newsletter sign-up as the main goal of self-published author websites

For self-published author websites the email list is the most valuable thing the site produces. It is the one way to reach readers that no retailer ranking or social media feed controls, and launch-week sales depend on it. The site collects addresses in three places:
a reader magnet — a prequel novella, a bonus epilogue or a deleted scene — delivered by BookFunnel, StoryOrigin or your email service
a short form on the home page, at the end of every sample chapter and on each book page
a separate landing page for the link in your back matter, so you can see how many subscribers the books themselves bring

Forms connect to MailerLite, Kit, Mailchimp or the service you already pay for, tag new subscribers by series or pen name where your tool supports it, and ask for consent in a form that also covers readers in the EU and the UK.
Preorder, launch and ARC request pages for a new book

A new book needs an address months before release day. The page opens with the cover reveal and preorder links, adds an excerpt and early review lines as the date approaches, and becomes the normal book page afterwards. Because the address never changes, links you shared in January still work in June.

Advance reader copies get their own form. Reviewers, bloggers and BookTok or Bookstagram readers apply with their platform, audience size and the genres they cover; you approve the ones you want, and copies go out through BookFunnel or NetGalley, wherever your publisher or your own account handles them.
Media kit and events page for authors
Podcast hosts, librarians, bookstore event managers and festival organizers need the same files every time. A media kit page saves both sides an email exchange:
bios in three lengths, written in the third person
author photos in print resolution, with the photographer’s credit
cover files and a one-page sell sheet for each book
interview topics, past podcast and radio appearances, and contacts for your agent or publicist

Readings, signings, school visits and panels go on an events page with date, venue, time zone and a link to tickets. Past events move to an archive, which shows an organizer you already know how a room works.
Self-published and traditionally published author websites: what changes
The structure is the same; the weight moves.
Author website for a traditionally published author

Your publisher has a page for each book, and you link to it. Your own site carries what the publisher’s page does not: all your books across imprints in one place, your voice, speaking and events, rights and translation enquiries routed to your agent, and a newsletter that stays with you if you change publishers.
Author website for a self-published author

You are the publisher, so the site does more of the selling. Next to the retailer links it can sell ebooks and audiobooks directly through a store such as Payhip or Shopify with BookFunnel delivery, offer bundles and signed paperbacks, and show the box sets that exist only on your site.
Author website examples: design that matches your genre
The best author website design follows the structure above and takes its look from the books. A reader should be able to guess the genre with the sound turned off.
Romance author website design

The covers set the colors. Readers often look for tropes and heat levels, so these become labels or filters on the book list, and couples or towns become series hubs. Bonus epilogues are reliable reader magnets in this genre.
Thriller, mystery, fantasy and nonfiction

Thrillers and mysteries use stronger contrast and short, tense copy. Fantasy readers come back for maps, character lists and glossaries between books, so those get their own pages. Nonfiction sites sell the author as an expert: speaking topics, media appearances, and an order form for bulk or corporate copies.
Own domain or a platform: BookBub, Squarespace or custom author website design services

You can create an author website for free or cheaply with BookBub’s author websites, Squarespace, Wix or a downloadable WordPress template, and for a debut author with one book that is a reasonable start. Your Amazon Author Central page, Goodreads and BookBub profiles are worth keeping current too, since readers look there. What these platforms do not hand you is an address you fully own and a list of readers’ emails.

Custom design starts paying off when a backlist or several series no longer fit the template’s book layout, when you write under more than one name, when translated editions need their own language versions — see
multilingual website development
— or when years of blog posts on an older WordPress site have to move without breaking links from old interviews, as described under

More and more readers type questions into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews, such as “a cozy mystery series with a bookshop owner, first book” or “in what order should I read the Harbor Lights novels?” An assistant answers from pages it can read. Your author name, pen names, genres, series and reading order are written as page text, and structured data marks up the author, every book with its ISBNs and formats, and each series with its order. Review lines carry their source and date, so they can be checked.

children.text: Auto detailing website design is what I do for detailing shops and mobile detailers: planning, design and the build all come from me, so a single person answers for the result and the price is fixed before work starts. A detailing website sells something customers find hard to judge before paying. A full interior detail, a two-step paint correction and a ceramic coating can look alike in a listing yet cost very different amounts, so the site has to show the difference, prove the results with photos and take a booking without a long exchange of messages.
Auto detailing website design for detailing shops and mobile detailers
Detailing businesses come in two shapes, and the site is built around the one you run:
a shop with bays, where customers drop the car off and need to know drop-off and pickup times, how long each package takes and where to leave the keys
a mobile detailer with a van, a water tank and a generator, where the work happens in the customer’s driveway and the site explains where you go and what you need there
a mix of both: maintenance washes and interiors on the road, paint correction and coatings in the shop, with the site steering each job to the right place

In each case the person who answers the phone is usually the person holding the polisher. The site takes the repeat questions — how long, how much, do you come to me, should I wash it first — so the messages you do answer are the ones that need you.
Detailing packages on the website: interior, exterior, ceramic coating and PPF

The package page is the one most visitors open. Customers compare packages rather than single services, so each package gets a clear name, a list of what is done, the time it takes and a starting price:
interior detail: vacuuming, shampoo and extraction of seats and carpets, leather cleaning and conditioning, pet hair, odor removal
exterior detail: hand wash, decontamination and clay bar, wheels and tires, a sealant or wax
paint correction: one-step or multi-step polishing that removes swirls and light scratches, usually done before a coating
ceramic coating: wash, correction, application, curing time and aftercare
paint protection film: full front, high-impact areas or full body, with the film brand you install
maintenance plans for coated and wrapped cars, if you sell them
Ceramic coating and PPF pages that answer questions before the quote

Coatings and film are the largest tickets in a detailing business and the jobs people research for weeks. Each gets its own page: what the product does and what it does not do, how the paint is prepared, how many days the car stays with you, what the manufacturer’s warranty covers and how the owner should wash the car afterward. A customer who has read that page writes to ask about dates rather than whether coatings are worth the money.
Detailing prices by vehicle size and condition

Prices on a detailing site are usually written as “from”, split by vehicle size: coupe or sedan, SUV, truck or minivan. One short line under each price says what raises it — heavy pet hair, sand, stains, a neglected finish. That line prevents arguments at pickup, because the customer read before booking that a car in rough shape costs more.
Before and after photos on an auto detailing website
Detailing is sold with pictures, and the gallery convinces when the photos are comparable:
the same car from the same angle in similar light, side by side or with a slider
each set labeled with the package and the vehicle, so the owner of a muddy minivan finds a muddy minivan
50/50 shots of paint correction and close-ups of water beading on a coating, which show what a wide photo cannot
short clips of extraction or foam, kept light enough to play on mobile data

Images are compressed and served in modern formats, so a gallery of eighty photos opens as fast as a page of text. The strongest sets also appear on the package pages, because a photo next to a price sells more than one hidden in a separate tab.
Mobile detailing service area: towns, ZIP check and what you need on site

For a mobile detailer the service area is part of the offer. It is written as a list of towns and ZIP codes, not only drawn as a circle on a map, and the booking form checks the ZIP code before asking anything else. If you charge a travel fee beyond a set distance, the form shows that fee instead of turning the customer away.

The same page says what the customer provides: a place to park the van, access to water and a power outlet if your rig needs them, and whether you can work in an apartment garage or an office parking lot. Building and HOA rules get one plain sentence. It prevents bookings that collapse on the morning of the job.
Online booking and deposits on an auto detailing website
A detail blocks a bay or a whole day on the road, so a no-show costs real money. The booking flow is built with that in mind:
The customer picks a package and a vehicle size, and the price range updates.
They add extras — engine bay, headlight restoration, pet hair removal — and see how long the job will take.
They choose a date from your calendar; coating and film jobs block enough days automatically.
They pay a deposit by card, with the cancellation and rescheduling rules shown above the button.

Most detailers already use a scheduling tool such as Square Appointments, Jobber or Urable, and the site embeds it, styled to match, rather than replacing it. The deposit amount, the refund terms and what happens if the car arrives in worse shape than described are written as text on the page, not only inside the widget, so the customer reads them before paying.
Auto detailing website templates, Jobber sites or a custom website

Searches for an auto detailing website template lead to theme stores and site builders, and field-service tools include a simple site with the subscription. For a detailer starting out with three packages, either is a sensible choice: it goes live in days and the booking link works.
Templates start to hold the business back when:
all packages sit on one page, so nobody finds you for “ceramic coating” or “interior detailing” in your town
the gallery is made for six stock photos, not hundreds of before/after sets
page titles, addresses and structured data are hard or impossible to change
the site lives on the platform and disappears when the subscription ends
A custom site keeps your booking tool and adds what the template lacks: a page per package, a fast gallery and service area pages under your own domain.
What the best auto detailing websites have in common
Lists of the best auto detailing websites mostly show dark themes and glossy sports cars. The sites that keep a calendar full share less visible habits:
the first screen says what you do, where, and how to book, with call and text buttons
work from your own shop and your own van rather than stock photos of supercars
packages with starting prices and durations, not a paragraph about a passion for perfection
reviews next to the booking button that name the car and the package, taken from your Google profile
for coatings and film: the product brand, your installer certification if you hold one, and the warranty terms in writing
Colors and fonts come after these. On a phone, a visitor decides within seconds whether their car and their problem are on the page.
Local SEO for an auto detailing website: “car detailing near me” and “ceramic coating near me”

People search by service and place: “mobile detailing near me”, “ceramic coating” with a city name, “interior car cleaning”. A shop’s Google Business Profile shows its address; a mobile detailer sets the profile up as a service-area business with the home address hidden. Either way the profile lists the same packages as the site, gets fresh photos from real jobs and collects reviews that mention the service and the town.

Each main package has its own page, and town pages exist only for places you actually drive to or draw customers from. A full site ships with the profile and these pages in place; the monthly side of map work is covered on the
local SEO services
page. If your business also repairs cars, the search side of that work is on the
SEO for auto repair shops
page.
An auto detailing website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Car owners ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews questions like “is ceramic coating worth it on a new car” or “who installs PPF near me”. Assistants recommend businesses they can read about. Packages shown as images, prices hidden inside a booking widget and a gallery without captions give them nothing to quote. The same facts as text — packages, starting prices, duration, service area, coating and film brands — with structured data for the business and its services, can be read and repeated.
Getting named in those answers is ongoing work; see
AI SEO and GEO optimization
How an auto detailing website design project runs
Brief. You send your packages, rough prices by vehicle size, service area, booking tool and a folder of before/after photos; recorded voice notes work as well as a document.
Mobile mockups. You review the first screen, one package page and the booking steps as phone-sized mockups before anything is built.
Development. The site is coded for speed, with an editor where you change prices, add packages and upload new before/after sets yourself.
Launch. Booking, deposit payments, analytics and your Google profile are wired together, and a short written manual shows you how to update packages and galleries.
My general approach to building sites is described on the
website development
page.

Design and build are one price.
A simple auto detailing website — home page, packages with prices, gallery, about, service area and booking link: 700–1,400 €.
A full site with a page per package, before/after galleries, service area pages, booking with deposits and local SEO setup: from 2,000 €.
After launch you pay for hosting and the domain, and me only for changes you ask for. Full ranges are on the
pricing
page.

children.text: I provide B2B SEO services for companies that sell to other businesses — manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, software and IT service firms. I do the work myself, as a single consultant who also builds websites. The measure is simple: how many relevant companies find you in search and AI answers and ask for a quote, a sample or a demo.
What B2B SEO is: search work measured in qualified leads, not traffic

B2B SEO uses the same tools as any other SEO — keyword research, pages, technical fixes, links — but aims at a different result. A consumer shop can win on volume: thousands of visits, a small share buying. A B2B company may need ten good enquiries a month, and one signed contract can pay for a year of work. That changes three questions:
who searches: an engineer looking for a part, a procurement manager comparing suppliers, an operations lead looking for software
what they type: the problem, the specification, the application or the certificate — rarely the name of your company category
what counts as a result: a request for a quote, a sample, a demo or a call with sales, from a company that fits your customer profile
Traffic that never reaches a conversation with sales is not a result, and I do not report it as one.
SEO for B2B companies: low-volume, high-value keywords

Most keyword tools show zeros for B2B. “Hygienic stainless valve DN50”, “private label cosmetics manufacturer EU”, “WMS for a 3PL warehouse” may have ten searches a month or no measured volume at all. These are often the best phrases a B2B company has: the person typing them knows exactly what they need.
So keyword research starts with your sales team rather than a tool:
the words customers use in RFQs, emails and calls, which often differ from your catalog names
the problems buyers describe before they know which product solves them
the standards, materials, part numbers and certificates they filter by
the competitors and alternatives they compare you with
Then I check those phrases in search data, look at what the results show — suppliers, marketplaces, directories, guides — and choose the ones where a page of yours can rank and lead to an enquiry.
Buying committees and long sales cycles in B2B SEO

A B2B purchase is rarely decided by one person. An engineer checks that the product fits, procurement compares prices and terms, a manager signs off on the risk, sometimes finance or IT checks details. The cycle takes weeks or many months, and each person searches for different things at different moments. The SEO plan gives each of them a page to land on:
the engineer or specialist: specifications, tolerances, compatibility, installation, documentation
procurement: minimum order, lead times, delivery terms, certificates, how to request a quote
the decision-maker: case studies, references, how quality and risk are handled, who runs the company
everyone, early on: guides that explain the problem and the ways to solve it
Each page links to the next step, so a visitor who arrives on a guide reaches the spec page, and a visitor on the spec page reaches the quote form.
Industry and use-case pages in SEO for B2B companies

Buyers search by their own industry and task: “packaging film for frozen food”, “CRM for freight forwarders”, “antistatic flooring for electronics assembly”. A site organized only by your product categories misses these searches. Two page types fill the gap:
industry pages — one for each sector you serve, with its requirements, standards, typical problems and the products or services that fit
use-case or application pages — one for each task the product solves, with the conditions, the results you can document and a clear next step

These pages work only when they carry real industry knowledge: the terms, the regulations, the objections a buyer from that sector raises. A template with the industry name swapped is filtered out by Google and ignored by buyers. I build them from short interviews with your sales and technical people, so the content holds details competitors cannot copy.
Product and spec pages in B2B SEO: catalogs, datasheets and comparison content
For manufacturers and distributors, the product page is where most qualified searches land, and many catalogs lose that traffic:
specifications live only inside PDFs, so the page itself has no text to rank
thousands of filter combinations create duplicate addresses that waste crawling
product names are internal codes nobody searches for
the page ends without a way to ask for a price, a sample or a drawing

A product page that ranks has the key specifications as text, a short description in the buyer’s words, downloadable datasheets, product structured data and a quote request on the page. Case studies and comparison pages — your material against an alternative, your service against doing it in-house — help at the comparison stage, as long as every claim can be backed up.
How a manufacturer’s site is built around catalogs and quote requests is covered on the
manufacturing company website
page; the design side is on the
B2B website design
page.
Export and multilingual SEO for manufacturers and distributors

A manufacturer in Poland selling to Germany, a distributor in Cyprus covering the eastern Mediterranean, a software firm in the Baltics selling across the EU — each needs to be found by buyers searching in their own language. Those searches are not translations of yours: a German engineer and a Polish buyer describe the same part with different terms and different standards. What works:
a separate address for each language or market, written or edited by someone who knows the industry terms in that language
hreflang tags linking the versions, so Google shows each buyer the right one
keyword research per market, because volumes and competitors differ
local trust details: delivery to that country, local contacts or distributors, certificates recognized there
I work in English, Polish and Russian, and multilingual sites are a regular part of my work. An example of SEO for a manufacturer selling in several markets is the
SEO for lingerie manufacturers
page; the technical side of language versions is on the
multilingual website development
page.
B2B SEO for ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews: getting onto AI vendor shortlists (GEO, AEO)

B2B buyers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to suggest suppliers before they open a list of links: “which EU manufacturers make food-grade conveyor belts”, “compare WMS vendors for a mid-sized 3PL”. The assistant returns a short list, and a company that is not on it may never be considered. Getting onto that list is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a B2B company it means:
what you make or do, for which industries, in which countries and from what order size — written as plain facts on your pages
certificates, standards and capacities stated as text, not only as logos
use-case and comparison pages that answer the questions buyers put to assistants
the same company details on your site, LinkedIn, B2B directories and association listings, so assistants do not confuse you with another firm
I check how assistants describe your company and your competitors before the work and again after it. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Lead quality and CRM attribution in B2B SEO
In B2B the useful report is a list of enquiries and what became of them. I set this up at the start:
conversions in GA4 for quote requests, demo bookings, calls and downloads, with the page where the visit began
the source and landing page passed with each form into the CRM you use — HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive or another — so sales can see which enquiries came from search
a short monthly check with sales: which search leads were relevant and which became opportunities

This shows which pages bring buyers and which bring job seekers and competitors. With long cycles, revenue from a search lead can appear months later, and the CRM is the only place where it can be counted.
Technical SEO for B2B websites: catalogs, PDFs, gated content and speed
B2B sites share a set of technical problems that block rankings no matter how good the content is:
whitepapers and guides behind a form, with no open page that search engines can read — the fix is an open summary page with the form for the full file
PDFs ranking instead of the product pages, so visitors land on a file with no navigation and no contact button
customer portals, price lists and test pages left open to indexing
catalogs rendered only by JavaScript, which search engines and AI crawlers may read late or not at all
heavy product photos and scripts that push the main content past 2.5 seconds on a phone
Most are fixed in the first month or two.
B2B SEO agency or B2B SEO consultant: one specialist instead of an agency

A B2B SEO agency usually sells a team: an account manager, a strategist, writers, a link builder. Many sell a wider package of digital marketing for B2B — paid search, LinkedIn ads, email — with SEO as one part. That suits companies that need many channels and have someone in-house to manage the agency.

I work as a B2B SEO consultant: one person who does the research, interviews your experts, writes the briefs, fixes the code and reads the CRM data. Nothing gets lost between account manager and executor, and I build or rebuild the website when the site itself is the problem. I do not run ads or social accounts. Whoever you choose, ask:
Will you report enquiries and opportunities, or only rankings and traffic?
Who will talk to our technical people, and who writes the industry pages?
Who owns the content, the site and the accounts if we stop working together?
Is there a minimum contract, and why?
SEO services for B2B companies: what is included and how much it costs
B2B SEO audit — the site, keywords, catalog, technical problems and lead tracking: from 250 €, one-off, with fixes listed in order of impact.
One-off work — industry and use-case pages, product page templates, language versions, structured data, CRM tracking: 250–700 €.
Monthly SEO for a B2B company — new pages, export markets, AI visibility and reporting in enquiries: from 800 € per month; in very competitive markets from 1,300 € per month.

Many B2B companies with a niche product get most of the effect from the audit and a few strong industry and product pages; the audit shows whether monthly work is needed. How I approach SEO in general is on the

page, and all prices are on the

page.

page goes into capability pages, certifications and RFQs.
For software houses, MSPs and IT service firms, see

children.text: B2B website design is what I do for manufacturers, distributors and companies that sell services to other businesses, and I build the sites myself, so design and build come from one person at one price. A B2B site is read by people who are working, not browsing: an engineer checking a dimension, a buyer collecting three quotes, a manager who received a link from your sales rep. The design has to let each of them find their answer and take the next step without calling anyone.
B2B website design: what the site has to do for buyers and for the sales team

A good B2B website has two users. The first is the buyer, who visits several times over weeks or months, often with colleagues who never contact you. The second is your sales team, who send pages to prospects and need those pages to answer questions in their absence. The design serves both:
a first screen that says what you make or do, for which industries and in which countries
a visible way to request a quote or talk to sales on every page
pages long and complete enough that a rep can send one link instead of writing a long email
downloads, specifications and certificates that a buyer can forward inside their company
Website design for B2B: structure by industry, application and product
Buyers arrive with their own question: “do you make this part”, “do you serve my industry”, “can this solve my problem”. Website design for B2B gives each question its own path from the main menu:
products or services, grouped the way buyers think of them, not the way your ERP lists them
industries served, one page each, with requirements and the products that fit
applications or use cases, for buyers who know the problem but not the product
company, quality and certificates, for procurement and the final sign-off
This structure is agreed before any visual design, because it decides the menu, the page templates and how the site can grow when you add products or markets.
Dealer and distributor locator for “where to buy” visitors

Companies that sell through partners need a page that answers “who sells this in my country”. A locator with a map or a list by country and region, the partner’s contacts and the product lines they carry sends buyers to the right partner instead of to your general inbox. The partner list is edited in the admin panel, not in code.
Product catalogs, spec sheets and CAD downloads in B2B website design
For a manufacturer the product page does most of the selling. Its layout follows how an engineer reads it:
Product name, the buyer’s term for it and one sentence on what it is for.
Key specifications as a table in text: dimensions, materials, ratings, standards.
Variants and options, with part numbers.
Downloads: datasheet PDF, CAD files in the formats your customers use, certificates, manuals.
A quote request for this product, with the product already filled in.
Specifications written only inside PDFs cannot be read by search engines or compared on the page. The PDF stays for printing and forwarding; the data also lives on the page.
Gated content: which downloads go behind a form

Asking for an email before every download loses engineers who just need a drawing. A common rule is to keep datasheets and CAD files open and put longer material — guides, calculators, reports — behind a short form. Each gated file still has an open page describing it, so search engines and buyers can see what they will get.
RFQ and quote request forms in B2B website design
A contact form with “name, email, message” produces vague requests that sales must answer with questions. An RFQ form asks for what sales needs to quote:
product or service, quantity and target delivery date
drawings or specification files as attachments
company, country and industry, so the request reaches the right person
a field for anything special: certificates, packaging, terms
Long forms are split into short steps, and the product is pre-filled when the request starts from a product page. Phone, email and WhatsApp stay visible for buyers who prefer to talk.
Trust signals in B2B website design: certificates, years in market, real client logos

A buyer choosing a supplier is putting their own reputation on the line. The design places proof where decisions are made — next to the quote button and on product and industry pages — not only on an “About” page:
certificates such as ISO 9001 or industry approvals, as text with numbers that can be checked
years in the market, production capacity, countries you deliver to
client logos and case studies only with the client’s permission
named people for sales and support, with photos and direct contacts
Multilingual B2B website design for export markets

A B2B site for export is designed for several languages from the first sketch: German words run longer than English ones, menus must fit them, and each version may need its own contacts, distributors and certificates. The design keeps one system for all languages, with a clear language switch and no automatic translation widget.
I work in English, Polish and Russian and build multilingual sites regularly. The technical side — addresses, hreflang, editing workflow — is on the
multilingual website development
page.
CRM, ERP and PIM integration in B2B website design
A B2B site sits between systems you already have. In general terms, the connections that save the most time are:
RFQ and contact forms sending requests into your CRM — HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive or another — with the source page and attachments
product data coming from a PIM or ERP export, so specifications are entered once
stock or price information shown only where your systems and policies allow it
What can be connected depends on what your systems offer; I check that before quoting. A full B2B ecommerce shop with customer-specific prices and checkout is a separate, larger project.
A B2B website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Buyers increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to list suppliers for a product or a task. Assistants work from text they can read and check. A design that keeps capabilities in images, certificates in logos and specifications in PDFs hides them; the same facts as page text, with structured data for the company and its products, can be read and repeated.
Getting onto those lists is ongoing work, described on the

B2B website design best practices
Say what you make, for whom and where on the first screen.
Organize navigation by product, industry and application.
Put specifications on the page as text; keep PDFs and CAD files one click away.
Offer a quote request on every product page, pre-filled.
Show certificates and contacts as text, next to the call to action.
Design for the longest language you will publish in.
Patterns seen in B2B website examples across industries

Lists of the best B2B website designs mix large brands with small specialists. The patterns that work are the same at any size: a homepage that routes visitors by industry, product pages built like datasheets, case studies with facts rather than adjectives, and a contact path that names a real person. B2B SaaS websites add pricing, integrations and product screenshots, but the logic is the same.

A B2B website design agency or company usually splits the work between a strategist, a designer and developers. I do the structure, design and build myself, so decisions about the catalog, forms and integrations are made by the person who builds them.

children.text: Bakery SEO is the work that brings people who search for a bakery near me, a custom birthday cake in your town or holiday pies to order straight to your shop — through Google Maps, your own website and the answers AI assistants give. I do the audit, write the pages and change the code myself, for neighborhood bakeries, cake shops and patisseries with one or a few shops. Bakery searches are fewer than searches for places to eat, but many of them end in an order worth far more than a coffee: a tiered cake, a box of pastries for an office or a holiday pre-order.
Bakery SEO keywords: bakery near me, custom cakes and fresh bread
Before writing anything I pull search data for your city and the towns around it. For a bakery it splits into five groups, and each needs its own page or place:
the shop — “bakery near me”, “bakery open now”, “sourdough bread”, “croissants near me”
cakes to order — “custom cakes [city]”, “birthday cake order”, “smash cake”, “number cake”
weddings and events — “wedding cakes [city]”, “cupcakes for a baby shower”, “dessert table”
diet — “gluten-free bakery”, “vegan birthday cake”, “sugar-free cake”
dates and delivery — “birthday cake delivery”, “cake for tomorrow”, “Thanksgiving pie pre-order”
Most bakeries are found only for the first group, because the site is a home page with a phone number. The other four are where orders with a deposit come from.
Custom cake SEO: pages for birthday cakes, kids’ cakes and cakes for tomorrow

Someone ordering a cake types the occasion and the town, then looks for three answers: can you make it, by when, and roughly for how much. A page for each kind of cake you sell gives those answers in its first lines:
the starting price by number of servings, and what raises it — tiers, sugar figures, fresh flowers
the lead time: how many days ahead to order, and what you can still do for tomorrow
a gallery of real cakes, each photo captioned with flavor, size and occasion
how ordering works, in one sentence, with a link to the order form

Captions and file names matter more than they seem. A photo called IMG_4821 tells Google Images nothing; “two-tier unicorn birthday cake, vanilla and raspberry, 20 servings” can bring a parent who searched for exactly that. The form itself — sizes, dates, photo upload, deposit — is part of the website, not of SEO.
Wedding cake SEO: tastings, flavors and price per serving

Couples start looking for a cake months before the date and compare several bakers. Their searches are about the process as much as the cake: “wedding cake tasting [city]”, “wedding cake cost per slice”, “semi-naked wedding cake”. The page that ranks explains how a tasting is booked and what it costs, lists flavors and fillings, gives a price per serving with the minimum order, and says how delivery and setup work at the venue. A short page for each style you make often — buttercream, semi-naked, sugar flowers — catches the searches by style. Directories such as The Knot and WeddingWire send their own inquiries, and a listing there that links to your wedding page helps that page too.
Birthday cake delivery and pickup pages for a bakery: zones, fees and same-day cakes

Cakes are fragile, so most bakeries deliver within a short radius or not at all, and the usual advice about a page per town does not fit. One delivery page with zones, fees and the earliest delivery time works better, with equal space for pickup: hours, where to park, how to carry a tall cake. For “cake for today” searches, a page listing the cakes usually ready in the case each morning, with sizes and prices, catches people who remembered a birthday at noon. A town gets its own page only when you deliver there often and have something specific to say about it.
Gluten-free, vegan and allergy-friendly bakery pages

People who search for a gluten-free bakery or a nut-free birthday cake read your site more carefully than anyone else, and they stay for years once they trust you. The page that ranks for them is precise:
which products are made without gluten, eggs, dairy or nuts, and which only replace one ingredient
whether they come from a dedicated kitchen or a shared one, and what you do about cross-contact
ingredients and allergens for each product, in text, updated when a recipe changes

Vague claims lose these customers on the first visit and can harm someone. I write what you confirm about your kitchen and nothing more; the rules for labeling food “gluten-free” come from food law in your country.
Google Business Profile for a bakery: categories, product photos and early hours
“Bakery near me” is decided on the map, and a few settings carry most of the weight:
“Bakery” as the primary category, with “Cake shop”, “Pastry shop” or “Wedding bakery” added only if you do that work every week
the products section with your bestsellers, each with a photo, a price and a link to its page
photos taken in the morning when the shelves are full, not in the afternoon when they are empty
hours that say what really happens — if you close when the bread is sold out, the description says so

Reviews that name the cake, the occasion and the flavor help twice: with the map ranking and with the next customer deciding whether you can make their cake. A short request in the pickup message collects them. Map work in more depth is on the
local SEO services
page.
Seasonal bakery SEO: Thanksgiving pies, Christmas cookies and Easter pre-orders

Holiday orders are a large part of a bakery’s year, and they are decided earlier than most owners expect. People search “Thanksgiving pie pre-order [city]” from late October, Christmas cookie boxes from late November and Easter cakes a few weeks before. A pre-order page for each season goes live six to eight weeks ahead with this year’s menu, prices, the order deadline and the pickup days, and is linked from the home page and the profile. Out of season it does not disappear: it says when orders open next and offers a reminder by email, so the people who find it in January still become customers in November.
Wholesale bakery SEO: bread and pastries for cafes, restaurants and offices

A bakery that supplies other businesses has a second, quieter set of searches: “wholesale bakery [city]”, “bakery supplier for cafes”, “office pastry delivery”. There are few of them, but one account can mean deliveries six days a week. The page that wins them names what you supply, minimum orders, delivery days and times, the cut-off for next-day orders and how a new account starts — a tasting box or a trial week. Buyers compare suppliers on reliability, so a line on how you handle a missed delivery says more than any adjective.
Bakery SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Questions like “which bakery in Denver makes gluten-free birthday cakes”, “where can I order a smash cake by Saturday” or “how much is a wedding cake per slice in Austin” now go to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews as well. The assistant picks a few bakeries and a reason for each from what it can read. Getting into those answers is called GEO (generative engine optimization) or AEO (answer engine optimization); for a bakery it comes down to:
lead times, starting prices per serving and delivery zones written as sentences, not only inside an order form
dietary claims stated precisely, because assistants repeat them almost word for word
Bakery structured data with the address, hours and a link to the menu
the same facts on Google, Yelp, wedding directories and your own site
Before the work and a few months into it, I ask the assistants your customers’ questions and record which bakeries come up. More about this on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Measuring bakery SEO in cake orders, pre-orders and calls

The report counts what a bakery owner counts: custom cake requests and deposits that started from search, holiday pre-orders by source, calls and direction requests from the profile, and the pages that brought them. Order forms pass the source along with each request, so a wedding inquiry can be traced to the tasting page or a style page.
