children.text: Bakery website design, as I do it, covers both the look of the site and the working parts behind it — the catalog, the cake order form, pickup slots and online deposits — designed and built by one person at a price fixed before work starts. A bakery site serves two kinds of visitors. Some want to know what is on the shelves this morning and whether you are open; others are planning a cake for a date three weeks away and want to know whether you can make it.
Bakery website design: today’s hours, fresh bakes and the cake order button on the home page
Most visits to a bakery’s site come from a phone, often from someone deciding whether to stop on the way to work. The first screen settles that at a glance:
today’s hours, with a separate line on Sundays and holidays — “Open today 7 a.m.–2 p.m.”
what came out of the oven today, or a link to the daily list
a button for custom cakes that leads to a form, not to a phone number
the address with a one-tap route in Google Maps or Apple Maps

Regular breads, the bakery’s story and the wholesale page come further down. If you sell out early, a short line such as “Sourdough is usually gone by 11 a.m. — pre-order for Saturday” saves people a wasted trip and turns them into pre-orders.
A bakery product catalog with photos, prices and baking days
A bakery catalog works less like a web store and more like a timetable: cinnamon rolls every day, rye only on Fridays, stollen only in December. Each product page holds:
a photo of the item as it comes out of your oven, cut open where the crumb or the layers do the selling
the price per piece, per loaf or per dozen, and the weight where customers care about it
the days it is baked and whether it can be ordered ahead
ingredients and allergens as text

Seasonal items are switched off in the CMS rather than deleted, so next year the holiday bread page returns with its photos, text and address unchanged. Categories follow the way people shop at your counter — bread, pastries, cakes, cookies, savory — not the way a theme names them.
Custom cake order form on a bakery website: servings, date, photo upload and deposit
A custom cake is a small project with a deadline, and phone calls about one can go back and forth for days. The order form collects the brief in one go:
the pickup or delivery date first, with your lead time built in, so dates you cannot meet are greyed out
size by servings, not only by inches: a guide that shows how many guests a 6-, 8- or 10-inch round or a two-tier cake feeds
flavor, filling and frosting picked from your own lists, plus the inscription with a character limit
a photo upload for a reference design and a note field for colors or a theme
dietary requests — gluten-free, egg-free, nut-free — offered only where you can actually make them

Simple cakes can be priced on the spot and paid in full. Decorated and tiered cakes end in a request: you confirm the design and the price, and the customer pays a deposit through a link. Once the deposit is in, the order is confirmed by email and the date is blocked in your cake calendar, so a busy Saturday cannot be overbooked.
Pre-orders and pickup time slots for bread, pies and holiday baking

Pre-orders turn the busiest days of the year into a list you can bake to. Customers choose items and a pickup slot — Saturday 8–9 a.m., 9–10 a.m. and so on — and each slot accepts only as many orders as the counter can hand out. Around Thanksgiving and Christmas the pre-order menu becomes a page of its own, with pies, rolls and holiday breads and a closing date after which it switches to “walk-in only”. Weekend bread works the same way on a smaller scale: order by Thursday, collect on Saturday. The list for each slot prints from the admin panel, so the morning shift knows what to bag before the doors open.
Allergens and ingredients on a bakery website

People with allergies, and parents of children with them, read a bakery website more carefully than anyone. Ingredients and allergens sit on every product page as text, not in a photo of a label, and the catalog can be filtered by gluten-free, vegan or nut-free where you offer those. In the EU a bakery has to give information on 14 allergens, unpackaged goods included; in the US customers look first for the major food allergens. Either way the site states the cross-contact risk plainly — “made in a kitchen that also handles nuts, wheat and sesame” — so nobody reads one gluten-free brownie as a gluten-free bakery. Recipes change with suppliers, so ingredients are edited in the same place as prices and update across the site at once.
A wholesale page on a bakery website for cafes, restaurants and grocers

Many bakeries earn steady money from cafes, restaurants and grocers that take bread and pastries every morning. Wholesale buyers need other things than walk-in customers, so they get a page of their own:
what you supply, the minimum order, and the delivery days and times
an application form: business name, address, contact, products and frequency
a price list that opens for approved accounts, or one sent after the first conversation
standing orders that a cafe manager can change until a cutoff the day before
Walk-in visitors never see wholesale prices, and a wholesale buyer does not have to phone to change Tuesday’s order.
Bakery shop website design for several locations and a delivery area

A bakery with two or three shops needs a page for each, not one contact page with a list of addresses. Every location page carries its own hours and holiday hours, a map, what that shop bakes on site, parking or transit notes and its own phone number. Pickup orders ask for the shop first, so a cake never waits at the wrong counter. If you deliver, the site shows the delivery area — a ZIP code check or a map of zones, each with a fee and a minimum order. Orders through DoorDash or Uber Eats continue as they are; the site links to them where that helps and keeps your own pickup and cake orders, which carry no commission, in front.
If you also run a sit-down cafe or restaurant with table bookings, that side of the business is covered on the
restaurant website design
page.
Bakery photography and branding in the website design

Baked goods are photographed close and in daylight. What sells on a bakery site is detail: an open crumb, laminated layers, a glossy glaze, a slice cut from a layer cake. The design takes its colors and lettering from what you already use — boxes, paper bags, the shop sign — and puts the food on a warm, plain background that does not tint it. Product pages give the photos room and keep text short. Every image is compressed and served at the size of the screen, so a page with fifty pastries still opens quickly on mobile data.

If you have no photos yet, a phone and a window are enough to begin: one background, one angle per category, the same time of day. A professional session can come later and replace the pictures without touching the layout.
Bakery website template, theme or custom design

Search for bakery website templates or bakery website examples and you find WordPress bakery themes, Square Online and Shopify stores, and galleries of attractive home pages. A theme is a fair start for a bakery with a short list of products and mostly walk-in trade. The gaps appear when you add what makes a bakery different: lead times on cakes, pickup slots with a cap, items baked on set days only, wholesale accounts, allergens per product. Themes patch these with plugins that do not talk to each other, and the examples in galleries rarely show an order form at all.

A custom site is designed around your products and your kitchen’s rhythm, built on WordPress with WooCommerce or on Next.js with a headless CMS, and the domain, the code and the customer list stay with you. Moving from an old site keeps your search positions when every old address gets a 301 redirect to its new page.
A bakery website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Ask ChatGPT or Google’s AI Overviews where to order a gluten-free birthday cake nearby, or which bakery opens early on Sunday, and the answer is assembled from pages the assistant can read. So hours, locations, product names, prices, cake lead times and allergen notes are plain text in the HTML, and the bakery, its shops and its products are marked up with Bakery, LocalBusiness and Product structured data. Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan, has a site built on these rules, and ChatGPT already quotes pages added to it since launch.

page. Ranking for searches like custom cakes in your city is the work on the

page, and the Google Business Profile and the map pack are covered on the

page.

children.text: Band website design is the service on this page: I design and build websites for bands, solo musicians and DJs myself, so the person who picks your typeface is the one who connects your tour dates, players and mailing list. A music band website has a short list of jobs — tell a new listener who you are in seconds, show where you play next, play a track, collect an email address and give promoters what they need to book you.
Band website design: what fans, promoters and press check first

Three kinds of visitors open a band’s site, each with a different question. A fan who just heard you at a festival wants the next show and a song. A promoter or talent buyer wants live video, a sense of your draw and a contact. A journalist or blogger wants a bio, photos and a quote they can use. The home page serves all three without making anyone dig:
one band photo or the current cover art at full width, with the name as real text rather than part of the image
the next three shows with ticket buttons
a player with the latest release
an email sign-up and clear links to the EPK and booking
The visual identity follows the record. The hero image and the accent color are fields in the editor, so the site changes with every album cycle without a redesign.
Tour dates on a band website: one list fed from Bandsintown or Songkick

The shows page is the one fans open most and the one that goes stale fastest. Many artists already list dates on Bandsintown or Songkick, because those services pass them on to streaming apps and social profiles. The website reads from the same source, so a show added once appears everywhere. Each date shows the city, venue, support acts and a ticket link straight to the seller; sold-out and canceled shows are marked, and past dates move to an archive by themselves.

That archive matters too. A promoter in a new city looks at where you have played and how often. Event structured data on every upcoming show also helps Google show your dates directly in search results.
Music embeds on a musician website: Spotify, Bandcamp, Apple Music and YouTube

A player is the fastest argument a band has, and the heaviest element on the page: one Spotify or YouTube embed loads more code than the rest of the site combined. On my builds the player first appears as a light preview — cover art and a play button — and the real embed loads only when someone taps it. The page still opens quickly on a phone with one bar of signal in a crowded venue. Sasha Dith’s site works this way: its YouTube videos and players load only when needed, and the page opens in under one second.

Every release gets its own page: cover, tracklist, credits, lyrics if you want them, links to each streaming service, a buy link to Bandcamp or the vinyl, and the videos. The overview is a grid of covers, each with its streaming links, like the discography on Sasha’s site. A release page is also what a blog, a radio host or a playlist curator links to when they write about the record.
EPK page on a band website: bio, press photos, stage plot and rider
An electronic press kit is what a booker opens before replying. As a page on your own site it stays current, unlike the PDF you emailed last spring. It holds:
a short and a long bio in the third person, ready to copy
high-resolution press photos with the photographer’s credit, downloadable in one click
two or three live videos and the strongest tracks
press quotes and notable shows or festivals — real ones only
stage plot, input list and technical rider as files
contacts for booking, management, label and press
The EPK can be public or sit at an address you send only to industry contacts.
Merch store on a band website: Bandcamp, Shopify or print-on-demand
For many independent acts merch brings in more than streams. Three setups are common, and the site works with any of them:
Bandcamp for records and a few shirts, linked from the release pages
a Shopify store with buy buttons placed inside your own pages, for a larger catalog and your own checkout
a print-on-demand service that prints and ships each order, when you would rather not store boxes in the rehearsal room
The website shows the products in your design and hands the fan over to checkout. Tour-only items can appear on the page of the show where they are sold.

Video can be merch too: a recorded masterclass, a concert film or a backstage cut. Stripe Checkout takes the payment and the buyer gets a personal viewing link automatically. On the Landi Room course page I built, each link stops working after 14 days and the file stays stream-only; more than 100 courses sold, and nobody has passed access on.
Mailing list on a band website: owning your fan list instead of renting it

Followers on Spotify, Instagram and TikTok belong to those platforms. When the algorithm changes or an account is locked, the way to reach those people goes with it. An email list is the one channel you own: you can move it to another provider and write to every fan on release day.

So the sign-up box appears on every page, not only in the footer, and asks for an email and a city. The city lets you write only to fans near a new date instead of the whole list. It connects to Mailchimp, Kit or the service you already use. A small reason to join — an unreleased demo, a presale code — works better than “subscribe to our newsletter”.
Booking form on a band or musician website: date, city, venue and budget

A request that says only “how much?” costs both sides a day of messages. A short form asks for what you need to answer: date, city, type of event — club show, festival, wedding, corporate party — venue capacity, set length, whether sound and backline are provided, and a budget range. Requests go to you or your agent, with a copy to the sender. On Sasha Dith’s site the form for events and collaborations sits over a concert photo, so it reads as part of the show rather than an office contact page. Wedding and corporate bands get a separate page with song lists, set formats and what the fee covers, because those clients ask different questions than club promoters.
DJ website design: mixes, booking, rider and EPK for DJs

Sasha Dith, a DJ and producer, shows how this works: his official site, built on Next.js 14 to match his Figma design, has About, Video Gallery, Music and Contact sections and gives fans, media and booking agents one address instead of scattered profiles.

A DJ website follows the same logic as a band site with a different weight. The music is mixes rather than releases: a SoundCloud or Mixcloud player, recent mixes and radio shows, sometimes a recorded set on video. Club DJs need a gig calendar and an EPK listing residencies and the clubs and festivals they have played. Event DJs need packages — hours, sound system, lighting, MC duties — a calendar of booked dates and a form that asks for the venue and guest count.

The rider lives on the site too: decks and mixer models, booth monitors, set-up time. If your work splits between clubs and private events, one site serves both with two clear entry points from the home page.
SEO for musicians: how a band website gets found on Google

Most searches for a band are for its name, a release or “band name tour”, and you want your own site above ticket resellers and lyric pages. That takes a clear title and description, links back from Spotify, YouTube, Instagram and Bandsintown, and structured data for the group, events and albums. Bands for hire live in a different search: someone types “wedding band Chicago” or “party band for a corporate event”, and pages per service and region, a Google Business Profile and reviews decide who appears.

Bandzoogle, Wix or a custom website design for bands

Bandzoogle, Squarespace and Wix give a working musician website in an afternoon, with tour widgets, a store and email tools included. For a band with one release and a handful of shows that is a sensible choice, and I will tell you if it fits your stage.

A custom site pays off when the template no longer matches your record, when the site carries many releases, a long show archive or several languages for touring abroad, when club shows and private bookings run side by side, or when monthly plan upgrades add up. Before leaving a builder, export the mailing list and collect the addresses fans and press link to, so each one gets a redirect.
A band website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Fans and bookers now ask assistants things like “an indie folk band from Portland touring this spring” or “a jazz trio for a wedding in Denver”. An assistant can name only the band it has read about. The build serves pages as HTML from the server instead of assembling them with scripts, writes genre, home city, members, releases, upcoming shows and the booking contact as text, adds structured data for the group, events and albums, and lists in robots.txt the AI crawlers allowed in. Giuseppe’s site, a psychotherapy practice in Milan, was built the same way, and ChatGPT already cites the pages he added after launch.
Ongoing work on those answers is covered on the

page.

children.text: What a client checks on a salon website before booking

A salon site is opened with one treatment already in mind and a decision to make in about a minute. Four questions decide it: do you do this exact thing, what does it cost, who will do it, and is there a slot when I need one.

A site that answers those four in a minute wins against a prettier one that hides them behind a contact form. That is why the structure follows the questions and not the sections agencies default to — «about the salon», «our philosophy» and «why choose us» are read last, if at all.
A page per treatment, with the price and the duration on it

The backbone of a salon site is separate pages for the work rather than one list: colour and balayage, cuts, lash extensions and lifts, brows, manicure and gel, pedicure, facials and peels, laser, waxing.

Each one carries the price or a «from» price, how long it takes, who performs it, how long the result lasts, whether preparation or a patch test is needed, and what aftercare looks like. This is also the content that lets the page be found at all: a two-line description is not something search or an assistant can work with.

A price list as a photographed sheet or an Instagram screenshot does not count. Neither search engines nor AI assistants read text inside images, so a salon whose prices exist only as a picture is invisible to both.
Online booking: connecting the system your front desk already uses

The booking question is not «which widget» but «where does the front desk actually look». A site that books into a second system nobody watches creates double bookings, and that costs more than no booking at all.

So the form or the button connects to the calendar or the salon system already in use, and it sits on every treatment page rather than only in the menu. Where bookings run through Booksy or a similar platform, the site links straight into the right treatment instead of dropping the client on its home screen. And the page says what happens next — who confirms, and how soon.
The team page: people are usually the reason clients come back
In this business the client books a person as much as a treatment, and a site that lists «our professional team» without names throws that away.

Each specialist gets a photograph, what they do, how long they have been doing it, examples of their work and a booking link to them specifically. It helps the client choose, it gives new specialists a way to fill their first weeks, and it produces pages that rank for a name people already search for.
Photographs of your own rooms instead of stock images
A stock model with perfect hair reads as «not our salon». Real photographs of the interior, the chairs, the equipment and the actual work build more trust than any text about quality.
What is worth photographing before the build starts
the interior, in daylight, without people in frame;
each treatment room or station separately;
the work itself: before and after, same light, same angle;
the team, in a consistent style rather than whatever each person sent.

The same photographs feed the Google Business Profile, where they are often seen before the site is opened and sometimes instead of it. I advise on the style and on what is missing rather than leaving that to chance.
Speed on a phone, in the conditions where the site is actually opened

Salon sites are opened on phones, often between other things, frequently on a weak connection. A gallery of uncompressed photographs and a video header in those conditions mean the visitor leaves before finding the price.
So I build on Next.js with properly compressed images and without unnecessary scripts, and put the price, the booking button and the phone number where nobody has to scroll to reach them.

children.text: Bed and breakfast website design is the work I do for innkeepers and owners of small guesthouses: I plan, design and build the site myself, from the room pages to the booking engine, for one fixed price. A B&B website has one main job — turning a guest who found you on Booking.com, on Google or through a friend into a guest who books with you directly — and a second job that matters as much: showing people what a stay in your house is like before they arrive.
Bed and breakfast website design for innkeepers who run the house themselves

In most B&Bs the owners cook breakfast, turn over the rooms, answer the phone and wait up for late arrivals. The website has to work while all of that is going on, and it has to be easy for them to change. On an ordinary day it should:
show live availability and take a booking at two in the morning without waking anyone
answer the questions you hear at every check-in — parking, arrival times, pets, children, stairs, dietary needs at breakfast
let you change a rate, close a room for repairs or add a winter package from your phone
look like your house, not like a hotel chain: your rooms, your porch, your street

Guests choose a B&B for the hosts and the house as much as for the room. A photo of you, a few lines on why you opened and how breakfast works do more on the home page than a slogan about comfort and charm.
Direct bookings vs OTA commissions on a bed and breakfast website

Booking.com, Expedia and Airbnb bring guests a small inn could never reach alone, and most B&Bs keep their listings. The price is a commission on every stay and less contact with the guest before arrival. A website does not replace the platforms; it gives returning guests, and people who first saw you there, a reason and an easy way to book with you next time:
a booking button on every screen with live availability, so nobody has to email and wait for an answer
a short, true list of what booking direct gets them — first pick of rooms, flexible check-in, a bottle of local wine, easier changes — whatever you can actually offer
the same or a better rate than on the platforms, where your agreements allow it
a line in the confirmation email and a card in the room inviting guests to book their next stay on your site

Analytics count bookings made through the site each month and the pages they started from, so you can set that number next to what you pay the platforms. That comparison tells you whether the site is doing its job.
Choosing a booking engine for a B&B website: Lodgify, Little Hotelier and others

The booking engine is the part guests use to pick dates, choose a room and pay. Small inns rent one rather than build it: Lodgify, Little Hotelier, Cloudbeds, ResNexus, ThinkReservations and others. Most include a channel manager that keeps availability in sync with the platforms, so the same room is not sold twice. I build the site around the engine you already use, or help you choose one by checking:
whether it syncs with every platform you list on, and how quickly
whether the booking step can stay on your domain and match the site’s look
whether it takes deposits and card payments the way you want, with your cancellation policy shown before payment
how it behaves on a phone, where most guests book
whether it can send your direct rate to Google’s hotel results
If you have a system you like, the site uses its widget and links and leaves reservations where they are.
Room pages on a B&B website: photos, beds, bathrooms and stairs
In a bed and breakfast no two rooms are the same, and guests know it. Each room gets its own page, and a room overview lets people compare them without opening each one:
eight to fifteen daylight photos, including the bathroom and the view from the window
bed size and number of beds, and who the room suits — a couple, a family with a child, a solo traveler
the bathroom: private or shared, en suite or across the hall, shower or clawfoot tub
the floor and the stairs, so a guest who struggles with steps is not booked into the attic
the rate range across seasons and a booking button for that exact room

Photos are resized for each screen and load as the guest scrolls, so a room page opens quickly on a weak rural signal. Honest details mean fewer surprises at check-in and fewer reviews that begin with “the room was smaller than…”.
The breakfast page and the local guide on a bed and breakfast website

Breakfast is half the name and often the part guests remember. Its page says when and where it is served, what a typical morning looks like, what comes from nearby farms or your own garden, and how you handle gluten-free, vegan or allergy requests — with photos of your real plates, not stock pastries.
The local guide answers the question that comes right after booking: what is there to do here. Write it the way you would talk to a guest at the table:
how to reach you from the airport, the interstate or the train, and where to park
what is within walking distance: the restaurant you send people to, the trail, the beach, Main Street
day trips — wineries, state parks, historic towns — with driving times
the seasons: fall color, ski weeks, summer festivals, and what closes in winter
These pages also bring visitors from search, because people read about an area before they pick where to sleep, and they give AI assistants concrete facts to quote about your inn.
A multilingual bed and breakfast website for international guests

A B&B in a tourist region hosts travelers from abroad, and many of them prefer to book in their own language. The site gets a language version only where you actually see those guests — for example Spanish, French or German — and that version covers the whole path to a booking:
room pages, house rules and the cancellation policy, translated and read by a person
the booking engine switched to the same language, with prices shown in the guest’s currency where the engine allows
directions written for someone who has never driven in your state
hreflang tags, so Google shows each guest the right version
How I plan and build sites in several languages is described on the

Google hotel results, reviews and local search for a B&B

When someone searches for a place to stay in your town, Google shows a map and a list of lodgings with prices and reviews. A B&B gets there through its Google Business Profile, set up in a lodging category with the exact name, address and phone used on the website. Many booking engines can also send your direct rate to those hotel results, where it appears beside the platforms’ prices and links straight to your booking page.

Reviews carry the most weight: ask every guest at checkout, answer each review in a sentence or two, and keep the details of the house identical on Google, Tripadvisor and the platforms. The site is launched with these basics in place; ongoing map and review work is covered on the

Bed and breakfast website design ideas: what the best B&B websites share
Collections of the best bed and breakfast website design and boards of design inspiration show handsome first screens. The B&B sites that fill rooms share habits more than a style:
a large photo of the house and a date search on the first screen
the town or region named in the first sentence
rooms you can compare at a glance
rates or rate ranges, cancellation terms and check-in times in plain view
dated reviews close to the booking button
a phone number and email for guests who would rather ask first

Templates from website builders and the site builders inside booking engines can look fine and are a fair start for a two-room B&B. Their limits show with a long room list, a second language, breakfast and area guides, and the day you change booking systems and want the site to stay yours.
A bed and breakfast website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Many guests start trip planning in ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews, asking for “a quiet B&B near Asheville with a big breakfast” or “dog-friendly inns in the Berkshires”. The assistant names a few places and says why. It can only recommend what it can read: rooms, rates, policies and breakfast that exist only inside a booking widget or as text on images are invisible to it. The site writes them as plain text and adds BedAndBreakfast structured data with your address, rooms, amenities and reviews.

contentBlocks.title: Get a quote for SEO for your cafe

children.text: Cafe SEO is the work that makes your cafe or coffee shop the one people find when they search for coffee near me, a quiet place to work with a laptop or weekend brunch nearby — on Google Maps, in the regular results and in AI assistants. I do it myself, from the first audit to the last fix in the code, for independent cafes, specialty coffee shops and small groups of two or three locations. A cafe lives on frequent, small visits, so the goal is to be the obvious choice on someone’s way to work.
Cafe SEO keywords: coffee near me, brunch, laptop-friendly and specialty coffee
Cafe searches are short and practical. When I pull search data for your street and city, they usually fall into four groups:
right now — “coffee near me”, “cafe open now”, “coffee shop open early”, “coffee near [station or campus]”
a reason to stay — “cafe to work with a laptop”, “quiet cafe for studying”, “dog-friendly cafe”, “cafe with a garden”
food and diet — “brunch near me”, “vegan pastries”, “oat milk latte”, “gluten-free breakfast”
the coffee itself — “specialty coffee [city]”, “pour over coffee”, “local coffee roaster”, “buy coffee beans near me”
The first group is decided on the map; the others need pages on your site. A cafe with only a home page competes in the first group alone.
“Coffee near me” and the map pack: how a cafe competes within a few blocks

Someone looking for dinner may drive across town; someone looking for coffee usually walks. The map pack for “coffee near me” changes from one street corner to the next, so your real competitors are the four or five places within a short walk, not every cafe in the city. Small details decide more than they seem:
the pin — a cafe inside an office building, a station or a courtyard needs the pin on the entrance and walking directions in the description
the opening time — morning searches start before seven, and a profile that says 8:00 when you open at 7:00 drops out of the “open now” filter in your busiest hour
the name — your real sign, without extra keywords added to it, which breaks Google’s guidelines and can get the listing suspended
the first photos — the counter, the drinks and the seats, so a person deciding in ten seconds sees what kind of place it is
Google Business Profile for a cafe: Cafe or Coffee shop category, menu items and attributes

Google offers both “Cafe” and “Coffee shop” as categories, plus narrower ones such as “Espresso bar” and “Brunch restaurant”. The primary category should match why most guests come: a place where people sit down for food and coffee is usually a cafe, a counter where most orders leave in a cup is usually a coffee shop. The rest of the profile works as a short version of your menu board:
menu items filled in by name and price, so a search for “cortado” or “matcha latte” nearby can match your cafe
the attributes Google offers for Wi-Fi, seating, outdoor tables, pets and accessibility, set to match what is really there
posts for the seasonal drink, a new pastry or a change in hours, which keep the listing active between reviews
Map work in more depth — citations, Apple Maps, Yelp and other directories — is on the
local SEO services
page.
Specialty pages for a cafe: brunch, laptop-friendly, vegan and dog-friendly

People choose a cafe for a reason, and the reason is what they type. A page for each reason that holds for your place answers the search better than a line on the home page, and each one lives on facts a guest can check:
brunch — the days and hours it runs, whether you take reservations, how long the weekend wait usually is, which dishes sell out first
laptop-friendly — Wi-Fi, how many seats have outlets, whether there are laptop-free hours on weekends, where the quiet corner is
vegan and plant-based — which milks you offer and whether they cost extra, which pastries are vegan and how they are kept apart
dog-friendly — inside or on the terrace only, water bowls, house rules for busy hours
Write a page only for what you want more of. A cafe that wants fewer all-day laptop guests at lunch should skip the laptop page; that is a business choice, not an SEO one.
Coffee shop SEO: pages for beans, roasting and specialty coffee

For a coffee shop that roasts its own beans or works with a named roaster, the coffee is a second product with its own searches: “local coffee roaster”, “buy coffee beans [city]”, “Ethiopian single origin beans”, “coffee subscription”. These buyers compare roast dates, origins and brew methods, so the pages that rank for them read the way a good barista talks:
a page for each coffee on offer: origin, farm or cooperative, process, tasting notes, how fresh the roast is and how to brew it
a page about the roaster or your own roasting — how often you roast and where the green coffee comes from
a wholesale page for offices and other cafes that want to serve your beans
Beans travel further than drinks: a guest who buys a bag takes your name home.
Cafe events in search: latte art classes, cuppings and open mic nights

Events give a cafe something to be found for beyond coffee: “latte art class [city]”, “coffee cupping near me”, “open mic night”, “board game evening”. Each recurring event gets its own page with the date, price, how to sign up and what happens, marked up with Event structured data so Google can show the date in results. The page keeps its address from month to month and only the dates change, so it builds history instead of starting over. City event calendars and local newsletters that list the event link back to it — some of the easiest local links a cafe can earn.
Cafe reviews on Google: regulars, details and replies

A cafe sees the same faces several times a week, an advantage few businesses have: regulars write the most useful reviews if someone asks them. The reviews that help are specific — the flat white, the window seat, fast Wi-Fi, a barista who remembers orders — because their words match what the next person types. Ask a regular after the tenth coffee rather than a first-time visitor at the till, with a short link or a QR code on the receipt, and never in exchange for a free drink. Reply to each review with the same specifics, including the complaint about the Saturday line.
SEO for a cafe with several locations: hours, seating, moves and closures

Two cafes under one name often differ more than the owner expects: the station kiosk opens at 6 and is takeaway only, the main street location has a terrace and brunch, the one in the mall follows the mall’s hours. Each location gets its own profile and its own page that says exactly that, so “[your name] near me” sends people to the one that fits, and a guest who wants a seat does not walk to a counter with no chairs. When a location moves or closes, the old profile is marked as moved or closed and its page redirects to the nearest open one, instead of a dead listing sending people to an empty shop front.
Delivery apps vs your own cafe website: Uber Eats, DoorDash and pickup orders

Search your cafe’s name with the word “menu” and your Uber Eats, DoorDash or Grubhub page often sits next to your own site, sometimes above it. For most cafes delivery is a small part of sales; the morning pickup order from someone on the way to work matters more. So the profile’s order button points to your own pickup ordering where you have it, your menu page is the result for your name plus “menu”, and the app listings stay an extra channel for people at home. Reports separate pickup orders started from search from app orders, so you see what each one brings.
Cafe SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Questions such as “where can I work with a laptop in Portland on a Sunday”, “brunch near Union Square without a reservation” or “a cafe with oat milk and a quiet corner near me” now go to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews too. The answer names a few places with a reason for each, taken from pages, listings and reviews the assistant could read. Work on those answers is called GEO (generative engine optimization) or AEO (answer engine optimization), and for a cafe it means:
the facts guests ask about — Wi-Fi, outlets, laptop rules, brunch hours, plant milks, dogs — written as sentences on your site, not only on a photo of the menu board
CafeOrCoffeeShop structured data with the address, hours, menu link and price range
the same name, hours and address on Google, Apple Maps, Yelp and your site, so the assistant is not choosing between two versions
reviews with details, because assistants quote them when they explain a choice
At the start and again a few months later I put your guests’ questions to the assistants and record which cafes they name. The method is described on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Measuring cafe SEO in direction requests, calls and pickup orders

A cafe rarely gets a form submission, so rankings alone say little. The monthly report shows direction requests and calls from the profile by day and hour, visits to the brunch, laptop and bean pages, pickup orders and bean sales that started from search, and how the morning hours compare month to month.

Cafe SEO audit — Google Business Profile, website, cafes within walking distance and AI answers: from 250 €, one-off.
One-off work — brunch, laptop, vegan, bean or event pages, profile clean-up, structured data: 250–700 €.
Monthly SEO for a cafe or coffee shop — new pages, map work, reviews, AI visibility and reports: from 800 € per month.

A single cafe in a small town often gets most of the effect from the audit and three or four pages; monthly work pays off in a dense area or with several locations. If the site itself needs rebuilding — menu, pickup ordering, a bean shop — the

children.text: Cafe website design is part of every cafe site I build: I design the look and develop the site myself, and the design is included in the price of the website, not billed as a separate project. The design has one task. A guest who has never been to your cafe should know from the screen what it feels like to sit there — bright and quick, slow and cozy, a roaster with a long bar, a brunch place with a line on Sundays — and every choice below serves that impression on a small screen.
Cafe branding on the website: taken from your cups, bags and sign

A cafe has a brand even without a brand guide. It is printed on the takeaway cup, stamped on the bean bags, painted on the window and chalked on the board. The cup matters most: it is the object guests photograph and post, so the website takes its colors and marks from it first.
the palette comes from the cup, the bags and the room — often one strong color and two quiet ones
the logo stamp becomes the icon in the browser tab and a small mark in the corner of sections
a hand-lettered or display font, if the board uses one, appears in a few headings only; the menu and body text use a plain typeface that reads well in daylight
patterns or illustrations from your packaging frame sections, never sitting behind text

If you are still opening and have no brand yet, the design works from what you chose for the room — wood, tiles, the color of the espresso machine — and stays simple enough to adapt when the logo arrives.
Coffee shop website design on a phone: the first screen and the vertical crop

A desktop hero photo is wide; a phone screen is tall. A panorama of the room that looks good on a laptop becomes a slice of countertop on a phone. So the first screen is designed for the phone first, with a photo chosen for each shape: a vertical image for phones — the 4:5 format you already shoot for Instagram — and a wider one for desktop, each cropped so the cup, the bar or the window stays in frame.

Over the photo sits only what helps a guest decide: the name, one line in your own voice, such as “small-batch roaster, brunch until 3”, and two buttons. Everything else — the story, the team, the beans — starts one scroll down, where it gets the attention it deserves.
Photography for a cafe website: drinks, pastries, the bar and the room

The same stock photos of beans and latte art appear on thousands of cafe sites, and guests recognize them. A cafe is easier to photograph than most businesses: one morning before opening usually covers it, working from a list of shots I write for the layout:
signature drinks shot from above for latte art and from the side for iced and layered drinks, where the layers show
the pastry case and two or three plated items in window light
the bar in action: hands on the portafilter, milk being poured, beans going into the grinder
the room empty, for its shape and light, and the room with guests, for its mood
details that carry the brand: the cup, the bag, the sign, a corner of the tiles
Every photo then gets the same color grade — warmth, contrast, brightness — so the site reads as one cafe and not as a stack of posts from different years.
Cafe menu layout: sizes, milk options and prices that read at a glance
A cafe menu is a grid more than a list, and the layout follows how a guest reads it while waiting in line:
drink names on the left and sizes as columns — small, medium, large or 8, 12 and 16 oz — with prices in the grid, so a guest compares at a glance
milk alternatives, extra shots and syrups printed once, on a single line under each group, instead of after every drink
dietary labels — vegan, gluten-free, contains nuts — as small tags explained once at the top
seasonal drinks set apart with their own color and photo, so they read as news rather than another line

On a phone the size columns fold into a compact row under each drink rather than a table that scrolls sideways. The menu page borrows the look of your printed menu or board, so the screen and the counter feel like the same place.
Seasonal drinks and launches in a cafe website design

Cafes change with the seasons more than most businesses: a fall menu, summer cold brew, a holiday drink, a guest roaster for a month. The design plans for it. Each season can have its own accent color, a hero photo and a short banner, all set from the CMS with a start and end date, while the layout, the fonts and the menu structure stay the same. The site looks fresh four times a year without a redesign, and last season’s drink leaves the screen on the date you chose.
Cafe website designs on Dribbble and Figma, and a design built on your real menu

Search for cafe website designs and you find striking concepts on Dribbble, Behance and in Figma community files. Most were made for a designer’s portfolio: four drinks on the menu, perfect photos, no hours, no allergens, no holiday notice and no order button. They are useful for collecting what you like — a color, a type pairing, the way a photo is cropped. A design for your cafe starts from the other end: your real menu with every size and add-on, your photos and the buttons guests use. I lay these out on a phone screen first, so the look is tested against the content it has to carry.
Cafe website examples: what the best coffee shop websites have in common
Looking through galleries of cafe and coffee shop websites, the ones that work for guests share a few design choices:
one strong photo on the first screen, not a slider that changes before anyone reads it
copy that sounds like the person behind the bar, not like a template
the menu one tap away from every page
one color grade across all photos, so the site feels like one place
plenty of white space, so the drinks and the room bring the color
nothing standing between the guest and the first screen: no loading animation, no newsletter pop-up on arrival
Cafe website templates or a custom cafe website design

Cafe website templates are designed around their demo photos: warm, perfectly lit, all in one palette. Swap in your own photos and the template often stops looking like its preview, because its colors and spacing were tuned to images you do not have. Templates also expect a short menu with one price per item, so sizes and add-ons get squeezed into descriptions. A template is a fair choice if you like it as it is and your menu fits it. A custom design is built around your photos, your colors and your real menu, so what you approve in the design is what guests see, and its cost is part of the website price.
A cafe website design that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Design choices decide what search engines and AI assistants can read. A menu exported from Canva as an image, opening hours inside a photo of the door sign or a seasonal drink announced only in a banner graphic are invisible to them. In my designs, everything that looks like a graphic but carries information is styled text: the menu, the hours, seasonal names and prices. Photos get descriptive alt text — “oat flat white with a rosetta on the window counter” — which serves screen readers and image search alike. That is how a guest who asks ChatGPT or Google’s AI Overviews for a cafe with a certain drink or atmosphere can be pointed to yours.

children.text: I build cafe websites for owners of cafes and coffee shops: I design and develop the site myself, connect ordering and payments, and hand over an editor your team can use from behind the counter, at a price fixed before work starts. Guests open a cafe site to check a few facts — what you serve and for how much, whether you are open right now, where to pick up an order — and leave within a minute. The site does its job when those facts are correct and quick to find.
What a cafe website does that Instagram and a Google listing cannot

Many cafes run on an Instagram account and a Google Business Profile, and both are worth keeping. Instagram shows the mood of the week; the Google listing puts you on the map. Neither is a good home for facts that change and must be right:
the full drink menu with sizes, milk options and current prices — highlights go stale and captions cannot be searched
this week’s hours, including a holiday or a private event that closes the room early
a pickup order that goes straight to the bar without a platform commission
the gift cards, beans and event tickets you sell

The website is also the only one of the three you own. Platforms change their feeds and rules; your domain and your menu page stay where you put them. Your Google listing links to the site, and the site carries the same name, address and hours.
A cafe menu on the website: written as text, not a photo of the board

The most common cafe menu online is a photo of the chalkboard above the counter, taken at an angle, or a PDF made two price changes ago. A cafe menu has a structure a photo cannot carry: one drink in two or three sizes, a choice of milk, an extra shot, syrups, decaf. On the site I set it up as data:
drinks grouped the way guests order — espresso drinks, filter and pour-over, tea, cold drinks, non-coffee
each drink with its sizes and a price per size, and add-ons stored as options with their surcharge, so a new price for oat milk is one edit in the admin panel
food marked as baked in house or brought in, with vegan, gluten-free and allergen notes
a “today” line for the filter coffee of the day or a pastry that has sold out, changed in seconds
Written as text, the menu can be searched on the page and read by Google and AI assistants. The order-ahead page takes its items and prices from the same list, so the two never disagree.
Opening hours, holiday hours and directions on a cafe website

Cafe hours change more often than a restaurant’s: earlier openings in summer, a shorter Sunday, a 2 p.m. close on a holiday, a day off for a private booking. On the site the regular hours and the exceptions are separate fields, so a guest sees “Open today 7 a.m.–2 p.m. (holiday hours)” instead of a weekly table that is wrong for today. A line at the top of every page says whether you are open now and until when.
Under the hours come the things people check before they walk over:
the address with a link that opens directions in their own maps app
the nearest parking, bike racks or transit stop, and where the entrance is if it is easy to miss
seating facts guests ask about: Wi-Fi, outlets, whether laptops are welcome at busy hours, stroller access, dogs on the patio
Change the hours in your Google Business Profile at the same moment; a guest who sees two different closing times trusts neither.
Online ordering on a cafe website: pickup orders and delivery apps

Uber Eats and DoorDash bring delivery orders from people who would not have found you, and they take a commission on each one. A pickup order comes from someone who already knows the way, so there is little reason to pay a platform for it. A cafe website can take order-ahead orders itself:
the guest picks drinks with sizes and options, chooses a pickup time and pays by card, Apple Pay or Google Pay
the order reaches the bar as a tablet notification or an email, whichever your team already watches
each pickup slot has a limit, so the morning rush does not get more orders than the bar can make
a text or email tells the guest when the order is ready

If your point-of-sale system has its own online ordering — Square, Toast and Clover do — the site connects to it instead of keeping a second menu in sync. Delivery stays on the apps, with clear buttons from the site, and pickup goes through your own page. Gift cards sell the same way, with a code sent by email.
Coffee shop website: beans, subscriptions and wholesale for a roaster cafe
A coffee shop that roasts or sells specialty beans needs more than a menu. Its website is also a small shop:
a page for each coffee with origin, process, roast level, tasting notes and how fresh the roast is
bag sizes and grind options, shipping rates and local pickup at the counter
a coffee subscription every two or four weeks that guests pause and skip online
a wholesale form for offices, restaurants and other cafes: volume per week, brewing equipment, delivery address

Brewing guides for each method fit naturally on a coffee shop site and answer questions guests otherwise ask at the bar. The shop runs on WooCommerce or Shopify, depending on your volume, and follows the look of the rest of the site.
Events, workshops and private hire on a cafe website

Cuppings, latte art classes, book clubs, live music and board-game nights fill quiet evenings, and each needs a page with a date, a price and a way to sign up. A short calendar on the site lists what is coming; each event has its own address you can share on Instagram, and seats are paid online or reserved with a short form that closes when the room is full. Private hire — a baby shower, a team breakfast, a photo shoot — gets an inquiry form that asks for the date, time, number of guests, food and drinks and a budget range, so you answer with a price instead of a round of questions.
Instagram, loyalty programs and newsletter sign-up on a cafe website

Instagram stays the place for daily photos, and the site does not need to copy it. An embedded Instagram feed looks lively but slows the page and shows whatever you posted last, including a closed-for-the-holidays notice from months ago; one clear link to your profile does the job. Loyalty works the same way: if your POS runs a points program or you use stamp cards, the site explains it in two lines. What the site adds is an email list: a short sign-up for new seasonal drinks, events and holiday hours, sent from a tool such as Mailchimp. People who asked for your emails are guests you can reach without paying to boost a post.
A fast cafe website on a phone and on mobile data

Most visits to a cafe site come from a phone, often on the street with a weak signal. The site stays fast because it is built that way: pages are generated in advance and served from a CDN, photos are compressed and sized for each screen, fonts are few, and nothing heavy loads before the menu and the hours. Third-party widgets — a feed, a review carousel, a chat bubble — each bring their own scripts, so I keep only the ones that earn their place. A guest standing outside will not wait for a slow menu page.
Cafe website builder or a custom-built cafe website

AI website builders and templates on Squarespace, Wix or Square Online promise a cafe site in minutes, and the first page often looks fine. The real work starts after that: entering a menu with sizes and add-ons, setting holiday hours, connecting ordering and payments, keeping it current. A builder is a sensible start for a new cafe with one location and a short menu. Its limits show when you want pickup slots, a bean shop with subscriptions, events with seat limits or control over page addresses and structured data, and when the monthly plan grows with every feature. AI-written text also describes a cafe in general, not yours.

A custom site is built on WordPress or Next.js around your menu and your ordering, and the domain, the code and your email list stay with you. Moving from a builder, every old page address gets a 301 redirect to its new one. How the site looks — your colors, the drink photos, the menu layout — is covered on the
cafe website design
page.
A cafe website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Guests now ask ChatGPT or Google’s AI Overviews things like “a quiet cafe near Union Square where I can work on a laptop” or “a coffee shop open before 7 a.m. with oat milk”. The assistant answers from what it can read on your pages and in your Google listing. So the facts go into the HTML as text: hours and holiday hours, the menu with prices, milk options and dietary notes, Wi-Fi and seating, the neighborhood. The cafe gets CafeOrCoffeeShop structured data with its hours and a link to the menu. I built a psychotherapist’s site in Milan this way, and its new pages already show up in ChatGPT answers.

children.text: Car dealer SEO is the work that puts your inventory, your lot and your dealership name in front of people searching for a car in your area, and turns those searches into calls, test drives and credit applications. I do it myself, as a single SEO consultant and web developer, for independent used car dealers and small dealer groups: the person who audits your vehicle pages is the person who fixes the templates and writes the model pages.
What SEO for car dealers covers: inventory, the lot and the dealership name

A car shopper searches in stages: first a model and a budget (“used Honda CR-V Columbus”), then a type of dealer (“buy here pay here near me”, “Subaru dealer Plano”), and finally your name, typed by someone who already saw one of your cars on a marketplace. SEO for a car dealer works on:
vehicle detail pages and inventory lists that Google indexes and keeps current
make, model, body type and price pages built from the stock you actually carry
a Google Business Profile for each lot, with reviews
your name in search and the places where buyers check you: Google, DealerRater, Cars.com, CarGurus
answers in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
The site itself — how the inventory feed is wired, how a vehicle page looks, the financing and trade-in forms — is covered on the
car dealer website design
page.
Vehicle detail pages in Google: inventory SEO for a car dealer
Every car on the lot has a vehicle detail page (VDP), where people land when they search for a specific car. Dealer sites share the same problems with them:
the inventory loads with JavaScript after the page opens, so Google sees an empty grid or a spinner
addresses carry session IDs and filter parameters instead of one stable address per stock number
every title reads “Vehicle Details” instead of year, make, model, trim and town
descriptions are the same feed boilerplate on hundreds of pages and on every marketplace
the XML sitemap updates once a week while cars sell every day

These are fixed in the templates, once: vehicle pages rendered on the server, a stable address per stock number, titles built from the feed fields plus your location, a sitemap regenerated with each import, and a few lines per car from your staff — condition, options, who it suits — that no other site carries.
What to do with a vehicle page when the car is sold

Deleting a page the moment the car sells throws away the visits and links it had; leaving it live with a “buy now” button annoys people. What works for most dealers: keep the page for a short period marked as sold, with similar vehicles in stock and a link to the model page, then let it return 410 or redirect it to that model page.
Make, model and price pages: which inventory filters to index in car dealer SEO

Pages such as “used SUVs”, “Ford F-150 for sale” or “cars under $15,000” outrank single cars because they stay live while vehicles come and go. Meanwhile inventory filters can produce thousands of address combinations — color, mileage, year, sort order — and Google spends its crawl on them instead of on your stock. The structure I set up:
indexable pages for the makes and models you regularly stock, body types and price bands, each with a short text written for that page above the current cars
filter combinations beyond that kept out of the index with canonical tags or noindex
a model page that stays live when the model is temporarily out of stock, offering an alert sign-up instead of an empty grid
links from the home page and from vehicle pages to the model pages that matter for your lot
The list of pages comes from your sales history: a lot selling work vans needs different pages from one selling compact sedans.
Vehicle structured data for car dealers: Car, Offer and AutoDealer markup
For a dealer, structured data covers:
each vehicle page: schema.org Car with VIN, make, model, year, mileage, color, fuel type and transmission, plus an Offer with price, currency and availability
each lot: AutoDealer with name, address, phone, opening hours per department and links to your profiles

In the US, Google can show dealer inventory in its vehicle listings, which read Car markup or a vehicle feed in Merchant Center. Markup helps only when it matches the visible page: a price in the code that differs from the one shown, or a sold car still marked in stock, gives Google a reason to ignore it. I generate the markup from the same feed as the page, so the two cannot drift apart.
Local SEO for car dealers: a Google Business Profile for each lot

Most buyers shop within driving distance, and searches like “car dealership near me” or “used cars Fort Wayne” are answered from the map. Each physical lot gets its own profile with its real address and hours. Google’s guidelines also allow dealerships to list departments such as sales and service separately, and franchise dealers can list each brand they are authorized to sell; read the current guidelines before splitting anything, because a suspended profile is slow to get back. For every lot:
a primary category that matches the business — “Used car dealer”, or the brand dealer category for a franchise
a location page on the site with the address, hours, staff, directions and the cars parked there
photos of the real lot and building
the same name, address and phone on the site, the profile, marketplaces and directories
Map work in more depth is on the
local SEO services
page.
Car dealer reviews on Google, DealerRater, Cars.com and CarGurus
Dealer reviews are often about the finance office and the call after the sale rather than the car. A steady flow counts for more than a burst:
a review request after delivery, sent by the salesperson who sold the car, with a direct link
a reply to every review, including the angry ones, with no details of the deal or the customer’s credit
DealerRater, Cars.com and CarGurus reviews followed too, because those pages rank for your name
no reviews written by staff or bought: Google’s policies and the FTC rule on fake reviews forbid both
Cars.com, AutoTrader, CarGurus or your own site: where SEO fits for a dealer

Marketplaces bring most of a typical dealer’s online leads: a shopper comparing twenty CR-Vs starts on CarGurus or AutoTrader, not on one lot’s website. But you pay for every listing package or lead, the buyer sees competitors next to your car, and the price badge often decides who gets the click. SEO works on the searches marketplaces do not own:
your dealership name, typed by people who saw your car on a marketplace and want to reach you directly
local and dealer-type searches: “buy here pay here Dayton”, “used work trucks Polk County”, “Subaru dealer near me”
buyer questions a dealer can answer better than a listing site
A lead from your own site comes with no fee and no competing cars beside it. The aim is a mix in which the site carries a growing share, with the marketplaces still running.
Buyer-question pages in SEO for car dealers: credit, trade-ins and model comparisons

People search a lot before they search for a specific car: “can I buy a car with bad credit”, “how is trade-in value calculated”, “Tacoma or Tundra for towing”, “best used cars under $10,000”. A dealer can answer these from daily experience, using cars on the lot as examples:
guides for first-time buyers, low credit and self-employed buyers, checked by your finance manager
trade-in explainers: what changes the offer, the paperwork, what happens if you still owe on the car
model comparisons and “best for” pages for the vehicles you sell most

Credit pages are advertising: in the US, terms such as a monthly payment or down payment trigger Truth in Lending disclosures, and states have their own rules on advertised prices and fees. I write within the rules your compliance contact gives me; this is not legal advice. If you run a service department, its search work is described on the
SEO for auto repair shops
page.
Used car dealer SEO vs franchise dealer SEO: OEM programs and what you can change

An independent lot controls its website — and often runs a cheap template with no inventory SEO at all. A franchise dealer usually works inside the manufacturer’s digital program: a website from a certified provider, required brand pages and incentives, co-op rules on what is reimbursed. SEO for a franchise dealer starts with what the platform lets you edit — titles, page text, custom pages, redirects, tracking — and puts the effort where the brand does not set the content:
used and certified pre-owned inventory
location pages and the towns you sell into
your staff, your delivery and trade-in process, your service department
Car dealer SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Car shoppers now put questions to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews — “which dealers in Tulsa have good reviews for used trucks” or “is this dealership legit”. The reply names a handful of dealers and says why. Shaping these replies is what GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization) refer to. On a dealer’s side it takes:
what you sell, where, your hours, financing options and warranty terms written as plain sentences on the site
the same name, address and phone on the site, Google, marketplaces and directories
a steady flow of reviews that mention the car and the experience
AutoDealer and vehicle markup that matches the pages
I record how assistants describe your dealership, and which competitors they name, at the start and again a few months in. What that service includes is listed under

children.text: Car dealer website design is what I do for independent used car lots and small dealer groups: I plan, design and build the site on my own, connected to the system where your inventory already lives, so one person answers for the whole thing at one price. Car dealer websites are catalogs that change every day. Cars arrive and sell, prices drop, photos come in after detailing, and the site has to follow all of it without anyone typing a car in twice.
Car dealer website design around three pages: inventory, vehicle, contact

Most visits to a dealership website follow the same path. The buyer opens the inventory, narrows it down, opens one or two cars, and then calls, texts or sends a form. Everything else — about us, hours, directions, financing — supports that path. So the design work goes where the decisions happen:
the inventory list, which has to be scannable on a phone held in one hand
the vehicle page, which answers “is this the car, what does it cost, is it still here”
the contact step, which should take one tap and tell your team which car the person means
The first screen of the home page shows a search box or the main body types, your location and phone, and a few current arrivals — not a slider of stock photos of cars you do not have.
Inventory feed on a car dealer website: cars imported from your DMS or spreadsheet
The site reads your inventory from where you already keep it. Common sources:
a dealer management system — DealerCenter or Frazer at many independent lots, CDK or Reynolds and Reynolds at franchise stores — through its export
an inventory tool such as vAuto or HomeNet that already sends feeds to marketplaces
a CSV file or Google Sheet for small lots that keep stock in a spreadsheet

I map the fields once — stock number, VIN, year, make, model, trim, mileage, price, colors, options, photo links — and the import runs on a schedule, several times a day if your stock moves fast. New cars appear with their photos, price changes go through, and sold cars leave the list automatically. What happens to a sold car’s page afterwards is a search question, covered on the
car dealer SEO
page. Staff can still add a note or a highlight to any car in the site’s admin, and the next import keeps it.
Vehicle detail page design: what a VDP shows on the first screen
The vehicle detail page decides whether the buyer contacts you or goes back to the marketplace. On a phone, the first screen holds:
the photo gallery, swipeable, starting with a front three-quarter shot
year, make, model and trim in plain words, then price and mileage in large type
three or four key facts: drivetrain, engine, MPG, number of owners
buttons to call, text and check availability, plus a test-drive request
Below that: the full options list, the history report link (Carfax or AutoCheck, if you provide one), the window sticker for new cars, a short walkaround video and similar cars in stock.
Price, fees and monthly payments on a vehicle page

Buyers distrust prices that change at the desk. The page says what the price includes and lists any dealer fees next to it, in the same type size. If you show an estimated monthly payment, its assumptions — term, rate, down payment — sit directly under it, readable without zooming. Rules on advertised prices and fees vary by state, so the wording follows what applies to you.
Inventory search and filters on a dealership website

On a desktop, filters can sit in a sidebar. On a phone they open from one button and close with the result count visible, so the buyer never filters down to zero cars without noticing. Each car in the list shows a photo, price, mileage and one line of key facts. Sorting by price, mileage, year and newest arrivals covers almost every need; a saved search with an email alert keeps buyers who are not ready yet.
Financing forms on a car dealer website: pre-qualification and credit applications
Credit is where many dealer sites lose people, either with a long form on the first visit or with a form that is not safe. The design separates two steps:
Pre-qualification: a short form, often a soft credit check through a provider, that gives the buyer an idea of their terms without affecting their credit score.
The full credit application: sent through your lender platform, such as RouteOne or Dealertrack, or through a secure form that never sends Social Security numbers by plain email.

Dealers who take customer financial information fall under the FTC Safeguards Rule, which asks for protection of that data. The form, its storage and who can see it are built with that in mind; your compliance contact confirms the details.
Trade-in forms on a car dealer website: “value your trade” with VIN lookup and photos

A trade-in form only helps if it collects what an appraiser needs. The buyer enters a VIN or license plate, the form fills in year, make and model, and then asks for mileage, condition, accidents, payoff and a few phone photos. You can show an instant estimate from a valuation tool such as Kelley Blue Book Instant Cash Offer, or ask for an appraisal from your team. Either way, the lead arrives with the car they want to trade and, if they came from a vehicle page, the car they want to buy.
Photo speed on a dealership website: dozens of photos per car without slow pages
A lot with eighty cars and thirty photos each serves thousands of images, and that is the main reason dealer sites are slow. The build handles it at import, not in the browser:
photos resized into several widths and converted to WebP or AVIF when they are imported
only the first photo loaded with the page; the rest load as the buyer swipes
inventory lists showing small thumbnails, never the full-size originals
walkaround videos embedded from YouTube and loaded only when tapped
The result is a vehicle page that opens fast on mobile data at the lot next door, which is where many buyers compare prices.
Calls, texts and chat on a car dealer website: every lead tied to a car

Many buyers would rather text than call. A “Text us about this car” button opens a message that already contains the year, model and stock number, so your salesperson knows which car it is without asking. Calls from a vehicle page can be tracked the same way. Forms and texts go to your CRM or lead inbox with the car attached, and the site shows business hours next to the phone, so nobody calls a closed lot at 9 pm expecting an answer.
Car dealer website providers and templates vs your own website

Dealer website providers bundle a site with the inventory feed and a monthly fee: Dealer.com, DealerOn and Dealer Inspire mostly serve franchise stores, while DMS and marketplace vendors sell website packages to independents. Builders like Wix offer car dealership website templates, some of them free. For a new lot, a template or a vendor package is a fair start. The limits show later:
the same layout as hundreds of other dealers, with little room for your own design
a monthly fee that never ends, and a site that disappears when you cancel
little control over page speed, forms and what goes into the page code

Franchise dealers often have to use a provider certified by the manufacturer, so an own site fits independents and groups with their own used-car brand best. Your feed, lender platform and CRM connect to it the same way they connect to a vendor site.
What the best car dealership websites have in common

The best car dealership websites share habits rather than a look: real photos of every car taken in the same spot, prices with fees shown openly, one tap to call or text from any vehicle, and inventory that matches the lot to the hour.
A car dealer website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Some buyers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which dealers nearby have a certain model or offer financing for first-time buyers. These assistants can only use what they can read. A site that shows inventory, hours and financing terms as images, or loads everything inside a third-party widget, gives them nothing. The same facts as text, with Car and AutoDealer structured data generated from the feed, can be read and quoted.
Being recommended there is separate, ongoing work; see
AI SEO and GEO optimization
How a car dealer website design project runs and what it costs
Brief. You send your current site, feed source, lots, fees, financing partners and a few vehicle pages you like elsewhere.
Phone layouts. I design the inventory list, the vehicle page and the forms on a phone and agree them with you.
Build and feed. The import is connected and tested on your real stock before launch.
Launch. Forms, texts, call tracking and analytics are connected; you get a short guide.
A simple car dealer website — home, inventory list, vehicle pages, about, contact: 700–1,400 €.
A car dealer website with an automatic inventory feed, search filters, financing and trade-in forms and location pages: from 2,000 €.
Design is part of both prices. Once the site is live, your running costs are hosting and the domain; I bill only for changes you request. My general approach to building sites is on the

page; full ranges are on the
pricing
page.
