contentBlocks.title: Get a quote for SEO for your car rental company

children.text: Car rental SEO is the work I do for independent rental companies: making sure that a traveler looking for a car at the airport, a family that needs a minivan for a week and a local whose car is in the shop find your fleet and book with you directly. There is no account manager in between: I audit the site and the booking engine, and I am also the developer who changes the code.
Car rental SEO for independent rental companies: what the work covers

An independent company competes with global brands at the airport counters and with aggregators that put hundreds of offers on one page. Search is where a smaller fleet can win, because many renters want something specific: an automatic where most cars are manual, a seven-seater, a pickup truck, delivery to a hotel, a rental for a full month. The work connects four places:
the website — fleet, location and airport pages, the booking engine, and answers about deposits and insurance
a Google Business Profile for each office and pickup point
aggregator listings and directories, where your details must match the site
answers in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews
Car rental SEO keywords: how travelers and locals search for a rental car
Before any page is written I collect search data for your city, airport and fleet. The phrases fall into groups that need different pages:
location — “car rental” or “car hire” with a city or airport name, “rental car near me”
car type — “SUV rental”, “7 seater car rental”, “van rental”, “convertible rental”
conditions — “car rental under 25”, “car rental with debit card”, “one way car rental”
duration — “weekly car rental”, “monthly car rental”, “long term car rental”
Travelers search weeks before a trip, often comparing three or four towns; locals search on the day they need a car. Both are worth winning, and the data shows which group is larger in your market.
Fleet pages in car rental SEO: car classes and specific models

Most rental sites show the fleet only inside the booking engine, after the visitor enters dates. Search engines and AI assistants never get that far. Each car class — economy, compact, SUV, minivan, van, premium — gets a page that works without dates:
the models in the class, with photos of your own cars rather than manufacturer press shots
seats, luggage space, transmission, fuel type, and available child seats or roof racks
a price range by season and the deposit for this class
who the class suits: a couple with carry-ons, a family with a stroller, four golfers with bags

A popular model gets its own page when people search for it by name — a Tesla, a Jeep Wrangler, a Mercedes V-Class. Only cars you keep in the fleet get one; a page for a car the customer cannot actually book costs trust at the counter.
Location pages for car rental: city offices, hotel delivery and one-way rentals

Each office, pickup point and delivery zone gets its own page: address, hours, how to find the desk or the parking spot, a photo of the meeting point, and the delivery fee to hotels, ports and neighborhoods. One-way rentals between your locations get a page with the routes and the drop fee.

Fifty city pages with swapped names are treated as doorway pages and filtered. A location page is worth adding where you hand over cars and have something useful to say: parking near the old town, ferry connections, roads that need a 4x4 in winter.
Airport car rental pages: pickup, meet-and-greet and late arrivals

Airport searches bring the most valuable bookings and the hardest competition: the big brands have counters in the terminal and aggregators bid on every airport phrase. An independent company usually works from a lot near the airport with a shuttle, or meets customers in arrivals. The airport page turns that from a doubt into a reason to book:
where exactly you meet — the arrivals exit, the parking level, the shuttle stop — with photos
what happens when a flight is late, and whether night arrivals are included or cost a stated fee
how the return works, how long it takes and how far it is to departures
the airport code and terminal names in the text, because travelers search with them
Rentalcars, Discover Cars and Turo vs direct bookings: where car rental SEO fits

Aggregators bring bookings from the first day. Rentalcars.com, Discover Cars, Kayak, Expedia and similar sites take a commission or charge per booking, rank offers mostly by price and keep the contact with the customer; Turo lets small fleets list cars on its marketplace on its own terms. Many independents get a large share of bookings this way, and that is fine.

A direct booking keeps the commission, gives you the customer’s email for the next trip and lets you sell your own extras. SEO is how direct bookings grow: travelers who compared prices on an aggregator often search the company name before paying, and returning customers search for you straight away. My reports show direct bookings next to what aggregators delivered, so you see the shift in money, not only in rankings.
Deposit, insurance and driver requirements: car rental FAQ pages that bring bookings
The questions that stop a booking are almost always about money at the desk. Each one gets a clear answer on the site, matching your terms:
the security deposit — amount by car class, credit or debit card, when the hold is released
insurance — what is included, what the collision damage waiver covers, the deductible, the price of full coverage per day
drivers — minimum age, the young driver fee, years with a license, an international driving permit
fuel policy, mileage limits, cross-border trips, extra drivers, tolls and traffic fines

These pages rank for searches like “car rental under 25” with your city, and they cut disputes at pickup. Insurance and liability rules differ between countries and states, so the text follows your contracts and local law; this is general information, not legal advice.
Car rental SEO for tourists: languages and seasonal demand

Rental demand follows the tourist calendar: summer at the coast, ski weeks in the mountains, holidays and large events in cities. A new page needs weeks or months to rank, so seasonal pages and price updates go live well before the rush, and quiet months go to fleet pages, location pages and fixes.

In tourist areas many renters search in their own language. Each language version is written for that market’s searches, not translated word for word, and the versions are linked with hreflang tags. How I build them is on the
multilingual website development
page.
Google Business Profile and reviews for car rental locations

For “car rental near me” the map decides many calls. Each office or pickup point with staff gets its own profile with “Car rental agency” as the primary category, real hours including late arrivals, and photos of your cars and the meeting point. A delivery-only business uses a service-area profile rather than an address where nobody works.

Rental reviews are mostly about the deposit, the return and extra charges. Asking every customer after the return and answering each complaint calmly in public does more than a row of five-star ratings. Profiles, categories and review routines for several locations are covered on the
local SEO services
page.
Car rental website design in car rental SEO: booking engine, speed and indexable pages
Rental sites usually run a booking engine from rental software — Coastr, RentRabbit and others — or a WordPress plugin. The engine handles availability and payment; the SEO problems sit around it:
the fleet and prices exist only inside an iframe or a script, so search engines see an empty page
result pages with dates in the address get indexed by the thousand and crowd out real pages
heavy car photos and scripts make the first screen slow on a phone at the airport
the form asks for every detail before showing a price
Keeping the booking engine and rebuilding the pages around it

Usually the engine stays. Fleet, location and FAQ pages are rebuilt as fast, plain pages with structured data, and the engine opens at the booking step. If the whole site needs replacing, I build that too.
Car rental SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Renters planning a trip put questions to ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews, such as “can I rent a car at 21 in Florida”, “is it cheaper to book a rental car directly or through Kayak” or “which local rental company meets you at arrivals in Maui”. Assistants build answers from pages they can read and check. This work is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO), and for a rental company it means:
deposit, insurance, age and fuel rules written as plain sentences on your own pages
fleet, locations, hours and airports as text and structured data
the same name, address and phone on Google, aggregators and directories
I save what assistants say about your company, and which competitors they suggest, before the work and again after it. How that work is done is explained on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
How much car rental SEO costs
Car rental SEO audit of the website, booking engine and Google profiles: from 250 €, one-off, with fixes ranked by their effect on bookings.
One-off work — fleet, location and airport pages, deposit and insurance answers, structured data: 250–700 €.

Monthly SEO for a car rental company — new pages, maps, reviews, AI visibility and reports in bookings: from 800 € per month; in big US metros, where national brands and aggregators bid on every airport phrase, from 1,300 € per month.

items.question: Should I stop listing on Rentalcars or Kayak once SEO works?

children.text: Yes, with a page that names the airport and terminals, shows the meeting point or shuttle stop with photos and explains late arrivals and returns. Travelers often prefer a clear meet-and-greet to a long counter line.

children.text: Yes, by car class, with the card types you accept and when the hold is released. Unclear deposits are the most common reason for abandoned bookings and angry reviews.

children.text: Not always. Often the booking engine stays and only the fleet, location and FAQ pages around it are rebuilt. The audit shows whether fixing the current site is enough.

children.text: Carpentry website design is the service I offer carpenters, cabinet makers and joinery workshops: I plan, design and build the whole site myself, so there is no hand-off between a designer and a developer, and the price is agreed before the start. A carpentry services website sells something hard to sell online — a custom job worth thousands, made to measure, which the client cannot see until it is installed. The site has to replace the showroom, the first conversation and part of the estimate.
Carpentry website design for carpenters, cabinet makers and joinery workshops

A website for carpenters covers businesses that sell very different things. A finish carpenter working alone sells trim, crown molding and doors to homeowners and remodelers. A cabinet shop with a CNC router sells kitchens and closets. A joinery workshop builds windows, doors and stairs. A deck builder works outdoors from spring to fall. What they share is a buyer who compares two or three shops over weeks, looks at past work many times and wants to know the price range before inviting anyone to measure.
So the site is built around proof of work and a request that carries real data. If most of your jobs are small repairs, the
handyman website design
page fits better; if you build or renovate whole houses as a general contractor, see the
construction company website
page.
A carpentry project gallery sorted by type of work
The gallery is the page clients return to most, and a single wall of photos does not help them. Projects are grouped the way people shop:
kitchens and kitchen islands
built-in wardrobes, closets, media walls and bookcases
stairs, railings and landings
interior doors, trim and wainscoting
decks, pergolas and outdoor structures
custom furniture: tables, beds, desks
commercial fit-outs for restaurants, offices and shops

Each project has its own page: the room, the wood and finish, the hardware, how long it took and a short note on the problem it solved, such as a closet under a sloped ceiling. Photos from the workshop — joints, glue-ups, a finish being sprayed — show the craft that a finished kitchen hides. You add a project from your phone in a few minutes, and the photos are compressed on upload so the gallery stays fast.
Wood species, materials and finishes explained on a carpentry website

Clients ask the same questions before every custom job: solid oak or veneer, plywood or MDF boxes, oil or lacquer, painted or stained. A short materials page answers them once and explains why your quote differs from a flat-pack kitchen. It covers:
the species you work with, each with a photo of a real piece, not a stock sample
solid wood, veneer, plywood and MDF — where you use each and why
finishes and how they age, with care instructions
hardware: hinges, drawer runners and soft-close options
Every project page links back to the materials it used, so a client who likes a walnut vanity can see what walnut costs relative to maple.
A carpentry quote request with photos, measurements and drawings
A good request saves a wasted measuring visit. The form asks what you would ask on the phone, in short steps:
Type of work, chosen from your list.
Rough dimensions — with a small diagram showing which walls or openings to measure.
Photos of the room or the old staircase, taken on a phone.
Drawings or plans from an architect or designer as PDF or image files, plus inspiration photos.
Wood or finish preferences, a budget range picked from options, and the date the job must be done by.

The request reaches your email with every file attached, or a shared folder if files are large. You can reply with a ballpark figure, ask for one more measurement or book a measuring visit — and decline politely when the budget and the job do not match.
Starting prices and price ranges for carpentry work on the website

Custom work has no fixed price, but clients still need a range to decide whether to call. Each type of work gets a starting price in the unit you already quote in: cabinets per linear foot, stairs per step or per flight, decks per square foot, doors per unit. Next to it is a short line on what moves the number — species, finish, hardware, site access, installation height.

If you charge for measuring and drawings, or credit that fee against the order, the page says so. A starting price filters out the client who expected flat-pack prices and gives the rest a reason to send a request.
The carpentry process from measuring to installation, shown step by step
Clients hiring a carpenter for the first time do not know what happens between the first call and the finished room. A process section shows it:
Measuring visit and a conversation about use, style and budget.
Drawings or a 3D view, revised until approved.
Deposit and material order.
Building and finishing in the workshop.
Installation, adjustment and cleanup.

Above the steps sits one line you edit yourself in the CMS: your current lead time, for example “Booking installs from March”. It answers the question asked in almost every call and sets expectations before the deposit.
A trade page on a carpentry website for builders, architects and interior designers

For many shops, repeat work from the trade matters more than single homeowners. Builders, architects and interior designers look for something different: whether you work from their drawings, produce shop drawings, meet a schedule and send an insurance certificate without being asked twice. A separate trade page answers that:
the work you take for the trade — millwork, built-ins, stairs, commercial fit-outs
drawing formats you accept and how you handle revisions
capacity, typical lead times and the area you install in
a trade enquiry form with a drawing upload and the project schedule
ScanM2, a 3D laser scanning and BIM company, sells to the same architects and builders; after I moved its site off a no-code builder, it gets leads every week.
Reviews, licensing and insurance on a carpenter’s website

Rules differ across the US: in many states and cities, cabinet installation or deck building counts as contractor work and needs a license above a certain job value. children.text: I do carpet cleaning SEO for owner-operators and small carpet cleaning companies: pages for each kind of job, a Google profile that wins the map, and prices and photos that make a homeowner book. Carpet cleaning is a small-ticket service that people buy again, so search has two jobs here. It has to bring the first booking at a fair price, and it has to make sure the same customer finds you again next year instead of a coupon from someone else.
Carpet cleaning SEO is a different search from house cleaning SEO

Someone who types “carpet cleaning near me” or “couch cleaning” wants a van with a wand and a specific stain gone, not a weekly maid. Google treats these as separate markets: the results for carpet cleaning SEO and for cleaning company SEO share almost no pages. The competitors are different too — Chem-Dry, Stanley Steemer and Zerorez franchises, local truck-mount operators and lead platforms — and so are the words customers use: hot water extraction, low-moisture, drying time, pet urine, rug pickup.
That is why a carpet cleaning business needs its own page structure and its own keywords. Maid services and janitorial firms have different needs, described on the

Carpet cleaning SEO keywords: how homeowners search for each job
Before anything is written I pull search data for your services and towns. In carpet cleaning, searches split by what is dirty and why:
carpet — “carpet cleaning near me”, “steam carpet cleaning”, “carpet cleaning cost per room”
upholstery — “couch cleaning”, “sectional cleaning”, “mattress cleaning”
rugs — “area rug cleaning”, “oriental rug cleaning”, “wool rug cleaning near me”
hard surfaces — “tile and grout cleaning”, “grout sealing”
problems — “pet urine smell in carpet”, “red wine stain on carpet”, “carpet smells after cleaning”
commercial — “office carpet cleaning”, “carpet cleaning for rental properties”

The data shows which of these bring up the map, which bring up franchise sites and which already get an AI Overview. That decides what gets built first: usually the service that earns you the most per visit where local competition is weakest.
Service pages for carpet, upholstery, area rug and tile and grout cleaning
A single “Services” page that lists everything loses each of these searches to a more specific page. Each service gets its own page that answers what that customer worries about:
carpet cleaning — your method (truck-mount hot water extraction or low-moisture), drying time, whether furniture is moved, protector
upholstery cleaning — fabric codes, microfiber and leather, sectionals, dining chairs, mattresses
area rug cleaning — in-plant washing for wool, silk and hand-knotted rugs, pickup and delivery, fringe repair
tile and grout cleaning — kitchens, bathrooms, showers, color sealing

Rug cleaning deserves extra attention if you run a rug plant. Rug owners search further from home, accept pickup and pay more per item than wall-to-wall customers, so one well-built rug page can reach well beyond your van routes. Commercial work — offices, short-term rentals, property managers between tenants — gets its own page too, because those buyers ask about scheduling, invoicing and insurance rather than stains.
Pet odor and stain removal pages in SEO for carpet cleaning

Pet urine is one of the most searched carpet problems and one of the better-paid jobs, because it needs more than a standard clean: finding spots with a UV light, treating the pad, sometimes replacing a section. Homeowners search in their own words — “dog pee smell won’t go away”, “cat urine in carpet” — and want to know whether it can be fixed before they pay for a visit.

A pet odor page says what you can remove and what you cannot, when the pad or subfloor is involved, and what the treatment adds to the bill. The same goes for stains: coffee, wine, rust, and bleach spots, which are color loss rather than a stain. Pages that are clear about limits bring fewer disappointed customers and rank for the long questions people type.
Carpet cleaning prices per room: price pages that rank and build trust

“Carpet cleaning cost per room” and “how much to clean a couch” are common searches, and AI Overviews answer them with national averages when your site gives nothing better. Customers have also learned to distrust low per-room offers that grow at the door with pre-treatment, deodorizer and heavy-soil fees.

A clear price page works against both problems: what counts as a room, the minimum charge, the price per sectional seat, per square foot for rugs, and which add-ons cost extra and when. Exact numbers are optional if your prices change; ranges and the rules behind them are enough for search, for assistants and for the customer.
Before-and-after photos and Google reviews for carpet cleaning companies

Carpet cleaning is one of the few services where the result fits in one photo. A gallery that ranks has pairs taken from the same angle, each with a line on what it was — “pet stains on a beige berber carpet in [town]”, “red wine on a cream sofa”. Untitled photos in a slider give Google nothing to read.

Reviews matter as much, since customers let a stranger into their living room. Ask the day after the job, when the carpet is dry and looks its best, with a direct link to your Google profile. Reviews that name the service and the problem — a rug, a sofa, pet odor — help on the map more than “great job”.
Local SEO for carpet cleaning: Google Business Profile and service-area pages

Most carpet cleaners work from a van and do not receive customers, so the profile is set up as a service-area business: address hidden, real towns listed, “Carpet cleaning service” as the primary category and upholstery or rug cleaning as secondary ones where Google offers them. A rug plant where customers drop off rugs can be shown with its own address. Weekly job photos and answers to common questions keep the profile active.
Town pages make sense where you have jobs and reviews to show; a page per suburb with only the name changed is filtered out. The map side of the work is described on the

Seasonal demand and repeat bookings in carpet cleaning SEO

Searches rise in spring, before Thanksgiving and the winter holidays, and around move-out dates, when tenants need a receipt for the deposit. Pages for those moments — move-out carpet cleaning, holiday booking, spring cleaning — go live a couple of months ahead, because new pages need time to rank.

The larger opportunity is the second booking. Families with pets and children clean carpets regularly, and some carpet warranties ask for professional cleaning at set intervals. A maintenance plan page, booking reminders and a profile that is easy to find by name keep last year’s customers from searching again and choosing someone else.
Carpet cleaning advertising vs SEO: mailers, coupon deals, Local Services Ads and lead platforms
Carpet cleaning advertising usually means some mix of these:
door hangers, postcards and coupon mailers in the neighborhoods you serve
deal sites, where a low price brings volume but rarely loyal customers

Each of them brings bookings while you keep paying. SEO costs work up front and then brings people who chose you by your pages, photos and reviews, without a fee per job. My part is the search side: the site, the profile and the pages your ads point to, so paid and unpaid visitors land on the same strong pages.

Homeowners now type questions into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews: “is steam cleaning or dry cleaning better for carpet”, “can pet urine be removed from carpet” or “who cleans area rugs near me”. Assistants build those answers from pages they can read and listings they can cross-check. Work on being named in those answers goes by two labels, generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO). For a carpet cleaner it comes down to:

children.text: The two halves of a working catalogue

A catalogue has to satisfy two audiences that behave nothing alike: the visitor already on your site, and the search engine deciding whether to send you visitors at all. Most catalogues are built for the first and quietly fail the second.

For the visitor, the requirements are ergonomic. Filters that respond without reloading, so narrowing a selection feels immediate. A filtered view that has its own address, so it can be sent to a colleague or reopened tomorrow. Sensible behaviour when nothing matches — nearest alternatives rather than an empty page. And speed that doesn't degrade as the catalogue grows.
For search engines, the requirement is different: something to index. Dynamically generated filter results usually aren't indexed,
which is why so many catalogues rank for the company name and nothing else
. The fix is
dedicated pages for the combinations that carry real demand
— a category within a location, a parameter range, a type of product — each with its own address, its own text and its own selection of items. That's where catalogue traffic actually comes from.

Then there's the part nobody sees until it fails: the connection to your data. If items live in a CRM, an ERP or a spreadsheet and the site is maintained separately, the two will drift. Automatic synchronisation isn't a convenience feature — it's what keeps the catalogue trustworthy.
This applies well beyond any single industry.
A property catalogue
, an equipment rental fleet, a B2B supplier's product range,
a manufacturer's specification-driven line-up
— the parameters differ, the structure doesn't.
A real estate catalogue I built runs in four languages
and brings over 1,500 organic visits a month with no ad spend
, and it does so because of dedicated pages behind the filters, not the filters alone.

children.text: I do SEO for catering companies: the work that puts your business in front of the office manager who searches for corporate catering in your city, the couple comparing wedding caterers a year before the date and the planner who needs lunch for two hundred at a conference venue. People shortlist three or four caterers and send several quote requests, so search decides who makes that shortlist. Catering SEO keywords: how planners, couples and office managers search for a caterer
Catering searches split by who is buying and what for, and each group needs its own page:
corporate and office — “corporate catering [city]”, “office lunch catering”, “boxed lunches for a meeting”, “breakfast catering for 50 people”
weddings and private events — “wedding catering [city]”, “rehearsal dinner catering”, “graduation party catering”, “BBQ catering for a backyard party”
format and diet — “drop-off catering”, “buffet catering”, “food stations”, “halal catering”, “vegan catering for an event”
cost — “catering price per person”, “how much is catering for 100 guests”

My first step is the search data for your city and the towns around it. Corporate searches are usually fewer than wedding searches, but they bring repeat orders; wedding searches often rise after the winter holidays, when newly engaged couples start booking. The data shows which group to start with in your market.
Event-type pages for caterers: corporate, wedding, office lunch and private party catering
A single “Services” page that lists weddings, conferences and birthdays in one paragraph ranks poorly for each of them. Each event type gets a page written for the person who books it:
corporate events — conferences, product launches, holiday parties: the headcounts you handle, service styles, staff and equipment, how far ahead to book
office lunch — daily or weekly drop-off, individually labeled boxes, the order cutoff the day before and how a company sets up a standing order
weddings — sample menus, tastings, whether you cook on site or bring food from your kitchen, what the price per guest includes
private parties — birthdays, graduations and anniversaries at home or in a rented hall, with the smallest order you accept
Each page carries photos from real events of that type, a sample menu and the questions people ask before booking, so the planner who reads it writes with a date and a headcount already decided.
Service-area and venue pages for a catering company

A caterer has no dining room, so people search by where the event will happen: “catering in [suburb]”, “caterers near [venue name]”. Service-area pages answer those searches when they describe places you really serve and say something specific about each one:
the delivery fee or travel minimum for that area, and how much notice you need
venues there where you have catered — event halls, wineries, office parks, community centers — with what you know about their kitchens, load-in times and house rules
photos from events in that area, published with the client’s permission

Venue pages tend to work especially well. A couple that has just booked a venue searches for “caterers at [venue]”, and few caterers have a page that answers it. A new town or venue gets its own page once you have events and photos to show there; until then a single list of the areas you serve is enough.
Catering menus and price per person: pages that answer the cost question

“How much does catering cost per person” is one of the most common questions in the business, and many caterers leave it unanswered on their site. A page that gives real ranges attracts the visitor who is building a budget, and that visitor is close to booking. The menu and pricing pages I write for caterers show sample menus as text for each event type, a price-per-person range for each service style — drop-off, buffet, family style, plated, stations — the minimum headcount or order value, and what moves the total: staff hours, rentals, travel and service charges.

Menus are written as facts, not mood. On the property platform in Cyprus that I built and run, project descriptions were once rewritten as lifestyle copy and commercial pages lost traffic; returning to factual descriptions with price, area and location brought clicks back by 16%. Catering pages behave the same way: dish names, portions, dietary marks and the price range are what searchers and AI assistants pick up.
B2B catering SEO: reaching office managers and corporate event planners

Corporate buyers search differently from couples. An office manager has a budget, a headcount and a meeting tomorrow at noon; an event planner has a brief and three caterers to compare. Both look for signs that you can serve a business without surprises:
a page for recurring office catering — weekly lunches, breakfast meetings, how standing orders and monthly invoicing work
clear labeling of each meal and allergen information on request, which HR and facility teams ask about
case pages or client names only where the client agreed to be named
short answers to procurement questions: insurance, food safety certificates, payment terms, the paperwork you send
The volume of these searches is small, but a company that likes your Tuesday lunches rarely switches caterers, so each of these pages is worth more than its traffic suggests.
ezCater and catering marketplaces vs quote requests from your own website

Search for office catering in a large US city and the top results often belong to marketplaces: ezCater, the catering sections of delivery apps and local ordering platforms. They bring orders from companies that already buy there, and many caterers keep their menus listed. The price is a commission on each order, a listing next to dozens of competitors sorted by price and rating, and a client relationship that stays with the platform: the office manager remembers the marketplace, not your company.

SEO builds a second channel next to it — pages that rank for your event types and areas, and a Google listing under your real name, so repeat clients come to you directly. My reports keep direct inquiries and marketplace orders in separate columns, so you can watch the share change and decide later which listings are worth keeping.
Google Business Profile for a catering company: service area, category and reviews

Many caterers work from a commercial kitchen that clients never visit. Google lets such businesses hide the street address and show a service area instead, and the profile can still appear for “caterer near me”. For a catering profile the work is concrete:
“Caterer” as the primary category, and the event types you serve listed as services
a service area that matches where you really go, not the whole state
photos from real events — the buffet before guests arrive, boxed lunches packed for delivery, your team at work — added after each larger job
a review request sent the day after the event to the person who booked, asking them to mention the type of event and the venue
The rest of the map work — citations in other directories, duplicate listings, service areas — is described on the

Seasonal catering SEO: holiday parties, wedding season and graduations
Catering demand follows the calendar, and a page needs weeks to be crawled and to climb, so the work runs ahead of the bookings:
late summer and early fall — holiday party pages refreshed with this year’s menus, because companies book December events early
winter — wedding pages updated with new menus and tasting dates while couples plan the next season
early spring — graduation parties, corporate picnics and summer events
January and September — office lunch pages, when companies return to routines and set new budgets
During its season a page is linked from the home page; afterwards it stays live, so the photos and reviews from this year’s holiday parties help sell next year’s.
Catering SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Planners increasingly type their questions into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews: “who does corporate catering in [city] for 150 people”, “which caterers near [venue] offer halal menus” or “how much should I budget for wedding catering for 120 guests”. The answers are put together from pages the assistant can read and compare with other sources; the work of getting into them is called GEO (generative engine optimization) or AEO (answer engine optimization). For a caterer it rests on four things:
headcounts, service area, lead time and price-per-person ranges written as plain sentences
event-type pages that answer planning questions directly, signed by the owner or the chef
structured data that describes the business, its services and the area it serves
the same name, phone number and service area on the site, on Google, in wedding directories and on marketplaces
I record what assistants say about your company and which caterers they suggest instead, at the start and again a few months later. The service itself has its own page: the

A good month in catering is counted in booked events, not in positions. Reports show quote requests that came from search, calls and messages from the map listing, which event-type and area pages brought them, the date and headcount of each inquiry, and how many of them became booked events. The booking figures come from your inbox, CRM or catering software, so they match your calendar.

A catering site has two kinds of visitors: a planner preparing an event weeks ahead who needs enough detail to send a request, and an office assistant who needs lunch for twelve people tomorrow and wants to order in a few minutes.
What the first screen of a catering website shows
The visitor decides within seconds whether to keep reading, so the first screen on a phone answers four things without scrolling:
what you cater and where — “Corporate and wedding catering in Denver and the Front Range”, with your own words and area
two clear paths: Request a quote for events, and Order lunch for offices if you sell drop-off
one photo from a real event of yours, not a stock buffet
a call and a text button for planners who would rather talk
On phones the quote button sits pinned to the lower edge. The story of the company, the chef and the awards comes further down, where the people who are already interested will read it.
Catering menus by event type on the website

A caterer’s menu is not one list. The same kitchen sells boxed lunches, a plated wedding dinner and a canapé reception, and each buyer wants to see only their part. The site organizes menus by event type — corporate, wedding, office lunch, private party — and each menu page shows:
packages or sample menus as text, with dish names and portions
dietary marks — vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, halal or kosher where you offer them — and a note on allergen information
the service styles each menu comes in: drop-off, buffet, family style, plated, stations
a “start a quote with this menu” button that opens the form with the menu already selected
Menus are edited in the CMS. A seasonal menu replaces the old one in a few minutes, and the layout stays the same whatever you add.
Price per person and minimum orders on a catering website

Planners want to know whether you fit their budget before they write. A pricing block on each menu page shows a “from” price per person for each service style, the smallest guest count or order total you accept, and the extras: staff hours, rentals, travel outside your area, service charge. If you would rather not publish exact figures, ranges do the job. Clear numbers filter out requests you would decline anyway and make the rest more serious.

For buffets and drop-off menus a small estimator helps: the visitor chooses a package and enters the guest count, sees a ballpark figure and continues to the form with both values carried over. The final quote is still yours to make.
A catering quote form: event date, guest count, venue, budget and dietary needs
The quote form is where a catering website earns its money. It asks for what you need to send a real quote, and nothing more:
event type and date, with fully booked dates marked so nobody asks for a day you cannot take
guest count and the venue or address, with a question about kitchen access on site
service style and a budget per person chosen from ranges
dietary needs: how many vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free or allergy meals
contact details and whether the client prefers a call, an email or a text

The form is split into three short steps, so on a phone it does not feel like paperwork. Each request reaches your inbox or CRM in the same format, and the client gets an automatic reply saying when to expect your quote.
Online ordering for office lunches and drop-off catering

Drop-off catering works more like a web store. The site shows a menu of boxed lunches, platters and breakfasts with prices, an order cutoff such as 2 p.m. the day before, delivery windows and the minimum order. Clients pay by card, Apple Pay or Google Pay, upload a list of names if each box should be labeled, and repeat last week’s order in two clicks.

Companies that order every week get an account with saved addresses, several people allowed to order, and a monthly invoice instead of card payments. Purchase order numbers and billing contacts are stored with the account, so accounting gets what it needs without a round of emails.
Deposits and online payments for catering events

An event is confirmed by a deposit. After you accept a request and send the quote, the client receives a payment link, pays the deposit by card through Stripe or another payment provider, and the date is marked as booked; a second link for the balance goes out closer to the event. Nobody has to read a card number over the phone, and you see at a glance which events are paid.

I built the same pay-then-confirm flow for Landi Room, a Warsaw beauty salon whose landing page sells an online course through Stripe Checkout: the buyer pays and gets access automatically, with no manual step on the salon’s side.
Photos of real events in catering website design

Stock photos of buffets look the same on every catering site, and planners recognize them. The design is built around your own pictures: the set-up before guests arrive, plated dishes, boxed lunches lined up for delivery, your team serving. Galleries are sorted by event type, so a couple sees weddings and an office manager sees lunches and conferences.

A catering gallery can grow to hundreds of photos, so images are resized for each screen and loaded as the visitor scrolls. The DJ and producer site I built has a video gallery and still loads in under one second; a catering gallery uses the same technique. If you have few photos yet, I give your photographer a shot list for the next events.
Service area and delivery details on a catering website

Planners need to know early whether you come to their venue. A service-area block shows the cities and suburbs you cover on a simple map, the delivery fee or travel minimum for each zone, and how much notice you need for each kind of event. The quote form checks the address against those zones and tells the visitor right away if the venue is outside your area. All zones and fees are settings you change yourself.

A template is a fair start for a new caterer with one menu: it is live in days. The limits show as the business grows. The quote form is a generic contact form, deposits and office ordering need several plugins that do not talk to each other, menus by event type become one long page, and the site looks like the competitor down the road who bought the same theme.

A custom catering site is built around your event types, your quote process and your own photos, on WordPress or on Next.js with a headless CMS, and the code, the domain and the client data stay yours. children.text: Charity website design is the work I do for UK charities, from small local groups to organisations with their own fundraising teams, and I build the sites myself, so design and development come from one person at one price. A UK charity site has to win supporters and meet rules at the same time: showing registered status, collecting Gift Aid declarations, following fundraising standards and getting consent for every email. Building those into the design from the start costs far less than adding them after a supporter complains.
Website design for charity organisations: what supporters, funders and trustees look for

Supporters arrive from a fundraising page shared by a friend, a local news story or a search for the cause. Within seconds they look for three things: what the charity does and where, whether it is a real registered charity, and how to give or get involved. Grant-makers read further — governance, accounts, outcomes — and trustees want a site they are happy to link to in a bid. The home page serves the first group; a clear “About us” section with governance serves the rest.
Showing your registered charity number on a charity website

Registered charities in England and Wales above an income threshold must state that they are registered on their official documents, and the Charity Commission’s guidance counts websites and emails among them. Charitable companies and CIOs have further naming rules of their own, so check the current Charity Commission guidance for your structure. In the design this becomes routine:
the full registered name and charity number in the footer of every page
the number repeated on the donation page and in email receipts
for a charitable company, the company number and registered office as well
a link to the charity’s entry on the regulator’s register, where supporters can check the accounts themselves
Designing an online donation form with a Gift Aid declaration

Gift Aid lets a charity claim basic-rate tax back from HMRC on donations from UK taxpayers — 25p for every £1 given — but only with a valid declaration from the donor. The donation form is built around that step:
a clear Gift Aid tick box with HMRC’s model wording, the donor’s full name and home address, with a postcode lookup to save typing
one line explaining that the donor must pay enough Income Tax or Capital Gains Tax to cover the claim
one-off and monthly options, with regular gifts by card or Direct Debit through your payment provider
each declaration stored with its date and the wording shown, so you can produce it if HMRC asks
Check the current HMRC Gift Aid guidance for the exact wording; the form is built so the text can be changed without a developer.
JustGiving, Enthuse or CAF Donate on a charity website

Many UK charities already use a donation platform, and the website works with it rather than replacing it. JustGiving is familiar to supporters and widely used for event sponsorship pages; Enthuse is often chosen for donation forms in the charity’s own branding; CAF Donate suits charities that want a simple form linked to the Charities Aid Foundation’s services. Fees, Gift Aid handling and how far each form can be styled differ, so I look at the platform you use before quoting. The design then works around it: appeal pages, event pages that point supporters to their sponsorship pages, and a thank-you page on your own domain.
Charity web design and the Fundraising Regulator’s Code of Fundraising Practice

The Fundraising Regulator sets standards for charitable fundraising in England, Wales and Northern Ireland through its Code of Fundraising Practice; Scotland has its own arrangements. On a website the Code shows up in small, visible choices:
appeals that are honest about what a gift does, without countdown timers or pressure
no pre-ticked boxes for extra amounts or regular giving
an easy, clearly described way to cancel a regular gift
a fundraising complaints route that is easy to find

Charities registered with the Fundraising Regulator can display its badge, and the design gives it a place next to the donation form. Check the current Code for the sections that apply to your charity.
UK GDPR and PECR on a charity website: newsletter consent, cookies and supporter data
Email and text updates to supporters fall under PECR as well as UK GDPR. In practice the design needs:
separate, unticked opt-ins for email, text and post on donation and sign-up forms
a privacy notice written for supporters, linked beside every form
a cookie banner that lets visitors refuse analytics as easily as accept them
consent recorded with its date and the form it came from, so your supporter database knows who agreed to what

The rules on the “soft opt-in” for charities have been changing, so check the ICO’s current guidance before relying on it. The forms are built so their wording and options can be updated as the guidance moves.
Accessible charity website design and the Charity Digital Code of Practice

The Charity Digital Code of Practice, a free framework for UK charities, asks boards to treat digital as part of their strategy and to design around the people they serve. Accessibility sits at the centre of that. The design aims at WCAG AA: readable contrast, text that scales, keyboard navigation, captions, alt text and plain English. Many charities serve people with disabilities or low literacy, and some funding agreements ask for a specific accessibility standard, so check your contracts and grant terms.
Trustees, annual report and accounts pages on a charity website
Funders and major donors look at governance before they give. A short governance section answers them:
trustees with names, roles and a line about each, as the people legally responsible for the charity
the trustees’ annual report and accounts as a short web summary, with the full document to download
safeguarding, complaints and privacy policies, each one click from the footer
the charity’s objects and area of benefit in plain English
Staff edit each item in the admin panel, so next year’s report goes up without waiting for a developer.
Charity websites in Scotland and Northern Ireland: OSCR and CCNI

Charities registered in Scotland answer to the Scottish Charity Regulator (OSCR), which has its own rules on showing the charity’s name, number and status on documents and websites. Charities in Northern Ireland register with the Charity Commission for Northern Ireland (CCNI). A charity registered in England and Wales that also operates in Scotland may need to register with OSCR too. The footer and donation pages are designed to carry more than one number where needed; check the guidance from each regulator that applies to you.
A charity website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Supporters ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which charities help with a cause near them, or whether a particular charity is legitimate. Assistants rely on facts they can read and match against the regulator’s register: the charity’s name and number, what it does, where, and how to give. The design keeps these as page text with structured data for the organisation, never only inside a logo, an image or a PDF.

Charity website design examples and templates: patterns that work

Template galleries offer charity themes ready to fill, and inspiration sites collect polished charity website examples. Look past the colour schemes and photography, and the charity websites that serve people best share a few patterns:
one primary action per page — donate, volunteer or get support — in one reserved colour
support services kept apart from fundraising, so a person in need never has to read an appeal first
stories told with consent, by or with the people involved
appeal pages that staff can launch in an afternoon from a ready layout
A template is a fair start for a newly registered charity with one activity. Once you run several services, appeals and events, a design system your staff can extend saves more than it costs.

children.text: I do chiropractor website design and build the site myself, so the layout, the code and the launch come from one person at one price. A chiropractic website is often opened by someone whose back hurts right now, on a phone, in a short break. The design has one job above the rest: show that person that you treat their problem, let them trust the doctor and get them to a booked first visit in under a minute.
Chiropractor website design: the first screen a patient in pain sees
On a phone, the visible part of the first screen has room for four things, and they go in this order:
what you treat and where — “Chiropractic care for back pain, neck pain and sports injuries in [town]”, not a slogan about wellness
a book button and a call button, fixed to the bottom of the screen on every page
opening hours, especially early mornings or Saturdays if you offer them
a real photo of the doctor or the office instead of a stock illustration of a spine

Everything else — mission, the full list of techniques, the blog — goes below. Sliders, autoplay video and pop-up offers push the booking button out of view; they are the first things I remove from existing chiropractic websites.
Chiropractic websites from vendor platforms and templates vs a custom design

Search for “chiropractic websites” and most results are platforms made for chiropractors — a monthly plan with a theme, hosting, a newsletter and a library of pre-written articles — plus galleries of chiropractic website templates. They launch fast, and for a new solo office that only needs hours, a phone number and a booking link online, a template can be enough.
The limits appear later:
the pre-written articles are on hundreds of other chiropractors’ sites, so they add little in search
the layout changes only as far as the theme allows
the content, and sometimes the domain, stays with the platform when you cancel
the monthly fee runs for as long as the site exists
A custom chiropractor website costs more at the start, belongs to you in full and is built around how your office works: your techniques, your doctors, your scheduler.
Design for patients in pain: calm layout, large buttons and plain words

Someone with acute low back pain may be lying on the floor with the phone held above their face. That sets the design rules: large buttons with space between them, body text of at least 16 pixels, strong contrast and one accent color reserved for booking. Nothing moves unless the visitor asks it to.

The words stay calm as well. “Instant relief” or “fix your spine” sound like promises no clinician can make, and cautious patients leave. A sentence describing what happens during an adjustment does more for them. Layouts follow WCAG at level AA — keyboard navigation, visible form labels, captions on video — which also helps the many older adults who see a chiropractor.
First-visit, pricing and insurance pages in chiropractic website design

Most calls to a chiropractic front desk ask the same things: how long the appointment lasts, what clothing to wear, whether imaging is part of it, the fee and whether insurance covers any of it. I design one page that answers them in that order, with a photo of the room where the first exam takes place, and link it from every condition page.

Cash prices and care plans are shown as text, and accepted insurance as a written list rather than a strip of logos, because patients search the page for their plan name. If you advertise a new-patient offer, the layout leaves room next to it for any disclaimer your state requires, at a readable size rather than in fine print.
Doctor bios and technique pages on a chiropractic website

Patients choose a chiropractor as much as an office. Each doctor gets a page built on one template: a photo taken in your own office, DC degree and school, state license, years in practice, the techniques they use — Gonstead, Diversified, Activator, Thompson Drop — and the patients they see most, such as runners, office workers, pregnant women or older adults.

Technique pages explain each method in a few short paragraphs, next to a short video of a real adjustment recorded with the patient’s written consent. A reader who is nervous about the sound of a joint release understands more from twenty seconds of video than from a page of text.
Online scheduling and intake forms on a chiropractic website

Booking is the main route through the site. Behind the button sits whatever your practice software offers — an embedded scheduler, a booking link or a short request form followed by a call back — and the visitor sees at once whether the time is confirmed or the office will phone them.

Intake paperwork is where health information enters. There are two safe designs: the public form collects a name, a phone number or email and a good time to call, with a note asking people to leave symptoms for the visit, or intake paperwork goes through a HIPAA-ready service that signs a business associate agreement with the office. Analytics scripts stay off booking and intake pages. Your compliance adviser confirms the final setup.

Some five years back I was part of building a medical system that handled patient data. An NDA covers it, so I cannot say more, but it taught me to treat every extra field on a health form as a liability: if the visit can be booked without it, the field goes.
Video and photos on a chiropractic website without slowing it down

Adjustment clips, exercise demonstrations and an office tour make a chiropractic site feel real, and they are also what makes it slow. Each video loads only when tapped and shows a still image until then; photos are cropped for phones and served in modern formats. The target is the main content visible in under 2.5 seconds on a mid-range phone, measured before launch, not assumed.
A chiropractic website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

People ask assistants which chiropractor nearby works on Saturdays, takes their insurance or treats sports injuries. Assistants can only repeat what they can read and verify, so those facts live on the page as text and in structured data — doctors, techniques, conditions, hours, insurance and languages, matching your Google Business Profile. Giuseppe’s site was built this way, with structured data for the practitioner, his consulting rooms, conditions and therapies and explicit rules for AI crawlers in robots.txt; its new pages already appear in ChatGPT answers.
Getting your office into those answers over time is described on the

page, and ranking in Google and the map pack on

Redesigning a chiropractic website without losing Google rankings

Older chiropractic sites often carry years of blog posts and condition articles that still bring visits. When I moved Giuseppe’s site from WordPress to Next.js, all 468 blog posts kept their place in search through 301 redirects from every old address. A chiropractic redesign gets the same treatment: each old URL mapped to its new page, structured data carried over and Search Console checked after launch.
Details of that process are on the

page.
How the chiropractor website design process works
Brief. You send the list of doctors, techniques and conditions, your hours, prices and insurance plans, and the questions the front desk hears most.
Patient routes. I map the three that matter — book a first visit, read about a condition, call the office — and agree them with you on a phone screen.
Design. The home page, a doctor bio and the first-visit page are designed in full; other pages follow the same system.
Build and checks. Scheduling is connected, forms, speed and accessibility are tested, and you get a short manual for editing hours, prices and doctors.

For scale: Giuseppe’s site, with two languages and hundreds of pages, was handed over 44 working days after the first line of code, together with owner’s manuals in two languages and video walkthroughs. My general approach to builds is described on the

Design is not sold separately; it is part of the build, and the price covers both.

children.text: Two questions decide it, and most sites answer neither
Someone looking for a cleaning company arrives with two questions in mind. What will this cost, and can I trust these people in my home.
Almost every site in the field answers the first with "contact us" and the second not at all
. Whether that comes from
a page builder or custom-built code
is a decision worth making deliberately, not by default.

The price question is the more surprising omission, because cleaning is genuinely calculable. Area, number of rooms, frequency, whether it's routine or post-renovation — a handful of inputs produces a defensible estimate. A calculator that returns a number on the spot converts a large share of visitors who would never have filled in an enquiry form just to ask what it costs, and it filters out those whose expectations were never going to match.
I've built parameter-based calculators of exactly this kind
, where a few selections produce a price immediately.

For harder jobs, photographs solve what a form can't. Post-renovation work or heavily soiled spaces can't be estimated from a description, and the usual answer is a site visit that costs both sides time. Letting a client upload photos in the enquiry gives an accurate quote without leaving the office — I've implemented this for a client, and it changed the character of incoming enquiries entirely.

Trust is the second question, and the one competitors leave open. Cleaning is unusual among services: you are asking for access to someone's home or office, frequently with keys and no one present. Who your people are, whether they're vetted, whether the company carries insurance, and what happens if something is damaged — these aren't reassurance copy, they're the actual decision criteria. Saying them plainly is the strongest available differentiator precisely because so few do.

Underneath both sits the split between private and commercial clients. They are not the same business. A household books on price and convenience and decides in an afternoon; a company signs a contract, needs invoicing and references, and decides over weeks. One page addressed to both persuades neither and ranks for neither set of searches. This is what

children.text: I build websites for construction companies from start to finish — structure, design, development and launch — so one person is responsible for how the site looks and how it works. A construction company website has one job: turn people who are comparing builders into requests for a price. Everything on it is planned around that.
What a construction company website needs: pages and features
Most construction company websites are a home page, an “about us”, a gallery and a contact form. That is not enough to be found or to be chosen. A website that brings work has:
a page for each service you sell — new builds, renovations, extensions, roofing, finishing
a page for each town or area you cover, with projects from there
a project portfolio where every project has its own page with facts and photos
a quote form that asks the questions your estimator needs and accepts photos and drawings

page.
A project portfolio your team updates from a phone

A portfolio only works if it stays current, and it stays current only if adding a project takes a few minutes. On the site I build, a new project is a short form in a simple admin panel: type of work, location, size, duration, a few sentences and photos straight from the phone. The page is laid out automatically, gets its own address, and appears in the right service and area lists.
Photos are compressed on upload, so a site manager can add twenty pictures from the site without slowing the website down.
A construction quote form with photo and drawing upload

The quote form is where the website earns its cost. It asks, in a few short steps, what your estimator would ask on the phone: type of project, location, approximate size, stage, budget range and start date. Clients can attach photos of the site and plans from their phone or computer.
Requests arrive by email with everything in one place. If you use a CRM or a shared inbox, the form can send requests there instead, so nothing gets lost between the office and the site.
Speed, hosting and security of a construction company website

Clients often look at a builder’s site on a phone, on mobile data, sometimes standing on their own plot. Pages are built to appear in under 2.5 seconds on a mobile connection — the threshold Google uses for a good page — even with many project photos, because images are served in modern formats and loaded only when they come into view.

The site runs on fast hosting with SSL, automatic backups and protection of the forms against spam. When a site is built well, it often needs no maintenance for months; when it does, you pay for the work done, not a monthly retainer.
A construction company website that AI assistants can read

More clients ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to recommend a builder. Assistants can only recommend what they can read. The site is built so that the facts about your company are machine-readable from day one:
services, areas, years in business and credentials written as text, not only shown in images
structured data for the company, its services, service areas and reviews
one page per service and area, each answering the questions clients ask
the same company details as in your Google profile and directories

A construction website is judged the way a client judges a builder: by finished work, by whether you take on jobs like theirs in their area, and by how easy it is to ask for a price. What a construction company website design has to show in the first minute
A client looking for a construction company is comparing three or four firms, often on a phone, often between other things. On the home page the design answers four questions before anything else:
what you build — new homes, renovations, extensions, commercial fit-outs — in plain words, not “quality construction solutions”
where you work — the towns and regions, named
proof — two or three recent projects with real photos, one tap away from the full list
how to get a price — a quote button that stays visible while scrolling on a phone
Company history, values and the team come after that. They matter for the final decision, but nobody reads them before checking that you do their kind of job in their area.
Construction project pages: the core of a construction website
Projects sell construction work better than any text about the company. A project gallery with forty unlabelled photos does not. Each project gets its own page with the facts a client compares:
type of work and what was in scope — from groundwork to finishing, or one stage
size, location and how long it took
photos in order: the site before, the work in progress, the finished result
the client’s problem and how it was solved, in two or three sentences
a link to the matching service page and a quote button

Projects are filtered by type, so a homeowner planning a loft conversion sees loft conversions, not warehouses. Real site photos taken on a phone are better than stock images of hard hats: clients recognise stock photos immediately. I prepare a short checklist of shots for the site team, so every new project is photographed the same way.
Services and service areas in construction website design

“Construction company” is too broad for both clients and search engines. The site gets one page for each service you actually sell — new builds, renovations, extensions, roofing, interior finishing, whatever applies — and, if you cover several towns, a page for each area with projects from that area.

This is what lets the site be found for “house extension” plus a town name rather than only for the company name. The structure is planned in the design stage, because adding it later usually means rebuilding the navigation.
A construction website quote form that collects what an estimator needs

children.text: Daycare website design is the service I offer owners of private daycares, preschools, nurseries and early learning centers: I plan the pages, draw the design and build the site myself, so the person who sketches the tour form is the one who makes it work. Parents choosing childcare are matching a child’s age, a start date and a commute against the places that might have room, and they leave a site the moment it makes them hunt for an answer.
Daycare and preschool website design: what parents look for first
Ask a center director what parents want to know on the first call, and the list is short. The home page answers it before anyone picks up the phone:
the ages you take, in one line such as “Infant care, toddlers and pre-K in [neighborhood]”
your opening and closing hours, and whether you follow the school calendar or stay open all year
the address with drop-off notes: parking, the entrance families use, the nearest bus stop or main road
tuition from a weekly or monthly amount, and whether a place is free right now
Two buttons follow these facts: book a tour and join the waitlist. Your philosophy, history and curriculum sit further down, for parents who are already interested.
Program pages on a preschool website: age groups, daily rhythm and curriculum

Each age group gets its own page built from the same parts, so the parent of a toddler reads about toddlers instead of a general “Programs” overview. The page covers the age range, the group size and staff-to-child ratio you keep, a typical day from drop-off to pickup, what children learn and how you report progress, and what to pack on the first morning. Ratios and group sizes are numbers parents compare between centers, so the page shows the figures you can stand behind and changes when they do.

Programs built on a named approach — Montessori, Reggio Emilia, play-based or faith-based — explain it in plain words with an example from your own classroom rather than a quote from a textbook. Bilingual and immersion programs get the same treatment, and the site itself can run in both languages; how that is built is on the
multilingual website development
page, and schools that teach languages to older children and adults have their own page on
language school website
design.
Tuition and openings on a daycare website: starting prices and a waitlist by age group

Many centers keep tuition off the site and give it on the phone. The result is predictable: the director spends afternoons on calls that end at the price. A short table does that work instead — weekly or monthly tuition from a stated amount for each program, full-time and part-time, the registration fee, what tuition covers (meals, diapers, field trips, whatever is true for you) and whether you accept state child care assistance. The table names the school year it applies to, so last year’s rates never mislead a family.

Openings change every month, so they live in one small block that the director edits in the CMS: for each age group, “full, waitlist open”, “two places from March” or “enrolling now”. Shown on the home page and on each program page, that one line saves more calls than anything else on the site.
Tour booking and waitlist forms on a childcare center website

A visit is where most enrollments start, and centers run it in one of two ways. Some hold group tours at fixed times; then the form lists the next dates and closes each one when it is full. Others show families around one at a time; then a parent picks a few slots that suit them and the director confirms one. The confirmation repeats the address, the door to use and how long the visit takes.

The waitlist form asks only what you need to hold a place in line: the parent’s name and contacts, the child’s birth month or due date, the wanted start date, the program and the days per week. Medical details, allergies and custody papers belong to the enrollment packet, which comes later and lives in your childcare software, not on a public website. If you charge a waitlist or registration fee, parents can pay it by card on the spot through Stripe Checkout — the same flow I built for Landi Room, where payment and confirmation happen in one step.
Teacher and staff pages on a daycare website

After tuition, the staff page is often the next one parents open. Each lead teacher gets a portrait, the room they teach, their early childhood education or credential, years in the field and a sentence or two in their own voice. Below the team, a short paragraph states what every new hire goes through — background checks, CPR and first aid training, ongoing professional development — in general terms that match your state rules and your handbook, and never more than you actually do.
Turnover is a real question in childcare, so if your teachers have stayed for years, the page can say how long each one has been with you. Profiles are edited in the CMS by your staff.
Licensing, safety, meals and allergy policies on a daycare website

Your license is stated as text rather than as a badge image: the license type, its number, the agency that issued it and, if your state runs a quality rating system, your current rating. A single policies page then answers what parents worry about without turning the site into a handbook:
how drop-off and pickup work, and who may collect a child
how the building is secured and how visitors are let in, described in general terms
the sick-child policy and when a child should stay home
meals and snacks: this month’s menu, who prepares it, and how you handle food allergies and special diets
the full parent handbook as a PDF for families who want every detail
Requirements differ from state to state, so you confirm the wording against your licensing rules; the site gives each item a fixed place, which makes it easy to keep current.
Photos of children on a daycare website: parent consent and safer choices
Parents scroll past stock photos of smiling toddlers, and photos of your own children are the most sensitive content a childcare business publishes. The approach I follow:
a photo release in the enrollment packet, and a simple list of which children may appear online
rooms, materials, art on the walls, the play yard and the kitchen as the main subjects
children shown from behind, at a distance or as hands at work, when a child appears at all
no names next to faces and no captions that tie a child to a room or a schedule
location data removed from every image file before upload
Everyday photos for parents belong in your childcare app, where only the families of that room can see them.
A parent portal through brightwheel or your childcare app, linked from the website

Most centers already use childcare software — brightwheel, Procare, Playground or similar — for check-in, daily reports, messages and billing. The website does not copy any of it. A parent login link sits in the header, a short page shows new families how to install the app, and child records stay in the system built to protect them. Beyond a waitlist entry, the public site keeps nothing about children.
Daycare SEO: local search, Google Business Profile and reviews

Parents search close to home: “daycare near me”, “preschool in [neighborhood]”, “infant care [town]”. The build prepares for those searches with a location page for each center carrying its own address, hours and openings, a business name and address written exactly as on your Google Business Profile, and pages that open fast on a phone. A review from a parent carries more weight than anything you write about yourself, so the site links to your profile and asking for a review takes families two taps.
The ongoing work on the map listing and local rankings is described on the

page.
A daycare website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Parents now ask assistants things like “which preschools near [neighborhood] have a place for a two-year-old” or “a bilingual daycare with extended hours in [town]”. ChatGPT and Google’s AI Overviews answer from what they can read on your pages. So ages, programs, hours, tuition from, license details, languages spoken and the address are written as plain text, kept identical to your Google profile, and marked up with schema.org ChildCare or Preschool data. Giuseppe’s practice site in Milan follows the same rules: he found me through ChatGPT, and his new pages already appear in its answers.
Staying in those answers takes continuing work, described on the

page.

More people search for daycare website templates than for daycare website design, and for a new home daycare a template, or the builder your childcare software includes, is a sensible start. Lists of the best daycare websites and preschool website examples help too: look past the colors at what the good ones share — ages and hours at the top, real rooms, tuition stated, a tour form that works on a phone.

A template starts to cost more than it saves once you run programs with different schedules, keep a waitlist per age group, need a second language or want the parent login, the payment and the tour form to feel like one site. A custom design is built around those routines on WordPress or Next.js, with an editor your director can use, and the domain and content stay in your name. Rainbow letters and cartoon fonts look cheerful and read badly on a phone; the people deciding are adults weighing money and safety, so the design keeps one or two brand colors, clear type and room for photos of your spaces.

children.text: Why dental clinic websites work differently

Choosing a dentist is a decision made under two competing pressures: urgency and fear. A patient in pain wants an appointment today. A patient considering implants may research for months. The same website has to serve both.
That shapes the structure. The urgent visitor needs the phone number, the address, the opening hours and
a booking option
visible immediately, on a page that loads in a second on mobile

. The deliberate visitor needs depth — who will perform the treatment, what qualifications they hold, what technology the clinic uses, how the procedure actually goes, what it costs, and what happens if something goes wrong.

Local search is where most of this begins. People search for a dentist near them, and the results they see are shaped by structured data about the clinic — address, opening hours, services — that most template sites never implement properly. Getting this right is often the difference between appearing in map results and being invisible in the area you actually serve. That kind of
local SEO work
is usually priced separately from the build itself.

Then there's the treatment structure. A clinic offering implants, orthodontics, prosthetics and hygiene isn't one business in search terms — it's four. Each treatment has its own patients asking their own questions, and each deserves a page answering them. That's also what makes a clinic legible to AI assistants, which increasingly answer questions like "where can I get implants in this city" with a shortlist rather than a page of links.

Finally, there's a constraint most agencies ignore: advertising medical services is legally restricted, and patient images require documented consent. A dental website has to persuade within those limits. Done well, that isn't a handicap — clear, factual, well-structured information builds more trust in this field than promotional language ever does. This is what
website development
