contentBlocks.title: Get a quote for SEO for your flower shop

children.text: I do SEO for florists: the work that makes your flower shop the one people find when they search for same-day flower delivery in your town, a florist near me or wedding flowers for a date next June. Flowers are often bought on short notice, the same day or the day before, so the shop that shows up at that moment gets the order and the one that does not loses it to a national website. There is no account manager in between: I also build websites, so the problems I find in the audit are the ones I fix in the code.
Florist SEO keywords: how people search for flowers and same-day delivery
Flower searches fall into four groups, and each one needs its own kind of page:
delivery — “flower delivery [town]”, “same day flower delivery near me”, “send flowers to [hospital or neighborhood]”
occasion — “birthday flowers delivered today”, “anniversary roses”, “Mother’s Day flowers [town]”
the shop itself — “florist near me”, “flower shop open now”, “florist on [street]”
weddings and events — “wedding florist [city]”, “bridal bouquet prices”, “centerpieces for a company dinner”

Before writing anything I pull search data for your town, the towns around it that you deliver to and the occasions you sell. Delivery searches are usually where wire services and national flower sites compete hardest, while shop and wedding searches are where a local florist wins most easily. The data decides where to start in your market.
Same-day flower delivery pages for the neighborhoods and towns you serve

Someone sending flowers types the recipient’s town, not yours. A shop in one suburb may deliver to eight towns around it, and each of those towns is a separate search. Delivery area pages answer it, but only for places your drivers really reach and only with details that belong to that place:
the delivery fee and the same-day cutoff time for that area
hospitals, senior communities, office parks and venues there, with the rules they set for flower deliveries
photos from real deliveries in that town, without recipients’ faces
how to order for a front desk, a gated community or a business address

Twenty town pages that swap only the town name are treated as doorway pages and filtered out. Eight pages with real local details do more than forty copies, and each new area gets a page only once you deliver there regularly.
Occasion pages for a flower shop: birthdays, anniversaries, Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day

People shop for flowers by occasion far more often than by flower name. Birthday, anniversary, new baby, get well, thank you, Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day, prom and graduation, holiday centerpieces — each has its own searches and deserves its own page. The page shows the arrangements that suit the occasion with prices, the delivery terms and cutoff, and a few lines for the card for people who do not know what to write. Google and AI assistants get a clear answer to “what should I send for…”, with your shop next to it.

Holiday pages keep the same address every year. A Mother’s Day page that is deleted in June and rebuilt in April starts from zero each spring; a page that stays live and is refreshed with the season’s arrangements keeps the links and history it has earned.
Wedding and event florist SEO: real weddings, venue pages and price ranges

Couples look for a wedding florist many months before the date, and event planners book flowers for galas and launches weeks ahead. They search in their own words: “wedding florist [city]”, “boho wedding flowers”, “event florist for a gala”, “how much do wedding flowers cost”. They want to see weddings you have done, not catalog bouquets. Wedding pages that rank are built from your own work:
a page for each real wedding with the venue, the season, the flowers used and the couple’s permission to show the photos
venue pages where you have decorated several weddings, written from experience: load-in times, ceiling heights, what works in that room
a price-range page that explains what moves the budget — guest count, installations, season, imported flowers
Venue pages also attract links from planners and photographers who worked the same day, and for a local shop such links are worth more than any directory listing.
Corporate flower SEO: offices, hotels and restaurants

Weekly lobby arrangements, reception desks, restaurant tables, client gifts, holiday orders for a whole team — business buyers search for “office flower delivery [city]”, “weekly flowers for business” or “corporate flower gifts”. These searches are few, but one account can mean an order every week for years. A business page names the services, how a recurring order is set up, how invoicing works and how fast you handle a last-minute gift for a client. How the account is ordered and paid for is a website task; making the page findable is SEO.
Wire services and order gatherers vs your own flower shop in search

Search for flower delivery with a town name and the top results often include national websites that are not local shops at all. Some are wire services such as FTD and Teleflora, which pass orders through a network of member florists. Others are order gatherers that look like a local shop in search, take the customer’s payment and forward the order to a real florist after keeping a share of it. The customer pays full price, the shop that makes the bouquet receives less, and neither the sender nor the recipient learns your name.

Wire orders can fill quiet days, and many shops keep their membership. SEO wins the orders that do not need a middleman: a site that ranks for your delivery areas, a Google listing with your real name, address and photos, and pages that make clear the order goes straight to the shop that arranges it. Reports separate direct orders from network orders, so you can watch the share move.
Google Maps for florists: Google Business Profile, photos and reviews
“Florist near me” and “flower shop open now” are decided by the map. For a flower shop the profile work is concrete:
“Florist” as the primary category, delivery listed as a service, and hours kept right on holidays, when people check them most
photos of the week’s arrangements, the shop front and the counter, so the listing shows a shop that is open and busy
a review request sent with the delivery confirmation, asking the sender to mention the occasion and the town
your best sellers added as products in the profile, each linked to its page on the site
Map work in more depth — categories, service areas, listings in other directories — is on the
local SEO services
page.
Seasonal SEO for flower shops: Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day and holiday peaks

A florist’s year has a few sharp peaks: Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day, the winter holidays, prom and graduation season, and the wedding months. Searches rise weeks before each date, and a page needs time to be crawled and to climb. The working calendar runs ahead of the sales calendar:
six to eight weeks before a holiday — the holiday page refreshed with this year’s arrangements and prices and linked from the home page and the delivery pages
two to four weeks before — holiday hours, holiday photos and a post with the order deadline in the Google profile
the week itself — cutoffs and sold-out notices written plainly on the page, so search traffic does not turn into disappointed calls
after the peak — the page stays live and the reviews it brought are answered
Quiet months go to new delivery area pages, wedding pages and technical fixes, so the site is stronger before the next peak than it was before the last one.
Florist SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

People now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews things like “which florist in [town] delivers on Sunday”, “what flowers to send for a 50th anniversary” or “how much do wedding flowers cost in [city]”. Those answers are assembled from pages the assistant can read and cross-check; the work of getting into them goes by the names GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization). In a flower shop it comes down to four things:
delivery areas, fees, cutoff times and hours written as plain sentences, not only inside a checkout widget
occasion guides and wedding price ranges answered directly on your pages, signed by the owner or the lead florist
structured data that describes the business as a Florist, with its address, hours and delivery area
one name, address and phone everywhere — site, Google, Yelp, wedding directories — because assistants cross-check listings
I save what assistants say about your shop, and which competitors they suggest, at the start and again later, so the change is visible. More about this work on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Measuring florist SEO in orders, calls and delivery areas

Rankings are a means, not the result. Reports for a flower shop show online orders that came from search, calls and direction requests from the map, which delivery area pages and occasion pages brought them, and how the share of direct orders compares with wire-service orders over the season. Orders come from your shop platform and point-of-sale system, so the numbers match what you see in the till.

children.text: Florist website design is the service I offer flower shops that want to take orders on their own site: I design and build the whole shop myself — the look, the product pages, the delivery rules and the checkout — so one person answers for how it looks and how it sells, at a price fixed in advance. A flower shop site has an unusual job. It sells something perishable and handmade, delivered at a set time to someone who is not the buyer, usually to a customer on a phone who decided a few minutes ago.
Florist website design: what the first screen of a flower shop shows
A visitor to a florist’s site rarely wants a brand story first. The first screen answers four questions:
whether you deliver today and until when — “Same-day delivery in Austin and nearby towns, order by 1 p.m.”, with your own cutoff
where to start — best sellers, shopping by occasion or by price
a call and a text button for people who would rather talk to the shop
the address and hours for those who want to pick up

On phones a fixed bar holds the cart and the call button. The cutoff line changes by itself once the day’s same-day orders close, so nobody orders a “today” bouquet in the evening that cannot be made.
An online flower shop with delivery areas, time windows and cutoff times
Delivery rules are what separates a flower shop from any other web store, and they are where generic templates break. The shop I build knows:
your delivery areas — an address or ZIP code check before checkout, with the fee for each zone
the same-day cutoff, which can differ on weekends, and the dates you do not deliver
the delivery windows you can promise — morning, afternoon or none — and how many orders each window takes
holiday capacity: on Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day a window closes when it is full, instead of taking orders your drivers cannot carry
Pickup in store is an option of its own, with its own hours. All of these rules sit in the CMS, so you change a fee or block a date without calling a developer.
Product photos on a florist website: your arrangements, sizes and substitutions

Catalog photos from a wire service show bouquets your shop may never make, and customers notice when the delivered flowers look different. Product pages sell better with photos of your own arrangements, shot in one consistent way:
the same background, light and angle for every product, so the catalog looks like one shop
each arrangement in two or three sizes, with the size made visible — a vase, a hand, a measurement
a second photo from the side or in its wrapping, because gift buyers care how it arrives

Flowers change with the season, so each product page carries a short substitution note: the florist may replace a stem with one of equal value in the same color palette. Saying this before checkout heads off the calls that begin with “this is not what I ordered”. Images are compressed and served in modern formats, so a catalog of a hundred bouquets still opens quickly on a phone.
A checkout for flower orders: recipient, card message and delivery date
A flower checkout serves two people: the sender who pays and the recipient who opens the door. What the shop needs is collected in a few short steps:
the delivery date first, because it decides what is available and what delivery costs
the recipient’s name, address and phone, with a note field for a front desk, a hospital room or a gate code
the card message with a character limit and a few ready lines for people who cannot find the words
the sender’s details, payment by card, Apple Pay or Google Pay, and an option to stay anonymous

Guest checkout is the default: asking someone to create an account before buying a birthday bouquet loses the order. A confirmation by email or text, and a second message when the flowers are delivered, save the shop a round of “did they arrive?” calls.
Flower subscriptions on a florist website: homes, offices and restaurants

Subscriptions bring steady revenue between holidays. On the site they are a product of their own: weekly, every two weeks or monthly, with a size and a delivery day. Customers pause, skip or cancel online, and payments recur through Stripe or your shop platform, so nobody chases invoices. Offices, hotels and restaurants get a business form for the number of arrangements, the delivery day and the billing contact, and you agree terms before the first delivery.
Wedding and event inquiries on a florist website

Nobody adds a wedding to a cart. The site shows real weddings — venue, season and flowers, published with the couple’s permission — and leads to an inquiry form that asks what you need before the first call:
the date and the venue, so you can check availability at once
the guest and table count, and the pieces they want — bouquets, boutonnieres, centerpieces, arches
a budget range chosen from options rather than typed
an upload for inspiration photos or a link to a Pinterest board

Inquiries reach your inbox in one format, or your CRM if you use one, and a consultation can be booked through a calendar link. Dates you are fully booked can be marked on the form, so couples do not wait for an answer you cannot give.
Florist branding on the website: a calm design that lets the flowers lead

A flower shop site should look like the shop: its palette, its wrapping paper, the lettering on its window. The flowers bring all the color, so the design keeps to a few neutral tones, one accent color for order buttons and type that reads well on a small screen. Large photos lead, text stays short, and seasonal banners never cover the products.

I took the same approach for a Warsaw renovation and property-investment company: a premium site where large photos of finished interiors do the selling and the design stays out of their way. On a florist’s site the arrangements take that place.
Florist website templates, wire-service sites or a custom design

Many florists start with a site from their wire service or a florist platform, or with a Shopify or Squarespace template, and lists of the best florist websites include shops built every way. A template or a florist website builder is a fair start: it takes orders on day one. Its limits appear as the shop grows. The catalog fills with network photos, the delivery settings cannot express your zones and windows, the shop looks like every other one on the platform, and the domain or the customer list may stay with the vendor if you leave. A custom site is built around your delivery rules and your own photos, on WordPress with WooCommerce or on the shop platform you already use, and the code, the domain and the customer data remain yours.

If you already have a site, its rankings survive the move as long as each old product and category URL gets a 301 redirect to its new page; that is how all 468 of Giuseppe’s blog posts moved without a single lost URL. The process is on the
website redesign
page.
A florist website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

When someone asks ChatGPT or Google’s AI Overviews which florist nearby delivers on Sunday or has wedding packages within a budget, the assistant answers from what it can parse on your pages. So delivery areas, fees, cutoff times, hours, product names and prices are written into the HTML as text — not baked into banners or hidden in the cart script — and the shop and its products get Florist and Product structured data. Giuseppe’s site in Milan is built on the same rules, and ChatGPT already cites its new pages.

children.text: Food truck website design is how I help a truck owner put the moving parts of the business — where you park today, what you serve, how to hire you — on one site you update from the phone in the cab. I design and build it myself, so the look and the working schedule come from one person at a price agreed in advance. A truck changes location more often than any other food business, and the site exists to keep up with that.
Food truck website design: today’s location and hours on the first screen
Most visitors arrive with one question: where are you today? The first screen answers it before anything else:
today’s stop — a street corner, a brewery, a business park — with service hours and a button that opens directions
when the stop was last updated, so nobody wonders whether the information is from last week
tomorrow’s stop, for people planning lunch a day ahead
a button for event bookings that stays on screen while the visitor scrolls
On a day off, the same space says so and points to the next stop. A clear “Closed today — back Thursday at Riverside Park” beats an old post that sends people to an empty parking lot.
A food truck schedule and calendar you update from your phone

Most trucks repeat a weekly pattern — Tuesdays at an office park, Fridays at a brewery, weekends at markets — with events in between. The calendar on the site is built the same way: regular stops entered once and repeated, one-off events added on top, and any single date cancelled with one tap when it rains or the generator quits.

Editing happens in a small form made for a phone screen: pick a date, pick a saved location or type a new one, set the hours, save. Each stop has its own address and map pin, and customers can add your week to their own calendar. Breweries and markets you visit often can be listed as partners with a link to their sites, and they tend to share the page in return.
A food truck menu customers can read while standing in line
A truck menu is short and shifts with the event, the season and whatever ran out at noon. On the site it stays text, not a photo of the chalkboard:
eight to fifteen items with prices, one short line each and marks for vegetarian or gluten-free dishes
a sold-out switch you flip during service, so people in line see it before they reach the window
specials for the day or week shown above the regular items
a separate menu for private events where you serve a set selection
A QR code on the side of the truck opens this page directly. Customers read the menu on their own phones while the line moves, and you no longer reprint a board every time a price changes.
Private event and festival booking form on a food truck website
Weddings, birthdays, office lunches and school events often bring in more than a day of street service, and organizers want answers before they call. The booking form asks for what you need to quote:
the event date, start and end time, and the address
the number of guests, and whether guests pay at the window or the host covers a set menu
space and power: where the truck parks, whether there is an outlet or you bring a generator
a budget range or the minimum spend you work with, picked from options

Requests arrive in your inbox in one format. If you take deposits, a confirmed booking ends with a payment link through Stripe Checkout, the same tool Landi Room uses to sell its online course, and the date is marked as taken in the calendar.
What festival organizers and corporate clients look for on a food truck website

Organizers compare several trucks before they choose, and they look for facts that rarely make it onto Instagram. A page for organizers lists the truck’s length and width, its power needs, how many guests you can serve in an hour, your permits and insurance, and photos of the truck set up at real events. Corporate clients also want to know that you send invoices and answer email. Keeping all of this on one page saves a round of questions and shows you are ready for larger bookings.
Instagram, Facebook and the food truck website: what goes where

Many trucks post their location on Instagram or Facebook every morning, and that habit does not have to change. Posts reach people who already follow you. The website holds what strangers search for — the week’s schedule, the menu, the booking form, photos from past events — and it appears in Google for people who have never heard of you. The site links to your profiles and the profiles link back. Social feeds embedded into a page are heavy and break often, so the site shows its own schedule instead of a stream of posts.
A fast food truck website on mobile data at a crowded event

Your customers open the site standing next to the truck, often at a festival where hundreds of phones share one cell tower. A page that takes six seconds to load there is a page nobody sees. So the site is built light: the first screen is text and one compressed photo, fonts are kept to a minimum, there is no autoplay video and no tracking scripts beyond the ones you need. Sasha Dith’s site carries a full video gallery and still loads in under one second; a food truck site has far less to carry.
One-page food truck website or a site with several pages

A single page is often enough at the start: today’s stop, the schedule, the menu, the booking form and links to your profiles in one scroll. Separate pages start to pay off when private events become a large share of revenue, when you run two trucks with different routes, or when you add a commissary kitchen or a market stall. Each of those needs its own address so people can find it in search and share it, and a one-page site can grow into a larger one later without changing its domain.

Food truck website templates, builders and examples

A builder works if you are fine typing your schedule into a text block and receiving booking requests by plain email. The limits show in daily use: someone has to rewrite the schedule every week, the editor is awkward on a phone, and the page grows heavier with every app you add. A custom site gives you a schedule that repeats itself, a sold-out switch and a booking form shaped around your events, and the domain and the code stay yours if you ever change developers.

Questions like “which food trucks are at the waterfront this weekend” or “taco truck for a wedding near Austin” now go to ChatGPT and Google’s AI Overviews as often as to a regular search. children.text: What a driver has to find on a garage website inside a minute

People arrive on a garage website in one of two states: the car is already off the road and it is urgent, or they are planning maintenance and comparing. Either way the decision is quick and runs on the same questions — do you do the specific thing, roughly what does it cost, when can I come in, and who will be working on my car.

A site that answers that in a minute beats a prettier one that makes people hunt. So the structure follows the questions, not the sections agencies default to: «About us», «Why choose us» and «Our advantages» are read last, if at all.
A page for every repair rather than a single services section

The backbone of a garage site is separate pages for the actual work: clutch replacement, transmission repair, diagnostics, wheel alignment, suspension, bodywork, tyres. That serves both the driver, who arrives with one specific problem, and search, which has a different query for each.

Each page answers what gets asked on the phone: what is included, how long it takes, whether the car stays overnight, what moves the price, what warranty applies and what happens if the fault returns. If you specialise in particular makes, those get their own pages — less competition and a more committed customer.
Getting those pages found is a separate job:
SEO for auto repair shops
Prices on the site: a range instead of «call us»
«Call for pricing» loses more customers than a high price does. Somebody with a broken car will not ring five garages to find the ballpark.

The site carries a range and explains what moves it: scope, OEM or aftermarket parts, the condition of neighbouring components that only shows once it is apart. State whether diagnostics is charged and whether it comes off the bill. A price list as an image or a PDF does not work — neither search engines nor AI assistants read text inside pictures.
Online booking: what the form should ask and what it should not
A booking form is not a questionnaire. Every extra field costs you bookings, and the detail comes out in conversation anyway.

Four things are enough: what is wrong, make and year, phone, preferred time. The make matters because it decides whether you will take the job at all. If bookings run through a calendar or a shop management system, the form connects to it so nothing is lost in an inbox.
And the thing most sites forget: say what happens after the form is sent — when somebody will call and what they will ask.
Photographs of your bays instead of stock images

A stock mechanic with perfect teeth reads as «no workshop of our own». Real photographs of the lifts, the equipment, the waiting area and the people who do the work build more trust than any «about us» page.
The same applies to the Google Business Profile: those photos are seen before the site is opened, and often instead of it.
Speed on a phone, in the conditions where the site is actually opened

A garage website gets opened on a phone, outdoors, often on a weak connection and frequently while standing next to a car that will not start. A heavy gallery and a video hero in those conditions mean the visitor leaves before finding the phone number.
So I build on Next.js with light images and without unnecessary scripts, and put the phone number and the booking button where nobody has to scroll to reach them.

children.text: I do SEO for garage door companies: separate pages for repair, new door installation and openers, a Google Business Profile that covers your service area, and the brand and project pages that sell a new door. Garage door SEO serves two very different customers — the homeowner whose door will not open this morning and the one choosing a door that will face the street for years — and a site that treats them as one customer loses both.
Garage door SEO: repair, installation and openers are three different searches
Search data for garage door companies splits cleanly into three groups:
repair — “garage door won’t close”, “broken garage door spring”, “garage door off track”: urgent, local, decided by phone
installation and replacement — “new garage door cost”, “insulated garage doors”, “carriage house garage doors”: researched for weeks and decided after a quote
openers — “garage door opener installation”, “opener light blinking”, “quiet belt drive opener”: somewhere between the two

“Garage door repair” alone is searched hundreds of thousands of times a month in the US, which is why national franchises and lead platforms fight over it. A local company wins the longer, more specific searches in its own towns: a page per problem, a page per door type, a page per opener brand you service.
Broken spring and off-track door pages: garage door repair SEO

A broken torsion spring is the classic urgent call: the door will not lift and the car is stuck inside. Searches are specific — “garage door spring broke”, “spring replacement near me”, “garage door came off track”, “cable snapped” — and each deserves its own page, written for someone reading on a phone in the garage.

The page says in its first lines whether you replace springs the same day and which areas you reach, then explains what the price depends on: spring type, one spring or a pair, whether rollers and cables are replaced too. It also says plainly that torsion springs are under high tension and should not be adjusted by the homeowner. That warning helps the reader, and it is the kind of direct answer search engines and AI assistants pick up.
New garage door installation pages: styles, materials and wind ratings

A new door changes how the house looks from the street, so buyers browse before they ask for a price. They search by style (modern, carriage house, traditional raised panel), by material (steel, wood, aluminum and glass, composite), by insulation and, on the coast, by wind rating. Pages that help them choose include:
one page per style or material, with photos of doors you installed on real houses next to the catalog images
what moves the price — size, insulation, windows, hardware, a new opener — with a range if you are willing to give one
how the job runs: measuring visit, ordering time, removal of the old door, install day
a quote request that asks for the opening size and a photo of the house
In hurricane regions such as Florida and the Gulf Coast, wind-load rated doors and local code approvals deserve a page of their own.
Garage door opener SEO: brands, drive types and smart openers

Opener searches mix repair and sales. Homeowners type the brand printed on the unit — LiftMaster, Chamberlain, Genie — plus the symptom: “remote not working”, “opener makes grinding noise”. Others compare chain, belt and wall-mount openers, or want app control and battery backup; some states, California among them, require battery backup on newly installed residential openers. A page per brand you service and per drive type catches both groups, and each opener repair page links to replacement for units too old to fix.
Manufacturer brand and dealer pages in SEO for garage door companies

Most garage door companies sell doors from a few manufacturers — Clopay, Amarr, Wayne Dalton, C.H.I., Raynor and others — and many appear in those manufacturers’ dealer locators. Two things follow for SEO. A page for each brand you carry, with your own installs, ranks for “[brand] garage door dealer [city]” searches that national sites cover poorly. And the link from a manufacturer’s dealer locator is one of the strongest local links a garage door company can have, so it should point to the right page and use your current business name. Manufacturer specifications can be quoted; descriptions copied whole from the brand’s site rank for nobody.
Commercial garage door SEO: rolling steel doors, dock equipment and service contracts

Warehouses, fire stations, car dealers and storage facilities buy differently. They need rolling steel and commercial sectional doors, high-speed doors, dock levelers and fire doors that require regular inspection. Their searches are few, but each can turn into a maintenance contract that lasts for years. A commercial page lists the door types and equipment you service, planned maintenance and emergency response, insurance, and how a site visit is booked.
Local SEO for garage door companies: Google Business Profile, town pages and reviews
Repair searches end on the map. A garage door company’s profile needs:
the garage door category that matches your main work as primary, and services listed one by one: spring replacement, opener installation, new doors, commercial
the towns you really cover as the service area; a showroom shows its address, a van-only business hides it
photos of installed doors and finished repairs every week or two, named by job and town
a review request sent on the day of the job, asking the customer to mention the door or the repair
Town pages on the site follow the profile: a town gets a page when you have installs and reviews there to show, with the door styles common in its neighborhoods. Map work in more depth is on the
local SEO services
page.
Garage door marketing: Local Services Ads, lead platforms and where SEO fits

“Garage door marketing” usually means a mix of Google Local Services Ads, search ads, lead platforms and SEO, and for garage doors the split between them is fairly clear. Paid leads suit repair calls: urgent, short, won by whoever answers first. New door sales are researched for weeks and compared on photos, reviews and quotes, and that is where pages and galleries on your own site do the selling. Local Services Ads also weigh your reviews when ranking, so the review routine built for SEO helps the ads too. I do the SEO and leave ad accounts to whoever runs them now.
Garage door SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Homeowners ask assistants “how long do garage door springs last”, “belt or chain opener” or “is an insulated garage door worth it”, and AI Overviews answer before anyone clicks. Work on being one of the sources behind those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO), or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a garage door company it needs:
clear answers to repair-or-replace and cost questions on its own pages, with what changes the price
the brands it is a dealer for, its service area, warranty terms and insurance written as plain sentences
structured data for the business, its services and areas
the same company details on Google, Yelp, BBB, Houzz and the manufacturers’ dealer locators
Before the work starts and again after it, I ask the main assistants about your company and compare what they say. Details are on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Choosing a garage door SEO company: questions to ask
Specialist garage door agencies, field service software vendors that bundle websites, and general marketing firms all sell SEO for garage door companies. Questions worth asking any of them:
Will reports show booked repairs and signed door sales from my field service software, or only rankings?
Do you work for another garage door company in my towns?
Will the style and brand pages use my installed doors or stock photos?
Who owns the website, the content and the profile if we stop?
I work alone and also build websites, so the audit and the changes are done by one person. Other trades will find their version on the

children.text: Gym SEO is the work that puts your club in front of people nearby when they search for a gym, a class or a trial pass — in Google’s map pack, in the regular results and in AI assistants — and turns those searches into trial sign-ups and memberships. The work is mine from start to finish — I am one SEO consultant who also builds websites — and I take on independent gyms, boutique studios and small groups of clubs. Most members train within a short drive of home or work, so gym SEO is won neighborhood by neighborhood, not nationally.
What gym SEO covers: “gym near me”, class searches and membership questions

“Gym near me” is one of the most searched phrases in fitness, and Google answers it with a map before any website. Around it sits a long tail that says what the person actually wants. I start with search data for your town and your programs, and it usually falls into four groups:
type and access — “24 hour gym”, “gym with sauna”, “women’s gym”, “powerlifting gym”
classes — “spin class near me”, “kickboxing for beginners”, “hot yoga” plus your town
price and commitment — “gym membership cost”, “gym no contract”, “gym day pass”, “free trial gym”
people and services — “personal trainer at gym”, “kids jiu-jitsu”, “senior fitness classes”

Those searches end in four places: your Google Business Profile, your website, listings such as Yelp and ClassPass, and AI answers. Gym SEO keeps all four consistent and points each search at the page that answers it. Trainers who work for themselves, without a club, have a separate
personal trainer website design
page.
Local SEO for gyms: the map pack and your Google Business Profile
For a local search Google shows three businesses on a map, chosen by relevance, distance and prominence. Your building fixes the distance; relevance and prominence are work:
a primary category that matches what you are — gym, fitness center, boxing gym, yoga studio, Pilates studio — and secondary ones only for what runs every week
hours that match reality: staffed hours in the profile, 24/7 keycard access explained in the description and on the website
services and amenities filled in, from childcare and parking to wheelchair access
new photos of the floor, studios and locker rooms every month, and posts for challenges and schedule changes

Each profile links to the page for that location rather than the home page, with tracking, so calls and direction requests from the map are counted. Citations, categories and map work in more depth are on the
local SEO services
page.
Class and program pages in gym SEO: HIIT, boxing, yoga and functional fitness

One “Classes” page listing twenty formats does not rank for any single one. Every program people search by name gets its own page, written around what a beginner wants to know: what a session looks like, which level it suits, how hard the first week is, what to bring, who coaches it and when it runs. A page for “beginner boxing class” that names your coach, shows your heavy bags and links to Tuesday’s 6 p.m. session beats a national fitness article for someone who lives ten minutes away.

One naming detail: CrossFit is a registered trademark that only licensed affiliates may use. An affiliate can target “CrossFit” plus the town; a gym running similar workouts writes about functional fitness or strength and conditioning, which is also what many people type. How the class page template and the timetable look is a design question, covered on the
gym website design
page.
Membership prices and trial passes: gym SEO for searches right before sign-up

“How much is a gym membership”, “gym no annual fee”, “day pass near me”, “free week pass” — these come from people deciding this week. A club that hides prices behind “stop by for rates” loses many of them to clubs that answer. Gym SEO puts the answers on pages search engines can index:
a membership page with real or “from” prices, enrollment and annual fees, contract length and how to cancel
a trial or intro-offer page that says what the pass includes, how to claim it and whether a tour with a membership advisor is part of it
a day-pass or drop-in page for travelers and people new to the area

Demand follows the calendar: the January peak, a smaller rise in spring before summer and a restart in September. A new page needs weeks to climb, so January pages go live in October or November, not on New Year’s Eve.
Gym SEO for multiple locations: a page and a profile for every club

A club with three addresses and one “Locations” page gives Google one page for three different searches. Every location gets its own page: address, staffed hours, parking, the classes held there, the manager and coaches, photos of that room and its own reviews. Its Google profile links to that page. When clubs differ — one has a pool, another only a floor and a studio — the pages say so, which is exactly what a person choosing between them wants to read.

Pages for nearby neighborhoods without a club help only when they carry facts, such as drive times or classes that fit a lunch break; dozens of copies with the town name swapped are doorway pages that Google filters.
Gym reviews in local SEO: members who mention classes and coaches

Reviews are one of the signals behind the map pack and often the deciding factor between two gyms at the same distance. The most useful ones are specific — the 5:30 a.m. class, a coach’s name, spotless showers, a sign-up without pressure — because their words match what the next person searches for. A routine that fits a gym:
ask after a good moment — a first month completed, a class milestone, a finished challenge — not at the front desk on day one
send the review link by text or through your gym app, with no reward attached, since Google’s rules forbid incentives
reply to every review, including complaints about billing or cancellation, with what was done about it
Instagram vs Google search for gyms: what each channel brings

Many gyms put most of their marketing into Instagram, and it does something search cannot: it shows energy, community and coaches to people who already follow you. Someone who has just moved to the area, or decided today to start training, does not scroll Instagram to find a gym; they search Google or ask an assistant. Search catches existing demand, while a post fades from feeds in days and a class page can rank for years. The two work best linked: the profile link points to the trial page, not the home page, and reels are embedded on the class pages they show.
Competing with Planet Fitness, Anytime Fitness and other franchises in local search

Franchise clubs hold the generic searches through brand strength, a large national site and hundreds of reviews per location. An independent gym rarely outranks them for “gym near me” in every direction, and it does not need to. It wins the searches where it is different: classes the franchise does not run, coaching included in the dues, a turf lane, a recovery room, women-only hours, staff who know members by name. Pages that say this plainly, with prices and real photos, rank for those searches and give a person comparing clubs a reason to pay more.
Gym booking software and SEO: Mindbody, Glofox and schedules Google can read

Most gyms run classes, bookings and billing in software such as Mindbody, Glofox, Wodify or ClubReady. Two things matter for SEO. A schedule loaded inside an iframe or a script is often invisible to search engines and assistants, so the class list and regular class times also need to exist as text on your own pages. And some platforms run a consumer app or marketplace of their own — Mindbody does — where your classes appear next to other studios, so your own pages should be the stronger result for your gym’s name. I check what your setup shows to Google and pass the traffic source into the software, so each sign-up can be traced back to a page.
Gym SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Future members also type questions into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews: “which gyms in Austin have a pool and childcare”, “a beginner-friendly boxing gym near downtown” or “is reformer Pilates good for back pain”. The reply lists a handful of clubs, each with a reason taken from a source the assistant could read. Work on those replies is known as GEO (generative engine optimization) or AEO (answer engine optimization); at a gym it covers four things:
membership types, prices, contract terms, hours and amenities written as text, not only inside a PDF or a booking widget
class pages that answer beginner questions directly, with a named coach as the author
structured data for the business, each location, its opening hours and classes
the same name, address, hours and offers on Google, Yelp, ClassPass and your site, because assistants cross-check sources
Before the work starts and again a few months in, I put the same questions to the assistants and record which gyms they suggest in your place. The method is described on the

page.
Measuring gym SEO in trial sign-ups, memberships and calls

Rankings are a means, not the result. The monthly report shows trial sign-ups, class bookings, calls and new memberships that came from search and the map, by page and by location. Forms and booking links carry the source into your gym software, calls from the profile are tracked, and rankings sit next to these numbers rather than in their place. Pages with visits but no trials get rewritten or merged.

children.text: I do SEO for HVAC companies: the website, the Google Business Profile and the pages that come up when a house is too hot, too cold or the system is twenty years old. HVAC SEO services have an unusual mix to serve — urgent repair calls that must be answered today, expensive replacements that are researched for weeks, and maintenance plans that turn one call into a customer for years.
What HVAC SEO services cover for heating and cooling companies
An HVAC company sells at least three different things, and search treats them differently:
repairs — urgent, local, decided in minutes, mostly from the map and the first few results
replacements and new installs — furnaces, central air, heat pumps, ductless mini-splits; compared by price, efficiency and financing
maintenance — tune-ups and memberships, searched before each season
HVAC SEO builds pages and profile content for each of these, measured in booked calls, not in rankings.
HVAC SEO keywords: emergency repair, replacement and maintenance searches

People rarely search for “HVAC”. They describe the symptom: “AC not cooling”, “furnace not working”, “heat pump blowing cold air”, “AC repair near me”, often at night or on a weekend. Before writing anything I pull the search data for your towns and group it:
symptom searches that need a short, fast page with the phone number at the top
service searches like “furnace repair” or “ductless AC installation”
cost and comparison searches: “heat pump vs furnace”, “AC replacement cost”
maintenance searches: “AC tune-up”, “furnace maintenance before winter”
Pages for 24/7 emergency HVAC calls

An emergency page is read on a phone by someone who is cold or overheated. It has to load in under 2.5 seconds, show whether you are open now, say how fast a technician can come and offer a call button before anything else. Long texts go lower on the page, for search engines and for the visitor who wants to check you first.
Heating and cooling season peaks in SEO for HVAC companies

HVAC demand swings twice a year. The first heat wave sends “AC repair” searches up within a day; the first cold night does the same for furnaces. Pages need weeks to rank, so SEO for HVAC companies works one season ahead: cooling pages are updated in late winter, heating pages in late summer. The quiet shoulder months are when replacement and heat pump content is written, because homeowners plan those purchases when nothing is broken.

The profile follows the same calendar: posts about AC tune-ups in spring, furnace checks in late summer, extended hours during a heat wave or a cold snap, and photos of the season’s installs. In mild climates, where cooling runs most of the year, the plan leans on air conditioning and heat pumps instead.
Maintenance plans and memberships in HVAC contractor SEO

A maintenance membership is worth more to an HVAC business than a single repair: it brings visits twice a year, priority for members in a heat wave and the first call when the system needs replacing. HVAC contractor SEO gives the plan its own page with what each visit includes, the price, the member benefits and an online sign-up. Searches like “AC tune-up near me” in spring and “furnace inspection” in the fall lead to this page, not to the generic home page.
Replacement installs, heat pumps and rebates: SEO for HVAC contractors who sell systems
System replacements are where most HVAC revenue sits, and the buyers research before they call. SEO for HVAC contractors who sell systems means pages that answer their questions:
repair or replace: age of the system, repair costs, efficiency
heat pumps: how they work in your climate, cold-climate models, dual-fuel set-ups
efficiency ratings, utility rebates and tax incentives available in your area, kept up to date
financing options and what an in-home estimate includes
Rebate and incentive programs change often, so these pages carry a date and a link to the official source rather than promises.
Manufacturer dealer pages as part of an HVAC SEO service

children.text: I design websites for HVAC companies and build them myself, so design and build come from one person at one price. HVAC website design decides what a homeowner in a too-hot or too-cold house sees on a phone, and what they do next: call for a repair, ask for a replacement estimate or join a maintenance plan. Layout, photos and wording are chosen for those three actions and nothing else.
Website design for HVAC: a seasonal home page for heating in winter and cooling in summer

HVAC is the trade where the right first screen changes with the weather. In winter the hero shows one of your furnace or heat pump jobs and leads with “No heat? A technician today”. In summer it shows an outdoor unit and leads with AC repair. In spring and fall it turns to tune-ups and planned replacements, when nothing is broken and homeowners have time to compare.

Each season is designed as a complete set — photo, headline, the two main buttons, the featured services and the current offer — so a change of season changes the whole first screen, not a single picture. Warm and cool tones can mark heating and cooling inside the hero, but the call button keeps one color all year, so a returning customer finds it where it was.
How the seasons are scheduled and switched in the admin panel is covered on the
HVAC websites
page.
Emergency repair or planned replacement: two paths in HVAC website design

The repair visitor is uncomfortable now and wants a time, not a brochure. The replacement visitor is about to spend several thousand on a system that will run for fifteen years or more, and has two other quotes open in other tabs. Right under the hero, the home page splits into two doors with different labels and different weight:
“Need a repair today” — a large call button, today’s availability, nothing to fill in
“Planning a new system” — a quieter button to request an in-home estimate, leading to replacement, heat pump and ductless pages

The replacement pages are longer and calmer: equipment options set out as good, better and best, what the estimate visit includes, how long installation takes, financing and current rebates. The repair pages are short and end at the phone.
Mobile-first HVAC website design for a homeowner at the thermostat
HVAC visitors often hold the phone in one hand while standing at the thermostat, in a basement next to the furnace or in the yard beside the outdoor unit. The layouts are tested for those places:
a call bar fixed at the bottom of the screen, within reach of the thumb
text size and contrast that stay readable in bright sun outside and in a dim utility room
a request form that invites a photo of the unit’s data plate or the error code on the thermostat, so the technician brings the right parts
no pop-ups, chat bubbles or cookie walls over the call button
Desktop layouts are adapted from the phone versions, not the other way round.
Presenting maintenance plans and memberships in HVAC website design
A maintenance plan sells when a visitor can compare the options in a few seconds. The plan page is a short table:
two or three tiers, with names that say what they cover, such as one system or the whole home
the price shown the way you bill it, per month or per year, never both mixed
what each tier includes: tune-ups a year, priority scheduling, repair discounts, waived after-hours fees — whatever your plan really offers
one sign-up button under each tier

Elsewhere on the site the plan shows up where it makes sense: a member price next to the regular one on repair pages, a short invitation after a booking, a line on the summer and winter hero. The plan becomes a habit of the page, not a menu item.
Showing financing and a payment calculator on an HVAC website

For a replacement customer the monthly payment often matters more than the total. Financing is shown where the price question comes up — on replacement, heat pump and ductless pages — rather than only on its own page:
a line under each price range saying financing is available, with a link to the terms
a simple calculator: choose a system range, see an indicative monthly payment, with the conditions your financing partner requires right beside it
a button to check eligibility that opens your partner’s application
Rates and terms are never invented in the design. They come from your financing partner and change when theirs do.
Trust signals in HVAC website design: licensed, NATE-certified technicians, warranties and reviews

An HVAC technician works inside the house and often recommends an expensive purchase. Visitors look for reasons to believe that advice. The design places those reasons next to the buttons that ask for a decision, not in the footer:
license and insurance, written out so they can be checked
certifications your technicians really hold, such as NATE, and manufacturer dealer status if you have it
warranties in plain words: the manufacturer’s parts warranty, your labor warranty and whether the equipment needs registering
reviews that name the technician and the job, on the matching service page
a satisfaction guarantee only if you offer one
Real technicians and trucks instead of stock photos on an HVAC website

Stock HVAC photos are easy to spot: a model in a spotless uniform pointing a screwdriver at a unit that has never been connected. Homeowners want to see who will come to the door and how the finished job will look. The design is built around your own photos:
portraits of your technicians, so the customer recognizes the person who arrives
your trucks with the logo — the same trucks neighbors see in the street
finished installs: a level condenser pad, tidy line sets, a clean furnace and duct connection
the old system next to the new one on replacement pages
A recent phone takes good enough pictures; light and a tidy background matter more than the camera. Before the design starts I list the shots each page needs.

Searches for HVAC website design examples and ideas lead to Dribbble shots and agency galleries. They help with type and color, but many are concept screens that never took a real call. Across HVAC company sites that do bring work, the ideas worth borrowing are plain:

HVAC website templates and HVAC company website templates promise a finished site in a weekend. They are designed for the demo: one hero, a grid of service icons, a contact form and a stock technician. With real content the gaps show — no seasonal versions of the first screen, no separate repair and replacement paths, no plan comparison, financing pushed into the footer.

A template is a reasonable start for a new one-truck company. A custom design pays off once you sell replacements and memberships, or pay for ads that send visitors to the site. Leaving a template later usually means designing again from the start.

Homeowners now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to compare HVAC companies nearby or explain whether a heat pump suits their house. Assistants read text, not pictures. A new system is a large purchase, and many buyers decide on the monthly payment. The financing page explains the plans you offer through your financing partner, in the partner’s own terms, and links to its online application, so a customer can apply before the estimate visit.

Rebates change more often than anything else on an HVAC site: utility programs open and close, federal and state incentives are revised. Area pages are generated from one template and a short entry per town, so when a new technician lets you cover another suburb, adding it takes minutes.

children.text: Hair salon website design is the work I do for salon and barbershop owners who want new clients to see the stylists, understand the price list and book a chair without sending three DMs first. I plan, design and build the site myself, connect it to the booking software you already pay for and hand it over with an editor your front desk can use. The goal is that a client who finds you on a phone ends up in your calendar, not in a list of competitors.
Do I need a hair salon website if I already have Booksy or Vagaro?

It is the first question most owners ask, and the answer depends on where your new clients come from. Booking apps such as Booksy, Vagaro and Fresha are very good at taking appointments, sending reminders and holding deposits. Their public profile, though, is a page inside someone else’s marketplace: the layout is fixed, the text fields are short, and the same screen often suggests other salons nearby.
If your book is full of regulars and referrals, the app profile plus Instagram can be enough for now. A website starts to pay off when you want to:
be found in Google for services, not only for the salon’s name — “curly haircut Denver”, “blonde specialist”, “skin fade near me”
explain prices and policies in more words than an app field allows
show each stylist’s work under their own name
sell something beyond appointments: courses, products, gift cards
The site does not replace the app. Every Book button opens your existing calendar, so the front desk keeps one schedule.
Hair salon price list on the website: by service, hair length and stylist level

A price that only says “from” makes a new client guess, and a guess often ends with them choosing a salon that shows a number. Hair pricing is complicated for real reasons — length, density, the color already in the hair and who holds the scissors — so the price list shows that structure instead of hiding it:
services grouped the way clients think: cuts, color, blonding, treatments, styling, extensions
a small table per service with columns for short, medium and long hair
a second axis for stylist level where your prices differ — junior, senior, creative director
the appointment length next to the price, so a client knows full highlights take an afternoon
one line on what changes the final price, and a consultation button for color corrections and big changes

The table lives in the CMS as text. When you raise prices in January, you change the numbers in one place and every page that shows them updates; search engines and AI assistants read the same numbers your clients see.
Stylist and barber pages on a hair salon website

Many clients follow a person, not a brand. A page for each stylist or barber keeps that loyalty inside your salon’s site: a real photo, years behind the chair, what they love doing (lived-in blondes, textured hair, precision bobs, beard work), the days they work, the languages they speak and a Book with… button that opens the app with that stylist already chosen, where the app allows it.

Stylists can get their own login, limited to their page and gallery, so updating a portfolio does not have to go through the owner. When someone leaves, their page is taken down and its address redirected to the team page instead of showing an error.
Hair salon booking website: connecting Booksy, Fresha or Vagaro

A hair salon booking website works when the jump from reading to booking is one tap. How that tap is built depends on your software: most systems give you a public booking link, and many also offer a button script or an embeddable widget. Before quoting, I look at your account and choose what fits:
a direct link per service and per stylist, so the client lands on the right step
a widget that loads only after a tap, so it does not slow the page down
a Book button fixed to the bottom of every phone screen
a short line under the button on deposits and cancellations, so the policy is read before card details are asked for

Marketplace fees and new-client rules differ between apps and change over time, so we check your current terms together. The aim is that clients who arrive through your own site book with you directly.
Hair color gallery and before-and-after photos on a salon website

Color work sells itself in pictures, yet a gallery of two hundred random shots helps nobody. On the site, the gallery is filtered by service — balayage, copper, gray blending, curly cuts, men’s cuts — and by stylist, so a client who wants a soft blonde sees soft blondes and who made them. Before-and-after pairs are shot in the same light and at the same angle where possible, and published with the client’s agreement.

Photos arrive from phones in large sizes. The CMS crops and compresses them on upload and loads them as the client scrolls, so a gallery page with sixty images still opens quickly on mobile data. Your Instagram feed can sit at the bottom of the page, but the main gallery stays on your site, where it is tagged and does not depend on a feed algorithm.
Barbershop website design: walk-ins, wait times and a men’s grooming menu
A barbershop runs on a different rhythm: shorter services, fewer price lines, regulars every three weeks and plenty of people who just walk in. The website follows that rhythm:
“walk-ins welcome” or “appointments only” on the first screen, next to today’s hours
a live queue or wait-time widget, where your barbershop software offers one
a short menu: haircut, skin fade, beard trim, hot towel shave, kids’ cut, combo
each barber’s style in four or five photos, not forty
a direct, plain look for a mostly male audience that wants the price and the next free slot
Many shops are best served by one fast page the owner edits himself. A second location or a growing team adds pages later, without a rebuild.
Selling hair courses and products from a hair salon website

Some salons earn as much from teaching as from the chair. Landi Room, a beauty salon in Warsaw, sells an online course in nanoplasty, a hair-smoothing treatment. I designed and built its landing page on Next.js with Sanity: payment through Stripe Checkout, then a unique video link sent automatically, valid for 14 days and not downloadable. Its first Google Ads campaign sold more than 100 places on the course, and no access link has been passed on without permission.

The same setup works for a balayage class for other stylists, a home-care lesson for clients or a short list of the shampoos and treatments you use at the station, sold for pickup at the salon. A course or product page becomes a section of your site rather than a separate platform with its own monthly fee.
Hair salon website templates vs a custom hair salon website

“Hair salon website template” is searched more than any other phrase in this niche, and for a good reason: a template is cheap and fast. A one-chair studio with a booking link and a steady Instagram following can start on one and be fine — and if that describes your salon, my reply will say so.

Templates start to cost you as the salon grows. Stylist pages, price tables by length and level, filtered galleries and course sales each become a plugin or a paid upgrade, and the result looks like hundreds of other salons on the same theme. A custom site is built around your price list and your team from day one, belongs to you, and keeps working if you switch booking software.
What the best hair salon websites do on a phone
Lists of the best hair salon websites tend to praise big videos and unusual fonts. Opened on a phone, the sites that actually fill chairs share plainer habits:
the salon’s specialty and neighborhood in one line at the top
a Book button that never leaves the screen
prices a client can read without zooming
real photos of the team and the space
an address that opens straight in maps
pages that load before the client gives up on a bus
Hair salon SEO: Google Maps, “hair salon near me” and service pages

Most new clients type “hair salon near me” or a service plus a neighborhood and pick from the map. The site supports that from launch: the same name, address, phone and hours as your Google Business Profile, a page for each service you want more of, a page per location and structured data describing the salon, its services and its opening hours.
The ongoing ranking work — the Google profile, reviews, local links and keyword research — is described on my

Clients now ask ChatGPT or read Google’s AI Overviews with questions like “a salon in Austin that is good with curly hair” or “a barber open on Sunday in Queens”. An assistant can only recommend a salon whose facts it can read. So services, stylists and their specialties, prices, hours and walk-in rules are written as text in the page code, delivered by the server rather than drawn by scripts after loading, and repeated in structured data that matches your Google listing.

children.text: Handyman website design is what I do for owner-operators and small handyman teams: I plan the site, design it and build it myself, so one person answers for all of it at one price. A handyman services website has a specific job. It has to sell many small tasks at once, tell a stranger what a visit will roughly cost, and collect enough detail that you can say yes, no or “send me a photo” without a twenty-minute phone call.
Handyman website design for a one-person business

When the business is you and a truck, nobody sits by the phone. You are on a ladder, under a sink or driving between jobs, and every call you miss goes to the next number on the list. The website covers the hours you cannot:
it answers the questions you hear ten times a week — do you hang TVs, do you do small jobs, what is the minimum
it turns a vague “I need some things fixed” into a request with a job type, an address and photos
it offers a text button next to the call button, so a customer can write while you are working and you reply at lunch
it shows one face, yours, because people hire a handyman as a person, not as a brand
A small team needs the same base, plus a line on who comes to the door and how jobs are assigned.
A handyman job list with “from” prices

The page most visitors open first is the list of jobs. A handyman sells dozens of tasks that customers do not group the way you do, so the list is written in their words and sorted by room or by problem:
mounting and hanging: TVs, shelves, curtain rods, mirrors, pictures
doors and windows: sticking doors, new locks and handles, screens, weatherstripping
plumbing fixes within your license: faucets, toilet parts, caulking around tubs
walls and ceilings: drywall patches, touch-up painting, ceiling fans where allowed
assembly and odd jobs: furniture, grab bars, baby-proofing, small repairs before a sale
How to write “from” prices on a handyman website

A starting price next to each job saves both sides time. It filters out the person who expected a two-hour job to cost the price of a coffee and tells everyone else that you are not going to surprise them. The design gives each price a short note on what is included and what raises it: height, wall type, parts you bring. If you charge a minimum visit or a trip fee, it is written once, near the top, in the same size as everything else. Hourly pricing works as well; the page then shows the rate and a typical time for common jobs.
Photo uploads in a handyman request form
Most handyman jobs can be priced, or at least sorted, from two or three photos. The request form is built around that:
The customer picks a job type from your list, or “several small jobs”.
They enter a ZIP code; the form says at once whether you cover it.
They add photos from the phone camera — the form shrinks them so the upload does not fail on mobile data.
They describe the job in a sentence and pick two or three possible days.

The request arrives by email and as a text, or goes straight into Jobber or Housecall Pro if you use one. You see the cracked tile or the bent track before you call back, and you can quote, ask for one more angle or decline in a minute. Photos of a home’s interior are personal, so the form says what happens to them, and they are kept only as long as you need them for the job.
Trust signals for a handyman who works inside customers’ homes

A handyman is usually a stranger who comes into the house, often while one person is home alone. Before they book, customers look for reasons to feel safe. The design puts those reasons next to the buttons, not on a page nobody opens:
your photo and first name, and the same for anyone else who might come
liability insurance, and a license where your state or city requires one for the work you do — stated as text so it can be checked
a background check, if you have done one, with who ran it
reviews that name the job and the neighborhood, pulled from your Google profile
a short “what a visit looks like” section: you call when you are on the way, wear shoe covers, clean up, and take payment by card or app
Licensing rules for handyman work differ widely between states and countries, so the wording follows what applies to you and nothing more. A badge you do not hold costs more trust than it earns.
Handyman service area on the website and a ZIP code check

Most handymen work from home and drive to customers, so the service area is the address. It is shown in two ways: a simple map for people who think visually, and a list of towns and ZIP codes as text for everyone else and for search engines. The request form checks the ZIP code before the customer writes anything, so people outside your area are told politely, before they spend five minutes describing the job. If you go further for a higher trip fee, the form says so instead of refusing.
Handyman website templates, Jobber and Housecall Pro sites, or your own website

Field-service tools such as Jobber and Housecall Pro offer a website as part of the subscription, and site builders sell handyman website templates. For someone starting out, either is a fair choice: it is online in a weekend and the booking link works.
The limits show up as the business grows:
one page for all jobs, so nobody finds you for “TV mounting” or “drywall repair” in your town
little control over titles, page addresses and structured data
a site that lives on the platform, so if you cancel the subscription it disappears
templates built for demo photos, not for a long list of jobs with prices
An own site does not mean dropping the tools. Your Jobber or Housecall Pro request and booking forms can sit inside it, styled to match, while the pages, the domain and the content belong to you.
What the best handyman websites have in common
Searches for the best handyman website and for handyman website examples turn up galleries of polished screens. The ones that bring jobs share a few plain habits rather than a look:
the first screen says what you do and where, with a phone number and a text button
real photos — you, your truck, finished jobs — and no stock carpenter with a perfect smile
a job list with prices or ranges, not a paragraph about quality and passion
a service area stated in towns, not “and surrounding areas”
reviews close to the buttons, with dates
Color, fonts and logo come after that. On a phone, the site is judged in a few seconds on whether the customer’s job is on the list and how to reach you.
Local SEO for a handyman website: being found for “handyman near me”

People rarely search for a handyman by name. They type “handyman near me”, or the job itself — “TV mounting”, “fix sticking door” — and choose from the map. A handyman usually has no storefront, so the Google Business Profile is set up as a service-area business: home address hidden, towns listed, the Handyman category and the same job list as on the website. The site supports it with a page for each main type of job, consistent name, phone and area across directories, and reviews that mention the work.
Town pages are added only for places you really drive to, each with jobs done there. The setup is part of the full site; ongoing work on the map and search results is described on the

page.
A handyman website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Some customers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews who can fix a door or hang a heavy mirror nearby. These assistants recommend businesses they can read about. A site that shows its jobs, prices, service area and insurance as images or inside a booking widget gives them nothing; the same facts written as text, with structured data describing the business and its services, can be read and quoted.
