children.text: I do healthcare SEO for hospitals, health systems, multi-site clinic groups, urgent care networks, diagnostic labs and telehealth companies: provider directories, location and service-line pages, medically reviewed content, schema and the technical work on large websites. I am a single specialist, not an agency, so I take a defined piece of work — an audit, one section of the site, a migration plan — or work alongside your in-house marketing and web team.
What healthcare SEO covers for hospitals, health systems and clinic networks

A health system website can hold thousands of pages: a profile for every physician, a page for every hospital, clinic, urgent care center and imaging site, service lines, a condition library and the patient portal. Most of the search demand that brings patients lands on four types of page:
provider profiles — searches for a physician’s name, or for a specialty with a town
location pages — “urgent care near me”, “hospital in [town]”, “MRI near me”
service-line pages — “cardiologist in [city]”, “knee replacement surgery”, “maternity hospital”
condition and treatment content — “what causes atrial fibrillation”, “recovery after hip replacement”

Each type has its own template and its own owner inside the organization. Healthcare SEO services at this size are mostly about getting those templates right once, so that one fix applies to hundreds of pages. Telehealth companies add a fifth type: pages for each state or country where their clinicians are licensed, because that is how patients search for online care.
Provider directory SEO: “find a doctor” pages that rank for physician names

Patients search for doctors by name to check a referral, find a phone number or read reviews before a visit. On those searches the organization’s own profile often ranks below Healthgrades, WebMD, Vitals or Zocdoc, because it is thin: a name, a photo and a specialty from the credentialing database. A provider profile that can rank includes:
full name with credentials, specialty and subspecialties, board certifications
every location where the physician sees patients, linked to those location pages
languages spoken, whether they accept new patients, and the insurance plans accepted
training and the conditions treated, written as text, not only as filter tags
a direct path to booking or to the phone number of the right office

The directory search is the other half. Filters by specialty, location, language and insurance can create millions of URL combinations that waste crawling and produce near-duplicate pages. I map which filtered pages deserve to be indexed — “cardiologists in [town]” usually does, a page for Spanish-speaking cardiologists accepting one plan on Tuesdays does not — and how the rest should be handled.
Location pages at scale for hospitals, urgent care networks and clinic groups

A clinic group with forty sites or an urgent care network with a hundred needs a page for each location, and those pages have to differ in substance, not only in the address. What separates a location page that ranks from a template copy is the information patients use: hours, including holidays; services available at that site; the providers who work there; parking and public transport; accepted insurance. For urgent care, whether walk-ins are accepted and how to check in online. For a lab or imaging network, the tests offered at that site and how to prepare for them.

Each location page connects to its own Google Business Profile listing with the same name, address, phone and hours. After mergers and moves, large organizations often have duplicate or outdated listings; cleaning them up is usually the fastest local SEO for healthcare win, because the map decides most “near me” searches.
Service-line pages in healthcare SEO: cardiology, orthopedics and maternity

Service lines compete with other systems, specialty groups and national centers. A service-line section works best as a small hub: an overview, pages for the main procedures and programs, and links to the physicians and locations of that line.
Orthopedics and joint replacement pages
Patients compare hospitals for hip and knee replacement weeks in advance. They look for the surgeon, the approach used, the expected length of stay and the rehabilitation program.
Cardiology and heart care pages
A mix of urgent and planned searches, from chest pain to “cardiac rehab near me”. The pages have to send urgent cases to emergency care at once and still answer the planned-care questions.
Maternity pages
Expecting parents choose a hospital months ahead and search for tours, birthing options and which obstetricians deliver there.
Condition and treatment content under YMYL: medical review and E-E-A-T

Google treats health content as “Your Money or Your Life” and holds it to a higher standard of experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust (E-E-A-T). A hospital has what smaller publishers lack — real clinicians — and the pages only have to show it:
a named clinician who wrote or reviewed the page, with credentials and a link to their profile
a publication date, a “last reviewed” date and a review schedule that someone owns
content tied to the care the organization provides, with a path to the right specialist or location
no claims beyond what the clinical team signs off on, and a clear note that the page is not individual medical advice

Licensed health libraries with thousands of generic articles rarely rank, because the same text sits on hundreds of other sites. Fewer original pages on conditions the system treats in volume, reviewed by its own specialists, do better.
Schema markup for healthcare organizations, hospitals, physicians and clinics

Structured data tells search engines and AI assistants what each page describes. Schema.org has types for this — MedicalOrganization and Hospital for the organization and its facilities, MedicalClinic for outpatient sites, Physician for provider profiles — with properties for specialty, address, hours and the link between a doctor and the places where they practice. On a large site the markup should come from the same data as the visible page, so it stays correct when a physician leaves. Schema does not guarantee rich results; it removes guessing.
Technical SEO for large healthcare websites and site migrations

Hospital websites usually run on enterprise CMS platforms such as Sitecore, Drupal or Adobe Experience Manager, with the directory, the location finder and the patient portal often served by separate systems. Most technical problems come from the joins:
directory and location pages rendered by JavaScript that search engines read late or incompletely
the same physician available under several URLs from different systems
old campaign pages, PDFs and microsites of acquired hospitals still indexed
slow templates on pages patients open on a phone

Migrations need their own plan. Mergers, rebrands and CMS moves are common in healthcare, and a migration that breaks provider and location URLs can cost a long time in search. The plan covers the URL inventory, a redirect map for every profile and location, template and markup changes, a check on staging and monitoring after launch.
HIPAA, tracking pixels and analytics in healthcare SEO

In the US, measuring SEO on a healthcare website has a privacy side. Tracking pixels and analytics tags on pages where patients read about conditions, book appointments or log in to a portal can pass health-related information to third parties, and this has drawn regulator guidance and lawsuits. Forms that collect health information can fall under HIPAA, which usually means using vendors that sign a business associate agreement, or keeping clinical details off the form.

I measure SEO with the tools your privacy team has approved and flag tags found on sensitive pages during the audit. I do not give legal opinions; that stays with your privacy officer and counsel. In the EU, GDPR treats health data as a special category, and the principle is the same: collect less.
Healthcare SEO approval workflows with compliance, legal and clinical reviewers
In healthcare the slow part is the approval. A change to a service-line page can pass through marketing, a clinical reviewer, compliance, legal and brand. To keep SEO work moving I:
separate technical changes — titles, redirects, markup, internal links — from changes to clinical wording, so the first group does not wait for medical review
write content briefs that reviewers can approve in one pass: the search data, the questions to answer and the claims that need sign-off
agree page templates with compliance once, so new location and provider pages follow an approved pattern
keep a change log that shows what was changed, when and why
Healthcare SEO for ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Patients now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which hospital is good for a knee replacement, which urgent care is open now, or whether a doctor takes their insurance. The answers draw on what assistants can read and cross-check: your pages, Google listings, directories such as Healthgrades, and news. Getting into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a healthcare organization it means:
provider, location and service-line facts written as plain, current text, not only inside filters and widgets
the same names, addresses and specialties on the website, the listings and the directories
structured data that connects physicians, locations and the organization
condition pages with named clinical reviewers, which assistants treat as more reliable sources
I check how assistants describe the organization, its locations and its main service lines before and after the work. More on the

A builder’s website is not visited once. A family returns to it for months — after a drive through a community, after a talk with a lender, before each weekend of model tours — and every visit should bring them one step closer to a contract.
Home builder website design: what buyers look for on the first screen
On a phone, before any scrolling, the first screen answers four questions:
where you build — towns, counties or communities, named
what you build — custom homes on the buyer’s land, homes in your communities, or both
the price level — “from the low 400s” or a range for custom work, if you publish one
the next step — browse communities, see plans, or start a custom build conversation
A full-screen video of a finished kitchen at sunset looks good in a pitch and pushes all four answers off the screen. It belongs further down, on project and model pages.
Custom home builder websites and production builder websites: different structures
Custom home builder websites

The custom buyer is choosing a team for a project of a year or more. The site is organized around trust: finished projects with their stories, the build process, the people who run the job, the architects and designers you work with, and how pricing works. Proof that you finish what you start matters more than lots and plans.
Production and semi-custom builder websites

The production buyer is choosing a place and a plan. The site works as a catalog: communities, floor plans and move-in-ready homes, all linked to each other, with filters by area, price, size and bedrooms. The design job is making a large catalog easy to browse on a phone. Builders who do both get two clear entry points on the home page, so a custom client never lands in an inventory list.
Community pages and interactive lot maps in home builder website design

The community page is where a buyer decides whether to drive out. Its center is the site plan: homesites marked available, reserved, sold or under construction, and a tap on a lot shows its size, orientation, lot premium and the plans that fit. On a phone a detailed site plan is hard to tap, so a list view sits next to it — lot number, size, status and price, sortable.

Status changes weekly, so your sales team updates it in the admin panel, or it comes from the lot inventory tool you already use if that tool offers an export. Around the map: the location and drive times, amenities open today, HOA dues, the plans offered, and the sales office hours with a tour button.
Floor plan pages on a home builder website: elevations, options and comparison
Plan pages get the most repeat visits on a builder site. Buyers print them, send them to a parent and put two side by side. Each plan gets:
a large plan image that zooms, with room dimensions, and a printable version
elevations as a switch on the same page, not as separate pages
the main options — extra bedroom, extended patio, third garage bay — shown on the drawing where possible, or listed with pictures
the key numbers in a fixed block: square feet, beds, baths, garage, stories
a compare button that keeps the buyer’s shortlist on their device
every community that offers the plan, with its starting price there
Model homes and quick move-in homes on a builder website your sales team can update

Models and finished or nearly finished spec homes bring buyers in this month. Each appears as a card: photo, lot or address, plan, completion month, a status label — under construction, ready in June, move-in ready, sold — and a button to book a tour. Your sales team changes status and price in a short form, without waiting for a developer. When a home closes, it leaves every list and its page offers similar homes instead of an error.
Project galleries, video and 3D tours on a custom home builder website
For a custom builder the gallery is the sales pitch, and it works when each project is a page, not a pile of photos:
a professional shoot of the finished home, inside and out, in one style across all projects
a few lines on the brief, the lot, the architect if there was one, the size and the build time
construction-stage photos for buyers who want to see what sits behind the drywall
a 3D tour or video walk-through that starts on tap, so the page stays light
a quote from the owners, with their name, if they agreed to it
A build process page for home builders: steps, timeline and what the price includes

Custom and semi-custom buyers fear two things: the budget growing and the schedule slipping. A process page answers both before the first meeting. It shows the steps with typical durations — design and selections, permits, site work, foundation, framing, mechanicals, finishes, final walkthrough — and separates what the base price includes from what counts as an upgrade. Selections at the design center get a short section of their own, because that is where budgets usually move.
Lead forms for a long buying cycle: interest lists, tour bookings and your CRM
Few buyers want to talk on the first visit, so every stage gets a step that fits it:
an interest list for each community, for lot releases and price news — one email field, community already selected
model tour booking with the times the sales office is open
a custom build inquiry that asks about the lot, the size and the timing, and nothing more at first
call and text buttons for those who would rather talk now

Each lead reaches your CRM — HubSpot, Salesforce, Lasso, BuildBook or whatever your sales team works in — with the community and plan attached. How it gets there depends on your plan with that CRM, so I confirm the connection method before giving a price.
Financing, incentives and warranty on a home builder website

Many builders work with a preferred lender and run incentives — help with closing costs, rate buy-downs — that change by month and by community. The design gives them a fixed place: a slim banner on community and inventory pages with an end date and a link to the conditions, and the lender’s own wording and disclosures for anything about rates. The warranty — a one-, two- and ten-year structure, or whatever you offer — has its own page and a one-line summary near the contact buttons.

Lists of the best home builder websites mix national builders with small custom shops. Set the budgets aside and the patterns repeat:
real photos of finished homes, with renderings only for what is not built yet
communities, plans and available homes linked within two taps
prices or price ranges shown, not hidden behind a form
a clear path for a custom build next to the catalog
pages that stay fast on a phone despite heavy imagery
Inspiration galleries show home pages; open a plan page and a community page too. That is where a buyer decides to book a tour.

A buyer can ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to “compare new home builders near Boise” or “find single-story new homes near Raleigh with a big lot”. An assistant can suggest only what it can read. The design keeps community names, locations, price ranges, plan specifications, warranty terms and years in business as page text, not inside renderings, PDFs or map widgets, with structured data describing the company, its offices and the homes for sale. Prices and availability carry the date they were last checked.

children.text: Hotel SEO services are the work that puts a hotel’s own website in front of travelers who search for a place to stay in your destination, and turns those visits into direct bookings instead of commission paid to an OTA. I do it myself, as a single SEO specialist who also builds websites, and I report on bookings that came through your own booking engine from search.
What is SEO in hotels: how an independent hotel gets found and booked through Google
SEO in hotels, or SEO for the hotel industry, means making your website and Google presence the place where a guest finishes the booking. A guest usually touches search several times:
choosing the area — “hotel near the convention center”, “quiet hotel in the old town with parking”, “family hotel by the lake” — often on a phone, weeks before the trip
comparing rates and reviews on Google Hotels, Booking.com or TripAdvisor
checking the hotel by name, which is the moment that decides whether the booking goes through your engine or through an OTA
“Hotels in [city]” is filled with OTAs, metasearch sites and chains. Independent and boutique hotels win on longer searches that describe what a guest wants, and on their own name.
Hotel SEO and OTAs: why Booking.com outranks your own hotel website for your name

Search the name of almost any independent hotel and Booking.com, Expedia or TripAdvisor often appear above the hotel’s own site. OTAs have very strong domains, and in many markets they also bid on hotel names in paid search. Each booking that goes that way carries a commission — typically 15–25% for hotels on major OTAs, depending on the contract — for a guest who was already looking for you.
SEO will not remove OTAs, and most hotels still need them. What it can do is win the brand search:
a home page whose title, text and structured data clearly belong to the hotel, with the exact name, town and address
a visible “check availability” button that opens the booking engine with dates, not a contact form
a clear note on what booking direct gives — breakfast, late check-out, a free cancellation window — within what your OTA contracts and local rules allow
the Google Business Profile linking to your site, not to an OTA listing
I check what appears for your name and its misspellings in each main guest market; a guest in Germany may see a different result than one at home.
Google Hotels and free booking links: showing your direct rate next to the OTAs

When someone searches for a hotel, Google often shows a booking panel with prices from several sites. A hotel can appear there with its own rate through Google Hotel Center and a connectivity partner — usually a booking engine, channel manager or PMS provider such as Cloudbeds, SiteMinder or Mews; whether yours offers this is a question for the provider. The basic listings, called free booking links, are not charged per click. Paid Hotel Ads are a separate option.
Your direct rate then sits next to OTA prices at the moment the guest compares. That only pays off if the engine is fast on phones and shows the same rates and room names as the listing.
SEO keywords for hotels: destination, room type, occasion and the kind of guest
Useful SEO keywords for hotels describe the stay, not only the town. Guests combine a place with something that matters to them:
place and detail: “hotel near [station or stadium]”, “hotel in [town] with free parking”, “hotel with sea view [town]”
room type: “two-bedroom family suite”, “room with hot tub”, “accessible room with roll-in shower”
occasion: “wedding venue with accommodation [region]”, “conference hotel [city]”, “romantic weekend [region]”
guest: “pet-friendly hotel”, “adults-only hotel”
I pull volumes for your destination in your guests’ languages, check what the OTAs hold, and give each phrase one page — choosing the ones a small property can realistically win.
Room and suite pages, location pages and event pages on a hotel website
One “Rooms” page with a gallery is not enough.
Room and suite pages
Each room type gets its own page: size, beds, view, occupancy, accessibility, real photos and a booking button that opens the engine for that room if the engine allows it.
Location and nearby-attraction pages written from what the hotel knows

An area page ranks when it is accurate: walking times you have measured, which bus goes to the airport, where to park. “Minutes from” everything, or forty thin pages for every museum in town, do the opposite. One good area guide and a few pages for places guests really come for — a congress center, a ski lift, a hospital — are enough.
Meetings, weddings and group pages

Planners and couples search separately from leisure guests, and one wedding can fill the hotel for a weekend. These pages need capacity per layout, catering, room blocks, open dates and a request form. If the hotel restaurant takes outside guests, it can rank on its own; the
restaurant SEO
page explains how.
Local SEO for hotels: Google Business Profile, the map and guest reviews

For “hotels near me” and searches in Google Maps, the Google Business Profile matters more than the website: the primary category “Hotel” (or bed and breakfast, inn), check-in and check-out times, amenities such as parking, pool, breakfast and pets, current photos, and the website link pointing to your own site.
Hotel reviews on Google and TripAdvisor

Guests read Google and TripAdvisor reviews before booking, and AI assistants summarize them. A routine works: a request in the post-stay email and a reply to every review within days, critical ones included. Buying reviews or asking only happy-looking guests breaks Google’s rules.
Multilingual hotel SEO: language versions and hreflang for international guests
Guests from abroad search in their own language, and their searches are not translations of yours. What works:
a separate URL for each language, written or edited by someone who speaks it, rather than an automatic translation widget
hreflang tags linking the versions, so Google shows each guest the right one
the same rooms, prices, policies and amenities in every version, so guests and AI assistants do not get conflicting facts
Multilingual SEO is a regular part of my work; an example is in the portfolio above.
Technical SEO for a hotel website: booking engine pages, speed and Hotel structured data
The usual technical problems in SEO for hotel websites:
a full-screen video or photo slider, so the main content appears on a phone after more than 2.5 seconds
a booking widget script that slows every page, including those where nobody books
a booking engine on another domain without cross-domain tracking, so bookings from search show up as referrals from the engine
no structured data, or markup that does not match the page

Structured data of the type Hotel (a LodgingBusiness in schema.org) gives search engines and assistants the address, check-in times, amenities, the official star rating if there is one, and room types. It must match what the page shows.
If the site needs rebuilding rather than fixing, the
hotel website development
page describes how I build one, and
hotel website design
covers the design side. Owners of apartments and villas will find their version on the

page.
Seasonality in hotel SEO: publishing before the high season, not during it
Guests plan summer holidays, ski trips and event weekends months ahead, and a new page needs weeks or months to rank. So seasonal pages go live or get updated well before the season:
seasonal pages keep the same URL every year, with new dates and prices
events that bring guests — a trade fair, a festival, a marathon — get a page as soon as the dates are announced
low-season offers such as spa weekends or long stays get their own pages, because that is when a direct booking is worth most
Hotel SEO for ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews: when travelers ask AI where to stay (GEO, AEO)

Travelers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews for a quiet hotel near the old town with parking, and the answer names properties before anyone sees a list of links. Getting a hotel into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a hotel it means:
the location described in words, with distances to the places guests ask about
amenities and policies — parking, pets, children, breakfast hours, accessibility, check-in — written as plain text, not only in icons and images
who the hotel suits and who it does not, which assistants often repeat
the same name, address and details on your site, on Google, TripAdvisor and the OTAs, which assistants compare
I check how assistants describe your hotel before the work and again after it. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Hotel SEO strategy and tips: what to fix first, and who should do it
A sensible hotel SEO strategy follows the money. These hotel SEO tips are in the order I usually work:
Win the search for your own name in every main guest market.
Fix the Google Business Profile and ask your booking provider about Google Hotels.
Make the booking engine fast and its bookings measurable.
Give each room type, event space and key location its own page.

children.text: I design hotel websites for independent and boutique hotels, guest houses and small hotel groups, and I build them myself, so the design and the build come from one person at one price. A guest who opens a hotel’s own site has usually seen it on Booking.com, Expedia or Google Hotels already, and asks two things: does the place look as good as the listing promised, and is it worth booking here rather than on the platform. The design answers both within seconds on a phone.
Hotel website design for mobile: a photo-led first screen with a booking bar
Most hotel visits begin on a phone. The first screen carries four things:
one strong photograph of what the stay feels like — the view from a room, the terrace at dusk, the breakfast table — rather than a wide shot of the facade
the hotel name, the town and one line on what kind of place it is
a booking bar with check-in, check-out and guests, visible without scrolling
a short reason to book on this site, right next to the bar

On a phone the booking bar folds into one button fixed at the bottom of the screen; a tap opens dates and guests, and the chosen dates are passed to your booking engine so the guest does not type them twice.
How the booking engine is connected, and how rooms and rates are managed behind the site, is covered on the
hotel website development
page.
Large hotel photos that still load fast on a phone

Hotels sell with pictures, and pictures make hotel sites slow. The design plans for weight from the start: modern image formats at the size each screen needs, the first photo loaded first and the rest as the guest scrolls, short muted video with a still frame until it plays, and galleries that open on tap. Speed is measured with Google’s Core Web Vitals on an average phone, not on an office laptop.
Book-direct reasons and guest reviews next to the hotel booking bar

Online travel agencies charge hotels a commission on each booking — typically somewhere in the 15–25% range on the major platforms, depending on contract and market. A guest needs a reason to book on your site, given at the moment of decision, so the design keeps a permanent space beside the booking bar for it:
the best available rate when booking direct, if your agreements allow you to say so
perks that cost little and matter to guests: breakfast, late checkout, parking, a room upgrade when available, flexible cancellation
the benefit of dealing with the hotel itself: special requests go straight to reception

What you may offer compared with the platforms depends on your country and OTA contracts; I design the space, you decide what goes in it. Beside it sit the signs guests check before paying: your Google or TripAdvisor score with a few recent reviews quoted as text, awards you actually hold, and a line saying payment is handled securely by your booking engine.
Room-type pages in hotel website design: rooms guests can compare
A guest choosing between a classic double and a junior suite wants the difference at a glance. Every room type gets its own page in one layout, and a rooms overview puts them side by side:
size, bed type and maximum occupancy
view and floor, said plainly — “courtyard side, quiet” is useful information
the bathroom: shower or bath, and what is in it
four to eight photos of that room type, one of them of the bathroom
a “from” price where your booking engine can supply it, and a button that opens this room for the chosen dates
On a desktop the overview is a comparison table; on a phone, cards the guest swipes through. Clear differences mean fewer calls to reception.
Luxury hotel website design and boutique hotel website design: telling the story of the stay
A luxury hotel website or a boutique hotel website sells what a room list cannot: the character of the place. The design gives that story room:
a short sequence after the first screen — the building, the people, the details — in photographs with one sentence each
the owner’s or the chef’s voice where it is real, in a few lines rather than a mission statement
type, space and restraint doing the work of “luxury”, instead of gold gradients and script fonts

The story must not bury the facts: a guest paying a high rate still wants check-in time, parking and the transfer in one tap. Boutique hotels with ten or twenty rooms gain most, because the story is what separates them from the chain hotel nearby, and what OTA listings show least.
Location and map on a hotel website: where the hotel is and what is nearby
“Where exactly is it?” decides many bookings. The location section shows:
a map with the hotel pinned, loaded only when the guest opens it so it does not slow the page
walking or driving times to the old town, the beach, the station or the airport
how to arrive: parking, public transport, transfers and what to do when arriving late
a few places your staff actually recommend
Address and directions are written as text and match the hotel’s Google Business Profile, so guests and search engines read the same details.
Restaurant, spa and event sections in website design for hotels
Many hotels earn a large share of revenue outside the rooms, and each area gets a section designed for its own visitor:
restaurant and bar: the menu as text, opening hours, table booking, and a clear note on whether non-residents are welcome
spa: treatments with duration and price, hours for hotel guests and for day visitors, and a way to book
meetings, weddings and events: capacities, floor plans, photos of real events and an inquiry form asking for date, guest count and type of event
These pages lead to their own action, not to the room booking bar. A hotel restaurant with its own name and following may deserve a separate site;
restaurant website design
covers that case.
Language switcher, currency and accessibility in hotel website design

The language switcher sits in the header of every page, lists language names rather than flags and keeps the guest on the same page after switching. Rooms are charged in the hotel’s currency; if your booking engine can show an estimate in the guest’s currency, the design labels it as an estimate and names the currency the card will be charged in.

Accessibility has two sides. The site follows the WCAG guidelines: readable text, enough contrast, a date picker that works with a keyboard and a screen reader. And guests with reduced mobility need facts, not a wheelchair icon: step-free entrance, lift, door widths, roll-in shower, which rooms are adapted — on an accessibility page and on each adapted room page.
A hotel website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Travelers increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews where to stay: “a hotel with a spa and sea-view rooms, good for a long weekend”. Assistants answer from what they can read and verify. Room sizes, amenities and check-in times inside images and sliders are hidden from them; the same facts as text, with Hotel structured data and details that match your Google Business Profile and OTA listings, can be read and repeated.
Becoming a source for those answers takes ongoing work, described on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page. Being found in Google search, on the map and in Google Hotels is covered on the
hotel SEO
page.
Hotel website design templates and website builders for hotels vs a custom design

Hotel website design templates and website templates for hotels look convincing in a demo full of professional photos and invented suites. A website builder for hotels, including those bundled with some booking engines and property-management systems, adds a working link to rates and availability. With a real hotel’s content the limits show: rooms that cannot be compared, one layout for restaurant and spa, a booking bar you cannot move and little control over image weight or language versions.

A template or builder is a fair start for a small guest house that sells mainly through OTAs. A custom design pays off when the site must win direct bookings: a boutique or luxury property, a restaurant, spa or events, several languages, or a small group where guests choose the hotel first and the room second.
Best hotel website design: what the best hotel websites have in common
Awwwards, Dribbble and Behance are full of hotel website design ideas, and many admired concepts never had to take a real booking. What the best website design for hotels shares is less dramatic:
a photograph that shows the stay, not the building
dates and guests one tap away on every page
a stated reason to book direct, close to the booking bar
room pages that let guests compare
the location explained in minutes on foot and by car
pages that open quickly on a phone despite large images
Choosing a hotel website design company or agency

Hotel website design companies range from booking-engine vendors that bundle a website, to hospitality agencies with their own templates, to independent developers like me. Questions to ask any hotel website design agency:
Who owns the site, the domain and the content if we change booking engine or stop working together?
Can we move the booking bar and the book-direct offer, or only change colors?
How fast does the home page load on a phone — measured, not promised?

Phone layouts of the first screen, a room page and the rooms overview, agreed with you.
The rest of the site in the same system, built by me.

A hotel website with room-type pages and comparison, a booking bar on every page, restaurant, spa and event sections, language versions and image speed work: from 2,000 €.

contentBlocks.title: What a hotel website includes for direct bookings

children.text: Direct bookings vs OTA commission: what a hotel keeps

Hotels are among the few businesses where the value of their own website can be calculated exactly. Every reservation made through a booking platform carries a commission — a double-digit percentage of the stay — and along with it goes the guest relationship: their contact details, their preferences, the ability to reach them again. A booking taken on your own site carries neither cost. The difference is not marketing theory; it's a line in the accounts. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.
Which is what makes the common situation strange.
Most hotel websites don't take bookings at all

. A guest arrives, likes what they see, and then goes back to a platform to reserve — because that's where the button was. The site did the work of persuading and handed the transaction to someone who charges for it.
Fixing that starts with
the booking path itself

, integrated with whatever system you already use so a reservation can be completed without leaving your site. But a booking engine alone doesn't change behaviour, because guests genuinely believe platforms are cheaper or safer. Whatever advantage you can offer for booking direct has to be stated where the decision is being made — plainly, not buried in a policies page.

Then there's the structure guests need in order to decide. Platforms are good at one thing in particular: making room types comparable. Your own site often isn't — rooms appear as a gallery rather than as choices, with no clear statement of what's included, for how many people, at what price. A visitor who can't compare on your site will go and compare somewhere they can.

Language is the other half, and it's more technical than it looks. Guests arrive from many countries and search in their own languages, so versions aren't optional for most properties. But translation is the easy part: without correct routing and markup, the versions compete with each other and the site performs worse than a single-language one would. I've built
multilingual sites
whose visitors come from more than twenty countries, and what makes that work is the structure underneath rather than the words on top.

And finally the images. Hotels are chosen visually, so photography is the product — and photography is also what makes hotel sites slow, particularly on the phones where most browsing happens. That's solvable without compromising quality: on a client project with a large gallery, the right approach took mobile performance from around 50 to 92 while the images stayed exactly as they were. I've built exactly that kind of multilingual, image-heavy site for
a real estate client whose buyers come from more than twenty countries

children.text: I offer IT company website design to development studios, MSPs, outsourcing providers and cloud or security consultancies, and I code the result myself in Next.js or WordPress, so the design and the build are a single price. An IT company sells something nobody can see — code, infrastructure, uptime, security — and the design has to make that work visible to a buyer who is not always technical.
IT company website design: what a CTO, a business buyer and a candidate look for
Three groups read an IT company’s site, often on the same day:
technical buyers — CTOs and engineering managers — who check the stack, the architectural thinking and the seniority of the team
business buyers — founders, operations or finance leads — who want the problem you solve, how the work is organized and what it costs
candidates — engineers deciding whether to apply
The first screen speaks to the business buyer in one plain sentence. The menu then gives each group its own way in: services, technologies, case studies, team, careers.
Diagrams and architecture schemes instead of stock photos of people at laptops

Stock images of people pointing at screens, glowing circuit boards and handshakes sit on thousands of IT sites and explain nothing. A diagram does: how a monolith is split into services, how data moves from a legacy system to the cloud, what the client’s team does and what yours does. I draw them as SVG in the site’s colors, starting from the sketches your engineers make on a whiteboard:
process diagrams — the stages of a migration, a support request, a team onboarding
architecture schemes on case studies, simplified so a non-engineer can follow them
before-and-after system views for modernization projects
one icon style drawn for the site instead of mixed icon packs
SVG diagrams stay sharp on any screen, weigh very little, and their labels are real text.
Service and technology page design for IT companies

Every service page follows one template so a buyer can compare services side by side: the problem in the client’s words, what you deliver, how an engagement runs step by step, the technologies, typical team and timeline, related case studies and a contact button. Technology pages use a lighter version of the same layout — what you build with that stack, versions and tools, the team’s experience and projects. Shared templates also let your team add a service later without a designer.
Case study page design for software and IT service companies
Case studies are where technical buyers spend the most time. The layout lets them scan first and read second:
A title with the service, the technology and the industry.
A summary box: client type, region, team size, duration, stack.
The situation and its constraints in a few short paragraphs.
The architecture diagram and the key decisions behind it.
Outcomes the client approved, with numbers where they exist.
A client quote, if allowed, and links to similar projects.
Under an NDA the same layout works with an anonymized client: “a mid-sized logistics company in Germany” still tells a buyer a lot.
Team and engineer pages: real photos, roles and experience

A buyer outsourcing development wants to know who will write their code. An engineers page with photos from one session, names, roles, years of experience, main technologies and, where people agree, links to GitHub or conference talks answers that better than a single group photo. Leadership gets short bios; delivery leads, who are the client’s daily contact, get as much space as the founders.
Trust on an IT company website: ISO 27001, partner badges and client logos
Procurement and security teams check proof before a contract. The design puts it near the contact button and on service pages, not only on an “About” page:
certifications such as ISO 27001 or a SOC 2 report, with scope and date, as text — only the ones you hold
Microsoft, AWS or Google Cloud partner status and earned specializations, each badge linked to the partner directory where possible
client logos and quotes only with written permission
a security page: where data is stored, who has access, how incidents are handled
A badge with no source invites doubt; one linked to the issuer’s listing settles it.
Careers page design: hiring is half of an IT company’s audience

For many IT firms, more visitors come for jobs than for services. A careers section designed as its own part of the site helps both sides: candidates find roles, stack, salary ranges where you publish them, the hiring steps and how remote work is organized, while the sales pages stay focused. Open positions can come straight from your applicant tracking system, so HR updates them without touching the site. Photos of the team and real project work do more for applications than a list of perks.
Dark and light themes, interactive demos and code samples on IT company websites

Many engineers prefer a dark theme, and developer tools have made it common. Designing both themes from the start — with contrast checked in each — and following the visitor’s system setting is cheap at the design stage and expensive later. children.text: I design insurance agency websites and build them myself, for independent agencies, captive agents and small brokerages in the US, the UK, Canada and Australia. People open an agent’s site in one of two moods: shopping for a better price on auto or home coverage, or worried — about a claim, a non-renewal letter, a contract that demands a certificate of insurance by Friday. The design has to work for both, and for the existing clients who come back to pay a bill or download an ID card.
Insurance agency website design: what the best agency websites show on the first screen
Look through insurance agent website examples and the best ones answer four questions before the visitor scrolls:
which coverage the agency writes and where — “Auto, home and business insurance in Tulsa”, not “Protecting what matters most”
whether it is an independent agency that compares several carriers or an agent of one company
who the visitor will talk to — real photos of the agents with their names and the languages they speak
how to get a quote now — a quote button, the phone number with office hours and texting if you offer it
A family under an umbrella or a slider rotating three slogans leaves all four questions open. Your office, your team and your town make the agency recognizable before the first call.
Independent agency or captive agent website: carrier logos and brand rules

An independent agency sells choice: several carriers and one agent who shops the policy. The site shows it with a “carriers we work with” section, and each logo is used the way that carrier’s appointment terms and brand guidelines allow — some carriers supply approved logo files and wording, others prefer a plain list of names.

A captive agent sells one company’s products and works under that company’s brand rules. Many carriers give their agents a ready-made microsite and limit what an agent may publish elsewhere: colors, the carrier name in a domain, product descriptions, claims about rates. Check your agent agreement or ask your field office before ordering an independent site. Where a personal site is allowed, the design puts you first — your office, your community, your languages — and shows the carrier’s brand exactly as its guidelines describe.
Insurance agency website pages for auto, home, life, health and commercial coverage
Each line of business gets its own page, built from one template so all of them read alike:
a heading that names the coverage and the area — “Commercial auto insurance for contractors in Collin County”
who the coverage is for and what it usually includes, in plain words rather than policy language
what the agent needs for a quote, so the visitor can gather documents before the call
the questions clients ask about this line, answered briefly
the agent who handles it and a quote request built for this line

Commercial lines need more depth than personal ones. The owner of a restaurant, a trucking company or a roofing contractor wants to see their trade named — general liability, workers’ compensation, commercial property, a business owner’s policy — and an agent who knows which certificate a general contractor will ask for. Life and health pages get a calmer layout with fewer buttons, because that decision takes longer and is often made by two people.
Quote request forms or phone calls on an insurance agent website
Many shoppers call; others want to start a quote in the evening without talking to anyone. Every line page offers both:
a short quote request — line of coverage, ZIP code, current carrier and renewal date, name and phone — that takes under a minute
a longer form per line, if your team prefers to receive vehicles, drivers or property details before calling back
an online quoting tool or comparative rater your agency already licenses, embedded and styled to match the site
tap-to-call with office hours, texting and a callback request when the office is closed

The forms never ask for Social Security numbers, full driver’s license numbers or medical history. Those belong in a phone conversation or the carrier’s own application, not in an email sent from a website. A short note next to the button says so and tells the visitor when to expect a call.
A service center page for current clients: claims, payments and ID cards

Many visitors are already clients: they need to report a claim, pay a bill, get an ID card, add a driver or request a certificate for a job site. When the site has no answer, they call, and service calls crowd out new business.

A service center page handles most of this: a block for each carrier with its claims phone line, payment link and mobile app; forms for policy changes and certificate requests that reach the right person on your team; and the office number for everything else. The page is linked from the header on every screen, so a client standing next to a dented car finds the claims number in two taps.
License numbers, disclosures and compliance on insurance agency websites

An agency website is advertising, and insurance advertising is regulated state by state. Some states expect the agency’s or producer’s license number on advertising, websites included, and agencies writing in several states often list where they are licensed. Medicare plan pages fall under federal marketing rules with required disclaimers, and life insurance and annuity pages have advertising rules of their own. Words like “cheapest” or “guaranteed savings” cause trouble almost everywhere.

The design gives these items fixed places: license details in the footer and on the about page, a disclaimer slot on each line page, a privacy policy linked from every form. I am a designer and developer, not a compliance officer: confirm the wording with your state department of insurance, your carriers or your compliance contact before launch. In the UK, the FCA’s rules on financial promotions and status disclosure apply.
Insurance agency website templates and builders or a custom design

Insurance agency website templates and builders sold to agents launch quickly and come with coverage pages already written. The trade-offs show later: the same pre-written pages appear on hundreds of agency sites, the design changes only within the platform’s limits, and when you stop paying the monthly fee, the site usually stays behind.

A template or an agent platform is a sensible start for a new agent with one or two lines and no time to write. A custom design pays off when the agency has several lines or offices, wants to stand out in its town, writes commercial business for specific trades or serves clients in a second language. Pages are written for your agency, and the code, content and domain are yours.
Office pages and Spanish versions of an insurance agency website

Carrier documents may exist only in English, so each page says what is available in which language. The technical side is on the

Shoppers ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews things like “independent insurance agent in El Paso who speaks Spanish” or “who insures food trucks in Austin”. Insurance is a “Your Money or Your Life” topic for Google, held to a stricter standard of trust, and AI assistants lean on the same signals. The design keeps the facts as page text: lines of coverage, carriers, towns served, hours, languages, license details and the agents’ names, with InsuranceAgency structured data and the same name, address and phone as your Google profile. Pages appear in under 2.5 seconds on a phone, without a heavy page builder. I do the structure, the design and the build myself, so the person who draws the quote form also connects it — no account manager in between and no website bundled into a monthly marketing package.

children.text: Insurance agent SEO is the work that brings people shopping for auto, home, life or business coverage to your agency’s own website when they search, and turns those visits into quote requests and calls. I do insurance agency SEO myself, as a single SEO consultant who also builds websites, for independent agencies, captive agents whose carrier allows their own site, and small agency groups with a few offices.
What insurance agency SEO covers: line pages, office profiles, reviews and AI answers

Someone who needs insurance types a coverage and a place — “cheap car insurance Dayton”, “homeowners insurance agent near me”, “workers comp for roofers Texas” — or a question such as “does renters insurance cover theft from a car”. Carriers, comparison sites and lead marketplaces hold much of the first page; an agency wins where local knowledge, a choice of carriers or a niche matters. The work covers:
a page for each line of insurance you write and for the niches where you want more policies
a Google Business Profile for every office, and the reviews behind it
license details, author bylines and careful wording, because insurance is a YMYL topic
technical fixes: speed, indexing, structured data, tracking of quote forms and calls
visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
Insurance agent SEO and insurance agency SEO are one job: Google shows nearly the same results for both searches, so one plan serves a solo agent and a ten-producer agency.
Independent vs captive insurance agent SEO: carrier names, co-branding and your own domain

Independent agents can name the carriers they are appointed with, and that list is a search asset: people look for “Progressive agent in Columbus” when they want a person, not a call center. A page showing which carriers you place each line with answers that search.

Captive agents usually get a page on the carrier’s website, and many carriers set rules on separate sites, logo use, which products may be described and who approves the text. I ask for those guidelines first; check with your carrier’s marketing or compliance team. Where an own domain is allowed, it is the asset you keep if you change carriers or sell your book. Where it is not, the work moves to the carrier page fields you control, the Google Business Profile and reviews.
Insurance agency SEO by line of business: auto, home, life, commercial and health
One “Products” page listing twelve coverages cannot rank for any single one. Each line gets its own page, and niches get pages when there is demand and you can place the risk.
Auto and home insurance pages for personal lines

Personal lines searches combine coverage with place and situation: “SR-22 insurance Phoenix”, “insurance for a teen driver”, “homeowners insurance in a flood zone”, “condo insurance HO-6”. A page for each situation explains what affects the price, what you need for a quote and how bundling works, with state details such as minimum liability limits or wildfire exclusions.
Life insurance pages: term, final expense and coverage for health conditions
Life insurance buyers research for weeks. Pages answer early questions — how much coverage a family needs, term or whole life, buying with diabetes — and end with a call or a short appointment form.
Commercial insurance pages by trade and contract requirement

Business owners search by their trade and by what a client or a city asks of them: “general liability for landscapers”, “insurance for a contractor license”, “commercial auto for food trucks”, “workers comp for restaurants”. A trade page listing the usual coverages, the certificates clients ask for and your quoting questions brings fewer visits than personal lines, but larger premiums.
Health insurance and Medicare pages

Medicare Advantage and Part D marketing falls under federal rules with required disclaimers, and many agents work through an FMO that reviews materials. I write those pages within the rules you or your FMO give me, and nothing goes live before your compliance contact has seen it.
Local SEO for insurance agencies: a Google Business Profile for each office and “near me” searches

“Insurance agent near me” and “insurance agency in [town]” show a map with three businesses above the regular results. Each office where you meet clients gets a profile with the right category, your lines as services, hours, real photos and a link to that office’s page. An agent working from home hides the address and shows a service area instead.
Several offices mean a page per town with its own team and lines, not one text with the town name swapped. The map side in depth is on the

page.
Reviews for insurance agents: when to ask and how to answer

Insurance is bought on trust and tested at a bad moment, so a review that mentions a claim handled well carries weight with readers and in the map results. Ask after real help — a claim, a renewal that saved money — with a direct link to the review form. Google’s rules forbid offering anything in return for a review, and many states limit gifts to clients under anti-rebating rules, so keep the request free of rewards.

Answer every review without confirming that the person is a client or mentioning a policy or claim: privacy rules for insurance customer data apply in public replies too. A calm, general reply to a one-star review about a denied claim is read by more people than the review.
License numbers, YMYL and trust signals on an insurance agency website

Google calls topics that affect someone’s money or safety “Your Money or Your Life” (YMYL) and expects stronger evidence of expertise on those pages. Insurance belongs there. On an agency site that means:
the states each agent is licensed in, and license numbers where your state requires them in advertising — showing them on every page costs nothing
an author byline on guides with the agent’s name, license and designations such as CIC or CPCU where they hold them
a “last reviewed” date on pages that describe coverage, limits or state rules
no promises of the lowest price or guaranteed approval; coverage described as typical, with the policy wording as the final word

In the UK, brokers show their FCA authorization on the site; Canada and Australia have their own disclosure rules. Check with your state insurance department, carrier or compliance contact, and I write within what they require. Clients and AI assistants can verify a license in the state’s public lookup, so names on the site should match the license records.
Insurance agent SEO content: coverage questions and Spanish-language pages

Content that brings policyholders answers what people type before they call: “does home insurance cover a roof leak”, “how much is business insurance for an LLC”. I build the list from search data and the questions your account managers hear, draft from your notes, and a licensed agent approves every coverage statement.

An agency earns on policies, not visits, so I report quotes and policies by line of business:
calls from search, counted with a tracking number shown only to organic visitors while your main number stays everywhere else
quote requests from each line page in GA4, with the page where the visit began
bound policies, if your agency management system — Applied Epic, HawkSoft, EZLynx or another — records the lead source

A form that asks for a Social Security or driver’s license number on the first step loses visitors and creates data to protect; leave that for the second contact. Reports hold counts, never client details.
Insurance agent SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

People now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which agency in their town writes contractor insurance or whether umbrella coverage is worth it. Assistants treat insurance as YMYL and lean on sources that show licenses and plain facts. Work on those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For an insurance agency it means:
lines written, carriers represented, states licensed, towns served and languages stated as plain sentences
answers to common coverage questions on the line pages, with the agent’s byline and the state
structured data that ties the agency, its offices and its agents together
the same agency name, address and phone on the site, Google, carrier agent locators and association directories
I check how assistants describe your agency and which competitors they name, before the work and after it. More on the

page.

The first page for “insurance agency SEO” is insurance marketing platforms and agencies. Many sell a bundle — template website, newsletters, social posts, SEO — on a contract that ties the site to their platform. That suits an agency that wants all marketing in one place.

I work alone: I talk to the principal or producers, write the line pages, change the site on WordPress, Next.js or another system, and read the quote data. I do not run ads, sell leads or post on social media. Whoever you compare, ask who reviews the coverage content, whether reports show bound policies, and who owns the domain if you leave.
Insurance agency SEO audit: what I check before monthly work
Every project starts with an audit; for a one-office agency it is often most of the work. I check:
which lines and niches have no page, or share one page
indexing, speed on a phone and titles duplicated by a template

children.text: I do interior designer website design and build the site myself, for solo designers and small studios, so the person who lays out your portfolio is the person who writes the code and launches it. Instagram and Houzz show your rooms; your own website is where a homeowner who already likes the pictures learns how you work, what a project with you involves and how to start one.
Interior designer website design: what a client checks before booking a discovery call

A homeowner who heard your name from a friend, saw a feature in a magazine or followed you on Instagram usually opens your site in the evening, on a phone, with one question: is this designer right for my project? The home page answers it in this order:
your work — one large photo of a finished room rather than a slideshow of twelve
who you are and where — “Interior design studio in Austin, residential and boutique hospitality” as one line of text
what you take on — whole homes, single rooms, new builds, renovations, e-design
how to start — a “Start a project” button that leads to the inquiry form, plus your phone and email
A home page with only a logo and a full-screen video wins attention in design galleries, but a visitor on a phone is left guessing which of those four answers applies to them.
Portfolio pages in website design for interior designers: large photos that still load fast

Interior design is sold on photographs, and a professional shoot arrives as large high-resolution files. Placed on a page unchanged, they make the portfolio crawl on mobile data, and the visitor leaves before the second image. The build carries the weight so you keep the quality:
every photo cut into several widths and served as WebP or AVIF: a phone gets a small file, a large monitor gets a sharp one
the first image of each project appears at once, the rest load as the visitor scrolls
galleries that open full screen and swipe, instead of a slider that hides images behind arrows
a portfolio overview filtered by project type — kitchens, whole homes, primary suites, commercial — instead of one endless grid

Photo credits and usage rights get a fixed place too: the photographer’s name under each project, and only the images your agreement with the photographer allows on your site. Shots taken for a magazine feature may be held for the publication for a while, so check before they go into the portfolio.
Interior design project pages: the brief, the constraints and the solution
A grid of beautiful rooms shows taste. A project page shows how you think, which is what a client paying a design fee wants to see. Each project page follows one structure:
the brief in two or three sentences: the household in general terms, what did not work in the space, what they asked for
the constraints: a narrow galley kitchen, a load-bearing wall, a rental where nothing can be drilled, a fixed budget or a move-in date
the solution: layout changes, materials and finishes, custom pieces, where the budget went
before photos or plans next to the finished rooms, where the clients agreed
credits: architect, contractor, photographer, stylist
The story sits beside the images as page text, not lettered onto graphics, so a client, a search engine and an AI assistant can all read it.
Services and fee structure on an interior designer website: flat fee, hourly or per square foot

Someone who has never hired a designer does not know whether you charge a flat design fee, an hourly rate, a fee per square foot or a percentage of the project, and some leave because they assume the worst. A services page removes the guess without forcing you to publish numbers:
each service as its own block: full-service design, consultation, single-room design, e-design, purchasing and procurement
what each one includes — concept boards, floor plans, 3D renderings, specifications, site visits, contractor coordination
how you charge, in your words, with a starting point or a minimum project size if you choose to show one
the steps from the first call to installation day
A stated minimum turns away projects that would not fit before anyone spends an hour on a call. Whether you publish it is your decision; the page has a place for it either way.
E-design and online interior design services on your website

E-design lets you work with clients outside your city: they send measurements and photos, you send a design board, a floor plan and a shopping list. It needs its own page, apart from full-service work, because the buyer and the decision are different:
a package price or a price per room, which suits a purchase made online
a plain list of what the client receives and how many revisions are included
what the client sends you — room measurements, photos, images they like — step by step
online payment and booking, or a short form if you prefer to talk first
An inquiry form for interior designers that qualifies projects before the call

A plain contact form brings everything from a request to choose one paint color to a full renovation two states away. A project inquiry form asks what you would ask in the first five minutes of a call:
the project type and the rooms involved
the location, and whether it is a new build, a renovation or furnishing only
the timeline and a budget range picked from options you set
how they found you, so you see which channel sends the right clients

Inquiries go to your email or into the software you run the studio on — Studio Designer, Houzz Pro, Programa or a CRM — where your account accepts outside forms. Booking the discovery call can follow through Calendly or the calendar tool you already use.

Interior design website templates on Squarespace, Showit, Wix or WordPress are where most designers start, and for a new studio a template is a sensible choice.

children.text: I do SEO for jewelry stores: the work that puts your rings, earrings and necklaces in front of people searching for exactly that piece, and your showroom in front of people who want to see it in person before they buy. Jewelry is bought slowly and checked carefully. Buyers compare metal, stone, price and return terms across several shops, and the store whose pages answer those questions plainly gets the sale. I work alone and do the whole chain myself — keyword research, page structure, product data, code changes and reports — for local jewelers, online jewelry shops and designer brands.
How people search for jewelry: SEO keywords by type, metal, stone and occasion
A jewelry search is usually built from a few attributes, and every combination that people really type deserves an answer somewhere on your site:
type and metal — “gold hoop earrings”, “sterling silver chain for men”, “platinum wedding band”
stone and origin — “lab grown diamond engagement ring”, “sapphire stud earrings”, “moissanite vs diamond”
recipient, occasion and budget — “silver bracelet for women”, “anniversary gift for wife under $500”
style — “vintage engagement rings”, “dainty gold necklace”, “art deco ring”
service and place — “jeweler near me”, “ring resizing [town]”, “custom engagement ring [city]”
SEO keywords for jewelry: why a keyword list is not a plan

Lists of “top jewelry keywords” go around the internet, and every store that copies one ends up chasing the same phrases. What matters for your store is narrower: which attribute combinations you really stock, how many people search for each in your market, and which single page answers each one. I map every search to one URL, so two of your own pages never compete for the same query.
Category and filter pages for a jewelry website: what to index and what to keep out

A jewelry catalog multiplies fast. Metal × stone × type × size × price produces thousands of filter URLs, and only a small share of them match real searches — “white gold engagement rings” or “pearl drop earrings” do, “size 6.5, under $300, sorted by newest” does not. Faceted navigation needs clear rules:
an indexable page for each combination with real demand and enough products, with its own title, heading and a short paragraph of text
filters without demand stay usable for shoppers but are kept out of the index with canonical tags or noindex
sorting and price-range parameters do not create new URLs for Google to crawl
menus and category pages link to the combinations chosen to rank, and empty or single-product combinations never become pages
On most shop platforms, WooCommerce included, this is set in the theme and filter plugin, sometimes with a small code change. I make those changes myself.
Jewelry product page SEO: metal, stone, size, certificate and returns

A buyer about to spend several hundred dollars on a ring reads the product page line by line. So does Google, and so does an AI assistant asked to compare two rings. A product page that ranks and sells states:
metal and purity — 14k, 18k, 925 sterling silver, platinum — the weight in grams and any plating
the stone: type, natural or lab-grown, carat weight, cut, color and clarity where they apply, and the grading report if there is one, for example from GIA or IGI, with its number
sizes and how to find yours, chain lengths, and whether the piece can be resized later and for how much
care, warranty, returns and delivery time, including for engraved and made-to-order pieces

Lab-grown and simulated stones need to be named exactly as your market’s rules require — in the US, the FTC’s Jewelry Guides — on the product page, in the title and in the feed. If you sell pieces that other retailers also carry, the supplier’s text sits on dozens of sites already; your own description with the facts above is the one that can rank.
Jewelry product descriptions that rank: facts first, lifestyle copy second

On the property platform in Cyprus that I run, descriptions were once rewritten as lifestyle copy — mood, dreams, the feeling of living there. Commercial pages lost traffic. When factual descriptions came back, clicks rose by 16%. Jewelry copy is tempted in the same way: “a symbol of eternal love” gives a buyer, a search engine and an assistant nothing to work with, while “18k yellow gold, 2.1 g, 0.5 ct lab-grown round diamond, IGI report” answers three questions at once. A line of feeling is welcome after the facts, not instead of them.
Image SEO for jewelry: photos, video and Product structured data
Jewelry is chosen by eye, and Google Images and the Shopping tab show pictures before text. What I check and fix:
file names and alt text that describe the piece — “18k yellow gold hoop earrings 20 mm on ear”, not IMG_0042
several angles, a photo on the hand or ear for scale, and a short video for stones that need light to show
images compressed and sized, so a category page with forty photos still loads fast on a phone
Product structured data with Offer — price, currency, availability, priceValidUntil on sale prices — plus shipping and return details for merchant listings

The same data feeds Google Merchant Center, where free listings can put your products in the Shopping tab without paying for ads. Feed errors such as mismatched prices or missing identifiers are fixed at the source.
Engagement ring and wedding band SEO: a separate section for the biggest purchase
An engagement ring is researched for weeks, often in secret, and the questions are specific. This section deserves its own structure:
pages by shape and setting — oval, emerald cut, solitaire, halo, three-stone — only for what you stock or make
guides that answer what buyers worry about: lab-grown vs natural diamonds explained without running down either, how to find out her ring size discreetly, what moves the price
the custom ring process written step by step — consultation, design, approval, making, timeline — with a form to book a consultation
wedding bands as the next step, linked from every engagement ring page
These pages bring the most valuable visits, so I track them separately.
Gift and occasion pages for jewelry: Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day, Christmas and anniversaries

Gift buyers search by person and budget — “gift for wife”, “jewelry for mom under $200”, “anniversary gift by year” — rarely by metal or stone. Gift pages group your pieces that way and state what a giver needs to know: the last day to order with engraving, gift wrapping, delivery cutoffs and exchange terms for the recipient.

I plan them with your buying calendar: when you order stock for a season, the page for that season gets written, so it is crawled and indexed before searches rise. Flower shops work to a similar calendar with a far shorter buying window, described on the
florist SEO
page.
Jewelry store local SEO: Google Business Profile, repairs, resizing and engraving
For a store with a showroom, many searches end on the map: “jeweler near me”, “jewelry repair [town]”, “ring resizing near me”, “watch battery replacement”. A local jeweler wins these with:
a page for each service — repair, resizing, cleaning, engraving, custom work, appraisals if you offer them — with typical turnaround and a starting price
“Jewelry store” as the primary category in your Google Business Profile, plus secondary categories that match your real services
showroom photos, opening hours that stay correct, and a booking link for consultations
reviews that mention the piece or the service, answered by you
The wider map work — categories, citations, service areas — is on the
local SEO services
page.
SEO for handmade jewelry brands: your own website next to Etsy and Instagram

Many designer and handmade jewelry brands start on Etsy, and Etsy SEO — titles, tags, attributes inside the marketplace — is its own discipline that stays inside Etsy. A brand’s own site works differently: it can rank for your brand name, for the collections you make and for the materials you work with, and every sale there is yours without a marketplace fee. Its pages are built around the maker’s name, techniques, collections and custom work, with the same facts on the site, Etsy and Instagram so search engines and assistants connect them.

Questions like “where to buy a lab-grown engagement ring in Austin”, “best jewelry store for custom rings in Chicago” or “is 14k or 18k gold better for an everyday ring” now go to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews as well as to search.
