They search for the thing that has to go and the situation they are in: “couch removal near me”, “hot tub removal cost”, “estate cleanout company”, “construction debris pickup”, “same day junk removal”. Each of those can be a page that ranks, and together they make SEO for junk removal its own discipline:
“what we take” pages for items and materials
cleanout pages for estates, rentals, foreclosures and hoarding situations
a pricing page built around truck loads
service-area pages and the Google Business Profile
answers in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
If residential moving is your main line and hauling a side business, the
SEO for moving companies
page fits you better.
“What we take” pages in SEO for junk removal: furniture, appliances, hot tubs and debris
An item page answers the three things a customer wants to know: do you take it, roughly how much, and where it ends up. That is enough to rank for searches a general services page never catches.
Furniture and mattress removal pages
Sofas, sectionals, recliners, mattresses and box springs; whether the crew carries them down from upstairs or up from a basement; what happens to pieces still in good shape.
Appliance removal pages
Refrigerators, freezers, washers, dryers and window AC units. Units with refrigerant fall under environmental rules, so say in general terms how you dispose of them.
Hot tub, shed and playset removal pages
Bigger jobs that involve cutting and dismantling. Customers look up the cost before calling, so a price range and photos of one removal from start to finish do most of the selling.
Construction debris and yard waste pages

Drywall, old flooring and cabinets after a remodel; branches and soil after yard work. Contractors and do-it-yourself renovators are the two audiences, and both ask about weight, mixed loads and whether a dumpster would be cheaper. If you also take on demolition jobs, that side is covered on the
SEO for contractors
page.
Estate cleanout, rental turnover and hoarding cleanup pages for executors, landlords and realtors

Cleanouts are larger tickets and usually come from people in a hard spot: an executor emptying a parent’s house, a landlord whose tenant left everything behind, a realtor who needs a listing empty by next week. They search “estate cleanout services”, “house cleanout after death”, “foreclosure cleanout”, “hoarder house cleanup”. These pages need a calm tone, a clear process — walk-through, setting aside what the family keeps, donation, removal, broom-clean finish — discretion, and a way to book a viewing.

Property managers and realtors who hire you once tend to call again. A short page written for them — how you invoice, how fast you can schedule, before-and-after photos, keys and access handled without the owner present — turns a single cleanout into repeat work.
Junk removal pricing pages: truck-load prices customers and AI answers can quote

“How much does junk removal cost” is among the most searched questions in the trade, and AI Overviews answer it with national averages unless a local page gives a better answer. Most haulers price by how much of the truck a load fills — minimum, quarter, half, three quarters, full — with surcharges for mattresses, tires or appliances. A pricing page can show that structure with your own ranges, explain what moves the price (weight, stairs, heavy materials like concrete and dirt) and offer a quote from a photo sent by text. It does not have to publish your whole price sheet to work.
A comparison with dumpster rental — when a roll-off bin is cheaper and when full-service removal makes more sense — ranks well too, and brings customers who were about to rent a bin.
Same-day junk removal searches: booking a pickup from a phone

Many junk removal searches carry a deadline: “junk removal today”, “same day junk pickup”, “junk removal this weekend”. If your crews take same-day jobs, put that in the page title and the first line, show the booking cut-off time, and let people pick a slot or text a photo straight from the page. When online booking runs through Jobber, Housecall Pro or similar software, the widget should load fast and pass the lead source into the job, so bookings from search can be counted.
Competing with Junk King, 1-800-GOT-JUNK and other franchises in local search
Franchise brands have national advertising, a page for every territory and trucks people recognize. An independent hauler beats them locally with what a franchise template cannot show:
the owner’s name and face, and the crew who will actually arrive
prices or price logic on the site, so customers know the range before the truck comes
photos and reviews from jobs in each town, not stock pictures
quick replies by text and flexible pickup windows
On the map, a complete profile with more recent reviews than the nearest franchise location often counts for more than the size of the brand.
Recycling and donation pages for junk removal companies: where the junk goes

Customers increasingly ask what happens to their things, and searches like “eco-friendly junk removal” or “furniture donation pickup” show it. A page that names the charities, recycling centers and scrap yards you really use, explains what gets donated, recycled or landfilled, and mentions donation receipts if you hand them out, builds trust and earns links. Local charities and recycling programs sometimes link to haulers who bring them items — one of the few natural local links in this trade.
Service areas and Google Business Profile for junk removal companies
Most haulers run as service-area businesses from a yard or a home, so the profile hides the address and lists the towns served. What decides the map:
the category “Junk removal service”, with each service listed: furniture, appliances, cleanouts, debris
photos of loaded trucks and cleared rooms, uploaded after jobs
a review request by text once the truck leaves, asking the customer to mention what was hauled
a business name without added keywords, which the map penalizes sooner or later

Town pages make sense where you have jobs to show and something local to say: which transfer station you use, how the city’s bulk trash pickup works and when paying for removal is faster. Profile categories, reviews and listings get their own treatment on the
local SEO services
page.
Junk removal SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Searches such as “what do junk removal companies do with old furniture”, “how much does it cost to remove a hot tub” or “junk removal near me that recycles” are now often answered by ChatGPT, Perplexity or an AI Overview before anyone clicks. Work on those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a hauler it comes down to:
item, pricing and recycling pages with direct answers in text, not only in images
service area, hours, same-day policy, license and insurance stated plainly
structured data describing the business and each service
the same company details on Google, Yelp, Nextdoor and the BBB
I put your customers’ questions to the assistants before the work and again later, to see whether your company gets named. How that works is on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Junk removal SEO next to Thumbtack, Yelp ads and Google Ads

Junk removal jobs are small and frequent, so a paid lead eats straight into the margin of a single pickup. Platforms such as Thumbtack and Angi pass one request to several haulers, and Google Ads for “junk removal near me” gets expensive in larger cities. SEO costs time and work instead of a fee per call; once item and town pages rank, each extra pickup they bring lowers the cost of the next. Many owners keep one paid channel running while organic pages grow. I work on search and AI answers, and on the pages your ads can use as well.

Junk removal SEO audit — website, Google Business Profile, pricing page, reviews and AI answers: from 250 €, one-off, with fixes ordered by impact.
One-off work — item, cleanout, pricing and town pages, booking and source tracking, structured data: 250–700 €.

Monthly SEO for a junk removal company — fresh item and town pages, the Google profile, review requests, AI checks and a pickup count every month: from 800 € per month; in very competitive markets from 1,300 € per month.
For a single-truck hauler outside the big cities, the audit, a tidied profile and a handful of item and price pages usually do most of the work. Ongoing work is described on the

children.text: I do SEO for landscaping companies: keyword research, pages for each service and suburb, project galleries, Google Maps and a plan that follows the seasons. Landscaping SEO differs from other trades in two ways. The work is judged before it is bought — customers look at photos of finished gardens and patios before they call. And a large share of the year’s demand arrives in a few spring weeks, so the work has to be done before them.
SEO for landscaping: design-build, maintenance and hardscaping are separate markets

A homeowner planning a new backyard, a property manager looking for weekly mowing and someone who wants a paver patio search for different things, at different times, with different budgets. SEO for landscaping treats them as three markets.
Design-build landscaping searches

Large projects: full yard redesigns, planting plans, outdoor living areas. Searches such as “landscape designer near me” or “backyard landscaping ideas” come months before the work starts. These customers research, compare portfolios and expect a site visit and often a design fee.
Lawn care and maintenance searches
Mowing, fertilization, aeration, leaf removal, shrub trimming. The searches are short and local — “lawn mowing service [suburb]” — and price-sensitive, but one customer can stay for years.
Hardscaping searches

Patios, retaining walls, walkways, outdoor kitchens, fire pits. The searches name materials — “paver patio”, “natural stone retaining wall” — and the customer wants to see similar finished projects and a price range.
One “Services” page listing all three ranks for none of them. Each needs its own pages and its own photos.
SEO keywords for landscaping: keyword research by service, season and suburb
Keyword research for landscapers starts from your price list and your map, not from an export of a keyword tool. What I collect:
the services you want more of, in the words customers use — “lawn care” or “yard maintenance”, “landscaper” or “landscape contractor”, “pavers” or “patio”
the suburbs and towns you work in, and which of them people search by name
the months when each search rises and falls — mowing and planting in spring, irrigation in early summer, cleanups and aeration in fall
which searches show the map, which show directories like Yelp or Angi, and which show AI Overviews
The result is a short list of pages to build, ordered by what each service earns you, rather than a spreadsheet of thousands of phrases.
Landscaping SEO through the seasons: planning pages before spring

In the northern US, Canada and the UK most landscaping demand comes in March to May; in Australia, in September to November. New pages take two to four months to rank, so the pages for spring work have to go live in winter. A yearly plan looks like this:
winter — new service and suburb pages, write-ups of last season’s projects, technical fixes while the crews are quiet
early spring — new photos and updates in the Google profile, review requests to last year’s customers, quote forms checked
summer — irrigation, drought-tolerant planting and outdoor living pages, published ahead of the next wave
fall — cleanups, aeration and overseeding, then snow removal or holiday lighting if you offer them in the off-season
Off-season services deserve their own pages: they keep crews busy and the website active all year.
Landscaping project galleries that rank: photos with text
Landscaping is sold on photos, but a gallery of eighty images without words gives Google nothing to rank. A project page that works for search and for customers has:
a title naming the job and the place — “Paver patio and seat wall in [suburb]”
before and after photos, compressed so the page still loads quickly
a few paragraphs: what the customer wanted, the plants and materials, how long it took, what was difficult
links to the matching service page and suburb page
Ten projects described like this do more for a landscaping website than a hundred untitled photos, and they are what AI answers can point to when someone asks for examples.
Lawn care SEO: pages for recurring customers and maintenance plans

Maintenance pays the bills between large projects, and its customers want something different: reliability, a fixed weekly or monthly price and easy communication. Lawn care and maintenance pages should:
explain what a weekly, biweekly or seasonal plan includes
show the suburbs your crews cover and, if routes allow, the days they are there
let the customer request a quote or sign up online, connected to the software you use — Jobber, LMN, Aspire, Service Autopilot or similar
mention treatments that need a license where your state or region requires one, such as pesticide application, and that you hold it
Recurring customers also become the steadiest source of reviews over the years, as long as someone asks them.
Commercial landscaping SEO: maintenance contracts with HOAs and property managers

Commercial maintenance contracts — homeowners’ associations, apartment complexes, office parks, retail centers — are decided by property managers and boards, often through a bid. They search for “commercial landscaping company [city]” or “HOA landscape maintenance” and check whether you can handle the size of the site, carry the insurance, give references and keep a fixed schedule. A commercial page lists the property types you maintain, what a typical contract includes — mowing, seasonal color, irrigation checks, snow removal — your crew size and equipment, and how a site walk and a bid are arranged. These searches are few, but a won contract can run for several seasons.
Local SEO for landscaping companies: Google Maps by suburb
For “landscaper near me” and “lawn care near me” Google shows the map first. A landscaping company’s Google Business Profile needs:
a primary category for the main work — “Landscaper”, “Lawn care service” or “Landscape designer” — and secondary ones for the rest
a service area made of the suburbs you really cover, with the address hidden if customers do not visit you
photos of finished projects every week or two during the season, named by job and suburb
reviews that mention the work and the area, asked for at project handover or after the first month of maintenance
The rules for contractors’ map results in general are on the
local SEO for contractors
page.
Technical SEO for landscaping websites: photo-heavy pages and speed

Landscaping websites are full of large photos, sliders and drone video, and they are often slow. Google treats a page that needs more than 2.5 seconds to show its main content on a phone as slow, and visitors leave. The usual fixes: images resized and served in modern formats, galleries that load as the visitor scrolls, a quote form that works on a phone, titles that name the service and the suburb, and structured data for the business, its services and areas. If the site has to be rebuilt, the

and
lawn care websites
pages describe how I design and build them.
AI SEO for landscapers: visibility in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Homeowners ask ChatGPT and Google’s AI Overviews “how much does a paver patio cost”, “what grass grows in shade” or “best landscaping companies near me”. The answers come from pages the assistant can read and trust. For a landscaping company, generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO) mean:
cost ranges for patios, retaining walls, sod and maintenance plans written on your pages, with what changes the price
planting and lawn care answers for your climate, not copied from a national guide
project pages with text that assistants can cite as examples
the business name, suburbs, licenses and insurance stated the same way on the site, the profile and listings
I check how assistants describe your company before and after the work. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Choosing a landscaping SEO company or agency: questions to ask

Some agencies work only with landscapers and lawn care companies, many general SEO companies take any trade, and there are specialists like me who work alone and also build websites. Questions to ask any landscaping SEO company:
Will the work be planned around my season, or the same amount every month?
Will you report quote requests and signed contracts, or only traffic?
Who owns the website, the photos and the Google profile if we stop?
Are the suburb pages written with my projects, or copied with the name changed?

children.text: I design websites for landscaping companies and build them myself — design-build firms, hardscape contractors and landscapers who also run maintenance crews — so design and build come from one person at one price. A landscaping company sells something the customer cannot see yet: a backyard that exists only as a plan. The design has to make that future garden believable through your finished work, then turn the visitor into a consultation or estimate request. This page is about websites for landscaping businesses, not about tools for homeowners who want to plan their own yard.
What landscaping website design has to do: sell the project before the site visit

A homeowner planning a new patio or a full backyard looks for weeks before calling anyone. They save photos, compare three or four companies and judge each one by the work it shows. Landscaping website design is built around that habit:
finished projects are the main content of the site, not a section near the footer
every project page ends in a request for a consultation or an estimate
the kind of work is clear at once — design-build, hardscape, planting, maintenance — so visitors know they are in the right place
the towns you work in are stated near the top, so nobody falls for your portfolio and then learns you do not come to their street
A company that mostly mows and treats lawns needs a different site, organized around recurring service and online sign-up. That is covered on the
lawn care website
page.
Separate paths for design-build and maintenance customers on a landscaping website

Many landscaping companies do both: large projects in spring and summer, and weekly maintenance that keeps the crews working all season. The two customers want different things. A design-build customer brings a large budget and wants to see taste, skill and a clear process. A maintenance customer wants reliability, a defined scope and a price per visit or per month.
The design separates them from the first screen with two clear entrances:
“Plan a new landscape” — portfolio, design process, consultation request
“Keep my property maintained” — what weekly or seasonal service includes, the areas you cover, a quote request
Each path has its own pages, photos and button wording, so a visitor planning a pergola never lands on a mowing price, and a property manager is not pushed into a design consultation.
Landscaping project galleries: large photos, before and after, plan to finished garden
Landscaping is bought with the eyes, and the gallery is where visitors spend most of their time. In the design each project is a page of its own, not one thumbnail in a grid of eighty:
a wide lead photo of the finished space, full screen width on a phone
before and after from the same spot, with a slider the thumb can drag
photos from the build — excavation, base, drainage, wall courses — because the work hidden under a patio is what separates a careful installer from a cheap one
a short description: what the client asked for, the materials and plants, how long it took, the town
Design-build project pages: from the first sketch to the planted garden

For full designs the story sells as much as the result. A project page follows it in order: the site as it was and its problems — a slope, poor drainage, deep shade, a view to hide — then the plan or 3D rendering, the build, and the finished garden. A photo of the planting a year later, if you can take one, shows the design was meant to last. A visitor who sees the drawing next to the real garden trusts that what you draw is what gets built.
Hardscape project pages: patios, retaining walls and outdoor kitchens

Hardscape customers search by material and want to see the exact thing: paver patios, natural stone, retaining walls, steps, fire pits, outdoor kitchens. Projects can be filtered by type and material, so someone planning a stone wall sees only walls, with close-ups of joints, caps and edges where the quality of the work shows.
A seasonal first screen on a landscaping website: spring, summer, fall and winter
A landscaping site that shows a snowy yard in May, or a tulip bed in November, looks abandoned. The first screen is designed to change with the season, using your own photos:
late winter and spring — design-build and planting, with “Book a spring design consultation”
summer — outdoor living, patios, landscape lighting, irrigation
fall — cleanups, fall planting, and design work booked over the winter
winter — snow removal or holiday lighting if you offer them, and early booking for spring projects
Switching is a setting in the admin panel: a photo, a headline and a button for each season, prepared once and reused every year.
Trust signals in landscaping website design: licensed, insured, certified

A landscaping project means heavy machinery on someone’s property, digging near utility lines and a large bill paid in stages. Visitors look for proof that you are a careful, established company. The design puts that proof next to every request button and on every project page:
contractor license and insurance, written as text, where your state or region requires them
certifications you or your crew hold — industry association credentials, manufacturer installer programs for pavers or wall systems, pesticide applicator licenses — only the real ones
a written warranty on hardscape work and your terms for replacing plants that fail
reviews that name the type of project and the town
years in business and crew size
Consultation and estimate requests in landscaping website design

Landscapers price their work in different ways, and the request follows yours. Some give free estimates for hardscape and maintenance; many design-build firms charge for a design consultation and credit it against the project. The design states which applies before the visitor types anything.
The form is short and asks only what you need to prepare the visit:
Type of project: new design, patio or wall, planting, maintenance.
Address, so you can check the area and look at the property from above.
A rough budget range, which saves both sides a visit that cannot end in a contract.
Timing: this season, next spring, still planning.
Photos of the yard and, if they have one, a property survey or plot plan.
Requests arrive by email or go into the CRM or estimating tool you use. How forms are connected to your tools, and what goes into the build, is covered on the
websites for contractors
page.
Image-heavy landscaping websites on a phone: large photos that still load fast
A landscaping portfolio can hold hundreds of photos and some drone video, and most visitors open it on a phone. The design decides how images behave before anything is built:
photos are cropped for a vertical phone screen as well as a wide desktop one
galleries open as swipeable full-screen views, with captions that stay readable
only the first image loads at once; the rest appear as the visitor scrolls
drone video plays on tap, with a still frame in its place until then
Planned this way, a page full of photos can still show its main content within 2.5 seconds, the threshold Google uses for a good page load.
Landscaping website templates or a custom landscaping website design

Landscaping website templates — the free ones that come with website builders and the paid themes — are made to look good with stock photos of perfect lawns. Filled with a real company’s content, they show the same gaps: a photo grid with no project pages, one services list for design-build and maintenance together, a generic contact form, and no place for a seasonal first screen.

A template is a sensible start for a new company with one crew and a dozen projects to show. A custom design pays off once you sell large projects, run design-build and maintenance side by side or cover several towns. Moving off a template later usually means building the site again.
Landscaping website design examples and inspiration: what to take from them

Pinterest boards and design showcases are full of landscaping sites with full-screen video and elegant type. Use them for mood, then look at what each one asks the visitor to do. The examples that bring work share a few decisions:
a first screen that says what the company builds and where
projects as separate pages, with words as well as pictures, and a request button on each
photos of the company’s own work and crew, not stock gardens
Landscaping website design that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Homeowners ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to suggest a landscape designer nearby or to explain what a retaining wall costs. The answers name companies whose facts the assistant can read and check. A design that keeps everything inside photos and sliders gives it nothing to work with. Here, services, areas, licenses, warranty terms and project descriptions stay as real text, with structured data for the business, its services and its projects.

children.text: A website that has to work for a few weeks a year

Language schools have an unusual traffic pattern. For most of the year the site ticks along; then enrolment season arrives and a large share of the year's decisions get made in a matter of weeks. That concentration changes what matters. A structure that's merely adequate in March costs real groups in September, because everyone who hesitates during the window doesn't come back later — they come back next term, if at all. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.

What survives that window is a site where a person can complete the decision themselves. That means course information readable on the page rather than in a downloadable timetable, prices visible, formats compared side by side, and — critically —
a way to sign up and pay without a phone call
Enrolment completed at the moment of decision is a different conversion rate from enrolment that requires a callback tomorrow
. I've implemented Stripe payments on a client's educational product for exactly this reason: taking course fees directly on the site rather than deferring the transaction.

The second structural decision is segmentation. An adult learning for career reasons, a parent choosing for a child, and a company arranging training for its staff are not variations of one customer. They search differently, weigh different things, and ask entirely different questions — the parent about who teaches and how children are supervised, the company about invoicing, scheduling around work and progress reporting. A page written for all three persuades none of them, and ranks for none of their searches either.

Then there's self-assessment. Choosing a level is the point where a motivated visitor most often stalls, because guessing wrong is embarrassing in both directions. A short level test resolves that in two minutes and changes the nature of the enquiries that follow — they arrive already knowing which course they want. Whether that comes from
a page builder or custom-built code
is a decision worth making deliberately, not by default.

And one point specific to this field: a school teaching a language usually shouldn't speak only in it. If your students are foreigners learning the local language, the site has to address them in a language they already have. That's
a multilingual structure question
, and it's worth getting right technically — otherwise the versions compete with each other instead of each reaching its own audience.

children.text: Law firm SEO is the work that brings people with a legal problem to your firm’s own website when they search for it, and turns those visits into consultation requests and signed cases. I provide lawyer SEO services myself, as a single SEO consultant who also builds websites, so the person who audits your site is the person who writes the pages and changes the code.
What law firm SEO includes: practice-area pages, attorney profiles and AI answers

A prospective client rarely searches for “law firm”. They search for their problem — “how to get full custody”, “green card through marriage”, “first DUI what happens” — and law firm SEO makes sure a page on your site answers that search and that Google trusts it. The work covers:
a structure of practice-area pages and pages for the specific legal problems inside each area
attorney profiles and content that meet Google’s higher standard for legal topics
wording that stays within your bar’s advertising rules
technical fixes: speed, indexing, structured data, tracking of calls and forms
visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
Most firms also get calls from Google Maps. The profile, reviews, legal directories and office pages are a separate job with their own rules, described on the
local SEO for lawyers
page.
SEO for legal firms and YMYL: why Google holds legal content to a higher standard

Google calls topics that can affect someone’s money, health, safety or legal rights “Your Money or Your Life” (YMYL), and its quality guidelines ask for more evidence of experience and expertise on those pages. An anonymous post on child support competes badly with a page that shows who stands behind it. On a law firm site that means:
an author byline on every guide, with the attorney’s name, the states or courts they are admitted in and a link to their profile
a “reviewed by” line and a “last updated” date on pages that describe the law
the jurisdiction named on the page, because divorce or DUI rules differ by state
links to statutes, court websites and official forms where they help the reader
Texts generated by AI and published without an attorney’s review are a poor fit for YMYL. I draft from your notes and answers, and an attorney at the firm approves every legal statement.
Lawyer SEO and bar advertising rules: what a law firm website may say

In the US, state bar rules on lawyer advertising follow the ABA Model Rules: a communication about a lawyer’s services must not be false or misleading. States add their own details, and lawyer SEO has to respect them:
some states require an “Attorney Advertising” label on certain pages or materials
case results usually need a disclaimer that past results do not guarantee a similar outcome
words like “specialist” or “expert” are restricted in many states unless the attorney is certified by an approved body
rules on client testimonials and endorsements differ from state to state

In England and Wales, the SRA requires price information for certain services, and law societies in Canada and Australia have their own rules. Check your state bar’s or regulator’s rules; I write within them, and the final wording is the firm’s decision. Forms on the site carry a note not to send confidential information and that sending a form does not create an attorney-client relationship. None of this page is legal advice.
Practice-area SEO for lawyers: one page for each legal problem a client searches for

A single “Practice Areas” page listing ten services cannot rank for any of them. Each area gets a main page, and each common problem inside it gets its own page, linked from the attorney profiles of the lawyers who handle it. The structure looks different for each practice.
Family lawyer SEO: custody, child support and protective orders

Family law clients search for the issue: “modify child support”, “grandparents’ visitation rights”, “relocate with child after divorce”. Each issue gets a page explaining the process in your state and how a first consultation works. Pages about protective orders need a quick-exit button and discreet wording, because some readers are searching on a shared device.
SEO for divorce attorneys: contested, uncontested and high-asset divorce

People research divorce for months before they call. Divorce lawyer SEO answers the early questions — how long it takes, what mediation is, how property is divided — and leads to pages for contested, uncontested, high-asset and military divorce.
SEO for immigration lawyers: visa types, languages and clients abroad

Immigration clients search by visa or process: marriage-based green card, K-1 fiancé visa, naturalization, removal defense, skilled worker or spouse visa in the UK. Many search in their own language, so separate language versions of the key pages often bring more consultations than another English article. Clients are warned about unlicensed “notarios”, so the attorney’s bar admission belongs on every page.
DUI lawyer SEO and criminal lawyer SEO: urgent searches by charge and county

DUI and criminal searches often come at night, right after an arrest. Pages are built by charge — first DUI, DUI with injury, license suspension hearing, drug possession, expungement — and by the courts and counties you appear in. The phone number sits at the top of every mobile page, and the content explains deadlines in plain words without promising outcomes.
Business lawyer SEO and employment lawyer SEO: owners and employees search differently

Business clients search for tasks: forming an LLC, a commercial lease, a partnership dispute, selling a company, and compare firms over weeks. Employment law splits by side: employees search for wrongful termination, unpaid overtime or discrimination; employers search for handbooks and compliance. The site has to make clear which side you represent.
Personal injury works by its own rules — case types, city pages, intake speed and very high competition — described on the

Technical SEO for law firm websites: speed, structure and structured data
Law firm sites often lose positions to a heavy home-page video, a chat widget that slows every page or one title repeated across practice areas. Law firm website SEO fixes:
the main content of each page appearing within 2.5 seconds on a phone (Core Web Vitals LCP)
clear addresses such as /family-law/child-custody/, with practice-area pages linked from attorney profiles and back
structured data for the firm (LegalService), the attorneys (Person) and the FAQs on a page
forms and click-to-call buttons that are tracked, so each consultation request is counted
If the site needs to be rebuilt rather than fixed, see
lawyer website development
and
law firm website design
Legal content and links in law firm SEO: answers clients search for, earned mentions

Content that brings clients answers what people type before they call: what a consultation costs, what happens at the first hearing, whether they need a lawyer at all. I build the list from search data and from the questions your intake staff hear every week.

Links come from real activity: bar association sections, law school alumni pages, articles quoting an attorney, CLE talks, community sponsorships. Paid link packages put a YMYL site at risk and are not part of my work.
Law firm SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

People now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews how to find a family lawyer in their city, whether they need an attorney for an uncontested divorce, or what a DUI case usually involves. Assistants answer legal questions with more care because they are YMYL, and they lean on sources that show credentials. Work on those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a law firm it means:
practice areas, bar admissions, counties served, languages and fee structure written as plain sentences
answers to common legal questions on the page, with the attorney’s byline and the jurisdiction
structured data that ties the firm, its attorneys and its offices together
the same firm and attorney details on the site and on the directories assistants read
I check how assistants describe your firm before the work and after it. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Attorney SEO from a consultant or a legal marketing agency: who does the work

Legal marketing agencies serve many firms at once: a salesperson, an account manager, writers, a developer, often a twelve-month contract, plus ads, social media and video. That suits a firm that wants every channel from one supplier.

As a law firm SEO consultant I work alone: I read your search data, write the pages with your attorneys’ input, make the changes on WordPress, Next.js or another system, and explain the report. I do not run ads, social media or video. Whoever you hire, ask who writes the legal content, who reviews it, and who owns the site and its texts when the contract ends.

Every project starts with an audit, and for a small firm it is often most of what is needed. I check:

How law firm SEO results are measured: consultations and signed cases
A firm pays for consultations and signed cases, so that is what I report, by practice area:
calls from search, counted with a call-tracking tool such as CallRail that swaps the number on the site for organic visitors and keeps your main number everywhere else

Reports hold counts, never client details. New practice-area pages usually need three to six months to bring steady consultations; in large cities and crowded practices, longer.

children.text: I design law firm websites and build them myself, so design and development come from one person at one price. Someone looking for a lawyer is usually worried — about a divorce, a visa, an arrest, an injury, a dispute with a business partner. They open two or three firms’ sites on a phone and decide within seconds which one feels safe to call. Web design for lawyers is mostly about those seconds.
Law firm website design: what a potential client checks in the first seconds
The first screen of a law firm site answers four questions before the visitor scrolls:
which matters the firm handles and where — “Divorce and custody lawyers in [county]”, not “Justice. Integrity. Results.”
who the lawyer is — a real photo of the attorney or the team, with names
how to reach the firm now — the phone number, the hours and a consultation button
why this firm — years in practice, languages spoken, a review score, in one line
Everything else goes below. A slider rotating three slogans hides all four answers on a phone.
Web design for lawyers without stock gavels: attorney photography and a calm style

Gavels, scales of justice, marble columns and handshakes appear on so many law firm sites that visitors no longer notice them, and they say nothing about you. A design built on your own photos — attorneys at work, in a meeting, outside the courthouse your clients know — makes the firm recognizable and the attorney familiar before the first call.

Before the photo session I send a shot list: portraits in the same light and framing for every attorney, a few working scenes, the office entrance so clients can find it. The rest of the style follows the practice: restrained colors, sober type, generous white space and text large enough to read without zooming. Serious does not have to mean navy and gold; a family firm can look warmer than a corporate one.
Attorney website design: the bio page layout clients read before calling
For many clients, choosing a firm means choosing a person, and bio pages are among the most visited on a law firm site. The layout follows the order of the client’s questions:
A portrait, the attorney’s name, role and practice areas.
One paragraph in plain language: who they help and with what.
Bar admissions, courts, education and languages as a short list.
Representative matters, articles or talks, with any disclaimer your state requires.
A consultation button and a direct phone line or email, if the firm allows it.
Long CV-style biographies with every award move below these, where readers who want them still find them.
Lawyer website design for practice-area pages
A practice-area page is read by someone trying to understand their own situation. The layout leads them from the problem to a call:
a heading that names the matter in the client’s words and the place
a short answer to “can you help me with this”, then the process step by step
what the first consultation involves and whether it is free or paid
the attorneys who handle these matters, with photos
questions clients ask, answered briefly, and a consultation request at the end
All practice pages share one design system, so a new matter page your team adds looks like the rest. How the templates, intake and hosting are built is covered on the
lawyer website development
page.
Designing case results and client reviews with the required disclaimers

Case results and reviews persuade, which is exactly why bar rules regulate them. Some states require a statement that past results do not guarantee a similar outcome, some restrict testimonials or prescribe wording, and no result may create unjustified expectations. The design shows the proof and its limits together:
each result as a short card — the type of matter and the outcome, without client names
the disclaimer on the card or directly under the group of results, in readable type, not behind a footer link
reviews taken from your Google profile or a legal directory, with the platform named, instead of unattributed quotes
a layout that still holds together if a state rule makes you remove a section
Check your state bar’s rules before publishing results or testimonials; in England and Wales the SRA’s rules apply.
Mobile click-to-call and consultation requests in law firm web design

Many legal clients call, and they call from a phone: after an arrest at night, an accident on the road, a court letter in the mailbox. On a phone, a fixed bar at the bottom of every screen holds three actions — call, text or WhatsApp, and request a consultation. The hours show next to the number, and outside them the bar can switch to a callback request so the client is not lost to the next firm.

The consultation request takes two short steps, the type of matter and then a name and phone number. A one-line note beside the button tells the visitor to keep confidential details for the conversation, because the request alone does not make the firm their lawyer.
Law firm website design templates or a custom design

Law firm website templates — WordPress themes, Squarespace and Webflow layouts for lawyers — look polished in their demos because the demos use professional photos and invented attorneys. With a real firm’s content the same gaps appear: one practice page for everything, a team grid instead of bio pages, no place for a disclaimer next to a result, and a contact form with an open message box.

A template is a reasonable start for a new solo practice with one or two practice areas and a small budget. A custom design pays off when the firm has several attorneys and practices, competes for clients in search, or needs a second language. Leaving a template later usually means building the site again.
Best law firm website design: patterns that top law firm websites share
Lists of the best law firm websites mix national firms with small local practices. Set the budgets aside, and the same patterns repeat:
a first screen with the practice, the place, real people and a phone number
navigation by the client’s problem, not by the firm’s internal departments
attorney bios that read like an introduction, not a résumé
results and reviews close to the call to action, each with its disclaimer

Legal clients rarely call the first firm they find. They read the practice-area page, look at the attorney, check that the firm handles their kind of matter, and only then call or send a form. The build is planned around that path and around the rules a lawyer’s website has to follow.
Law firm website development: what a website for lawyers must contain
A law firm website is more than a brochure with an “Our Team” page. To bring consultations it needs several kinds of pages, each built as its own template:
a page for each practice area and, under it, pages for the matters clients actually search for
a bio page for each attorney, with bar admissions, education and languages
case results or representative matters, where your state allows them, with the disclaimer attached
a contact and intake page with a form that does not invite confidential details
legal guides and FAQs with the author’s name, the date and who reviewed them
disclaimers: “Attorney Advertising” where state rules require it, “not legal advice” on articles, a privacy policy for the forms
How these pages look and lead a visitor to call is covered on the

page; this page is about how they are built.
Practice-area pages and attorney bio pages: how they are built
Practice-area pages built around the matters clients search for

People rarely search for “family law”. They search for “uncontested divorce”, “child custody modification” or “prenup lawyer”. Each practice area gets a parent page and child pages for those matters, linked so a visitor can move from the general topic to their own situation and back. The template has fields for the description, the process step by step, typical timelines, fees where you choose to publish them, the attorneys who handle the matter and an FAQ, so every page your team adds later has the same structure.
Attorney bio pages with bar admissions, education and languages

The bio template stores admissions, courts, education, memberships, languages, publications and practice areas as separate fields rather than one block of text. The site then lists the right attorneys on each practice page automatically, marks up each person with structured data, and keeps every fact in one place when someone is admitted in another state or leaves the firm.
Intake forms for law firms: confidentiality notice and no attorney-client relationship

A contact form on a lawyer’s website is where two risks meet: a prospective client writes the whole story, including facts against them, before the firm has checked for conflicts — and may later argue that sending it made you their lawyer. The intake form is built to avoid both:
a short notice above the button: sending the form does not create an attorney-client relationship, and confidential details should wait until the firm confirms it can take the matter
a field for the names of other parties, so your office can run a conflict check before the first call
a choice of practice area and a short, length-limited description instead of an open “tell us everything” box
a privacy notice checkbox and consent to be contacted

Data travels over HTTPS, the form is protected against spam, and requests go to the inbox or tool you choose instead of piling up on the web server. The exact wording of the notice is your decision; I place it where visitors actually read it.
Connecting website intake to practice-management and call-tracking tools

Most firms already use a practice-management or intake system — Clio, MyCase, Lawmatics or a similar tool — and often a call-tracking service such as CallRail. In general terms, the website can work with them in three ways:
embedding the intake form the tool itself provides, styled to match the site
sending the website’s own form to the tool through its API or an automation service, where your plan allows it
email with every field filled in, when neither is available

Call tracking shows which pages and channels bring calls without changing the main number in your Google profile and directories. Which option fits depends on the tool and your subscription, so I check it before the quote instead of promising a connection that may not exist.
Attorney Advertising disclaimers and state bar rules on a lawyer website

In the US, a law firm website is lawyer advertising. State bar rules follow the ABA Model Rules in principle — communications about a lawyer’s services must not be false or misleading — but the details differ by state: some require an “Attorney Advertising” label, some require disclaimers on case results, many limit the word “specialist” to lawyers certified as such, and rules on testimonials vary. In England and Wales, the SRA requires price information for certain services to be published.

The site gives these elements fixed places: a label slot in the header or footer, a disclaimer field attached to every case result, a review section that can be switched off. I am a developer, not ethics counsel: check your state bar’s rules, and you approve the wording before launch.
Multilingual law firm websites for immigration and international practices

Immigration, family and business firms often serve clients who prefer another language — Spanish, Polish, Ukrainian, Chinese, Arabic and many more. A page in the client’s own language, written by a person rather than a translation widget, makes the first call far easier. Each language version gets its own addresses, a visible language switch, the attorneys who actually speak that language and the contact channels that audience uses; for many immigration clients a WhatsApp button matters more than a form.
I work in English, Polish and Russian and build multilingual sites regularly. The technical side — hreflang, translated addresses, an editing workflow for translators — is on the
multilingual website development

Website speed and ADA accessibility for law firm websites

Most legal searches start on a phone, often at a bad moment. Pages are built to appear in under 2.5 seconds on a mobile connection — the Largest Contentful Paint level Google rates as good — with optimized images, few scripts and no heavy page builder.

Accessibility matters twice for a law firm. People with disabilities are clients too, and in the US accessibility claims under the ADA against business websites are common, law firms included. The site is built against WCAG 2.1 level AA, the standard most often used as the reference: real headings, labeled form fields, keyboard navigation, enough contrast, alt text for images and captions for video. An accessibility overlay widget does not replace this work.
WordPress website for lawyers or a custom Next.js build
Both are sound choices for a law firm; they suit different firms.
WordPress suits a team that wants a familiar editor and a plugin for every task. It needs regular core and plugin updates, and a plugin-heavy site becomes slow and harder to secure.

A custom build in Next.js with a headless CMS such as Sanity is faster, has fewer moving parts to attack and no plugins to update; the team edits practice pages, bios and articles in a clean admin panel. It suits firms that publish often and care about speed.
I build both and recommend one after seeing how your team works. Either way, the templates let the site grow from ten pages to a hundred without a rebuild.
Hosting, security and ownership of a law firm website

Some legal marketing agencies rent the website to the firm: the monthly fee covers the site, and when the contract ends, the site stays with the agency. Here the domain is registered in the firm’s name, the hosting account is yours, and the code and content are handed over at launch. You can move to another developer at any time.

The site runs on fast hosting with SSL, automatic backups, updates and spam protection. Admin access uses individual accounts with two-factor login, so a departing employee is removed without changing everyone’s password. There is no monthly retainer to me; changes are paid as work done.
Law firm website redesign and migration without losing rankings

A firm that has had a site for years usually ranks for some searches and has links from bar associations, directories and articles. A law firm website redesign keeps that value. Before launch, every old address is mapped to its new page and redirected, titles and structured data are carried over, and after launch Search Console is watched for errors. Moving from a rented agency site follows the same steps once the content is exported. The process is described on the

People ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews how custody works in their state or which immigration lawyer speaks their language. Google treats legal content as “Your Money or Your Life” and holds it to a higher standard, and assistants lean on the same trust signals. What a lawn care website has to do for a recurring-service business

Most lawn care company websites are built like a contractor’s: a services list, a gallery, a contact form and a promise to call back. The customer waits for a price on something they expected to buy in five minutes, and often signs up with whoever answers first. A website for lawn care works more like a small subscription shop:
a price, or at least a range, before the customer gives a phone number
programs the customer can compare and choose: weekly mowing, a fertilization and weed control program, a full-season plan
sign-up and payment details taken online and passed to the software that runs your routes
pages for the neighborhoods your crews already drive through
add-on services offered to existing customers at the right time of year
Instant quotes by lawn size on a lawn care website
Lawn care is priced by area, and customers rarely know the square footage of their lawn. Measuring used to mean a drive-by. Now the website can ask for the address and show a price on the spot:
a property measurement tool estimates the turf area from satellite or aerial imagery — some lawn care software includes one, and separate services exist
your price table — per visit or per treatment, by lawn size band — is applied to that area
lots the tool cannot measure well, with heavy tree cover, steep slopes or shared driveways, go to you for a manual quote

If you prefer not to show automatic prices, the form still asks for the address and the approximate lawn size, and you reply with a quote the same day. Either way, price is the first question, and the sooner the customer has an answer, the less reason they have to call a competitor.
Online sign-up for mowing, fertilization and aeration programs
Once the customer has a price, they choose what to buy. Each program has a page with a clear scope, and the sign-up starts from it:
weekly or biweekly mowing — what is included (trimming, edging, blowing off clippings), when the season starts and ends, what happens when it rains
fertilization and weed control — the number of visits, roughly when each comes, and the applicator license you hold where your state requires one
core aeration and overseeding — usually once a year, in fall for cool-season grasses, late spring or early summer for warm-season ones
full-season plans that bundle these at one monthly price, with prepayment terms if you offer them

A comparison table of two or three plans lets the visitor choose without a call. The sign-up form asks for the address, the program, the start date, gate codes, dogs in the yard and agreement to your service terms.
Recurring billing and scheduling: connecting a lawn care business website to Jobber, FieldRoutes or LawnPro

Lawn care companies run their routes and invoices in field-service software — Jobber, FieldRoutes, LawnPro, Service Autopilot and other lawn care apps for providers. Most offer an online request form, a client portal or a sign-up flow that can be placed on the website. The build connects it so that:
a new sign-up appears in the software as a customer with a program and start date, not as an email someone has to retype
the card is stored in the software for autopay, so the website itself never holds payment details
existing customers find “Pay my bill” and “Client login” links in the header
each completed sign-up is counted in analytics, so you see which pages and ads bring paying customers
Where the software has no suitable sign-up flow, the website collects the request and payment is set up afterward through the software’s own payment link.
Neighborhood service-area pages that follow your lawn care routes

For a lawn care company, a new customer on a street you already mow is worth more than one twenty minutes off the route. Service-area pages are planned around route density, not around every town in the county:
a page for each neighborhood or suburb where your crews work every week, with the days they are usually there
a ZIP code or address check on the quote form, so people outside your area find out at once
local details that matter for lawns: the common grass types, typical lot sizes, HOA rules, watering restrictions
reviews from customers in that neighborhood
Pages come from one template and a short entry per area, so when a route grows, a new neighborhood takes minutes to add.
Upsells on a lawn care website: aeration, overseeding, leaf cleanup and snow removal
The easiest new sale is to a customer you already serve. The site follows the lawn care calendar and offers the next service when it is needed:
spring — cleanup, pre-emergent weed control, mulch
summer — grub control, irrigation checks, mosquito treatment if you offer it
fall — core aeration and overseeding, leaf cleanup
winter — snow removal and holiday lighting, which keep crews and cash flow going

Each add-on has a short page with a price and a request form, a banner on the home page in its season, and a link in the client portal or in the reminder emails your software sends. Add-ons ordered this way go into the same customer record, so the crew sees them on the next visit.
Lawn care website design and web design: a quote box, a program table and real lawns

Lawn care web design is simpler than a landscaper’s portfolio site, but it has its own order. On a phone the first screen holds an address field with “Get my price”, not a slogan over a stock photo of a golf course. Below come the programs in a short table, then proof: your trucks and crews in uniform, lawns you maintain photographed through the season, your review score, and your applicator license and insurance written as text.

Customers ask the same questions every spring, and the answers belong next to the sign-up button: whether the products are safe for children and pets, how long to stay off the lawn after a treatment, whether they need to be home, what happens on a rainy day. Answered on the page, they stop being phone calls.
Lawn care website templates or a custom-built lawn care website

A lawn care website template, from a website builder or bundled with lawn care software, puts a site online in a day. For a one-truck start-up with a few dozen customers, a template and a link to your software’s request form are enough.
As the business grows, the template starts to cost customers:

A custom-built lawn care website is paid for once; the code, content and domain are yours. It connects to whichever software you use and keeps working if you move from one to another.

children.text: I design and build life coach websites for career, business, health and relationship coaches who work one to one, in groups or through recorded programs. I do the design, the code and the launch myself, for one fixed price. A coaching site has a narrow job: within a minute a stranger should see whether you coach people like them, trust you enough to book a discovery call or join your email list, and know roughly what working with you costs.
Life coach website design starts with your niche

“I help people live their best life” fits every coach and therefore nobody. The life coach websites that convert name a person and a problem: “Career coaching for engineers moving into management”, “Coaching for founders who work alone”, “Health coaching for nurses on night shifts”. That phrase goes into the headline, the page titles and the first paragraph of each page, because it is what a future client recognizes — and what they type into Google or ChatGPT.

If you coach two audiences, say managers and the teams they lead, each one gets its own page with its own examples and call to action. Naming a niche does not turn other clients away. It lets the right ones see themselves in the first sentence.
Coaching programs and pricing on a life coach website
Coaching is an invisible product, so the program page makes it concrete:
format: one-to-one sessions, a group cohort, an intensive day, a company engagement
length and rhythm: twelve weeks, a session every two weeks, messages in between
what the client gets: session notes, worksheets, recordings, course access
the price or a starting price, payment plans and what happens if someone stops early

A starting price on the page filters out calls with people who expected something else. When an employer pays, one line such as “team and corporate programs are quoted after a call” is enough. Programs are stored as fields in the CMS, so launching a new cohort does not mean redesigning a page.
Discovery call booking on a coaching website

On most coaching sites the discovery call is the main conversion, so its button sits in the header and after every program. The scheduler — Calendly, Acuity, TidyCal or the one inside your coaching platform — shows only discovery slots, in the visitor’s own time zone. That matters once clients live in New York, London and Dubai at the same time.

Three intake questions before the call save time for both of you: what they want to change, which program caught their eye, how they found you. The last answer shows which pages and channels bring clients. A line under the button says what the call is: 20 or 30 minutes, by video, free, with nothing to buy at the end.
Credentials, ICF and the About page on a coach website

In the US, anyone can call themselves a coach, so visitors look for other proof. The About page, written in the first person, covers your coach training and where you did it, an ICF credential if you hold one (ACC, PCC or MCC) or membership in another body, your earlier career when it fits the niche, and what a session with you is like. Where the credentialing body keeps a public directory, the site links to your listing.
The page also says where coaching stops and when you refer someone to a therapist or doctor. That sentence protects the client and you, and it reads as experience rather than caution.
Testimonials on life coach websites: permission and no promised outcomes

Testimonials carry a lot of weight on coaching sites, and every one needs the client’s permission for the words, the name or initials and any photo. In the CMS each testimonial has a consent field and an approval date; without them it stays unpublished. Many coaching clients prefer anonymity, and “Engineering manager, Seattle” works well when the quote itself is specific.

Quotes describe what changed for that person, not what the reader is guaranteed. Lines like “double your income in 90 days” draw complaints and, in the US, attention from the FTC, which treats claims made in endorsements as claims made by you. Video testimonials load only when tapped, so they never slow the page.
Lead magnet and email list: what a coaching website offers before the call

Most visitors are not ready for a call on their first visit. A lead magnet offers a smaller step: a self-assessment, a workbook, a five-day email course, a recorded workshop. It appears on the pages where it fits — a career-change checklist on the career-change page — instead of a pop-up that greets everyone.

The sign-up form connects to your email tool — Kit, MailerLite, Mailchimp or Flodesk — and tags each subscriber by the page they joined from, so the welcome emails match their problem. It asks for an email and a first name, links your privacy policy and sends the download by email, which also confirms the address. On the retail analytics consultant’s site I built, downloadable templates and five calculators play this role: tools a visitor can use long before buying a course.
Courses and group programs sold from a coaching website

A self-paced course or a group program needs three parts: a sales page, payment and access to the lessons. A course platform such as Kajabi, Teachable or Thinkific can host the lessons while your site carries the sales page, your story and the search traffic. Or the lessons live on your own site behind a payment, as the consultant’s courses with video do.

For Landi Room, a Warsaw beauty salon selling an online course, a Stripe Checkout payment sends the buyer a unique link to the lessons. Fourteen days later the link is dead, and the video was never downloadable. Over 100 people paid for the course after its first Google Ads campaign, with zero cases of unauthorized sharing. A coach selling a recorded workshop or a mini-course can use the same flow without paying a monthly platform fee.
Life coach website examples, templates and builders: Wix, Kartra or custom

Search for life coach website examples and you mostly find builders and all-in-one platforms: Wix and Squarespace templates, Kartra and Kajabi with pages, email and courses in one subscription. For a coach still testing a niche, a template with a booking link is a fine start, and I will say so on the first call.

A custom site makes sense when you have content worth ranking — articles, a podcast, a book — when you coach in two languages, or when the platform fee and its limits on page structure and speed start to cost more than they save. Whatever you choose, keep your own domain and your email list. Those are the assets that move with you.
SEO for coaches: how a life coach website gets found in Google

“Life coach” as a search is crowded with directories and big platforms; a niche is not. SEO for coaches works through pages that match how future clients describe their problem: “career coach for nurses leaving the bedside”, “ADHD coaching for adults”, “executive coach in Chicago”. Each niche or program gets a page with its own title and answers to the questions you hear on discovery calls. Articles help when they answer those questions in depth, and a podcast or YouTube channel helps when each episode has its own page with a written summary.

A blog grows in value over years, so a redesign must not throw it away. When I rebuilt Giuseppe’s site, all 468 posts moved with 301 redirects from every old address, and their search history moved with them. Ongoing work on rankings after launch is described on
SEO optimization and strategy
A life coach website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

People now ask ChatGPT for “a career coach for software engineers who want to become managers” and get names back. An assistant can name you only if it can read who you coach, on what, in which languages, in what format and at what price. On your site those facts are plain text on pages rendered by the server, with structured data for you as a person, your services and your FAQ, and robots.txt rules that let AI crawlers in.

The retail analytics consultant’s site was planned this way from the start: demand researched before design, and pages written to be quoted by AI assistants. Giuseppe’s new pages already show up in ChatGPT answers. The ongoing side is on the

page.

A simple life coach website — home, about, one or two programs, discovery call booking, email sign-up, contact: 700–1,400 €.
A site with several niche or program pages, a lead magnet flow, course sales with protected video, blog or podcast pages, or a second language: from 2,000 €.

children.text: I do local SEO for contractors: the work that puts your business in the map results when someone nearby searches for your kind of job. For a contractor those three businesses on the map are often where most calls come from — they sit above the regular results, show a rating and a call button, and homeowners rarely scroll past them.
How Google picks the contractors in the map results
Google ranks local businesses on three things:
relevance — how well your profile and website match the job searched for
distance — how close the searcher is to your business or your service area
prominence — reviews, mentions on other sites, links and how well known the business is
Distance you cannot change. Local SEO for contractors works on the other two, and on making sure nothing in your profile holds you back.
Google Business Profile for contractors: categories, services and service area
The profile is the core of local SEO for a contractor. What I set up and keep current:
a primary category for the job you most want — “Roofing contractor”, “Kitchen remodeler” — not only “General contractor”, plus secondary categories for the rest
each service listed with a short description and a price range where you can give one
a service area that matches the towns you really work in
photos of real jobs, added every week or two, with the job named
hours, a direct phone number and a link to the matching page on your website
answers to the common questions in the profile itself
Service-area businesses: local SEO for contractors without an office

Most contractors go to the customer, so Google treats them as a service-area business: the address can be hidden, and the profile shows the area instead. That is fine for ranking, but it brings rules contractors often break by accident:
the address must be a real place you work from — not a virtual office or a mailbox
the business name must be the real name, without keywords added to it
one profile per real location; several profiles at one address get suspended
A suspended profile disappears from the map until it is reinstated, which can take weeks. Setting it up correctly costs less than getting it back.
Reviews for contractors: how many, how fresh, what they say
Reviews move a contractor up the map and decide whether the homeowner calls. What counts is not only the score but how many there are, how recent they are and what they mention. The routine I set up:
every customer is asked at the end of the job, by text with a direct link to the review form
every review gets an answer within a few days, including the bad ones
customers are asked to mention the job and the town in their own words
Bought reviews, reviews only from happy customers and discounts in exchange for reviews break Google’s rules and are easy to detect, so none of them is used.
Local citations and listings for contractors

Your business is listed in many places: directories, review sites, platforms like Houzz, Yelp or Angi, the local chamber, supplier “find an installer” pages. Google compares them. If the name, address or phone number differ, it trusts the profile less. I check the main listings, correct what is wrong and add the ones that matter in your country and trade. Hundreds of low-quality directory submissions are not part of this — they bring nothing.
Local SEO for general contractors: one profile, many jobs

A general contractor has one profile but sells many jobs, and the map results for “basement finishing” and for “roof repair” are separate. The profile carries the main category and secondary ones, every service is listed, photos cover the different kinds of work, and each service has its own page on the website. That is how one general contractor shows up for several jobs instead of only for “general contractor near me”.
For single trades, the map work is described on the

Area pages on the website and local SEO

The map results look at your website too. A page for each town you cover — with projects, reviews and details from there — helps the profile rank in those towns and also ranks on its own in the regular results. Pages that only swap the town name in the same text do the opposite: Google filters them out.
The website side of contractor SEO — service pages, technical fixes, content — is described on the
SEO for contractors
page.
Local AI search for contractors: how ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews pick local businesses (GEO, AEO)

When a homeowner asks ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to recommend a contractor nearby, the assistant puts the answer together from the same sources as the map: the business profile, reviews, listings and your own pages. That makes local SEO the base of generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO) for a contractor:
the same business details on every listing, so the assistant is sure who you are
reviews that name the job and the town, which assistants quote
services, areas, licence and insurance written as text on your website
structured data that links the website to the profile
I check how assistants describe your business before and after the work. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
How local SEO for contractors is measured

Positions in the map change with where the searcher stands, so a single “rank” says little. I report what matters to a contractor: calls and direction requests from the profile, estimate requests from the website, the map position measured on a grid across your service area, and the number and score of reviews month by month. Calls from the profile are tracked separately from calls from ads, so you see what each channel brings.
How much local SEO for contractors costs
Local SEO audit — profile, listings, reviews and website: from 250 €, one-off. You get a list of fixes in order of impact.
One-off set-up — profile, categories, services, listings clean-up, review routine: 250–700 €.
Monthly local SEO for a contractor — photos and updates, reviews, listings, area pages and reporting: from 800 € per month; in very competitive cities from 1,300 € per month.

For many contractors a correct profile and a working review routine bring most of the effect, and the audit shows whether monthly work is needed. Local SEO for other kinds of businesses is described on the
