children.text: I do local SEO for dentists: the work on the Google Business Profile, patient reviews and dental listings that decides whether your practice is one of the three offices on the map when someone nearby searches for a dentist. Patients choose a dentist near home or work, open when it suits them and in their insurance network, and the map shows all of that before your website is opened.
What local SEO for dentists covers, and what stays on the website

A search such as “dentist near me”, “emergency dentist” or “pediatric dentist [town]” shows a map with three practices, a rating, opening hours and a call button. Local dentist SEO is the work on that map: the profile, the reviews, the listings on other sites and the office pages that support them. Google ranks practices there on three things:
relevance — how well the profile’s categories and services match the search
distance — how close the office is to the person searching
prominence — reviews, listings, links and how well known the practice is
Treatment pages, content and the technical side of the website rank in the regular results below the map. That part of dental search is described on the
dentist SEO
page; this page is about the map.
Google Business Profile for dentists: primary category “Dentist” and specialty categories

The primary category tells Google what the practice is, and for a general practice it should be “Dentist”, because most patient searches match it. Secondary categories add the work you really do and for which Google has a category:
“Cosmetic dentist” if veneers, whitening and smile makeovers are a real part of the schedule
“Emergency dental service” if the practice sees same-day emergencies and answers the phone for them
“Pediatric dentist” only if a pediatric dentist works at the office, not because you see a few children

A specialist practice is different: an orthodontist, an oral surgeon or a periodontist uses that specialty as the primary category. Extra categories added “in case” blur the profile and bring patients you then turn away.
Dental services, emergency hours and photos in a dentist’s Google profile
Next to the categories, the profile carries the details patients compare between two practices before they call:

a services list in patients’ words — cleanings and checkups, fillings, crowns, root canal treatment, implants, Invisalign or clear aligners, whitening, dentures, extractions — each with a short description
regular hours, holiday hours set before each holiday, and emergency hours shown only if someone really takes those calls
an appointment link to your online booking, whether that is your own form, NexHealth, ZocDoc or the booking tool linked to Dentrix or Open Dental
attributes that matter to patients, such as a wheelchair-accessible entrance and parking
photos of the building and entrance, the reception, the treatment rooms and the team, added every few weeks
For an anxious patient, seeing the waiting room and the people in it lowers the barrier to booking more than any description; stock images are not used.
Patient reviews for dentists: asking without incentives

Reviews move a practice up the map and decide whether a new patient books. Their number matters, but so do how recent they are and what they say. A line like “they fixed my cracked crown on a Saturday, ten minutes from my flat in [neighborhood]” helps the next nervous patient decide, and gives Google words to match against searches. The routine:
after the visit the patient gets a text or email that opens Google’s review box in one tap, sent by the practice’s reminder tool such as Weave or NexHealth, or by hand
the message says that a few words about the kind of visit and the area help other patients, and leaves the choice of what to share to the patient
every patient is asked, not only those who looked happy in the chair
Discounts, free whitening, prize draws or any other reward for a review break Google’s rules, so none is used — and neither are reviews written by staff or bought from a service.
Responding to dental patient reviews without revealing patient information

Replying to reviews is part of local SEO for dentists, but in a dental practice a reply is also a privacy question. In the US, HIPAA protects patient information, and a reply that confirms the reviewer is a patient, mentions their treatment or quotes their records can count as a disclosure — even when the patient described the visit first. In other countries data protection law, such as the GDPR in the EU, raises the same concern. This is general guidance, not legal advice; your compliance officer or lawyer has the last word. The rules I follow when writing replies:
thank the reviewer without saying “we were glad to treat you” or naming any procedure
answer a complaint with the practice’s general policy — how billing questions or wait times are handled — never with details of the case
invite the person to call the office manager, so the conversation moves off the public page
never argue about the treatment, even when the review is unfair
A short, calm reply reads well to future patients.
Dental listings beyond Google: Healthgrades, ZocDoc, Yelp and insurance directories
Patients compare dentists in several places, and Google compares those places with your profile. The listings that matter for a dental practice:
Healthgrades and ZocDoc, where patients search by specialty, insurance and availability
Yelp, Apple Business Connect and Bing Places, which feed maps and voice assistants
the find-a-dentist directories of the insurance plans you are in network with, which patients check before booking
professional association directories you belong to

Dental listings go stale in typical ways: the address from before the practice moved, a dentist who retired three years ago still shown as accepting patients, a phone line the previous owner cancelled. Google trusts the profile less when sources disagree. I go through the listings that exist, fix them and add the few that matter in your country; bulk directory packages are left out.
Local SEO for multi-location dental practices: one profile per office

A group practice with three offices needs three Google profiles, each verified at its own address, with its own phone number, hours, photos and reviews. A single profile for the whole group shows in one place only. What usually needs fixing in dental groups:
duplicate profiles left over from a previous owner or an old address
all offices linking to the home page instead of to their own office page
one central phone number on every profile, which makes the offices look alike to Google
profiles for individual dentists that compete with the office profile for the same searches
Google allows profiles for individual practitioners; they can help a well-known specialist, but for most general dentists the office profile should carry the weight.
Location pages for dental offices on the practice website
Each office needs its own page on the website, linked from its Google profile. The map reads it, and patients land on it. A good location page has:
the address, a map, parking and public transport, and a photo of the entrance
hours, emergency arrangements and the direct phone number of that office
the dentists who work there, with their credentials, and the languages spoken
the treatments offered at that office and the insurance plans it accepts
reviews from patients of that office, shown with their consent
Ten office pages that differ only in the street name add nothing; each page needs the facts that make that office different. How the website is structured and built is covered on the
dental clinic website
page, and its look on the
dental website design
page.
Proximity in dentist local SEO: why you cannot rank on the map where you have no office

Distance is the factor local SEO cannot change. Dental practices are not service-area businesses: patients come to the chair, so Google ranks the office from its real address. A practice in one town will not appear on the map in the next town for “dentist near me”, however good its profile. A virtual office or a mailbox address used to get there breaks Google’s guidelines and is a common reason for suspension.

What does work for patients from neighboring towns: a strong profile that ranks for searches with the town name, an office page that names the area and the travel time, listings on Healthgrades and ZocDoc, which do not limit by distance in the same way, and the regular results, where a good page can rank beyond the map’s radius.
Local AI search for dentists: how ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews recommend a dentist (GEO, AEO)

Lawyer local SEO and the map pack: how a law firm gets into Google’s top three

For searches like “family lawyer near me” or “criminal defense attorney [city]”, Google shows a map with three firms above the regular results. On a phone they fill the screen, each with a star rating, a call button and directions. Google picks them by three factors:
relevance — how well the profile’s categories, services and website match the search
distance — how close the office is to the person searching, or to the place named in the search

Distance matters more in law than many firms expect: a firm with an office downtown may not appear for someone searching from a suburb ten miles away. Law firm local SEO cannot move the office, but it can make the firm the most relevant and most trusted choice within its reach.

Choosing Google categories for a law firm

Google has categories by practice area: “Family law attorney”, “Divorce lawyer”, “Immigration attorney”, “Criminal justice attorney”, “DUI attorney”, “Employment attorney”, “Personal injury attorney” and others; the list changes, so I check it when setting up the profile. The primary category should be the practice that brings the most valuable cases; secondary categories cover the other practices you really handle. “Law firm” alone is too broad to win specific searches.
The firm name in the profile: no keywords added

The name must match what is on your sign, your letterhead and your bar registration. “Smith & Lee Law” is correct; “Smith & Lee Law — Best Divorce Lawyer Chicago” breaks Google’s guidelines, invites edits from competitors and can get the profile suspended.
What else to fill in on a lawyer’s profile
services listed per practice area, each with a short plain description
hours, including whether you take calls after hours
photos of the office entrance, the reception and the attorneys
attributes such as languages spoken, online appointments and wheelchair access
the website link pointing to the matching office page, not to the home page
Google’s rules for lawyer profiles: individual practitioner profiles and firm profiles
Google treats lawyers, like doctors, as individual practitioners: a public-facing attorney may have a profile of their own in addition to the firm’s profile. That brings rules firms often get wrong:
an attorney’s own profile carries only the attorney’s name, with no firm name or practice keywords added
a solo attorney whose name is the firm usually needs one shared profile, not two that compete with each other
when an attorney leaves, their profile is not deleted but marked as moved or closed, so calls do not go to a dead number
Several profiles at one address with overlapping categories split reviews and can trigger suspension. I decide with you which profiles should exist and merge or close the rest.
Office location pages for law firms, and why virtual offices get suspended

A profile needs a real office where clients are received and where someone is present during the hours shown. Firms that want to appear in a neighboring city often rent a virtual office or a mail address there. Google checks such addresses, often by asking for video verification, and suspended profiles disappear from the map until reinstated.

What works instead is an office page for each real location: the address with directions and parking, the attorneys who work there, the courts nearby, office hours and reviews from clients of that office. For areas without an office, a firm can still rank in the regular results with practice-area content about that county, while the map stays tied to real addresses.
Google lawyer reviews and bar rules on testimonials

Reviews are what a prospective client reads before calling, and the number, freshness and wording of reviews also lift a firm in the map. Lawyers have to collect them with more care than other businesses.
Asking clients for reviews without breaking the rules

Ask after the matter is closed, with a direct link to the review form, and ask every client rather than only those you expect to be happy. Do not offer anything in exchange — a discount or a gift card breaks Google’s policies and, in many states, bar rules as well. Some bars also limit how reviews may be quoted on your own website, and may require a disclaimer next to testimonials; check your state bar’s rules before republishing reviews.
Replying to lawyer reviews without revealing client confidences

A negative review tempts an attorney to explain what really happened. Bar ethics opinions have warned that such a reply must not reveal anything about the client’s matter. A short reply that thanks the reviewer, states that the firm cannot discuss client matters and invites them to call the office protects the firm and still shows future clients that you respond.

How the Google map pack works for “plumber near me” searches

For a plumbing search Google shows a map with three businesses above the regular results, and on a phone they fill most of the screen. Which three appear depends on what was typed, where the person is and what Google knows about each business. For plumbers a few points carry extra weight:
closeness — urgent searches lean towards businesses near the searcher, so the service area has to cover the right towns
opening hours — a profile shown as closed at 11 pm is less likely to appear for a search made at 11 pm
the primary category and the services list — they have to match what the person searched for
reviews — how many, how recent and what they say
Local SEO for plumbing works on all of these except where the customer happens to be standing.
Google Business Profile for plumbers: category, services and description
The profile is the center of local SEO for plumbers. What I set up and keep current:
“Plumber” as the primary category, because most searches match it
secondary categories only for work you really do and Google has a category for — drain or septic work, for example — not a long list added in hope
a full services list: drain cleaning, leak repair, water heater installation, sewer line repair, repiping, fixture installation, backflow testing — each with a short description
a business description that names the trade, the towns and your license, without stuffing phrases into it
a link from the profile to the matching page on your website, not only the home page
Service-area business set-up for plumbers working from home

Most plumbers have no shop for customers to visit; many run the business from home with the vans in the driveway. Google’s answer is the service-area business: the address stays hidden and the profile shows the area you cover. What often goes wrong:
the home address is entered but not hidden, so it appears on the map for anyone to see
the service area is drawn far wider than the crews drive, which does not help ranking and brings calls you turn down
a second profile is created for a “branch” that is a mailbox or a virtual office — a common reason for suspension
“24/7 Emergency Plumber” and a city name are added to the business name, which breaks Google’s guidelines
Getting a suspended profile back can take weeks, and for a plumber that means weeks of emergency calls going to someone else.
Hours, 24/7 emergency service and photos in a plumber’s Google profile

If someone really answers the phone at night, set the hours to open 24 hours and say so in the description and the services. If nobody does, do not: customers who call at 2 am and reach voicemail write the reviews that hurt most. Holiday hours are worth setting before each holiday, because pipes freeze and burst on public holidays too.

Photos need regular attention as well: the team, the vans with the company name, finished work under a sink or in a utility room, a new water heater in place. Real photos added every week or two show that the business is active and help a customer trust the person they are about to let into the house.
Reviews for plumbers that mention the job and the neighborhood

A review along the lines of “came out at midnight for a burst pipe in [neighborhood] and fixed it within the hour” does more than five stars with no text: it tells the next customer and Google what the job was and where. The routine I set up:
the job is closed and the customer gets a text with a direct link to the review form the same day
the message suggests mentioning what was fixed and the neighborhood, in the customer’s own words
every review gets a reply within a few days, including the angry one about the call-out fee

Housecall Pro, ServiceTitan and Jobber can send the review request automatically when a job is closed, so nobody has to remember. Paid reviews, requests sent only to happy customers and discounts in exchange for reviews break Google’s rules, so none of them is used.
Local SEO for plumbing companies: citations and listings beyond Google

Beyond Google, a plumbing company is listed in many places: Yelp, BBB, Angi, Nextdoor, Apple Business Connect, Bing Places, the local chamber of commerce, and the “find an installer” pages of the water heater and fixture brands you fit. Google compares these with your profile. A company that has moved, changed its number or rebranded often has old details spread across a dozen sites, which weakens Google’s confidence in the profile. I find the listings that matter for plumbing in your country, correct the name, address and phone, and add the missing ones. Mass submissions to hundreds of directories are not part of the work.

For plumbing searches, Local Services Ads with the Google Guaranteed badge often sit above the map. They are paid per lead, require background checks and license verification, and their order depends on things like distance, reviews and how quickly you answer. They do not change your position in the map results, and the map does not depend on whether you buy them.

The two work side by side: the ads take the top of the screen for those who pay, and the map takes the next three places for free. Many plumbers use both. I do not run Local Services Ads, but the habits that help the map — quick answers, a verified business, a steady flow of reviews — help there too, and the reports show map calls separately from ad leads.
Fake plumber listings in Google Maps: how to report spam competitors

Plumbing is one of the trades with the most spam in Google Maps: names stuffed with keywords, addresses at empty lots or mailbox stores, and lead-generation networks that forward calls to whichever plumber pays. They hold map positions that real companies would otherwise have. What can be done:
“Suggest an edit” on the listing for a stuffed name or a business that does not exist at that address
Google’s Business Redressal Complaint Form for networks of fake listings, with evidence: street photos of the address, screenshots, notes on where the number forwards
a check after a few weeks, because removed listings sometimes return under a new name
Google decides what to remove, and not every report succeeds. But reporting is allowed, costs nothing, and can free a map position faster than months of other work.
Call tracking for plumbers without breaking NAP consistency

To know how many calls come from the map, the profile needs its own tracking number. Done carelessly, this creates the very problem local SEO tries to avoid: different phone numbers in different places. The safe set-up:
the tracking number as the primary phone in the Google profile, your main number as the additional phone
your main number on the website, in listings and in the structured data
on the website, dynamic number insertion only for visitors from ads or other tracked sources, with the main number kept in the page code
the profile’s website link tagged with UTM parameters, so visits from the map show separately in analytics
The report then shows calls from the map, calls from the website and calls from ads as separate lines, which is the only way to see what each one brings.

children.text: Local SEO for small business is the work that gets a shop, an office or a business that travels to its customers into Google Maps and the three map results when people nearby search for what it offers. I do it myself — the Google Business Profile, reviews, listings and the location pages on your website — so you get the map side handled without learning every Google Maps rule yourself.
Why local SEO is important for small business: the map pack and “near me” searches

For searches with local intent — “dry cleaner”, “bike repair near me”, “accountant in [town]” — Google shows a map with three businesses above the regular results. On a phone those three fill most of the screen and carry a call button, directions and a star rating. A small business outside them stays unseen by most people searching nearby, however good its website is.

Google picks the three by how well a business matches the search, how near it is to the person searching, and how well known it is through reviews, mentions and links. Where your customer stands is fixed; everything else can be worked on.
Google Business Profile for a small business: the setup that matters
The profile is the center of local SEO for a small business. The parts that carry the most weight:
the primary category — the most specific one that describes your main service, such as “Bakery” rather than “Food”, plus secondary categories only for things you really do
services or products listed one by one, each with a short description
regular hours, and special hours set before every public holiday
photos of the entrance, the inside, the team and finished work, added every few weeks
a description of what you do, where and for whom, without a list of keywords
the website link pointing to the page that matches the profile, plus booking or menu links where they apply
attributes such as wheelchair access, payment methods or online appointments
New profiles, and profiles with changed details, may need verification by video of the premises and signage. Plan for it before changing an address or a name.
Where the profile sits in the rest of the work, and what to do in the weeks after it is set up, is in the
small business SEO guide
Storefront or service-area business: setting up a small business profile correctly
Google treats a business differently depending on where it serves customers.
Storefront: customers come to you. The address is shown, the map pin must sit on your entrance, and the sign outside should carry the same name as the profile.
Service-area business: you go to customers — cleaning, repairs, mobile pet grooming. The address is hidden, and the profile lists the towns or postcodes you cover.
Hybrid: both. The address is shown and the service area is added.

Typical mistakes on small business profiles: a home address left visible by accident, a virtual office or mailbox used as the address, keywords added to the business name, and a second profile for the same business. Each can lead to suspension, and a suspended profile drops out of the map until Google reinstates it.
Getting Google reviews for a small business without breaking the rules

Reviews move a business up in the map, and they are what people read before they call. The steady way to get them is to ask at the moment the customer is pleased: a short link in the receipt email, a QR code at the counter, a line in the invoice or a text after the visit. Every review gets an answer within a few days. To an unfair one, reply calmly with facts, because future customers read the reply more than the complaint.

What breaks Google’s rules: paying for reviews, giving discounts in exchange, and sending requests only to customers you expect to be happy. Yelp goes further and asks businesses not to request reviews at all, so on Yelp the only thing to do is keep the listing accurate and answer what comes.
NAP consistency for small business local SEO: one name, address and phone

NAP stands for name, address and phone number. Google and other maps compare how your business appears across the web, and mismatches make them less sure the details are right. Small businesses collect mismatches without noticing: a move to a new street, a new phone number, an old trading name, “Suite 4” written three ways, a call-tracking number that ended up in a directory.

The fix starts with one agreed version of the name, address and phone. It goes into the website footer and contact page, into LocalBusiness structured data, into the Google profile, and then into every listing that shows a different version.
Local citations for small business: Yelp, BBB, Apple Business Connect and Bing Places
A citation is any listing of your business with its name, address and phone. The ones worth having for most small businesses:
Apple Business Connect — the listing in Apple Maps and Siri, which iPhone users see when they ask for directions
Bing Places — the listing in Bing and in services that take map data from it
Yelp and BBB, which many US customers check before choosing
Facebook and Nextdoor pages, kept with the same details
directories for your trade and your country, and the local chamber of commerce
A few dozen accurate listings do more than hundreds of automatic submissions. Mass directory packages are not part of my work.
Location pages and service pages for a small local business website

The map results look at your website too: the site must confirm what the profile says. A business with one address needs a home page and service pages that name the town and the area. A business with two or three locations needs a page for each, with its own address, hours, directions, photos and reviews, and each Google profile linking to its own page rather than the home page.

A service-area business can have pages for its main towns when there is something real to put on them: jobs done there, local details, reviews from those customers. Dozens of pages with only the town name swapped are treated as doorway pages and filtered out.
Local links for a small business: sponsorships, partners and local press
Links from local websites show that a business is part of its community, and they help both the map and the regular results. Small businesses can usually earn them without buying anything:
sponsoring a youth sports team, a school event or a charity run that lists its sponsors
supplier and partner pages that list where their products are sold or installed
local news sites when you open, expand, mark an anniversary or run a community event
local business associations and the chamber of commerce
Local SEO for small business in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews where to get keys cut nearby or which bakery makes gluten-free cakes in their town, the assistant builds the answer from map data, listings, reviews and business websites. Getting into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO), and for a local business it rests on local SEO:
the same details on Google, Apple, Bing, Yelp and your website, so the assistant can be sure which business it is describing
reviews that say what was done, which assistants summarize
your services, area and hours written as text on the website, not only shown in images
LocalBusiness structured data that links to your profiles
I check how assistants describe your business before and after the work. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Measuring local SEO results for a small business
Checking your rank from your own phone at the shop says very little: map positions change with where the searcher stands. What I report instead:
calls, direction requests and website clicks from the profile’s performance data
visits from the profile in GA4, separated with UTM tags on the profile’s website link
map positions measured on a grid of points across your area
the number of reviews and the average rating, month by month

Local SEO audit — profile, listings, reviews and location pages: from 250 €, one-off, with fixes ranked by impact.
One-off set-up — categories, services, hours, NAP clean-up, main citations, review routine: 250–700 €.
Monthly local SEO for a small business — photos and updates, reviews, listings, location pages and reporting: from 800 € per month; in very competitive cities from 1,300 € per month.

contentBlocks.title: Get a quote for SEO for your locksmith business

children.text: I do locksmith SEO for local locksmith businesses: the Google Business Profile, the website and a page for each job — home and car lockouts, rekeying, key programming, commercial locks — so that the person standing outside a locked door calls a real locksmith, not a call center renting out its listing. Almost every locksmith customer phones rather than fills in a form, so the result is counted in calls answered and jobs done.
Why SEO for locksmiths differs from other local trades

Three things set locksmiths apart in search. Most searches are urgent and made on a phone, often in a parking lot or a hallway. The map carries more weight than the website, because people tap the first number that looks trustworthy. And the map itself is crowded with listings that are not real businesses. Locksmith SEO deals with all three at once: a profile Google trusts, pages that answer the job on the first screen, and visible proof that you are the business you claim to be.
Fake locksmith listings on Google Maps: how a real locksmith competes

Locksmiths have long been one of the categories hit hardest by spam on Google Maps. Lead-generation networks create listings with invented names, borrowed addresses and titles like “24 Hour Locksmith [City]”, then forward the calls to whoever is free. The customer hears a low price on the phone and gets a far larger bill at the door; the honest locksmith down the street never gets the call. What helps:
keeping your own profile clean — the business name you trade under with no keywords added, a real address, hours you actually keep

documenting fake listings near you, with a street view of the empty address or a call where nobody can name the company, and reporting them through “Suggest an edit” and Google’s business redressal complaint form
reporting listings that copy your name, photos or reviews
checking your own profile for edits suggested by others, because spammers sometimes change competitors’ phone numbers or hours
Spam removal takes weeks and some listings come back. It is still worth the effort: every listing that disappears moves the real businesses up.
Google Business Profile for a mobile locksmith without a storefront

Most locksmiths work from a van. Google allows that as a service-area business: you list the area you cover and hide the street address. The address must still be real and able to pass verification — a virtual office, a mailbox store or a coworking desk is exactly what gets locksmith profiles suspended. Locksmiths are also often asked for stricter verification than other businesses, such as a video showing the work vehicle, tools and business documents, so have these ready before changing the name, address or category. Suspensions often follow changes made in a hurry, and reinstatement is slow.

If you also run a counter where customers come to cut keys, that location shows its address and counter hours; the mobile work is described through the service area. On the website these become two pages: one for people who will walk in, one for people waiting at a door.
Locksmith service pages: home, car and commercial lockouts, rekeying and safes

A single “Services” page listing fifteen jobs does not rank for any of them. Each job customers search by name gets its own page, and its first lines say what you do, where and how quickly you arrive.
Residential lockout and rekey pages

House lockouts, lock changes after a move, rekeying after a lost key or a tenant leaving, smart lock installation. The page explains when rekeying is enough and when the lock has to be replaced, and states that you ask for proof of residence before opening a door.
Car lockout and key programming pages

Car customers search by situation and by make: “keys locked in car”, “lost car key no spare”, “Honda key fob replacement”. A key programming page names the makes and key types you handle — transponder keys, remote fobs, push-to-start smart keys — and says whether you program on site, so the car does not have to be towed to a dealer. A make gets its own page only if you do it often.
Commercial locksmith pages

Property managers, offices and shops look for master key systems, panic bars, high-security cylinders, access control and safe opening. They decide slowly and stay for years, so the page lists the building types you serve and how to book a site survey.
Emergency locksmith SEO: 24/7 hours, arrival times and price logic

“Emergency locksmith”, “locksmith open now” and “24 hour locksmith” are searched at the moments when a call is worth most. Google uses your listed hours when deciding whom to show at night, so a locksmith who really answers at 2 a.m. should say so in the profile and on the site. One who does not should leave 24/7 out: the calls you cannot take come back as poor reviews.

An emergency page names the areas you reach with a realistic arrival time for each, explains how the call-out and the job are priced, and lists what to have ready — ID, the car’s registration, proof of address. Explaining the price before you arrive is the clearest line between you and the bait-and-switch operators.
A locksmith website that turns a search into a call

Locksmith websites tend to fail in the same places: a heavy slider at the top, the number hidden in the menu, the same text on every city page and not a word about price. A locksmith site needs less than people expect:
a tap-to-call button and opening hours on every page, visible without scrolling
main content shown within 2.5 seconds on a weak mobile connection
the business name, the license number where your state requires one, and photos of your own van and team instead of stock images
a short form or a text option for jobs that can wait, such as rekeys and commercial quotes
structured data of the Locksmith type with your service area
If the current site cannot be fixed, I build a new one; how that works is on the
website development
page.
Locksmith reviews and trust signals: license, ID checks and upfront pricing

People who have heard about locksmith scams read reviews more closely than in most trades. Ask each customer for a review the same day, by text with a direct link, and ask them to mention the job and the area — “rekeyed all locks after we moved in, Westside”. Reply to every review under your own name. On the site, show what fake operators cannot: insurance, a license number in states that license locksmiths, trade association membership if you have one, a company name that matches the van and a sentence on how you price jobs. Search engines and AI assistants use the same details to tell a business from a listing.
Call tracking for locksmiths without breaking the map listing

Since nearly every job starts with a call, call tracking is how locksmith SEO is measured. Done carelessly it damages the map: a tracking number that replaces your main number everywhere breaks the consistency of your business details. The safe setup is dynamic numbers on the website, a tracking number as the primary number in the Business Profile with your main number kept as an additional phone, and the main number in directories. The monthly report then shows calls from the map, the website and AI referrals, with missed calls counted — at night a missed call is a lost job.
Dispatch networks and Local Services Ads vs your own locksmith SEO

Many locksmiths take work from dispatch networks and lead platforms that keep part of each job or charge per call. They fill quiet days, but the customer belongs to the network and the reviews often go to a listing you do not control. Google Local Services Ads also run for locksmiths in many US areas, with background checks and a fee per lead. SEO builds the part that stays yours: a profile and pages under your name, where every review and every repeat customer adds up. The question is what share of your calls you want to own; I work on that share and do not run ads.
Locksmith SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

People also ask assistants “how do I find a legit locksmith”, “can a locksmith make a car key without the original” or “how much does it cost to rekey a house”. ChatGPT and AI Overviews answer from a few sources and sometimes name businesses. Getting a locksmith into those answers — generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO) — rests on the same facts that beat fake listings:
business name, license, service area and hours written as plain text on the site
answers to lockout and key questions on your own pages, including how jobs are priced
Locksmith structured data tied to your Business Profile
identical details on Google, Apple Maps, Yelp and BBB
I check how assistants describe your business before and after the work. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Choosing a locksmith SEO company or consultant
Search “locksmith seo” and most of the first page belongs to one vendor. That shows the niche is small, not that the choice is made. Before signing with anyone, ask:
Will you add keywords to my business name or create extra listings? If yes, walk away — that is how profiles get suspended.
Do you work for another locksmith in my area?
Will reports show calls and jobs, including missed calls?
Who owns the website, the profile and the tracking numbers if we stop?
I work alone, so the person who audits your profile writes the pages and changes the code. What monthly work includes is described on the
SEO optimization and strategy
page.

Locksmith SEO audit of the profile, the website, map competitors and AI answers: from 250 €, one-off, with fixes in order of impact.

contentBlocks.title: Get a quote for your makeup artist website

children.text: Makeup artist website design is what I offer here: I design and build sites for freelance makeup artists and small bridal teams myself, from the portfolio layout to the booking form and launch. Brides, wedding planners and photo producers usually see your Instagram first; your website is where they check what you charge, whether you travel to their venue and how to secure the date.
Makeup artist website design: what brides and producers check before they write

A bride often starts looking six to twelve months before the wedding, on her phone, with a shortlist of three or four artists. A producer or photographer looks for someone who can handle a specific brief next week. Both decide fast, so the first screen says:
one photo of your work on a real face in natural light, not a collage
what you do and where — “Bridal and event makeup in San Diego, travel across Southern California”
the kinds of work you take: bridal, events, editorial, film and SFX
a “Check my date” button and a text button, visible without scrolling
A line such as “Soft, long-wearing bridal makeup for all skin tones” tells a bride more than a tagline about beauty and confidence.
Makeup artist portfolio website: bridal, events, editorial and SFX by category

An Instagram grid mixes soft bridal looks with graphic editorial work and prosthetic wounds. A bride scrolling for a glowing, natural face gets lost; a film producer has to scroll past twenty weddings. A portfolio website splits the work into categories, each with its own page, short intro and button. Within bridal, the gallery shows a range of ages, skin tones and skin types, so each bride can find someone like her.

Close-ups are what clients study, so they open full screen and stay sharp. Each photo is resized for every screen and saved in a modern format, the first image loads at once and the rest as the visitor scrolls. Credits sit under each look — photographer, hair stylist, model — and a bride’s photos are published only with her written consent. If a photo was retouched, saying so builds more trust than hiding it.
Bridal makeup artist website: trials, wedding-day schedule and bridal party prices
Brides ask the same questions in every inquiry, and a bridal page answers them before the first message:
what the bridal package includes: trial, lashes, a touch-up kit, staying for photos
where the trial happens and how long before the wedding it is best booked
time per person and a sample schedule counted back from the ceremony
prices for the bridal party, mothers and flower girls, and the minimum for peak Saturdays
whether you bring an assistant or a hair stylist for larger parties
A short FAQ on the same page covers allergies, skin prep and what to wear on the morning, so the consultation call can be about the look itself.
Makeup artist prices and travel fees on the website

Many artists keep prices in a PDF or an Instagram highlight, where they are hard to find and easy to forget to update. On the site they are plain text you edit in the CMS: a “from” price for each service — bridal, bridesmaid, trial, event, lesson — and what changes it. Travel is the second question after price, so it gets its own section: the area included in the price, zones beyond it, early-start fees before a set hour, and destination weddings quoted individually with travel and lodging. Editorial and film work can show a day rate or “on request”, as you prefer.
A makeup artist booking website: date check, deposit and contract

Wedding bookings work by date rather than by time slot: one artist usually takes one wedding a day. The form asks for the date, the venue or city, the number of people and the time everyone must be ready. You confirm the date is free, then the client signs the agreement and pays a deposit — many US artists call it a retainer — that secures it. HoneyBook and Dubsado handle the contract and deposit in one flow; a Square or Stripe payment link works for simpler setups. Lessons and studio appointments, which do run by time slot, can go through a scheduler with a deposit, such as Acuity or GlossGenius.
The deposit amount, what happens if the wedding moves and the cancellation terms are shown before the form is sent, so nobody learns them from the invoice.
Editorial, film and SFX makeup artist website: a separate path for producers

Producers, photographers and agencies look for something else: tear sheets with publication names, a short reel for film and TV, set experience, kit and skills — beauty, grooming, aging, prosthetics, wounds — and an agent’s contact if you have one. That path starts from its own button on the home page and leads to pages without bridal prices, with a downloadable PDF portfolio for quick sharing. Credits and clients are listed only where the work was published and you are allowed to name them.
Models building their own book need a different site, described on
website design for models
Makeup classes and courses on a makeup artist website: selling video lessons online

Teaching fills the months between wedding seasons. One-to-one lessons and small group masterclasses in your studio are booked by time slot with a deposit. A recorded course — bridal skin prep, a soft glam routine, a pro course for new artists — reaches people far outside your travel area. Its page shows who the course is for, the lesson list, a short preview and the price, and Stripe Checkout takes the payment.

I built this setup for Landi Room, a Warsaw beauty salon selling an online nanoplasty course. Each buyer receives a unique viewing link by email the moment the payment clears; it works for 14 days and the lessons can be watched but not saved. Its first Google Ads campaign sold over 100 courses, and no link has been shared onward. A makeup course runs the same way, on your own site, without sending students to a separate course platform.
Instagram or a website for a makeup artist

Instagram is where many brides find you, so keep posting. Its limits show when someone is ready to book: the feed runs in the algorithm’s order, prices hide in highlights, inquiries arrive among spam in DMs, and a hacked account can disappear overnight. The website holds what a profile cannot — prices, travel zones, the booking form, your terms and the full portfolio by category — and your bio link points to the right page. When someone searches “makeup artist near me” on Google, the results show websites and the map, not posts.
Local SEO for wedding makeup artists: service areas and Google Business Profile

Brides search “bridal makeup artist” with a city or region, and planners search by the area of the venue. A page for each area you actually serve, with real weddings from there, gives Google something to match. In Google Business Profile you list the regions you cover and hide your home address, as service-area businesses do. children.text: Manufacturing SEO is the work that brings engineers, buyers and procurement teams to your own website when they search for a process, a material or a supplier, and turns those visits into requests for quotes. I do it myself, as a single SEO consultant who also builds websites, for machine shops, fabricators, molders, contract manufacturers and companies that make their own components.
What SEO in manufacturing is: matching the way engineers describe a job

An engineer with a part to source does not search for “precision manufacturing solutions”. They type the job: “5-axis CNC machining titanium aerospace”, “tight tolerance Swiss turning medical”, “low-volume aluminum die casting”, “powder coating extrusions Ohio”. Each search combines a process, a material, often a tolerance or a volume, and sometimes an industry or a region. SEO for manufacturers makes sure that a page on your site matches that combination, says plainly that you can do the job, and leads to an RFQ.
Manufacturers share a lot with other B2B companies — long sales cycles, several people involved in a decision, leads that need tracking into a CRM. That general side is on the
B2B SEO
page. This page is about what is specific to industrial SEO: capabilities, materials, equipment, certifications, directories and the RFQ.
SEO for manufacturers starts with a capability matrix: process, material, tolerance, industry
Before any page is written, I build a grid of what the plant can actually do, from your quote history and a short call with whoever estimates jobs:
processes — milling, turning, laser cutting, bending, welding, injection molding, extrusion, assembly
materials you run regularly, with grades buyers name: 6061 aluminum, 316 stainless, Ti-6Al-4V, PEEK
the tolerances and surface finishes you can hold, and the largest part that fits your machines
lot sizes, from prototypes to production runs, and secondary operations such as anodizing or heat treatment
industries you already ship to, and the ones you want more work from

Then every combination is checked against search data. Some have steady demand and deserve their own page; most are covered by a broader page that lists them in text. Generating hundreds of near-identical “process + material + city” pages is a pattern Google treats as low-value, and engineers notice it too.
Capability and process pages: the core of industrial SEO
A capability page is the main landing page for a manufacturer. It ranks when it answers the engineer’s questions before they ask them:
what the process is used for, in the words buyers use
materials, tolerances, finishes and the maximum part envelope, as text
prototype and production quantities, typical lead times and secondary operations
photos of real parts you are allowed to show, with a short caption on each
a link to the RFQ with the process already selected
Material pages for the alloys and plastics you run most

When a material is hard to work — titanium, Inconel, PEEK, copper alloys — buyers search for it directly, because many shops refuse it. A page per difficult material, with what you machine or mold in it and for which industries, often brings better RFQs than the process page itself.
Equipment list as text, not a photo gallery

Engineers check whether your machines can hold their part. A list with make, model, number of axes, work envelope and spindle or press size, written as text, answers that and gives search engines the terms to match. A gallery of machine photos without captions does neither.
Industries-served pages and certifications in SEO for the manufacturing industry

A buyer from a regulated industry searches with that industry in mind and checks your quality system before anything else. Each sector you serve gets a page with the certifications and documents it expects. Examples:
aerospace — AS9100, first article inspection reports, material traceability
automotive — IATF 16949, PPAP documentation
medical devices — ISO 13485, cleanroom or controlled assembly if you have it
general industry — ISO 9001, material certificates, certificates of conformance

Certifications are written as text with the standard, the scope and the certifying body, with the certificate file linked. A row of logos in the footer cannot be read by search engines or quoted by AI assistants.
Local SEO for manufacturers: regional and “contract manufacturing near me” searches

Many buyers prefer a supplier they can drive to for an audit, a first-article review or an urgent rework, and shorter shipping matters when supply chains are under strain. That shows up in searches like “CNC machine shop near me”, “sheet metal fabrication Midwest” or “contract manufacturer Texas”. What helps:
a Google Business Profile for each plant, with the right category and a link to the matching capability page
the plant address, the regions you ship to and delivery times stated on the site
regional pages only where you have a plant, a sales office or a real customer base
The map side in depth — profiles, categories, reviews — is described on the
local SEO services
page.
Thomasnet, industrial directories and trade shows in manufacturing SEO

For many industrial searches, Thomasnet and other directories rank above the suppliers themselves, and a “manufacturing directory” is where some buyers start. A directory profile is part of the work, not a replacement for it: the capabilities, certifications and locations there should match the site, and the profile should link to the relevant capability page rather than the home page. Association member lists, regional manufacturing networks and supplier portals of your customers work the same way. For buyers in Europe, Europages plays a similar role.

Trade shows bring face-to-face conversations for a few days; search brings buyers the rest of the year. The two connect: the exhibitor listing links to your site, new equipment shown at the show gets a page, and the people who took your card look you up afterwards and find the capability they discussed.
Manufacturers of one product type have their own patterns. An example of SEO for one industry in depth is the
SEO for lingerie manufacturers
page.
Manufacturing SEO for ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews: supplier shortlists (GEO, AEO)

Procurement teams and engineers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews for a first list of suppliers: “contract manufacturers in the US with ISO 13485 that do silicone overmolding”, “machine shops in Ohio that work Inconel”. The assistant answers with a few names and a reason for each. A plant that is not described clearly anywhere does not make the list. Work on those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a manufacturer it means:
processes, materials, tolerances, lot sizes and industries written as plain sentences on your pages
certifications with their scope, and the plant locations, stated as text
structured data for the company and its locations
the same facts on your site, Thomasnet, LinkedIn and association listings, so assistants do not mix you up with another firm
I check how assistants describe your company and which competitors they name, before the work and after it. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Measuring SEO for manufacturing companies in RFQs, not traffic
Manufacturing lead generation is judged by requests that can be quoted. I set up tracking for:
RFQ submissions, with the page where the visit began and whether a drawing was attached
calls and email clicks from capability and industry pages
datasheet and certificate downloads, as a sign of interest from engineers

Once a month I compare that list with your estimating team: which requests fit your machines, which were quoted and which became orders. Manufacturing sites also attract job seekers searching for machinist or welder jobs; that traffic goes to a careers page and is kept out of the sales report.
Manufacturing SEO agency, manufacturing SEO companies or one consultant

A manufacturing SEO agency usually sells a team and a wider package: paid search, directory advertising, LinkedIn, trade show campaigns. That fits a company that wants every channel from one supplier and has a marketing manager to run it.

I work alone: I talk to your estimator or production manager, write the capability pages, make the changes on WordPress, Next.js or another system, and read the RFQ data. I do not run ads. Whoever you compare, ask them:
Who will speak to our engineers, and who writes about tolerances and materials?
Will the report show RFQs and quoted jobs, or only rankings?
Who owns the site, the content and the accounts if we stop working together?

children.text: Your buyer already knows what they need

Industrial buying differs from almost every other kind in one respect: the person searching usually knows precisely what they're looking for before they start. A material in a grade. A component within a tolerance. A process for a given volume. A supplier holding a particular certification. They aren't browsing for inspiration, and they aren't going to be persuaded by a description of your company's values. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.

Which is why the standard manufacturing website underperforms. It opens with when the company was founded, its commitment to quality and its modern machinery — while the visitor is trying to establish whether you can produce a specific part in a specific alloy at a specific volume. If the answer isn't on the page in the form they're looking for,
they leave, and they leave without contacting you
, because there was nothing to suggest an enquiry would be worth their time.

Publishing specifications changes both halves of this. For the visitor, it answers the actual question. For search, it creates pages that can match the terms buyers use — a material name, a standard, a process, a capability — which is how technical buyers find suppliers they hadn't heard of. The same applies to capabilities as a category: buyers looking for a contract manufacturer search for what a plant can do at least as often as for what it already makes.

Documentation deserves a decision most companies get wrong. Datasheets and drawings are frequently placed behind a contact form, on the reasoning that a download is a lead. In practice it means evaluation happens without you: an engineer comparing four suppliers downloads three sets of documents and requests none. Publishing openly costs some contact data and buys inclusion in the comparison, which is the stage that matters.

Certifications belong in the same category of decisions. In this field they aren't reassurance — they're the filter that determines whether a supplier can be considered at all. A buyer who has to search or ask whether you hold a required standard has already found someone whose site stated it plainly.

Finally, language. Manufacturers export as a matter of routine, and technical searches happen in the buyer's own language. A site in a single language is absent from most of the markets the company already sells into — and the fix is structural rather than linguistic: versions with correct routing and markup work independently, while incorrectly configured ones compete with each other and can leave a site worse off than before. that multilingual structure

a filterable product catalogue

children.text: Manufacturing website design is what I do for machine shops, fabricators, molders, contract manufacturers and companies that make their own components, and I build the sites myself, so design and development come from one person at one price. A manufacturer’s site is read by people with very different jobs — a design engineer at a CAD workstation, a buyer collecting quotes, a quality manager checking certificates, a production lead looking something up on a phone next to a machine — and the design has to work for each of them.
Manufacturing website design: who reads the site and on which screen
The same capability page is opened on a wide monitor in an engineering office and on a phone in a noisy plant. Design decisions follow from that:
type large enough and contrast strong enough to read under shop lights or near a window
buttons big enough to tap without zooming, spaced so a thumb does not hit the wrong one
menus that name processes and industries plainly, so nobody has to guess what “Solutions” contains
pages that stay light, because plant Wi-Fi and mobile signal inside steel buildings are often weak
A modern industrial website design does not need dark backgrounds, sparks and slow video to look serious. It needs clear pages that open fast.
Industrial website design without stock photos: your plant, machines and parts

Stock images of robot arms, sparks and glowing factories appear on so many industrial websites that they tell a buyer nothing about you. Your own photos do: the machines, the people running them, the inspection room, the parts that leave the dock. Before a photo session I send a shot list:
each machine type with an operator, in the same light and framing
close-ups of finished parts with something that shows scale, against a plain background
the inspection area, measuring equipment and the clean or controlled area if you have one
raw material stock, packing and loading, which show capacity better than adjectives

Customer parts appear only with permission, and drawings or part numbers visible in a shot are blurred. Short silent video loops of a process can work on a capability page, as long as the page still loads quickly on a phone.
Capability and process page layouts in website design for manufacturing companies
A capability page answers one question: can this plant make my part? The layout puts the answers in the order an engineer looks for them:
The process and one sentence on what it is used for.
Materials, tolerances, finishes and the largest part size, in a short table.
Quantities from prototype to production, typical lead times, secondary operations.
Photos of real parts made with this process.
A request button with the process already selected.
Every capability page uses the same template, so a new process your team adds looks like the others.
Equipment list layout: a sortable table rather than a gallery

An equipment page designed as a table — machine type, make and model, axes, work envelope, quantity — lets an engineer sort by size and see in seconds whether a part fits. A small photo can sit in each row; the data stays as text.
Spec tables an engineer can read on a phone on the shop floor
Specification tables break on phones more than any other element of a manufacturing site. The design handles them deliberately:
on narrow screens, wide tables turn into stacked cards, with the parameter name next to each value
units sit in the column header, and values are given in millimeters and inches where your buyers use both
decimal separators follow the language: a point in English, a comma in German and Polish
tolerances use the ± sign and the same notation everywhere
tables are real text, never images, so they can be copied into a quote or an email
The datasheet PDF sits one tap away from the table for anyone who needs to print or forward it.
Industries-served and quality page designs for a manufacturing website

Buyers from aerospace, medical or automotive open the page for their industry first. Each one follows the same layout: the requirements of that sector, the certifications that apply, the kind of parts you make for it (shown generically where customer work is confidential) and a request button.

The quality page is designed for the person who signs off on a new supplier. It shows each certificate with the standard, scope, certifying body and expiry date, a download of the certificate itself, the inspection equipment and the documents you provide with a shipment. Laid out as text, it can be checked in a minute instead of requested by email.
RFQ form design with CAD file upload
The request form decides whether an engineer sends you a job or moves on to the next supplier. Its design details matter as much as its fields:
an upload area that accepts several files at once and names the formats you take, such as STEP, IGES, DXF and PDF
the maximum file size written next to the upload, and a progress bar that also works on a phone
files stored in a secure place for your team, not sent as large email attachments
a short note on confidentiality, and an option to request an NDA before sending drawings
a confirmation page that says who will reply and when, with a reference number
Product configurators on manufacturing websites: when they pay off

For standard products with options — enclosures, cables, fasteners, filters, conveyors — a configurator lets the buyer choose size, material and options step by step and ends with a part number and a pre-filled request. It saves your sales team many repeated questions. For a job shop where every part is different, the RFQ with a drawing does the same job better. A configurator is built from the rules you give me; a full quoting system with live prices from your ERP is a separate, larger project.
Manufacturing website design for export: German and other language versions

Many European manufacturers sell to German-speaking buyers, and German words run long: menus, buttons and table headers designed in English often break. The design is drawn for the longest language from the first sketch. I work on my own and also build websites, so one person reads your search data, drafts the treatment pages with your providers and edits the code.
What med spa SEO covers: treatment pages, Google Maps and AI answers

A med spa client usually knows the treatment before choosing the place. They search “Botox near me”, “lip filler Scottsdale” or “laser hair removal cost”, look at the map, read reviews, open two or three websites and compare providers, prices and photos. SEO for a med spa works on each of those steps:
a page for every treatment you want more bookings for, built around what clients type
a Google Business Profile for each location, with the right category and services
provider and medical director pages that show who performs each treatment
price, membership and package pages that answer the cost question before the call
galleries and reviews handled within consent and endorsement rules
facts that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read and repeat
I report results in consultations and booked treatments by treatment line, not in traffic.
Treatment pages for med spa SEO: injectables, laser and body contouring

A single “Services” page listing twenty treatments cannot rank for each of them. Each treatment line gets a main page, and each treatment clients search by name gets its own page: who it suits, who performs it, what happens at the visit, downtime, the usual number of sessions, how the price is calculated, aftercare and a booking button.
Injectable pages: neurotoxins, fillers and biostimulators

Clients search by product and by area: “Botox for forehead lines”, “Dysport vs Botox”, “cheek filler”, “Sculptra”. A page per area or product family answers those searches better than one injectables page. It names the products you use, explains pricing per unit or per syringe and states who injects — a physician, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or registered nurse, as your state allows.
Laser and skin treatment pages

Laser hair removal, IPL photofacials, resurfacing, RF microneedling and chemical peels attract different clients with different questions: skin type, number of sessions, the device, time off work. Facial and peel pages also compete with day spas, so they need the medical detail a spa cannot offer.
Body contouring and medical weight-loss pages

Fat reduction, muscle toning and skin tightening are researched for weeks and compared by device name and price per area. Medical weight-loss programs need extra care: who prescribes, what the first consultation includes, and no promise of a number of pounds lost.
Surgical procedures belong with a surgeon and have their own page on

Local SEO for med spas: Google Business Profile and “near me” searches

For “med spa near me” and “Botox near me” the map results take most of the clicks, and they depend on distance, the profile and reviews. The profile needs “Medical spa” as its primary category, secondary categories only where true, a services list with short descriptions, real photos of the rooms and team, hours and a booking link. Each location gets its own profile and its own page on the site, with directions, parking, the providers who work there and the treatments offered at that address — not every location has every laser.

Med spa provider and medical director pages: E-E-A-T for aesthetic treatments

Google treats pages about medical treatments as “Your Money or Your Life” topics and looks for experience, expertise and trust (E-E-A-T). Clients ask the same thing in plainer words: who will hold the needle? Each provider gets a page with the credential written as text — MD, NP, PA, RN or licensed aesthetician — training, the treatments they perform and a button to book with them. The medical director is named, with specialty and role.

State rules on who may inject, who must supervise and who may own a med spa differ and change. I build the pages around the arrangement you actually have; check the details with your state medical and nursing boards. Treatment pages carry a named clinical reviewer and a last-reviewed date, describe risks and side effects, and promise no outcome.
Prices, memberships and packages in SEO for med spas

“How much is Botox” and “lip filler cost” are typical questions before a first booking. A page that answers them — price per unit or per syringe, typical ranges by area, what the consultation costs and whether it is credited — keeps the comparison on your site. If you prefer not to publish exact prices, a range with an explanation still answers the search.

Memberships and packages deserve their own pages: what the monthly fee includes, how credits roll over, how a laser series is priced, financing and the manufacturer rewards programs you take part in. Existing clients search for these too, by your name and the word “membership”.
Before-and-after photos and reviews in med spa SEO: consent and FTC rules

Clients study galleries closely before booking. They help in search when each case has text: treatment, area, sessions, time between photos and provider. Photos go online only with the client’s written consent, taken in the same light and angle, without filters or retouching.

Reviews move a location up the map. A routine beats a campaign: a text with a direct review link after every visit, to every client. Paying or rewarding clients for reviews, or posting reviews by staff, breaks Google’s policies and the FTC’s rules on reviews and endorsements; the same rules cover influencers who get free treatments. Public replies never confirm that someone is a client or mention their treatment.
Instagram or search: how med spa clients find you when they are ready to book

Many med spas win their first clients on Instagram, and it remains good at showing results and personality to people who already follow you. It is weaker at the moment of decision: someone who types “lip filler in Austin” into Google or asks an assistant for a med spa nearby gets map listings, websites and directories first. SEO does not replace Instagram; it catches the demand Instagram creates. The cases, provider stories and treatment explanations you post can become pages that keep working after the post scrolls away.
I do SEO and websites; I do not run Instagram, paid social or ads.
Med spa SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Clients now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews questions like “Botox or Dysport for crow’s feet”, “how many laser hair removal sessions do I need” or “which med spa in Tampa has a nurse practitioner for lip filler”. An assistant builds its answer from sources it can compare — treatment pages, the map listing, review sites and directories — and favors a med spa whose facts agree across all of them. Getting a med spa into those answers goes by two names, GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization), and in practice it comes down to:
treatments, providers and credentials, the medical director, locations, hours and price ranges written as plain sentences
two- or three-sentence answers to frequent treatment questions, signed off by your medical director
the same business details on the site, Google, Yelp and RealSelf
structured data that connects the business, its providers and its locations

Strict rules on wording are no obstacle: Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan, works under tighter advertising rules than a med spa, and the new pages of the site I rebuilt for him are already quoted by ChatGPT. The method is described on the

Med spa sites tend to lose positions for the same reasons:

Most firms selling med spa SEO services are agencies that bundle SEO with ads, social media, email and often a website on their own platform, usually under a long contract. That suits a group that wants every channel from one supplier. With me there is no account manager in between: the person on your calls is the one who plans the treatment pages, edits your WordPress or Next.js site and walks you through the monthly numbers. Whoever you hire, ask who writes the clinical content, who approves it and who owns the site when the contract ends.

children.text: Med spa website design shapes what most clients see before they walk in, and I design and build the site myself, so the look, the booking flow and the code come from one person at one price. A medspa website has a narrower job than it seems: help someone who already wants a treatment choose you, trust the person who will perform it and book — usually on a phone, often late in the evening.
Medspa website first screen: treatments, location, provider and a booking button
Visitors arrive with a question, not to admire a hero video. The first screen answers it in four lines:
what you do and where — “Injectables, laser and skin treatments in Scottsdale”, not “Reveal your glow”
a booking button and a text or call button, the same on every page
the location, or each location, with hours
a sign of medical oversight: the medical director or the provider team, named
The membership offer, gallery and reviews sit below. On phones a fixed bar at the bottom holds Book and Text, so the client never has to scroll back up to act.
Med spa treatment menu design: navigation by treatment and by concern

A med spa menu grows fast: neurotoxins, fillers, biostimulators, lasers, peels, facials, body treatments, weight loss. Visitors think in two ways. Some know the treatment — “Morpheus8”, “lip filler”. Others know only the concern — “forehead lines”, “sun spots”, “loose skin after weight loss”. The navigation offers both routes: a treatment menu grouped into injectables, laser and skin, and body, and a page for each concern that links to the treatments used for it, without promising that any of them will fix it.

Every treatment page follows one template, so a client comparing two treatments finds the same facts in the same place: what it is, who performs it, the visit, downtime, sessions, price basis, aftercare, gallery cases and a booking button preset to that treatment. Your team adds a new device or product in the CMS without a designer.
Online booking on a med spa website: Boulevard, Mangomint, Vagaro and deposits

Most med spas already book through a system built for them — Boulevard, Mangomint, Vagaro, Zenoti or similar. The website does not replace it; it hands the client over at the right moment. Depending on what your system allows:
a booking button that opens the system’s own flow with the treatment or provider already selected
an embedded widget on treatment pages, loaded only when the client taps, so the page stays fast
a consultation request form for new clients and for treatments that need an assessment first

Deposits and cancellation terms are shown before booking starts, not as a surprise on the last step. New-client consultations are kept apart from rebooking: returning clients want two taps, new clients want reassurance first.
Membership, package and price pages on a med spa website

Memberships keep a calendar full, yet they are often explained in a block of small print. A membership page is designed like a product page: the monthly fee, what it includes, how credits roll over, member prices, how to cancel and a sign-up button that leads into your system’s membership checkout. Packages — a laser series, a facial program — get a small table that shows the price per session.
Prices are text, not images, and staff edit them in the CMS. Where you prefer ranges, the layout shows the range and what moves it: units, syringes, size of the area.
Before-and-after gallery design for med spas: consent, consistent photos, no editing

The gallery is where clients slow down and look closely, so it should help them judge rather than dazzle them. Each case shows the treatment, area, number of sessions, time between photos and the provider, with filters by treatment and concern. Design rules keep it honest:
photos published only with the client’s written consent, kept with the case record
the same light, angle and background before and after, no filters and no retouching
faces cropped or eyes covered where the client prefers
a short note that results vary, next to the photos rather than hidden in the footer
Thumbnails load first and open larger on tap, so a page with fifty cases still opens quickly.
Provider and medical director pages in med spa website design

Clients book a person as much as a treatment. Every provider gets a profile from one template: a real photo in your rooms, name and credential as text, training, the treatments they perform, languages and a “Book with” button. The medical director’s page explains the role in plain words — protocols, supervision, handling complications — without suggesting they perform every treatment when they do not.
In aesthetics, where clients look closely at faces, stock models are spotted at once. A half-day shoot of your team, rooms and devices does more for the site than any template image.
Med spa branding on the website: photography, typography and a calm visual style

Med spa branding often borrows from luxury hotels and cosmetics. It works while it stays calm: a short palette, one accent color kept for booking, a refined serif or sans for headings, space and real photographs. It stops working when it turns into sliders, discount pop-ups and countdown timers. Many clients are nervous about needles or about how they will look afterwards; the design should lower that tension, not add to it.

Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan, needed the same effect for people arriving in a state of anxiety. His site uses a dark base broken by light sections, a serif typeface whose italic is drawn separately, very few colors and nothing that hurries the reader. His profession has strict advertising rules, so the CMS warns the editor when a text contains wording his profession’s advertising rules make risky — promised outcomes, patient testimonials, discounts. A med spa site can carry the same kind of check for phrases like “guaranteed results” or “painless”.
Intake forms, consent and client privacy on a med spa website

Medications, allergies, pregnancy, past treatments — aesthetic medicine needs this information, but a website contact form is the wrong place for it. The public form asks for a name, contact details, the treatment of interest and a preferred time, with a note not to share medical details. Intake questionnaires and consent forms run in your booking or charting system, which is built for them. In the US, whether HIPAA applies depends on how the practice is set up; where it does, any form provider that receives health information signs a business associate agreement, and state privacy laws can add their own rules. Analytics and ad pixels stay off booking and intake pages.

About five years ago I worked on a medical software project with patient records; an NDA keeps its name private. It left me with one rule for clinic sites: ask online only for what the booking needs. Your compliance adviser confirms the final setup.
A med spa website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

When a client asks ChatGPT or Google’s AI Overviews which med spa nearby offers a treatment or has a nurse practitioner for lip filler, the answer is built from text the assistant can read. The build keeps treatments, providers and credentials, locations, hours, prices and membership terms in plain HTML rather than images or scripts, adds structured data for the business, its providers and locations, and matches your Google profile. Giuseppe’s site shows how this pays off: explicit rules for AI crawlers in robots.txt and structured data for the practitioner and services, and his new pages already appear in ChatGPT answers.

What makes them work sits further down: a treatment menu that fits a phone, booking two taps away, galleries with real cases, named providers and prices that answer the question. A builder template or a site from a med spa marketing vendor is a fair start for a new practice with one provider. A custom design pays off with several providers or locations, a long treatment menu, memberships and plans to grow from search.
