children.text: I do medical SEO for private practices and small clinics — dermatology, plastic surgery, med spas, physical therapy, chiropractic, primary care and specialist practices: procedure pages, a Google Business Profile for each location, reviews, booking and insurance pages. Medical practice SEO is measured in new patient appointments, not in traffic, and I do the work myself, from the audit to the code.
What medical SEO covers for private practices and small clinics
A patient choosing a dermatologist or a physical therapist usually looks in three places before booking:
the map results — three practices with a rating, hours and a phone number, shown first for “near me” searches
the regular results, where your site competes with Zocdoc, Healthgrades, WebMD and the hospital system in town
AI answers — Google AI Overviews and assistants like ChatGPT, which recommend practices by name

SEO for a medical practice works on all three: the website pages that answer what patients search, the Google profile, reviews, and the facts assistants read. Unlike a hospital, a private practice has a handful of locations and a short list of treatments it wants more of, so the work is focused and results are easier to trace.
Procedure and treatment pages in medical practice SEO

Patients search for the treatment or the problem, not for “a practice”: “Botox near me”, “mole removal”, “sciatica physical therapy”, “rhinoplasty cost”. One “Services” page cannot rank for all of them. Each treatment you want more of needs its own page: who it is for, what happens at the visit, recovery, a price range or insurance coverage, the clinician who performs it and how to book.
Dermatology and skin treatment pages

Medical and cosmetic dermatology bring different patients. Skin checks, acne and eczema are often covered by insurance; laser treatments, fillers and peels are paid out of pocket and compared by price. Separate pages keep each patient on the page meant for them.
Plastic surgery and med spa pages

Patients research for weeks and compare surgeons. They look for board certification, the steps of the procedure, recovery time, a price range and before-and-after photos — published only with written patient consent and without retouching.
Physical therapy and chiropractic pages

Searches are built around pain and injuries: “lower back pain”, “sports injury rehab”, “physical therapy after knee surgery”. Pages that explain the first visit, the usual number of sessions and whether a referral is needed answer what patients ask the front desk.
Primary care and specialist pages

For primary care the questions are practical: accepting new patients, same-day visits, which insurance. Specialists get many patients by referral, but the patient still searches the practice and the doctor’s name before the first visit.
Local SEO for medical practices: Google Business Profile for each location

For “dermatologist near me” or “chiropractor open Saturday” the map results decide most of the calls. They depend on the Google Business Profile: the right primary category (Dermatologist, Physical therapy clinic, Chiropractor, Medical spa), the services list, hours, real photos of the practice and a link to the matching page on the site, not the home page. A practice with two or three locations needs a profile and a page for each.

Google also allows profiles for individual practitioners. In a practice with several doctors they should be set up deliberately, so they support the practice listing instead of competing with it. Practices built around one or two physicians will find more on the
SEO for doctors
page.
Patient reviews in SEO for medical practices: Google, Zocdoc and Healthgrades

Reviews move a practice up the map and help patients choose between two names. A routine works better than a campaign: a short text after each visit with a direct link, sent to every patient, not only the happy ones. Buying reviews or rewarding patients for them breaks Google’s rules and, in the US, consumer protection rules on reviews.

Healthcare adds one rule other businesses do not have: a reply must not confirm that the reviewer is a patient or mention anything about their care. A polite, general answer that invites the person to call the office protects privacy and still shows readers that the practice responds.
Online booking and appointment forms on a medical practice website

Every extra step between the search result and an appointment loses patients. Online booking through your practice management system or a tool such as NexHealth or Zocdoc, a tap-to-call button at the top of each page and text reminders through a service like Weave cover most of them.

Forms need care. In the US, a form that collects health information can fall under HIPAA. The usual options are a form provider that signs a business associate agreement, or a form that asks only for name, contact details and a preferred time and leaves symptoms for the call. Tracking pixels on booking pages deserve the same caution. This is general guidance, not legal advice; your compliance adviser has the final word.
Insurance pages for medical practices: “does this doctor take my insurance”

Many patients filter by insurance before anything else: “dermatologist that accepts Medicare”, “physical therapy covered by Blue Cross”. A page that lists the plans you accept, per location if they differ, explains out-of-network visits and shows self-pay prices where you have them answers these searches and saves calls to the front desk. The list has to stay current: a wrong insurance listing brings angry reviews, not patients.
YMYL and E-E-A-T on medical practice websites: author, reviewer and date
Google treats health pages as “Your Money or Your Life” and expects clear experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust (E-E-A-T). For a practice this means:
each treatment page names the clinician who wrote or reviewed it, with credentials and a link to their bio
pages show a publication date and a “last reviewed” date
results are described with risks and alternatives, without guarantees
pages give general information, not individual medical advice, with a clear path to book a consultation
I write the structure, the search data and the drafts; your clinicians check and approve the clinical content before it goes live.
Technical SEO for medical practice websites: speed, booking widgets and schema
Most practice websites lose positions on the basics:
pages slowed down by booking widgets, chat pop-ups and video, taking longer than 2.5 seconds to show content on a phone
template sites from medical marketing vendors with the same text on hundreds of practices
practice name, address and phone written differently on the site, the profile and directories
no structured data — MedicalClinic or Physician — naming the practice, its specialties, locations and hours
If the site needs more than fixes, the
medical website design
page describes how I build practice websites.
Medical SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Patients now ask an assistant “which dermatologist in [town] does skin checks on Saturdays” or “is a chiropractor or a physical therapist better for back pain” before they open a single site. The answers come from what assistants can read and cross-check: your pages, your Google profile, reviews and directories. Getting into them is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a practice it means:
specialties, treatments, locations, hours, languages and accepted insurance written as plain facts
answers to common patient questions on the treatment pages, reviewed by a clinician
the same practice details on the site, the profile, Zocdoc and Healthgrades
structured data that connects the practice, its clinicians and its locations
I check how assistants describe your practice before and after the work. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Medical SEO and medical marketing: what an SEO specialist does and does not do

Medical marketing is the wider field: paid ads, social media, email, reputation management, sometimes a call center. Many firms that sell medical SEO are practice-marketing companies that bundle all of it with a website on their own platform. I am a single SEO specialist who also builds websites. I do not run ads or social media; I make the pages, the profile and the facts that search and AI answers rely on, and the site stays yours.

children.text: I design medical websites for doctors, private practices and clinics, and I build them myself, so the design and the build come from one person at one price. A medical website is opened by people who are worried, unwell or caring for someone who is — often on a phone, and often older than the average web user. The design has to make three things easy: choosing a doctor, understanding what the practice treats and booking a visit without waiting on hold.
Medical website design for patient trust: a calm layout and plain language

Patients do not choose a practice by its logo. They look for signs that the doctors are qualified, that the place is real and that the visit will be simple to arrange. A calm design helps them find those signs: generous white space, one accent color reserved for the booking button, readable type and no sliders that move while someone is trying to read.
The first screen of a practice website answers four questions, in this order:
who you are and what you treat — “Family medicine and pediatrics in [your town]”, not “Your health is our priority”
whether you are accepting new patients
how to book: online, by phone or both
address, hours and parking or transit, one line each
The language stays plain: “hypertension” once, then “high blood pressure”. Medical practice websites fail more often on jargon and on menus that copy internal departments than on looks.
Doctors website design: profile pages with credentials and photos of the real team

For many patients the doctor matters more than the clinic. Every physician, nurse practitioner and physician assistant gets a profile page, and doctors website design starts with that template, because it is reused more than any other:
a real photo taken in your own rooms, in natural light, framed the same way for everyone
full name, title, specialty and board certification, written as text
medical school, residency and hospital affiliations
languages spoken and the patients the doctor sees: adults, children, new patients
the services this doctor provides, linked to their pages, and a button to book with this doctor

Stock photos of models in white coats are recognized at once and work against you; a short session photographing the real team and rooms does more for trust. Group practices also get a page per location, listing the doctors who work there.
Web design for clinics: service and condition pages reviewed by a clinician

Patients search for what bothers them — knee pain, a skin check, a sports physical — and land on a service or condition page, not on the home page. Web design for clinics therefore gives each service and each main condition you treat its own page, laid out the same way: what it is in plain words, who it is for, what happens at the visit, how to prepare, whether insurance usually covers it, which doctors provide it and a booking button.

Google treats health content as “your money or your life” and holds it to a higher standard. The design makes room for the signals that standard looks for: the name and credentials of the clinician who wrote or reviewed the page, the date of the last review and sources where a page states facts. The site describes your services; it does not give medical advice, and every condition page leads to an appointment rather than to self-treatment.
Online booking, patient portal, telehealth and insurance in medical website design

Booking is the most important route through the site, and it should be a few taps from any page. On phones, a fixed bar at the bottom of the screen holds two actions: book and call. Behind the book button sits whatever your scheduling system offers — an embedded widget, a link to your booking page or a short request form when online self-scheduling is not possible.
Around it, patients look for:
a link to the patient portal for existing patients, kept apart from booking so new patients are not sent to a login screen
a telehealth entry: which visits can be done by video, how to join and what to prepare
insurance accepted: the plans you take, as a text list, and what self-pay patients pay for common visits
new-patient forms to fill in through the portal before the first visit
Accepted insurance belongs in text, not in a picture of logos: patients search the page for the name of their plan, and so do search engines.
Accessible medical website design: WCAG for older and visually impaired patients

Older adults are among the most frequent users of medical websites, and many of them see poorly, use a screen reader or find small targets hard to tap. Accessibility is part of the design from the first sketch and follows the WCAG guidelines:
body text of at least 16 pixels and contrast that meets WCAG level AA
large buttons with space between them, and links that say where they lead
forms with visible labels, clear error messages and no time limits
full keyboard navigation and a correct heading order for screen readers
captions on videos and text alternatives for images that carry information
I design to the guidelines and test the result with automated tools and a screen reader; your legal obligations toward patients with disabilities are a question for your lawyer.
Multilingual medical websites for patients who speak other languages

Many practices see patients who are more at ease in Spanish, Polish, Ukrainian or another language. A language switch that leads to one machine-translated page disappoints them. A multilingual medical website gives each language its own address, translated service pages and doctor profiles that say which languages each doctor speaks, so a patient can book with someone they can talk to.
I build the structure, the language switch and the search setup for each version; clinical wording in another language is checked by a clinician or a medical translator from your side.
Privacy-safe forms on a medical website: HIPAA and patient data

A contact form looks harmless until a patient types a diagnosis into it. In the United States, a form that collects health information for a practice can fall under HIPAA, and a service that receives that data may need to sign a business associate agreement. There are two safe ways to design for it:
keep clinical details off the website: the form asks for a name, contact details and a preferred time, and says plainly not to describe symptoms
where a clinical form is needed — intake, referrals, refill requests — run it through a form or portal provider that signs a business associate agreement, not through ordinary email

Analytics and advertising scripts are set up so that pages and forms do not pass health information to third parties. Whether a setup meets your legal obligations is confirmed by your compliance officer or lawyer.

I have built a medical system that handled patient data, under NDA, so I cannot name it. The rule I carry from that work into every medical website: collect as little health information on the site as the task allows.
A medical website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Patients increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which doctor nearby treats a condition, takes their insurance or speaks their language. Assistants answer from what they can read and check. The design keeps those facts in text and in structured data: doctors with their specialties and credentials, services, locations, hours, insurance plans and languages — matching your Google Business Profile and directories such as Healthgrades or Vitals.
Getting a practice into those answers is ongoing work, described on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page. Being found in Google for your specialty and town is covered on the
SEO for doctors
page; clinics with several departments or locations will find the
medical SEO
page more useful.
Medical website design templates and healthcare website templates vs a custom design

A medical website design template or a free healthcare website template looks complete in a demo, because the demo is filled with stock doctors and invented departments. With a real practice’s content the gaps show: one page for all doctors, no place for credentials, a contact form where booking should be, no language versions and accessibility nobody has tested.

A template is a fair start for a solo physician who needs an address, hours and a phone number online. A custom design pays off with several doctors or locations, online booking, more than one language or a dependence on new patients from search.
Best medical websites: what top medical clinic websites have in common

Lists of the top 10 medical websites mix hospital groups and small clinics; they give medical website design ideas only if you look past the budgets. What makes the best medical websites work fits a three-doctor practice too:
what the practice treats and where, stated on the first screen
booking visible on every page, with the patient portal kept separate
a profile for every clinician, with credentials and a real photo
service and condition pages written for patients, signed and dated
insurance, hours and directions as text
readable type, strong contrast and forms that work with a screen reader
How the medical website design process works
Brief. You send the list of doctors, services, locations and insurance plans, and the questions your front desk answers most often.
Patient paths. I map the three routes that matter — book a first visit, find a doctor, reach the portal — and agree them with you on a phone screen.
Design. The home page, a doctor profile and a service page are designed in full; the other pages follow the same system.
Build and checks. The site is built, booking and portal links are connected, and accessibility and forms are tested before launch.

children.text: Model portfolio website design is the service on this page: I plan, design, code and launch personal websites for fashion, commercial, fitness and runway models, and the whole job stays with me. Bookers, casting directors and clients first meet you on an agency board, through a referral or on Instagram, then look you up by name. A website for models is where that search should end: your current look, your stats and one clear way to reach you or your agent.
Model portfolio website: what agents, casting directors and clients check first

Someone building a casting list gives each model a few seconds, often on a phone between appointments. They want to know whether your look fits the brief and how to book you. The opening screen answers both:
one strong recent image instead of a grid of twenty
your name as real text, with height and the city you work from
“Represented by” with your mother agency and a link to your board page
buttons for polaroids, comp card and contact

The design stays quiet. Neutral type, generous white space and a restrained palette let the photos carry the page, and nothing in the layout needs changing when you cut your hair or dye it for a season.
Polaroids, digitals and an online comp card with current measurements

Agencies trust polaroids — digitals in US agency language — more than the book, because they show you as you are this month: daylight, no retouching, little or no makeup, plain fitted clothes, front, profile, full length and close-up. On the site they get their own page with the date of the set. You replace them from the editor after each new round, so nobody has to email you for “recent pictures”.

The comp card, called a zed card in much of Europe, becomes a page instead of a file: four or five images and your stats. Height, bust or chest, waist, hips, dress or suit size, inseam, shoe size, hair and eyes are fields in the CMS, shown in centimeters and in feet and inches, with US and EU sizes side by side. The same data builds a printable PDF, so a booker attaches this season’s card, not the one from two years ago.
Modeling portfolio website by category: editorial, commercial, fitness and runway

A catalog client looking for a warm, everyday face and a magazine editor looking for an editorial look should not scroll through the same mixed feed. The book is split into categories — editorial, commercial and e-commerce, fitness and sportswear, runway — and each gets its own short edit. Many models work in two of them; the home page then offers two entry points instead of one endless gallery.

Credits sit under each image: photographer, stylist, hair and makeup, and the client or publication where the work is out and you may name it. Test shoots are marked as tests. Photos stay sharp without making pages heavy: each one is saved in several sizes and modern formats, the first image loads at once and the rest load as the visitor scrolls.
The photographers you shoot tests with may want a site built on the same principles; theirs is covered on
photographer website design
Runway walk video and intro video on a model website

Casting teams more and more often ask for an intro video — name, height, agency and base city, said to camera in under a minute — and runway models add a walk video. Fitness models show a short movement clip; commercial models keep a recent self-tape. A video page holds them all, each behind a still frame, and the player starts loading only when someone taps it. The page stays fast on a phone even with several clips. Sasha Dith’s site, a DJ and producer’s portfolio I built, treats its video gallery the same way and opens in under one second.
Mother agency and booking contact on a model website

If you have a mother agency, it is named on every page with a link to your profile on its board, and placement agencies in other cities are listed under it. Booking requests then go through the agency, as most contracts expect: the contact button opens your booker’s email with your name already in the subject line. Freelance models, and models between agencies, get a direct form that asks for date, city, kind of job, image usage and budget, so each request arrives ready for an answer.

New faces use the same site to get signed. An agency’s first questions are height, city and current polaroids, and one clean link sends all three. For models under 18 a parent signs and manages the site.
Privacy on a model website: city only, no home address

The site names the city you work from, never a street. Location data is stripped from photos when they are uploaded, your email address sits behind a form so spam bots cannot collect it, and the polaroids page can live at an unlisted address you share only with agencies and clients.
Modeling portfolio examples: what strong model websites have in common
Search for modeling portfolio examples and most results are template galleries and design concepts. The model sites that work for bookers share a few plain habits:
a tight edit of fifteen to twenty-five images rather than every frame ever shot
polaroids from the last few months, with the date shown
stats right next to the photos, not three clicks away
one line about the agency and one contact path
the newest work first, even when an older campaign is better known

Design showcases on Dribbble or Behance rarely include polaroids or measurements; they show layouts. Use them for mood, then check every idea against what a booker needs from your page in the first ten seconds.
Instagram or a model website on your own domain

Instagram shows personality and fresh work, and casting teams do look at it. It is still a feed someone else arranges: the latest post is rarely your best, stats and agency details are squeezed into a bio, follower numbers pull attention from the pictures, and an account can be limited without notice. Models move between markets: a season in Milan, a few weeks in Paris or New York, a contract in Asia, then home. English is the working language of most castings, so it comes first. A second language helps when you also book clients in your home market — Polish, German, Spanish or Italian, for example. Each version gets its own addresses and hreflang tags, so Google shows the right one, and measurements switch units with the language. Whichever route you take, register the domain in your own name — not your agency’s and not a photographer’s.

children.text: Mortgage broker SEO is the work that brings home buyers and homeowners to your own website when they search for a loan, a program or a broker in their area, and turns those visits into applications and funded loans. I do it myself, as a single SEO consultant who also builds websites, for independent brokers, small brokerages and loan officers who want borrowers who found them, not leads shared with five other lenders.
What SEO for mortgage brokers covers: loan programs, local markets, compliance and AI answers

A borrower rarely types “mortgage broker”. They type their situation: “FHA loan with 580 credit score”, “VA loan for a condo”, “mortgage for self-employed with bank statements”, “first-time home buyer programs in Ohio”. Mortgage broker SEO puts a page on your site in front of each of those searches and makes it easy to start a conversation. The work covers:
a page for every loan program you offer and every borrower type you want more of
local pages for the cities and counties where you are licensed and active
licensing details and rate wording that hold up in a compliance review
a site that loads fast on a phone and leads to the application without detours
visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
Mortgage broker SEO and YMYL: NMLS ID, Equal Housing Opportunity and licensing on the website

Google treats mortgage content as “Your Money or Your Life” (YMYL): a wrong answer can cost a family real money, so pages need visible proof of who stands behind them. For a broker that proof is largely the same information regulators already expect:
the company NMLS ID and each loan officer’s NMLS ID, with a pointer to NMLS Consumer Access
the states where you are licensed, written as text, not only in a footer image
the Equal Housing Opportunity statement or logo (lenders often use “Equal Housing Lender”)
a named author with an NMLS ID on every guide, plus a “last reviewed” date

Federal and state rules generally treat a website as advertising, and some states add their own disclosure wording. This is a general description, not legal advice: your compliance team, sponsoring company or state regulator has the final word.
Rate pages and mortgage advertising rules: trigger terms and rates that stay accurate

“Today’s mortgage rates” pages attract searches, and they are also where most advertising problems start. Under Regulation Z, some figures in an ad — a monthly payment, a down payment, the number of payments — trigger extra disclosures such as the APR and the repayment terms. When I write or edit a page, I flag every trigger term and every rate claim so your compliance reviewer can approve, change or remove it.

A rate shown on a page must be true on the day someone reads it. If you publish rates, the page carries the date, the assumptions and the APR, and it updates from a source you control. A page that explains what moves rates and invites a personal quote often ranks better than a table that goes stale by Tuesday. In the UK, Canada and Australia, the FCA, provincial regulators and ASIC set their own rules; the approach is the same.
Loan program pages for mortgage brokers: FHA, VA, first-time buyer, self-employed and refinance

One “Loan Options” page listing eight products cannot rank for any of them. Each program you want to grow gets its own page: who it suits, typical requirements in plain words, documents to prepare, how long it usually takes and a clear next step.
FHA, VA and USDA loan pages: government programs with their own vocabulary

Government-backed loans attract precise searches: “VA loan funding fee”, “FHA loan limits” in a county, “USDA eligible areas” near a town. A page that answers these with your county’s details and your own experience with the program beats a generic national article.
First-time home buyer pages: down payment assistance and local programs

First-time buyers search for help as much as for a loan. State and city down payment assistance programs, homebuyer education courses and closing-cost grants are strong topics for local pages, as long as each program’s current status is checked before the page goes live.
Self-employed, investor and non-QM loan pages

Bank statement loans, DSCR loans for rental investors and other non-QM products are where a broker’s access to many lenders matters most. These borrowers have often been turned down by a bank, so the pages bring fewer visits but better applications.
Refinance and home equity pages
Refinance searches rise and fall with rates. Pages on cash-out refinance, rate-and-term refinance and HELOCs written now are already indexed and trusted when the next wave of demand comes.
Local SEO for mortgage brokers: city pages, Google Business Profile and reviews

“Mortgage broker near me” and “mortgage lender in [city]” searches show a map with three businesses. A Google Business Profile with the right category, your real office address and hours, and reviews that mention the loan type a client closed, is often the quickest source of calls. Brokers who meet clients at their homes rather than in an office can set a service area and hide the address, within Google’s rules.

City and county pages are worth building where you have a reason: you are licensed there, you close loans there, you know the local programs and the realtors. Fifty identical pages with only the city name swapped are a pattern Google discounts. The map side in depth — categories, reviews, listings — is on the
local SEO services
page.
Mortgage calculators and guides: content that wins searches before a borrower calls

Borrowers research for weeks: “how much house can I afford on $90k”, “closing costs in Texas”, “how long does pre-approval last”. Calculators and short guides answer those questions on your site instead of on a national portal. A calculator page needs clear assumptions and a note that results are estimates. Each guide ends with a link to the matching loan program page.
Realtor partnerships in mortgage broker SEO: co-marketing pages and referral rules

Much of a broker’s business comes from real estate agents, and search can strengthen those relationships. Neighborhood pages, open-house financing pages and joint guides with partner agents give both sides something to link to, and agents look up your name before referring a client.

Co-marketing between brokers and agents falls under federal rules on referral payments (RESPA): each side pays its fair share, and nothing of value is exchanged for referrals. Your compliance team sets the limits. Agents who want their own search work will find it on the
SEO for realtors
page.
Mortgage lead generation from your own site versus bought leads, measured in funded loans

Mortgage lead generation companies sell inquiries that are often sent to more than one lender at once, so the fastest caller wins. A borrower who found your program page and filled in your form chose you, and organic leads do not disappear when you stop paying. I report both sources side by side, by loan program and city:
calls and form submissions from search, tracked in GA4
started and completed applications, if your portal can pass the source back
pre-approvals and funded loans, if your LOS or CRM records where the borrower came from
Reports carry counts only, never borrower data. New program pages usually need three to six months to bring steady applications; in big metros, longer.
Mortgage broker website design: the path from search to application

Most loan officer websites provided by a lender are templates shared by hundreds of loan officers with the same text, so Google has little reason to rank any one of them, and the domain belongs to the lender. A broker’s own site, built where your company or sponsor allows it, can be fast and specific. What matters for the application path:
the main content of each page visible within 2.5 seconds on a phone
a short first form — loan goal, price range, state, contact — before any sensitive data
a clear handoff to your secure application portal for documents and full details
click-to-call and scheduling links visible on every page
accessible forms and text a screen reader can follow
If the site needs a rebuild, a focused broker site costs 700–1,400 € and a full site with program pages and calculators from 2,000 €, design included. The build is described on the
website development
page.
Mortgage SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Borrowers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews whether to use a broker or a bank, who does VA loans in their city, or how bank statement loans work. Because mortgages are YMYL, assistants prefer sources that show licensing and expertise. Work on those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a mortgage broker it means:
states, NMLS IDs, loan programs and languages spoken written as plain sentences
direct answers to borrower questions on program pages, with an author and a date
structured data that ties the company, its loan officers and its offices together
the same details on your site, Google Business Profile, Zillow and other lender profiles
Before the work starts and again after it, I ask the assistants about your market and record who they name. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Mortgage broker SEO consultant or a mortgage marketing company: who does the work

Mortgage marketing companies often bundle a website platform, a CRM, ads and lead lists on a long contract. I work alone: I read your search data, write the pages with your input, change the site on WordPress, Next.js or another system, and explain the report. I do not run ads or sell leads. Whoever you choose, ask who checks compliance wording and who owns the site when the contract ends.

children.text: Mortgage broker website design is the planning, design and build of a site that a borrower trusts with a first conversation about a loan: who you are, where you are licensed, what you can arrange and how to start. I do web design for mortgage brokers myself — independent brokers, small brokerages and loan officers allowed to run their own website — so layout, code and compliance details come from one person at one fixed price.
Mortgage broker website design: what the first screen tells a borrower

Borrowers reach a mortgage broker website from a realtor’s text, a search or a friend’s tip, usually on a phone, and a realtor deciding whether to refer you checks the same screen. Before the first scroll it answers four questions:
who you are — a face, a name and the company, not a photo of keys on a table
where you can lend — the states you are licensed in, written out
who you help most — first-time buyers, self-employed borrowers, veterans or investors, in one plain line
how to start — “Book a call” and a short form, plus tap-to-call for people who would rather talk
Rate tickers, stock photos of families on porches and slogan sliders push those answers out of sight.
Compliance built into mortgage website design: NMLS ID, Equal Housing and state licensing
Every page of a mortgage broker website is advertising, so licensing details belong to the design from the first sketch. I build them as fixed components that the site fills in by itself:
a footer on every page with the company name, company NMLS ID, office address and the Equal Housing Opportunity logo or statement
a licensing page listing each state with its license type and number and the state disclosures your licenses call for
each loan officer’s individual NMLS ID next to their name wherever they appear, including the form confirmation

When you add a state or a loan officer leaves, you change one record in the CMS and every page follows. This describes what US brokers commonly show, not legal advice: your compliance contact, sponsoring company or state regulator decides the exact wording.
Mortgage broker website design in the UK, Canada and Australia

Outside the US the same fixed places hold other details. In the UK: the firm’s FCA status and reference number, the repossession risk warning that mortgage promotions usually carry and how you are paid. In Australia: the Australian Credit Licence or credit representative number and a link to your credit guide. In Canada: the provincial license numbers of the brokerage and of each agent.
Rate disclaimers and dated payment examples in the CMS

Mortgage broker website content with numbers in it gets one extra rule. If you show a rate or a sample payment, the CMS asks for the date, the APR and the assumptions and will not publish the block without them. The date prints next to the figure, so last month’s example cannot pass for today’s offer, and your compliance reviewer sees every rate block in one list before launch.
A short first form on a mortgage broker website, then a booked call

An application-length form on the first visit loses people who are only starting to compare brokers. The site asks four or five things — purchase or refinance, rough price range, state, timeline, contact — and the confirmation screen offers a slot from your calendar. The full application happens later, in your own system.
no Social Security number, date of birth, income figures or account numbers on the website form
consent wording for calls and texts supplied by your compliance contact, with a box left unticked
each request tagged with the page and campaign it came from and sent to your CRM, email or both
spam protection that does not make borrowers solve puzzles
Secure document upload for mortgage borrowers: your portal, not email attachments

Pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns and bank statements should never sit in an inbox or travel as attachments. The website has no upload widget of its own; it sends borrowers to the secure portal of your loan origination system, point-of-sale platform or CRM:
an “Upload documents” button in the header that opens your portal login, so returning borrowers find it in one tap
a page that lists what borrowers are asked for at each stage, so files arrive complete
a short note on how their information is protected, consistent with your privacy notice
US financial companies work under federal rules for safeguarding customer information, UK and EU firms under GDPR; one secured system for documents makes both easier to follow.
Mortgage calculators on a broker website that show their assumptions

Borrowers use calculators for three real questions. I write them into the site’s own code rather than embedding a third-party widget, so they load fast, match the design and pass their result to your form.
affordability: income, monthly debts and down payment in, a price range out, with the debt-to-income limits used shown beside the result
payment: principal and interest plus property tax, homeowners insurance, mortgage insurance and HOA dues, each one editable
refinance: current balance and rate against a new loan, with closing costs and the month the switch breaks even

Every value the borrower does not type — sample rate, tax rate, insurance estimate — is visible, editable and dated. The result is labeled as an estimate, and one button carries the scenario into the short form, so you see the numbers before the call.
Loan officer profile pages and Google reviews on a mortgage broker website
Borrowers and realtors choose a person, not a logo. Each loan officer gets a page from one template:
a recent photo, a short first-person introduction and the languages they speak
their individual NMLS ID and the states where they are licensed
their own booking link and, if your system issues one, their personal application link
the kinds of borrowers they work with most, in a sentence or two

Reviews come from Google and other platforms with source, date and star rating as given, newest first rather than hand-picked five-star quotes, and never trimmed to change the meaning. US rules prohibit fake or misleading reviews and testimonials; showing them as written, with their source, stays clear of that.
Lender panel and “who we work with” on a mortgage broker website

A broker’s advantage over a bank is access to many lenders, and the site says so in words: how many wholesale lenders you work with, which kinds — banks, credit unions, non-QM lenders — and what that means for a borrower turned down elsewhere. A wall of logos says less and can cause trouble, since some wholesale lenders restrict use of their names and logos in consumer advertising; check your agreements first. A line on how you are paid, by the lender or by the borrower, answers a question many borrowers never ask aloud.
Speed, mobile layout and accessibility on a mortgage website

Most first visits happen on a phone, often from a link in a text message. The build aims at Google’s Core Web Vitals thresholds: main content visible within 2.5 seconds, an instant response to taps and no layout jumps while fonts or reviews load. Calculators and chat load only when someone uses them.

Accessibility matters twice: borrowers include older homeowners and screen reader users, and ADA accessibility claims against websites are common in the US. The site follows WCAG 2.2 AA — labeled fields, enough contrast, full keyboard use, announced error messages and calculators that work without a mouse.
Mortgage broker website templates and builders or a custom mortgage website

Many loan officers start with their lender’s page or a mortgage website builder with ready templates and a rate widget. That is sensible when you need a compliant page this week and most business comes from realtors and past clients who already know you.

A custom site pays off when the template looks like every other broker in your market, when calculators and forms should feed your CRM, when the domain and content must stay yours after a change of lender or software, or when you serve Spanish-speaking borrowers and need a real second version — see
multilingual website development
. Free mortgage broker website templates for WordPress sit in between: workable, but the licensing components, rate rules and portal handoff usually have to be added.
What the best mortgage broker websites have in common
a person and a licensed area on the first screen
a first step that takes under a minute
disclosures that are complete without crowding the page
calculators that explain their numbers
A landing page for mortgage brokers running ads

A campaign aimed at one audience — first-time buyers in one metro, a refinance offer — works better on its own page with one form and the same compliance footer than on the home page. I build these on the same system; see
landing page development

Borrowers now type questions into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews such as “a mortgage broker in Phoenix who works with self-employed buyers” or “a loan officer in Houston who speaks Spanish”. An assistant can only name someone whose details it can read, so the build keeps them as page text — names, NMLS IDs, licensed states, languages, borrower types, contacts — consistent with your Google Business Profile and NMLS record. FinancialService and Person markup describe the brokerage and each loan officer; disclosures are HTML, not images or PDFs.

children.text: Nonprofit website design is what I do for community organizations, foundations and charities, and I build the sites myself, so design and development come from one person at one price. A nonprofit site has more audiences than most: a donor deciding whether to give, a volunteer looking for a Saturday shift, a family looking for help, a program officer checking the organization before a grant, and a board member who just wants to fix a typo. The design gives each of them a short path and keeps the site easy for a small staff to run.
Nonprofit website design: what donors, volunteers and people seeking help look for first
The first screen answers four questions before anyone scrolls:
what the organization does and for whom, in one plain sentence — “Free after-school tutoring for kids in East Austin”, not “Empowering futures together”
where it works — the city, county or region
how to give — a Donate button that stays in the header on every page
how else to take part — volunteer, come to an event, or get help
People who need your services often arrive on a phone and in a hurry. A “Get help” link next to Donate keeps them from scrolling past fundraising appeals to find a phone number.
Donation page design for nonprofits: one-time and monthly gifts on a phone
The donation page is where design pays for itself. The visitor has already decided to give; every extra field, slow script or redirect is a reason to stop. The layout:
A one-time and monthly switch at the top, with monthly shown first if recurring gifts matter most to you.
Three or four suggested amounts, each with a line on what it pays for, written from your own figures.
An “other amount” field, name, email and card or wallet payment on one screen.
Optional extras below: a gift in honor or memory of someone, covering the processing fee, employer matching.
A thank-you page that says what happens next and offers one more step: share, volunteer or sign up for updates.

Payments run through a processor such as Stripe or PayPal, or through a donation platform such as Givebutter, Donorbox or GoFundMe Pro (formerly Classy). A form kept on your own page, in your own design, usually loses fewer donors than a jump to another site with a different look. How far a platform’s form can be embedded and styled differs, so I check yours before quoting. The emailed receipt carries the details the IRS expects in a donor acknowledgment; confirm the current wording with your accountant.
Mission, impact and program pages in website design for nonprofit organizations
Donors and grantmakers want to see what changes because of your work. Impact pages that persuade share a few habits:
figures you can document — people served, meals, hours of tutoring — with the year, as text rather than inside a graphic
one story per page with a real photo, used with the person’s consent, instead of a wall of stock smiles
a page for each program: who it serves, where, how to join or refer someone and who funds it
a donation option on each program page, if you accept gifts restricted to a program
A program on its own page also lets staff send one link to a partner or a family instead of writing the explanation again in every email.
Volunteer and event sign-up pages on a nonprofit website

Volunteers look for something concrete: a shift, a skill, a place. The volunteer page lists roles with the hours they take, age limits or background checks and where the work happens, then a short form or a link to the scheduling tool you already use. Each event gets its own page with the date, place, accessibility notes, a map and registration or tickets. Past events move to an archive on their own, so the site never invites people to last year’s gala.
Transparency on a nonprofit website: annual reports, Form 990 and your Candid profile
Before a larger gift or a grant, people check that the organization is real and well run. A transparency or “Financials” page puts the proof in one place:
the latest annual or impact report as a web page, with the PDF for printing
links to your recent Form 990 filings and to your Candid (formerly GuideStar) profile, plus Charity Navigator if you are rated there
the board and senior staff with names and roles
your EIN and 501(c)(3) status in the footer, so a donor can confirm them
Staff replace these each year from the admin panel; a report from four years ago raises more questions than it answers.
Accessible nonprofit website design to WCAG 2.1 AA

Many nonprofits serve older people, people with disabilities and people reading in a second language, so accessibility is part of the mission. The design targets WCAG 2.1 AA: contrast that passes, text that resizes, every action reachable by keyboard, labeled form fields with clear error messages, captions on video and alt text on photos. The donation form is tested with a screen reader before launch, because an inaccessible step there costs both a gift and a supporter.
Donor CRM integration for nonprofits: Bloomerang, Neon CRM or Salesforce
Most nonprofits keep donors in a CRM, and the website should feed it rather than start another list. In general terms:
donations, volunteer forms and newsletter sign-ups passing their data to the CRM you use — Bloomerang, Neon CRM, Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud or another — directly or through the donation platform
one email list, with consent recorded at sign-up
events and volunteer shifts run in the tool your team already knows, linked from the site
What can be connected depends on each tool’s options and your plan. I check that before the quote and do not promise a connection the tool does not offer.
Website builder or a custom website for a nonprofit
Much of the search for a website for a nonprofit is really a search for a free or cheap builder, and for some organizations that is the right answer.
When Wix, Squarespace or a free program is enough for a nonprofit
you are a new or all-volunteer group with one program and a donation link
someone on the board has time to build the site and keep it current
donations run through a platform’s hosted page anyway
free help fits your needs — Google for Nonprofits gives eligible organizations Google Workspace and other tools, and programs such as Free for Charity build basic sites; check their current terms
Wix or Squarespace? For a small nonprofit either works: Squarespace templates look tidy with little effort, Wix has a freer editor. Choose the one your volunteer finds easier to update.
When a custom nonprofit website pays off
several programs, locations or languages that each need their own pages
a donation page on your own domain, designed for your appeals and campaigns
donor CRM and donation platform working together without copy-paste
staff turnover — an admin panel where a new coordinator adds an event without breaking the layout
control over speed, accessibility and search settings that a builder limits
Best nonprofit websites and nonprofit website templates: patterns worth copying
Lists of the best nonprofit websites mix global charities with small local groups. Across budgets the same patterns repeat:
a mission sentence and a Donate button on the first screen
real photos of the people and places the organization works with
impact told with a few documented figures and one story
a separate path for people who need help
one accent color kept for the donation button

Nonprofit website templates copy the look of these sites, rarely the structure: one generic “Our work” page, a Donate button that opens a bare payment link, no place for reports. When you browse nonprofit website design examples for ideas, look past the home page at the donation and program pages.

Donors and volunteers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which organizations work on a cause in their city. Assistants can only mention what they can read. The design keeps the mission, programs, service area, EIN, walk-in hours and contacts as page text, adds structured data for the organization and keeps key facts out of images, sliders and PDFs.

children.text: I do optometrist website design for eye care practices and optical shops, and I build the sites myself, so the layout, the code and the booking setup come from one person at one price. Visitors to an eye care website are often reading without their glasses, on a phone, sometimes right after an exam with dilated pupils. That one fact shapes most of the decisions below.
The first screen of an optometrist website: exam booking, offices and frames
Someone opening your site wants one of four things, and the first screen points to each of them without scrolling:
book an eye exam — the main button, in the one accent color the site uses
find the nearest office, with today’s hours and a tap-to-call number
see which frames and brands you carry
reorder contact lenses or pick up glasses that are ready

The headline says what you are and where: “Eye exams, glasses and contact lenses in [your town]”, not “See the world clearly”. A rotating slider with brand campaign images looks good in a vendor demo and hides all four actions on a phone.
Accessible optometrist website design for visitors with low vision
An eye care practice has more visitors with poor eyesight than almost any other business, so accessibility here is the brief itself. I design to the WCAG guidelines and test the result:
body text of at least 18 pixels on phones, line spacing that keeps lines apart, no light gray text on white
contrast at WCAG level AA or better, including buttons and form fields
layouts that still work when the browser zooms to 200% or the phone uses large system text
no text inside images, so screen readers and zoom both work
clear focus outlines and full keyboard navigation
Low-vision patients notice when a practice that treats eyes has a site they cannot read. The opposite is a quiet sign of care.
Eye exam booking on an optometry website: three steps from any page

Booking follows the order people think in: choose the office, choose the type of visit — routine exam, contact lens fitting, child’s exam, dry eye or an urgent problem — then a time. The scheduling itself comes from the system you already run — its embedded calendar or booking link — and where patients cannot pick slots themselves, a three-field request your front desk answers. On a phone, “Book” and “Call” stay pinned to the bottom edge of every page.

The confirmation page tells people what to bring: current glasses, contact lens boxes, the insurance card and a list of medications. It also says whether the exam includes dilation, so nobody arrives planning to drive straight back to work.
A frame catalog on an optical shop website: brands, real photos and reservations

Frames are what people browse for fun, and a catalog gives them a reason to visit the shop. It works as a catalog, not an online store: filters by brand, shape, material, size and price; real photos taken on your shelves; and a “reserve to try in store” button that sends the frame and the office to your staff. I built the same pattern — filters, a map, structured listings — for a real estate catalog in Cyprus.

Your staff update frames in a simple editor, one entry per model with several photos. Virtual try-on tools exist and can be embedded, but they are heavy on phones; I add one only if your patients ask for it.
Contact lens reorders and insurance details on an eye care website

Existing patients who wear contacts need one short path: name, contact details and the office, sent to your staff, who look up the prescription on file and reply with the price and pickup date. No prescription details typed into the form, no uploads through plain email. This keeps reorders with you instead of with an online seller.

Insurance is shown as text in a short table: vision plans and medical plans accepted, per office if they differ, plus a line on what happens with plans you do not take. Logos alone fail twice — screen readers skip them and nobody can search the page for a plan name.
Calm design for an eye care practice: doctor profiles and real photos

Trust comes from seeing the people and the place. Each optometrist gets a profile with a real photo taken in your own exam room, the OD degree, license, fellowships, languages and the days they work at each office. Photos of the frame wall, the waiting area and the equipment replace stock models in white coats.

For Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan, I designed a calm site for anxious visitors: a dark theme with light sections, a serif with a true italic, a map of his three consulting rooms. An eye care site needs a lighter palette, but the same restraint — one accent color, generous spacing, nothing that moves while someone is reading.
Privacy-safe forms on an optometry website: HIPAA and patient data

Patients will type anything into an empty message box, including a diagnosis or their last prescription. For a US practice that information is likely protected under HIPAA, and any outside service that stores it may need a business associate agreement with you. Three design choices avoid most of the risk:
general forms ask for a name, contact details, office and preferred time, and say plainly not to describe symptoms
intake forms and prescription questions go through your practice management system or a form provider that signs a business associate agreement
analytics and advertising scripts never run on booking and reorder pages

Years ago I worked on a medical system that processed patient records; it is under NDA and stays unnamed. The habit it left me: a practice website should hold the least health data its job needs. Whether a setup meets your obligations is confirmed by your compliance adviser.
An optometrist website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Questions like “which eye doctor near me fits contacts for astigmatism” or “who sees kids and takes my vision plan” now go to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews as often as to the search box. An assistant can only repeat facts it finds as text. So offices, doctors and their credentials, services, hours, languages and plans live in HTML and structured data, word for word the same as on your Google profiles.
Giuseppe found me by asking ChatGPT, and the new pages of his site already appear in ChatGPT answers. Earning a place in those answers takes steady work after launch — see the

page; ranking in Google for exams and frames in your town is covered on the

page.
Eye care website templates from vendors vs a custom optometrist website

Eye care vendors such as iDoc, EyeCarePro and iMatrix sell websites on their own platforms, often with marketing services attached. For a single office that needs an address, hours and a booking link, that can be enough. The limits appear later: shared template text, a frame section that is a row of brand logos, little control over speed, and a site you cannot take with you if you leave.

A custom site belongs to you — code, content and domain. Leaving a vendor platform does not have to cost rankings: I list every old URL and point it at its new home with a 301 redirect before launch. Giuseppe’s practice kept all 468 blog posts this way, each old address redirected.
Best optometry websites: what the good ones have in common
Galleries of the best optometry websites mix national chains and small practices. What the good ones share fits a two-office practice too:
exam booking visible on every page, with the type of visit chosen before the time
an office page for each location, with doctors, hours and plans
frames shown from the real shelves, by brand
text that stays readable at large zoom
a reorder path for contact lens wearers

Eye exam pages in optometry SEO: routine, pediatric and medical eye care

A person searching for an exam wants to know what happens, how long it takes, what it costs without insurance and whether there is a slot soon. One page per type of visit answers that better than a list.
Routine and pediatric eye exams
Parents search for a child’s first eye exam and for back-to-school vision checks. The page says what is checked at each age, how long the visit lasts, whether pupils are dilated and what to bring.
Medical eye care: dry eye, red eyes and diabetic eye exams

Visits billed to medical insurance rather than a vision plan — dry eye evaluation, eye infections, diabetic eye exams, glaucoma monitoring — bring people who search for a symptom. Each page describes the visit and the options in general terms and leads to booking. No page promises a result.
Myopia management for children

Parents of nearsighted children search for myopia control lenses, orthokeratology and atropine drops. These pages explain the options, who they suit and that results differ from child to child, and they name the optometrist who reviewed them.
Vision insurance pages for eye care practices: VSP, EyeMed and medical plans

Many patients start from their benefits: “eye doctor that takes EyeMed”, “VSP provider near me”, “does Medicare cover eye exams”. A page that lists the vision and medical plans you accept, per office if they differ, explains why a dry eye visit is billed differently from a routine exam, and shows self-pay prices for an exam and a contact lens fitting ranks for those searches and takes pressure off the phones. Someone has to own that list: a plan you dropped last spring, still listed, turns into an angry one-star review.
Frame brand and lens pages: optical shop SEO that brings buyers

People search for frames by brand — “Oakley frames near me”, “Tom Ford eyeglasses” plus a city, “Lindberg dealer” — and by lens type: progressives, blue-light filters, sports and safety glasses. A page for each brand you carry, with photos from your own shelves, a price range and a line on fittings, catches searches that a row of logos never will. Brands with selective distribution deserve their own page: being an authorized dealer is a fact buyers look for.

Contact lens pages work the same way: fittings for astigmatism and multifocal lenses, specialty and scleral lenses, and a clear reorder path for existing patients, so they do not drift to online sellers.
Patient reviews in optometry SEO: Google, Yelp and privacy-safe replies

Reviews move a practice up the map and decide between two nearby offices. A routine works better than a campaign: a text after every exam or glasses pickup with a direct link, sent to every patient. Rewarding reviews or asking only satisfied patients breaks Google’s rules and the FTC rules on reviews and endorsements.

Replies need one extra care in healthcare: never confirm that the reviewer is a patient and never mention a prescription or a visit. Thank the person, keep it general and offer a phone number for the office manager; readers see a practice that listens, and nothing private is said. A complaint about a late order or a broken frame can be answered more concretely, as long as no health detail appears.
E-E-A-T and HIPAA on an optometry website: reviewer, credentials and safe forms

Google holds eye health pages to the same standard as other “Your Money or Your Life” topics. Each clinical page names the optometrist who wrote or reviewed it, with the OD degree, state license and any fellowship, and shows a “last reviewed” date. I prepare the structure, search data and drafts; your doctors check clinical content before it goes live.

Booking and contact forms collect as little as possible: name, contact details, office and preferred time. If a form must collect health details, it runs through a provider that signs a business associate agreement under HIPAA, and tracking pixels stay off booking pages. This is general guidance; your state board and compliance adviser have the final word on advertising and privacy.

children.text: I design orthodontist websites and write their code myself; there is no hand-off between a designer and a developer, and the quote is a single figure. An orthodontic site serves two very different visitors — a parent deciding about a child’s treatment and an adult who wants straighter teeth without anyone at work noticing — and both have to reach a consultation request without hunting for it.
Orthodontist website design for parents and adult patients: the first screen

The home page gives each visitor a door. One block for “Braces and early treatment for children and teens”, one for “Clear aligners and discreet braces for adults”, a single consultation button and the phone number under both. Below that, one line each: the orthodontist’s name and specialty, the offices, and how payment works.

Stock photos of grinning teenagers and moving sliders do not belong here. A photo of your own treatment room and team, in natural light, tells a parent more about the practice than any slogan, and a calm layout with one accent color for the booking button keeps attention where it should be.
Pages for parents on an orthodontist website: age, first visit and treatment timeline

Parents read on phones, often in the car outside school. A child’s treatment is easier to follow as a timeline than as paragraphs: first check, observation visits if it is too early, a first phase if needed, braces or aligners, then retainers. I design it as a row of short steps, each with the usual age range and how often the family comes in, written and dated by your orthodontist.

The first-visit page shows what happens in the chair, how long it takes, whether a parent can stay and which records are taken. These are the details that decide whether the parent of a nervous ten-year-old calls.
Braces vs clear aligners: comparison pages for adult orthodontic patients

Adults compare options side by side, so a comparison table does more than three separate sales pages: visibility, typical length range, visit frequency, eating and cleaning, what the patient has to do every day. Each column links to the full page for that option, with the orthodontist who provides it.

The adult section uses photos of adult patients, shared with consent, not teenagers, and offers a way to ask a question in writing for people who cannot call during work hours. Discretion is part of the design, not only of the treatment.
Before-and-after smile galleries on an orthodontist website: consent and honest photos
The gallery is the most visited page on many orthodontic sites, and its design keeps it honest:
written consent for every case, signed by a parent or guardian for minors, kept in the practice records
the same views — front, both sides, bite — and the same lighting before and after
no retouching, whitening or cropping that hides crowding
the treatment and its length next to each case, and a plain note that results vary
filters by treatment and age group, so an adult does not scroll through teenagers
image descriptions that name the case type for screen readers, never the patient
Treatment cost and payment plan pages on an orthodontic website

Cost works best as a set of cards: one per treatment, each with a price range, what it includes and a sample monthly plan. A payment calculator can help if it shows ranges and states its assumptions; it must never look like a quote. Insurance and flexible spending accounts get a short, plain paragraph rather than a wall of logos.

If your consultation has no fee, the card says what it includes, right beside the button. How such offers may be worded depends on your state board, so check before launch. Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan, works under Italian rules on advertising health services, so his editor flags any draft that promises an outcome, quotes a patient, mentions a discount or offers a “free consultation”. A similar check can flag the phrases your own board restricts.
Online booking and virtual smile assessments on an orthodontist website

Every page leads to the consultation request. On a phone it stays within thumb reach in a bar pinned to the bottom of the screen, next to the phone number. Tapping it opens your scheduling system’s online booking, or a short request form asking for a name, contact details, the patient’s age group and the preferred office — nothing clinical.

Virtual consultations, where a patient uploads photos of their teeth, suit adults and families far from an office. Those photos are health information, often of a child’s face, so they go through a service that has signed a HIPAA business associate agreement with the practice, never through email or an ordinary form. I design the flow around the provider you choose, and your compliance adviser approves it. Five years ago I helped build a system for patient records, under an NDA that keeps its name private; it taught me to let a public website store nothing clinical it can do without.
Multi-office orthodontic websites: an office finder with days, doctors and directions

Practices with several offices need an office finder: a map and a list, each office with its own page showing the days it is open, the orthodontists who treat there, parking, the entrance and a photo of the front door. Families choose by the school run, so the list can show nearby towns, and the request form asks which office suits them.

Giuseppe’s site follows the same pattern on a smaller scale: one map showing where he sees clients — Milan, Monza, Cernusco sul Naviglio — a page for each place and a separate page for online sessions with Italians abroad.
Orthodontist profile pages and a section for referring dentists

Parents and dentists both read the doctor page. It shows the dental degree, the specialty residency, board certification where it applies, years in practice and the offices where the orthodontist sees patients, with a real portrait. Assistants and coordinators get a photo and a line each; families meet them more often than the doctor.

Referring dentists get a small section of their own: how to refer, a form that sends records through a secure provider, what you report back after the first visit and a direct number. Two pages save a busy dental office a phone call for every referral.
Pages for current orthodontic patients: emergencies, appliance care and aligners

Patients in treatment visit the site more often than new ones. A section for them keeps the home page clear and reduces calls: what to do about a poking wire or a loose bracket, which problems need a call the same day, cleaning around braces, how long to wear aligners and how to clean them, retainer care, and the link to the patient portal or payments. Short videos recorded by your own team work better here than stock footage.

Parents ask AI assistants which orthodontist nearby treats young children, has evening hours or offers monthly plans. The replies are assembled from page text the assistant can parse and compare with your Google profiles. The design keeps those facts in the page itself, not inside images: offices with days and hours, ages treated, treatments, languages, payment options, and structured data that connects each orthodontist to each office. children.text: Personal injury SEO is the work that brings people hurt in an accident to your firm’s website when they search for help, and turns those visits into calls and signed contingency cases. I do SEO for personal injury attorneys myself, as a single consultant who also builds websites, and I start where your firm can realistically win, because in this market the head terms belong to firms with national budgets.
Why SEO for personal injury lawyers matters: injured people search before they call

After a crash or a fall, most people do not have a lawyer’s name. They search from a phone, sometimes from a hospital bed or the roadside: “do I need a lawyer after a car accident”, “truck accident lawyer near me”, “how much is my settlement worth”. The firm whose page answers that search, and whose phone is answered, gets the call.

Referrals still matter, but the referred client also searches your name and compares you with the firms they see. TV and billboards make people remember a name; search decides who they call when the moment comes. SEO for personal injury law firms is how a smaller firm takes part in that decision without matching the advertising budgets of the largest firms.
SEO for personal injury law firms: the hardest legal search market

Personal injury is the most contested corner of legal search. Ad clicks for these terms are among the most expensive in Google Ads, because a single signed case can be worth a great deal to the firm. For “car accident lawyer” in a large city you compete with:
firms that have invested in SEO for years, with hundreds of pages and reviews
national advertisers and lead-generation sites that sell the same enquiry to several firms
directories, legal information sites and Local Services Ads above the regular results
That is why personal injury SEO agencies charge more than general SEO shops, and why big-city PI firms often spend on SEO what smaller firms spend on their entire marketing.
A personal injury SEO strategy against national budgets: start with a narrow case type or a suburb

A single consultant cannot outspend those firms, and I will not pretend otherwise. For a big-city PI firm, a page aiming at “car accident lawyer [big city]” from day one usually means a year of costs with little to show. The strategy I propose instead:
pick one case type where competition is thinner and your firm has real experience — motorcycle crashes, dog bites, rideshare accidents, premises cases
or pick the suburb or county around your office, where national firms have no real presence
build the strongest pages on the web for that niche, collect reviews from those clients, and only then widen to the next case type or area
For a PI firm in a mid-size city or a small town the picture is different: there the main terms are often within reach, and the work can start broader.
The same approach for any practice area — choose what to win first, then fix the profile, the pages and the reviews — is laid out in the
attorney SEO guide
Case-type pages for personal injury attorney SEO

Each case type you take gets its own page, because injured people search for what happened to them, not for “personal injury”. A good case-type page explains the steps after the accident, who usually pays, the evidence that matters, typical deadlines in your state described in plain words, and how your firm handles that kind of case.
Car accident and truck accident lawyer pages

Car accident pages split further into rear-end collisions, uninsured drivers, rideshare crashes and accidents with injured passengers. Truck accident pages deal with commercial carriers, trucking regulations, black-box data and several insurers at once — searchers and their cases differ, so the pages do too.
Motorcycle accident, slip and fall and dog bite pages

Motorcycle riders face bias from insurers and juries, and the page should show that the firm knows it. Slip and fall pages explain premises liability and what to photograph at the scene. Dog bite pages cover owner liability rules in your state and what to do about medical records and animal control reports.
Wrongful death and medical malpractice pages: the most careful tone

Families searching after a death read slowly and are sensitive to any sales tone. These pages need calm language, clear explanations of who may bring a claim and how long it may take, and a quiet way to contact the firm. Medical malpractice pages should be cautious about outcomes and explain expert review in general terms.
City and case-type pages for personal injury law firms without doorway spam

“Car accident lawyer in [suburb]” pages work when they contain something specific to that place: the dangerous intersections and highways, the courthouse where cases are filed, the hospitals and trauma centers nearby, the police department that writes the reports, reviews from clients who live there. A hundred pages that only swap the town name are doorway pages; Google filters them and they weaken the whole site.
I build city pages one at a time, for places where the firm has clients and an office or court presence, and link each from the matching case-type page.
Personal injury SEO keywords: what injured people type
The obvious terms are the hardest. Many signed cases start from longer searches that show a real person with a real problem:
questions — “what to do after a car accident that wasn’t my fault”, “how long does a personal injury claim take”
money — “who pays my medical bills after an accident”, “average settlement for a back injury”
specific situations — “hit by an uninsured driver”, “injured as an Uber passenger”, “bitten by neighbor’s dog”
I pull the volumes for your state and city, check which searches show AI Overviews and Local Services Ads, and give each topic one page.
Contingency-fee messaging on a personal injury website

Most PI clients worry about cost before anything else, so “you pay nothing unless we recover compensation” belongs high on the page. But this message is regulated: several states require that it be accompanied by an explanation of whether the client may owe case costs and expenses, and how the fee percentage is calculated. A short, clear section on how your contingency fee works answers the client’s main fear and keeps the wording within your state bar’s rules — check them before publishing; the final wording is yours.
Intake speed for personal injury firms: calls, chat and callbacks
In personal injury, a visitor who reaches voicemail calls the next firm. SEO traffic is wasted if intake does not answer quickly, so part of my work is checking the path from search to conversation:
the phone answered around the clock, by staff or an answering service that knows which questions to ask
chat that reaches a person or a callback within minutes, not a form that waits until Monday
click-to-call at the top of every mobile page and a short form with a notice not to send confidential details
a test call and a test form at night and on a weekend, to see what a real visitor gets
Intake staffing is your decision; I show where search visitors are lost and make the site side fast.
Settlements, verdicts and reviews on a PI website: disclaimers bar rules require

Results pages persuade, and they are among the most regulated content on a law firm site. State bar rules commonly require a disclaimer that past results do not guarantee a similar outcome, and some states set conditions on how settlements and verdicts are described. Each result should state the case type and, where your rules require it, whether the figure is gross or net of fees. Reviews and testimonials follow the same caution. I build these pages with space for the disclaimers your state requires.

These are YMYL questions, and assistants prefer sources that show who wrote them and where the law applies. the case types you take, counties you serve, languages and fee structure written as plain facts
structured data and directory profiles that agree with each other
