children.text: I design and build personal trainer websites for independent trainers who coach in a gym, in clients’ homes, in a park or online. One person does the design, the code and the launch, for one fixed price. Instagram shows how you train. The website answers what a ready-to-start client checks before paying anyone: where you train, what a package includes, what it costs, how to book a first meeting and how to pay — all without sending you a DM.
Personal trainer website design: what the first screen tells a new client

Most people open a trainer’s site on a phone, from your Instagram bio, a Google search or a link a friend sent. In a few seconds they look for three answers: is this coach for someone like me, can I train with them where I live, and what happens if I tap the button. The first screen answers all three in text:
who you train and how, in one sentence — “Strength coaching for women over 40, in Denver gyms and online”
your formats: gym, in-home, outdoor, online, small group
one main button, the same on every page: “Book a free consult” or “See packages”

Photos come from a real shoot where you actually work. You correcting someone’s squat sells better than a model on a stock image. A short looping video can work too, as long as it is compressed and does not hold up the page on mobile data.
In-person and online personal training: two offers on one website

An in-person client and an online client buy different things. The local client cares about the gym or the home visit, time slots, travel radius and session length. The online client cares about the app, how the program arrives, how often you review form videos and answer messages, and what happens in a week they miss. Mix both on one page and each reader skips half of it.

So the home page splits visitors early — “Train with me in Denver” and “Coaching online, anywhere” — and each format gets its own page, packages and button. Hybrid clients, who see you twice a month and follow your app plan in between, get a block on both pages. People also search for an “online personal trainer and nutritionist”: if you hold a nutrition credential, the page names it and its scope; if not, it says you give general eating guidance and refer to a registered dietitian.
Personal training packages and prices on the website
Price is the question people hesitate to ask and most want answered. You decide whether to show exact amounts or a starting price; either way the package page makes the structure easy to compare:
a single session, packs of 10 or 20, or a monthly plan
session length, place and the travel fee for in-home training
what happens between sessions: an app program, form checks, messaging hours
how long a pack stays valid, how to pause, the cancellation window

Three packages side by side read well on a phone; a fourth usually belongs on its own page. Packages are stored in the CMS as fields — name, number of sessions, price, what is included — so a price change takes a minute and cannot break the layout.
Booking and payments on a personal trainer website
Two moments turn a visitor into a client: a booked first meeting and a paid package. The site handles both, so you are not chasing anyone through direct messages.
Booking a free consult or a paid assessment

The consult button opens a calendar with consult slots only — from Calendly, Acuity or the booking module of your coaching app — or a short form: name, contact, the goal in one line, in person or online, preferred times. Screening questions about injuries or a doctor’s clearance go to your inbox or app, never to a shared spreadsheet, and the form asks only what you will use. A line under the button says how long the consult takes and that nothing has to be bought on the spot.
Taking payment for packages, deposits and monthly plans

Package buttons lead to Stripe Checkout or to your coaching app’s checkout: one-off packs, monthly plans billed automatically, or a deposit that holds the first session. Cancellation and refund terms sit next to the button in plain words, and a confirmation email tells the client what happens next. Card details never pass through your website; the payment provider handles them.
Selling workout programs online from your personal trainer website

A ready-made program — a 12-week strength plan, a return-to-training course after pregnancy, a mobility series — sells while you coach other people. The weak spot is delivery: a PDF or video link that one buyer forwards to a group chat of twenty.

For Landi Room, a beauty salon in Warsaw, I built a landing page for an online hair treatment course on Next.js and Sanity, with Stripe Checkout. Payment triggers an automatic email with a unique video link. That link stops working 14 days later, and there is no download button or file to pass around. More than 100 people bought the course from the first Google Ads campaign, and nobody got access without paying. A trainer’s video program fits the same setup: a sales page showing the plan week by week, the equipment and who it suits, then payment and access with no files sent by hand.
Client results on a personal trainer website: before-and-after photos with consent

Before-and-after photos are the most persuasive part of a trainer’s site and the easiest to get wrong. A story goes live only with the client’s written permission for the photos, the name or initials and the quote. In the CMS each story has a consent field; without it, the story stays in draft, and removing one when a client asks takes a click.

Captions describe what the client did — three sessions a week for five months, a first pull-up, back pain gone in their own words — rather than promising the reader a number of pounds by a date. A line near the gallery says results depend on the person, their health, sleep and food. In the US, testimonials used in advertising fall under the FTC’s endorsement guides, so check the wording around them with your adviser.
Local search for in-home personal trainers: “near me” and service areas

People type “personal trainer near me”, and “in-home personal trainer near me” alone gets about 1,300 searches a month in the US. Google answers from your Business Profile, the location written on your site and pages that match the query. So the site names the gym you work from, with the address and a map. If you travel to clients, a service-area page lists the neighborhoods or ZIP codes you cover and how the travel fee works, while your Business Profile keeps your home address hidden. Two gyms mean two short pages with their own details.
Reviews come from clients you ask after a few weeks of training, on Google; the site links to them instead of copying them. Growing local visibility month by month is the work described on
local SEO services
; the website gives that work pages to point at.
Coaching app, template or your own personal trainer website

Coaching platforms such as Trainerfu, PT Distinction and FitBudd include a simple trainer website, and Wix or Squarespace sell personal trainer website templates. If you are starting out, train in one gym and need four pages, a template is enough — I will say so on the first call, and the budget is better spent on a photo shoot.

Your own site pays off when you sell local and online coaching side by side, sell programs, need area pages or a second language, or expect to switch apps one day. The app keeps the training itself — programs, check-ins, progress logs. The site takes the first impression, search, booking and sales, and links to the app for login. Before signing with any platform, ask whether your domain, pages and addresses stay yours when you leave.
What the best personal trainer websites have in common
Lists of the best personal trainer website examples mostly show handsome home pages. What the useful ones share is less visible:
the city, or “online”, in the first line
one button, repeated, leading to a consult
packages explained before anyone has to ask
a real face and the real training place
pages that open fast on a phone

Speed is the point people forget. On the site I built for Sasha Dith, a DJ and producer, video and music load only when needed, and pages open in under one second, replacing slow builder pages. The look follows your brand — a powerlifting coach and a Pilates-based trainer should not resemble each other — while the order of information stays the same.
A personal trainer website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Ask ChatGPT for a trainer who works with beginners in your part of town, or read Google’s AI Overview for an online strength coach, and the answer is assembled from pages the assistant could read. Your site gives it facts as text: name, certifications by name and issuing body — NASM, ACE, NSCA or ACSM, for example — formats, area, languages and starting price. Structured data describes you as a person and your services, FAQ answers are marked up, pages arrive from the server as ready HTML, and robots.txt states which AI crawlers may read them.

Credentials belong in text, not only in a strip of logos: assistants do not read logos. Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan who works alone, as most trainers do, already sees new pages of the site I built for him in ChatGPT answers. The ongoing side of this is on the

children.text: I do SEO for pest control companies: your site, your Google Business Profile and the pages people land on after spotting droppings in the pantry or winged ants by the window. Pest control lives on repeat visits — a customer won on one bed bug call can stay on a quarterly plan for years — so each new customer from search is worth far more than the first invoice. I work alone and also build websites, so whoever finds a problem on your site fixes it too.
Pest control SEO keywords: what people type when they find a pest
Pest searches often start with a problem the customer cannot name yet. Before any page is written I pull search data for your pests and towns, and the phrases fall into four groups:
identification — “small brown bugs in bed”, “what do termite droppings look like”, “scratching noise in attic at night”
treatment — “bed bug exterminator near me”, “termite treatment [town]”, “wasp nest removal”
cost and plans — “termite treatment cost”, “is quarterly pest control worth it”
safety — “is pest control safe for dogs”, “how long to stay out after spraying”

Identification and safety searches are where people meet your company first, often weeks before they need a technician. Treatment searches are where the map and Local Services Ads decide most calls. The data shows which group needs work first in your market.
Pest pages in SEO for pest control: termites, bed bugs, rodents and mosquitoes

A single “Services” page listing twelve pests ranks for no single pest. Each pest you treat has its own searches, its own season and its own worries, so each gets a page with your method, the prep the customer has to do, how many visits it takes and what happens if the pest comes back.
Termite inspection and treatment pages

Termite work is the largest ticket in residential pest control and the most researched. The page explains swarmers versus flying ants, liquid treatments versus baiting systems, how long protection lasts, the renewal or warranty you offer, and the wood-destroying insect inspection a buyer or lender asks for when a house is sold.
Bed bug treatment pages

Bed bug customers are embarrassed and in a hurry. They want to know whether you use heat, chemical treatment or both, how to prepare the room, whether they can sleep there tonight and whether the neighbors will see your truck. A page that answers all of this gets calls that a two-line service blurb loses. Hotels and landlords search for it in other words and deserve their own section.
Rodent control and exclusion pages

Mice and rats move indoors when the weather cools, and the searches follow. Owners want the noise in the attic gone and the entry points sealed, not only traps set. Pages on exclusion work — gaps, vents, rooflines — with photos from your jobs show why your visit costs more than a box of bait from the hardware store.
Mosquito and tick yard treatment pages

Yard treatments are sold as a program from spring to fall, plus one-off visits before weddings and backyard parties. The page names the months, the number of visits and what the customer should expect between them. Companies that also do lawn treatments will find the other side of that work on the
landscaping SEO
page.
Recurring pest control plans: SEO pages that sell quarterly service

Most residential revenue comes from service plans: an initial treatment, then a visit every quarter or every other month, with free re-service if pests show up in between. The plan is your product, and its page has to be as clear as any product page:
what the initial visit includes and how it differs from the regular ones
which pests are covered, and which — termites, bed bugs, wildlife — cost extra
how re-service calls work between visits
the price per visit or per month if you publish it, and how the customer cancels
People compare plans before signing and search questions like “is $70 a month good for pest control”. A plan page that answers them on your terms turns those comparisons into sign-ups.
Commercial pest control SEO: restaurants, warehouses and property managers

Commercial buyers search differently from homeowners. A restaurant manager looks for a contractor whose service reports a health inspector will accept; a food warehouse needs records for third-party food safety audits; a property manager wants one company for forty units and a clear routine for tenant complaints. Commercial pages name the facility types you serve, your integrated pest management approach, the paperwork left after each visit, after-hours service, insurance and how a site survey is booked. Such searches are few; one won account can run for years.
Pest control cost pages: answering “How much will it cost for pest control?”

“How much will it cost for pest control?” is one of the questions Google shows most often for this topic, and AI Overviews answer it with national averages when your site offers nothing better. A cost page, or a cost section on each pest page, says what moves the price: the size of the home, the pest, how far the infestation has gone, one-time or recurring service, follow-up visits. Ranges are enough; your price book stays private. Visitors who read a range before calling are the ones who book, and assistants get a figure with your company name next to it.
Local SEO for pest control companies: Google Business Profile, service areas and reviews
For “exterminator near me” and “pest control near me” the map decides most calls. Local SEO for pest control starts with the profile:
“Pest control service” as the primary category, each pest listed as a service, and the towns your routes really cover
weekly photos from jobs — technicians, trucks, sealed entry points, bait stations by a foundation — rather than dead pests
a review request texted after each visit, asking customers to name the pest and the town
service-area pages only for towns where you have customers, each with details only you could write: termite pressure, older housing, HOA rules
Fifty town pages with the same text are treated as doorway pages and filtered. The map side in more depth is on the
local SEO services
page.
Seasonal pest control SEO: termite swarms, mosquito summers, rodent winters

Pest demand follows a calendar that varies by region: termite swarms in spring, ants and wasps in early summer, mosquitoes and ticks through the warm months, stinging insect nests late in summer, rodents from fall into winter. A page needs weeks to rank, so each season’s pages go live a couple of months ahead. Quiet weeks go to new pest pages, job photos and fixes; the weeks before a rush go to the profile, reviews and forms.
Pesticide licensing and safety questions on pest control pages
Pest control is licensed work, and customers ask about chemicals before they let a technician in. Pages that answer plainly earn trust with people and with search engines:
the company’s license number and the state agency that issued it, written as text
the kinds of products you use, applied according to their labels, and when pets and children can go back into treated rooms
options for sensitive households, if you offer them, described without promises the label does not support

Words like “non-toxic”, “100% safe” or “harmless” about pesticide services can conflict with label and advertising rules in many states. Check wording with your state regulator; I follow the rules you pass on to me, and this is general information, not legal advice.
Local Services Ads, lead platforms and pest control marketing: where SEO fits

At the top of most pest searches sit Google’s Local Services Ads, the ones with the Google Guaranteed badge, charged per lead. Below them come national brands and franchises with large budgets, and lead platforms such as Angi or Thumbtack that pass one request to several companies. Paid leads arrive this week and end when the spending does; SEO takes months, then brings calls that are yours alone and cost nothing per lead. Many local firms keep Local Services Ads for the busy season and let SEO take over a growing share of calls. My part is the website and the map, and I make sure the pages your ads land on are the pages that rank.

Pest control marketing companies often sell SEO together with ads, call answering and door hangers, sometimes to several firms in one market. Whoever you hire, ask whether reports show booked services from your routing software — PestPac, FieldRoutes, GorillaDesk or similar — whether they work for a competitor in your towns, and who owns the site and profile if you part ways.
Pest control SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Homeowners type questions such as “how do I know if I have termites”, “is heat treatment better than spraying for bed bugs” or “who does rodent exclusion in [town]” into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews. Assistants assemble those answers from sources they can read and verify. Work on being included is known as generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a pest control company it comes down to:
direct answers to identification, prep and safety questions on your own pages, with the owner or a named technician as author
plan contents, cost ranges, license and service area written as plain sentences
structured data describing the business, its pest services and the towns it covers
the same company details on Google, Yelp, the BBB and other listings, since assistants compare them
Before the work starts and again after it, I record how assistants describe your company and who they name instead. The method is on the

page.

the one-time caller has wasps by the door or a mouse in the kitchen and needs your number, the pest, the area and how soon you come
the plan buyer compares quarterly service between two or three companies and reads what is covered, what it costs and how to cancel
the commercial manager runs a restaurant, a warehouse or apartment buildings and looks for service reports, insurance and someone to arrange a site survey
The home page shows three doors at once — call now, see plans, commercial service — and each looks different, so nobody ends up in the wrong form.
Website design for pest control: the first screen on a phone
The first screen carries five things and nothing more:
what you do and where: “Pest control in [county] — homes and businesses”
a call button and a second button to book or request a quote
the pest finder, as one row of icons
one line of proof: licensed, review score, years in the area
a photo of one of your technicians at work
Slogans about a pest-free life and full-screen video of someone spraying a baseboard move down the page or go. On every page the call and booking buttons stay fixed at the bottom of the phone screen.
A pest finder with photo upload on a pest control website

Many callers do not know what they have: “little black bugs” could be ants, carpet beetles or young cockroaches. A pest finder — simple drawings of ants, cockroaches, termites, bed bugs, rodents, wasps and mosquitoes, with “Not sure?” at the end — takes the visitor straight to the right page. “Not sure?” opens a short form with a photo upload, so the office can name the pest before quoting.

The drawings are clean line icons in your brand color, not close-up photos of insects next to your logo. Real pest photos belong further down the pest pages, sized small, where a visitor compares them with what they found.
Designing recurring plan pages for a pest control company

A recurring plan is sold like a subscription, and its page is designed like one. If you sell two or three levels — an exterior plan, a plan with interior visits, a plan with mosquito or termite cover — they sit side by side as cards that still read well on a phone:
the plan name and what it protects against
how often the technician comes and what the first visit includes
re-service between visits, worded as a promise you keep
a monthly or per-visit price if it is public, or a “from” price
one button per plan: sign up, or ask a question
Below the cards come the questions people ask before committing: contract length, cancellation, whether someone must be home, what happens when it rains on service day.
Online booking, plan sign-up and a customer portal in pest control website design

Routing software such as FieldRoutes, PestPac or GorillaDesk usually offers a booking form, an online sign-up or a customer portal for bills and service history. Each one helps only if visitors see it at the right moment, so the layout places it:
as the second button in the fixed bar on phones
at the end of every plan page and every residential pest page
as “Customer login” and “Pay your bill” links in the header, for people already on a plan
The embedded form gets your colors and fonts wherever the tool lets it. Whether your account supports embeds, an API or only a hosted page, I check before quoting.
Trust signals on a pest control website: license, products, pets and children
A technician sprays inside the house where children play and the dog sleeps. Visitors look for reasons to let you in, and the design puts those reasons next to the booking buttons:
the license number and the agency that issued it, in text
one short line on re-entry times and pets, linked to a fuller safety page
the guarantee in plain words — free re-service between visits, or what your termite warranty covers
your star rating and a couple of fresh reviews that mention the pest
association memberships, only those you really hold
Technician and truck photos instead of hazmat stock images on a pest control website

Stock photos of a masked figure in a hazmat suit frighten people and say nothing about you. Your technician in uniform at a front door, a truck with your logo, a bait station placed neatly by a foundation, a sealed gap under a garage door — these show a careful company the neighbors would not mind seeing. Phone photos work if they are taken in daylight; I send your team a short shot list.
Some customers, bed bug customers above all, prefer that nobody sees a pest control truck outside. If you send unmarked vehicles, the bed bug page says so right beside its button.
Pest control landing pages for Local Services Ads and Google Ads campaigns

Paid clicks that land on the home page waste part of the budget. A pest control landing page is built for one pest and one offer — “Bed bug inspection this week” or “First quarterly visit” — with the same words as the ad, the call button, a three-field form, three reviews that mention that pest and no menu that leads away. The layout is part of the site, so your office can copy it for each new campaign without a designer.
Commercial pest control pages: service reports, audits and site survey requests

Commercial buyers rarely book online. They want proof that you understand inspections and paperwork, then a conversation. The commercial section gets its own menu entry and a calmer look: facility types with a photo each — restaurants, food plants, warehouses, multi-unit housing, offices — a sample service report to download, and a request form that asks for the facility type, its size and the inspection or audit being prepared for. Those requests go to whoever sells commercial contracts, not into the residential booking queue.
Best pest control websites: templates, builder sites or a custom design

Searches for the best pest control websites lead to template stores, Dribbble shots and sites made with field service software builders. A template or builder site is a fair start for a one-truck operator: a few pages, a call button, a form. The gaps appear as the company grows — no room for a pest finder, plan cards squeezed into a sidebar, one page for every pest, booking that opens on someone else’s domain. A custom design pays off when recurring plans carry the business, when you sell commercial contracts or when paid ads land on the site.
A pest control website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Customers ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which local company treats termites or whether a quarterly plan is worth paying for. Assistants read text, not icons. A design that keeps the license inside a badge image, plan contents inside a graphic and service areas on a map picture hides them; the same facts as page text, with structured data for the business, its services and its areas, can be quoted.

children.text: Wedding photographer website or portrait portfolio: style is judged in seconds, and genres don't mix

Choosing a photographer is unlike choosing most services. There's no specification to compare and little to research — the decision is made by looking, quickly, and asking whether this person's work looks like what I want my own photographs to look like. Everything the site does either supports that judgement or gets in its way. Whether that comes from
a page builder or custom-built code
is a decision worth making deliberately, not by default.

Which makes the most common structural mistake expensive: a single portfolio containing everything. A couple planning a wedding and a company commissioning staff portraits are not browsing the same collection. When both are shown the same mixed feed, each spends the first thirty seconds filtering out work irrelevant to them — and thirty seconds is most of the attention available. Genres separated into their own paths let each visitor see a coherent body of work immediately, and they also let each genre rank on its own for the searches people actually make, which combine a genre and a city.

Speed matters here for a reason specific to the field. In photography the image quality is the product, so uncompromised files are the natural instinct — and the natural result is a gallery that doesn't appear fast enough to be judged at all. This is solvable without any compromise in what's shown: modern formats, sizes generated per device, and a loading strategy that prioritises what's on screen. On a client project with an extensive gallery of work, that approach took mobile performance from around 50 to 92 while the images stayed exactly as they were.
Two questions then arrive with nearly every enquiry: what it costs, and whether you're free on a particular date. Both can be handled on the page.

Private galleries on your own site make delivery part of the experience rather than an afterthought — and it's the last impression a client takes away, which they'll repeat to whoever asks them for a recommendation. children.text: I design and build plastic surgeon websites — for solo surgeons, group practices and surgery centers — and I do both the design and the code, so one person answers for how the site looks and how it works. A plastic surgery website has a narrow job: help someone who is considering an operation decide that your surgeon is the right one and ask for a consultation. Every page is measured against that job.
Plastic surgeon website design: what a patient checks before requesting a consultation

Visitors arrive with specific doubts: is this surgeon trained for my operation, do the results look natural, how long will I be off work, can I afford it. The home page and the menu are built around those doubts, not around how the practice is organized:
the surgeon’s name, specialty and board on the first screen, with a real photograph
procedures grouped by face, breast and body, with reconstructive work shown on its own if you do it
the gallery one tap away from every procedure
consultation request, call and text in a fixed bar at the bottom of the phone screen

The look is discreet rather than glossy: photographs of the surgeon, the team and the facility, a restrained palette and readable type. Stock images of models signal a template and show nothing about your work.
Surgeon profile page design: board certification and training shown correctly
Patients reread the surgeon profile before the consultation, and it is where they look for what credentials a plastic surgeon should have. The template holds:
full name and the exact name of the certifying board — in the US, for example, the American Board of Plastic Surgery — rather than a bare “board-certified”
medical school, residency, fellowship and hospital privileges
professional memberships, written as each society names itself
the procedures this surgeon performs, linked to their pages and galleries
a short video or a note on the surgeon’s approach, and a button to request a consultation with them

Some states regulate how certification and specialty may be advertised, so the wording is checked with your state medical board or counsel before launch. Board and society logos appear only where their own rules allow it.
Procedure page design for plastic surgery websites: face, breast and body

Every procedure page follows one layout, so a patient who has read about rhinoplasty knows where recovery is described on the breast reduction page. A summary comes first — what the operation changes, how long it takes, the anesthesia, typical downtime — then the detail: candidates, technique options, a recovery timeline, risks, a cost range linked to financing, and the matching gallery. A table of contents lets readers jump, and long medical text is split under headings that say what each part contains.
Each page shows the surgeon who reviewed it and the date of the last review. Results are described with their limits, and the page ends at a consultation request, not at a promise.
Before-and-after gallery design for plastic surgeon websites
The gallery is where many patients spend the most time and where most plastic surgery sites are slowest. The design I use:
a gallery per procedure, with filters patients care about — technique, implant type, age range — only where there are enough cases to fill them
each case as a pair at the same size, with a caption: procedure, time since surgery, surgeon
a notice before images with nudity, which open on tap
images in modern formats that load as the visitor scrolls, so the gallery opens quickly on a phone

The gallery depends on discipline in the photos: written consent from each patient for use on the website, the same lighting, angle and background, no retouching. Each case can be removed in one step if a patient withdraws consent.
Consultation requests and virtual consultations: secure forms for patient photos

Many practices ask for photos with a consultation request. A photo of a patient’s body attached to an ordinary contact form and delivered by email is health information traveling through tools never meant for it, and in the US it can fall under HIPAA. The design keeps the paths apart:
the short request asks only for name, contact details, procedure of interest and a preferred time
photo uploads and medical history go through a form or practice-management provider that signs a business associate agreement
analytics and ad pixels stay off the request and upload pages

Years ago I worked under NDA on a medical system that stored patient records; I can’t name it, but it left me with one rule: the website itself collects as little as possible. Your compliance adviser confirms the final setup.
Website design for out-of-town and international plastic surgery patients

Patients who fly in for surgery need a different set of pages: how a virtual consultation works, how many nights to plan nearby, where to stay during recovery, when the follow-up visits are and how aftercare continues at home. A “Traveling for surgery” section answers this in one place, with a checklist and a map of the practice, the surgery center and nearby accommodation. For international patients the section exists in their languages, each version at its own address rather than behind a translation widget. I build
multilingual websites
, including Hebrew, a right-to-left language, on the Cyprus VIP Estates platform.
Financing and price pages in plastic surgery website design

Price is the question patients hesitate to ask on the phone. A pricing page with ranges per procedure and a plain list of what is and is not included — anesthesia, facility, garments, follow-up — plus a financing page with the providers you accept and a link to apply, filters out requests from people who cannot go ahead and makes it easier for those who can. On each procedure page a short cost block links to both.
Advertising rules built into a plastic surgeon website’s editor: the Milan practice case

My strongest case is a private medical practice with strict advertising rules: Giuseppe, a psychologist and psychotherapist in Milan. I rebuilt his site on Next.js and Sanity with a calm design for anxious visitors — dark backgrounds broken by light sections and serif type with a real italic. While he types, the editor points out anything Italian rules on advertising health services make risky: promises of results, patient testimonials, discounts, a “free consultation”. Key pages cannot be deleted, published URLs are locked, analytics runs only after consent, and he got an owner’s manual in English and Italian with video walkthroughs. The build, from first code to handover, took 44 working days.

For a plastic surgery practice the same approach means the editor flags “guaranteed”, “painless”, “risk-free” and discount wording before a page goes live, and a gallery case can require a consent date before it is published. Staff add procedures and cases without breaking the layout.
A plastic surgeon website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Patients ask assistants which surgeon in their city does revision rhinoplasty or breast reconstruction after cancer. Assistants answer from text they can read and check, so the site keeps surgeons, boards, training, procedures, locations, languages and financing as text and structured data, matching your Google profile and RealSelf. children.text: I design websites for plumbers and plumbing companies and build them myself, so design and build come from one person at one price. Plumbing website design is about what a customer sees and does in the first seconds on your site — usually on a phone, sometimes with water spreading across the floor. Everything on the page is arranged to lead to one of two actions: a call now or a booked visit later.
Plumbing website design for two visitors: the emergency and the planned job

The same site is opened by two very different people. One has a burst pipe or a sewer backup and wants a plumber at the door within the hour. This person does not read; they scan and tap the first phone number that looks right. The other is planning a water heater replacement or new bathroom fixtures and is comparing companies on price, reviews and how professional they look. This person reads.
Good plumbing website design serves both without making either one wait:
the emergency visitor sees a phone number and whether you are available now, without scrolling
the planning visitor finds a clear list of services, prices or ranges and a way to choose a time
the two actions look different — a strong call button for urgent help, a quieter one for booking — so nobody has to think which is theirs
Website design for plumbers: what the first screen shows on a phone
The first screen of a phone is small, and on a plumbing site it carries four things and nothing else:
what you do and where, in plain words: “Plumbers in [your town] — emergency and scheduled repairs”
the phone number, large, with your hours or “24/7” if that is true
one line of proof: licensed and insured, review score, years in business
a photo of your own van or one of your plumbers
Slogans, sliders and welcome paragraphs move further down or disappear. A visitor in a hurry should be able to call without reading a single sentence.
A sticky call button in plumbing website design

On every page the call button stays fixed at the bottom of the phone screen, where the thumb already is. It dials the number on a tap; it does not open a contact page. Next to it sits a second, smaller button — book online, or send a text — for the visitor who would rather not talk. On a desktop the number sits in the top right corner of the header, where people look for it.

The label matters as much as the position. “Call now — a plumber answers 24/7” is right only if someone really picks up at 3 a.m. If calls after hours go to voicemail, the button says when you call back. A promise the phone does not keep costs more than it brings.
Trust signals on a plumbing website: licensed, insured, upfront pricing, guarantees, reviews

A plumber comes into the house, sometimes when nobody else is home, and the final bill is not known when the customer calls. Visitors look for reasons to believe you are safe and fair. The design places those reasons near every call button, not in the footer:
license number and insurance, written out so they can be checked
upfront or flat-rate pricing explained in one sentence: the price is agreed before work starts
a guarantee in plain words — on parts, on labor, on cleaning up after the job
a review score with two or three recent reviews that name the job: a drain, a water heater, a leak
badges such as Google Screened or a trade association membership — only those you really hold
Photos of your vans and plumbers instead of stock images on a plumbing website

A stock photo of a smiling model holding a wrench is recognized at once and says nothing about you. Your own van with the logo, a plumber in your uniform at a real job, a neat water heater installation, a cleaned-up crawl space — these show that the company exists and cares about its work. They also help the customer recognize the van that pulls up outside and the person who knocks.

Phone photos are enough if they are taken in daylight and the same way each time. I give your team a short shot list: each van, each plumber, before and after of typical jobs, and the shop or warehouse if you have one.
Layout of a plumbing service page: from the problem to the call
A service page — say, water heater replacement — follows the order in which the visitor thinks:
The problem in their words: “No hot water? Water heater leaking?”, with the call button.
What you do about it and how soon you can come.
The price or range, and what changes it.
The options — repair or replace, tank or tankless — one sentence each.
Two or three photos from real jobs and a review that mentions this service.
The questions customers ask on the phone, answered briefly.
Booking or a second call button at the end.
Emergency pages are shorter: a few steps to limit the damage, then the call. Planned-job pages are longer and finish with booking.
How these pages are organized by service and town, connected to your software and kept fast is covered on the
websites for plumbers
page.
Where the booking widget goes in plumbing website design

Online booking from ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, Jobber or a similar tool helps only if people see it at the moment they decide. Hidden on a separate “Book” page, it is found by few. In the design it appears:
as the second button in the sticky bar on phones
at the end of every planned-job service page
never on emergency pages, where it would suggest that a burst pipe can wait until Thursday
The widget is styled to match the site as far as the tool allows, so the customer does not feel they have landed on another company’s form.
Color, contrast and text size of a plumbing website for a visitor under stress
Someone with water on the kitchen floor reads badly and taps fast. The design is checked for that:
body text at 16 pixels or larger, short headings, one idea per line
text and background contrast that meets the WCAG accessibility guidelines
one strong accent color kept only for the call button, so it is never confused with decoration
large tap targets with space between them, so a wet thumb does not hit the wrong link

Blue and white are common on plumbing sites because they suggest clean water; they work as long as the call button stands out against them. Your van and uniform colors carry the brand, but the button color is chosen for visibility first.
Plumbing website templates or a custom plumbing website design

A plumbing website template, free or paid, looks good in the demo: perfect photos, invented reviews, a 24/7 banner. With a real company’s content the gaps appear — no place for emergency pages, one page for all services, a contact form instead of a call button, booking squeezed into a sidebar. A search for a plumbing website design template, or inspiration boards on Dribbble and Pinterest, will show attractive screens, but they are made to be admired, not tested with real customers and real calls.

A template is a fair start for a one-van business. A custom design is worth it when you take emergency calls, sell several services, cover several towns or pay for ads that land on the site. Moving off a template later usually means designing from the beginning.
Plumbing website design that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

More customers ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to suggest a plumber or explain a repair before calling anyone. Assistants work from text, not pictures. A design that keeps licenses, guarantees, prices and service areas inside images and badges hides them; the same facts set as real text, with structured data for the business and its services, can be read and repeated.
Getting into those answers is ongoing work, described on the

page. Being found in Google search and on the map is covered on the

children.text: Pressure washing website design for owner-operators and small crews is work I do from start to finish — plan, design and build — so one person is responsible and the price is fixed. A pressure washing website has an easier job than most trade sites in one way and a harder one in another. The result is visible, so photos sell; but every property is a different size and surface, so customers want a price before they call, and they worry about damage you know how to avoid.
A pressure washing website for a one-truck owner-operator

Many pressure washing businesses are one person, one trailer or truck rig and a long season. Between April and October you are on driveways and roofs from morning to evening and answer the phone with wet gloves. The website has to work without you:
show the result in the first seconds, so the visitor does not need convincing by phone
collect surface, size and address in one request, so you can price it from the truck
say plainly what you wash and what you do not, so you are not called for interior cleaning or graffiti you would not take
look as clean and orderly as the work: a messy site is a strange advertisement for a cleaning service
Before-and-after photos on a pressure washing website

Before-and-after is the whole sales pitch of this trade, and the design is built around it. A slider the visitor drags across the photo is more convincing than two pictures side by side, because the eye sees the same brick or the same board change. For that to work, the photos have to be taken properly:
the same position, the same height and the same zoom for before and after — mark the spot with your foot or a chalk line
landscape orientation on the phone, in daylight, without the sun shining straight into the lens
one shot halfway through, with a clean stripe across a dirty driveway — it shows the difference in one picture
no filters or extra saturation: customers have seen edited “afters” and stop trusting all of them

Under each pair, one line: the surface, the town, the method — soft wash or surface cleaner. The gallery can then be filtered by surface, so a homeowner with a green roof sees roofs and not parking lots.
Instant quotes by square footage on a pressure washing website
Most pressure washers already price by square foot or by size band, so the quote form asks for the same things you would ask on the phone:
Surface: house siding, roof, driveway, patio, deck, fence.
Size: square footage if the customer knows it, or small, medium and large with a picture of each for those who do not.
Condition and extras: light dirt, heavy algae, oil stains, sealing after cleaning.
Address, photos, and a way to reach them.

The form can show a price range on the spot if you want that — using your own rates and your minimum job charge — or simply send the request so you reply with a number. A range on screen brings more requests; a firm price stays your decision after you see the photos. The form can feed Jobber, GoSite or your email, whichever you already use.
Service pages for house washing, roof soft washing, driveways and decks
Each surface has its own customer and its own question, so each gets its own page rather than one long list.
House washing and soft washing siding

Homeowners worry about water behind vinyl siding and stripped paint. The page explains low-pressure soft washing with a cleaning solution, shows siding before and after, and says how windows and outlets are protected.
Roof soft washing

Black streaks and moss on a roof make people fear for the shingles. The page says that roofs are cleaned without high pressure, what the solution does to algae, how long results last, and that you follow the shingle manufacturer’s cleaning guidance where one exists.
Driveways, patios and concrete cleaning
These buyers care about stains: oil, rust, tire marks, gum. The page shows which ones come out fully and which only fade, and offers sealing as a second step.
Decks and fences
Wood needs care: the page explains lower pressure, brightening and the wait before staining, so the customer does not expect a new deck in an afternoon.
A commercial pressure washing page for property managers and storefronts

Commercial work — storefronts, sidewalks, drive-thrus, parking areas, dumpster pads, building exteriors — is bought by a different person. A property manager or a store owner is not moved by a dramatic slider alone; they want to know you can be trusted with their site and their schedule. That page has its own layout:
proof of insurance available on request, written as a line of text
night, early-morning and weekend work so customers and tenants are not disturbed, if you offer it
recurring cleaning by month or quarter, described as your product with your terms
a request form with company fields: business name, number of locations, who approves the work
How a pressure washing website answers fears of damage to siding, roofs and plants

The most common doubt is not the price; it is damage. Siding cracked by too much pressure, plants killed by runoff, etched concrete, water inside windows. A short block on each surface page answers it in plain words: what pressure you use on what, how you wet and rinse the plants, what you cover, and what your liability insurance covers if something goes wrong. Reviews that mention care — “they covered everything and rinsed the flower beds” — sit right next to it.
Seasonal services and maintenance plans on a pressure washing website

The season shapes the site. In spring the first screen leads with house and driveway washing; later in the year it may lead with fall cleanups, and if you add gutter cleaning, window washing or holiday lighting in the cold months, those get their own pages instead of a line at the bottom. A slim banner announces booking for the new season and is switched on and off by you. A yearly or twice-yearly maintenance plan, if you sell one, has a short page with what it includes and how renewal works.
Pressure washing website templates, Jobber and GoSite, or a site of your own

Field-service tools like Jobber and GoSite include simple websites, and builders sell pressure washing website templates, some of them free. They get a new business online fast, and that is worth something in the first season.

They show their limits once the work grows: one page for all surfaces, galleries that do not filter, a quote form that cannot ask about square footage, and a site that lives on the platform. A site of your own keeps the tools for scheduling and invoicing and embeds their forms where they help, while the pages, the photos and the domain stay yours.

Customers search “pressure washing near me”, “roof cleaning” or “driveway cleaning” plus the town, and choose from the map. A pressure washing business is usually a service-area business with no storefront, so the Google Business Profile hides the home address and lists the towns you drive to. The website matches it: a page per surface, the towns written as text, the same phone and name everywhere, and before-and-after photos posted to the profile as well. Reviews that name the surface and the town help most.
Profile setup comes with the full site; month-to-month work on map positions and reviews is a separate service, explained on the

People also ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews whether roof soft washing is safe, how often to clean siding, or who does it nearby. Assistants answer from text they can read. Surfaces, methods, the area you cover and your insurance written as text, with structured data for the business and each service, give them something to quote; a price list set inside a photo gives them nothing.
Getting your business named there is its own line of work — more on the

page.

children.text: Why a developer website has to sell something the buyer cannot see yet

A developer sells a building that does not exist. There is nothing to walk through, nothing to touch, and often nothing on site but a fence and a board. Everything the buyer uses to decide has to be carried by the website, which makes it a different instrument from an agency site: not a catalogue of what is available, but the substitute for a physical object.

That changes what belongs on it. Floor plans and renders are the easy part. What decides the enquiry is the material that makes an unbuilt property feel real and safe — construction progress with dates, the permits and the legal structure of the purchase, the payment schedule, and who exactly is behind the company.
What a buyer of an off-plan unit checks on a developer website

Someone buying before completion is managing risk, not choosing a kitchen layout. They look for what has already been delivered, whether the previous projects were finished on time, whether progress is documented rather than promised, and whether the terms of the deal are written down before a call.

A site that answers those questions loses fewer buyers at the point where they hesitate. A site that shows only renders leaves the question open, and an open question at that price point usually ends the visit.
The availability board: the object a developer site is judged by
An agency site never needs one; a developer site is judged by it. The board shows every unit in a building with its floor, area, layout, price or price range, and status — available, reserved, sold.

Two rules decide whether it works. Sold units stay visible and marked sold, because a board that quietly loses rows reads as a board nobody maintains, and because sold-out floors are the strongest evidence a project is selling. And the status has to be editable by the sales team in minutes, not by a developer on a ticket — a board that goes stale is worse than no board at all.
How a catalogue with filters is built underneath it is covered separately:
catalogue website with filters
Floor plans, renders and construction progress: what belongs where
Renders sell the idea, floor plans sell the unit, and progress photographs sell the company. Mixing them into one gallery wastes all three.
What each one has to do
floor plans: open full-size on a phone, areas in square metres per room, orientation marked, downloadable;
renders: labelled as renders, with the view and the floor they are taken from;
progress: dated, in order, from the same angles each time, so a buyer can see movement rather than a mood board;
the finished previous project: the strongest page on the site, and usually the one nobody builds.
This is also the material that ages, so it needs to be editable by whoever is on site, not by whoever built the website.
Why a developer website needs traffic before the launch, not after

Search visibility takes months to build. A developer's selling window is fixed by the construction schedule, so a site that starts earning organic traffic at launch has already missed the part of the cycle where enquiries matter most.
The work has to begin while the project is still in permits — the pages, the structure and the search visibility built ahead of the sales phase, not alongside it.
Renovation and investment website with a premium feel and 96/98/100/100 performance
is a case study from the same market, where speed and trust signals were treated as part of the sales instrument rather than as a finishing touch.
CRM integration: one enquiry path per development
A developer selling three projects through one shared inbox loses enquiries to sorting. Each development has its own sales people, its own stage and often its own agency partner.

I connect the forms over your CRM's API so an enquiry arrives tagged with the development, the unit and the source, and is routed by the rules you already use. Where a project is sold through a partner agency, the routing reflects that instead of fighting it.
Languages for cross-border buyers

Off-plan property is bought across borders more often than finished property, because the price advantage is the reason for buying early. A single-language site filters those buyers out silently — they never appear in the statistics.

The second and third language are separate work, not translation: their own keyword research, text adapted to how that market reads, and a URL structure search engines can tell apart. Built into the structure from the start, each extra language is cheap; retrofitted later, it is the expensive version of the same job.

children.text: Real estate developer website examples: what the best ones show
Lists of the best real estate developer websites are dominated by 3D tours and video headers. The parts that actually help a buyer decide are simpler, and they work for a developer of any size:
a page for every development with the location, completion date, unit types and prices or price ranges;
an availability board that is kept current — sold units marked as sold, not removed;
floor plans that open properly on a phone, with areas in square metres;
construction progress updates with dated photos;
one enquiry path per development, sent to the people selling it.

A real estate developer website template can present one project well. It rarely copes with several developments, each with its own units and sales status, without turning into pages nobody keeps up to date.

A basic catalogue site with developments, units and enquiry forms starts at €2,500. A site with CRM integration and advanced functionality starts at €4,000. A full platform starts at €7,000 and is scoped individually. Design is included, never a separate line. The breakdown by tier is in

How long building a developer website takes

A basic catalogue site takes three to six weeks. The availability board, CRM integration and each additional language extend that, and I give the figure before we start rather than during. A full platform is scoped with its own timeline because the functionality decides it.

What stretches a build here is material rather than code: floor plans in a usable format, the unit list with current statuses, progress photographs, and who on your side will keep them current after launch.
What stays with you after launch
the code, the domain, the content and the CMS logins are yours from day one;
the availability board is editable by your sales team, not only by a developer;
the site does not live on my hosting account and exports are not blocked;
the project can be handed to another developer at any point;
the work runs on a contract with a fixed scope, timeline and stages.

children.text: A developer website that AI assistants can read

Buyers and investors increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google's AI Overviews which developments are being built in an area, who the developer behind one is, what a completion date and payment schedule look like, and whether previous projects were delivered on time. The assistant answers from text it can read and restate, and it names sources — so the structure of the site decides whether your company appears in that answer at all.

In practice: a direct answer at the top of each section, facts about locations, dates, areas and terms rather than adjectives, Schema.org markup for the organisation and the developments that matches the visible text, and content available without running scripts. A render carousel with the facts inside the images is invisible to all of it.

contentBlocks.title: What a real estate agency website build includes

children.text: Why an agency website loses to the portals it competes with

An agency website almost always starts as a catalogue. Listings go up, filters get added, and the site is considered done. The problem is that a catalogue is the one thing an agency will never win on: portals hold more inventory, more traffic and larger search budgets, and a buyer looking only for listings goes there first. A site that competes on inventory competes on the single axis where it is guaranteed to lose.

What the agency does own is everything a portal cannot show: which districts you actually work in, which segment you know, which language your buyers speak, and what happens after the first enquiry. That is the material the site should be built from.
What a buyer checks on an agency website before making contact

By the time someone reaches your site they have usually seen the property somewhere else. The visit is not a search, it is a check: they are deciding whether to send the enquiry to you or to the agency open in the next tab.

They look for how long you have worked this market, whether the listings are current, whether a named person answers, and whether terms are stated or withheld until a call. None of that is decoration — it is the content that decides between an enquiry and a closed tab, and it is exactly what a catalogue with a contact form at the bottom leaves out.
A property catalogue and its filters: what to filter by and what to drop
Filters are where agency sites are over-built and under-used. Eight filters look thorough and produce a page nobody can operate on a phone, plus a crawl problem the site then carries for years.

Four or five decide almost every search: price, location, property type, rooms, and whichever one matters in your segment — plot size, floor, yield, completion date. The rest belong in the listing, not in the filter bar. What does matter is that a filtered result can be sent to someone as a link and still show the same properties, and that the combinations worth ranking become real pages instead of parameters.
How a catalogue with filters is built is covered separately:
catalogue website with filters
Listing import and updates: where the data comes from and what breaks

The question that decides the build is where listings live today. A feed from a portal or an MLS, an export from your CRM, a spreadsheet, or three agents each keeping their own — each answer produces a different site.
What breaks in practice
a listing sells and its page disappears, leaving a dead end or a soft 404;
the same property arrives twice from two sources under two addresses;
photographs come in at full camera resolution and the catalogue slows to a crawl;
prices update in the feed but not in the text somebody wrote by hand.
All four are solvable, and all four need deciding before the first page is designed rather than after launch.
CRM integration: where an enquiry lands and who sees it
An enquiry that arrives in a shared inbox is an enquiry somebody will eventually answer. One that arrives in the CRM with the property, the source and the time attached is a lead with an owner.

I connect the forms to whatever you already run, over its API, so enquiries are distributed by the rules you already use. Where there is no CRM, the forms still carry the property and the source into the notification, because knowing which listing produced the call changes what you say when you make it.
Several languages: why it matters more for an agency than for most businesses

Property is one of the few categories where the buyer routinely sits in a different country from the asset. A single-language site quietly filters out everyone searching in another language, and the agency never finds out — those buyers simply never appear in the statistics.

Building the second and third language properly is not translation. It means separate keyword research per language, content adapted to how that market reads, and a URL structure search engines can tell apart.
Build and optimize a multilingual real estate platform
is the case study for exactly that work.

children.text: An agency website that AI assistants can read

Buyers increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google's AI Overviews which agencies work a particular area or development, what buying costs a foreign buyer, and which district suits them. The assistant answers from text it can read and restate, and it names sources — so the structure of the site decides whether your agency appears in that answer at all.

In practice: a direct answer at the top of each section, facts about areas, segments and terms rather than adjectives, Schema.org markup for listings and the agency that matches the visible text, and content available without running scripts. This is built in during development, because adding it afterwards costs more than doing it at the start.

children.text: I do realtor website design and build the site myself, for individual real estate agents and small teams, so design and development come from one person at one price. You already appear on the brokerage site and on Zillow and Realtor.com; a website of your own is the one place shaped around how you work that carries your name from one brokerage to the next.
Realtor website design: what buyers and sellers check on an agent’s website

Buyers usually find a home first and look up the agent afterwards; sellers compare two or three agents before a listing appointment. Both open your site on a phone, and the first screen answers them before they scroll:
who you are — your photo, your name, the brokerage you work with and the area you cover, in one line such as “Homes in [neighborhood] — [Name], [Brokerage]”
what you are best at — first-time buyers, luxury homes, condos, relocation or investors
the next step for each side — “What is my home worth?” for sellers, search or featured listings for buyers
how to reach you now — call, text and email, each one tap away
A full-screen drone video pushes all four answers below the fold on a phone; video belongs on the listing and neighborhood pages.
IDX website builders for realtors or a custom real estate agent website

Most agents choose between three things: the free agent page their brokerage provides, a subscription IDX website builder — Placester, Real Geeks, Luxury Presence, the site that comes with kvCORE and similar platforms — or a custom site. Each fits a different stage, and a builder is not a wrong choice.
When an IDX builder or a brokerage page is enough
you are new, the budget is small and you need MLS search on the first day
most of your business comes from referrals and your sphere, not from search
the builder’s layouts suit you and you do not plan many pages of your own
When a custom realtor website design pays off
your brand and your neighborhoods should look like you, not like a layout many agents in your market already use
you want neighborhood guides, market updates and video pages that build up under your own domain
you work in two languages or with relocation and international buyers
the site, the domain and the content must stay yours when you change brokerage or software

A custom site does not mean giving up listing search. MLS data still comes from an IDX provider you subscribe to, such as iHomefinder, embedded in your design; your MLS and your broker approve the feed, and the MLS display rules apply. The trade-off in plain terms: a builder is cheaper to start and has saved searches and alerts ready; a custom site costs more at the start and gives you control over everything around the search.
Realtor website design templates

Realtor website design templates — WordPress real estate themes, Squarespace or Webflow layouts — sit between the two. With a real agent’s content their gaps show: one “Communities” page instead of a page per neighborhood, no place for a valuation request, an IDX plugin styled differently from the theme. As a start, with those limits accepted, a template works.
Agent bio and personal brand in real estate agent website design
People choose an agent before they think about the brokerage, and the About page with its photos carries most of that choice. That is why it is designed first:
portraits and working photos taken for the site — at a showing, on your streets, with your team — in the same light and framing
a bio written as an introduction: where you live, which areas and property types you know, how you work with buyers and with sellers
designations, certifications and languages as a short list in text, not inside badges
reviews from Google, Zillow and Realtor.com, each with its source named
your own colors and logo next to the brokerage’s, in the proportion your brokerage’s brand rules allow
Neighborhood and community pages on a realtor website
Neighborhood pages show local knowledge that a portal cannot. They share one layout, so the set stays consistent as you add areas:
a description in your own words: streets, housing types, commute
your photos and a short video walk rather than stock images
schools, parks and transit as facts with links to official sources, not your rating of them
active and recently sold listings from that area through the IDX feed
a market note refreshed monthly or quarterly, with the date shown
a contact block that names you as the agent for this area
Getting these pages found in Google and on the map is SEO work, described on the
SEO for realtors
page.
Listing pages, photos and video tours in realtor website design
Your own listings are marketing, not only data. A listing page designed for your site does more than a standard IDX template:
a large photo gallery that opens quickly and swipes on a phone
a video tour or 3D walk-through near the top, loaded only when the visitor taps play
price, beds, baths, size, lot and fees in a fixed block, as text
a floor plan, a map and a short story of the home in your words
a showing request button, with the listing brokerage credited as your MLS requires
Home valuation and lead forms that reach your real estate CRM

Most leads on an agent’s site come from three forms: a home valuation request, a showing request and a buyer consultation. Each asks only what the first reply needs — the address and the home’s basics for a valuation, the listing and a preferred time for a showing.

I do not put an invented instant estimate on the page. The valuation form starts a conversation, and you answer it with your own market analysis, which is why sellers ask an agent in the first place. If your IDX or valuation tool provides an automated estimate, it can sit on the page with its own disclaimer.

Leads go where you already work — Follow Up Boss, kvCORE, Lofty or another CRM — through the CRM’s own form, its API or an automation service, depending on your plan. Each lead carries the page it came from, so you see which neighborhood or listing brought it. I check what your account supports before quoting.
A fast realtor website on a phone, even with heavy listing photos

A realtor’s site carries far more weight than a typical service business site: dozens of photos per listing, video, maps and an IDX script. The build keeps the main content of each page visible in under 2.5 seconds on a phone, the level Google rates as good:
photos resized for each screen and served as WebP or AVIF
galleries that load the first image at once and the rest as the visitor swipes
video and 3D tours shown as a poster image until someone taps play
maps and IDX search loaded only on the pages that use them
Brokerage name, license details and Fair Housing on a real estate agent website

An agent’s website is advertising, and real estate advertising has rules. In the US, state license laws generally require the brokerage name in advertising, some states require license numbers, and the Fair Housing Act applies to every word on the site. The design gives these items fixed places:
the brokerage name and contact details on every page, where your state and your broker require them
your license number and the Equal Housing Opportunity logo in the footer
MLS attribution and the IDX disclaimer next to listing data
neighborhood copy that describes homes and places, not the kind of people who should live there

Rules differ by state and by brokerage, so check the wording with your managing broker before launch. In Canada, the UK and Australia other regulators set the rules, and the same fixed places hold what yours require.
Best websites for realtors: what top real estate agent websites have in common
Lists of the best real estate agent websites mix luxury teams with solo agents in small towns. Set the budgets aside and the same patterns repeat:
one person or one team clearly in charge of the first screen
separate paths for sellers and buyers from the home page
neighborhood pages with the agent’s own photos and dated market notes
listing pages with video that still load fast
reviews with their sources, placed next to the contact buttons
Galleries on Awwwards or Dribbble show home pages; open the neighborhood and listing pages too — that is where a visitor decides to call.
Owning your realtor website and domain instead of renting a platform

Agents change brokerages and software more often than careers. A brokerage page stays with the brokerage when you leave, and a builder site usually stays with the builder when you cancel: the domain can be pointed elsewhere, but the design, the neighborhood guides and years of market notes rarely move with it.

Here the domain is registered in your name, the hosting is on your account, and the code and content are handed over at launch. When you join another brokerage, the logo and footer change and everything else stays. After launch you pay for hosting, the domain and your IDX provider, if you use one — there is no monthly fee to me.
A realtor website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Buyers and sellers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews for “a realtor in [suburb] who speaks Spanish” or “an agent who sells condos in [neighborhood]”. An assistant can only suggest an agent it can read about. The design keeps the facts as page text — your name, brokerage, license, areas, languages, property types and contact details — matching your Google Business Profile and your Zillow and Realtor.com profiles. RealEstateAgent structured data describes you, neighborhood pages answer common questions directly, and every market note shows its date.
Being named in those answers is ongoing work, described on the

page.

contentBlocks.title: Recruitment agency website design: what the site includes

children.text: Web design for recruitment agencies: two audiences that want opposite things

A recruitment agency's website has a structural problem few other businesses face: it has to persuade two groups whose interests point in different directions, on the same domain, at the same time. An employer wants evidence of rigour — how candidates are found, how thoroughly they're screened, what happens when a placement doesn't last. A candidate wants the opposite qualities: speed, ease, and discretion.
Written as one page for both, it convinces neither
. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.

Separating them is the first decision, and it's structural rather than cosmetic. The employer path answers the questions that decide a briefing: sourcing method, screening depth, timelines, how fees work, what guarantees exist. The candidate path is built for browsing and applying, with the friction removed. They can share a brand and share nothing else.

On the candidate side, the technical piece matters more than it looks. Job listings published as ordinary page content, without proper structured markup, are invisible to job search results — which is where a large and growing share of candidates begin. Publishing each vacancy on its own page with correct JobPosting data doesn't guarantee anything about ranking, but it makes the listing legible to systems that otherwise can't see it at all. Given how much effort goes into writing and distributing vacancies, leaving them unreadable to the largest search surface is an odd place to economise.

Discretion is the other half of the candidate question, and it's rarely addressed. The strongest candidates are almost always employed, and applying carries risk for them. A site that states plainly who sees an application, how the data is handled and how long it's retained removes a real hesitation. So does an application path short enough to complete on a phone in a break, rather than a form demanding a full profile before anything is submitted.

Then there's specialisation. Employers don't search for recruitment agencies in general — they search for agencies that recruit for their sector. An agency covering several sectors from one page competes for none of those searches, while a page for each competes for all of them. The same applies to language: in markets where candidates come from other countries, the languages your candidates read may have nothing to do with the language your clients speak, and the site needs both — set up so the versions work independently rather than against each other. The same principle — dedicated, filterable pages — is what makes
a job catalogue
findable, and it's
a multilingual structure question
as much as a translation one.
