children.text: I do SEO for restaurants myself — the Google Business Profile, the website and the local pages — so the person who audits the site is the one who fixes it. Restaurant SEO is mostly local: guests choose from the map results and the first few links, on a phone, within minutes of deciding to eat out.
What restaurant SEO covers: Google Maps, local search and the website

Restaurant SEO is the work that makes a restaurant appear when someone searches for a kind of food, a dish or a place to eat nearby, and makes the restaurant’s own website win the search for its own name. Three places decide this:
the map results — three restaurants with a map, rating and hours, shown above everything else for searches like “sushi near me”
the regular results, where the restaurant’s website competes with booking portals, delivery apps and review sites
AI answers — Google AI Overviews and assistants such as ChatGPT, which recommend places and quote menus and opening hours

Each needs different work. The map results depend mostly on the Google Business Profile and reviews, the regular results on the website, and AI answers on both, plus facts written in a form a machine can quote.
Local SEO for restaurants: Google Business Profile, reviews and the map results

For a restaurant, local SEO matters more than anything else on this page. Guests compare three places in the map block and often choose before opening any website. What moves a restaurant into that block:
the right primary category — “Georgian restaurant”, not just “Restaurant” — and secondary categories for what you also are: bar, café, takeaway
opening hours that are always correct, including public holidays; wrong hours cost more trust than a missing photo
a menu link that leads to a text menu on your own website, not to a PDF
recent photos of dishes that are on the menu now
the attributes guests filter by: outdoor seating, vegetarian options, wheelchair access, reservations
the same name, address and phone number on the website, the profile and the main directories

Reviews weigh more for restaurants than for most businesses. I set up a routine: guests are asked at the right moment, every review gets an answer within a few days, and answers name dishes and occasions in plain words. What I do not set up: bought reviews or asking only happy guests. Both break Google’s rules, both are detectable, and in hospitality they cost more reputation than they bring.
Restaurant website SEO: menu, cuisine and location pages
The website is the one place portals cannot copy, and it is where a restaurant wins searches beyond its name. Restaurant website SEO starts with:
the menu as text on its own page, with dish names and short descriptions, so a search for a dish can lead to you
one page per location, with address, hours, map, booking and the menu for that location
pages for what guests search besides the name: the cuisine, private dining, group bookings, events, a lunch menu
Restaurant and Menu structured data, so opening hours, price range, cuisine and the booking link are read correctly
speed on a phone: the page and its main photo appear in under 2.5 seconds on mobile data
If the current website cannot do this — a builder template, a PDF menu, one page for everything — rebuilding it usually costs less than working around it. That is covered on the
restaurant website development
and
restaurant website design
pages.
AI SEO for restaurants: visibility in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

More guests now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews where to eat — “a quiet Italian place near the old town”, “where to get good ramen tonight”. The answer names a few restaurants and quotes what the assistant could read about them. Getting into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO), and for a restaurant it rests on the same work as local SEO:
the menu, cuisine, price range and opening hours written as text on your own site and in the Google profile
reviews that mention dishes and occasions, so an assistant can match you to “a place for a birthday dinner”
Restaurant and Menu structured data that states the facts in a form machines read reliably
the same name, address and hours everywhere, so assistants do not mix you up with a place with a similar name
I check how assistants describe and recommend your restaurant before and after the work. More on this on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
SEO keywords for restaurants: what guests actually type
Restaurant searches fall into four groups, and each needs its own place on the website or the profile:
the restaurant’s name — your own site should come first, above portals that take a commission for guests who were already yours
cuisine plus area: “ramen near me”, “pizza in the old town”, “vegan restaurant” with a district
dish names: “khachapuri”, “pho”, “beef tartare” — found through a text menu
occasions: “private dining room”, “restaurant for a birthday”, “business lunch”, “Sunday brunch”
Before any work I pull the real search data for your city and cuisine, so the pages are built around the phrases guests use, not around how the restaurant describes itself.
SEO strategy for restaurants with several locations

With two or more locations, the usual mistake is one website page and one profile doing the work for all of them. A working setup gives each location its own Google Business Profile linked to its own location page, a separate menu where the menus differ, its own reviews, and a link from the home page. Searches for the brand then lead guests to the nearest place, and each location can rank in its own area.
Restaurant SEO agency, marketing agency or an SEO specialist

A restaurant marketing agency usually sells social media, photo shoots, ads and influencer campaigns, with SEO as one line in the package. A restaurant SEO agency focuses on search, but the work often goes to junior staff and templates. I am a single SEO specialist who also builds websites: the same person audits the Google profile, rewrites the menu page and fixes the code.
What I do not do: social media management, paid ads and photo shoots. If you need those, a marketing agency is the better choice, and the SEO part can still be done separately.
Restaurant SEO tips you can do yourself this week
Search your restaurant’s name on a phone and note who ranks above your own website.
Check the hours in your Google Business Profile against the real ones, including the next public holiday.
Replace a PDF menu link in the profile with a link to a text menu page, even a simple one.
Upload five recent photos of dishes that are on the menu now.
Answer every review from the last three months, good and bad.
Make sure the name, address and phone number on your website match the profile exactly.
These steps are free and take an afternoon. They do not replace work on the website, but they often move a restaurant up in the map results within weeks.

children.text: I design restaurant websites and build them myself, so the design and the build come from one person at one price. The design starts from how guests choose a restaurant: on their phone, in a few seconds, often while standing outside another one. In those seconds the site has to show what you cook, whether you are open and how to get a table.
What restaurant website design has to answer in the first five seconds

Almost every visit to a restaurant website starts with one of three questions: what do they serve, are they open, can I get a table. A good design answers all three on the first screen of a phone, before anyone scrolls.
That first screen holds four things and nothing else:
the name of the place and what kind of food it serves, in plain words
today’s opening hours, not the whole week
two buttons: Menu and Book a table
one photograph that shows the food or the room as guests will actually see it

The story of the chef, the interior, the awards and the gift vouchers go below. They matter, but nobody reads them before deciding where to eat tonight. On a phone the booking button stays fixed at the bottom of the screen, so it is one tap away from anywhere on the page.
Restaurant menu design: readable on a phone, not a PDF

The online menu is the page guests open most, and it is where most restaurant websites fail. A PDF menu opens in a separate viewer, needs zooming, is slow on mobile data and is often out of date because updating it means sending a new file to someone.
A menu designed for the web works differently:
sections in the order guests read them — starters, mains, desserts, drinks — with a jump bar at the top
every dish as a line of text: name, one short description, price aligned on the right
dietary and allergen marks as small symbols with a legend, not a footnote
body text at 16 px or larger, so nobody has to zoom
seasonal or daily dishes marked, so a guest knows what is on today

Because the menu is text and not a picture, search engines and AI assistants can read the dishes and connect them to your restaurant. Someone looking for “ramen near me” or asking an assistant where to eat khachapuri can find you by what you actually cook. How the menu is edited from your phone is covered on the
restaurant website development
page.
Food photography in restaurant web design: fewer photos, better ones
A restaurant website needs eight to twelve strong photographs, not sixty. Guests remember two or three images; the rest only slow the page down.
What works:
dishes that are on the current menu, shot in the same light, so the menu and the photos tell the same story
the room at the time of day guests come — a dinner place photographed in the evening, a breakfast place in the morning
people in the frame where it fits the venue: a busy room sells a bistro better than an empty one

Every photo is compressed into modern formats and loaded only when it comes into view. The goal is that the main image on the first screen appears in under 2.5 seconds on a mobile connection — the threshold Google uses for a good page. If you do not have photos yet, I prepare a shot list for your photographer so the session covers exactly what the design needs.
Restaurant brand on the website: colours, fonts and tone taken from the venue

The website should feel like walking in. The design system comes from what already exists in the restaurant: the sign, the printed menu, the materials and colours of the interior. A new visual identity is not part of the job unless you want one.

In practice that means two typefaces at most, a small palette built from the venue’s own colours and text that meets the WCAG contrast ratio of 4.5:1, so it stays readable in sunlight on a phone screen. The tone of the copy follows the place: a neighbourhood wine bar and a hotel restaurant should not sound the same.
Restaurant website design examples: what the best restaurant websites have in common

Galleries of restaurant website examples are full of slow, image-heavy pages that look good on a large monitor and fall apart on a phone. The restaurant sites that bring bookings tend to share a few plain decisions:
one clear booking path, repeated on every page, instead of a phone number hidden in the footer
the address with a map link and directions near the top, not only on a contact page
private events and group bookings on their own page with their own enquiry form
language versions where the guests are tourists or expats, with the menu translated, not only the home page
no autoplay video, no full-screen intro, no music
Restaurant website design or a restaurant website template

A free or paid restaurant website template on a builder is a reasonable choice for a small café with a short, stable menu and no plans to grow. You get a tidy page quickly and pay a monthly subscription.

Custom design starts to pay off when the restaurant has more than one location, runs events and group bookings, needs several languages, or depends on being found in local search. Templates make all of these possible but rarely make them work well, and moving away from a builder later usually means rebuilding the site from scratch.

children.text: Restaurant website menu: real pages, not a PDF
Almost every visit to a restaurant website is driven by one of three questions: what do they serve, are they open, and
can I get a table

. Answering those three on a phone within a few seconds is most of what the site is for. Everything else — the story, the interiors, the chef's biography — matters only to visitors who got past those first questions satisfied.

Which makes the standard habit of publishing the menu as a PDF the most expensive decision in the field. It fails on all three counts at once. On a phone it requires pinching and zooming to read, which is enough to lose people. It's invisible to search engines, so
the restaurant competes only for its own name rather than for the food it actually serves
. And because updating it means regenerating a file, it drifts out of date until the version people are reading isn't the one being cooked.

Publishing the menu as ordinary pages fixes all of it. Dishes become text your kitchen can change the same day, readable without effort, and — with the right structured data — legible to search engines and AI assistants, which increasingly answer questions like "where can I eat something specific nearby" with a short list rather than a page of links. People search for dishes and cuisines far more than for restaurant names, and a menu locked in a file participates in none of that. Whether that comes from
a page builder or custom-built code
is a decision worth making deliberately, not by default.

Opening hours deserve more care than they usually get, for a simple reason: checking whether somewhere is open is one of the most common things a person does before leaving the house. Hours that are wrong are worse than hours that are missing, because the second sends someone to call and the first sends them to a closed door. A live indicator based on your real schedule, including a kitchen that closes before the room, is straightforward to build — I've implemented exactly that for a client whose customers routinely check before setting out.

Then there's the part most restaurant sites leave almost invisible: private events. Group bookings and closed events are frequently the most profitable evenings of a month, and on the majority of sites they amount to a sentence in the contact page. Giving them a real page — capacities, formats, what's possible, how far ahead to ask — makes them plannable, which is the only way anyone books them. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.
Restaurant website builder or a custom website

A restaurant website builder — a general one such as Wix or Squarespace, or a platform made for restaurants — puts a simple site online in a day for a monthly fee. For a café with a short menu that rarely changes, that is a reasonable start.

The limits appear exactly where this page is about: a menu as real pages the kitchen edits, hours that are always right, bookings without a portal, private events, language versions and local search. A builder offers each of these in a basic form, but the site cannot be shaped around them, and leaving the builder later usually means building again from scratch. A custom website is built around them from the start, and the code, the content and the address stay yours.
Development is one of three pieces of work on a restaurant website. How the site looks and reads on a phone is covered on the
restaurant website design
page, and getting found in Google Maps and local search on the

page.

children.text: I do SEO for restoration companies that handle water damage, fire and smoke damage and mold: emergency pages that load fast and get the call, a page for each kind of damage, a Google profile set up for round-the-clock work and plain answers to the insurance questions homeowners ask on the worst day of their year. In restoration a single job can be worth more than several months of SEO, and the customer usually calls the first company that looks local, available and competent.
Restoration SEO starts with the emergency call: searches made in a flooded basement

Most restoration work begins with a search like “water damage restoration near me”, “basement flooded what to do” or “emergency water removal”, typed on a phone, often at night. The person calls one of the first two or three names and rarely compares. Those searches show Local Services Ads and the map first, then franchise sites — SERVPRO, Paul Davis, PuroClean, BELFOR — and lead-generation pages built for every city.

If you answer around the clock, your emergency pages have one task: say in the first lines that a crew can come now, show the response area and put the phone number in a button, and prove you are a real local company with an address, photos of your trucks and team, and certifications. Longer explanations go lower on the page, for the careful reader and for Google.
Water damage restoration SEO: pages for burst pipes, flooded basements and sewage backups
Water damage brings most of the search volume in restoration, but it is not one search. Each cause brings a different customer and needs its own page:
burst and frozen pipes, appliance and water heater leaks — the typical insurance job in a house or apartment
flooded basements after heavy rain or rising groundwater — coverage often depends on the cause and the policy, so price questions come first
sewage backups — category 3 water, health risk, removal of soaked materials
water extraction and structural drying — equipment, moisture readings, how many days the dehumidifiers stay

Each page explains what happens in the first hour, the first day and the first week, what the homeowner should and should not do before you arrive, and when drywall, flooring or cabinets have to come out. Water category, drying time and mold risk are the details both readers and assistants look for.
Fire and smoke damage restoration pages in restoration company SEO

Fire jobs are rarer and larger. The homeowner is usually not searching at night but in the days after, often with an adjuster already involved, and compares companies more carefully. A fire and smoke page covers board-up and tarping, soot cleaning, smoke odor removal by the methods you use — thermal fogging, ozone or hydroxyl — contents cleaning and pack-out, and whether you also handle the rebuild. Separate pages for smoke odor and for contents pack-out pick up searches that one general “fire restoration” page misses.
Mold remediation SEO: testing, removal and clear limits

Mold searches come from worried homeowners, buyers after an inspection and landlords: “black mold in bathroom”, “mold remediation cost”, “mold after water leak”. A mold page explains the difference between testing and remediation, containment and air scrubbers, what happens to drywall and insulation and how you check the result. Some US states license mold assessment and remediation, sometimes as separate activities; where that applies to you, the license number belongs on the page.

Mold is also where trust is lost fastest. Pages that frighten people into large jobs collect reviews that say so. Pages that explain when a small patch can be cleaned by the owner and when a professional is needed rank for those questions and bring the callers who need you.
Insurance claims on a restoration website: coverage and adjuster questions in general terms

Almost every restoration customer asks about insurance, and the searches show it: “does homeowners insurance cover water damage”, “how to file a water damage claim”, “do I have to use the restoration company my insurance recommends”. what to document before work starts — photos, the source of the water, damaged belongings
how your estimate is prepared and shared with the adjuster, and the estimating software you use, such as Xactimate, if that is your practice
whether you bill the insurer directly and what stays with the homeowner — the deductible and anything not covered
who chooses the company that does the work, in general terms
Coverage depends on the policy and the cause of the loss, and the page should say so in one plain sentence. A company that explains the process calmly is the one a stressed homeowner calls back.
IICRC certification, licenses and trust signals in SEO for restoration companies

Homeowners and adjusters both check whether the people entering the house are trained. IICRC certifications held by your technicians — water damage restoration, applied structural drying, fire and smoke, mold remediation — a contractor license where your state requires one, insurance, years in business and a real address are facts that readers and search engines use. Put them as text on the pages where they matter, not only as logos in the footer. Team pages with real names and photos count for more here than in most trades, because your crew will come back to the same home for days while it dries.

Restoration is one of the map categories crowded with lead-generation listings. What holds up over time is a real profile with consistent details: “Water damage restoration service” as the primary category, fire and mold categories added where Google offers them, the address shown or hidden according to whether customers visit, 24/7 hours only if someone really answers at 3 a.m., and photos from jobs, equipment and the warehouse.

Organic search is the source that charges nothing per job. It takes months to build, so most companies keep the other sources while it grows. My work is on the search side, and I make sure the pages that rank are the same pages your ads and referral partners send people to.
Reviews for restoration companies after water, fire and mold jobs: when to ask

A restoration customer is not happy on the day the crew arrives; they are relieved weeks later, when the house is dry and the claim is settled. That is the moment to ask for a review, with a direct link. Reviews that mention the damage type, the response time and the help with paperwork match what the next customer is searching for. Answer every review, including angry ones about insurance outcomes you did not control, calmly and without the customer’s details.

Questions like “how long does it take to dry a flooded basement”, “is mold after a leak dangerous” or “who does fire damage cleanup near me” are now answered by ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews before anyone clicks. children.text: I do SEO for roofing companies: the website, the Google Business Profile and the pages a homeowner finds when the roof leaks, the hail has passed or the shingles are twenty years old. Roofing jobs are large and rare — a homeowner replaces a roof once or twice in a lifetime — so a single extra replacement job a month pays for the work many times over. That is also why every roofer in town fights for the same searches.
Why SEO for roofing is harder than for most local trades
Roofing is one of the most competitive local niches in search. On a search like “roof replacement” in a mid-sized city you compete with:
local roofers who have collected reviews for a decade
national replacement brands with big advertising budgets
lead sellers and directories that rank pages for every town
Google Local Services Ads with the Google Guaranteed badge at the very top

Generic SEO packages rarely move a roofer up in this crowd. What works is depth: the most useful page in your area for each kind of roof job, a profile with more fresh reviews than the competitors on the map, and pages that answer the questions a homeowner has before letting a roofer climb up.
Roofing SEO keywords: what homeowners type before they call a roofer
Before any page is written I pull the real search data for your jobs and towns. Roofing searches fall into a few clear groups, and each group needs a different page:
emergency and damage — “roof leak repair”, “storm damage roof repair”, “emergency roof tarp”
replacement and cost — “roof replacement cost”, “new roof near me”, “how long does a roof last”
roof type — “metal roofing contractor”, “flat roof repair”, “shingle roof installation”
checks and paperwork — “roof inspection”, “roof inspection for home sale”, “roof insurance claim help”
The data also shows which of these searches trigger the map, which trigger Local Services Ads and which already show an AI Overview — and that decides where effort goes first.
Storm and hail damage searches in SEO for roofing companies

After a hailstorm or a windstorm, searches for roof inspection and storm damage in the affected towns jump within hours and stay high for weeks. The roofing company whose storm pages already rank gets those calls; pages written after the storm usually start ranking when the demand is gone. So storm content is prepared in advance: a page on hail damage, a page on wind damage, each with photos of real damage you have repaired and a clear way to book an inspection.

Homeowners are also wary of out-of-town crews who appear after every storm. Your pages should show the opposite: a local address, years in the area, a license number and roofs you have done on nearby streets.
Insurance claim questions on roofing storm pages

Most storm jobs go through the homeowner’s insurance, and searches like “does insurance cover hail damage on a roof” are common. A good storm page explains the steps in plain words: the inspection, the photos you take, the adjuster’s visit, what you do if the claim is approved. It does not promise that insurance will pay; that is not yours to promise, and pages that do it lose trust.
Roof replacement, repair and inspection pages in roofing company SEO
Replacement, repair and inspection are three different decisions, and putting them on one “Services” page loses all three searches. Roofing company SEO gives each one its own page:
roof replacement — materials, the order of work, how long a tear-off takes, a price range per square if you give one, warranty and financing
roof repair — leaks, missing shingles, flashing, when repair is enough and when it is not
roof inspection — after storms, before a home sale, for insurance, what the report includes

The “repair or replace” question is one of the most searched in roofing. A page that answers it fairly, with the signs that point either way, ranks well and brings homeowners who trust you before the first call.
Metal, shingle and flat roofs: SEO for roofing contractors with several roof systems

A roofer who installs asphalt shingles, standing seam metal and flat roofs (TPO, EPDM, modified bitumen) is really in three markets, with different customers and different searches. Metal roofing buyers compare lifespan and cost; flat roof searches come mostly from commercial buildings and property managers; shingle searches are the volume of residential work. Each system gets a page with your projects, the manufacturers you are certified with and the questions buyers of that material ask.
Local SEO for roofing companies: Google Business Profile and service-area pages after storms

The map results bring a large share of roofing calls. Local SEO for roofing companies starts with the profile: “Roofing contractor” as the primary category, every service listed, the real service area, weekly photos from jobs and answers to common questions.

Area pages are where roofers most often cross the line. After a storm it is tempting to publish fifty town pages with the same text. Google treats those as doorway pages and filters them. An honest service-area page has roofs you replaced in that town, reviews from customers there and local details such as typical roof age or HOA rules. A town gets a page when you have work to show there. More on the map side on the

page.
Reviews, project photos and financing in roofing contractor SEO

A new roof is one of the largest bills a homeowner pays, so they read reviews before they call. Roofing contractor SEO sets up a routine: a text with a review link the day the crew leaves, an answer to every review within days, and customers asked to name the job and the town. Before-and-after photos with the roof type and town written next to them work both for search and for the decision.
Financing deserves its own page if you offer it. “Roof financing” and “roof replacement with no money down” are searched by homeowners who would otherwise postpone the job.
Buying roofing leads vs SEO: Local Services Ads, lead platforms and your own calls

Roofing leads are sold by lead platforms such as Angi or HomeAdvisor and by specialized roofing lead sellers. The same lead often goes to several roofers, and you pay for it whether you win the job or not. Google Local Services Ads charge per lead too, and show only a handful of businesses with the Google Guaranteed badge.

Bought leads start working this week and stop when the payments stop. SEO for roofing companies takes months to build, but the calls it brings come to you alone, without a per-lead fee. Many roofers keep Local Services Ads for the storm season and use SEO to depend less on bought leads over time. I do the SEO part; I do not run ads or sell leads.

Seasonality in roofing SEO marketing: a year-round plan

Roofing demand follows the weather: spring and summer storms, the rush to finish replacements before winter, a quiet period when snow and cold stop most tear-offs. Roofing SEO marketing uses the quiet months to build what the busy months need — storm pages, replacement guides, new project photos — because pages need weeks to rank. In regions with hurricane or hail seasons the plan is set around those dates.

Roofing website design decides what a homeowner sees and does on your site — usually on a phone, sometimes standing in the yard looking at shingles the wind tore off, sometimes weeks into planning a new roof. Every screen is laid out to end in one of two actions: a call about a roof that leaks now, or a request for an inspection and estimate.
Roofing website design for two visitors: an urgent leak or storm, and a planned roof replacement

The urgent visitor has a stain spreading on the ceiling or debris in the yard after last night’s storm. They want to know whether you can come and how soon. The planning visitor has a roof near the end of its life and will compare three or four roofers on finished roofs, materials, warranties and monthly payments before inviting one to measure. They read the same site in very different ways, and the design gives each a path of its own:
the urgent path is short: a call button, emergency tarping if you offer it, one line on how soon a crew can come
the planned path is longer: materials and colors, finished roofs, warranty, financing, then an estimate request
the two buttons look different, so the urgent visitor never lands in a multi-step form and the planner is not pushed to phone before they are ready
Website design for roofing: what the first screen shows on a phone
The first screen of a roofing site carries four things and nothing else:
what you do and where: “Roof replacement and repair in [your area]”, not a slogan about quality
two buttons: call, and book a roof inspection — marked free only if it is
one line of proof: licensed and insured, years in business, review score
one photo of a roof you finished, taken from above
Sliders, video backgrounds and welcome paragraphs move down the page or go. They push the buttons out of view, and a homeowner looking at a damaged roof does not scroll to find them.
Inspection and estimate buttons in mobile-first roofing contractor website design

The layout is designed on a phone screen first; the desktop version is adapted from it. On phones the call button and the inspection button sit in a bar fixed at the bottom of the screen, where the thumb already is, on every page. On a desktop the phone number sits top right, where people look for it.

The wording changes with the page: “Book a hail damage inspection” on storm pages, “Get a replacement estimate” on replacement and material pages, “Call for emergency tarping” where that is the job. One “Contact us” across the whole site makes the visitor translate their problem into your menu.
What the form asks, where requests go and how they reach your CRM is covered on the
roofing websites
page.
Aerial, drone and before-and-after roof photos in roofing website design

Homeowners rarely see their own roof from above, and a roof is hard to judge from the street. Aerial and drone photos show the finished job the way a ground shot cannot: straight courses, clean valleys, neat ridge caps, flashing around the chimney. A before-and-after pair from the same angle — the worn, patched roof and the new one — does more than any paragraph about workmanship. On each project:
before and after from the same position, as a slider or side by side
the roof system, color and product line under the photos
the town or neighborhood, so visitors see roofs near their own
one or two close-ups of details — drip edge, vents, flashing — for the visitor comparing roofers

Commercial drone flights are regulated in most countries — in the US they need a pilot with an FAA Part 107 certificate — so drone shots come from a certified pilot on your team or a hired one. Phone photos from a ladder still work for details. Stock roofs are recognized at once and say nothing about your crew.
Trust signals in roofing company website design: license, insurance, manufacturer certifications, warranties

Every big storm brings storm chasers who knock on doors, take deposits and are gone before the first leak. Homeowners know it, and they look for signs that you will still answer the phone when the warranty matters. The design puts those signs next to every button, not in the footer:
license number and insurance, written out so they can be checked
manufacturer certifications — only programs you belong to, shown the way the manufacturer’s rules allow
warranties in plain words: what the manufacturer covers, what your workmanship warranty covers, and for how long
a local address and the year the company started
a review score and recent reviews that name the roof, the town or the storm
A storm-season banner on a roofing website: when it appears and what it says

After hail or high wind, visitors arrive with one question: can you inspect my roof this week? A slim banner above the header answers it before they look for anything else — the storm date and area, how soon you can inspect, and a button to book. Your office switches it on and off in the admin panel; a banner still announcing a storm from three months ago makes the site look abandoned.

The banner is designed before the season, with fixed wording, color and position, so it does not look improvised on the day. It uses the same accent color as the call button and never covers the button bar on phones.
How to display financing in roofing website design

A full replacement costs more than many homeowners keep in savings, so the planner looks for a monthly payment as much as for the total. Financing is shown where the decision is made, not on a page few people find:
a short line under the estimate button on replacement and material pages: “Financing available”, linked to the details
an example payment only if your lending partner gives you one you may publish
the lender’s name, so the visitor knows who they would be borrowing from
Financing stays off the urgent path: someone with water coming through the ceiling needs a crew, not a loan offer.
Best roofing website design: what to take from Dribbble and Pinterest examples

Searches for the best roofing website design lead to Dribbble shots and Pinterest boards: big aerial heroes, dark backgrounds, heavy type. They are useful for color, type and photo style. They are made to be admired as pictures, though, and rarely show the screens that decide whether a homeowner calls: a phone layout with the button bar, a replacement page with real text, an inspection form, a storm banner. When you send examples you like, I take the look from them and keep the layout that works for a roofing company.
Free roofing website templates or a custom roofing website design

Free roofing website templates and paid themes look finished in their demo: drone shots, invented reviews, a storm banner. With a real company’s content the gaps show — no separate urgent and planned paths, one page for every service, a contact form instead of an inspection request, no place for certifications or financing beside the buttons.

The choice depends on what the site has to carry. A roofer doing repairs in one town by referral can run on a well-chosen template with real photos for years. A company that depends on storm seasons, sells financed replacements and wants certifications next to every button ends up overriding the template piece by piece, and that usually costs more than a design made for the company from the start.
Choosing a roofing website design agency or a single designer

A roofing website design agency brings a team and often sells the site together with ads, lead generation and monthly marketing, sometimes to several roofers in one market. A single designer who also builds the site — that is how I work — means the person who drew the layout makes it work on a phone, at one price, without a retainer. Whoever you choose, ask:

Are you designing for another roofer in our area?

Roofing website design that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Homeowners increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews which roofers nearby are certified, or how a metal roof compares with shingles. Assistants read text, not pictures. A design that puts certifications in badge images, warranty terms in a graphic and service areas on a map image hides the very facts an assistant needs. children.text: I build roofing websites for roofing companies and roofing contractors: a site for your own business, planned, designed, built and launched by one person, with a page for every roof job you sell, inspection requests that arrive with photos and land in your CRM, and code that stays yours. How it looks and what a homeowner sees first is on the
roofing website design
page.
What roofing contractor websites have to handle: storm calls, active leaks and replacement decisions

Work reaches a roofer’s website in three moods. After a hailstorm, homeowners in a few zip codes want an inspection this week. A homeowner with water dripping through a ceiling wants a tarp on the roof today. A homeowner with twenty-year-old curling shingles reads for weeks about materials and payments before inviting anyone to measure. A roofing contractor website takes in all three:
a quick path to a phone call for active leaks and emergency tarping
an inspection request that collects the address and photos, for storm damage and planned work alike
depth on replacement, materials and payment for the homeowner still deciding
a way for the office to switch storm messages and storm-area pages on and off without calling a developer
Roofing company website pages for replacement, repair, storm damage and inspections
On many roofing company websites every job sits on one “Services” page, which cannot be found for any single job. Each service you want more of gets its own page, generated from one template:
Roof replacement — tear-off and installation, the materials you install, typical timeline, warranty, financing
Roof repair — leaks, flashing, missing or lifted shingles, ventilation problems
Storm and hail damage — what you check, how the inspection runs, what happens after it
Roof inspections — after a storm, before buying or selling a home, for an insurance renewal
Gutters, skylights and siding, if you sell them
Every service page has the same parts: the job in your words, finished projects of that type pulled in automatically, customer questions, and the inspection request at the end.
Metal, shingle and flat roof pages on a roofing contractor website

Each roof system you install — asphalt shingle, standing seam or exposed-fastener metal, flat roofs in TPO, EPDM or modified bitumen — gets a page built from structured fields: the products and manufacturers you install, the warranty that comes with them, the colors you offer and a project list filtered to that material. Commercial work gets its own section and its own request form asking for building type, approximate roof size and access, so property managers are not sent through a homeowner’s form.
Service-area and storm-area pages on roofing websites: real towns, real jobs

Homeowners search for a roofer with a town name. Service-area pages come from one template plus a short entry per town: roofs you have done there, reviews from customers there, the building department that issues roofing permits, local details such as HOA rules. A town gets its own page when there is real work to show; one with nothing behind it stays a line in the coverage list.

Storm-area pages use the same template but are tied to a date. After a hailstorm the office opens a page for the affected area — the storm date, the zip codes, what a homeowner can check from the ground, a link to book an inspection — and later closes it or turns it into a normal area page with the roofs you replaced there. What the build never does is stamp out fifty copies of one text with the town name swapped.
Roof inspection requests with photos, sent to JobNimbus, AccuLynx or your CRM

The inspection request is the main form on a roofing website, and it is built in short steps that work on a phone: address, what happened (leak, storm, old roof, home sale), whether an insurance claim is open, a preferred time, and photos. Photos from the ground or the attic tell the office whether to send a repair tech or an estimator. Photos are resized on the phone before upload, so a request does not fail on a weak signal.

Requests go where your office already works. Roofing CRMs such as JobNimbus, AccuLynx and Roofr, and field-service software such as ServiceTitan, can take website leads through their own web forms, an integration or a connector like Zapier. Without a CRM, requests arrive by email with the photos attached. Each request carries the page and the search or ad it came from, so you see which pages bring replacements.
Instant estimate and roof measurement tools on a roofing website

Some homeowners want a number before they talk to anyone. Several roofing software products and measurement services offer instant estimate widgets: the visitor types an address, the tool measures the roof from aerial or satellite imagery and shows a price range for the materials you set up. Its limits:
the range is only as good as the price per square you enter and keep up to date
complex roofs, steep pitches and tree cover make measurements from imagery less reliable
a third-party widget loads its own scripts, so it sits on the replacement page and loads on demand, not on every page
every instant estimate still ends in an inspection request, because the final price depends on what the crew finds
Financing and insurance claim help pages on a roofing company website

Many homeowners put off a new roof until they see a monthly figure. If you offer financing through a lending partner, the site gets a financing page with the terms your partner lets you publish and a link to its application, plus a short mention on every replacement page. The terms are stored in one place and edited once.

Storm work usually goes through the homeowner’s insurer. An insurance claim help page sets out what your company does at each step — the inspection, the photo report, meeting the adjuster, a supplement if items were missed — and what the homeowner should keep: the policy number, the claim number and photos taken right after the storm. It never promises what the insurer will pay. The inspection form asks for the claim stage, so the office sees whether it is a fresh storm or a claim in progress.
Speed of a roofing website full of aerial and project photos

Roofing websites carry heavy images: drone shots, close-ups of hail hits, galleries from every job. Uploaded straight off the camera, they make a page crawl on mobile data. Images are compressed and resized on upload, served in modern formats and loaded only as they scroll into view, so pages appear in under 2.5 seconds — the threshold Google uses for a good page load. The phone number and the inspection button load first, before photos, chat and review widgets.
Hosting includes SSL, daily backups and spam filtering. No monthly retainer; changes after launch are paid as work done.
Roofing website builders, rented agency sites or a roofing website you own

Roofing website builders — general builders, sites bundled with roofing software and template sites sold by marketing companies — put a page online fast for a monthly fee. Some roofing marketing agencies keep the site on their own account: when you leave, the site and sometimes the domain stay with them.
For a small crew in one town, a builder can be enough. The limits show as the company grows:
no real way to add a page per service, roof system, town or storm area
a request form that cannot pass leads to your CRM, or only on a higher plan
a fee that continues for as long as the site exists
A roofing website you own is paid for once, the code, content and domain are in your name, and it can move to any host or developer.

Brief. You send the roof jobs and systems you sell, the towns you cover, your certifications, financing partner and CRM, and finished projects with photos.
Structure. I propose the pages — services, roof systems, areas, storm, insurance, financing — and the path from each one to a call or an inspection request.
Design and build. Pages are designed on a phone first, then built and filled with your content.
Connections. The inspection form, CRM, call tracking, analytics and your Google Business Profile are connected and tested with real requests.
Launch and hand-over. You get access to everything and a short guide to adding projects and opening storm-area pages.

Lists of the best roofing websites judge the home page by its looks. From the build side, the sites that keep bringing inspections share a few plain decisions:
a page for each job, roof system and town instead of one services page
an inspection request that takes photos and goes straight into the CRM
storm messages and storm-area pages the office controls itself
financing and insurance questions answered on the site, not left for the phone
A roofing website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Homeowners now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews things like “how long does a metal roof last”, “does homeowners insurance cover hail damage” or “which roofers near me are certified by the shingle manufacturer”. An assistant can only use what it can read and check, so the build hands it clear facts:
license number, insurance, manufacturer certifications and warranty terms written as text, not only inside badge images
structured data for the business as a roofing contractor, for each service and for the areas it covers
answers to cost, lifespan and repair-or-replace questions on the service pages, in plain sentences
the same company name, address and phone as in your Google Business Profile and directories
Getting into those answers is ongoing work, described on the

page. Ranking in Google search and on the map is covered on the

children.text: Why most accounting firm websites are invisible in search

Open the search results for «website for accounting firms» and the top of the page is held by two template vendors who build sites for the profession by the hundred. That is the whole explanation. A large part of the industry sits on near-identical templates: the same page structure, the same service list, the same «we provide tax, audit and advisory services to businesses of all sizes». To a search engine those firms are interchangeable, so none of them can outrank another on anything except its own name.

The second reason is that the pages describe the service and not the client. «Tax planning» is what you do; «tax planning for an S-corp owner paying himself a salary» is what somebody searches. A firm that keeps the first wording competes with every other firm in the country, and a firm that writes the second competes with almost nobody.
A page per client type is the one change that moves accounting firm SEO

Accounting is bought by segment, not by service. An e-commerce seller with inventory in three states, a construction company with retainage and progress billing, a dental practice with equipment leases, a freelancer who just crossed a VAT threshold — these people have different questions, different software, and different fears, and they search in those terms.

So the structure is one page per segment you actually serve, each naming the segment, the specific problems it brings, the software you work in, and what the engagement costs. That is also the honest filter: a firm that cannot name three segments it is better at than average has a positioning problem rather than an SEO problem, and more content will not fix it.
name the segment in the heading, not in the third paragraph;
say which software you work in — the segment searches by it;
state what the engagement includes and what it costs, or at least a floor;
show who on the team actually handles that segment;
and do not create a segment page for work you would rather not take.
Local search for an accounting firm with one office or several

Most accounting work is bought locally even when it could be done remotely, because people want someone they can reach. That makes the Google Business Profile as important as the site: the categories, the service list, the hours, and the reviews, with the same firm name and address everywhere they appear. A firm with two offices needs a real page per office with its own address and team, not one page listing both.
What this covers in detail is on the
local SEO page
. Where the firm serves clients across a country rather than a city, the local side matters less and the segment pages carry the weight.
Publishing prices: how far to go and what it changes

The single most common complaint from accounting-firm visitors is that no price is shown anywhere. Buyers read «contact us for a quote» as «this will be expensive and awkward to ask about», and the ones who are price-sensitive leave without contacting you — which is also the point: a stated floor filters them out before they take an hour of your time.

Going as far as you are willing is enough. A monthly fee for a defined scope, a fixed price for an annual return at a stated revenue level, or a range with what moves it. The firms that refuse any figure are usually the ones whose enquiries are hardest to qualify.
Publishing content before the busy season, not during it

Search demand in this profession is seasonal and the content calendar has to run ahead of it. A page written during the filing rush is indexed and starts gathering positions after the rush has ended; the same page published a few months earlier collects the season it was written for. The practical rule is that anything tied to a deadline is written in the quiet months, and the quiet months are exactly when nobody feels like writing it.
SEO for bookkeepers: a smaller market with a different buyer

A bookkeeping practice is not a smaller accounting firm — it sells a recurring operational service, usually to owners who do not want to touch their own books, and the buyer compares on monthly price, software and responsiveness rather than on credentials. Measured demand here is small: «seo for bookkeepers» and «bookkeeper seo» together run about thirty searches a month in English, which is why this is a section rather than a page of its own.

What differs in the work: the software is the keyword, because owners search «QuickBooks bookkeeper» or «Xero bookkeeper» and not «bookkeeping services»; the monthly price belongs on the page because that is the comparison being made; and a clear statement of what is and is not included prevents most of the bad-fit enquiries.
What SEO for accounting firms costs and when it shows results

An audit is €250 and covers the site, the Google Business Profile and what AI assistants currently say about the firm. One-off work — segment pages, pricing, structured data, the local profile — runs €250–800 depending on scope. Ongoing work is €800 a month. First movements are usually visible after about a month and a half; steady growth sits on a three to six month horizon, and anyone promising a position by a date is selling a date rather than a result. If the firm sits on a vendor template where pages cannot be added, text cannot be edited without a support ticket and the address structure is fixed, SEO work on it is paying rent. In that case the cheaper route is a site you own:

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for an artist's website actually consists of

children.text: Which artists this page is about, and where the other meanings are covered

«Artist» carries several trades, and they need different work, so to be clear about what is on this page: it is for visual artists who make objects — painters, printmakers, sculptors, ceramicists, illustrators — selling originals, prints or commissions from their own site.
If you are a recording or performing artist, the work is different and it is on the
SEO for musicians page
. A makeup artist needs local bookings rather than collectors, which is
makeup artist website design
, and a tattoo artist the same, which is
tattoo studio website design
Why an artist's website usually gives a search engine nothing to read

The standard artist site is one portfolio page holding forty images, a short bio, and a contact form. To a visitor it reads as confident restraint. To a search engine it is a single page with almost no text, where forty works are indistinguishable from each other and none of them has an address of its own, so there is nothing to match against any search a collector could type.

This is not a matter of writing more for the sake of it. A search engine cannot see a painting: it cannot tell oil from acrylic, it cannot measure the canvas, and it has no idea the piece is predominantly blue. Every fact a buyer would filter by has to exist as text somewhere, and on most artist sites it exists nowhere — not in the image file names, not in the alt text, not on the page.
A page per artwork: what the page for a single painting has to contain

The unit of SEO for an artist is not the portfolio and not the series — it is the individual work. Each piece that is for sale, or that represents the kind of thing you take commissions for, gets its own address and its own text, and that text is mostly facts a collector asks for before they ask the price.
title, year, medium and exact dimensions, written out rather than abbreviated;
the series or body of work it belongs to, linked;
price and availability, or the plain statement that it is sold;
what the piece is of and what it is about, in two or three sentences;
framing, hanging, edition size for prints, and what shipping involves;
and an image with alt text that describes the work rather than repeating the title.
Sold works should stay published instead of being deleted

Artists routinely remove a piece from the site once it sells, which is understandable and costs them twice. The sold pages are the body of text that makes the site legible to a search engine in the first place, and they are the strongest evidence a hesitant buyer can be given — that work at this size, in this medium, at this price, has been bought before by somebody.

The version that works keeps the page, marks it sold clearly so nobody enquires about it in vain, and links from it to the series and to available work of a similar size. Over a few years that turns into the part of the site that brings people in, and it costs nothing to build because the pages already existed.
Nobody searches for «artist»: the words collectors actually use

Searches that end in a sale almost never contain the word artist. They describe the thing wanted: a large abstract painting for a living room, an original seascape in oil, a bronze figure under a certain height, a botanical print in a particular colour. Buyers search by subject, medium, size, colour and sometimes by the room the work is going into, and those are precisely the searches a page about one piece can answer and a portfolio page never will.

The practical consequence is that keyword work for an artist is not about finding a term to rank for; it is about making sure the facts already true of your work are written down in the words buyers use. Somebody looking for a two-metre canvas does not search «large» if they mean two metres, and an artist who writes «large» instead of the measurement has opted out of the search.
Owning the search for your own name, which marketplaces and galleries have taken

Type your own name into a search engine. For most artists the first results are Saatchi Art, Artsy, Etsy, a gallery's roster page, an Instagram profile, and a Behance account abandoned in 2017 — with the artist's own website somewhere below. This matters more than any other search, because the person typing your name has already seen the work: at a fair, in a group show, on a wall at a friend's house.

That visitor is the most valuable one you will ever get, and they arrive at a marketplace that takes a commission, or at a gallery page listing two works from four years ago, and in the worst case at a profile you no longer update. Winning your own name is the cheapest and most profitable piece of SEO available to an artist, and it is mostly a matter of structure rather than content: one clear address for you, consistent naming, and the right pages linked from the right places.
That groundwork is the
SEO audit
, and where you also want to be found by city — a studio open to visits, a local commission market — it extends into
local SEO
Commissions and prints are two separate searches and two separate pages

Commissions and prints look like extensions of the same business and behave like different ones. Someone commissioning a portrait or a large piece for a specific wall wants process, timeline, price range and reassurance that they can see progress; someone buying a print wants size, paper, edition and delivery. They search differently, they decide differently, and a single page trying to serve both converts neither.

Commissions are a service page: what you take on, what you decline, how long it takes, what it costs from and to. Prints are closer to a shop, and once there are more than a handful the work overlaps with
SEO for online stores
. What the site itself needs to look like is on the

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for an author actually consists of

children.text: Three different things are called author SEO, and this is one of them

The phrase is used for three unrelated jobs. Academic publishers use it for helping researchers get papers found and cited. SEO software uses it for author bylines and expertise as a ranking factor on any website. Writers use it for getting books and themselves discovered by readers. This page is about the third one: novelists, non-fiction authors and self-published writers with a backlist to sell.
What an author site can win in search, and what it cannot

Start with the limit. Search your book title and the first screen is Amazon, Goodreads, a retailer or two and possibly a pirate site. Your page will not take that first place, and chasing it is how authors waste a year. Title search is also the least valuable query you could win, because the person typing it already knows the book exists and will buy it wherever they land.

Three things are winnable and worth more. Your own name, which readers search after finishing something and liking it — that search should reach you, not a retailer page that sells one book and shows nothing else you wrote. Your series, which readers search in confusion about reading order more often than anything else. And the recommendation questions, where somebody does not know your name at all and asks for a book like one they loved.
Why a series page earns more than a book page

A reader who finished book two does not search for book three by its title; they search for the series and the order. A reader who heard about a series searches for where to start. A reader halfway through searches whether the spin-off matters. These are small, specific, repeating queries that retailers answer badly, because a retailer page is built to sell one item rather than to explain a shelf.

So the structure is a page for the series that states the reading order plainly, what each book covers without spoiling it, where the novellas and prequels fit, and what to read next when the series ends. It is the page readers bookmark and send to each other, and it is the one an assistant can quote when asked where to start.
state the reading order in text, numbered, near the top;
say what to read first for a newcomer and what is optional;
name every format and edition, because readers search by format;
link to every retailer rather than one, including the library option;
and keep the series page updated before the release, not after.
What the site itself needs — a page per book, retailer links, media kit, newsletter — is a different job and is described on the
author website design page
The recommendation question is where new readers come from

«Books like Project Hail Mary», «best historical novels set in Poland», «something to read after finishing a series» — these are the queries that reach a reader who has never heard your name, and they are also the exact shape of question people now ask an assistant rather than a search engine. Being an answer to them is not done by repeating keywords; it is done by having a page that describes your book the way a reader would describe it to a friend: the setting, the period, the feel, the comparable titles, the content warnings.

Most author sites cannot be used this way, because the only description on them is the publisher's cover copy, which is written to sell and not to inform. The version that works says what the book is actually like, for whom, and when it is not the right choice. That last part is the one authors resist and the one that makes the page quotable.

children.text: No, and I would not take money to try. Amazon and the retailers own title search and that is not going to change. The work is on your name, your series and the recommendation questions, which are winnable and bring readers who do not yet know the book exists.

items.question: Can you get my book above Amazon for its own title?

children.text: It works better. Non-fiction readers search for the problem rather than the title — a topic, a question, a method — and those searches can be answered by pages around the book, which is a larger surface than fiction offers.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for an auto repair shop includes

children.text: Why searches for an auto repair shop work differently from other local services

A driver almost never chooses calmly. The car is already off the road, or it started making a noise nobody wants to drive on. So the search is urgent and very specific: not «car repair» but make plus part plus symptom — «clutch replacement Golf», «suspension noise Focus», «P0171 code what to do».

Two things follow. The driver will not read your site; they will open two or three tabs and call whoever answered fastest. And a single «our services» page answers none of those searches, so it does not appear for them.

There is a second audience that behaves nothing like the first: scheduled maintenance, pre-purchase inspections, getting a car ready to sell. They search ahead, compare and read. One page written to serve both usually loses both.
The map pack decides before your website does

On urgent searches most people never reach the regular results: the decision happens in the map pack, on distance, rating and whether you are open now. At that moment the site is not a showroom, it is confirmation — people open it to check that you do the specific repair and roughly what it costs.

So local SEO here starts with the Google Business Profile, not the copy: the right primary category, services with descriptions, real photos of the bays and the lifts, hours, and a phone somebody answers. And I will say plainly what cannot be fixed: distance is not optimisable. If you are out of town and a competitor is round the corner, «auto repair near me» goes to the competitor whatever anyone does. Repair-specific and make-specific searches depend on distance far less — and that is where there is something to win.
A page for every repair instead of one services list

The main SEO work on a garage site is turning the service list into separate pages. Clutch replacement, transmission repair, diagnostics, wheel alignment, suspension work, bodywork — different searches, different volumes, different questions, each needing its own page.

On that page a driver should find what they would otherwise ask on the phone: how long it takes, whether the car stays overnight, what is included, what the price depends on, what warranty applies and what happens if the fault comes back. That is the content — not «quality repairs on modern equipment», but answers.
If you specialise in certain makes, those get pages too: «transmission repair» and «transmission repair Passat» behave differently, and the second is usually less competitive with a warmer customer.
Price is the first question and most shop sites refuse to answer it
«Call for pricing» is the most expensive line on a repair shop website. Somebody with a broken car will not ring five places to learn the ballpark; they will ring the one that showed a range.

So repair pages carry a range and an explanation of what moves it: the scope of work, OEM part or aftermarket, the condition of neighbouring components that is only visible once it is apart. Say whether diagnostics is charged and whether it comes off the repair bill.
A price list as a PDF or an image does not count: neither search engines nor AI assistants read text inside pictures.
Tyre season is two short windows a year, and preparing for them takes longer than they last

Seasonal tyre work produces two demand spikes a year and both are short. The problem is that a page published during the rush will not rank during that rush: search needs time to crawl it and judge it.

So seasonal pages are prepared ahead and not deleted afterwards — the URL lives all year and gains weight before the next window. The same goes for tyre storage, which is a subscription in all but name and brings a customer who comes back for servicing.

children.text: How long it takes before the calls change

The first movement in visibility usually shows after about six weeks — new pages starting to collect impressions on long-tail searches. The growth the work is for builds over three to six months, and it is not slower because of effort but because search needs time to crawl pages and accumulate data on them.
Anyone promising calls in two weeks is promising something they do not control.
Who auto repair SEO suits and who it does not
SEO for an auto repair shop suits:
shops with a steady service list and their own address;
owners willing to show at least a price range;
shops where somebody answers the phone in working hours;
owners who can wait three to six months.
And it does not suit:
one-off or temporary operations;
owners committed to «call for pricing»;
shops with nobody to handle calls and forms;
owners who need customers this week.
The last line is not a formality. If you need work in the bays this week, the honest answer is paid ads, not SEO, and I do not run campaigns.

children.text: Auto repair shops in ChatGPT and AI Overviews: what GEO and AEO mean

Drivers increasingly ask an assistant directly: «where can I get a transmission rebuilt in this city», «how much is a timing belt», «what does code P0420 mean». ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews answer and name specific shops — taken not from advertising but from text they can read and restate.

Two related jobs sit behind that. GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) is about being mentioned in generative answers, and mentioned correctly. AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) is about the page giving a direct answer in its opening sentences, because that is what gets quoted. Classic SEO does not go away: it decides your position in Google, while GEO and AEO decide whether you are named when the customer asks instead of searching.

In practice: a direct answer at the top of each section, facts instead of adjectives, structured data that matches the text, and content readable without running scripts. Plus measurement on a fixed set of questions before and after — otherwise AI visibility is just talk.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a beauty salon includes

children.text: How clients actually search for a salon, and why it decides the page structure

Beauty searches are almost never generic. Nobody looks for «beauty services»; they look for one treatment, in one place, often for one evening. That single fact decides everything about how the site should be built.

Two groups carry the demand. Treatment plus location: «balayage <city>», «lash lift <district>», «laser hair removal <city>», «gel manicure near the office». And the «near me» group: «nail salon near me», «beauty salon open now», «brow bar near me». The second group is where local SEO lives, because the client has already decided what they want and is choosing only by distance and availability.
A site built around one «Services» page cannot answer either group. A site built around treatments answers both, and the same structure is what an AI assistant can read later.
A page for every treatment instead of one services list
The backbone of salon SEO is separate pages for the work: colour and balayage, cuts, lash extensions and lifts, brows, manicure and gel, pedicure, facials, peels, laser, waxing.

Each page answers what gets asked at the desk and in DMs: how long it takes, what it costs or starts at, which specialist does it, how long the result lasts, whether preparation or a patch test is needed, what aftercare looks like. That is the content a client needs before booking, and it is also the content that ranks — a two-line treatment description ranks for nothing.
If one specialist is the reason people come, that specialist gets a page: name, specialisation, portfolio of work, and a direct booking link.
Google Business Profile and the map pack decide before the website does

For a salon, the local results and the map usually appear above the ordinary links, and often the client books without opening a site at all. Treating the profile as an afterthought while optimising the website is the single most common mistake in this niche.

So the work starts there: the full treatment list in the profile, hours that are actually right including the evenings, real photographs of the interior and of the work, reviews answered, and a booking link that leads to the treatment rather than to the home page. Then the site and the profile are made to agree with each other, because a client who sees two different prices stops trusting both.
Prices and durations on the site, not in a photographed price list
«Prices on request» costs a salon more bookings than a high price does. The client is choosing between three salons on a phone, and the one that states the number gets the message.

A price list as an image or a story screenshot does not work either: neither search engines nor AI assistants read text inside pictures, so it is invisible to exactly the channels this page is about. A range with what moves it — length and density of hair, condition of nails, the specialist's level — works better than a single number and loses fewer people.
Why most salon websites do not rank, in order of frequency
two lines of text per treatment, which is nothing to rank with;
no location signals at all beyond an address in the footer;
the price list only as an image;
page titles like «Services» and «Prices», identical on every page;
a heavy gallery of uncompressed photographs, slow on a phone;
no structured data, so the hours and prices an assistant repeats are guesswork.
None of these is exotic, and none needs a redesign to fix. That is why an audit on a salon site usually finds more than a year of advertising would have bought.
Booking: the shortest path from the treatment page to a filled slot
A salon lives on schedule density: an empty slot at six on Friday is revenue that does not come back. So the site is judged by bookings, not by positions.

In practice that means a booking button on every treatment page rather than only in the menu, the same booking system the front desk actually uses, visible evening and weekend availability, and a phone number that is tappable. If bookings run through Booksy or a similar system, the site links straight into the right treatment instead of dropping the client on its home screen.

First movement appears in about six weeks: treatment pages that did not exist get indexed and start collecting impressions on long-tail searches. Steady growth in bookings builds over three to six months as the pages accumulate authority and the profile work compounds.

The map pack can move faster than that — sometimes within weeks — because the profile is a smaller object than a website. Anyone promising bookings in two weeks is promising something they do not control.

An audit of the site, the Google Business Profile and the AI answers is €250. One-off work — treatment pages, prices, structured data, the booking path — runs €250–800 depending on scope. It suits a salon with a steady treatment list and its own premises, willing to publish prices at least as a range, with somebody who answers messages during opening hours, and able to wait three to six months for the compounding part.

It does not suit a salon that works purely from Instagram and has no site to improve, one where «prices only by phone» is a rule, one with nobody to handle enquiries, or one that needs the chairs filled this week — that is an advertising budget, not SEO, and I do not run campaigns.

children.text: Beauty salons in AI search: what GEO and AEO mean and how they are done

More clients now ask an assistant before they open a booking app: «which salon near me does a lash lift after 7 pm», «who does balayage on dark hair without it turning orange, and for how much», «is there a salon in my district with laser and online booking». The assistant answers from text it can read and restate, and it names the places it found.

Two acronyms describe the work. GEO, generative engine optimization, is getting your salon picked up and named when an assistant assembles a recommendation. AEO, answer engine optimization, is having a sentence on your site that the assistant can repeat almost word for word.
What an assistant actually needs to find
every treatment as text: duration, a price or a «from» price, the technique, and which specialist offers it;
BeautySalon, HairSalon or NailSalon markup with address, opening hours and services, so the hours an assistant repeats are the ones on your door;
Service markup with a price for each treatment, so nothing has to be guessed about what «facial» includes;

identical name, hours and treatment names on the Google Business Profile, Booksy, Bing Places and Instagram — a salon open on Booksy but closed on Google gives an assistant two answers to choose from;
short answers on each treatment page to what clients ask at the desk: how long a lash lift lasts, whether a patch test is needed, whether a peel needs preparation.

Before I change anything, I put the same booking-style questions about your area to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews and note whether your salon comes up and how it is described; once the work is live, I repeat exactly those questions. How this works in more detail is on the
AI-ready SEO and GEO page

They bring the clients who already know you. Search brings the ones choosing a salon right now, and neither Instagram nor a booking platform answers «how much is balayage on dark hair» in a way Google or an assistant can read. The site is also the only one of the three that belongs to you.
