contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a carpentry business actually consists of

children.text: Carpentry is two businesses with one name, and that decides the whole site

A carpenter on a building site and a joiner in a workshop share a trade and almost nothing else commercially. Site carpentry is sold to contractors, developers and builders, who search for capacity, certification, day rates and whether you can start on the fourteenth. Workshop joinery is sold to homeowners, who search for a thing in a room — a wardrobe in an alcove, a kitchen, a staircase, shelving for a loft — and who compare photographs and lead times.

These two clients do not read the same page, do not use the same words, and do not decide on the same timescale. Most carpentry websites address both at once, which produces a home page saying «domestic and commercial carpentry, no job too small» — a sentence that answers no search anybody makes. The first decision in this work is which of the two you want more of, and then the site is built to say so.
if you want contractors: capacity, insurance, certifications, day rates, references from sites;
if you want homeowners: rooms, materials, photographs of finished work, lead time, price ranges;
if you genuinely want both: two distinct sections, each written as though the other client did not exist;
and in either case, name the trade the way your market names it — carpenter, joiner, cabinetmaker, furniture maker are not interchangeable in every country.
A page per piece of fitted furniture, because homeowners search by room and by timber

The valuable domestic searches are specific and they almost always name a room or a material: fitted wardrobes in a city, a bespoke kitchen, an under-stairs storage unit, alcove shelving, an oak staircase, a walnut dressing table. The person searching has a space in their house they have been looking at for two years, and they want to see that exact thing made by somebody nearby.

Most joinery sites answer this with a gallery. A gallery is images, and images are not readable: a search engine cannot see that the piece is oak, cannot tell it is a wardrobe rather than a cupboard, and does not know which room it is in. Every job type you want more of therefore needs a page that says what it is, in what material, at roughly what cost, with what lead time, and with the photographs attached to that text rather than floating in a grid.
Bespoke woodworking and furniture making as a separate line of work

Making furniture to order is adjacent to joinery and sells differently again. The buyer is not solving a storage problem; they want a specific object — a dining table of a certain length, a desk to fit a recess, a piece in a particular timber — and they are prepared to wait and to pay for the maker rather than the product. The searches are correspondingly narrow and low in volume, which is precisely why they are winnable: almost nobody writes a page about making a four-metre dining table in a specific timber.

If this is the part of the business you want to grow, it needs its own section with its own language — species, finishes, joinery methods, commission process, deposit terms — and it should not be filed under the same heading as fitting out a developer's apartments.
Quotes, minimum project size and lead time: the three things to publish

The most expensive thing in a carpentry business is quoting for work you would not have wanted. Measuring up, drawing, pricing and following up a job that was never going to happen costs days a month, and the usual cause is a site that invites everyone to get in touch without saying what the business does, what it costs from, or when it could start.

Publishing three facts fixes most of it: a minimum project size, a realistic range for the common jobs, and the current lead time. Fewer people will write. The ones who do will be describing jobs you want, with budgets that exist, and they will already know they are waiting until spring.
Where you want to be found by city, the groundwork is on the
local SEO page
. What the site itself should contain — galleries tied to job types, enquiry forms that collect room dimensions, material pages — is on the
carpentry website design page
, and if you want to know what is wrong before committing to anything, that is the
SEO audit
The local pack and the Google profile, where most domestic enquiries are decided

For a homeowner, the first screen is usually the map results: three businesses, their ratings, their photographs and their hours. A joinery business with no photographs of finished work on the profile loses to one with twenty, regardless of which makes better furniture, and a profile listing «carpenter» as the only service loses the search for fitted wardrobes to one that lists fitted wardrobes.

This is cheap work with a fast return, and it is usually where I start on a carpentry business, because it tends to move within weeks while the pages are still maturing. It also needs maintaining: photographs added as jobs finish, hours corrected before holidays, and replies to reviews written by the person who did the work rather than by an agency.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a coaching practice actually consists of

children.text: Why most coaching websites are invisible in search

Read ten coaching websites in a row and they merge into one. Unlock your potential, step into your power, transform your life, a three-month journey, a free discovery call. That is not laziness — much of it comes from certification programmes, which hand out a website structure and sample copy along with the credential. Thousands of coaches launched from the same script, so to a search engine they are interchangeable, and interchangeable pages cannot outrank each other on anything except the coach's own name.

The second reason is that the pages describe the method rather than the person in trouble. «Transformational coaching» is what you do; «I have managed people for fifteen years and I have just been made redundant» is what somebody types. A coach who writes the first competes with everyone holding the same certificate; a coach who writes the second competes with almost nobody.
Naming who you coach is the one change that moves coaching SEO

Coaching is bought at a moment, not as a category. Someone whose company was just sold, a founder who cannot get past the same revenue number two years running, a doctor leaving clinical practice, a new manager promoted over former peers — each arrives with a different fear and searches in their own words, and none of them searches for «coaching».

So the structure is one page per situation you genuinely work with: the situation named in the heading, the questions it brings, how the engagement runs, and what it costs. It is also an honest filter. A coach who cannot name three situations they are better at than average has a positioning problem rather than a search problem, and publishing more pages will not fix it — it will spread the same sentence over more addresses.
name the situation in the heading, not in the third paragraph;
use the words the client uses about themselves, not the words of your method;
say how long the engagement runs and what it includes;
state a price or at least a floor;
and do not build a page for work you would rather not take.
Search for a coach who works remotely: why local SEO matters less here

Almost every other profession I write these pages for is bought locally: the clinic, the garage, the law firm, the accountant. Coaching mostly is not. Sessions happen on a video call, so the buyer is not filtering by city, and that changes the strategy in both directions. The good news is that a coach in a small town competes on equal terms with one in a capital. The bad news is that the field is the entire language rather than the twenty practices within driving distance, and the pages that already rank are often large publishers and directories rather than other coaches.

There are two exceptions worth being honest about. Coaching genuinely delivered in person — team workshops, on-site executive work — is local, and then the Google Business Profile and a city page do matter. And coaching sold to companies rather than to individuals is bought the way consulting is bought: through procurement and reputation, where a case study somebody can forward does more than a ranking.
If you work in person as well as online, both halves are worth doing, and the local half is described on the
local SEO page
. If the site itself is the problem rather than its visibility, that is a different job:
website design for coaches
Proof and credentials a search engine can actually read

Coaching has no licence, so proof does the work a licence would do elsewhere, and most of it is published in a form that cannot be read. Testimonials inside slider images, credential badges as logos with no text, results described as «transformational» with no number or timeframe. Written as text, the same material does its job: the credential and its level spelled out, how long you have practised, how many hours, and outcomes a reader can check — a promotion, a role change, a figure, a date.
write the credential and its level as text, not as a badge image;
give testimonials a name, a role and a situation, with permission;
say what changed and over what period;
and keep the same name, credential and wording on the site and on any directory that lists you.

children.text: Which delivery businesses this page is for, and where the neighbours are covered
This page is about courier work: parcels, documents, pallets and time-critical consignments, moved same day or next day, for businesses and for people who need something somewhere by a deadline.
If you move households and offices, the purchase is entirely different — it is planned, priced per volume and sold on trust rather than speed — and that is
SEO for moving companies
. What a transport or logistics site itself should contain is on the
logistics company website page

One structural note before the rest: most courier firms are two businesses sharing a van fleet. There is contract work, sold to a procurement or operations manager on rates, service levels and reliability over months, and there is ad-hoc work, sold in ten minutes to somebody who has a problem today. Search mainly reaches the second, and the second is where the margin usually is, so the pages below are built for it.
Route pages: the highest-intent search in transport, and almost nobody has them

Courier searches name two places and a time. Somebody needs a parcel from one city to another today, a pallet across a border by Thursday, documents to an office two hundred kilometres away this afternoon. They do not search for a courier company and then work out whether it covers their route — they search the route.

A page per route you genuinely run is therefore the strongest asset a courier firm can build, and the competition for those searches is almost nil, because every competitor publishes one page saying «nationwide and international delivery». Each route page says how long that run takes, what time you have to collect by for it to arrive the same day, what it costs for a typical consignment, what you will and will not carry on it, and how often you run it.
one page per route you actually run regularly, named by both places;
the transit time and the collection cut-off for that route, not a general promise;
a worked price for a typical consignment on it;
whether it is a dedicated van or a consolidated run, because senders care;
and the border or document requirements where the route crosses one.

Write only the routes you run. A page for every city pair in the country, generated from a list, is the oldest mistake in this industry and it produces exactly the thin pages search engines discount and senders distrust.
Cargo type and constraint, which is how senders really describe the job

The second half of the search is what is being moved. A pallet, a document, something fragile, something oversized, something that must stay cold, something that must not be left with a neighbour. Each of those is a different operation with a different price and a different set of worries, and a sender searching for one of them wants to see it named.

This is also where a courier firm can decline work gracefully and profitably. Saying plainly what you do not carry — and there is always a list — saves the phone calls and makes the rest of the site more credible, because a company that carries everything for everyone describes no actual service.
Cut-off times: the single fact that decides the order

For same-day work the question is not whether you can do it, it is whether you can still do it today. «Booked before two o'clock, collected by three, delivered this evening» is the sentence that wins the order, and it is missing from most courier websites, which prefer «fast and reliable delivery» — a phrase that commits to nothing and therefore answers nothing.

Publish the cut-off per route and per service, and keep it true. It converts, it ranks for the urgent searches, and it also stops the enquiries that arrive at half past four for something that needed collecting at two.
Pricing when a price list is genuinely impossible

Courier pricing depends on weight, distance, deadline and vehicle, so a simple price list is not dishonest to omit — it is actually impossible. But «request a quote» loses the sender who is comparing three firms in five minutes, and that is most of them.

The workable answer is worked examples: a named weight, a named route, a named service level, and the price. Three or four of those per route tell a sender what to expect, give them a reason to call rather than click away, and provide search engines and AI assistants with figures to quote. A calculator does the same job better where the business can support one.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a daycare or nursery actually consists of

children.text: Why a nursery is the one business where more traffic is not the goal

Almost every business I work with wants as many enquiries as it can handle. A nursery is the exception: the building holds a fixed number of children, the law sets how many of them can be in each age group, and the intake is seasonal. Success is not a larger number of visitors — it is four free places in the toddler group filled before September, and the parents of those four children living close enough to walk.

That changes what the work is for. The aim is to fill specific gaps, which means the site has to say which gaps exist, and it means the campaign has a natural end. If you are full across every group with a waiting list already, there is nothing for me to sell you that month, and I would rather say that than take a retainer for traffic you cannot use. What is worth doing in that situation is preparing for the next intake and keeping the waiting list growing.
Parents search an age band and a walking distance, not «daycare»

Nobody types the name of your category and reads a list. A parent types what they need in the words their country uses — daycare, nursery, crèche, preschool, kindergarten, or the local term — and attaches either their district, their street, their child's age, or the hours they need. The searches that end in an enrolment look like a nursery near a named street, a place for a two-year-old starting in January, somewhere open from seven, somewhere with hot meals included.

Each of those is a page or a clear section, and the words have to match the market rather than the brochure. This matters more in childcare than in most trades, because the age bands are legally defined differently from country to country, and a parent searching for care for a child under three is often looking for a different kind of institution than one searching for a preschool. A site that calls everything «our programme» answers neither.
a page or section per age group, with the hours and the ratio for that group;
the area and the nearby streets named the way parents name them;
the hours written as times, including the earliest drop-off and the latest pick-up;
what the fee includes — meals, nappies, trips — and what costs extra;
and the local term for your type of setting, not an internal label.
Publishing availability, which almost no nursery does and every parent wants

The single most useful sentence a nursery can put on its website is how many places are free, in which group, and from when. Parents are not browsing; they are trying to solve a date — a return to work, the end of parental leave, a move. A site that answers «two places in the toddler group from January, infant group full until September» converts the visit immediately, and a site that says only «contact us for availability» sends the parent to the next result.

The objection is that availability changes and the page would go stale. It does change, and keeping it current is a five-minute job that belongs to whoever answers the phone. A stale availability note is worse than none, so the honest version is a dated line — availability as of the first of the month — which is both true and far more useful than silence.
Waiting lists are an asset, not an apology

A full nursery usually treats being full as a reason to stop marketing, which gets it exactly backwards. The parent searching today for a place next autumn is the easiest enrolment you will ever make, and they are often pregnant or on leave, deciding a year out. A waiting-list page that explains how the list works, where it currently stands and what happens when a place comes up collects those parents instead of losing them to whoever had a free place this week.
It also protects the intake. A nursery with forty names on a list does not have to discount in August, and it can plan staffing on something firmer than hope.
Trust is checked before a parent ever calls, so put the record on the page

Childcare is the one service where the buyer verifies you before making contact. Parents look for the register entry, the inspection outcome, the staff qualifications, the ratios, the safeguarding policy and the insurance, and they look for them off your site as well as on it. A nursery that publishes its registration number, its most recent inspection result and its staff qualifications plainly is both easier to trust and easier to find, because those are pages with facts on them rather than adjectives.

One thing to keep off the site entirely: claims about what the setting will do to a child's development, reading age or future schooling. They cannot be substantiated, they read as sales copy to exactly the parent you want, and in several markets they attract regulatory attention. Describe the day, the staff, the room and the food, and let the parent draw the conclusion.

The local pack and the Google profile, where most parents decide to call

For a search made within walking distance, the map results are the whole shortlist: three settings, their ratings, their photographs, their hours. A nursery with current photographs of the rooms and the garden, correct hours including the weeks you close, and replies to reviews in the voice of the director will take calls from one that has none of these, whatever the quality of the care.

This is also the fastest-moving part of the work. The profile tends to respond within weeks, while age-group pages take longer to mature, which is why I usually start there when a setting has places to fill in the current term rather than the next one.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a debt collection agency actually consists of

children.text: Which firms this page is for, and where the neighbouring services are covered

This page is for agencies recovering money owed: unpaid invoices, overdue accounts, receivables handed over after a company's own reminders have stopped working. It is not about litigation and not about bookkeeping, and the distinction matters because the three are often confused by the people searching.
If you are a law firm conducting proceedings, the work is on
SEO for law firms
and
local SEO for lawyers
. If the service is credit control, invoicing and ledgers rather than recovery, that is closer to
SEO for accounting firms
What your client is actually afraid of, and why it decides every page

Agencies in this trade usually write as though the client's question were whether the money can be recovered. In my reading of how businesses actually choose, it is not. A company handing over an unpaid invoice is afraid of something else: that an agency acting in their name will be heavy-handed with a customer they would still like to work with, or with a person whose circumstances they do not know, and that the damage will come back to them.

That fear is the lens every page on the site is read through, and it explains why the aggressive register this industry often adopts — firm, relentless, uncompromising — loses business it was written to win. The client is not shopping for aggression. They are shopping for someone who will be effective without creating a problem that outlasts the debt.

So the pages that convert describe the process in order and in plain language: what happens first, what the debtor receives and in what tone, how long each stage lasts, when the client is consulted before anything escalates, what you will not do, and how a case is closed when the debtor genuinely cannot pay. A page that explains restraint reads as competence.
the sequence of steps, with the time each one takes;
what the first contact with the debtor looks like, described honestly;
where the client's approval is required before escalation;
your compliance position and which rules govern your conduct;
what you decline to take on, and what happens when a debt is uncollectable;
and how the client is kept informed, since silence is the second complaint in this trade.
The client searches mid-frustration, in words that are not your service name

Nobody wakes up wanting a debt collection agency. They have an invoice that is ninety days late, a customer who has stopped replying, and a cash-flow problem, and what they type is the problem rather than the service: a customer who will not pay, how to recover an unpaid invoice, what to do when a client ignores reminders, whether a late-payment charge can be added.

That makes process and explanatory content unusually effective here, more so than in most business-to-business work, because the searcher does not yet know what kind of help exists. The agency that answers the question clearly — including the parts where the answer is «send one more letter yourself first» — is the one they contact when the reminders fail, and that honesty is also what distinguishes the page from a competitor's sales copy.

Where the answer involves what the law allows, keep the page to the process you follow and point readers to proper advice. I am not a lawyer, this is a regulated area in most markets, and content that reads as legal guidance is a risk to the client that commissioned it.
Commission bands, because that is the comparison every client makes

Almost every business comparing agencies is comparing two things: whether there is a fee if nothing is recovered, and what percentage you take if there is. Keeping both off the site does not protect the margin; it just removes you from the comparison, and the client assumes the higher of the figures they have seen elsewhere.

Bands with the conditions attached work better: what the commission is for recent invoices, what it becomes for older ones, where the minimum sits, what changes if the debt is disputed or the debtor is abroad. It is also the kind of concrete figure a search engine or an AI assistant can quote, which matters more each year.
Business and consumer debt are two different pages with two different sets of rules

Recovering money from a company and recovering it from a private individual are different operations with different obligations, and in most markets consumer debt is the more tightly regulated of the two. A single page addressing both tells a business client nothing specific and signals to a regulator's eye that the distinction is not being taken seriously.

If you work in both, they need separate pages written for separate readers. If you work only in business-to-business recovery, say so prominently: it removes enquiries you cannot take and it reassures the corporate client that your practice is built for their situation.
Sector pages where late payment is chronic

Late payment is not evenly distributed. Construction has retention and subcontract chains, transport has long payment terms and disputed deliveries, staffing agencies carry wages before they are paid for them, and professional firms have clients who simply stop answering. Each of these sectors has a characteristic pattern, and an agency that describes that pattern in the sector's own language reaches a client who recognises their situation in the first paragraph.
These pages are also the most winnable searches in the trade, because the competition is writing about debt collection in general. Where you want to be found by city as well, the groundwork is on the
local SEO page
, and if you want the state of your own site established before committing to anything, that is the
SEO audit

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a driving school actually consists of

children.text: Automatic or manual: the search that decides the enrolment before anything else

Nobody searches for a driving school in the abstract. The first thing a learner settles is the gearbox, and it is now the sharpest division in the industry: automatic-only licences have gone from a niche to a large and growing share, pushed along by electric cars, and a learner who has decided on automatic will not consider a school that does not say it teaches in one.

Yet a great many school websites mention it nowhere, or bury it in a sentence on a general lessons page. If you have automatic cars, that is a page: how many, which instructors drive them, what the licence restriction means in practice, what it costs, and how the waiting time compares with manual. If you only teach manual, say so plainly, because the enquiries you lose that way are enquiries you could not serve anyway.
a page for automatic lessons and a page for manual, not one page mentioning both;
what the automatic-only licence does and does not allow, in plain terms;
how many cars of each type you run, since availability is the real constraint;
prices for each, because they usually differ;
and the waiting time for each, which usually differs more.
Test-centre pages: the content only a local driving school can write

There is a large, permanent search demand around test centres — the routes used, the junctions that catch people out, where to park beforehand, which centre has the shorter wait, what the examiners there are strict about. Learners search this obsessively in the weeks before a test, and it is answered today mostly by forums and national sites that have never been to the place.

A school that teaches at a centre every week knows all of it, and that knowledge is the one asset a national competitor cannot copy. A page per test centre, written from experience, will rank because nothing better exists for that query, and it reaches the learner at precisely the point they are deciding whether to buy a few more lessons before the test.

One caution: write what helps a learner drive well at that centre, not a claimed list of official routes. Routes change, publishing a supposed definitive list ages badly, and the useful version — what the roads there demand of a driver — is both more honest and more durable.
Test waiting times, which are the most urgent thing a learner wants to know

In many markets test slots are booked out for months, and the wait is the single most pressing question a learner has. A school that publishes the current wait at the centres it uses, explains how it books tests and says what it can and cannot do to bring a date forward answers something nobody else answers, and it builds trust in the process — this is also the question most often answered dishonestly in this trade, so being plain about it stands out.
Intensive courses and weekly lessons are two different purchases

A learner taking an hour a week for eight months and a learner who needs a licence in three weeks for a job are not the same customer. The second has a deadline, a reason, usually a higher budget, and a completely different set of questions: how many hours a day, whether a test is included, what happens if they are not ready, what the refund position is.

Intensive courses therefore deserve their own page with the price, the structure and the honest caveats, and they tend to be the most profitable thing a school sells. The weekly-lessons page can be calmer and should carry the things that worry a first-time learner instead: who the instructor will be, what happens in the first lesson, whether the car is dual-controlled, and how progress is tracked.
Instructors are your second audience, and almost no school writes for them

Driving schools are usually limited by instructors rather than by learners. Finding them is a recruitment problem, and it is also a search problem, because instructors looking for a school to join or franchise with search for exactly that — terms about joining, franchise fees, car provision, how much of the lesson fee they keep, how pupils are allocated.

A page answering those questions is rarely found on a school's website, which means the search is almost uncontested, and it addresses the constraint that actually caps the business. If you are turning learners away because you have no capacity, this is the page worth writing before any of the others.

local SEO page
, and if you want the state of your own site established before committing to anything, that is the
SEO audit
Prices, instructors and the phone in the learner's hand

Three shorter points. Publish hourly and block prices: learners compare several schools in one sitting and a school without figures is skipped. Keep individual instructor information short but real — a learner wants to know who will be in the car, and a named instructor with their own gearbox and area beats a stock photograph of a smiling person with a clipboard.

And remember there are two readers on most enquiries: the learner, who is young and on a phone, and whoever is paying, who is often a parent reading the same page with different questions about safety, cost and whether the money is refundable. A page that answers both converts a conversation that is happening at a kitchen table rather than on your website.

children.text: Why furniture searches are dimensions and doorways rather than product names

Furniture is the one retail category bought against a physical space. The customer has already measured the alcove, counted the stairs and worried about the front door, and that is what they type: a console under eighty centimetres, a two-and-a-half-seat sofa, a corner unit facing left, a wardrobe for a sloped ceiling, a table that seats eight in a room four metres long. Nobody searches the name of a sofa they have never heard of.

Almost every furniture site makes those facts unsearchable. The dimensions live in a diagram image, the configuration lives in a dropdown, and the page text is three sentences about Scandinavian warmth. A search engine cannot read a drawing, so a shop with four hundred products that would each solve somebody's measuring problem is invisible to all of them.
every dimension in the page text, in the units your market uses, not only in an image;
the measurements people actually search: seat height, depth, overall width, and the narrowest point it has to pass through;
configuration spelled out — left or right facing, extendable to what length, reversible;
the room constraint named, because that is the search: narrow, low-ceilinged, awkward stairs, rented flat;
and a page for each constraint you can genuinely solve, not a filter nobody links to.
Pages built around the problem, which no competitor is targeting

The strongest pages a furniture retailer can publish are not categories. They are constraints: sofas that fit through a seventy-centimetre door, wardrobes for rooms with sloping ceilings, dining tables for narrow rooms, beds with storage for flats without a loft, furniture that can be carried up a tight staircase. These are real searches made by frustrated people with money ready, and the competition for them is almost nil, because every other shop is competing on the word sofa.

Each page is a short piece of advice plus the products from your own range that satisfy the constraint. It ranks because nothing else answers it, and it converts because the visitor has spent two weekends failing to find exactly this.
Lead time and stock, which decide the purchase more often than price

A sofa on order can be eight to fourteen weeks away, and a large share of furniture buyers are working to a date: a move, a renovation finishing, a baby, a lease starting. For those people availability outranks everything, and «in stock» is a search term rather than a logistics detail. A shop that shows lead time on each product and keeps a genuine available-now section wins them from a shop with better prices and no dates.

This is also the part most retailers get wrong in the opposite direction — a cheerful «fast delivery» banner with no figure anywhere. A number that is true, even a disappointing one, outperforms an adjective: somebody deciding between twelve weeks and four will not be annoyed by twelve, they will be annoyed in week six of a delivery they thought was quick.
The showroom is the conversion step, so publish the brands you stock

Furniture is one of the last categories where people want to sit on the thing before paying for it. That makes two searches unusually valuable, and most shops answer neither: a brand or collection name together with a city, and the question of where a particular piece can be seen in person.

Shops bury this. The brands they carry appear as a strip of logos on the home page, unlinked and unreadable, when each one deserves a page saying which collections are on the floor, which fabrics can be seen and touched, what can be ordered, and where in the showroom it is. Somebody searching a brand plus your city has already chosen the product and is only looking for the nearest place to try it — which is the shortest path to a sale a furniture retailer has.

Delivery access, assembly and taking the old piece away

Before the price, customers ask whether it will get up the stairs, whether anyone will build it, and what happens to the thing it is replacing. Each is a page, each is searched, and each removes a reason not to buy. Charging for assembly is fine; not saying whether it exists is what costs the order.

Returns on large items belong in the same group and carry the most weight of all. A page that states plainly what happens if a sofa does not fit, who pays to take it back and within how many days does more for conversion than any amount of lifestyle photography, and it is also a page that ranks, because every competitor keeps the answer in a terms document nobody reads.
Interior designers and trade accounts as a second, separate reader

A designer specifying furniture for a client's project buys differently from a household: they want lead times they can plan around, trade pricing, specification sheets, fabric samples, and confidence that a piece will still be available in four months. A page written for them reaches a buyer who orders repeatedly rather than once a decade.

The work is done by one person, me, an SEO consultant who also builds sites in React and Next.js, and I take it on for software houses, managed service providers, IT outsourcing firms and cloud, DevOps and security consultancies.
What SEO for IT companies is: service, technology and industry in one search

Buyers of IT services describe a need, not a vendor category: “Azure migration partner”, “React development company for fintech”, “managed IT services for dental practices”, “Kubernetes consulting Germany”, “SOC 2 readiness help”. Each phrase joins a service, often a technology, and sometimes an industry or a region. IT company SEO builds pages for the combinations you can deliver and prove.
IT services share long sales cycles and buying committees with other B2B companies; that general side is on the
B2B SEO
page. Companies selling their own software by subscription follow other patterns, covered on the
SEO for startups
page. This page is about firms that sell expertise and delivery.
Keyword research for IT services: what CTOs, IT managers and procurement search
Most IT keywords have small volumes and high value: one new client can mean a contract that runs for years. Research draws on four sources:
the services in your proposals and statements of work, renamed the way buyers name them
the technologies and platforms your engineers are certified in or use every day
the industries of your current clients, whose regulations and jargon you already know
questions from sales calls: migration risk, team size, time zones, security, pricing

Each phrase is then checked in search data and in the results themselves. If the first page holds only directories and global consultancies, a smaller firm needs a narrower angle — a technology plus an industry, or a region.
Service, technology and industry pages in IT company SEO
A single “Services” page with twelve icons cannot rank for any of them. The structure that works has three layers, linked to each other:
service pages — custom software development, cloud migration, managed IT support, DevOps, QA, security assessments
technology pages — the stacks you deliver in, what you build with each and who builds it
industry pages — the sectors you serve, their compliance needs and the projects done for them
Tech stack pages: React, .NET, Python, AWS, Azure and Kubernetes

Technical buyers often start from the stack: a .NET system to modernize, a React front end to extend, a workload to move to AWS. A stack page shows the versions and tools you work with, typical projects, how many engineers have the skill and links to case studies built on it. A wall of forty logos does not rank; three or four stacks described in depth do.
Industry pages: IT support for law firms, software for logistics, cloud for healthcare

An industry page earns trust by naming the sector’s own problems: document management and confidentiality for law firms, uptime and route data for logistics, HIPAA or GDPR constraints for healthcare. Without real projects or knowledge behind it, an industry page is a template, and both Google and buyers notice.
Case studies as SEO pages for software companies and IT service firms

SEO for software companies that build for clients rests on case studies, because a good one ranks for the exact service, technology and industry a buyer types. A case study that ranks has a title with those three elements, the client’s situation, the architecture chosen and why, the stack, the timeline and team size, and outcomes the client approved. When an NDA hides the name, the industry, company size and region still make the page useful. Each project gets its own page — not a PDF behind a form.
SEO for MSPs and managed service providers: location pages and local search
Managed service providers mostly sell to companies within driving distance: on-site visits still happen, and owners want a local partner. That makes local SEO central for an MSP:
a Google Business Profile for each office, with the right category and service area
a page for each city or region you cover, with response times, on-site options and local clients who agree to be named
pages for industries common in your area, such as IT support for law firms, accountants or clinics
client reviews, answered without revealing anything about their systems
City pages that differ only by the city name get filtered out; each needs real local detail. The map side is described on the
local SEO services
page.
Comparison and pricing-model pages: “vs” searches, T&M and fixed price

Before a call, buyers compare options: an in-house team or outsourcing, nearshore or offshore delivery, one cloud or another, time and materials, fixed price or a dedicated team. Pages that explain these choices fairly — including the cases where your model is the wrong fit — rank for those searches and bring buyers who already understand how you work. Published rate ranges, even approximate ones, answer the question every buyer asks first. Many IT firms hide them, which leaves the answer to directories and competitors.
Clutch, G2 and GoodFirms profiles in SEO for IT companies

For many IT searches, Clutch, G2, GoodFirms and similar directories rank above the vendors themselves, and buyers use their reviews to build a shortlist. AI assistants read them too. So the profiles are part of SEO:
services, technologies, industries, team size and rate range filled in to match the site
reviews collected after each finished project, through the platform’s own verification
a link from each profile to the matching service page
one company description used everywhere, so facts never conflict
Paid placement in directory rankings is advertising, not SEO; whether it pays off depends on the category.
Developer-written content and E-E-A-T for IT service companies

Google’s quality guidelines look for experience and expertise behind content, summarized as E-E-A-T. In IT, readers spot generic text at once. The articles that bring the right visitors come from your engineers: a migration post-mortem, two frameworks compared on a real project, a checklist from your security reviews. I turn engineers’ notes, recorded calls or internal documents into articles, published under the engineer’s name, role and profile. A few of those do more than a long run of keyword posts.
Technical SEO for IT company websites built on React, Next.js and other JavaScript frameworks
IT companies often build their own site in the stack they sell, and JavaScript sites have their own SEO problems. React, Next.js and TypeScript are my daily tools, so I fix these in the code:
pages rendered only in the browser, which Google renders later and many AI crawlers not at all — moved to server rendering or static generation
titles, descriptions and canonical tags set by client-side code and missing from the HTML
navigation built from buttons with click handlers instead of real links
heavy animations and scripts that push Core Web Vitals out of the good range
staging and preview deployments indexed next to the live site

Before they open a single vendor site, many CTOs and IT managers ask an AI assistant — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google’s AI Overviews — for a shortlist: “software development companies in Poland with healthcare experience”, “MSPs in Chicago that support Mac environments”. The assistant names a few firms with a reason for each. Getting into those lists is the job of GEO and AEO, generative and answer engine optimization. services, stacks, industries, team size, time zones and locations written as plain sentences

I capture what assistants say about your company, and which rivals appear next to it, at the start and after the work. Details are on the

IT company sites attract many visitors who will never buy: developers reading a technical post, job seekers, students, other vendors. The report keeps them apart:

A technical article that brings thousands of developers and no leads is reported as exactly that, and judged by whether it helps hiring or brand.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a massage practice actually consists of

children.text: Which practices this page is for, and where the neighbouring trades are covered

This page is for therapeutic and sports massage practised as its own discipline: a single practitioner or a small studio, by appointment, selling sessions to people who come back. The neighbouring trades on this site need different work, and separating them matters more here than anywhere else, because the search terms overlap while the buyers do not.
For a salon selling appearance treatments alongside massage, the structure is on
SEO for beauty salons
. For a clinic doing assessment and rehabilitation it is
SEO for physiotherapists
, and for aesthetic medicine
med spa SEO
. If your practice genuinely spans two of these, it needs two clearly separate sections rather than one page trying to be both.
The problem no other trade has: the word attracts the wrong enquiries

Massage is the one service where the plain description of the work also draws enquiries that a licensed practice will not take. Every therapist knows this, most have a story about it, and almost nobody addresses it on the website — which is where it could actually be solved, because the text of a page decides who writes to you.

The work is not defensive, it is specific. A practice that names its modalities in professional terms, states its qualifications and registration, says that it works by appointment from a listed address, publishes rates per session length, and chooses the right category in its map profile reads unambiguously to both a client and a search engine. The practices that get the worst of this are usually the ones whose sites say the least — a page with a photograph, the word relaxation, and a phone number is ambiguous by omission.
modality names in professional form, not atmospheric language;
qualifications, training and any professional registration, with the body named;
by appointment, from a stated address, with the hours you actually work;
rates per session length, on the page, not on request;
the correct primary category in the map profile, which is a surprisingly common misconfiguration;
and, if you work mobile, say what mobile means in your practice — where, when and for whom.
Mobile and studio are two different searches, and a mobile practice needs more precision, not less

Visiting clients at home is a legitimate and well-paid part of many practices, and it is also where ambiguity does the most damage. A mobile practice therefore benefits from being more explicit than a studio one: the area covered, the hours, what equipment is brought, what space is needed, what the client should expect on arrival, and the same qualification and registration details. Written that way, it ranks for a separate set of searches and reads as a professional service rather than an unspecified call-out.
What a massage practice may claim, which sits between the clinics and the salons

Much of the valuable demand is about a purpose: people search for massage after surgery, during pregnancy, for desk-bound shoulders and necks, for marathon preparation and recovery. That demand is real and specific, and capturing it requires walking a line that neither the clinics nor the salons have to walk.

The clinics are governed by rules on advertising health services, which in several markets restrict what a practice may publish at all. The salons mostly sell appearance and are barely touched by those rules. Massage sits between them: it is not a medical treatment in most jurisdictions, and a page promising to treat a condition, relieve a diagnosis or replace medical care invites exactly the regulatory attention the clinics live under — and is also simply unprovable.

The version that works describes the session rather than the result. What happens during it, how long it lasts, what the therapist will ask beforehand, what clients commonly come for in their own words, who should speak to a doctor first, and what the practice does not do. This captures the search, because the search is phrased as a purpose rather than a promise, and it keeps the page defensible. Where the line falls exactly depends on your market and your professional body, and a borderline page is worth a question to them rather than to me.
One pair of hands: the capacity ceiling and what it does to the work

A solo therapist has perhaps twenty-five to thirty treatable hours in a week, and that number does not move no matter how well the site performs. So the goal of this work is not more enquiries. It is a fuller book at a better rate, with fewer gaps in awkward parts of the day and fewer of the appointments you take reluctantly.

That has two consequences I would rather state before invoicing. If your book is already full and you have a waiting list, there is nothing worth buying monthly, and the useful work is an audit plus the pages that let you raise your rate. And if your book is half empty at eleven on a Tuesday but full on Saturdays, the work is not general visibility — it is making the quiet hours findable and bookable, which is a much smaller and cheaper job.
Rebooking: search buys the first appointment, the practice keeps the client

The economics of this trade are repeat custom. A client who comes monthly for two years is worth thirty first visits, and no amount of search traffic substitutes for that. What search can do is buy the first appointment, and what the site can do is make the second one effortless: the same therapist shown by name, availability visible rather than requested, a course of sessions priced, and a reminder that does not require anybody to remember.

children.text: Where Google helps a musician and where it does not

Start with the part most SEO pages for musicians leave out. If your goal is more listeners, Google is not the main instrument: discovery of music happens inside Spotify, YouTube and TikTok search, and the work there is metadata, playlists and release strategy, which is a different job from this one. Hiring me to do Google SEO for streaming numbers would be selling you the wrong thing.

Google decides a different half, and it is the half that pays. Who gets booked for the wedding, the corporate night, the festival slot. Who is found by the journalist writing about the scene. Who owns the first screen when somebody hears a track in a bar, remembers the name and searches it. That half is winnable by a site you control, and it is what this page is about.
Owning your own name in search is the first job for a band or DJ

Search your act's name and look at what you get. For a great many musicians the first screen is Spotify, Apple Music, a lyrics site, a YouTube auto-channel, a Discogs entry and a Bandcamp page — all describing them, none of them theirs, and not one with a booking contact on it. The person searching has already decided they are interested; they just cannot find you, only your distribution.

Fixing it is unglamorous and quick: one canonical site that states who you are in text, the same act name spelled identically everywhere, the links that tie the profiles together, and structured data that lets a search engine understand this is a musical act with these releases and these upcoming dates. The site does not have to outrank Spotify. It has to be on that first screen with the one thing Spotify does not carry — how to hire you.
spell the act name identically on every profile, including capitalisation;
put a booking contact in text, not inside an image or a contact form only;
link your profiles from the site and the site from your profiles;
mark up releases and dates so an assistant can read them;
and claim the name in the directories that already outrank you.
Pages for the work you are hired for, not for the music you make

A booker does not search for your genre; they search for the occasion. A wedding in a particular city, a corporate event, a club night of a certain style, a session player on a certain instrument, a teacher for a certain level. Each of those is a page, and each page answers what that buyer needs to know before writing: what the set looks like, how long it runs, what the line-up and equipment are, what it costs or starts at, and how far you travel.

This is also where the local half belongs and where it should stop. A city page is worth having for a city you actually take work in and worth nothing for a city you would decline — the measured experience on this site is that a page for a place where the service is not really delivered settles in the fifties and stays there.

children.text: What this page adds to the general salon advice, and what it does not repeat

If you run a salon offering several kinds of treatment, the structural work — a page per treatment, prices and durations on the site, the map profile, the path from a treatment page to a booked slot — is on the
SEO for beauty salons page
, and all of it applies to nails too. There is no point repeating it here.

This page is about the four things that make a nail business behave differently from the rest of the salon trade: a vocabulary that changes every season, a clientele that walks in rather than books, a hygiene question nobody writes about, and a return visit that happens on a predictable cycle. Those four are where a nail salon gains or loses search traffic, and none of them is a general salon problem.
Nail technique names change every season, which makes this a maintenance job

No other beauty service renames itself as quickly. Over the last few years the searched vocabulary has moved through gel and acrylic to dip powder, builder gel in a bottle, Russian and Japanese manicures, chrome, ombre and whatever is currently rising — and each of those is a term clients type, compare and judge a salon by. A salon still advertising a technique that peaked three years ago is not just missing searches; it reads as dated to the client it most wants.

The practical consequence is unusual for this kind of work: the technique pages are not a build, they are a standing task. Terms get added as they rise, pages get renamed or merged as they fall, and once or twice a year the whole set is reviewed against what people are actually searching. This is also the one part of nail salon SEO where a monthly arrangement genuinely earns its fee rather than filling time.
name every technique you do in the words clients use, including the ones you find imprecise;
say what each one actually is, because half the clients searching cannot define it;
give the price and how long it lasts, since that is the comparison being made;
attach your own photographs to the technique rather than to a general gallery;
and retire the pages for techniques you no longer offer instead of leaving them up.
Walk-ins and «open now»: why hours matter more here than content

Hair and beauty appointments are planned. A large share of nail business is not: somebody is in town, has forty minutes, and searches for a salon that is open and can take them. That makes this trade unusually dependent on two things that are not content at all — opening hours that are correct everywhere they appear, and a plain statement of whether you take walk-ins and when.

A salon that says «walk-ins welcome, usually a short wait before four on weekdays» answers the search better than a page of beautiful photographs, and a salon whose published hours are wrong loses the client permanently, because they walked to the door. Before writing anything else on a nail salon I check the hours in every place they are published, and in most cases at least one of them is wrong.
Hygiene and tools: the question clients ask each other instead of asking you

Among clients who have stopped going somewhere, the reason is often hygiene rather than the result, and the worry is specific: what happens to the files between clients, whether the tools are sterilised and how, whether a drill is used and by whom, what happens if a nail is damaged. Almost nobody searching will ask a salon this directly, and almost no salon answers it on the website.

A page that describes the practice plainly — single-use items, how reusable tools are processed, who is trained and in what — converts the cautious client, who is also usually the one who comes back every three weeks for years. Describe the practice rather than making claims about health or safety outcomes: what you do is verifiable, what it prevents is not, and the careful client is reassured by the first and suspicious of the second.
The infill cycle makes rebooking schedulable rather than hopeful

Gel and builder work needs attention every two to four weeks, which is the most predictable return cycle in the beauty trade. That changes what the website is for after the first visit: not persuasion, but making the next appointment the easiest thing in the client's week — the same technician shown by name, visible availability, a prepaid course of visits if you offer one, and a reminder timed to the technique rather than to a generic month.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a pharmacy actually consists of

children.text: Which pharmacies this page is for, and what it deliberately leaves out

This page is about community pharmacies — a dispensary serving the people who live and work nearby. It is not about pharmaceutical manufacturing or distribution, which shares the word and almost nothing else: that is a business-to-business market with its own regulations, its own buyers and a completely different kind of website.
If you run a clinic or a practice rather than a pharmacy, the governing rules are different and the pages for that are
medical SEO
and
SEO for doctors
. The distinction is not cosmetic: a pharmacy is not a healthcare provider in the legal sense used by those rules, and the norm that applies to it is stricter.
Why the advertising rules decide this work before a single keyword is looked at

In most of Europe a pharmacy cannot advertise itself the way a shop can, and in several markets it cannot advertise itself at all. That is not a detail to be managed later; it decides what the website is allowed to contain, and therefore what the work can consist of. An agency that sells a pharmacy the standard package — promotional landing pages, offers, product promotions, review campaigns — is selling something that in some markets carries an order to take it down and a fine.

So the first thing I do on a pharmacy is not keyword research. It is establishing which regime applies where you operate, what the published exceptions are, and what is left. That usually turns out to be less than the owner was promised by somebody else and more than the owner feared, because being findable and advertising are not the same activity, and search rewards the first.

This page describes rules as they stood when it was written and is not legal advice. I am not a lawyer, and for a pharmacy the stakes are high enough that the final word on a borderline page should come from one, or from the supervising inspectorate.
Poland: advertising a pharmacy is prohibited today, and the law is being replaced

Poland has one of the strictest regimes in the European Union. Article 94a of the Pharmaceutical Law states that advertising of pharmacies and pharmacy points, and of their activity, is prohibited, and that information about the location and opening hours of a pharmacy does not constitute advertising. That exception is the whole of it — two items. Supervision sits with the voivodeship pharmaceutical inspector, who orders the advertising stopped by a decision that is immediately enforceable, and the penalty today runs to fifty thousand złoty.

That regime is in the middle of being replaced. A law lifting the total ban passed the Sejm in September 2026, was amended by the Senate in October, and went to the President on 23 October 2026 for a decision within twenty-one days; it takes effect fourteen days after publication. The replacement is not simply a liberalisation: the penalty ceiling rises from fifty thousand złoty to a million, and where a breach covers several pharmacies, a separate fine applies to each one.

The practical consequence for anyone commissioning work on a Polish pharmacy right now is that the answer depends on the date the page goes live, and the cost of getting it wrong is going up twentyfold. This is a reason to check the position on the day rather than to rely on what an agency wrote in a blog post last spring — including what is written here, which I will keep current but which is dated by definition.
What remains legal and still works: being findable rather than advertised

Strip out everything promotional and a surprising amount is left, because the searches that bring somebody to a pharmacy are not persuadable. Nobody is talked into needing a dispensary. They need one now, near where they are standing, that is open, and the pharmacy that answers those three things first gets the visit.
the location, written as an address a search engine and a map can both read, with the entrance described;
the opening hours, accurate, including the days and weeks you are closed;
duty and night hours, which change on a roster and go stale faster than anything else on the site;
accessibility, parking and which languages are spoken at the counter;
and the technical state of the site, which no advertising rule touches at all.

Nothing in that list is promotion. All of it is information somebody is actively searching for, and most pharmacy websites get at least half of it wrong — most often the hours, which is the single most consequential field on the entire site.
«Pharmacy open now» and the duty roster, the most urgent search in the sector

The largest and most valuable pharmacy search is someone standing in the street at nine in the evening looking for somewhere open. It is answered almost entirely from opening hours and location data — the two things explicitly permitted even under the strictest regime — and it is won or lost on whether those are correct in every place they appear.

Duty rosters are where this falls apart. A pharmacy on night duty one week in six has hours that differ from its published ones on exactly the nights when demand is highest, and a site showing the standard hours sends that person elsewhere. Getting the roster onto the site and into the map profile, in a form that updates rather than rots, is the highest-value piece of work available to most pharmacies and is entirely inside the exception.
Prescription medicines cannot be advertised to the public, in any market in the European Union

Separately from whether the pharmacy itself may advertise, advertising prescription-only medicines to the public is prohibited across the European Union. That rules out product pages, promotions and content built around prescription products, whatever the pharmacy's own regime permits, and it is the mistake I see most often on pharmacy sites built by general web agencies.

Non-prescription products are advertisable but regulated, with requirements about what claims may be made and how the product is described. The safe default for a community pharmacy's website is to describe services and availability rather than to promote products, and to treat any product content as something to clear before publishing.
Services and specialisms, where the market permits mentioning them

Many pharmacies do considerably more than dispense: vaccinations, blood-pressure and other measurements, medication reviews, compounding, equipment hire, dressings. Where the local regime permits describing the services offered, these are worth their own pages, because each is a distinct search made by somebody who does not know which pharmacy near them does it.

Where the regime does not — and Poland today is the clearest case, with an exception covering only location and hours — the honest answer is that those pages cannot go up yet, and that the work worth paying for is the permitted material plus the technical state of the site. I would rather tell a pharmacy owner that in the first conversation than build a set of service pages that an inspector orders taken down.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a photographer actually consists of

children.text: Why the best portfolio in the city can be invisible in search

A search engine cannot see your photographs. It cannot tell a beautifully lit ceremony from a snapshot, and no amount of talent changes that. What it can read is the text around the pictures: the headings, the descriptions, the file names, the alt text, the page addresses. A portfolio of four hundred untitled JPEGs in a slider is, to a search engine, an empty page that takes nine seconds to load.

This is why photographers who are plainly better than their competitors sit below them in the results, and it is also good news, because the gap is closed with writing rather than with equipment. The photographer who describes the wedding — the venue, the season, the light, how the day ran — gets found for the searches the photographs themselves can never answer.
Genre, place and date: the three things a photography client searches with

Nobody searches for «photographer». They search for a genre and a place, usually with a date implied: a wedding photographer in a particular city, a newborn session in a district, a brand shoot for a product launch, a graduation in a particular month. Each genre you want more of is a page, and each page says what that session involves, how long it takes, how many images are delivered and when, and what it costs.

Each genre also belongs to a different buyer with a different anxiety. A couple is afraid of hiring the wrong person for a day that cannot be repeated. A parent of a newborn is afraid of the baby crying for two hours. A brand manager is afraid of missing a launch date. The page that names the fear books the session.
one page per genre you want more of, not one page listing all of them;
say how the session runs, hour by hour, so the buyer can picture it;
state delivery: how many images, in what time, in what format;
put a starting price on the page;
and leave out genres you take reluctantly — they bring the enquiries you dislike.
Venue pages: the highest-intent query in the profession

This is the tactic the platform guides never explain, and it is the strongest one photographers have. Someone who searches a venue name together with «photographer» has already booked the venue. The date is fixed, the budget is set, and they are looking for somebody who knows the building — where the light falls at four in the afternoon, which corner works when it rains, where the registrar stands.

A photographer who has shot at a venue can own that search, because almost nobody competes for it: the venue itself writes nothing, and other photographers post the gallery to Instagram and move on. A page per venue, with the photographs you took there, what the light does through the day, the practical constraints and the timings that worked, is both the most useful page on the site for a couple and the easiest one to rank.
one page per venue you have genuinely shot at, named exactly as the venue names itself;
write what you learned about the place, not a gallery caption;
include the practical details a couple cannot find elsewhere;
and check with the venue before using their name prominently — many will link back.
Why blogging every wedding does not rank, and what to publish instead

The standard recommendation in photography circles is to blog every single wedding. As a content habit it is sound: it produces text, images and venue names regularly. As an SEO plan it produces two hundred near-identical posts titled with two first names, which compete with each other and rank for nothing, and the practice has a name in search — thin pages.

The version that works keeps the habit and changes the shape. The gallery post stays as a gallery post for the clients and for social media. The searchable material inside it — the venue, the season, the style, the logistics — is lifted into pages built around those things, where one strong venue page replaces eleven weak ones that happened to be shot at the same place.
Gallery speed: why a photography site loses the booking before the first image appears

Photography sites are the slowest sites I audit, for an obvious reason: the product is large images and the owner is unwilling to compromise on quality. The compromise is not necessary — modern formats and correct sizing keep full visual quality at a fraction of the weight — but the default setup of most portfolio templates does none of it, and a gallery that takes nine seconds on a phone loses the booking before the first frame appears.
That part overlaps with the
performance and code audit
, and the structure of the site itself — portfolios by genre, private delivery galleries, packages — is on the
photographer website page
. Where you work in one city in particular, the groundwork is the
local SEO page
SEO for wedding photographers: the same work on a longer horizon

Wedding photography is the same discipline with one difference that changes the schedule: couples book twelve to eighteen months ahead. Content published in the spring is not competing for this summer's weddings — it is competing for next year's, and a page that goes live in March for a season that is already booked has missed by a year rather than by a month.

The practical consequence is that venue and season pages are written in the quiet months and left to mature, and the measurement window stretches accordingly: first movement in about six weeks, bookings on a horizon that follows the couple's planning cycle rather than the search engine's. A wedding photographer who starts this work in peak season should expect the return a season later, and anyone promising otherwise is selling the calendar they do not control.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a physiotherapy clinic actually consists of

children.text: Why physiotherapy websites lose in search to software vendors

Search for almost any physiotherapy question and the first page is not clinics. It is practice-management software companies and billing vendors, who publish long guides about conditions and rehabilitation because content is how they sell subscriptions to clinics. They have budgets a four-therapist practice does not, and they are not going anywhere.

That sounds discouraging and is actually the opposite. Those vendors cannot treat anybody. They rank for «what is physical therapy» and «exercises for rotator cuff», which bring readers from everywhere and patients from nowhere. The queries that produce an appointment have a place attached — a condition and a district, a condition and a city — and on those the vendors do not compete at all.
A page per condition and area is what moves physiotherapy SEO

Nobody searches for «physiotherapy». They search for what hurts and where they live: sciatica that has lasted three weeks, a shoulder that will not lift above the head, week six after a knee replacement, a running injury before a race. Each of those is a different page, and each of those pages is the one a search engine can match to a person.

The structure that follows is a page per condition you actually treat, each one naming the condition in the heading, describing how the first session goes, how many sessions this usually takes, what it costs, and which of your therapists handles it. If you have more than one location, each location gets its own page with its own address, team and opening hours rather than one page listing both.
name the condition in the heading, in the words patients use, not only the clinical term;
say what the first appointment involves — the fear of the first visit stops more bookings than price does;
give a typical number of sessions and a price per session;
name the therapist who handles that condition and their qualification;
and skip conditions you would rather refer out — a page you do not want to fulfil is worse than no page.
Terminology: physiotherapy, physical therapy, and why the page needs both

The same profession is called physiotherapy in the UK, Ireland, Australia and most of Europe, and physical therapy in the United States. Patients search in the word their country uses, and clinics serving mixed populations — an expat district, a border city, a practice taking international patients — get searched in both. A page that only uses one of the two is invisible to half of them, so both appear here and both should appear on a real clinic's pages, in headings rather than hidden in body text.
Local search for a physiotherapy practice: profile, districts and reviews

Physiotherapy is bought within travelling distance of a painful body, which makes the Google Business Profile as important as the website: the categories, the services list, the hours, photos of the actual practice, and reviews with replies. The practice name, address and phone number have to match exactly across the site, the profile and every health directory that lists the clinic, because mismatched listings are the most common reason a clinic with good reviews still does not appear on the map.

local SEO page

SEO for chiropractors

for general practices and clinics.
What a physiotherapy website may and may not claim

Health advertising is regulated, and the rules differ by country — in Poland and much of the EU a clinic may inform but not advertise in the way a shop may, and patient testimonials are restricted or forbidden outright depending on the jurisdiction. This matters for SEO because the usual conversion advice — before-and-after photos, outcome promises, patient stories — can be the exact thing that is not allowed. The safe and effective version is describing the method, the qualification, the equipment and the process precisely, which happens also to be what a search engine can read and what a cautious patient is actually looking for. I write to the rules of the country the clinic operates in and flag anything I am unsure about rather than guessing.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a real estate website includes

children.text: Why a real estate website loses to portals in Google, and what can be changed

Most real estate websites are not invisible because of their design. They are invisible because the pages that could rank do not exist, and the pages that do exist are fragmented across hundreds of filter URLs.
A site that does not appear in Google
almost always has a structural reason, not a cosmetic one.

The second reason is the competition. Rightmove, Idealista, Zillow and their local equivalents own the head queries, and no amount of optimisation moves an agency above them on «apartments for sale in <city>». That is not where this work pays off.

Where it does pay off: the queries portals answer badly. A buyer asking which neighbourhood suits a family, what the purchase process costs a foreign buyer, what a particular development actually includes, or how rental yields differ between two districts gets a list of listings from a portal and no answer. That is the gap, and it is where your own site can win and keep the lead instead of paying for it.
A listing catalogue search engines can crawl: filters, pagination, canonicals

A real estate catalogue is the hardest technical object in this industry. Every filter combination can generate a URL, and a site with eight filters produces more addresses than it has listings. Search engines then spend their crawl budget on near-duplicate pages and split ranking signals between them.

The work here is unglamorous and decides everything else: which filter combinations become indexable pages and which stay out, canonical tags that point somewhere sensible, pagination that does not orphan page 14, structured data for listings, and a sitemap that reflects what actually exists. Done once, properly, it is the highest-leverage technical investment a real estate site has.
The same applies to listings that sell. A property page that disappears leaves either a dead end or a soft 404; neither is neutral, and at the volume these sites churn, it matters.
Location and neighbourhood pages: what a portal listing cannot answer
Location pages are the backbone of real estate SEO, and most sites either skip them or fill them with a map and a listing feed.

A location page earns its rankings when it answers what a buyer cannot get from a listing: what the area is like, who lives there, what transport and schools exist, how prices moved, what the service charges and taxes look like, what is being built nearby. This is content a portal structurally cannot produce, because a portal sells listings, not local knowledge.
Property-type pages work the same way: new builds, resale apartments, villas, commercial units, land. Each has a different buyer with different questions, and each has its own search demand.
Prices and conditions on the site: what buyers check before they call
Real estate buyers arrive with money questions, and a site that avoids them loses the enquiry to one that does not.

That means price ranges per area and property type, what the total cost of purchase includes beyond the price — fees, taxes, notary, agency commission — and what the process looks like step by step for a buyer who is not local. Putting this in writing filters out the enquiries you cannot serve and raises the quality of the ones you can.
Several languages on a real estate site, and the mistakes that cost rankings
Cross-border property buyers research in their own language and buy in another, so most real estate sites that matter are multilingual. That is also where the technical damage usually sits.

The recurring mistakes: hreflang that points at pages which do not exist, one language machine-translated from another and indexed as thin duplicate content, locations named differently in each language so none of them builds authority, and a language switcher that drops the visitor onto the home page instead of the same property. Each of these is fixable, and each one is currently costing rankings on sites that look fine from the outside.

children.text: How long real estate SEO takes to show results

First measurable movement appears in about a month and a half: pages that were not indexed get indexed, and queries the site never appeared for start showing impressions. Steady growth in enquiries builds over three to six months, as location and property-type pages accumulate authority and the catalogue fixes work through the index.

Real estate is slower than most industries on the head queries, because portals hold them, and faster than most on the long tail, because almost nobody writes proper location content. That is why the work starts with the long tail.
What SEO for a real estate website costs and what is included

An audit of the site, the catalogue and the AI answers is €250. One-off work — catalogue architecture, location pages, structured data — runs €250–800 depending on scope. Ongoing SEO is €800 a month and includes the technical work, the content plan, new pages and the reporting. The full price list is on the
pricing page

SEO audit
Whoever runs the audit also writes the fixes. You do not get a list of problems and an invitation to find a developer for them.
Who SEO for a real estate website suits, and who it does not

It suits you if you sell or let property through your own site, have a catalogue worth crawling, and are willing to publish content about locations and the buying process. It also suits an investment or development business where a single enquiry is worth enough that a few months of groundwork is obviously cheaper than the equivalent in advertising.

It does not suit you if the entire business runs through portal listings and the site is a formality, if nothing on the site may be changed, or if you need enquiries this week — that is an advertising budget, not SEO.
