children.text: Real estate in AI search: what GEO and AEO mean and how they are done

Buyers increasingly start in ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google's AI Overviews rather than in a list of ten links: «which district of Limassol suits a family», «what does buying an apartment cost a foreign buyer in Spain», «which agencies work with this development». The assistant answers from text it can read and restate, and it names sources.

Two acronyms describe the work. GEO, generative engine optimization, is getting a site used and named as a source by AI assistants. AEO, answer engine optimization, is getting it quoted in the direct answer rather than the link list. Both reward the same things, and they are not the same things that classic rankings reward.
What AI assistants actually use
a direct answer at the top of a section, before the context and the caveats;
facts — prices, areas, fees, timelines — instead of adjectives about the market;
Schema.org markup that matches the visible text rather than contradicting it;
consistent naming of locations, property types and your own brand across the whole site;
content that is in the HTML and does not need scripts to appear.
Real estate suits AI search unusually well, because the decisions run on trust and detail rather than on price alone. How this is done on an existing site is a separate job:
preparing a site for AI search

Three things: a large catalogue that changes constantly, direct competition with portals on every head query, and buyers who research in several languages. The work is therefore weighted towards catalogue architecture, location content and hreflang, rather than towards the generic checklist.

items.question: What makes real estate SEO different from general SEO?

children.text: Both, in different places. Portals bring volume but own the lead and the relationship. Your own site is the asset you control — the brand, the enquiry flow, the client data — and it wins on the depth portals cannot produce. Strong businesses rank in both and stop depending on either.

items.question: Should a real estate website compete with portals or complement them?

children.text: They are the main technical risk. Filter combinations can generate hundreds of near-duplicate addresses that split ranking signals and burn crawl budget. Deciding which combinations become indexable pages, and setting canonicals and pagination accordingly, is where most of the technical gain is.

children.text: By enquiries, not rankings. Organic enquiry volume, how many of them are qualified, what an organic enquiry costs next to a paid one, and organic's growing share of the total. Rankings are an input and I report them, but they are not the result.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a remodeling company actually consists of

children.text: Which businesses this page is for, and where the neighbouring trades are covered

This page is about renovating homes people already live in, sold to the homeowner: kitchens, bathrooms, loft and basement conversions, extensions, whole-house refurbishment. That client, that price and that decision process are specific enough to need their own approach, and different enough from the neighbouring trades to be worth separating before anything else.
If you build new houses, the buyer and the cycle are different and that is
SEO for home builders
. For commercial and structural work it is
SEO for construction companies
. For trade work across many job types it is
SEO for contractors
, and for design-led work without the building it is
SEO for interior designers
Publishing what your projects actually cost, which is the biggest search in the trade

The most searched question in remodeling is what it costs. A kitchen, a bathroom, a loft conversion, a square metre of refurbishment — these are typed hundreds of times a day in every city, and almost no remodeling company answers them. The field is left to national cost-estimator sites and lead platforms, which publish a country-wide average assembled from somebody else's jobs, and the homeowner reads a number that is wrong for their city, their building and their standard of finish.

A company that publishes real ranges from its own completed projects — in its own city, with the scope that produced each figure — outranks those sites for the local version of the question, because it is the only page on the subject that is actually about the place the searcher lives. It also does something more valuable than ranking: it ends the conversations with people whose budget is a third of the job, before the site visit, the measuring and the three days of quoting.
a range rather than a single figure, with what sits at each end of it;
the scope that produced the number — what was included, what was not;
your own finished jobs as the source, with the year, since prices move;
what pushes a job to the top of the range: structural work, moving services, a difficult building;
and the minimum project you take, which saves everybody the enquiry.
Why «from €X» and «every project is unique» both lose the search

Two habits keep remodelers off these pages. The first is a single «from» figure, which the homeowner correctly reads as the cheapest job you ever did and discounts entirely. The second is the sentence that every project is unique, which is true and answers nothing: the person asking knows their kitchen is not identical to the last one, and is asking for an order of magnitude so they can decide whether to keep reading.

The version that works gives three bands with what distinguishes them, and says plainly which band most of your work falls into. It takes an afternoon with your own invoices, and it is the highest-value page most remodeling companies do not have.
A five-figure job is decided over months, so the site has to survive being re-read

Remodeling has one of the longest decision cycles in local trade. The homeowner starts looking in January, gets three quotes in March, and signs in May, and in between they come back to each company's website several times — once to look at the work, once to show a partner, once to check something they half-remember. Most of this trade's SEO is sold as though the goal were a phone call on the first visit. The actual goal is to be the company that still looks like the right choice on the third visit, when they are comparing you with two others.

That shapes what the pages have to contain. Finished projects with the scope, the duration and the cost band rather than a carousel of photographs. The names of the people who would be in the house. What happens when something is found behind a wall. Who handles permits and building control. How payments are staged. None of this ranks on its own, and all of it decides the comparison that search produced.
Answering how long it takes and whether they can live there

After cost, the two questions are duration and disruption, and they are asked constantly: how long a kitchen takes, whether the family can stay in the house, whether there will be water, which weeks are the worst. Almost no remodeling site answers them, which is strange, because they are the cheapest pages to write — the answers are the same on every job — and they catch the homeowner at the exact moment they are deciding whether to do the work at all.
These pages also pre-empt the awkward part of the sale. A company that has already written down that the bathroom is unusable for nine days is not going to be accused of hiding it in week two.
Owning the search instead of buying the same enquiry four times

Most remodeling companies buy leads from a platform, where one homeowner's form is sold to three or four firms at once. You pay for the enquiry, you compete on price against two companies who paid for the same enquiry, and the homeowner — who never learned any of your names — picks on the cheapest quote. The margin for the whole arrangement comes out of the job.

Search works the other way round: the enquiry arrives with your name attached, having read your project pages and your cost bands, and usually without the other two quotes being in the same conversation. That is the economic case for this work, and it is also the honest limit of it: it takes months to build, it does not replace the platform in the first quarter, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling you a campaign rather than a plan.

children.text: Which security businesses this page is for, and which it is not

This page is about physical security: manned guarding, monitored alarms, access control, and camera installation and monitoring. If you sell information security — penetration testing, managed detection, compliance work — the word is the same and nothing else is: that is a business-to-business software market with its own buyers, its own publications and a sales cycle that has little to do with being found locally.
If you fit locks and respond to lockouts rather than monitor premises, the trade is closer to
SEO for locksmiths
, which is built around emergency searches instead of contracts.
A security company has two buyers, and one website usually fails both

Manned guarding is sold to an organisation: a procurement team, a facilities manager, a developer, a local authority. They work from specifications, insurance certificates, licence numbers and references, over months, often through a formal tender. Alarm and camera work is sold to a business owner or a householder who had a break-in last week, wants a quote, and will decide within days.

These two read nothing alike. The first needs evidence and documents; the second needs prices, response times and somebody who answers the phone. Most security company websites address the first in tone — corporate, formal, photographs of a man in a high-visibility jacket — while almost all of their searchable demand comes from the second. Separating them into two clear parts of the site is usually the first structural change worth making.
guarding: sectors served, licence and insurance, vetting and training, shift coverage, references;
installation and monitoring: what systems, what they cost from, how fast, who monitors them and from where;
one page per type of site you protect, because a warehouse and a building site are different problems;
and a separate page for events, which is a different purchase again — dated, short, and planned weeks ahead.
The honest limit: search will not win you a tender

I would rather say this before you pay me than after. Large guarding contracts are awarded through procurement, and procurement does not find suppliers through a search engine — it runs a process, often with a shortlist assembled before anything is published. No amount of content changes that, and an agency that tells you otherwise has not worked with a procurement timetable.

What search does do is three things that are worth real money: it brings installation and monitoring work, which is the higher-margin half of most security businesses and is bought like any other local service; it brings the small and mid-sized guarding contracts that are awarded by one person making a decision rather than by a committee; and it makes you findable to the procurement officer who has your name from a reference and is checking whether you look like a serious company. That third one is not lead generation, and it decides shortlists.
Response time, coverage and the specifications buyers actually compare

Security is bought on specifications, and the deciding one is almost always how fast somebody arrives. Yet most security company sites say «rapid response» and no figure, which reads to a buyer as a number too poor to print. A published range — the area you cover and the time you commit to within it — outperforms every adjective in the industry, and it also pre-empts the conversation where the customer discovers you are forty minutes away.

The same applies to the other comparables: how monitoring is staffed and from where, what happens when the connection drops, who holds the keys, whether patrols are logged and how the customer sees that log, and what the contract minimum is. None of this is marketing copy, all of it is searched, and publishing it is what distinguishes a company that has thought about the service from one that has bought a website template.
CCTV installation makes your customer responsible for personal data, and almost nobody explains it

The moment a camera is installed, the customer acquires obligations about what the cameras may see, what signage is required, how long recordings may be kept and who may access them. Across the European Union those duties fall on the customer as the data controller, not on the installer, and most customers have no idea they exist until something goes wrong.

A page that explains this plainly — what the installer is responsible for, what the customer must do, what retention period is defensible, where cameras should not point — is one of the most useful pages a security company can publish, and in my experience none of its competitors has one. It ranks because it answers a question people ask in those words, and it converts because a company that warns you about an obligation reads as one that will not cut corners on the installation either.

Where your market licenses security work, say so with the licence number and the scope it covers. It is a trust signal, it is checked by serious buyers, and it is also searched directly by people who have been told to verify that a contractor is licensed.
Local search, the map results and the sector pages that bring the contracts

Installation and small guarding work behave like any local service: the map results and a correctly built profile bring the first contact, and the sector pages decide whether it goes anywhere. Those sector pages are where this industry has the most unexploited room, because almost every competitor publishes one page called «our services» covering warehouses, construction sites, retail, residential estates, events and offices at once, and therefore ranks for none of them.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a tattoo studio actually consists of

children.text: What a tattoo client actually types, and why one studio page cannot answer it

Almost nobody searches for a tattoo studio by category. They search for a style in a place — fine line in a particular city, blackwork, realism, lettering, a specific traditional school — or they search for a problem, which is usually an old piece they want covered. The searcher has already decided what they want on their skin and is looking for the hand that can do it.

The standard studio site answers none of that. It has a home page, an «our artists» page with six names and six Instagram links, a prices page saying «from», and a contact form. One page cannot rank for eight different styles, and six artists sharing one page means a client searching for the one who does fine line is shown a page that is mostly about five people who do not.
A page per artist and a page per style, because clients choose the hand, not the shop

The unit of SEO in this trade is the artist and the style, not the studio. Each artist gets a page: the styles they actually work in, the pieces that show it, what they will and will not take on, how far out they are booked, and how to get on their list. Each style you want more of gets a page too, written so somebody who knows what they want can tell within a few seconds whether this is the right place.
name the styles the way clients name them, including the ones you find imprecise;
say what each artist declines — it saves everyone the enquiry;
state the waiting time and update it, because a stale «booking now» costs trust;
link each piece of work to the artist and the style it belongs to;
and keep healed photographs, not only fresh ones, since that is what a careful client looks for.
Cover-ups and reworks: the highest-intent search in the trade, and almost nobody writes it up

Somebody searching for a cover-up has a tattoo they regret and a budget ready. It is the most decided client who will ever contact a studio, and it is also the hardest work, which is exactly why it deserves its own page rather than a line in a FAQ. What that page needs is what the client cannot judge for themselves: what can realistically be covered and what cannot, how dark the new piece has to be, how many sessions it takes, whether laser fading first is the sensible route, and what it costs compared with a fresh piece of the same size.

The same applies to reworks and finishing other people's unfinished work. These searches are small in volume and large in value, there is rarely anyone competing for them, and the page that answers them honestly tends to bring the client who has been putting the decision off for three years.

One caution on adjacent work. If the studio also does scar or post-surgical camouflage, that text has to stay away from medical claims — describe the aesthetic result and the process, not healing, correction or anything resembling a medical outcome, and do not imply a clinical qualification the studio does not hold.
Walk-ins, waiting time and guest spots: the three answers that decide the enquiry

Three questions are asked constantly and answered on almost no studio site. Do you take walk-ins, and on which days. How long is the wait for each artist. Who is guesting, when, and how to book them. Each of these is a search in its own right — walk-in tattoo in a city is a large, urgent, local query — and each is also the reason a client writes or does not write.

Guest spots are worth their own treatment because they are time-bound: an artist visiting for a week has a name people already search for, and a page that goes up two days before they arrive catches nothing. Published three weeks ahead, with the dates and how to book, it catches the people searching that artist's name plus your city.
The local pack and your Google profile, where a tattoo studio is usually chosen

For a walk-in or a first consultation, most clients never reach a website. They look at the map results, the star rating, the photographs and the opening hours, and they go to one of the first three. That means the profile is not a side task — it is the main surface, and it needs the same discipline as the site: correct hours including the days you are closed, photographs of the studio and of healed work, services listed as clients name them, and replies to reviews in a voice that sounds like the shop.

local SEO page
, and what the site itself should contain — artist pages, booking enquiries with references attached, aftercare — is on the

SEO audit
Publishing a minimum charge and an hourly rate, and what it does to your enquiries

Most studios keep prices off the site to avoid scaring people, and get punished for it twice: the searcher who wants a sense of cost goes to a studio that states one, and the enquiries that do arrive are from people whose budget is a third of the piece they are describing. A minimum charge, an hourly or day rate, and a worked example of what a given size and style typically comes to will cut the volume of enquiries and raise the quality of them.

It also matters for a reason that has nothing to do with clients. A figure written on the page is something a search engine and an AI assistant can quote, and a studio that publishes nothing gets described by whatever a third-party directory guessed.

contentBlocks.title: What SEO for a wedding planner actually consists of

children.text: Your client is a first-time buyer who does not know what a planner does

Almost every other business I work with sells to someone who has bought the thing before. A wedding planner does not. The couple is buying this service once, they have no reference price, no vocabulary for the different levels of it, and no way to judge a portfolio of twelve beautiful weddings against another portfolio of twelve beautiful weddings.

The practical consequence is counter-intuitive: the pages that win enquiries are not the gallery. They are the pages that explain the service. Couples routinely believe that the venue's coordinator will do what a planner does, that a planner is only for very large budgets, or that hiring one costs a percentage they have invented. Each of those beliefs is a page, and the planner who writes them gets the enquiry, because they are the only one in the search results who answered the question the couple was actually asking.
what full planning includes, month by month, and when you join;
what partial planning means, since every planner defines it differently;
what day-of coordination is and, plainly, what it is not;
what the venue's coordinator does and does not do, stated without disparaging them;
how many weddings you take in a year, which tells a couple whether they get you;
and who should not hire a planner, which is the page that earns the most trust.
Package tiers and costs, because the couple is guessing and guessing high

The most searched question in this trade is what a wedding planner costs, and most planners answer it with a contact form. The couple then assumes a figure, and the figure they assume is usually either absurdly low or high enough that they do not write at all. Neither outcome is improved by keeping the number off the site.

Tiers with real figures fix it: what day-of coordination starts at, what partial planning runs to, what full planning costs for a wedding of a given size, and what moves a project between the bands. It filters the enquiries you cannot serve, it ranks for the question itself, and it gives search engines and assistants a number to quote rather than one a directory invented.
Destination weddings are an international SEO problem, not a local one

For a planner taking destination work, the search does not happen where the wedding happens. A couple in one country is searching, in their own language, for someone who can run a wedding in another — and the page that reaches them has to exist in that language, be aimed at that country, and answer the questions specific to marrying abroad: what paperwork is required, how far ahead it has to start, whether the legal ceremony has to happen elsewhere, who deals with suppliers who do not speak the couple's language.

This is a different technical job from local search. It involves which language versions exist, how they are signposted to search engines, and which country each one is meant for — and it is the part most planner websites get wrong by translating a page and stopping there.
That groundwork is
international SEO
, and it is the strongest opportunity in this trade, because a destination wedding is both the largest project a planner takes and the one with the least competition in search.
Why a wedding planner's pages have to be published for next season rather than this one

Couples book a planner twelve to eighteen months ahead, which means content published in spring is not competing for this summer. It is competing for the summer after, and a page that goes live in March for a season already full has missed by a year rather than by a month.

So the schedule matters more here than the volume. Pages written in the quiet months mature in time for the enquiry season that leads to the season after. And the measurement window stretches accordingly: first movement in search within about six weeks, enquiries on the couple's planning cycle rather than the search engine's. A planner who starts this work in peak season should expect the return a year out, and I would rather set that expectation now than explain it in August.

If you work repeatedly at particular venues or in a particular region, those pages are specific and almost uncontested, and they are worth writing where you genuinely know the place — what the logistics are, where the guests stay, what the weather does in September.

The wedding directories bring enquiries and share them: the couple sees you alongside competitors and the lead is rarely exclusive. Search works differently, arriving with your name attached and usually without three other planners in the conversation — though it takes months to build and will not replace a directory listing in the first quarter.

And this is a capacity business: fifteen to twenty-five weddings a year is a ceiling, not a target. If your season is full, the work worth paying for is the pages that support a higher fee and the destination market, not more visibility.

children.text: Why more enquiries usually makes a handyman business worse

Most trades come to me because the phone is not ringing. A handyman normally has the opposite problem: it rings constantly, with jobs that take forty minutes and sit on the other side of the city. The business is busy, the van is always moving, and the money at the end of the month does not reflect either, because half the working day was spent driving between jobs too small to carry the travel.

So the goal of this work is not volume. It is a higher average job value and a shorter average drive, and those two numbers are what I would look at before and after. That changes what gets built: not a site that ranks for the broadest possible term, but pages for the jobs you want, with the price floor and the radius stated plainly enough that the rest filter themselves out before they call.
«Handyman near me» is the biggest search in the trade and the worst one to win

It is the term every agency sells and every owner asks for, and it delivers precisely the job you should not take: someone two suburbs away who needs one shelf put up and is comparing you with a neighbour's teenager. Winning it fills the diary with work that loses money once the drive is counted.

The searches worth winning name the job. Mounting a television on a plasterboard wall, assembling flat-pack furniture for a whole flat, hanging internal doors, resealing a bathroom, clearing gutters, fitting blinds through a house, boxing in pipework, putting up shelving in an alcove. Each of those is a person who has already decided what they need, usually knows it is not a ten-minute job, and is comparing two or three tradesmen rather than five.
one page per job you want more of, named the way customers name it;
say what the job typically involves and what it typically costs;
say how long it takes, because that is what the customer is actually asking;
show finished work for that specific job, not a general gallery;
and leave out the jobs you take only to fill a gap — those pages bring more of them.
Selling a half-day instead of a single task, which doubles the job value

The most useful page a handyman can add is not about a job at all; it is about a block of time. Most households have a list — the door that sticks, two pictures to hang, a dripping tap, a curtain pole, a shelf — and they put off calling anyone because no single item feels worth a call-out. A page that sells a half-day or a full day, explains how many items typically fit into it, and tells them to send a photographed list converts that hesitation directly.

It also fixes the economics. One drive, one set-up, four hours billed, and a customer who now has a tradesman they will call twice a year. This is the single change I would make first on most handyman sites, and it requires no ranking improvement at all to pay for itself.
State the radius, the minimum charge and what you are not licensed to do

Three sentences remove most of the wasted phone calls. A radius in kilometres or a list of named districts, rather than a town plus «and surrounding areas». A call-out minimum and an hourly rate, so nobody rings about a job a third of the size. And a plain statement of the boundary — which gas, electrical or structural work you do not take on, and what you do take on, since in most markets that line is set by licensing rather than by preference.

The last of those does more than filter. A tradesman who writes down what he will not touch reads as someone who knows the rules, which is exactly the impression the customer with a larger budget is looking for. The opposite — a site promising that no job is too small or too large — reads as someone who will attempt either.
Landlords, letting agents and property managers as a separate, repeating client

One landlord with eight flats is worth more than forty households, and they search differently: they want response time, invoicing, whether you can be given keys, whether you work to a schedule of rates, and whether you can handle a changeover between tenancies in one visit. None of that is on a site written for homeowners, and a page that answers it reaches a client who calls every month rather than once.

children.text: I provide SEO for architects: the practice’s own website shows up when a homeowner, a developer or a company looks for an architect for their kind of building in their area, and those visits become project inquiries. There is no agency team behind me: I research, write and change the site myself, and I also build websites. The service is for residential studios, commercial and public-sector practices, interior architects and landscape architects.
What SEO for architects is: matching building type, place and service

Clients rarely type a studio’s name or the word “architecture”. They describe their own project: “residential architect Denver”, “architect for a rear extension”, “passive house architect near me”, “architect for a restaurant fit-out”, “barn conversion planning”. Each search joins three things — the kind of building, the place and the service — and architect SEO puts a page of yours in front of every combination that matches the work you want more of.

Search engines read text. A site made of full-screen images with one-word captions impresses a visitor who is already on it but tells Google almost nothing. Most of the work below turns what the studio knows into pages that can be found.
SEO keywords for architects: residential, commercial, passive house and extension searches
Keyword research for a practice starts from the commissions you want, not from a tool. The groups I check for most studios:
residential — new houses, renovations, extensions, loft and garage conversions, custom homes
commercial and public — offices, retail and restaurant fit-outs, schools, healthcare, mixed-use
sustainability — passive house, net-zero, timber construction, retrofit of existing buildings
services — feasibility studies, permit applications, interior architecture, landscape design
place — the city, its districts and suburbs, and the towns where you are willing to work

Volumes for these phrases are small, often a few dozen searches a month. That is normal for the profession: one private house or one office fit-out can be worth more than a year of SEO, so a small number with the right intent deserves a page.
Project pages as SEO pages: typology, location, size and sustainability

Most architecture sites already hold their best SEO material — the portfolio — and waste it. A page called “House K” with twelve photos competes for nothing. The same project described in words can rank for the next client with a similar brief:
a title that names the type and the place: “Timber family house extension in Evanston”
the brief in two or three sentences: who the client was, what they needed, what limited the site
floor area, construction method and main materials, and a budget range if the client agrees
the energy standard or certification where it applies, such as Passive House or LEED
the services you provided, from feasibility to construction oversight
links to the matching sector page and to two or three similar projects
Ten well-described projects usually do more than fifty with a caption each. I write the texts from your drawings, the design statement and a short talk with the architect who led the job.
Sector and practice-area pages in SEO for architecture firms

SEO for architecture firms working in several sectors needs a page per sector instead of one “Services” page that lists everything. A hospital board and a young family look for different proof. Each sector page explains the typical brief, the regulations that shape the design, the stages you cover and the projects of that type, linked from the page.
Planning, permit and fee guides that homeowners search for

Private clients read for weeks before they call: whether an extension needs planning permission, how long a building permit takes in their city, what an architect does at each stage, how fees are usually calculated. A short guide on each question, written for your jurisdiction and signed by an architect in the studio, meets those readers early and leads them to the matching service page. Rules differ by city and country, so every guide names the place it covers and the date it was checked.

Image SEO for architects: file names, alt text and fast project galleries
In architecture the images are the content, and they can bring visitors through Google Images and visual search. What makes them count:
file names that describe the picture: timber-extension-kitchen-evanston.webp rather than DSC_0412.jpg
alt text that says what is shown — “double-height kitchen in a timber rear extension, view to the garden” — instead of a string of keywords
captions under key images, which visitors read more than any paragraph
WebP or AVIF files in several sizes, so a phone downloads a phone-sized picture
the photographer’s credit, and a license that allows web use, checked before publishing

Awards, publications and architecture directories as authority and links

The profession has its own platforms — Archello, ArchDaily, Dezeen, Architizer and national journals — and a feature there brings a link, a mention and readers who already value design. SEO uses them in three ways:
each published or awarded project links back to its own project page, not only to the home page
the site lists awards and publications as text, with the year and a link to the source
the studio’s name and description match on every platform, so search engines and AI assistants see one firm
Competition entries, lectures at schools of architecture, articles by your architects and listings in professional bodies’ member directories work the same way. Buying links is not part of my work.
Multilingual SEO for architecture practices working in several countries

Practices that design abroad, or serve foreign clients at home, need the key pages in the languages those clients search in. A German client types “Architekt Einfamilienhaus” and expects details on fees and permits that an English page does not give. SEO for architects in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

A growing share of clients put the question to an AI assistant first: “find an architect in Seattle who does passive house retrofits”, “what does an architect charge for a home extension”. ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews reply with a handful of studio names or a summary of a few sources. Optimizing for these replies goes by two names, GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization). For an architecture practice the work looks like this:
services, project types, places and sustainability expertise written as plain sentences
project pages with facts an assistant can repeat: type, place, size, standard, year
structured data for the practice, its office and its architects
the same description on the site, the Google Business Profile and publication platforms

Fix the technical basics: indexing, titles and page speed with large images.

An architecture marketing agency usually adds PR, social media and ads to this list. I do the SEO part myself: research, writing with your architects, changes in the CMS or the code, and reports. Whoever you hire, ask who will write about your projects and how results will be counted.
Measuring architect SEO in project inquiries, not visits

children.text: SEO for chiropractors is the work that puts a chiropractic office in the map results for “chiropractor near me”, on the first page for the conditions you treat and in AI answers, and turns those searches into booked first visits. One person does all of it — I am an independent SEO consultant and web developer — so whoever reviews your Google Business Profile also writes the condition pages and changes the code.
What SEO for chiropractors covers: map searches, condition searches and name searches
People look for a chiropractor in three different situations, and each one is won in a different place:
in pain today — “chiropractor near me”, “chiropractor open Saturday”, “walk-in chiropractor” — they call one of the three offices shown on the map
researching a problem — “chiropractor for sciatica”, “is a chiropractor good for neck pain”, “chiropractor after car accident” — they read websites over several days
checking a name after a referral from a friend, a personal trainer or an attorney

The first group is decided mostly by the Google Business Profile, the second by your own pages, the third by both plus reviews; ChatGPT and AI Overviews draw on all of them. Physical therapy clinics appear in some of the same searches but compete for a different set of phrases and referrals, so this page stays with chiropractic offices.
Local SEO for chiropractors: Google Business Profile and the map pack
Most calls from new patients start in the three map results. Distance to the searcher cannot be changed, so everything else has to be right:
primary category “Chiropractor”, with secondary categories only for services you really provide
a services list — adjustments, spinal decompression, prenatal care, sports injuries — each linked to its own page on the site, not to the home page
hours that match reality, including early mornings and Saturdays, which people search for
photos of the front desk, adjusting rooms and the team, added regularly
one profile and one location page for each office in a group, with its own doctors and hours
Virtual offices, invented addresses and business names stuffed with keywords get profiles suspended, and I do not use them. Map ranking factors and citation work in more depth are on the
local SEO services
page.
Condition pages for chiropractors: low back pain, sciatica, neck pain and sports injuries

One “Services” page cannot rank for “chiropractor for sciatica”, “herniated disc chiropractor” and “sports injury chiropractor” at once. Each condition you want more patients for gets its own page, planned from search data for your town:
what patients usually feel, and the warning signs that mean they should see a medical doctor first — written or approved by you
how you assess the problem and which techniques you use, in plain words
how many visits a typical plan includes, given as a range, without promised outcomes
which chiropractor in the office treats it and how to book

I organized Giuseppe’s site in Milan on the same principle: 7 pillar pages by area of therapy, 21 subtopic pages under them, separate pages for each place he sees patients and 150 FAQ entries reused where they fit. A chiropractic office has fewer topics, but the pattern — one page per problem, linked to the place and the person who treats it — is what search engines and assistants pick up.
How many condition pages a chiropractic office needs

Start with five to eight conditions that fill your schedule and that you can describe from experience. Fifty thin pages generated from a template are what Google’s spam policies call scaled content abuse, and patients notice them too.
Auto accident and personal injury pages in chiropractic SEO

“Chiropractor after car accident” and “whiplash chiropractor” are searched by people who also worry about who will pay. If your office takes these cases, a separate page answers what the front desk hears every week: what to bring to the first visit, how auto insurance and, in no-fault states, personal injury protection usually work, whether you accept cases on a letter of protection and how injuries are documented. Coverage depends on the policy and the state, so the page stays general and invites a call.

Personal injury attorneys also look for chiropractors who keep clear records. A short section for attorneys with a named contact person serves them without mixing their questions into the patient pages.
New patient specials and state board rules in chiropractic SEO

Many chiropractic sites lead with a discounted first exam or a free consultation. Chiropractic advertising is regulated by each state’s board, and the FTC expects health claims to be supported by evidence. In general terms:
some states require a set disclaimer next to free or discounted services, and offers to patients with Medicare or other federal coverage raise separate questions
claims to treat conditions outside the musculoskeletal system draw complaints and regulator attention
“best chiropractor in town”, guaranteed results and posture photos published without written consent stay off the site
testimonials, where your state allows them, come from real patients, disclose any incentive and do not suggest typical results
I write within the rules you give me. Check current wording with your state board or a healthcare attorney; nothing here is legal advice.
Chiropractor reviews on Google: a routine that protects patient privacy

Reviews often decide between two offices in the map pack. A text after each visit with a direct link to the review form, sent to every patient rather than only the happy ones, works better than a campaign twice a year. Gifts or discounts in exchange for reviews break Google’s rules, and the FTC rule on consumer reviews prohibits incentives tied to positive reviews.

Healthcare adds one rule to replies: never confirm that the reviewer is a patient and never mention their treatment. A short thank-you answers praise; criticism gets a general apology and an invitation to call the office.
Online booking and first-visit pages: turning chiropractic searches into appointments

A visitor in pain decides quickly, so every condition page ends with two actions: book online and call. Booking runs through the scheduler you already use, loaded so that it does not slow the page. A “your first visit” page — how long it takes, what to wear, whether X-rays are taken, what it costs with and without insurance — removes the last reason to wait.

Forms that ask about symptoms can fall under HIPAA. Either keep the form to name, phone and a preferred time, or run it through a form service that will sign a business associate agreement with your office. Calls and bookings are tracked per page, so the monthly report shows which conditions bring patients, not only rankings.
Chiropractor credentials and YMYL: author, license and review date
Google treats health topics as “Your Money or Your Life” and looks for evidence of who stands behind the advice. For a chiropractic office that means:
a bio for each doctor of chiropractic with the DC degree, school, state license, years in practice and techniques used
condition pages that name the chiropractor who wrote or reviewed them, with the date of the last review
links to sources where a page states facts about a condition
MedicalClinic and Person structured data connecting the doctors to the office and its specialty
I write the structure, the search data and the drafts; the chiropractor checks every clinical statement before it goes live.
SEO for chiropractors in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Patients now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google “what does a chiropractor do for sciatica” or “which chiropractor near me takes Blue Cross and works on Saturdays”. The assistant names a few offices with reasons for each. Earning a place in those replies goes by two names, generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO); in a chiropractic office it comes down to:
conditions, techniques, doctors, hours, insurance plans and languages written as plain sentences
answers to common patient questions on the condition pages, signed by the chiropractor
the same office details on the site, Google, Yelp and Healthgrades
structured data that ties the office, its doctors and its locations together

Giuseppe found me through ChatGPT, and new pages on his site already appear in its answers — a small private practice can be named there. I check how assistants describe your office before and after the work. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Chiropractic SEO agencies, platforms and a single consultant: what to ask

Searches for SEO services for chiropractors are led by chiropractic marketing firms and website platforms that bundle SEO with templates, ads and newsletters, plus Reddit threads where chiropractors compare them. Before signing with anyone, me included, ask:
who writes the condition pages, and whether the same text runs on other clients’ sites
whether reports show calls and booked visits, not only rankings
whether you keep the domain, the content and the Google profile if you leave
how long the contract runs and how to cancel it

children.text: I do SEO for construction companies myself — the Google Business Profile, the website and the pages for services, areas and projects — so the person who audits the site is the one who fixes it. Construction SEO is local: a client looks for a specific job in a specific place, and most of them choose from the map results and the first few links.
What construction company SEO covers: Google Maps, service pages and project pages

SEO for a construction company is the work that makes the company appear when someone searches for the job they need — “house extension”, “loft conversion”, “commercial fit-out” — together with their town, and that makes its own website win the search for its own name. Three places decide this:
the map results — three companies with a map, rating and phone number, shown above the regular results for local searches
the regular results, where the company’s site competes with directories, lead-generation portals and big national firms
AI answers — Google AI Overviews and assistants such as ChatGPT, which recommend local companies and quote what they can read about them

The map results depend mostly on the Google Business Profile and reviews, the regular results on the website, and AI answers on both, plus facts written so a machine can quote them: services, areas, projects, years in business.
Local SEO for construction companies: Google Business Profile and service areas
For most construction companies the map block brings more enquiries than everything else together. What moves a company into it:
the right primary category for what you mainly do, and secondary categories for the rest — not a single generic “Construction company”
service areas that match where you really work, and an office address that is the same everywhere
photos from real projects, added regularly, with the job named in the description
services listed in the profile with short descriptions
the same name, address and phone number on the website, the profile and the main directories

A company with several offices gets a profile per office, each linked to its own page on the site. Fake addresses and virtual offices are not set up: Google suspends such profiles, and the company loses the map position it had.
Construction SEO keywords: searches for a service plus a town

Construction clients rarely search for “construction company”. They search for the job: “kitchen renovation”, “house extension”, “flat roof replacement”, “new build house”, usually with a town or district. Each such combination you actually sell needs a page that answers it:
one page per service, with what is included, typical timing and a price range where you can give one
one page per town or area you cover, with projects from that area
a link between them: the service page lists the areas, the area page lists the services
Before any work I pull the real search data for your services and towns, so pages are built around the phrases clients use and not around your internal names for the work.
Project pages as SEO content for a construction website

Finished projects are the strongest content a construction company has, and on most sites search engines cannot read them: a gallery of photos with no text says nothing to Google. A project page that ranks has the facts written out — type of work, location, size, duration, what the client needed — next to the photos, and links to the matching service and area pages.
Every new project then becomes a new page that can be found for the job and the place. How such pages are designed is covered on the
construction website design
page.
What the website itself needs — the pages, the portfolio your team updates, the quote form — is covered on the
construction company website
page.
Reviews and trust signals in construction SEO

Construction is an expensive decision, and clients read reviews more carefully than in most services. I set up a routine: the client is asked for a review at handover, every review gets an answer within a few days, and reviews mention the job and the area in plain words, which also helps the profile appear for those searches.

Credentials work the same way on the website: licences, insurance, warranties and memberships written as text and marked up as structured data, so both clients and search engines can read them. What is not done: bought reviews or reviews only from happy clients. Both break Google’s rules and are easy to detect.
AI SEO for construction companies: visibility in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

More clients now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to recommend a builder before they open any website. Those answers are put together from what the assistant can read and trust: your Google profile, reviews, directory listings and your own pages. Getting into them is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO), and for a construction company it is part of the same SEO work:
services, areas, years in business and credentials written as plain facts an assistant can quote, not only shown in images
structured data that names the company, its services and the areas it covers
the same company details on the website, the profile and directories, so an assistant does not confuse you with another firm
answers to the questions clients ask — price ranges, timing, permits — written on the service pages
I check how assistants describe your company before and after the work. More on this on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Construction SEO company, marketing agency or an SEO specialist

A construction marketing agency usually sells a package: social media, paid ads, video, sometimes leads bought from portals, with SEO as one part of it. A construction SEO company focuses on search, but the work is often split between junior staff and templates. I am a single SEO specialist who also builds websites: the same person audits the profile, writes the service and area pages and fixes the code.
What I do not do: paid ads, social media management and lead buying. If you need those, an agency is the better choice, and SEO can still be done separately.
Seasonality in construction SEO: start before the building season

Searches for most construction work rise in late winter and spring, when people plan the year’s projects. New pages need weeks to months to rank, so work started in spring brings results in autumn. The useful moment to start is before the season, so the pages are in place when clients begin to search.

children.text: SEO for dermatologists means that a person with a rash, a changing mole or a question about laser treatment finds your practice — on its own website, on Google Maps and in AI answers — and books an appointment. I do this myself, as a single consultant who also builds websites, for private practices that run medical, surgical and cosmetic dermatology under one name. One person audits the site, writes the condition pages with your dermatologists and makes the changes in the code.
What SEO for dermatologists covers: medical, surgical and cosmetic dermatology
A dermatology practice serves at least three kinds of patients, and each of them searches in a different way:
someone living with a condition — “adult acne dermatologist”, “eczema on hands won’t heal”, “psoriasis biologics” — who wants to know whether a specialist can help and whether insurance pays
someone worried about a spot — “mole changed color”, “full body skin check near me” — who wants an appointment soon
someone choosing a cosmetic treatment — laser, chemical peel, injectables — who compares prices, photos and who performs it

Dermatology SEO gives each of them a page that answers the search, keeps the practice details identical on the site, Google and directories, and reports results in appointments by service line. In any one town the number of dermatology searches is modest, so precise pages for real searches matter more than traffic charts.
Medical and cosmetic dermatology on one website: two paths for two kinds of patients

Most practices offer both, and the website often mixes them: a rosacea page that ends with a filler promotion, or a home page where a patient with a suspicious mole scrolls past laser packages. Patients and search engines both read that as a confused page. I split the site into two clear sections that share the practice name, the clinicians and the booking system:
medical dermatology: conditions, skin checks, procedures, insurance, referrals and new-patient paperwork
cosmetic dermatology: treatments, who performs them, price ranges and consultation requests

The two sections link where it helps a patient — acne scar treatment after acne care, for example — but each page has one job. If the cosmetic side runs as a separate med spa with its own brand, memberships and booking, that work is described on the
med spa SEO
page.
Dermatology condition pages: acne, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea and hair loss
People search for their condition long before they search for a practice. A condition page that ranks is written for the person who has it and checked by your dermatologist:
what the condition looks like and when it is worth seeing a specialist instead of waiting
what happens at the first visit, which tests may follow and the kinds of treatment the practice offers
whether treatment is usually covered, and what prior authorization means for biologics and other specialty drugs
which clinicians at the practice see patients for it, and how to book

Start with the conditions you want more patients for, not with the whole textbook. Giuseppe’s psychotherapy site in Milan is organized the same way: seven main pages, one for each area of therapy, carry 21 narrower Italian pages between them, and the conditions he works with are named in structured data, so search engines can tell which problems the practice treats.
Pediatric dermatology pages for parents

Parents search for “baby eczema specialist” or “birthmark doctor for kids”. They need to see that the practice treats children, from what age, which dermatologist sees them and how a first visit works for a child.
Skin cancer screening, biopsy and Mohs surgery pages in dermatology SEO

Skin checks are among the most searched dermatology services and the most sensitive to write about. A full-body skin exam page explains in general terms who it is recommended for, what happens in the exam room, how long it takes and what follows if something looks suspicious: a biopsy, the wait for pathology and how results are shared. Mohs surgery, excisions and other skin cancer treatment get their own pages with the surgeon named and the referral process explained, because many of these patients come from another doctor and look up the surgeon first.

These pages inform; they never diagnose, promise a result or use fear to fill the schedule. A self-check guide such as the ABCDE signs is useful if it ends with “book a skin check”, not with reassurance based on a photo.
Local SEO for dermatologists: Google Business Profile, locations and new-patient openings

Searches like “dermatologist near me” are decided mostly in the map pack. Local SEO for dermatologists starts with the Google Business Profile of each location: Dermatologist as the primary category, extra categories only where they are true, medical and cosmetic services listed separately, opening hours, photos of your own waiting room and treatment rooms, and a link to that location’s page instead of the home page.

New patients can wait weeks for a first dermatology visit, and many search for exactly that. If a location has earlier openings, a physician assistant who sees new patients sooner or same-week slots for spot checks, put it on the location page and in the profile. Reviews come from a short request after every visit; replies never confirm that the writer is a patient. The practice name, address and phone must match on the site, the profile, Healthgrades, Zocdoc and insurer directories. Maps work in more depth is on the
local SEO services
page.
Insurance and self-pay pages on a dermatology practice website

Insurance decides where many dermatology patients book. A page for each location with the plans you accept, whether an HMO referral is needed, how out-of-network visits work and what common visits cost without insurance answers searches like “dermatologist that takes Medicare” or “dermatologist no insurance”. Cosmetic treatments are paid out of pocket, so their pages show price ranges or the consultation fee instead. A wrong plan list brings frustrated calls and one-star reviews, so I agree with the front desk on a date each quarter to confirm it.
Teledermatology pages: online visits, skin photos and state licensure

Dermatology fits telehealth better than most specialties, and patients search for “online dermatologist” or “virtual acne visit”. A teledermatology page states which problems can be handled online and which need an in-person exam, how the visit works, which states the clinicians are licensed in — patients usually have to be located in one of them — and whether insurance covers it.

The photos patients send are health information. In the US they belong in a HIPAA-compliant patient portal or telehealth tool, not in a website form or plain email. The form on the site collects contact details and a convenient time, nothing about the skin. Treat this as general orientation rather than legal advice; the practice’s compliance adviser makes the call.
YMYL and E-E-A-T on dermatology websites: board certification, reviewer and date
Health pages fall into the group Google calls “Your Money or Your Life” (YMYL), where it wants to see who is behind the advice. In dermatology the proof is concrete:
each condition and procedure page names the dermatologist who wrote or reviewed it, describes board certification accurately and links to their profile
titles are exact: a physician assistant or nurse practitioner is introduced as one, with the conditions they treat
pages carry a “last reviewed” date and describe outcomes with risks and alternatives, without promises
clinical photos are the practice’s own, used with written consent; before-and-after pairs are shot in the same light and not edited

Advertising rules differ by state, and the FTC has its own rules on reviews and endorsements, so check with your state medical board and your adviser. Giuseppe’s editor gets a warning from the CMS whenever a draft uses wording that Italian rules on advertising health services make risky; a dermatology site can get the same kind of check for words like “cure” or “guaranteed results”.
Technical SEO for dermatology websites: images, speed and structured data
Dermatology sites are heavy with photos, and that is where most technical problems start:
photos compressed and served in modern formats, so the main content of a page shows within 2.5 seconds on a phone
alt text on clinical images that describes them for screen readers instead of repeating keywords
one address per condition and treatment, without near-identical copies for every suburb
structured data for the practice (MedicalClinic), each dermatologist (Physician) and the questions answered on a page
If the website itself is the obstacle — a vendor template you cannot edit, no room for new pages — read how I design and build sites for practices on the
medical website design
page.
Dermatology SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

More and more patients ask assistants “should I get this mole checked”, “which dermatologist in Denver treats hidradenitis” or “dermatologist or med spa for rosacea laser”. An assistant builds its reply from sources it can compare: the practice website, the Google profile, Healthgrades or Zocdoc listings and reviews. On health questions it favors sources that name a qualified author. Getting into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a dermatology practice it means:
conditions treated, procedures, locations, languages, accepted plans and new-patient availability written as plain facts
short, clinician-reviewed answers to the questions patients ask the front desk
the same practice and doctor details everywhere assistants look
structured data that ties the practice, its dermatologists and its locations together

A private practice can get there: ChatGPT already cites recently published pages from Giuseppe’s site, and Giuseppe himself first heard of me in a ChatGPT answer. I record what assistants say about your practice at the start and compare it a few months later. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.

children.text: I do SEO for doctors as individual physicians and specialists: the work that makes a patient who searches for your name, your specialty or their condition find you — and trust what they find. A practice or a hospital has its own website and marketing; you as a physician have a name, credentials and reviews that follow you from one employer to the next. This page is about that personal side of search.
What SEO for doctors covers: your name, your specialty and the conditions you treat
Patients look for physicians in three ways, and each needs its own work. These are the SEO keywords for doctors that matter most:
the doctor’s name — after a referral, a recommendation from a friend or a hospital stay, often typed with a spelling mistake
the specialty and the place — “rheumatologist [city]”, “pediatric cardiologist near me”, “female dermatologist”
the condition or procedure — “psoriatic arthritis specialist”, “knee replacement surgeon”, “second opinion thyroid nodule”

Name searches show directories first: Healthgrades, Vitals, ZocDoc, WebMD and the hospital’s find-a-doctor page. Specialty searches show the map. Condition searches show health publishers and AI Overviews. SEO for a whole practice, clinic or medical group — service lines, several locations, a marketing budget — is a different job, described on the
medical SEO
page.
A personal physician website or a doctor profile on the practice site

Many physicians have only a profile page on their employer’s website, written by someone else and lost when they change jobs. A personal physician website — even five pages — is the one place you control:
it ranks for your name above directories you cannot edit
it stays yours when you move hospitals, join a group or open a private practice
it can explain your approach and the conditions you focus on in your own words

If you stay with one practice for the long term, a strong profile page on its site may be enough, and the work goes into that page and the directories. How a doctor’s site is designed and built is covered on the
medical website design
page.
Doctor profile pages and E-E-A-T: credentials, board certification and hospital affiliation

Google treats health as a “Your Money or Your Life” subject and looks for E-E-A-T — first-hand experience, expertise, authority and trust — before it ranks medical pages. For an individual physician E-E-A-T is not abstract: it is the list of facts on your profile page that a patient, a colleague or a search engine can verify.
Credentials and board certification on a physician profile

Medical school, residency and fellowship with years; board certification with the board named; state licenses; memberships in specialty societies; publications and teaching roles. Patients and search engines can check board certification, so it is written exactly as the board states it.
Hospital affiliation and the hospital’s find-a-doctor page

The hospitals where you have privileges are both a trust signal and a source of links. Your profile names them, and the hospital’s find-a-doctor page should link back to your profile or personal site. Many US directories build profiles from public provider data such as the NPI registry, so an old address there spreads to sites you never touched.
All of this is also marked up as structured data for the physician — specialty, credentials, affiliated hospitals, offices — so search engines and assistants connect the page with the person.
Specialty and condition pages in SEO for doctors: written or reviewed by the physician
A page about a condition you treat — say, psoriatic arthritis for a rheumatologist — can rank for searches that no directory answers. In a YMYL field it only works if it is clearly yours:
written or reviewed by you, with your name, credentials and the date of the last review at the top
explains the condition, how it is diagnosed and what treatment options exist at your office, without giving advice to an individual reader
says when to seek urgent care and that the page is no substitute for a visit
cites guidelines or studies where it makes a claim, and makes no promises of a cure or outcome
I draft and structure the pages from search data and your notes; you correct the medicine. Pages nobody with credentials has reviewed are not published.
Physician reviews and reputation on Healthgrades, Vitals, ZocDoc and Google

Patients read ratings before they book a doctor they do not know. The directories hold profiles for most US physicians whether or not they have claimed them, often with wrong offices, old photos and missing insurance. The work:
claim and correct the profiles on Healthgrades, Vitals, ZocDoc, WebMD and Google, with the same name format, offices and phone numbers
add a recent photo, languages, accepted insurance and a short biography that matches the profile page
set up a request for a review after the visit, sent to every patient, with no incentives of any kind
report reviews that break a platform’s rules, such as ones about a different doctor

Replies need the most care. In the US, a reply that confirms someone is your patient or mentions their care can be a HIPAA disclosure, even when the patient wrote about it first; in the EU the GDPR raises the same concern. A reply thanks the person, states a general policy and invites them to call the office — nothing more. This is general guidance; your practice’s compliance officer has the last word.
Local SEO for doctors: practitioner profiles in Google Maps

Google allows a separate Business Profile for an individual practitioner at the practice where they see patients. For a specialist this profile often ranks for “[specialty] near me” alongside the practice. Local SEO for doctors means:
one practitioner profile for each office where you hold regular hours, with the specialty as the category
hours that match your clinic days at that location, not the building’s hours
an appointment link to the booking page for you, not the general switchboard
no duplicate profiles from an old practice; those are merged or marked as moved
Map results for a whole clinic or hospital, with many departments and locations, are part of
healthcare SEO
SEO for doctors who get patients through referrals

Many specialists depend on referrals from primary care physicians and other specialists, and a referred patient almost always searches for the name before calling. If that search shows an outdated directory profile with two stars and an old phone number, some referrals never arrive. For referral-based practice, SEO is mostly about the name search: a profile page that ranks first, directories that agree with it, a clear way to book, and a short page for referring physicians with your fax or e-referral details, the conditions you see and typical wait times.
Telehealth SEO for doctors: virtual visit pages and where you are licensed

Telehealth lets a physician see patients far beyond the commute radius, and it changes what search can bring. A virtual visit page states what can and cannot be handled by video, which platform is used and how to book. In the US a physician generally needs a license in the state where the patient is during the visit, so the page lists the states you are licensed in, and pages target those states rather than the whole country. Search does not override licensing; it only helps the patients you can lawfully see find you.
Doctors in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews: how patients ask AI to choose a physician (GEO, AEO)

Patients now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews “who is a good endocrinologist in [city] who takes my insurance” or “which surgeons do robotic hernia repair near me”. The answers are put together from directories, hospital pages, reviews and the physician’s own site. For a doctor, generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO) mean:
credentials, board certification, hospital affiliation and specialty written as plain facts on your profile page
the same name format and offices on every directory, so the assistant does not merge you with another doctor of the same name
condition pages with your name as the reviewer, which assistants can cite
structured data that ties the person, the specialty and the offices together
I check what assistants say about you before and after the work. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
SEO agency for doctors or a single specialist: questions to ask before you sign

Most firms ranking for “seo for doctors” are physician marketing agencies that bundle a website, ads, social posts and review software into one monthly fee; some reuse the same condition pages for every dermatologist or orthopedist they sign. I work alone, on SEO and on the site itself. The questions below are worth putting to me as much as to any agency:
Who writes the condition pages, and do I review every one before it goes live?
If we part ways, do the site, the domain and the Healthgrades and Google logins stay with me?
How do you handle review replies with patient privacy in mind?
Will you report appointment requests and referral calls, or only rankings?

I am a single specialist, not an agency, and I measure the work in calls and booked jobs, not in a list of positions.
SEO for electricians: emergency, upgrade and project searches
People look for an electrician in three very different situations, and each one needs its own page:

an emergency — half the house has no power, a breaker trips every few minutes, an outlet smells of burning. The search is short, on a phone, often at night: “emergency electrician”, “electrician near me open now”

a planned upgrade — a new electric car, a heat pump, a hot tub or an insurance letter about an old panel. The search names the job: “EV charger installation”, “200 amp panel upgrade cost”, “whole house generator installer”
a project — a renovation, an addition, a shop fit-out or a lighting retrofit in an office. Here the buyer is often a general contractor or a property manager, not a homeowner

A site that answers all three with one “Services” page loses each of them to a competitor who answers one well. Electrician SEO starts by deciding which of these you want more of, and building for that first.
Local SEO for electricians: getting into the Google map results

For “electrician near me” and most emergency searches, Google shows three businesses on a map above everything else. Getting there depends mostly on the Google Business Profile, and electricians lose positions in it in predictable ways:
“Electrician” as the primary category, with secondary categories only for work you actually do, such as lighting or electrical installation
each service listed in the profile — panel upgrades, EV chargers, generators, rewiring, inspections — with a short description
a service area drawn around the towns your vans really reach, not the whole state
hours that match reality: “open 24 hours” only if someone answers the phone at 2 a.m.
photos of finished work every week or two — a labeled panel, a mounted charger, a generator pad — with the job and the town named
Electricians who go to the customer are service-area businesses, and the rules on addresses and business names apply to them strictly. The general mechanics of the map results are described on the
local SEO for contractors
page.
SEO keywords for electricians: how homeowners and property managers search

Keyword research for an electrician shows a split that most sites ignore: homeowners search for the job or the symptom, while commercial buyers search for the type of contractor. Before any page is written I collect the real numbers for your area:
job searches: “panel upgrade”, “Level 2 charger installation”, “knob and tube rewiring”, “recessed lighting installation”
symptom searches: “lights flickering in the whole house”, “breaker keeps tripping”, “outlet not working”
cost searches: “cost to rewire a house”, “generator installation cost”
commercial searches: “commercial electrician” plus a city, “tenant improvement electrical contractor”
For each phrase I check whether Google shows the map, Local Services Ads, AI Overviews or lead platforms. That tells us which page can rank and which searches are better left to the profile.
Service pages for panel upgrades, EV chargers, generators and rewiring

Each job worth having gets its own page, written around the questions customers ask on the phone. An EV charger page covers charger types, the distance from the panel, whether the panel has room, the permit and the inspection. A panel upgrade page explains why it is needed — more load, an old fuse box, an insurer’s request — what the utility has to do and how long the power is off. A generator page covers sizing, fuel, the transfer switch and maintenance.

Rewiring, lighting, smart home installs, surge protection and electrical inspections for home buyers each follow the same pattern. Where your utility or state offers a rebate for chargers or panel work, the page says so, with a link to the program.
Emergency electrician searches: pages and calls that work at night

An emergency visitor does not read. The emergency page puts the phone number first, says which towns you reach and how fast, explains what to do before you arrive — switch off the breaker if it is safe, keep away from a downed line and call the utility — and states any after-hours fee plainly. Calls from that page are tracked on their own number, so you can see what emergency searches bring and whether the night line pays for itself.
Residential, commercial and industrial electrical work: separate pages in electrician SEO

Commercial and industrial buyers use search to build a shortlist, then check capabilities. A facility manager looking for a lighting retrofit or a GC looking for an electrical subcontractor wants to see project types, crew size, the license classes you hold, safety practices and the sectors you work in. Those pages are kept apart from residential service, so a homeowner with a dead outlet is not sent to a warehouse project, and a building manager is not shown smart thermostats.
Industrial work rarely starts from a search box, but a clear capabilities page is what a buyer checks after hearing your name from someone else.
License, permits and reviews: trust signals in electrician SEO

Electrical work is bought on safety. People want to know that a licensed master electrician is responsible for the job and that the work will pass inspection. On the website and in the profile, the license number, license class, insurance, permits pulled and inspections passed are written as text — not hidden in a logo — so customers, Google and AI assistants can all read them.

Reviews do the rest. The best moment to ask is when the inspection has passed or the power is back on: a text with a direct link, and an answer to every review within days. Reviews that mention “panel upgrade” or “EV charger” and the town help the profile rank for those jobs. Bought reviews break Google’s rules and are not used.
SEO versus Local Services Ads, Angi and Thumbtack for electricians

Google Local Services Ads put a few electricians with the Google Guaranteed badge above the map and charge per lead. Angi, HomeAdvisor and Thumbtack sell leads that several electricians often receive at once. Both bring calls from the first week and stop when the budget stops, and emergency leads in a busy city get expensive.

SEO takes longer — usually two to four months for new pages — but the calls it brings are yours alone. A common setup is to keep Local Services Ads for emergencies while SEO builds the planned-work pages that bring larger jobs. My work covers search; running ads or lead-platform accounts stays with you or your ad agency.
AI SEO for electricians: visibility in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Electrical questions are a natural fit for AI answers: “do I need a permit to install an EV charger”, “why do my lights flicker when the AC starts”, “how much is a panel upgrade”. Google’s AI Overviews and ChatGPT answer them directly, and when the question ends in “who can do this near me”, they name local electricians. This work goes by two names, generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO), and for an electrician it means:
service pages that answer the cost, permit and safety questions in a few clear sentences
license, insurance, service area and years in business written as plain facts
structured data that names the business, each service and the areas you cover
one business name, address and phone number across the site, the profile and every directory
I check how assistants describe your business before the work starts and again later. More on the

page.
Choosing the best SEO for electricians: questions to ask
Some agencies sell SEO to hundreds of electricians from the same templates, and some field-service software includes a marketing add-on. Before you sign with anyone, including me, ask:
Will reports show calls and booked jobs, or only rankings?
If we part ways, do the site, the Google profile and the texts stay with me?
Are service-area pages written with real jobs from those towns?
How will residential and commercial work be kept apart?
