children.text: I do SEO for flooring companies: keyword research by material and job, pages for installation and refinishing, brand and project pages, Google Maps and visibility in AI answers. Flooring sits between retail and a trade. The customer first chooses a material and a look, often in a showroom or on a phone at night, and only then needs someone to measure, prepare the subfloor and install it. The searches follow that order, and a flooring website has to answer both halves: a list of brands alone loses the people looking for an installer, and a phone number alone loses the people still choosing.
SEO for flooring companies: showroom retailers, mobile installers and refinishers
“Flooring company” covers three different businesses, and each one competes for its own searches:
showroom retailers that sell product and arrange installation — customers search by brand, material and “flooring store near me”, and visit before they buy
installers who work from a van, often subcontracting for stores and builders while taking direct jobs — customers search “LVP installation” or “tile installer” with the town
hardwood refinishers — customers search “floor sanding”, “refinish hardwood floors” or “dustless refinishing”, usually for a house they own or have just bought
Many companies do two or three of these. Each needs its own section of the site, its own photos and its own way to book.
Flooring SEO keywords: material, job, room and look
Keyword research for a flooring company is built from the materials you install, the jobs you take and the words customers use for rooms and problems. The usual groups:
material — “luxury vinyl plank installation”, “engineered hardwood flooring”, “porcelain tile installer”, “carpet installation”
job — install, replace, refinish, repair, stairs, removal of the old floor, subfloor leveling
room or problem — “basement flooring options”, “waterproof flooring for kitchen”, “squeaky floor repair”, “flooring for dogs”
look — “white oak floors”, “herringbone wood floor”, “wide plank flooring”, searched while the customer is still choosing

The data also shows which searches lead to the map, which to big retailers and which already show an AI Overview. That decides what to build first — usually the materials with the best margin, in the towns you want to work in.
Flooring installation pages: LVP, engineered hardwood, tile and carpet
Each material is a separate decision for the customer and a separate search, so each gets a page. What a good installation page explains, beyond “we install it”:
subfloor preparation — leveling, moisture testing on concrete, and what happens when the old floor has to come out first
how long a typical room or a whole floor takes, and whether the family can stay in the house
where the material fits and where it does not: vinyl plank in basements and kitchens, solid hardwood above grade, tile in bathrooms and entryways
transitions, stairs, baseboards and furniture moving — the details behind most complaints when nobody mentions them in advance
These pages need your jobs and your answers. A page assembled from a manufacturer’s brochure reads like every other installer’s page in the area, and Google has no reason to choose yours.
Hardwood floor refinishing SEO: sanding, recoating and the refinish-or-replace question

Refinishing is searched by a different customer: someone who found oak under old carpet, bought a house with worn floors or manages a rental between tenants. The searches are “hardwood floor refinishing near me”, “floor sanding cost”, “dustless floor refinishing” and “refinish or replace hardwood floors”. A refinishing page earns them when it covers:
a full sand and refinish versus a screen and recoat, and how you decide which one the floor needs
stain colors on the wood species you usually work with, shown on real floors
dust control, odor and the time before people, pets and furniture can go back on the floor
when boards are too thin or too damaged to sand again, and replacement is the better answer
The refinish-or-replace question is where the customer decides whom to trust. A page that lists the signs pointing either way often gets the call.
Flooring store SEO: brand pages, samples and in-home measure appointments

A showroom stocks Shaw, Mohawk, COREtec, Bruce or other manufacturers, and the easy move is to import their catalogs. Those descriptions already sit on the manufacturer’s site and on hundreds of retailer sites, so copied product pages rarely rank. What works better for a flooring store:
one page per brand or collection you carry, with where it suits, what you think of it and photos of it installed by your crew
a sample request and an in-home measure booking on every brand and material page
showroom hours, parking and what to bring — room sizes, photos, cabinet and paint colors
the warranty in plain words: what the manufacturer covers and what your installation warranty covers
Price per square foot on a flooring website: cost pages that bring calls

“How much does it cost to install LVP”, “hardwood refinishing cost per square foot” and “tile installation cost” are among the most common flooring searches, and AI Overviews answer them with national averages. A cost page with your own ranges keeps the customer on your site instead. It says what the per-square-foot price includes and what is added on top:
removal and disposal of the old floor
subfloor repairs and leveling
stairs, usually priced per step
moving furniture and appliances, trims and transitions
Published ranges filter out the customers who were never going to pay for proper preparation, and the ones who call already know roughly where they stand.
Flooring project photos for SEO: product, pattern and room in every caption

Flooring photos are searched as much as they are looked at. People type “herringbone white oak living room” or “gray vinyl plank kitchen” while choosing, and Google Images shows what it can read. A flooring project page names the exact product and color, the pattern, the room and the town — “Engineered white oak, herringbone, living room in [town]” — and shows the details that prove the craftsmanship: stair nosings, the transition to tile, the cut around a fireplace hearth. The same photos posted only on Instagram are close to invisible in Google search.
Commercial flooring SEO: builders, property managers and apartment turnovers

Commercial work arrives through other people: general contractors who sub out flooring, property managers replacing carpet between tenants, office and retail fit-outs, multifamily developers. They search “commercial flooring contractor [city]” or “carpet tile installation” and check whether you handle volume, schedules, insurance certificates and night or weekend work. A commercial page lists the building types you work in, the materials — carpet tile, sheet vinyl, rubber, polished concrete if you offer it — your crew size and how bids are requested. These searches are few, but one property manager can send work every month.
Local SEO for flooring companies: Google Business Profile for a showroom or a service area
For “flooring near me” and “floor refinishing near me” the map comes first, and the right setup depends on how you work:
a showroom keeps its address visible, with a primary category such as “Flooring store” and hours that match the door
a mobile installer or refinisher sets a service area of the towns the crew really covers and hides the home address, with “Flooring contractor” or “Floor refinishing service” as the category
photos of finished floors, named by material and town, added through the busy months
reviews that name the material and the room, requested when the last piece of trim goes on
The full map work for a flooring business — listings, review replies, spam competitors — is covered on the
local SEO services
page.
Angi, Thumbtack and big-box installation programs compared with flooring SEO

Many installers take part of their work from Home Depot and Lowe’s installation programs, from lead platforms such as Angi or Thumbtack, or from national brands like Empire Today. That work keeps crews busy, but the customer belongs to the store or the platform, and someone else sets the margin. SEO builds the other side: customers who found your name, booked your measure and pay your price. Most flooring companies keep both and shift the balance over a few years.
Remodelers and general contractors who do flooring as part of bigger jobs compete in a different search; their version is on the
SEO for contractors
page.
Flooring SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

A growing share of flooring questions never reach a search results page: “vinyl plank or engineered hardwood for a basement”, “how long does hardwood refinishing take” or “good flooring installers near me” go to ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews, which build the answer from sources they can read and verify. Work on those answers goes by two names, generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO). For a flooring business it covers:
material comparisons written from your installs, including where each material fails
cost ranges and timelines in plain text, not only inside a PDF quote
the brands you are authorized to sell or certified to install, stated the same way on the site and the profile
structured data naming the business, its services and its service area
At the start and again a few months later, I put questions about your company to these assistants and save their answers. The method is described on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.

children.text: SEO for home builders is the work that brings people searching for a new house in your area — by town, by community name, by floor plan or by “build on my lot” — to your website, and keeps them coming back over the months it takes to sign a contract. I do it myself, as a single SEO consultant who also builds websites, for custom, semi-custom and production builders, so the same person audits the site, writes the community pages and changes the code.
What SEO for home builders covers: communities, floor plans, custom builds and AI answers

A home builder is searched differently from a contractor called for a repair. Nobody needs a new house by tonight. A family starts looking a year or more ahead, compares areas, saves floor plans, tours models on weekends and talks to a lender long before signing. Search touches every one of those steps:
town and area searches — “new construction homes in [town]”, “new homes near [school district]”
community and builder names, typed after a drive past a sign or a mention by a realtor
plan and product searches — “single-story 4-bedroom homes”, “homes with a casita”, “quick move-in homes”
custom-build questions — “custom home builder [county]”, “build on your own lot”, “cost to build a house in [state]”
the same questions asked in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
Everything here is about companies that build houses. General contractors, remodelers and commercial construction firms are searched in other ways; their version is on the
SEO for construction companies
page.
Custom home builder SEO and production builder SEO: two different search maps
A custom builder and a production builder may work in the same county, but their buyers type different things, and one “Our homes” page serves neither.
Custom and semi-custom home builders

These buyers usually own land or are about to buy it. They search for a builder by area and style — “luxury custom home builder [lake or county]”, “modern farmhouse builder”, “barndominium builder [state]” — and for the process: design-build or with an architect, cost per square foot, how long it takes. Project pages, a clear build process and a fair answer on price ranges win these searches.
Production builders with communities

These buyers choose a place first and a builder second. Their searches name the town, the school district, the community or a type of home — townhomes, 55+, single-story. Community pages, plan pages and a current list of move-in-ready homes win here. Builders who do both get a separate set of pages for each side.
Community and lot pages in SEO for home builders
The community page is a production builder’s main landing page, and most are too thin: a rendering, a price “from” and a contact form. A page that ranks and convinces carries:
the location in words and on a map: nearest towns, main roads, commute times to the job centers your buyers care about
homesite sizes, how many remain and which plans fit them
the price range, HOA dues and special tax districts such as MUD or Mello-Roos where they apply, stated plainly
amenities that exist today, kept apart from those still planned
links to the school district’s own site and to the plans and homes on offer there
the sales office address and the hours someone is there
What to do with the page when a community sells out

Deleting it throws away years of links and rankings. The page stays, says the community is sold out, and points to your nearest active community. The same goes for plan names you retire: their pages redirect to the plan that replaced them.
Floor plan, model home and quick move-in pages that rank
Plan names are searched more than builders expect: buyers write down “the Madison” at a model and look it up at home. A plan page needs text, not only an image and a PDF:
square footage, beds, baths, garage, stories and minimum lot width as text
elevations and the main structural options — extra bedroom, covered patio, third garage bay — described in words
the communities where the plan is built, each linked
a video or 3D tour of the model, with a written summary next to it

Quick move-in, spec or inventory homes deserve their own pages and their own list, because “move-in ready homes [town]” comes from buyers with a deadline — a lease ending, a new job. Each page shows the lot, the plan, the completion month and the status, and redirects to similar homes once the house closes.
Cost to build and build process content: answering buyers months before they call

“How much does it cost to build a house in [state]”, “cost per square foot for a custom home”, “how long does it take to build a house” are searched all year, and they are often where a buyer first meets a builder. A builder who answers with real ranges earns the visit; “contact us for pricing” sends it to a forum. Pages that work cover:
price ranges by size or finish level, and what moves the number: site work, utilities, foundation, finishes, permits
the build process as steps with typical durations, from design and permits to the final walkthrough
what the base price includes and what counts as an upgrade
construction loans versus a mortgage on a finished home, with your lender partners named
Ranges age quickly, so each figure shows the month it was last checked, and anything about rates or incentives uses the lender’s own wording.
Local SEO for home builders: Google Business Profile, sales offices and homeowner reviews

Google’s guidelines do not accept a profile for a model home as such, because homes for sale are excluded, but a sales office or design center staffed during posted hours can have its own next to the company profile. For each eligible location:
a primary category that matches the work, such as “Home builder” or “Custom home builder”
the hours someone is really there, weekends included
photos of the community, the models and finished homes, added regularly
reviews from homeowners, requested at closing and again after the first-year warranty walkthrough
Answer every review, complaints about delays included; buyers read the replies as closely as the stars. Everything else about map rankings is on the
local SEO services
page.
New home listing sites and realtors in home builder SEO

NewHomeSource, Zillow’s new construction section and Realtor.com show your communities and inventory, and they often rank above builders for “new homes in [town]”. For SEO they are places where your data must match your site — community and plan names, prices, status — with a clear way to reach you. Sold homes still listed there make buyers and AI assistants doubt the rest.

In many markets realtors bring a large share of new-home buyers. A page for agents with co-op terms, registration rules and current inventory is searched by agents themselves and saves your sales team the same phone call every week.
Tracking home builder leads through a long buying cycle: from search to tour and contract

A buyer can visit your site many times over several months before booking a tour. A report that counts only forms sent in the month of the click misses most of what SEO does for a builder. What I set up:
interest-list sign-ups per community, tour requests and calls tracked as separate events in GA4
every form sent to your CRM — HubSpot, Salesforce, Lasso or the tool your sales team uses — with the first page and source of the visit
a simple way for sales to mark which leads became tours and contracts
The monthly report then shows tours and contracts by community and by type of search, with rankings beside them, not instead of them.
Technical SEO for home builder websites: lot maps, plan PDFs and inventory feeds
Builder websites hide a lot from Google. The usual cases:
interactive lot maps and plan tools from third-party vendors loaded in an iframe, whose content counts for the vendor or for nobody
floor plans published only as PDFs or images, with no page of text
inventory pulled in by script, with no separate address for each home
sold-out communities and closed homes returning errors instead of redirects
heavy renderings and tour embeds that make pages slow on a phone
I check what Google actually sees and fix it in the code or around the tool. If a rebuild makes more sense, the
home builder website design
page shows how I plan and build one.
SEO for home builders in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Buyers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews “who are good custom home builders near Boise”, “is [builder] good quality” or “production or custom builder for a first home”, and gets back a short list of builders with a reason next to each. Work on those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a builder it means:
areas, home types, price ranges, warranty terms and years in business written as plain sentences
cost, timeline and process pages that answer questions directly and show their dates
the same company, community and plan names on your site, Google, listing sites and Houzz
a steady flow of homeowner reviews that describe the build
Before the work starts and again afterwards, I ask the assistants about you and note which builders they name instead. The method is described on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.

children.text: I do SEO for home inspectors and multi-inspector companies: the website, the Google Business Profile and the pages a buyer under contract finds when the inspection period has started and a date is needed this week. The same pages are read by the real estate agent who checks your name before passing it on, so a home inspector’s site has two readers with different questions — and good SEO answers both.
Home inspector searches: who looks for an inspection and what they type
Inspection demand is narrow but steady, and the searches split by who is asking:
buyers with an accepted offer — “home inspector near me”, “home inspection [town]”, “how long does a home inspection take”
sellers preparing to list — “pre-listing inspection”, “should I get an inspection before selling”
owners of new homes — “new construction inspection”, “11-month warranty inspection”, “phase inspection before drywall”
buyers adding tests — “radon testing”, “sewer scope inspection”, “mold inspection cost”
agents looking for a backup when their usual inspector is booked
Each group needs its own page. A single “Services” page with a list of bullet points does not rank for any of these searches and leaves the buyer guessing whether you even do sewer scopes.
Realtor referrals and direct buyers in home inspector SEO

In many markets a large share of inspections still comes through agents. That work depends on relationships, and SEO does not replace them. What SEO changes is the other share: buyers who choose their own inspector, investors, sellers, owners of new homes and people relocating from another state who do not know any local agent. Those bookings come with no middleman, and they grow as your pages rank.

Agent referrals also pass through search. The agent, or the buyer the agent names you to, types your company name into Google before calling. What they see — reviews, a sample report, the license number, a clear price — decides whether the referral turns into a booking.
A page for real estate agents on a home inspector website

Give agents a page of their own: how to book for a client, report turnaround, who receives the report, how you handle re-inspections, and how findings are written — clear and factual rather than alarming. Agents worry about inspectors who frighten buyers; a sample report shows your tone better than any promise.
Home inspection marketing: where SEO fits next to agent visits and paid platforms

Home inspection marketing usually mixes several channels: presentations at brokerage offices, continuing-education classes for agents, social media, review sites, Thumbtack or Angi listings and Google Ads. They work, and most of them need your time or money every month to keep working. SEO is the part that keeps bringing bookings between those efforts, and it makes every other channel stronger, because each of them ends with someone searching your name. My part is the search side: the website, the profile and the pages.
Ancillary service pages for home inspectors: radon, mold, sewer scope, termite, septic

Add-on services raise the value of each inspection, and each one is searched on its own. A buyer reading about radon levels in their county, or worried about the 1950s clay pipe under the yard, searches for that test, not for a home inspector. Give every ancillary service a page with:
what the test finds and why it matters in your area — older sewer lines, radon-prone soils, termite pressure, homes on wells or septic
how it is done, how long it takes and when the results arrive
the price alone and as an add-on to a full inspection
photos or short video from real jobs, with the town named
Some loan types and states ask for a wood-destroying insect report; if that applies where you work, say so on the termite page. These pages also give AI assistants specific facts to repeat.
Sample inspection report and online booking on a home inspector website

“What will the report look like?” is the question most buyers cannot ask before booking. A sample report page answers it. Most inspection software — Spectora, HomeGauge, ISN and others — produces a web version of the report, so the sample can be a real report from a house you are allowed to show, with the address removed. Put a short summary on your own page — sections, number of photos, how defects are rated, delivery time — and link to the full sample. A PDF alone is hard to read on a phone and is rarely what ranks.

Booking is the next step. Show the price before the calendar: base price by square footage and age of the house, then add-ons with their prices. A buyer who sees the full figure and a free slot on Thursday books; a buyer who has to call for a quote often calls someone else.
Local SEO for home inspectors: Google Business Profile and service-area pages

Most inspectors work from home and travel to the house, so the profile is set up as a service-area business: “Home inspector” as the primary category, the counties you cover, real hours and photos from inspections — attics, crawl spaces, electrical panels, roof drones. Service-area pages on the website should carry local knowledge: the age of the housing stock, common foundation types, frequent problems such as galvanized plumbing in post-war neighborhoods or expansive clay soils. A page for a town where you have never inspected is a thin page, and Google treats it that way. More on the map side on the
local SEO services
page.
Reviews, InterNACHI, ASHI and state licensing on a home inspector’s site
A buyer is trusting a stranger with the largest purchase of their life, so the trust signals have to be on the page, not in a logo strip:
the state license number, where your state licenses inspectors, written as text
InterNACHI, ASHI or other memberships and certifications, with what they mean in one sentence
errors and omissions and general liability insurance, if you carry them
years in business and the kinds of homes you inspect

For reviews, ask when the report is delivered, while the buyer is still grateful, and ask agents too. Reviews that mention the town, the house type and something you found give both Google and the next buyer something concrete.
New construction and 11-month warranty inspection pages

Buyers of new homes often believe a new house needs no inspection. Pages for pre-drywall, final walk-through and 11-month warranty inspections reach them with that exact question. Show defects you have found in new builds and explain the timing around the builder’s warranty. Builders market these homes with their own SEO, described on the
SEO for home builders
page; your pages meet the same buyers after they sign.
Home inspection SEO through the year: busy spring, slower winter

Inspections follow the housing market: busy from spring through summer, slower in the colder months and when mortgage rates rise. The slow weeks are the best time to write add-on pages, update the sample report and collect photos, because new pages take weeks to settle in search. Pre-listing and new construction pages can help keep the calendar fuller when buyer inspections drop.

“What does a home inspection include?”, “Is a sewer scope worth it?” and “Who is a good home inspector in [town]?” are now often answered by ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews before anyone opens a website. structured data marking the business, its services and the area it covers
the same name, phone and details on Google, Yelp, the association directories and your site

Keyword research for a studio starts with how clients describe their project, not how designers describe their work. The searches that end in paid projects usually fall into five groups:
place: “interior designer Scottsdale”, “interior design firm Upper West Side”, “interior decorator near me”
room or project: “kitchen remodel designer”, “primary bathroom design service”, “new build interior design”

service model: “full-service interior design”, “e-design services”, “interior design consultation cost”
your name and studio name, including the ways people misspell them

Volumes for most of these are small, often a few dozen searches a month per city, and that is fine for a business that needs a dozen good projects a year. A page ranking for “kitchen designer [town]” does not need thousands of visitors; it needs the three people about to spend on a kitchen.
Local SEO for interior designers: Google Business Profile, cities and neighborhoods

For most studios the map results bring more inquiries than any blog post. Google treats an interior designer as a local business: a studio that receives clients shows its address, while a designer who works from home and visits clients sets up a service-area profile with the address hidden. the primary category “Interior designer”, with extra categories only for services you really sell
the studio name as it appears on your invoices, with no city or service words added
photos of finished projects added through the year, each with the town in the description
a review request when a project is installed, and a reply to every review

a title naming the work and the place, such as “Kitchen and dining room renovation in a 1920s Tudor, Evanston”
image file names and alt text that describe each room, written per image instead of copied
a few hundred words on the brief and the choices, linked to the matching service and area pages
photos compressed so the page passes Core Web Vitals on a phone

publications that featured your projects — ask for a link to the project page, not only a credit line

show houses, design awards and local home tours
Bought links and directory packages carry the risk; links earned from people you actually worked with carry the value.

E-design is the one service where an interior designer competes beyond the city. There is no map pack here, and the competition is national e-design companies and designers from everywhere. What ranks is a clear page for each package, answers to what buyers ask before paying — what they receive, how many revisions, how to measure a room — and finished e-design rooms with the clients’ own photos where they agree. E-design pages stay separate from local service pages, so each targets its own searches and neither weakens the other.

City-to-city route pages for movers: which routes deserve a page

Searches like “movers from Austin to Denver” or “Chicago to Phoenix moving company” come from people who already know the date and the distance — the most valuable visitors a long-distance mover gets. A route page ranks when it carries what only a company running that lane knows: how often your trucks go that way, typical transit time, whether customers can share a load to lower the price, the delivery window, and photos or reviews from moves on that route.

The usual mistake is generating hundreds of route pages from one template with the city names swapped. Google treats them as doorway pages and trusts the whole site less. I start with the five to fifteen routes you drive most and add new ones when the jobs are there.
Moving quote forms and estimates: in-home, video and online inventory

For a mover the quote request is the conversion, so the form decides how much search traffic becomes revenue. A good first step asks only what the estimator needs to call back: moving from and to, date or month, home size and a phone number. A fifty-item inventory list scares people off on a phone; it belongs in a second step or a video survey.
a video survey option — the customer walks the rooms on a call — is quicker to book than an in-home visit and gives a firmer price
a page explaining binding, non-binding and not-to-exceed estimates in plain words, because customers search those terms while comparing quotes
every request sent to your moving CRM — SmartMoving, Supermove or the one you use — with the page and search that brought it
a reply within minutes in business hours; in moving, the first credible quote often wins the job
USDOT number, insurance and reviews: trust signals in moving company SEO

“Moving scams” and “how to check a moving company” are searched by the same people who later search for movers. In the US, interstate household movers register with the FMCSA and display a USDOT number, and many states license movers who work inside the state. Showing those facts plainly helps both customers and search:
USDOT and state license numbers as text in the footer and on the about page, not inside an image
a page on valuation coverage — what basic released value covers and what full value protection adds — in general terms, with your own options
a real street address for the office and warehouse, photos of your own branded trucks and of the crew
reviews on Google, Yelp and the BBB that mention the route or type of move
Requirements change and differ by state; check the current rules for your operation. Nothing here is legal advice.
Local SEO for movers: Google Business Profile, service area and fake listings

For “movers near me” the map usually comes before the regular results, and the moving category has a known problem: lead brokers and out-of-state operators create listings that look like local movers. A company with a real yard and real trucks wins by being complete and consistent:
a moving category such as “Moving company” as the primary one, and a storage category only if you run a warehouse
a service area that matches where you really book local moves
new photos of trucks, crews and the warehouse every month
a review request after each delivery, asking customers to mention where they moved from and to
Listings of brokers posing as local movers can be reported to Google through its redress form. Map work in depth is on the
local SEO services
page.
Advertising ideas for a moving company: lead sites, Google Ads and SEO compared

Ask movers what works and you hear the same list: realtor and apartment-complex referrals, trucks as rolling billboards, Google Ads, Local Services Ads, Yelp and moving lead websites. Lead aggregators are where many owners lose the most: one form on a quote site is sold to several movers at once, so you pay to compete with four other companies for the same customer.

Paid channels bring calls this week and stop with the budget. SEO brings requests that come to you alone, with no fee per lead, but it needs months. A common mix is ads for the summer peak while route pages and the map profile grow. My part is search and AI answers, and the pages I build are the same pages your ads can land on.
Seasonality in SEO for moving companies: summer peak and slow months

Most household moves in the US happen between May and September, with spikes at the end of each month and around school calendars; college towns add move-in and move-out weeks. Searches follow the same curve, and new pages take weeks or months to rank, so the work runs ahead of it: route pages and summer content are written in winter, review requests are pushed hardest in summer, and the off-season goes to commercial moving and storage, which sell all year.
Storage, packing and commercial moving pages for the whole year

Storage is searched on its own — “moving and storage near me”, “storage in transit” — and a warehouse with vaults or containers deserves a page with sizes, access hours and how pricing works. Office and commercial moves keep crews busy when residential demand drops, and they are decided by managers who read about insurance certificates, after-hours scheduling and how equipment is labeled and set up again.
The moving company website: what the site needs for SEO and quote requests

Rankings bring visitors; the website decides whether they ask for a quote. Typical problems: a quote widget that breaks on a phone, stock photos of smiling movers, no price logic anywhere, and the USDOT number hidden in an image. A moving site that works is fast on a phone, shows your own trucks and people, has a short quote form near the top, and keeps one page for each move type and main route.

People now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews “how much does it cost to move a three-bedroom house across the country”, “how do I check a mover’s USDOT number” or “which movers in Denver are reliable”. The assistant answers with figures and a few company names. Getting into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). price logic and typical ranges written on your pages, so the assistant can cite you instead of a national cost guide
registration, insurance, years in business, fleet and service area in plain sentences

the same details and steady reviews on Google, Yelp and the BBB, which assistants cross-check

I do nonprofit SEO myself, as one consultant who also builds websites, so the person who finds the problems on your site is the person who fixes them.
What nonprofit SEO includes: searches for help, volunteering and giving
A nonprofit has three kinds of searchers, and each types something different:
people who need help: “free tax help for seniors Denver”, “food pantry open Saturday”, “shelter for women near me”
volunteers: “volunteer with animals on weekends”, “volunteer opportunities near me for teens”
donors: “donate to wildfire relief”, “where to donate a used car to charity”, “charities fighting childhood hunger”

Nonprofit SEO covers pages for each group, the technical health of the site, a Google Business Profile where you have a location, earned links, visibility in ChatGPT and AI Overviews, and reports in sign-ups and donations.
SEO keywords for nonprofits: how people search around a cause

Few people search for the name of an organization they have not heard of. They search for the problem, the action or the place. Research starts with your staff — the questions callers ask, the words families use, what new volunteers wanted to know — and then checks those phrases in search data:
problem searches, often urgent and local, which show where a program page is missing
“near me” and city searches for services, drop-off points and volunteering
giving searches around a cause, a disaster or a season such as Giving Tuesday and the year-end
questions about the issue itself, which a short guide from your experts can answer
A phrase with ten searches a month matters if the person typing it is someone you exist to serve.
Program and location pages in SEO for nonprofits

A single “What we do” page cannot rank for six programs in three neighborhoods. Each program gets its own page — who it serves, eligibility, how to apply or refer someone, hours and the address — and each location with walk-in services gets a page with directions, transit, the phone number and what to bring. Pages use the words clients use, “help paying rent” rather than “housing stabilization services”, with the formal program name below for funders. Where a community you serve searches in Spanish or another language, translated versions of the key program pages often bring more people than another English article.
Donation page SEO and volunteer page SEO

Donation and volunteer pages can rank on their own when they say more than a form does. A donation page on your own domain, with a paragraph on what gifts fund, your EIN and a few short answers, can appear for “donate to [cause] in [city]”; a page hosted only on a platform’s domain builds that platform’s visibility, not yours. A volunteer page that lists roles, time commitment, minimum age and the city can appear for “volunteer opportunities near me”. Listing the same roles on VolunteerMatch or Idealist brings more volunteers and a link back to your site.
Google Ad Grants and nonprofit SEO: why the grant needs a strong website

Google Ad Grants gives eligible nonprofits up to $10,000 a month in Google search ads. It complements SEO rather than replacing it: ads can appear for searches where you do not rank yet, while SEO covers the searches the grant’s rules make hard to win. Both depend on the same thing — landing pages that answer the search and lead to an action. The program expects a website with substantial content about your mission and working conversion tracking; check Google’s current Ad Grants policies.

I do not run ads or manage Ad Grants accounts. I build and improve the pages the ads land on and set up the conversion tracking that both the grant account and the SEO report use, so whoever manages the account works from clean data.
Google Business Profile for nonprofits with a physical location

If people come to you — a food bank, a clinic, a thrift store, a community center — a Google Business Profile puts you on the map and in “near me” results. Google’s guidelines allow a profile where staff meet people in person during stated hours, so a nonprofit run from a board member’s home usually should not create one; check the current guidelines. The profile needs the most specific category that fits, such as “Food bank”, hours that change with the season, real photos, your programs as services and a link to the matching program page rather than the home page. Reviews from volunteers and clients, answered by staff, help as they do for any local organization.
Earned links for nonprofits: partners, local media, .gov and .edu resources
Nonprofits earn links more easily than most businesses, because others want to send people to them:
partner organizations, funders and corporate volunteer programs listing you on their sites
local news coverage of events and reports, linking to the source page
city, county, library and school resource pages — .gov and .edu sites that rarely link to companies
community foundation directories, United Way listings and coalition member pages
Each existing mention is worth a polite request to link to the specific program page. Paid link packages are not part of my work; a nonprofit’s reputation is worth more than a ranking shortcut.
Impact reports and stories as nonprofit SEO content

Annual and impact reports usually sit in a PDF nobody finds. Turned into web pages — a summary page per year, a page per program outcome, client and volunteer stories used with consent — they answer searches about the issue, give journalists and partners something to cite and give assistants facts to quote. The PDF stays for the board; the text lives on the site, with a date and an author.

Donors ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews “which charities help refugees in Chicago” or “how can I volunteer with seniors on weekends”, and get a short list before any links. Getting onto that list is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a nonprofit it means:
mission, programs, service area, eligibility and ways to give written as plain sentences
the same name, EIN and address on your site, your Candid profile, Charity Navigator and volunteer platforms
impact figures with a year and a source, which assistants can cite
Organization structured data connecting the site with those profiles

page.

Nonprofit sites are often built by volunteers and grown over years, and the same problems repeat: an old WordPress theme with a dozen plugins, event pages from past years competing with current ones, a Donate button that leads to a platform page search engines never see, reports only as large PDFs, and pages that take five seconds to load on a phone. The report counts what the organization needs, by page and by month:

Positions and visits are in the report as context. Where a donation platform hides the final step, the report says what can and cannot be counted rather than guessing.

children.text: SEO for orthodontists is the work that puts an orthodontic practice in front of parents looking for braces for a child, adults weighing clear aligners and families a general dentist has just referred: treatment pages, cost and financing pages, a Google Business Profile for each office and the facts AI assistants repeat. I do every step myself, from the first audit to the code changes, because I am a single consultant who also builds websites. Results are counted in consultation requests and new starts, not in rankings.
How SEO for orthodontists differs from dentist SEO
Search results for orthodontic practices and for general dentists barely overlap, and the reason is the patient’s path:
the person searching is often not the patient: a parent researches treatment for a nine- or thirteen-year-old, and the decision is made at home, together
treatment runs for one to three years and is a large planned expense, so families read and compare for weeks before they book
many new patients arrive with a referral from their dentist and check the orthodontist online before calling
adults compare aligners with braces and care about discretion as much as about the result
A dental office sells many short visits; an orthodontic practice sells one long treatment. SEO for orthodontists is built around that one decision. General dental practices have their own page on
dentist SEO
Orthodontic keywords: what parents, teens and adults type into Google
“Orthodontist” on its own has huge volume, but most of it is people looking up a practice they already know. The searches that lead to new starts are more specific:
children: “braces for kids [city]”, “when should a child see an orthodontist”, “palate expander”, “early orthodontic treatment”
teens: “Invisalign for teens”, “braces colors”, “aligners or braces for a teenager”
adults: “adult braces”, “clear aligners [city]”, “ceramic braces”, “lingual braces”
cost: “how much are braces”, “Invisalign cost [city]”, “braces payment plan”, “does insurance cover braces”
after treatment: “lost retainer”, “retainer replacement”, “teeth moving after braces”

Before anything is written I pull real volumes for your towns and give each phrase to one page. Headings use the words families use — “expander”, not the full appliance name — and the clinical term appears once in the text.
Pages for parents in orthodontist SEO: braces for kids and teens

Parents are the largest audience of most orthodontic websites and the most careful readers. They want to know when to come — orthodontic associations commonly suggest a first check around age seven — whether early treatment is needed or can wait, what the first visit costs, how long appointments last and whether they clash with school. A page for each of these questions ranks for what parents search and answers what your front desk hears every day.

Write for the parent and show the doctor: who sees young children, how a first visit with a child goes, and what happens when treatment is not needed yet and the child comes back for observation. Teen pages can address the teen too: eating with braces, mouth guards for sports, wearing aligners at school.
Adult orthodontics and clear aligner pages: Invisalign, ceramic and lingual braces

Adults often start with a brand — “Invisalign near me” — and then compare: aligners or braces, how visible, how long, how many visits, what it costs. One page for adult treatment, one for clear aligners and a short, plain comparison of the options cover most of that research. Adults also ask about treatment combined with other dental work, so the page explains how you coordinate with their dentist.

If an aligner brand lists you in its provider locator, the listing should point to your aligner page, not the home page, and the page should describe your provider status exactly as the brand permits. Patients arriving from a locator compare three or four nearby names; the page wins them with the orthodontist’s name, the steps at your office and the cost range.
Treatment cost and financing pages for orthodontic practices

“How much are braces” is one of the most searched questions in orthodontics, and many practice sites answer it with “every smile is unique”. Families then find a number on a competitor’s site or a forum. A cost page that ranks and helps includes:
a typical range for each type of treatment, and what it covers: records, appliances, adjustment visits, retainers
how orthodontic insurance benefits usually work, such as a lifetime maximum, and that your team checks the patient’s plan
in-house payment plans: down payment, monthly amount, interest-free options if you have them, and HSA or FSA use
what the first consultation includes and whether there is a fee

Free consultations are common in US orthodontics. The wording around them is where practices get into trouble: state dental boards and consumer protection rules limit advertising claims, and some countries restrict “free” offers in healthcare entirely. Check with your board before publishing; I keep the conditions next to the offer, not in a footnote.
Referral pages for general dentists in SEO for orthodontists

Referrals are a search channel too. A family leaves the dentist with your name and types it into Google that evening; a dentist checks your site before adding you to their referral list. Two pages serve them:
for referred patients: what to bring, what happens at the first visit and how you report back to their dentist
for referring dentists: the orthodontist’s training, what you treat and what you send back, how to send records and whom to call

A referral that carries X-rays, photos or patient details needs a secure route. In the US, HIPAA points to a referral service bound to you by a business associate agreement, not a web form that mails attachments around. That is the general picture; your compliance adviser signs off on the actual setup.
Local SEO for orthodontists with multiple offices

Many orthodontic practices run two or more offices, and some are open only on certain days. Each office needs its own Google Business Profile with the Orthodontist category, its real days and hours, photos of that office and a link to its own page on the site. The office page names the orthodontists who treat there and on which days, parking, and the towns and schools families come from.

Satellite offices open one or two days a week lose most map positions: hours that read “closed” most of the week, no photos, no reviews. Accurate hours, regular photos and a review routine for each office fix most of it. Maps work is described in more detail on the
local SEO services
page.
Patient and parent reviews for orthodontic practices

Orthodontic reviews have natural moments: the day the braces come off, the last aligner, the first retainer check. A short message with a direct link at those moments, sent to every patient or parent, builds a steady flow. Two habits common in orthodontics break the rules: contests and prizes for teens in exchange for reviews, which Google forbids and which can run against the FTC’s endorsement rules, and asking only the happy families.
Many reviewers are minors or write about their child. Replies stay general and never confirm that someone is a patient or mention treatment details, even when the review itself does.
YMYL and orthodontist credentials: authorship and before-and-after photos

Google holds orthodontic pages to the standard of health information. The site should show what sets an orthodontist apart from a general dentist offering aligners: the specialty residency, the university, board certification where the doctor holds it, memberships — stated exactly, without suggesting a title the doctor does not have. Each treatment page names the orthodontist who reviewed it and the date.

Before-and-after photos persuade more than any text and are the most sensitive content on the site. Publish them only with signed permission, which for a minor comes from the parent, with matching angles and lighting, no editing, and the treatment type and length stated. No page promises a result or a fixed treatment time.
Technical SEO for orthodontic websites: speed, structured data and booking
The technical problems I find on orthodontic sites repeat:
smile galleries and autoplay clips that hold back the main text beyond 2.5 seconds on a phone
a vendor template whose text appears on hundreds of other orthodontic sites
one “Treatments” page for braces, aligners and expanders together
no structured data linking the practice, each office and each orthodontist
a consultation request hidden three screens deep
When the problems are deeper than a list of fixes,
orthodontist website design

SEO for orthodontists in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Parents ask ChatGPT what age a child should see an orthodontist, then which orthodontist in their town offers payment plans. Adults ask whether aligners suit them and who nearby offers both options. Earning a place in those replies is called GEO or AEO — generative or answer engine optimization. In orthodontics it comes down to:
treatments, ages treated, offices, days open, languages and payment options written as plain facts
cost ranges and what they include, in sentences an assistant can quote
identical names, addresses and hours on your site, Google, the aligner locator and dental directories

What SEO for painting contractors covers: interior, exterior and commercial work
A painting company usually sells several different jobs, and each has its own customers and searches:
interior painting — rooms, ceilings, trim, whole-house repaints before a sale or after a move
exterior painting — siding, stucco, brick, decks and fences, with weather and prep as the main questions

commercial painting — offices, retail units, apartment buildings, HOA communities
SEO for painting contractors gives each of these a page of its own, with photos, the steps of the job and the questions customers ask. One “Painting Services” page cannot rank for all of them.
How homeowners and property managers search for a painting contractor

Before writing pages I pull the search data for your services and towns. Homeowners search for the job and the place — “interior painters near me”, “exterior house painting”, “kitchen cabinet painting” — and for the price: “cost to paint a house exterior”, “how much to paint a room”. Property managers search differently: “commercial painting contractor”, “apartment painting services”, “HOA painting”. Interior painting pages

Interior customers worry about the house: furniture, floors, dust, how long the rooms are out of use, smell. The page answers that — how you prepare, which paints you use, low-VOC options, how many days a typical job takes.
Exterior painting pages

Exterior buyers ask about prep and lifespan: power washing, scraping, wood repair, caulking, primer, how long the paint will last in your climate, and what happens if it rains. Pages that explain the prep show why your price is higher than the cheapest quote.
Cabinet painting pages

Cabinet painting is a separate decision: refinish or replace. A page that compares the two, shows kitchens before and after and explains spraying, drying and curing time often brings well-paid jobs that fill the winter.
Before-and-after photos as SEO content for painting contractors

the town or neighborhood, the room or surface, the paint and color used

file names and alt text that describe the job, compressed so the page loads in under 2.5 seconds on a phone
The same photos go to the Google Business Profile every week or two. A profile that keeps showing fresh finished jobs gets more clicks than one with three photos from years ago.
Estimate and color consultation pages for painting companies

Most painting jobs start with an on-site estimate, and many homeowners hesitate because they do not know what it involves. A clear estimate page lowers that barrier: what you measure, how long the visit takes, whether it is free, when the written quote arrives, what the quote includes. If you offer color consultations, give them a page too — people search for help choosing colors, and the consultation is often the first step to the job.
Seasonality in painting: planning SEO for exterior and interior work

Exterior painting depends on temperature and dry weather, so in most of the US, Canada and the UK the season is spring to early fall. Homeowners start searching for exterior painters weeks before, so exterior pages and fresh project photos need to be in place by late winter. In the colder months interior and cabinet pages carry the business; in warmer climates the exterior season is longer and the plan shifts with it.
Commercial painting SEO: HOAs, property managers and commercial painting leads

Commercial work is a different market: fewer, larger jobs, bids instead of quick estimates, and buyers who check insurance, safety records and capacity. Some painting companies buy commercial painting leads from lead sellers or bid boards; SEO works on a different part of that market, the managers who search for a contractor themselves. The pages they look for:
services for HOA communities, apartment complexes, offices and retail
insurance, license and safety information written out, not hidden in a PDF
work done after hours or in phases, so tenants and businesses keep running

Commercial buyers rarely call from the first result. They shortlist two or three contractors and compare them, often over weeks. A clear page with a direct contact for bids, a short capability statement and references by building type keeps you on that shortlist. Commercial and residential pages stay separate, so a property manager does not land on a page about painting a child’s bedroom.

What SEO for plastic surgeons covers, and how it differs from med spa SEO

Nobody books a facelift after one search. A patient reads for weeks, compares two or three surgeons, looks through hundreds of photos, checks credentials and asks about cost and time off work. SEO for a plastic surgery practice follows that research: your practice should appear at each step, and each page should answer the question the patient had when they arrived.

This is a different job from SEO for a med spa. Injectables, laser and body contouring are frequent, lower-cost visits, often chosen by distance and price; surgery is one large decision made on the surgeon. Procedure pages in SEO for plastic surgeons: one page per operation

Patients search by operation and often by detail: “deep plane facelift”, “breast lift without implants”, “revision rhinoplasty”, “mommy makeover cost Houston”. A single “Procedures” page does not rank for searches this specific. Each operation you want more cases of gets its own page, and the main ones get supporting pages for variants and common questions. A procedure page that ranks and leads to consultations usually covers:
who is a good candidate, and who should not have the operation
how it is performed, the type of anesthesia and where — office surgical suite, ambulatory surgery center or hospital

I pick procedures and variants from search data for your area, so the pages use the words patients type rather than surgical terms from the operating notes.
Board certification, surgeon credentials and E-E-A-T in plastic surgery SEO

Plastic surgery is a “Your Money or Your Life” topic for Google, and the surgeon is the strongest trust signal a practice has. Patients ask what credentials a plastic surgeon should have; search engines and assistants look for the same facts: medical school, residency, fellowship, hospital privileges and board certification.

Certification has to be stated exactly. In the US, “board-certified plastic surgeon” usually refers to the American Board of Plastic Surgery; a surgeon certified by another board names that board in full instead of writing “board-certified” alone. Some states regulate how certification may be advertised, so the wording is checked against your state medical board’s rules. Each procedure page names the surgeon who reviewed it, links to the bio and shows a review date.

The same clarity answers a frequent search — the difference between a plastic surgeon and a cosmetic surgeon. A page that explains your training in plain words, without attacking anyone, helps patients and gives assistants a fact they can quote.
Before-and-after galleries in plastic surgeon SEO: consent, captions and image search
Galleries are the most visited part of most plastic surgery sites and the least readable for search engines: hundreds of images with no text, loaded through a slow plugin. A gallery can do more work:
one gallery page per procedure, linked from the procedure page and back
each case with a text caption: procedure, technique, implant size where relevant, time after surgery, surgeon
compressed images with descriptive file names and alt text about the procedure, never about the person
faces and identifying marks cropped or covered unless the patient agreed otherwise

Every photo needs the patient’s written consent for marketing use, the same lighting, angle and background before and after, and no editing beyond cropping. In the US, using patient photos in marketing generally requires a signed HIPAA authorization; your compliance adviser confirms the form.

In big metros patients search by neighborhood and suburb; in smaller cities they often accept a drive of an hour or two for surgery. Location pages are made for real offices only, and procedure pages say where patients come from and how consultations work for them.
Plastic surgeon reviews on Google and RealSelf: what helps SEO and what breaks the rules

Reviews move the practice up the map and decide the patient’s shortlist. For surgery, Google and RealSelf carry the most weight, and patients read the long reviews about recovery and how the surgeon explained risks. A steady routine — a request with a direct link after the post-op visit — works better than occasional campaigns.

The limits are clear: no paying or rewarding patients for reviews, no reviews written by staff, and no hiding the negative ones, all of which the FTC rules on endorsements and reviews address. Replies never confirm that the reviewer is a patient or mention their procedure, even if the reviewer did. A short, polite reply with an invitation to call the office protects privacy and shows readers that the practice responds.
SEO for out-of-town and medical tourism patients: travel, recovery and virtual consultations

Many plastic surgery patients travel: from rural areas to the nearest city, across state lines for a specific surgeon, or from abroad. They search differently — “rhinoplasty surgeon Miami out of town patients”, “how long to stay after tummy tuck before flying” — and need a page that answers practical questions:

For international patients the page exists in their language, and questions about licensing and aftercare abroad are answered as facts.
Plastic surgery cost and financing pages that answer price searches

“How much is a breast augmentation”, “tummy tuck cost near me” and “facelift financing” are among the most searched plastic surgery questions, and practices that hide prices lose them to directories and price articles. A cost page per procedure gives a range, explains what moves the price — technique, anesthesia, facility fee, garments, follow-up visits — and says that the exact fee is set at consultation. A financing page lists the medical credit providers you accept, such as CareCredit, and how to apply. Prices stay in text, not inside an image.

Before opening a single site, many patients type into an assistant “which surgeon in Dallas specializes in revision rhinoplasty” or “what is recovery like after a deep plane facelift”. This work goes by two names, GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization). Assistants quote facts they can read and confirm in several places, so the work is:

Plumbing SEO for emergency searches: burst pipes, blocked drains and “plumber near me”
A large part of plumbing work starts with a search made in a hurry, often at night, on a phone, by someone standing in water. The searches are short and urgent:
“emergency plumber near me”, “24 hour plumber”
“burst pipe”, “water leak under sink”, “toilet overflowing”

A person in that situation calls one of the first businesses they see and rarely compares prices. These searches show the map and Local Services Ads first, so the website has a narrow job: one emergency page per problem that loads fast, says in the first line that you come out tonight, puts the phone number in a tap-to-call button and lists the areas you reach within the hour. Longer text goes lower on the page, where Google and the more careful customer read it.

Planned plumbing work is searched differently. The homeowner has days or weeks, compares two or three companies and reads. Each of these jobs needs its own page, because each has its own searches and its own questions.
Drain cleaning and hydro jetting pages
Searches range from “drain cleaning near me” to “hydro jetting cost”. The page explains when snaking is enough, when jetting or a camera inspection is needed, and what the visit costs.

Tank or tankless, gas or electric, repair or replace — customers search for all of them. The page covers sizing, typical lifespan, the permit and installation time, and names the brands you install.
Sewer line repair and replacement pages
Expensive, rare and frightening for the homeowner. Camera inspection, trenchless options, what the permit involves and how long the yard stays dug up are the questions a sewer page has to answer.
Repiping pages
Mostly searched by owners of older houses with galvanized or polybutylene pipes. The page explains the materials, how long the house is without water and how walls are opened and patched.

A pricing page, or a cost section on each service page, can show ranges, what moves the price — access, materials, an after-hours call-out — and whether the diagnostic fee is credited against the job. It does not need to publish your whole price book. A page that answers the cost question keeps the visitor on your site instead of sending them to a national cost guide, and it gives assistants a figure with your name next to it.
Commercial plumbing SEO: restaurants, property managers and facilities

Commercial customers use other words and decide differently. A restaurant owner searches for “grease trap cleaning” or “commercial drain service”; a property manager wants a company that covers several buildings, invoices properly and picks up at weekends; a facility manager looks for backflow testing and certification. Commercial pages name the building types you serve, the maintenance agreements you offer, your response time and insurance, and who to contact for a site visit. Questions like “why is my water heater making noise”, “is a slab leak an emergency” or “who is a reliable plumber in [town]” are now often answered by Google’s AI Overviews, ChatGPT or Perplexity before anyone clicks a link. Getting a plumbing company into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a plumber it means:
answers to the common “what is wrong with my pipes” questions on your own pages, written with trade knowledge
cost ranges and what changes them, in text an assistant can quote

A ranking report does not pay for a van. What SEO for real estate developers covers

A developer’s site is not a brochure with a contact form. It is a catalog that changes every week: units sell, prices move, a new phase launches, a completed building leaves the market. Search engines rank it like any large catalog, and buyers judge it like a sales office. The work covers five areas:
search demand for your cities and products, from “pre-construction condos Miami” to “new construction townhomes Raleigh”

Real estate developer marketing: where SEO sits next to brokers, portals and ads

A real estate developer marketing strategy usually leans on channels that stop when the money stops: paid portal placements, brokers on commission, launch campaigns. Search works on a different clock. Buyers of new homes research for a long time, and many of them type the development’s name, your company name or the neighborhood dozens of times before they sign a reservation. If those searches land on a portal or a broker’s copy of your listing, you pay for a buyer who was already looking for you.

SEO keeps those searches on your own site and adds the ones you would not reach otherwise. The sales office still needs its own Google Business Profile with hours and directions; that map work is described on the

Real estate developer keywords: location, property type, stage and budget
Buyers of new builds combine four things in one query, and the mix tells you where they are in the decision:

property type and size — condo, townhome, villa, “3 bedroom”, “with a yard”
stage — pre-construction, pre-sale, off-plan, move-in ready, a completion year
budget — “under $500k”, “starting from”, payment plan

Before writing anything I pull the search data for every city where you build and for each combination with enough demand. Your own development name and brand searches are checked too, because they show where portals already take your traffic.
Landing pages by city, property type and budget for new developments

A page for “new condos in Tampa under $400k” only works if it lists real developments that match and says something a buyer cannot get from a filter: how the areas differ, what completion dates look like, what fees to expect. Pages generated for every possible combination with nothing behind them are thin content, and Google treats them that way.
Development pages that rank: prices, floor plans, completion date and location
Most searches that end in a reservation land on a development page, so it carries the most weight. It should answer the questions a buyer would ask the sales agent, as text:
price range and price per square foot, with the date of the last update
unit types, sizes and floor plans, each plan as a separate image with a text label
construction stage, expected completion and what is already built, with dated photos
location facts: distances to the beach, center, schools, airport or highway
fees, deposits and payment schedule in plain terms

Write it as facts, not mood. The Cyprus platform described below learned this the hard way: someone once replaced its project texts with lifestyle prose, and traffic to the commercial pages fell. Once the facts — price, area, location — were back, clicks recovered by 16%.
Unit availability and prices from a feed: keeping a developer catalog current

A price list that is three months old costs more than it earns: buyers call about units that are gone, and assistants quote the wrong numbers. The fix is a single source of truth. Most developers already keep prices and availability in a spreadsheet, a CRM or a sales system; that data can feed the website automatically, daily or more often, so each unit shows its current status without anyone editing pages by hand.

a sold unit stays on its page marked as sold, linking to similar units still available

Completed projects are your track record. Buyers and AI assistants both use them to decide whether a developer finishes what it starts.

Where a developer wins is narrower and closer to a sale: the development’s own name, the neighborhood plus “new construction”, the specific unit type, the questions about your construction quality and payment terms.

Keep your listings on portals — they are a source of leads and citations — but make your site the version with more detail: full floor plans, live availability, construction updates. Then a buyer who sees you on a portal and searches your name finds you, not another copy.

Resort and second-home developments sell to buyers from other countries, and each of them searches in their own language with their own words. A German buyer does not type a translation of the English query; the phrasing, the units of measure and the questions about taxes and financing are different. filter combinations that have search demand become real landing pages; the rest are not indexed

Bought links are the fastest way to a manual penalty and the slowest way to trust. children.text: SEO for realtors is the work that makes a real estate agent show up when people in your market search for your name, your neighborhoods or how to sell their home, and turns those visits into buyer and seller conversations in your CRM. What SEO for real estate agents covers: your name, your neighborhoods and seller leads

Most of an agent’s business comes from people who already know them or were referred, and most of those people still type the agent’s name into Google before they call. The rest search for a place or a decision: “realtor in Brookside Kansas City”, “best time to sell a house in Raleigh”, “condos near Lake Merritt”. Real estate agent SEO works on the four places where those searches end:
your own website: bio page, neighborhood pages, market reports, valuation and contact forms
your Google Business Profile and the map results for “realtor near me”
your profiles and reviews on Zillow, Realtor.com and your brokerage’s site
answers in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
This page is for individual agents and teams. Brokerages that run a full listings catalog and developers selling a project have different problems, described on the

and

Realtor name searches: personal brand SEO for an agent

When a past client recommends you, their friend searches your name. If the first results are an old brokerage profile with a dead phone number, a Zillow page with three reviews and someone else with the same name, part of that referral is lost. Name searches are the first thing I fix for an agent, because they are one step from a signed listing agreement:
a bio page on your own domain, titled with your full name, “Realtor”, your brokerage and your main area
a current headshot, years in the business, designations such as ABR or CRS if you hold them, languages spoken and the neighborhoods you work
Person structured data linking the bio to your Google Business Profile, Zillow and Realtor.com profiles and social accounts
the same name, phone and brokerage everywhere, including the brokerage’s agent roster
Agents who change brokerages lose the most here. Owning your domain keeps name searches pointing to you, whichever brokerage holds your license.
Neighborhood pages for real estate agents: community SEO for buyers and sellers

A neighborhood page is the main landing page in SEO for realtors. Broad “homes for sale” searches go to the big listing sites; what an agent wins is the local knowledge behind searches like “living in Brookside” or “Highland Park vs Lakeview”. A page that ranks answers what a buyer or a relocating family wants to know:
where the neighborhood starts and ends, the streets and subdivisions inside it, and a map
the housing: ages and styles of homes, typical lot sizes, condo buildings, HOA fees in general terms
commute times, parks, shops, transit, and a link to the official school district site
your own photos and a short walk-through video
a link to current listings in the area and to your market report for it
How many neighborhood pages a realtor needs

Start with the areas where you already have sales and can write from experience — usually five to ten. A hundred pages copied from one template and filled with census figures is what Google’s spam policies call scaled content abuse, and buyers notice it too.
Hyperlocal market reports: monthly neighborhood updates in real estate SEO

Homeowners search “home values in [neighborhood]” and “is it a good time to sell in [city]” months before they call an agent. A short monthly or quarterly report per area answers that: median sale price, days on market, months of inventory, price per square foot, and a few sentences on what you saw at showings and offers. The numbers come from your MLS; check its rules on publishing statistics and attribution before the first report goes out.

Each report links to its neighborhood page and to your valuation form. The page keeps one address while each new month replaces the old figures, so links and rankings build up; the same report goes to your sphere by email.
IDX and MLS listings on a realtor website: what helps SEO and what does not

An IDX feed shows MLS listings on your site, and most agent platforms — Luxury Presence, Real Geeks, Placester, or an iHomefinder plugin on WordPress — include one. Whether those pages help you in search depends on how they are built:
listings loaded in an iframe or on the vendor’s subdomain count for the vendor, not for your domain
the same listing descriptions appear on every IDX site in the MLS, so single listing pages rarely rank on their own
listing searches embedded in your neighborhood pages, under your own text, do help those pages
saved searches and listing alerts are worth keeping, because they turn a browsing buyer into a contact
I check what your IDX setup actually shows to Google and work around it. If the platform blocks basic changes such as page titles or addresses, the options are on the

page.

Google allows individual practitioners, real estate agents included, to have their own Business Profile, separate from the brokerage’s. An agent who meets clients at properties rather than at an office sets it up as a service-area business with the address hidden. What matters:
the primary category “Real estate agent”, the areas you serve, and a link to your bio or main neighborhood page
a name that matches real life — your name, or your name and brokerage — with no keywords added
a review request after every closing and a reply to each review that gives away nothing private about the deal
Zillow and Realtor.com profiles kept current, with sales history and reviews, because buyers and AI assistants read them too
Map results, categories and review work in more depth are on the

page.
Fair Housing and brokerage advertising rules in real estate agent SEO
Neighborhood pages and market reports are advertising, and in the US they fall under fair housing law and your state’s license law. In general terms:
describe the property and the place — square footage, parks, commute, schools by name — not the people who live there or who would “fit in”
phrases about who an area is “perfect for” are where most problems start
link to official school and crime data instead of rating schools or calling an area “safe”
display the brokerage name the way your state requires; many agents also add their license number and the Equal Housing Opportunity mark

Many states and brokerages also have rules on team names and on how prominent the brokerage name must be next to yours. Check with your managing broker or your state’s real estate commission; I write within the rules you give me, and nothing here is legal advice.
Lead capture on a realtor website: home valuation, saved searches and your CRM
SEO pays only when a visit becomes a conversation you can follow up. On an agent’s site that means a few clear paths:
a home valuation page for each main area, offering a comparative market analysis from you rather than an automated number
saved-search and listing-alert sign-up for buyers who are months away
call and text buttons on every mobile page
every form sent straight to your CRM — Follow Up Boss, kvCORE, Lofty or the one your brokerage provides — with the page it came from
Then the report shows valuation requests, buyer registrations and calls from search by neighborhood, with rankings next to them, not instead of them.

Buyers and sellers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews questions like “who are good listing agents in Naperville”, “what is it like to live in East Nashville” or “how do I choose a realtor for a first home”. your areas, specialties — first-time buyers, relocation, luxury, condos — brokerage and languages written as plain sentences on your bio

Paid leads — Google Ads, Zillow Premier Agent, social ads — start the day you pay and stop the day you stop.
