children.text: SEO for recruitment agencies is the work that brings two kinds of people to your site from Google and AI assistants: employers looking for an agency to fill a role, and candidates looking for that role. I do it myself, as an independent SEO consultant and web developer, for recruitment agencies, executive search firms and staffing companies, so the person who reads your search data is the one who writes the sector pages and fixes the job markup.
What SEO for recruitment agencies covers: candidate searches and employer searches

A recruitment agency is searched for from both sides of the hire. Candidates type “accounting jobs in Denver”, “remote Java developer jobs” or “staffing agencies hiring near me”. Employers type “IT recruitment agency Chicago”, “executive search firm for healthcare” or “temp agency for warehouse staff”. The two groups use different words, land on different pages and are worth different amounts to you:
the candidate side: job pages, Google for Jobs, permanent job category pages and advice for job seekers
the employer side: sector and city pages, recruiter profiles, salary guides and placement stories
the map: a Google Business Profile for each office, with reviews from candidates and clients
answers in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews

Candidates bring volume; employers bring the fees. On many agency sites the job board gets all the attention and the employer gets one “Hire talent” page. I usually start on the employer side and keep the candidate side technically clean.
Employer-side recruitment agency SEO: sector and city pages for hiring managers

A hiring manager with an open role looks for a specialist: “accounting and finance recruiters Dallas”, “construction recruitment agency Phoenix”, “cybersecurity headhunters”. A page that ranks for such a search answers what that person wants to know before picking up the phone:
the roles you fill in that sector and the seniority levels you cover
salary ranges and typical time to fill, taken from your own placements
how you work — contingent, retained or contract — and what the fee depends on, in general terms
the recruiter who runs the desk, with a photo and a direct line
short placement stories, with the client’s permission or without names
How many sector and city pages a recruitment agency needs

One for each pair you can back with a real desk and real placements. An accounting team covering Dallas and Houston means two pages. Fifty city pages that differ only in the city name fall under Google’s rules on doorway pages and get filtered, and they tell a hiring manager that nobody local wrote them. Start with the sectors that bring the highest fees and add a city once you have a recruiter and placements there.
Google for Jobs and JobPosting structured data on recruitment agency job pages

For many job searches Google shows its own jobs block above the regular results. A listing gets into it through JobPosting structured data on the job page, and agencies lose this traffic mostly through small errors in that data:
the title is a real job title, without “URGENT”, reference codes or pay in it
datePosted and validThrough come from your ATS, so closing dates are true
baseSalary carries a real range and unit — hourly for temp roles, yearly for permanent ones
jobLocation has a full address, and remote roles are marked as such, with the states or countries candidates may work from
hiringOrganization is filled the same way on every job, confidential searches included

Job pages usually come from an ATS plugin or a feed, so I check what Google receives in the Search Console job posting report and fix the template once. Google’s Indexing API, accepted for job pages, then reports new and removed jobs without waiting for a crawl.
Expired job postings: what to do with vacancy URLs after a role is filled

Every closed job leaves a URL behind. Left alone, those pages still say “Apply now” for a role filled in March, still carry markup and send candidates to a dead end. I set up one rule for the whole site:
the JobPosting markup goes, or validThrough moves into the past, the day the role closes
the page either returns 404 or 410, or stays live with “this position has been filled” and links to similar open roles
the URL leaves the sitemap and the Indexing API gets a removal notice
roles you hire for again and again — forklift operators in Columbus, registered nurses in Tampa — get a permanent category page that lists current openings and keeps its links between hires
Indeed, LinkedIn and Glassdoor in recruitment agency SEO: competitors and distribution

For broad searches like “jobs in Houston” or “marketing jobs”, Indeed, LinkedIn, Glassdoor and ZipRecruiter will stay above any agency site. An agency wins where it knows more than a board — a narrow specialism, a city, a type of contract — and in every search an employer makes. Boards remain a distribution channel, and the two work together when:
a job goes live on your site first, with fuller text than the board version
your LinkedIn company page and Glassdoor profile carry the same sectors, offices and details as the site, because candidates and AI assistants read them when they check you
reviews on Glassdoor and Indeed get the same calm answers as reviews on Google
Local SEO for recruitment agencies: a Google Business Profile for each office

Searches such as “staffing agency near me” or “recruitment agency in Columbus” are answered by the map, and they come both from candidates who want to walk in and from local employers. Each staffed office gets its own profile:
the primary category that matches the office — Employment agency, Temp agency, Executive search firm or Recruiter
the office’s own page on the site as the profile link, with its sectors and its team
hours for walk-in registration where you offer it
reviews requested from placed candidates and from clients, each answered without personal details
Categories, listings and review work in more depth are on the
local SEO services
page.
Recruiter profile pages: SEO for recruiters and the expertise behind the agency

Clients hire a recruiter, not a logo. A profile page for each consultant ranks for that person’s name and shows Google and AI assistants the experience behind your content — what Google calls E-E-A-T. Each profile carries:
the sectors, seniority levels and locations the recruiter covers, and years in the field
a LinkedIn link and Person structured data that ties the two together
articles and salary commentary signed with their name
a plan for when someone leaves: the page is redirected to the desk or sector page, never simply deleted
Salary guides and hiring market reports built on your own placement data

A salary guide is the content that earns links for a recruitment agency: HR blogs, local business press and job seekers cite it, and AI assistants quote it when someone asks what a role pays in a city. It works only when the numbers are yours — accepted offers, agreed rates, time to hire — with the method, the number of placements behind each figure and the period stated next to the table. Where the sample for a role is too small, the role is left out. Each guide keeps one permanent page, refreshed every year or quarter, with a one-sentence summary on top that a journalist or an assistant can repeat.
Staffing agency SEO: temp, light industrial and healthcare staffing
US staffing firms are searched for differently from permanent recruiters. Volume roles, many branches and shift work change the job:

candidate searches carry pay and urgency — “warehouse jobs hiring immediately”, “weekly pay jobs near me”, “night shift CNA jobs” — so pay rate, shift and start date go into the first lines of the job page and into the markup
branch pages matter more than sector pages: one per branch, with its open roles, hours and directions
employer pages answer “light industrial staffing [city]”, “temp to hire agency” or “healthcare staffing agency” with service levels, onboarding and safety written as text
in healthcare staffing, license and credential requirements are described per role and state in general terms and checked by your compliance team
Recruitment agency SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Hiring managers now ask ChatGPT or Perplexity “which recruitment agencies in Boston specialize in biotech” or “retained or contingent search for a CFO”, and candidates ask “are staffing agencies worth it for nurses in Texas”. The assistant names a few agencies and gives its reasons. Getting into those lists is what generative engine optimization (GEO), also called answer engine optimization (AEO), is about. For a recruitment agency it involves:
sectors, cities, fee models and the roles you fill written as plain sentences on sector and office pages
recruiter profiles and salary guides with named authors and dates
the same agency details on the site, Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, Glassdoor and industry directories
Organization, EmploymentAgency and Person structured data linked to one another
Before the work and a few months into it, I record which agencies the assistants name for your sectors and cities. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Measuring recruitment agency SEO in client inquiries and applications

A report that mixes both audiences hides the result, so in GA4 each conversion is labeled by audience: applications and CV uploads by job, sector and office on one side; client inquiries, “submit a vacancy” forms and calls to the business line on the other. If your ATS or recruitment CRM records the source, we follow clients who found you through search on to jobs registered and placements made. Rankings sit next to these numbers as a means, not as the result. First results usually show after about a month and a half, and steady growth takes three to six months.

Recruitment agency SEO audit — employer pages, job markup, expired vacancies, office profiles, competitors and AI answers: from 250 €, one-off.
One-off work — sector and city pages, JobPosting template fixes, recruiter profiles, a salary guide page, tracking by audience: 250–700 €.

children.text: I do SEO for solar companies: the work that puts an installer in front of homeowners and business owners while they research panels, batteries and incentives, and again when they compare who should do the install. Buyers spend weeks or months on cost, payback, roof suitability, financing and trust, and each step starts with a search; when your pages answer them, the buyer reaches your quote form already knowing your name. I work alone: the audit, the new pages and the code changes are mine, with no account manager passing messages.
Solar SEO keywords: how homeowners and businesses search before buying solar panels
Solar searches follow the buying process, and the research shows which stage your site is missing:
research and cost — “solar panel cost [state]”, “is solar worth it in Ohio”, “how long do solar panels take to pay off”
the installer — “solar installers near me”, “solar company [town]”, “best solar company in [city]”
products and jobs — “solar battery storage installation”, “commercial solar installer”, “solar panel repair near me”
checks — “[company] reviews”, “is [company] legit”, “solar complaints [state]”

Before any page is written I pull the volumes for your states and towns and look at who holds the first page now: other installers, national solar brands, quote marketplaces and lead sites dressed up as neutral guides. A ready-made list of “SEO keywords for solar” helps little: the same phrase needs a different answer in Arizona than in New Jersey, because rates, rules and roofs differ.
Solar service pages: residential solar, commercial solar, battery storage and EV chargers
One “Solar” page cannot rank for everything an installer sells. Each line of work has its own buyer and its own questions, so each gets a page:
residential solar — roof and ground mounts, the steps from site survey to permission to operate, what moves the price
commercial solar — rooftop, carport and ground arrays for an owner or finance manager who wants production and payback in writing
battery storage and backup power — whole-home or partial backup, or a battery added to an existing system
EV chargers, panel cleaning, repairs, monitoring faults, and removal and reinstall for a new roof
Service pages are often forgotten, yet owners whose installer has closed search for exactly this and later buy batteries. If solar is one part of a wider business, the neighboring pages go deeper:
roofing SEO
for re-roof work,

for heat pumps,

for panel upgrades, and

Local SEO for solar companies: service-area pages by town and utility

Solar installers travel to the customer, so Google treats them as service-area businesses: the Business Profile shows the area you cover, not a showroom address. Buyers rarely pick an installer straight from the map, but they open the profile to read the reviews before filling in a form.

For area pages, solar has a detail most trades lack: the utility. Two neighboring towns served by different utilities can have different rates, interconnection steps and export credit rules, and that is what buyers ask about. An area page earns its place when it has:
installs you have done there, with photos and system sizes
the utility, and how its interconnection and approval work in general terms, with a link to the utility’s own pages
permit and HOA notes from jobs in that town
reviews from customers who live there
A town with nothing to show stays on the general list until you install there. The profile side — categories, service area, photos, review requests — is covered on the
local SEO services
page.
Solar incentive, tax credit and net metering pages that stay accurate

Incentives drive more solar searches than any other topic: “solar tax credit”, “solar rebates [state]”, “net metering [utility]”. They are also the part of a solar site that ages fastest: federal credits, state rebates and utility export rules change, sometimes at short notice, and people keep searching for a program long after it has changed or ended. A page that gives the current status in plain words wins that search; a page still promising last year’s credit loses the visitor’s trust in everything else you wrote.
So incentive content lives on a few permanent pages, not in a new blog post every year:
one page per program or rule, updated in place, with a “last checked” date at the top
links to the official source — the tax authority, the state energy office, the utility tariff
who qualifies, in general terms: buying with cash, a loan, a lease or a PPA is treated differently
no incentive folded into a headline price, and no “free solar” wording anywhere
Solar savings calculator and payback estimates with stated assumptions
“How much will solar save me” sits behind most solar searches, and a calculator answers it on your site instead of a marketplace’s. It helps search and sales only when the method is visible:
inputs the visitor knows — monthly bill, ZIP code or utility, roof direction and shade
assumptions written next to the result: electricity price and how it may change, panel output loss over the years, which incentive status was used
a range rather than one exact figure, with a line saying the site survey sets the real numbers
the method explained in text on the page, because Google and AI assistants read words, not a script
The result leads to the quote form with the inputs filled in, so the first call starts from the buyer’s numbers.
Solar install case pages: system size, panels, inverter and roof type
Buyers want to see a system like the one they are weighing, on a house like theirs. A case page per install answers that and supports a town page and a product page:
the roof — tile, shingle, metal or flat, orientation, shade
system size in kW, panel model and count, inverter type, battery if any
the time from signed contract to permission to operate
production from the monitoring app and bill changes, only when the owner agrees to share them
Each case goes live only with the customer’s consent, without the street address. Stock photos prove nothing; one documented install a few streets away does.
Trust signals in solar company SEO: licenses, warranties, reviews and no-pressure selling

Every installer inherits the industry’s reputation for pushy door-to-door sales and companies that vanished after the install. Buyers search with that in mind — “is [company] legit”, “[company] complaints”, “solar scams [state]” — so the results for your name are part of your sales process. What helps:
license numbers, insurance and certifications written as text, with where to verify them
warranties set out one by one: panel and inverter product warranties, the production warranty and your own workmanship warranty
a review request once the system is switched on, and factual replies to bad reviews
sales pages that show how a quote is prepared, with no countdown offers or pressure to sign at the first meeting
How to advertise for solar: marketing companies, shared leads and owned search

“How to advertise for solar” has many answers: door-to-door teams, paid social, Google Ads, events, appointment setting and lead lists, and solar marketing companies usually sell a mix of them. Shared leads are the most common. A homeowner fills in one “see if your roof qualifies” form and gets calls from several installers within minutes, so you open the conversation as one more voice they are trying to get off the phone.

Search works the other way round: someone who read your battery page and then checked your reviews has chosen to contact you. Many installers keep buying leads while search grows and compare what a signed contract costs in each channel. My part is search: the site, the profile and AI answers. How monthly work runs is on the

page.

Many solar sites are a single landing page made for paid traffic, with nothing for search to read, or a template that crawls on a phone. When SEO needs pages the site cannot hold, the site is rebuilt first. A solar website that works for search has:

A site like this costs 700–1,400 €, and a full site with a case library and a calculator starts from 2,000 €; design is included in both. How I build them is on the

Every form and call carries its source page into your CRM, so you see which product pages, towns and cases bring requests and, where the CRM records it, which became signed contracts. children.text: I provide SEO for startups — early-stage SaaS and tech products — as one consultant who also builds websites in Next.js and React. The goal is not a traffic chart for the next investor update. It is buyers finding your product when they search for the problem it solves, compare tools or ask an AI assistant for a shortlist, and then starting a trial or booking a demo.
When SEO for startups makes sense, and when it can wait
SEO is slow. A new domain usually needs months before its pages rank for anything competitive, and a founder with twelve months of runway should know that before spending on it. A fair rule of thumb:

SEO makes sense when people already search for the problem you solve or the category you are in — “invoicing software for freelancers”, “open-source feature flags” — even if they have never heard of you
it makes sense when there is a signup, a trial or a demo request, so a visit can turn into something you can count
it can wait when the category is new and nobody searches for it yet; founder-led sales, communities and launch platforms bring the first users faster
it can wait while the positioning still changes every month, because pages written for last month’s audience will need rewriting

Even when full SEO can wait, the technical base should not. A site that renders properly, has clean addresses and keeps preview builds out of Google costs little at launch and much more to repair after a year of growth.
SEO strategy for startups: matching keywords to stage and runway
An SEO strategy for startups starts from the buyer’s searches, not from the top of a keyword tool’s list. I sort them into three groups:
problem searches — what people type before they know tools exist; good for content, slow to convert
category and use-case searches — “[category] for [type of team]”; the core of most SaaS sites
comparison searches — “[competitor] alternatives”, “[tool A] vs [tool B]”; small volumes, buyers close to a decision

With limited runway, the order is usually the reverse of the volumes: comparison and use-case pages first, because the people who land there are already choosing; problem content later, when the product and the message have settled. For each phrase I check who ranks now — a large directory, a well-funded competitor, a forum thread — and whether a young domain can realistically reach the first page within your timeline.
Technical SEO for startups on Next.js and React: rendering, metadata and previews

Many startup sites run on the stack I use every day — Next.js, React and TypeScript — often with the marketing site and the app in one repository. That stack ranks well when a few things are set right:

rendering: marketing pages delivered as HTML from the server or generated at build time, not assembled in the browser. Google can run JavaScript, but later and not always, and many AI crawlers read only the first HTML response
metadata per route: title, description, canonical and Open Graph set for each page, not one default inherited everywhere
preview and staging deployments closed to search engines, so Google does not index a copy of your site on a temporary address
the app kept apart: login, dashboard and settings pages out of the index; public pages linked and listed in the sitemap
speed: Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 seconds on a phone, which on Next.js usually comes down to images, fonts and third-party scripts
A React single-page app that loads all its text with JavaScript is the hardest case. The usual fix is to move the public pages to server rendering, which I can do directly in your codebase.
SEO for SaaS startups: use-case, integration and programmatic pages
Product-led SEO means pages that show the product doing a specific job. For SEO for SaaS startups the useful types are:
use-case and role pages — the product for agencies, for finance teams, for onboarding — each with real screens and steps, not the home page reworded
integration pages — one per tool you connect to, saying what syncs, in which direction and how to set it up
template and example pages, when the product works with templates, documents or workflows that people search for by name

These pages can be programmatic: generated from structured data in a CMS or from your product’s own database, so fifty integration pages share one design and stay up to date. Programmatic pages work when each one carries information the others do not — real settings, limits, examples. Pages that differ only by a swapped name are a known pattern, and Google tends to leave them out of results.
Comparison and alternatives pages for startups: “X vs Y” that buyers trust

People who search “[competitor] alternatives” or “[your tool] vs [competitor]” are close to buying. If you have no such page, a review site or the competitor answers for you. A comparison page that converts is fair:
it says where the other tool is the better choice and for whom
it compares on what buyers weigh — pricing model, limits, integrations, where data is stored, support
it dates the facts that change, and gets updated when they do
I prepare the structure and the factual parts; every claim about a competitor is checked against their public pages before it goes live.
Docs, changelog and help center in SEO for tech startups

In SEO for tech startups, documentation often ranks before the marketing pages do. Developers and admins search for error messages, API names and “how to connect X to Y”, and a well-built docs section answers them with your product in the answer. What helps:
docs on your own domain, in a subfolder or subdomain you control, not on a hosted service’s address
one page per task, with a title that names the task
a changelog with a page per release, so each new feature has an address that can be found and quoted
help-center articles open to search engines, unless they contain account-specific details
AI search optimization for startups: how ChatGPT and Perplexity shortlist tools (GEO, AEO)

Buyers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews “what is the best tool for X for a team of ten” and get a shortlist before they open a single website. Getting onto that list is the work of generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO). Assistants build such answers from what they can read and cross-check:
your own pages, when they state plainly what the product does, for whom, at what price and with which integrations
comparison articles, directories, review sites and community threads where your product is discussed
consistency: the same name, category and facts everywhere, so the assistant does not mix you up with a similarly named product

That is why pricing hidden behind “contact us” and features shown only in screenshots hurt a startup twice: in search and in AI answers. I check how assistants describe your product and which competitors they name before the work and again after it. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
SEO agency for startups or one SEO consultant: who does the work

A typical SEO agency for startups sells a monthly retainer with a fixed number of articles and links, done by a team you rarely talk to. That suits a company with a marketing lead who manages vendors. For an early-stage startup I offer the other model: one SEO consultant for startups instead of an agency — the same person audits, plans, fixes the code or writes the tickets, and reports to the founder. Whoever you hire, ask:
Will you report signups, trials and demo requests from search, or only rankings?
Who writes the pages, and who checks them against the product?
Can you work in our repository, or only send recommendations?
Is there a minimum contract, and what happens to the work if we pivot?
What SEO services for startups include in the first three months
Audit: crawling, rendering, indexing in Google Search Console, metadata, speed and the searches you can realistically win.
Technical fixes in the code — made by me or written as tickets for your developers.
The first pages: the most valuable use-case, integration and comparison pages, with structured data.
Measurement: GA4 events for signups and demo requests, so search traffic is tied to outcomes.
A plan for the next quarter, sized to your budget.

I work alone, from the audit to the code, so the person who finds a problem is the person who fixes it.
What SEO in mental health means for a private therapy practice

SEO in mental health is the work of making a practice visible at the moment someone looks for help: “therapist for panic attacks near me”, “couples counseling Denver”, “EMDR therapist online”. These are rarely casual searches. Many people read for weeks before they write to anyone, and they choose the therapist whose pages describe their situation in words they recognize.
A therapy practice is found in four places, and SEO for therapists works on all of them:
directories such as Psychology Today, which hold most top results for “therapist + city”
the map results shown for “near me” searches
your own website, for searches about one issue, approach or client group
answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, which now name individual practitioners
Psychology Today, Headway and directories vs your own therapist website

For a search like “therapist Austin”, page one is mostly directories: Psychology Today, GoodTherapy, Zocdoc, and marketplaces such as Headway or Alma. A good directory profile still brings inquiries, and I would not tell anyone to drop it. Its limits are plain, though: you sit in a list of twenty colleagues with the same photo size, the platform sets the rules, and the profile text is short.

Your own site wins other searches — your name, your niche in your town, questions about a modality — and it is the page assistants read when they describe you. The two work together when the directory profile links to the site and both show the same name, credentials, address and specialties. Directories also count as mentions of your practice for Google and AI tools, so a forgotten profile with an old phone number does real harm.
Insurance panels or private pay: which searches a therapy practice targets

Being in network changes which searches are worth winning. Clients with coverage search “therapist who takes Aetna in Chicago” or filter directories by plan; a page listing your panels, per state, answers them before they call. Private-pay practices compete on fit. Their clients search by problem and approach, ask about fees and superbills for out-of-network reimbursement, and compare what two or three therapists write about the same issue.
Group practices often have both kinds of clinicians. Then each profile states which plans that clinician takes, and the fees page explains the difference in a few plain sentences.
Niche pages in SEO for therapists: anxiety, couples, trauma and EMDR
Most therapist websites have one “Services” page listing fifteen issues. That page rarely ranks for any single one. People searching are specific, so the pages have to be specific too.
Pages for issues and conditions

Anxiety, panic attacks, depression, grief, burnout, OCD, postpartum depression. Each page says how the problem shows up in daily life, how you work with it, what the first sessions look like and how to start — without promising a result.
Pages for therapy approaches and modalities

EMDR, CBT, DBT, the Gottman Method, IFS, psychodynamic therapy. People search for a modality after reading about it or after a referral, and a page by someone trained in it, naming that training, answers them better than a directory line.
Pages for client groups
Couples, teens and their parents, LGBTQ+ clients, first responders, adults starting therapy for the first time. The same anxiety page reads differently to a parent looking for a teen therapist.

Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan whose site I rebuilt, has seven pillar pages by area of therapy with 21 Italian subtopic pages under them, and 150 Italian FAQ entries reused on the pages where each question belongs. A search for one kind of anxiety lands on the page written about it.
Local SEO for therapists: Google Business Profile and location pages

Local SEO for therapists starts with the Google Business Profile: a primary category that matches your license (Psychologist, Psychotherapist, Counselor, Marriage & family therapist), the office address, hours, a short description of who you help and a link to the matching page on your site, not the home page. Google lists businesses that meet clients in person, so a practice that works only online usually cannot have a map listing; its location pages and directory profiles carry the local searches instead.

A location page is more than a town name: how to find the office, parking or transit, which clinicians work there and whether they also see clients by video. Giuseppe has separate pages for Milan and Monza. More on map results on the
local SEO services
page.
Reviews and therapist ethics codes

Reviews push other businesses up the map; therapists have a narrower path. Ethics codes such as those of the APA and ACA discourage asking current clients for testimonials, and a reply to any review must never confirm that the person is or was a client. Many practices let reviews come on their own and put the effort into the profile and the pages. Check what your licensing board and association allow.
Telehealth SEO for therapists: online therapy pages and licensure across state lines

Video sessions let a practice in one city see clients across the state, so “online therapist Texas” or “virtual couples counseling California” matters as much as the town. In the US a therapist can generally treat clients located in the states where they hold a license, and interstate compacts cover some professions. An online therapy page for each state you are licensed in — with the license, the platform and your hours in that time zone — targets those searches without implying you can see anyone anywhere. Confirm the current rules with your board.
The same logic works for languages and clients abroad. Giuseppe has a page for online therapy for Italians living outside Italy — people no map listing in Milan could reach.
E-E-A-T for psychologists and counselors: license, training and careful wording
Mental health content falls in what Google calls “Your Money or Your Life”, so it is judged on E-E-A-T — signs of experience, expertise, authority and trust. For a therapist those signs are concrete:
license type, number and state on the about page and in structured data
training in each modality you name, with the institute and the year
an author and a review date on every clinical page and blog post
no promised outcomes such as “in six sessions”, and no client stories presented as results

Wording is an ethics question as much as a ranking one. Giuseppe works under Italian rules on advertising health services, which rule out promised outcomes, patient testimonials, discounts and “free consultation” offers, so every page written to be found has to stay inside it. US ethics codes are less detailed but point the same way.
SEO keywords for therapists: blog posts that answer questions before the first session

Keyword research for a therapy practice starts from the questions people bring to the first call: “how long does therapy for panic attacks take”, “psychologist vs therapist vs counselor”, “what happens in the first EMDR session”, “is online therapy as effective as in person”. Each answered question is a chance to be found and to be quoted by an assistant. I check real search data for your niches and area, give each phrase one page and draft the outline; you write or approve the clinical content.
An older blog is an asset. Before anything new is written, I check which posts already bring visits, merge the thin ones and link each post to the niche page it supports.
SEO for therapists in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

People now ask an assistant before they open a directory: “find a therapist in Brooklyn who does EMDR and takes Cigna” or “Italian-speaking psychotherapist online”. The work of getting into those answers goes by two names, GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization). Assistants name practitioners they can describe with confidence from several sources, so the work is:
issues, modalities, client groups, languages, fees, panels and locations written as plain facts
structured data naming the practitioner, the practice, the conditions treated and the therapies offered
the same facts on the Google profile and in every directory listing
robots.txt rules that let AI crawlers read the pages you want quoted
Giuseppe found me through ChatGPT, and his new pages already appear in ChatGPT answers. Before I start and again afterwards, I record what assistants say about your practice. More on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Measuring therapist SEO without exposing client privacy

Results for a practice are consultation requests, not traffic. I count calls, form messages and booking clicks from search and show which pages they came from. Two cautions. Advertising pixels on contact and booking pages can pass information that, in the US, may fall under HIPAA. And for visitors from Europe, analytics should run only after consent, as it does on Giuseppe’s site. Measurement can tell you what works without sending anything about a client elsewhere; your compliance adviser has the final word.

Each phrase has modest volume, but each sits close to a booking. Tour company SEO maps these groups to pages before anything is written, so two of your tours never compete for the same search.
Tour pages by destination and activity: the site structure that ranks
Many tour sites list every tour on one page under a booking widget. Search engines need one page per tour, aimed at one search, and hub pages that group them:
a page for each tour: what happens hour by hour, duration, meeting point with a map, what is included, group size, age limits, what to bring, cancellation terms and price from
destination pages that gather your tours in one place with a short guide to the area
activity pages that gather kayak, food or hiking tours across destinations, if you run several
photos and short videos from real departures, described in words
Original text matters more than length. Pasting the OTA description onto your own page gives Google two copies of the same text, and the platform usually wins.
“Things to do in…” searches and Google Things to do for tour companies

Searches like “things to do in Savannah” are broad, and lists from large travel sites hold the top of the results. A small operator reaches that demand in two ways. First, with planning articles for narrower versions — “things to do in Savannah with kids on a rainy day” — written from a guide’s experience and linked to the matching tour. Second, through Google’s Things to do listings, where tours appear with prices and booking links: your booking software or a connectivity partner sends your products there, and your own site can be one of the booking options next to the OTAs.
Viator, GetYourGuide and direct bookings in tour operator SEO

Viator, GetYourGuide, Klook and Airbnb Experiences sell tours to people who would never find a small company alone, and they take a commission on each booking. Most operators keep them. SEO works on the other side of that trade:
travelers who saw you on an OTA often search your name before booking, and your site should be the first result, with the same tours and a clear booking button
your own tour pages compete for searches where OTA pages are thin or generic
reviews, guide profiles and photos on your site answer the doubts that send people back to the platform
Reports put direct bookings from search next to OTA bookings, so you see the share move month by month.
Tour booking software and SEO: Rezdy, Bókun, FareHarbor and page speed

Booking software runs the calendar, payments and manifests, and few operators would work without it. Its widget can still hurt search: some load slowly, some keep the tour description inside a frame Google does not credit to your page, some send guests to another domain where tracking breaks. An audit checks:
whether tour details are text on your page or exist only inside the widget
how the widget affects load time and Core Web Vitals on a phone
whether each booking is tracked back to the page and search that brought it
whether availability and prices on the page match the system
The fix is usually in how the widget is embedded, not in switching software.
Multilingual SEO for tour companies with international guests

Travelers search in their own language: a German couple in Florida types in German, a family from Mexico in Spanish. Every language gets pages built on what that market types into Google, with its own titles and planning answers, tied together with hreflang. Start with the languages your guides speak on tours; a page selling a German-language tour without a German-speaking guide earns bad reviews. How I build sites in several languages is on the
multilingual website development
page.
Seasonality in SEO for tour operators: when to publish and update tour pages
Tour searches rise weeks or months before the season: people plan summer whale watching in spring and fall foliage trips in August. The SEO calendar follows that:
new tour pages and seasonal guides go live well before the season, so Google has time to find and rank them
dates, prices and departure times are updated before travelers start comparing
off-season and private tours get attention when the main season ends
pages for paused tours stay live with the next season’s dates instead of being deleted
Deleting a tour page each winter throws away the rankings it earned; keeping it with “next departures from May” keeps them.
Google reviews, Tripadvisor and the Google Business Profile of a tour operator

Reviews often decide between two similar tours. Ask every group after the tour, by email or with a QR card, and reply on Google and Tripadvisor. The Google Business Profile marks where tours start — an office, a dock or a meeting point — so travelers find it on the map that morning, with the same name, phone and website as everywhere else. Map rankings and reviews in more depth are on the

More travelers plan with an assistant: “plan three days in Charleston with a food tour”, “best small-group tour of Zion from Springdale”. ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews name a few companies and give reasons. Shaping those answers goes by two names, GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization), and for a tour operator it comes down to:
each tour’s facts — duration, meeting point, group size, season, languages, price from — as plain text
planning articles that answer the question directly, with the guide or owner named as author
the same facts on Google, Tripadvisor and OTA listings, plus a steady flow of new reviews
TouristTrip and Organization structured data tied to those profiles
Before and after the work I check how assistants describe your company and which operators they name instead. More on the

Before hiring anyone, ask who writes the tour pages, whether reports show bookings, and whether the content stays yours if you leave. What small business SEO services include: the website, the Google listing and AI answers
For a small business, search decides in three places whether a customer gets in touch:
your website — service pages, titles, speed, structured data and the text that answers customers’ questions
your Google Business Profile — the listing that appears in Google Maps and next to searches for your name
AI answers — ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, which name businesses they can read about

Benefits of SEO for small businesses: customers who are already looking
Advertising shows your business to people; SEO shows it to people who have already typed what you sell. For a small business with a small budget that is the main benefit, and there are a few more:
visits from search are not paid per click, so a page that ranks keeps bringing calls in months when you spend nothing on ads
the customer lands on a page that answers the question they typed: the price range, the area you cover, how to book
people who heard about you from a friend or a flyer also look you up, and a good result reassures them
the pages, the listing and the reviews stay yours; nothing switches off when a contract ends
The trade-off is time. SEO takes months, while an ad works the same day, so many small businesses keep a modest ad budget while search builds up.
SEO consultant for small business or an SEO company: who does the work

Searching for an SEO company for small business leads mostly to agencies, and agencies are built for many clients at once: a salesperson, an account manager, a strategist, and writers or developers you may never speak to. That suits a business that needs many channels in one contract. For a business with one location and a modest budget, those layers cost money that does not reach the website.

As a small business SEO consultant I work alone. The same person reads your search data, writes or edits the pages, changes the code — on WordPress, Next.js or another system — and explains the report. There is no handover between the one who audits and the one who implements, which is where a lot of agency work gets lost.
What I do not do: paid ads, social media and video. If you need all of that from one supplier, an agency fits better, and the SEO part can still be ordered separately.
SEO audit for a small business: the first step before any monthly work
Every project starts with an audit, and for many small businesses the audit and its fixes are most of what is needed. I check:
how Google sees the site: indexing, broken pages, duplicate titles, and speed on a phone, where the main content should appear within 2.5 seconds
which searches already bring visitors in Google Search Console, and which of your services have no page at all
whether the Google listing matches the site: category, services, hours, the link
what nearby competitors rank with, and which of their positions you can realistically take
how ChatGPT and AI Overviews describe your business today
You get a list of fixes ranked by impact, written so that you, your web developer or I can carry them out. The

What a monthly SEO service for a small business includes
Monthly SEO is worth paying for when there are more services, areas or competitors than one round of fixes can handle. A month of SEO service for a small business usually covers:
a new or rewritten page for a service or area you want more work in

Each month is planned from the audit list, so you know what you are paying for. My general approach to ongoing work is on the

Affordable SEO services for small business: what cheap packages leave out

Affordable and cheap are different things. Low-priced monthly packages usually save on exactly the parts that make SEO work: pages written about your real services, fixes in the code, and someone who reads the results. Signs of a package to avoid:
a guaranteed first position on Google — nobody controls the ranking
hundreds of backlinks a month from directories and article networks, which Google ignores or penalizes
reports full of positions for phrases nobody searches, with no calls or form requests
the provider keeps the website, the domain or the Google listing in its own name
For most small businesses the affordable route is a one-off audit plus fixes, and monthly work only when the audit shows a reason for it.
DIY SEO or hiring help: what a small business owner can do alone
If you want to learn SEO as a beginner, Google’s SEO Starter Guide and Google Search Console are free and cover the basics. A lot of small business SEO can be done by the owner:
give every service its own page, with a title that names the service and the town
write prices or price ranges, the area you cover and how to book as plain text
ask every satisfied customer for a review and answer each one

Hiring help pays off where mistakes are expensive or slow to notice: moving or redesigning a site, technical errors, a website builder that limits what you can change, or a market where competitors already have strong sites. A common split is that the owner keeps the listing and reviews going while I handle the structure, the technical side and the pages.

SEO for SaaS companies after first traction: from blog traffic to pipeline

By the time a SaaS company has its first few hundred customers, the site usually has a blog written for traffic, a features page, pricing and a login link. Visits grow; signups from search do not. The reasons repeat from company to company:
articles answer questions from people who will never buy — students, job seekers, competitors’ users looking for a tutorial
product pages target only the category term, where review sites and the category leaders hold the first page
nobody has linked organic signups to trial-to-paid, so the team cannot tell which pages earn money
If your product is still before product-market fit, the stage-by-stage plan on the

SaaS SEO strategy by funnel stage: bottom of the funnel first
Searches around a software product fall into four levels of intent:
product — “[your brand] pricing”, “[competitor] alternative”, “[tool A] vs [tool B]”
solution — “invoicing software for contractors”, “time tracking app for agencies”
problem — “how to reduce failed payments”, “client onboarding checklist”
category education — “what is a customer data platform”

A SaaS SEO strategy starts with the first two. Their volumes are small, but the people typing them are choosing a tool this month. Problem content comes next, each article linked to the solution page it leads to; broad education comes last, only where it is a natural road to the product. Beyond search data, I build the plan from sales call notes, support tickets and lost deals: the reasons buyers give for choosing a competitor are the pages you are missing.
SaaS content marketing that brings trials, not just visits
SaaS content marketing pays when an article does a job in the funnel. In practice:
each article solves the reader’s task and shows the product doing that task, with real screenshots
the call to action matches the article: a template that opens in the product, a trial with the right settings preloaded, a demo for a team-sized problem
articles that bring traffic and no signups are merged, rewritten for a buyer’s question or removed

Plain facts beat slogans in search. On the property platform I run, descriptions rewritten once as lifestyle copy lost traffic on commercial pages, and factual descriptions brought clicks back (+16%). Software pages behave the same way: features, plan limits, integrations and prices stated plainly outrank and outsell taglines.
Product-led SEO: templates, calculators and free tools built from your product

Searches such as “invoice template”, “SLA calculator”, “UTM builder” or “meeting agenda template” have steady volume and sit next to what a SaaS product does. A free tool that solves a small part of the job, with a clear step into the full product, is often the strongest page a SaaS site has. What makes one work:
it works without a signup, and the result can be copied, downloaded or shared
the page explains the method in text, so search engines and AI assistants can read it
templates come from what your users actually build, with permission
it is rendered on the server, not assembled in the browser

For a retail analytics consultant I built calculators and templates as part of a 153-page site in three languages; demand for each was researched before design, and the pages were written to be quoted by AI assistants.
Programmatic SEO for SaaS: pages from product data and when they become thin

Programmatic pages can come from data the product already holds: integration pairs, templates by industry, public directories, exchange or tax rates, benchmarks by country. They work when every page carries data a person needs that is not on the next page. Google’s spam policies call pages made mainly for ranking “scaled content abuse”, whether a person, a script or an AI wrote them. My test: would you link this page from inside your product? I launch in batches, watch “Crawled – currently not indexed” in Search Console, and merge or remove the pages that do not earn their place.
International SEO for SaaS: hreflang, localized landing pages and pricing for EU markets

A SaaS product can sell everywhere from day one, but search is local. A German buyer types “Zeiterfassung Software”, a French one “logiciel de facturation”, and neither reads an English page with a translated headline. A localized version needs:
keyword research per market, with your features named in local terms
prices in local currency, with VAT shown the way local buyers expect, and local payment methods named
customer stories and trust details from that market, including where EU data is stored
hreflang with x-default, one folder per language, and no automatic redirects by IP

The Cyprus platform I run has five languages and top positions for many German (DACH) queries; the education agency’s site grew from one country to ten on one structure. I write English, Polish and Russian myself; for German, French or Spanish I plan the pages and keywords, and a native speaker on your side or a translator you choose writes or checks the texts. At this stage a SaaS product website sells a working product to buyers comparing it with two or three others.
What is a SaaS website, and what it does once the product sells

A SaaS website is the public marketing site of a software-as-a-service product: the pages that explain what the product does, who it is for, what it costs and how to start, kept apart from the app customers log into. Once revenue comes in, it is a sales channel with its own targets — trial signups, demo requests, upgrades — read by the person with the problem, the manager who approves the spend and the IT team that signs off on a new vendor.
Products before launch or still looking for their first customers need fewer pages and different ones: a waitlist, an MVP page, material for investors. Those are on the
startup website design
page. Companies selling services or physical goods to other businesses will find catalogs and quote forms on the
B2B website design

Best SaaS websites: what the best SaaS website designs have in common

Galleries of SaaS web design on Awwwards, Behance or Webflow mostly show home pages. Open the inner pages of SaaS website examples that sell well and the shared principles concern structure, not style:
every feature has its own page answering one question — what job does this do for me
visitors find themselves by role, company size or industry within two clicks
the next step matches the buyer: signup to try, a call for a team that needs one
proof sits where doubt appears — a customer quote beside the claim it supports, a hosting note beside the signup button
plans, limits and integrations are written as text, so they can be searched, compared and quoted
SaaS website inspiration helps with taste; the structure comes from your product and your buyers.
Feature pages and use-case pages on a SaaS website, by role and industry
A single Features page with thirty icons convinces nobody and gives search engines nothing to match. A SaaS marketing site that sells is built from two page types, each with its own template:
feature pages, one per capability a buyer would search for or ask about on a call: the problem, how the feature handles it, a short walkthrough, which plans include it and which integrations it uses
use-case pages, one per role (“for finance teams”, “for agencies”) or per industry, written in that reader’s vocabulary and showing the features and customer stories that matter to them
Both are CMS content types, so product marketing adds a page for a new feature or segment without waiting for design or engineering.
An integrations directory on a SaaS website, generated from data

Buyers check early whether you connect to the tools they already pay for. Each integration is one record in the CMS — name, logo, category, what syncs in which direction, the plans that include it, a link to the setup article — and the site builds the rest from those records:
a directory with filters by category and plan
a page for each integration at its own address
a block on every feature page listing the integrations that feature relies on
A new connector means one new record, and its page appears in every language version. Records without a real description stay unpublished, so no page shows only a logo.
Self-serve trial signup or “book a demo”: two page flows on a SaaS website
Self-serve and demo-led products need different flows, and many products need both. The difference shows in every button:
self-serve: the main button opens signup inside the app, with no extra form on the marketing site; the chosen plan and campaign parameters travel along, so the app knows where the account came from
demo-led: a short form — work email, team size, the problem — then a calendar, so the meeting is booked before the visitor leaves and the request reaches your CRM with its source page
hybrid: small teams are sent to the trial and larger accounts to a call, split by team size or plan rather than by hiding one of the paths
Signups and demo requests are recorded as separate events, so each page shows which of the two it brings.
SaaS landing page design for paid campaigns
Ads, webinars and partner campaigns get landing pages assembled from the same components, with one offer, one action and no full menu. How I build them is on the

Proof pages on a SaaS website: customer stories, security and compliance
Customer story pages

A buyer reads a customer story to see whether the product worked for a company like theirs. The template opens with a facts box — industry, team size, region, plan, features used — then the situation and the result in the customer’s words, with numbers only where the customer approved them. Tags by industry and use case put each story on the matching use-case pages.
Security and trust pages for the buyer’s IT team
Before a contract the buyer’s IT team sends a questionnaire. A security page or trust center answers much of it in advance:
the reports and certifications you hold, such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001, with scope, date and how to request the report
GDPR: where customer data is hosted, a data processing agreement (DPA) to download or request, and a privacy contact
subprocessors with their purpose and location, and how customers hear about changes
a link to the status page and a way to report a vulnerability
These are your company’s facts; the site gives them fixed places, plain text and dates.
Docs, help center and changelog on a SaaS website: subdomain or subfolder

Documentation, the help center and the changelog serve customers, and prospects read them to judge the product. A subfolder such as /docs keeps one domain and one design, and search engines treat it as part of the main site. A subdomain such as docs.yourproduct.com suits a docs tool your engineers already run. Either works when the header and the links back to the marketing site match and the docs arrive as server-rendered text. A changelog with one dated entry per release, linked to the feature page it changes, shows prospects that the product keeps moving.
Localized SaaS website versions for European markets

Selling into Germany, France, Poland or Spain often stalls at a translated home page. A localized SaaS site carries the pages buyers decide on — features, use cases, security, plans in euros with VAT stated, the legal pages — under translated URLs with hreflang, written for each market instead of passed through a machine translator. Bandziuk.com is built this way in three languages, and so is the retail analytics consultant’s site with its 153 pages. The setup is described on the

Moving a SaaS website from Webflow or WordPress to Next.js without losing search traffic

SaaS marketing sites often start on Webflow or WordPress and hit limits as they grow: hundreds of pages that should share data, collection caps, conflicting plugins, language versions added as an afterthought. The rankings live in the URLs, so a move starts with a map of every address. Each one gets a 301 redirect, titles and structured data are carried over, Webflow collections or WordPress posts become structured CMS content, and the redirects are tested on a preview before the domain switches.

I moved Giuseppe’s site in Milan this way, from WordPress to Next.js 16 and Sanity, with a 301 for each of its 468 old posts; it took 44 working days to handover. After launch the marketing team publishes feature pages, stories and changelog entries in Sanity with a live preview, and the layout stays protected.

It fits a product with one audience and a short feature list; use-case pages, an integrations directory, trust pages and languages later mean working against it.

A SaaS website design agency brings a strategist, designers, developers and a project manager, which suits a large rebrand with many stakeholders. A SaaS website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Software buyers now type requests like “an invoicing tool that connects to QuickBooks and stores data in the EU” into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews and get a shortlist back. An assistant can only shortlist what it can read, and SaaS sites often hide those facts: plans in a JavaScript widget, integrations as a wall of logos, security details in a PDF. children.text: Senior living SEO is the work that brings families to your community from Google, Maps and AI assistants rather than from paid referral lists: a page for each level of care, a Google Business Profile for each community, clear cost information, reviews and a tour request that takes a minute. One person handles it end to end — audit, page plans, code and reports — for independent living, assisted living and memory care communities and for operators with several locations.
What senior living SEO covers: how adult children search for a community

The person typing “assisted living near me” is rarely the future resident. More often it is a daughter or son, sometimes in another state, searching at lunch or late at night after a fall, a hospital discharge or a worrying phone call. They open several tabs and call the two or three communities that answer their questions first. That search happens in three places:
the map results, where three communities with a rating and a phone number take many of the first calls
the regular results, crowded with referral services, directories and large operators
AI answers in Google and ChatGPT, which now name communities when asked which memory care nearby has good reviews
SEO for senior living works on all three: your pages, your profile, your reviews and the plain facts that assistants can quote.
Senior living keywords by level of care: independent living, assisted living and memory care pages

Families search by the care a parent needs, not by the name of your building. One “Our community” page cannot rank for “memory care Scottsdale”, “assisted living with nursing care” and “respite stay after hospital” at once. Each level of care you offer gets its own page, written around the questions that level raises.
Independent living and 55+ community pages
Here the future resident often searches alone: apartments, meals, activities, transportation, the monthly fee and what happens if care is needed later.
Assisted living pages
Adult children want to know what help with bathing, dressing and medication is included, how care needs are assessed, who is on site at night and how the monthly price changes with the care level.
Memory care pages

Searches here are anxious and specific: dementia care with a secured courtyard, care for someone who wanders. The page explains the secured setting, staff training in general terms, the daily rhythm and how families visit.
Respite and short-term stay pages
A short stay after surgery or while a family caregiver travels is often the first contact with a community. A separate page catches these searches and lets a family see the community from inside.
State licensing and fair housing rules on assisted living pages

Assisted living and memory care are licensed by each state, and the names, rules and allowed services differ: what one state calls assisted living, another licenses as a residential care facility or a personal care home. A care page should name your license type as text, describe only the services your license allows and make no promises about health outcomes. Senior housing is also housing, so fair housing rules apply to your pages and ads: describe the community and its services, not the kind of resident you prefer. These are general points; your licensing consultant or attorney checks the wording for your state.
Local SEO for senior living communities: a Google Business Profile for each community

For “assisted living near me” the map decides. Each community needs its own profile with the primary category that matches its license, the hours when families can tour, real photos of apartments and common areas, the services list and a link to that community’s page rather than the home page. Operators with several communities need a page and a profile per address, with the same name, address and phone on the site, the profile and senior care directories. More on maps work on the
local SEO services
page.
Referral services vs your own inquiries: A Place for Mom, Caring.com and the senior living website

Referral services such as A Place for Mom or Caring.com rank high for almost every “assisted living + city” search. They pass a family’s details to several communities and charge a fee when someone moves in. For many communities they remain a real source of residents; the price is a family that is already comparing you with others, and a fee on each move-in.

Senior living SEO does not replace those services. It adds a channel where the family finds you directly. Track the two separately in your CRM, so you can see what a direct move-in costs next to a referred one. A complete directory listing that links to your site also supports your own pages.
Assisted living cost pages: pricing transparency in senior living SEO

“How much is assisted living in [city]” and “memory care cost per month” are among the questions families type most, and many community sites answer them with “contact us for pricing”. The family then reads an average on a referral site instead. A cost page that gives a starting monthly price for each level of care, what it includes, how care levels add to it, whether there is a community fee and which payment sources you accept — private pay, long-term care insurance, veterans benefits or a state Medicaid waiver where it applies — answers the search on your own site. It also filters out families for whom the price does not work before your sales team spends an hour on them.
Tour requests from search: measuring senior living SEO in tours and move-ins

Rankings and traffic are not the result a community needs. The useful numbers are tour requests, calls and move-ins that started from search. I set up tracking so each inquiry carries the page it came from: the call button, the tour form and the brochure download are recorded as separate events and passed to your senior living CRM where it accepts web leads. After a few months you can see which care page brings tours and which only brings readers.
Reviews for senior living communities: Google, Caring.com and resident privacy

Families read reviews here more closely than for almost any other decision. A steady routine works better than a campaign: ask every family, not only the happy ones, a few weeks after a move-in, with a direct link to Google. Buying reviews or rewarding them breaks the platforms’ rules and US consumer protection rules on endorsements.

Replies need care. Never confirm that the reviewer’s relative lives with you and never discuss anyone’s care in public. A short, calm reply that invites the person to call the executive director shows readers that the community listens without exposing a resident.
Staff pages and E-E-A-T on senior living websites: who stands behind the care

Pages about dementia, nursing and daily care belong to what Google calls “Your Money or Your Life” topics, held to a higher standard. The signals it looks for are simple: pages for the executive director, the director of nursing or wellness and the memory care lead with their credentials; the name of the person who reviewed each care page and the date; a clear line between describing your services and giving medical advice. My part is the page plan and the first drafts; nothing about care goes live until your care team has signed it off.
Senior living SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Adult children now ask ChatGPT which assisted living near Tampa takes residents with diabetes, or ask Google how memory care cost compares with assisted living. Assistants answer from facts they can read and confirm in several places. The work of earning a place in those answers goes by two names, GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization). For a senior living community it comes down to:
levels of care, license type, apartment types, starting prices, payment options and visiting hours written as plain facts
answers to the questions families ask on tours, published on the care pages
the same details on your site, your Google profile and the directories
structured data that connects the operator, each community and its services

I have seen it work for a private medical practice: the site I rebuilt for Giuseppe, a Milan psychotherapist, now has new pages quoted in ChatGPT answers — the same assistant through which he first came to me. More on the

page.

Senior living marketing is usually a mix: paid search, social media, referral partners, events and a sales team that follows up every lead. Many firms sell that whole mix on their own platform. children.text: Senior living website design is my work for independent, assisted and memory care communities, and the person who draws the pages is the one who codes them, so nothing is lost between a designer and a developer. An assisted living website has two readers at once: an adult child comparing options on a phone between meetings, and a parent who may read the same page later on a tablet. The design has to serve both without talking down to either.
Senior living website design for two readers: the adult child and the future resident

The adult child arrives with a deadline and a list of questions: what care you offer, what it costs, whether an apartment is free, when they can visit. The future resident arrives with a different worry: whether this place will feel like home. The first screen answers the first list in plain words — “Assisted living and memory care in [town]”, a starting price, a tour button and a phone number — and the photography below it answers the second.
Menus follow the questions families ask, not your organization chart: Care, Living here, Pricing, Tours, Our team, Contact. Six items, a word or two each, readable without hovering.
Assisted living website design by level of care: one page for each care type

Independent living, assisted living, memory care and respite stays are different decisions, often made by different people. Each gets its own page with the same layout, so a family can compare them side by side: who it suits, what daily help is included, how needs are assessed and reassessed, which staff are on site day and night, the starting price and a tour button.

Memory care pages need the quietest design on the site, because the family reading them is often at the hardest point of the decision. Soft colors, short sentences and no countdown banners or “only two suites left” pressure. A plain description of the secured garden and the shape of the day does more than any slogan.
Photos, video tours and floor plans on a senior living website
Families judge a community by what they can see, and stock photos of smiling seniors are recognized at once. What works instead:
real photos of apartments, bathrooms with grab bars, the dining room, the garden and activity spaces, in daylight and without heavy editing
a floor plan for each apartment type with its size and an idea of what furniture fits
a short video walk-through that a sibling in another state can watch before the tour
this week’s menu and an activity calendar that your staff update themselves

Photos of residents need their written consent, or the consent of the person legally entitled to give it; for memory care it is often wiser to show spaces and staff. Your attorney confirms the consent form.
Pricing pages on an assisted living website: starting prices and what they include

Pricing is the page families look for first and many community sites hide. The layout I use shows a starting monthly price for each level of care, then plain text rows: what the base price covers, how care levels add to it, any one-time community fee and the payment sources you accept. A short note on what moves the final price prepares the family for the assessment. Families who see a number they can manage book the tour with less hesitation; those who cannot save your sales team a long call.
Tour booking and inquiry forms on a senior living website

The tour is where families decide, so the tour button sits on every page, and on phones a fixed bar holds two actions: schedule a tour and call. Behind it is either a calendar with real free times or a short request form when your sales staff confirm by phone. A text-message option suits adult children who cannot take calls at work.

Forms ask for the family member’s name, contact details, the level of care being considered and a preferred time. They do not ask for diagnoses or medications; those belong in the assessment with your nurse. Health details about a parent are sensitive whether or not HIPAA applies to your community, so any form that must collect them runs through a provider built for it. Years ago I worked on a medical system holding patient records; it is covered by an NDA, so it stays unnamed, but it left me with a rule: a public website should hold as little health information as it possibly can. Where your CRM accepts web leads, each inquiry goes there with the page it came from.
Accessible senior living website design: large type, contrast and WCAG
Many residents, and some of their children, see less well, tap less precisely or use a screen reader. The design follows the WCAG guidelines from the first sketch:
body text larger than on a typical site, with contrast that meets level AA
buttons large enough to hit with an unsteady hand, with space between them
no carousels that move by themselves and no text set inside images
forms with visible labels, clear error messages and no time limits
captions on videos and full keyboard navigation
I test the result with automated tools and a screen reader; your obligations under accessibility law are a question for your attorney.
Staff, license and inspection information on an assisted living website

Trust in a community is trust in its people. A team page with real portraits and a few lines from the people families will actually meet — the community’s director, the nurse in charge, the life enrichment lead — answers the question families ask on every tour: who will look after my mother. Your state license type and number appear as text in the footer and on the care pages, and where your state publishes inspection reports online, a link to its lookup shows families you are comfortable being checked.
Websites for senior living operators with several communities

An operator with several communities needs one design system and a full section per community: its own address, photos, care levels, prices, team and tour calendar. Families search for a town, not for your company name, so a community page has to make sense on its own when someone lands on it from Maps. Shared content — care philosophy, careers, company history — lives once at the brand level and links down to each community.
A senior living website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Adult children ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews to shortlist communities near a parent, with a memory care wing and within a budget. Assistants can recommend only what they can read. The design keeps the facts as text and structured data — levels of care, license, apartment types, starting prices, visiting hours, address — and in agreement with your Google Business Profile. Giuseppe’s site in Milan is built this way, and his new pages already appear in ChatGPT answers.
Earning a place in those answers takes continuing work — see the

Senior living website templates and vendor platforms vs a custom design

Several companies sell ready-made senior living websites on their own platform, and a builder like Wix or Webflow can produce a decent page in a day. For one small community with one level of care that can be enough. The limits show as you grow: one generic layout for every care type, pricing that cannot be shown the way you sell, a tour form that never reaches your CRM and a site you cannot take with you when the contract ends. A custom design is built around how you present care, prices and tours, and the code, content and domain stay yours.
If your current site already has pages that rank, a redesign keeps every address or redirects it, the way all 468 blog posts on Giuseppe’s site kept their old URLs. The

page explains the process.
