children.text: I design and build websites for small businesses, so design and development come from one person, at a price you can see before you contact me. Most owners I work with run everything themselves: they answer the phone, do the work, send the invoices and have maybe an hour a week left for the website. The site has to work without that hour — bring calls and requests, show what you sell and what it costs, and stay easy to change when prices or opening hours change.
Website design for small business: what the site has to do for an owner
A small business does not need a website that looks like a corporation’s. It needs one that does three jobs every day without supervision:
says in one sentence what you do and where, so the visitor knows within seconds they are in the right place
makes contact easy in the way your customers prefer — a call, a WhatsApp message, a form, or directions to your door
answers the questions you would otherwise answer on the phone ten times a week: prices or price ranges, hours, the area you serve, how long a job takes

Everything else — animations, sliders, a page about the company mission — comes after these three, and often not at all. Good web design for small business is mostly a matter of deciding what to leave out.
Website builder or a custom website for a small business

Wix, Squarespace, the GoDaddy website builder and WordPress.com put a site online in a weekend for a monthly subscription. Many people who search for a website for a small business are really choosing between these tools, and for some of them a builder is the right choice. Better to say that here than to sell a custom site to someone who does not need one.
When a website builder is enough for a small business
you sell one or two services in one place, and the site is mainly an online business card
you have the time to assemble it from a template and keep it up to date
your customers come through referrals, social media or foot traffic, not from Google searches
you are testing an idea and do not yet know whether the business will be running in a year
When a custom small business website pays off
you sell several services and want each one found in Google on its own, with its own page, text and price
you want full control over SEO: page addresses, titles, structured data, redirects and loading speed
the monthly bill keeps growing — a plan upgrade for a booking form, an app for reviews, another for a second language
the site has to work with other tools: a booking system, a CRM, invoicing, a delivery or reservation platform
you want to own the site and be able to move it to another host or developer without rebuilding it

A custom site costs more at the start and less over the years: no per-feature subscriptions, and hosting a small, fast site is cheap. If you start on a builder and outgrow it, moving later means building the site again, not exporting it — that is the real cost to weigh.
Web design for small companies: the pages a small business website needs
Small business websites need fewer pages than most owners expect, but they need the right ones:
a home page that says what, where and how to reach you, with the main services one tap away
a page for each service or product line people search for, with what is included, a price or range and your own photos
a page about you and the team — in a small business, customers choose people, not a brand
reviews, ideally the ones customers already left on your Google Business Profile or another platform they trust
contact and location: an address on a map, hours, the service area, parking or how to find the entrance
The best small business websites rarely have more than this at launch. A blog is optional: if nobody will write in it, it is better left out than left with three posts from years ago.
How to decide which service pages to write first, and what each one has to answer, is covered in the

Website developers for small business: one person from design to launch

An agency splits a small website between a project manager, a designer, a developer and a copywriter, and the price reflects four people. I do all of it myself: the structure, the design, the build in Next.js or WordPress, the page texts together with you, the SEO basics and the launch. You talk to the person who does the work, and a decision takes a message instead of a meeting.
What website design services for small business include
In both price ranges you get:
the design for phones and desktops, agreed with you before the build
development, hosting setup, SSL and your domain connected
page titles, descriptions, structured data and a sitemap, so Google can index the site from the first day
Google Analytics 4 and Search Console connected, with calls, messages and form sends counted
an admin panel where you change text, prices, photos and hours without calling anyone
The general way I build sites, for any size of business, is described on the

page.
A fast small business website with one-tap contact on a phone
Most visits to a local business website come from phones, often straight from Google Maps or a search for a service nearby. The design and build are checked against that visit:
pages load in under 2.5 seconds on a phone, the Largest Contentful Paint level Google rates as good
call, WhatsApp and directions buttons on every page, large enough for a thumb
forms with as few fields as the job allows: a name, a phone number and a short description are often all you need
text that can be read without zooming and colors that stay readable outdoors
A small business website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

People now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews for recommendations: a bakery that makes custom cakes, an accountant who speaks Polish, a bike repair shop open on Sunday. Assistants can only suggest what they can read and check. The site is built so the facts about your business are text, not pictures — services, prices, area, hours and languages — with structured data for the business, its services and reviews, and the same name, address and phone number as on your Google Business Profile and in directories.

Small business website redesign without losing Google rankings

Many owners come with a site that is five or ten years old, built by a relative or by an agency that has since closed, slow on a phone and impossible to edit. A small business website redesign keeps what still works — the domain, the pages Google already ranks, the reviews, the good photos — and replaces what does not.

Before the new site goes live, every old address is mapped to a new page and redirected, titles and structured data are carried over, and after launch Search Console is checked for errors. Moving away from Wix, Squarespace or GoDaddy follows the same steps: the content is moved over page by page and the old addresses are redirected. The full process is on the

page.
Website design for your type of small business

Some trades need specific things from a site: emergency calls for plumbers, appointment booking and patient trust for dentists, menus and table reservations for restaurants, direct bookings for hotels, project galleries and estimate forms for contractors. Each has its own page:

How the small business website design process works
Brief. You send what you sell, where and to whom, the questions customers ask, and any photos and texts you already have. A voice message is fine.
Structure and fixed price. I propose the list of pages and a price. If the scope changes later, the change is priced before it is made.
Design, phone first. The home page and one service page are designed and agreed with you; the other pages follow the same style.
Build and texts. I build the site and fill it in. If you have no texts, I write them from your brief and you correct the facts.
Launch and hand-over. Domain, analytics and Search Console are connected, you get a short guide to editing, and the site is yours.

After launch there is no monthly fee to me. You pay your hosting and domain provider, and you pay me only for changes you ask for.
Inexpensive website design for a small business: where the price can go down

The price goes down when you bring your own texts and photos, when the site has fewer pages, and when we launch the simple version first and add pages as the business grows. It does not go down by skipping mobile layout, speed or the SEO basics — those are the parts that make a site bring customers instead of just existing.

children.text: Spa website design is a quieter job than most web work: the site has to feel like your treatment rooms, yet answer practical questions fast — what a treatment includes, how long it lasts, what it costs, and how to book it or give it as a gift. I design and build websites for day spas, wellness centers, massage studios and hotel spas myself, from the page list to launch, and connect them to the booking and payment tools you already use.
Web design for spas: who opens the site and what they look for
A spa website has at least four kinds of visitors, and each needs a different first step:
someone booking time for themselves, who wants the menu and a free slot this week
a gift buyer, often in a hurry before a birthday or holiday, who wants a voucher in the inbox within minutes
a couple planning a day together, who compare packages
a hotel guest or tourist, who checks opening hours, day passes and what to bring
The home page gives each of them a clear door: Book a treatment, Buy a gift voucher, Packages for two, Visiting us. Everything else — your story, the products you use, the team — sits one tap deeper.
Spa treatment menu on the website: durations, prices and what each treatment includes

The menu is the page guests open most, and the one most spas publish as a scanned PDF. On the site it becomes a set of short, readable entries grouped the way guests think — massage, facials, body treatments, rituals, add-ons — each with:
the duration options side by side, for example 60 and 90 minutes, with a price for each
two or three sentences on what happens, in plain words rather than a list of oils
who it suits and when it is not recommended, such as pregnancy or recent sunburn
a Book button that opens that exact treatment in your system

Each larger treatment can have its own page with more detail, so a search for “hot stone massage” lands on hot stone massage. Prices and durations are edited in one place in the CMS and stay the same everywhere.
Selling spa gift vouchers online: payment, delivery and redemption
For many spas, vouchers are a large share of December and February revenue, and most of them are still sold over the phone or at the desk. Online, the purchase takes a minute:
the guest picks a value or a specific treatment or package
pays by card or wallet on a secure checkout
receives a designed voucher with a unique code by email, or has it sent to the recipient on a chosen date
your front desk checks the code at the visit, and it is marked as used

Some spa software includes gift cards; if yours does, the site uses it. If not, I build the voucher flow on Stripe Checkout. The page I built for Landi Room, a Warsaw beauty salon, sells its online course this way: a Stripe Checkout payment triggers automatic delivery of a unique video link, valid for 14 days. Its first Google Ads campaign brought more than 100 sales. A voucher uses the same mechanics with a code instead of a link. Expiry and refund rules for gift cards differ between states and countries, so the terms on the voucher follow the rules where you operate.
Spa packages and couples treatments: half-day, full-day and rituals for two

Packages are how a spa raises the average visit, and they need more explanation than a single massage. Each package page shows the full timeline — arrival, sauna or pool time, treatments in order, lunch or tea, departure — with the total time and price, and whether both guests are treated in the same room. Couples packages also answer the questions that stop a booking: can we stay together the whole time, what if one of us wants a different treatment, is there a private suite. A package can be booked directly or bought as a voucher from the same page.
Online booking on a spa website: linking your spa software

Most spas already run Mangomint, Vagaro, Fresha, Booker, or a hotel system such as Book4Time. The site does not replace it; it sends guests into it at the right place. Depending on what your system allows, Book buttons open the specific treatment, a widget loads after a tap without slowing the page, and package bookings go to a request form when they need a call to arrange. Deposits and cancellation rules appear in one line above the button, so guests read them before they pay.
Massage studio website design: techniques, therapists and the first visit

A massage studio is usually smaller than a day spa, and its guests choose by technique and by therapist. The site lists techniques — Swedish, deep tissue, sports, Thai, prenatal — with a clear description of pressure and purpose, introduces each therapist with a photo, training and the techniques they do, and explains the first visit: arriving early, the intake questions, what to wear, how to say the pressure is too much. A one- or two-person studio often needs five or six pages at most.
Hotel spa and day spa websites: day passes, facilities and outside guests

Hotel and resort spas sell to two audiences: hotel guests, who already have a room, and locals, who need to know whether they can come at all. A dedicated page answers that: day passes and what they include, pool and sauna hours, age limits, what to bring, parking and the entrance to use. For spas that welcome visitors from abroad, the menu and booking pages are translated with their own addresses, so a guest searching in German or Spanish finds a page in that language.
Calm, premium spa website design that still loads fast

Spa sites often look calm and load slowly: full-screen video, huge photos, three fonts. The design I build keeps the mood and drops the weight — your own rooms and treatment details photographed in natural light, two typefaces, a soft palette with one color kept for the Book button, generous spacing, and images compressed and loaded as the guest scrolls. On a phone, the menu, the voucher button and directions are reachable with the thumb.
Day spa or med spa website: wellness treatments without medical claims

A day spa sells relaxation and care; a med spa sells medical aesthetic treatments under a medical director, with consent forms, provider credentials and before-and-after rules. Mixing the two on one site confuses guests and invites claims a wellness business should not make. If you offer injectables or laser treatments, those belong on a separate site or section built for that purpose, described on my
med spa website design

children.text: I provide startup website design together with development: I design the pages and build them myself, so one person and one price cover both. A startup site changes faster than any other kind of website — the message shifts after the first fifty customer calls, a pricing plan appears, a new integration ships — so the design has to work on launch day and still hold together six months later.
Startup website design for an MVP or pre-launch product
Before the product is ready, the website has one job: explain the problem well enough that the right people leave an email. A pre-launch site needs less than founders expect:
one sentence that names the problem and who has it, and a second one that says how the product solves it
a picture of the product — a real early screen or a careful mock-up, labelled as a preview
one action: join the waitlist, request early access or book a call
who is building it, with names and faces, because early users and investors both check

Everything else — feature grids, testimonials, a blog — waits until there is something true to put in it. Placeholder logos and invented quotes on a pre-launch site are noticed, and they cost trust exactly when you have the least of it.
Landing page for startups: a waitlist page that collects the right signups
A landing page for startups is usually the first thing paid ads, launch posts and investor emails point to. A waitlist page works when it qualifies people as well as counts them:
a short form — email plus one or two questions such as role or team size — so you know who signed up
an honest promise of what happens next and when
signups sent straight into your email tool or CRM, with the source of each one recorded
a separate version of the page for each campaign, when messages differ, so you can see which one works
How I build landing pages for any kind of business, startups included, is on the

page.
Website design for a startup: what the best startup websites show on the first screen
Lists of the best startup websites are full of beautiful animation, but the sites that convert share plainer decisions. On the first screen, without scrolling:
what the product does, in the words buyers use — “Invoices that chase late payments for you”, not “The future of finance”
who it is for, when that is not obvious from the first line
one main button — start free, book a demo or join the waitlist — and at most one quieter second option
a real screen of the product, not an abstract illustration

Inspiration boards on Dribbble and Pinterest show attractive screens, but they are made to be admired. Website design for a startup is tested by a different question: can a stranger repeat what you do after five seconds?
Product screenshots, demo video and interactive demo in startup web design
Buyers want to see the product before they give an email. The design plans how it is shown:
screenshots cropped to the part that matters, with a short label, instead of a full dashboard at thumbnail size
a demo video of a minute or two, with captions, because many people watch with the sound off
an interactive demo or a sandbox account, when the product is easier to try than to explain
Screens change with every release, so they are kept as separate images or components that can be replaced without touching the layout.
Pricing page design for a startup: plans, limits and the next step
Buyers who reach the pricing page are close to a decision, and an unclear table is where many of them leave. A pricing page that works:
two to four plans, each named for who it is for, with the limits that differ written out
monthly and yearly prices, with the difference shown in money, not only as a percentage
a clear answer to “what happens when I go over the limit”
short answers to billing questions — trial length, cancellation, invoices, VAT — under the table

If the price is not settled yet, the page can show plans without numbers and a “talk to us” button, but the plans and limits should still be there. Buyers and AI assistants both treat a missing pricing page as a warning sign.
Pages for investors on a startup company website

Investors usually open the site after reading the deck. They are checking whether the company is what the deck says. Startup company website design takes this into account without turning the site into a pitch:
an about or team page with real names, roles and links to professional profiles
a press or news page with dated announcements, once there is something to announce
a media kit — logo files, product screens, a short description — so journalists and partners use the right ones
traction numbers only if you are ready to make them public and keep them updated
A design system for a startup website that grows with the product

A startup site that starts with five pages often has fifty a year later: use cases, integrations, comparisons, changelog, careers. Designing each page by hand does not scale. I build the site from a small set of components — section types, cards, pricing tables, screenshot frames, forms — defined once in code with shared colors, type sizes and spacing. A new use-case page is then assembled from existing parts in hours, and a change to a button style updates every page at once.
Analytics and events from day one on a startup website
Founders often add analytics after launch and lose the first months of data. In the design stage I list the actions that matter and track them from the first day:
waitlist and signup submissions, with the campaign or page they came from
clicks on start free, book a demo and pricing plan buttons
demo video plays and how far people watch

These go into GA4 and Google Search Console, or into the product analytics tool you already use, such as PostHog, Mixpanel or Amplitude. In the EU, a consent banner is part of the design, not an afterthought.
Webflow or Framer vs a custom Next.js site for a startup

Webflow and Framer are good tools. If the team has no developer, the site is a few pages and marketing needs to change text daily, one of them may be the right choice, and I will say so. A custom Next.js site pays off when:
the marketing site should share components, styles or data with the product, which is often built in React
you plan dozens of use-case, integration or comparison pages generated from data
you need several languages, custom forms or integrations without per-feature add-ons
speed matters: main content under 2.5 seconds on a phone, with no builder scripts on every page

contentBlocks.title: How I build it

children.text: The site has to change as often as the product

Early-stage companies have a website problem that established ones don't: the thing being described keeps moving. Positioning gets rewritten after customer calls, the target segment narrows, the pricing model changes, features that seemed central turn out not to be. A site built to describe the product accurately on launch day is describing something else within a quarter.

That reframes the requirement. The question isn't how good the first version is — it's how cheaply the tenth version happens. Which comes down to two things: who can change the copy, and what the platform allows.

On the first, the answer should be whoever owns positioning, without a deploy and without an engineering ticket. If changing a headline requires a developer, the site drifts out of date quietly, and the drift is invisible until someone external points it out. Content in a CMS solves this completely and costs nothing to build in from the start.
On the second, the usual early decision is
a website builder

, and at the beginning it's often correct — being live this week beats being ideal next month. It stops being correct at a specific and predictable point: when you need real content structure, technical SEO beyond the basics, or any integration the platform didn't anticipate. By then the site has accumulated links and rankings, and moving means
a migration
rather than a rebuild. Choosing a stack you'd be comfortable owning avoids that step entirely. The same forward planning applies to
language versions
— building the structure in from the start costs far less than adding it after the fact.

Search deserves attention earlier than most founders give it, for a reason specific to new companies: a new domain has no authority, so it can't win on strength. Structure is the only thing available early, and it compounds — pages built correctly at launch accumulate, while pages built badly need redoing before they can. That includes
readiness for AI assistants
, which increasingly answer specific questions with a short list rather than a page of links. My own site is the working demonstration of that:
a client found me through ChatGPT
rather than a search engine, and everything the assistant repeated back was simply what the site states plainly about itself in structured form.

And then ownership. Startups hire engineers. When yours arrives, the site should be something they can take over — your repository, a stack they recognise, decisions documented. The alternative is a conversation where the first recommendation of your first technical hire is to throw away the site you paid for.
A rushed redesign
carries the same risk — which is why it's worth planning one in advance.

children.text: Tattoo website design is my service for tattoo studios and independent artists who want their work, their artists and their booking rules on a site they own, not only in an Instagram grid. I plan, design and build it myself, at a price fixed before work starts, and at launch the studio manager gets an admin panel for new work and dates. A good tattoo shop website does three jobs: it shows a stranger enough of the right work to trust you, it filters out requests your artists would turn down, and it turns a serious request into a paid deposit and a date.
Does a tattoo shop need a website when Instagram already shows the work?

Instagram is where most clients first see an artist, and it should stay that way. A feed, though, is made for scrolling, not for deciding. Someone who wants a fine line botanical piece on the forearm has to dig through months of posts, stories and giveaways to find three examples, and older work slips out of sight even when it is your best.
Your own tattoo shop website adds what the feed lacks:
a page that comes up when someone searches “tattoo shop” or “fine line tattoo” with your city, which a profile rarely does
work grouped by style and by artist, kept for as long as you want it
deposit, cancellation, age and aftercare rules written out in full, in one place
a booking request that arrives with the details an artist needs, instead of “how much for a small one?” in DMs
an address that survives a restricted or hacked account
Instagram keeps feeding the site. Each artist page links to their profile, and the best posts are moved into the portfolio with a tag, so the site never depends on an embedded feed.
Tattoo portfolio by style: fine line, blackwork, realism, traditional and Japanese
Clients pick a tattoo artist by style before anything else, so the portfolio follows the way they search. Every photo carries two tags, the style and the artist, and the gallery filters by either:
the styles your studio really does — fine line, blackwork, realism, American traditional, neo-traditional, Japanese, lettering, dotwork, color, cover-ups
placement where it helps: sleeves, back pieces, small work on hands and fingers
healed photos next to fresh ones and marked as healed, because a fine line piece six months on is the picture that convinces a careful client

Photos go online with the client’s consent. The style list comes from your studio, not from a template’s categories: if a style is missing from the filter, visitors assume nobody in the studio does it.
Tattoo artist pages for residents, guest spots and flash days

Each artist gets a page under the studio’s address: a photo, the styles they take on and the ones they decline, years in the trade, the languages they speak and one status line — books open, closed or waitlist only. A request sent from that page already names the artist.

Guest artists get the same kind of page for the dates they work with you. A short calendar lists upcoming guest spots and flash days with the artist, the dates and how booking works: requests in advance, or first come, first served on the day. Flash sheets can be published with fixed prices and marked as taken once tattooed, so nobody asks for a design that is gone. After a guest leaves, the page stays as an archive of the visit or points to the artists page.
A tattoo booking request form: placement, size, references and budget
Most custom work starts with a conversation, not an instant slot, so the site collects a request first. The form asks what an artist would ask in the first three messages:
the idea in a few sentences, and whether it is new work, a cover-up or a touch-up
placement and approximate size in inches, with a simple body outline to tap for those who are unsure
up to five reference images uploaded from the phone
color or black and grey, a budget range picked from options, the preferred artist and the dates that suit
confirmation of age and the contact the client prefers for the reply

Requests reach the studio inbox in one readable format, tagged by artist, or go into your tattoo studio software where it accepts them. An artist with a full waitlist closes their form with a short note, and requests flow to the others.
Tattoo deposits paid online, with a policy clients read first

Once an artist accepts a request, the client gets a link to pay the deposit with a card or a phone wallet, and the date is held when the payment clears. I built the same pay-then-confirm flow for Landi Room, a Warsaw beauty salon: buyers of its online course pay via Stripe Checkout and a protected video unlocks on its own, and the course passed 100 sales on the very first Google Ads campaign. For a studio, the payment holds a date instead of opening a video.
The deposit policy sits right above the payment button in plain words, and the client ticks a box to accept it:
the amount, and that it comes off the price of the final session
how much notice a reschedule needs and how many times a date can move
what happens to the deposit after a no-show or a late cancellation
what happens when the artist has to cancel
The wording is yours; the site makes sure it is read before the card is charged, which settles most disputes before they start.
Aftercare, age and ID, and hygiene pages on a tattoo studio website

A few short pages answer what the front desk hears every day. The aftercare page holds your instructions — washing, the film or bandage you use, what to avoid in the first weeks — and its link goes to every client after the session, so a paper sheet is not the only copy. The age and ID policy states your minimum age and the documents you accept, as local law and your rules require. Where your state or county requires a license or health permit to be displayed, its number sits in the footer, next to a short note on how you sterilize equipment and use single-use needles. The rules come from the studio; the site makes them easy to find.
Image-heavy tattoo websites that still load fast on a phone

A tattoo site is mostly photos, and that is where slow sites come from: full-size images straight from a phone, autoplaying video, an Instagram widget pulling dozens of posts. On the sites I build, each image is resized for the screen that requests it and served in a modern format, galleries load as the visitor scrolls, and video plays only when tapped.

The site of Sasha Dith, a DJ and producer, is built this way on Next.js from his own Figma design: a video gallery, a discography and a booking form, loading in under one second after it replaced slow builder pages. children.text: I design and build therapist websites for psychologists, counselors, marriage and family therapists and small group practices — design, code and launch by one person, at one price. A private practice website is read by someone who is not sure they are ready to ask for help. Its job is to make the next step feel small: see who you are, recognize their own problem in your words and send a short message.
Therapist website design for anxious visitors: calm, slow and readable

Many visitors arrive late in the evening, on a phone, after weeks of hesitating. A busy page makes them close the tab. What I leave out: pop-ups asking for an email, chat bubbles, sliders, stock photos of people holding their heads, red buttons. What I put in: wide margins, a muted palette, type large enough to read without zooming, real photos of you and your room, and one accent color kept for the button that starts contact.

For Giuseppe, a psychologist and psychotherapist in Milan who works with anxiety and panic attacks, I made a custom calm design: a dark theme with light sections, a serif typeface with a true italic for quieter emphasis, and only open-licensed resources. It does not look like a template because it is not one.
What a private practice website shows on the first screen
Before scrolling, a visitor should know four things:
who you help, in their words — “Therapy for anxiety and panic attacks in Portland and online”, not “A safe space to grow”
whether you see clients in person, by video or both
whether you are taking new clients
the fee or insurance in one line, next to the button to get in touch
Your photo belongs near the top. People choose a therapist more than a practice, and a natural portrait in your own office tells them more than any headline.
The path from a psychologist website to the first session
The step people fear most is the first message. A short “what happens if I write” section on the contact page and the home page removes the guesswork:
You write a few lines: your name, how to reach you, in person or online.
You get a reply within the time stated on the page.
A short call to see whether we are a good fit.
The first session, with the fee and the cancellation policy known in advance.

Booking link or contact form? A scheduler from your practice-management system, such as SimplePractice, or a tool like Calendly suits therapists who offer a bookable consultation slot. Many prefer a short message first, so they can check fit before anything is scheduled. The site can offer both, with one of them clearly the main path.
Privacy on a counselor website: forms, email and HIPAA

A message to a therapist often says more than the sender meant to share. The form asks for little — a name, an email or phone, in person or online, a convenient time — with a line asking people not to describe symptoms. Where a real intake form is needed, it runs through a provider that signs a business associate agreement, as HIPAA can require in the US, not through ordinary email.

The rest is plumbing visitors never see. Giuseppe’s contact form sends through mail on his own domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC records in place, so replies do not land in spam, and analytics starts only after consent. About five years ago I worked on a medical system built around patient records, under NDA; what stayed with me is to collect only what the site cannot do without. Your compliance adviser confirms the setup.
Template, website builder or a custom therapist website

Builders such as Wix and Squarespace and therapy-website vendors sell calm templates for a monthly fee. For a solo therapist with one office, no blog history and a handful of pages, that is often enough, and I will tell you so.

A custom site pays off when the practice outgrows the template: several clinicians or offices, a second language, a blog that already brings visits, wording rules you want enforced, or plans for many specialty pages. Before choosing any vendor, ask whether you can take your pages, posts and addresses with you when you leave.
Pages a private practice website needs: about, specialties, fees and FAQ
Beyond the home page, most private practice websites need the same small set of pages, each with one job and one button to get in touch:
an about page in the first person: license, training, how a session with you feels
specialty pages built from one template, so each reads and looks alike
a fees page: session length and price, insurance or superbills, cancellation policy
an FAQ with what people ask on the first call
a contact page with a map when you see clients in person
Giuseppe’s site has a map of his consulting rooms in Milan, Monza and Cernusco sul Naviglio, so each client sees at once which room is nearest and how to get there.
Online therapy pages on a therapist website: video sessions and other time zones

If you work by video, a separate page explains how it goes: the platform, what to prepare, a quiet room, how payment works and where you can legally see clients. For clients in other time zones, session times are shown in their local time, not only in yours. Giuseppe works with Italians living abroad; his site is Italian first, with an English version under /en where every URL is translated rather than copied.
Moving a therapist website without losing the blog: migration and 301 redirects

Many therapists have written for years on WordPress, and those posts carry their search history. On Giuseppe’s site I moved all 468 blog posts from WordPress to Next.js 16, with Sanity as the editor, and set 301 redirects from every old URL to its new address, so links and positions follow the posts. The new site also got seven pillar pages, 21 Italian subtopic pages and pages for Milan, Monza and online therapy. It took 44 working days from the first line of code to handover.

Before any move I list every existing address, match it to a new page, carry over titles and structured data, and check after launch that nothing returns an error. The same process is described on the
website redesign
page.
A CMS with guard rails: editing a therapy practice website safely

After launch you edit the site yourself, often late and in a hurry, so the editor should make mistakes hard. In Giuseppe’s CMS the editor warns him when a text contains wording Italian rules on advertising health services make risky: promised outcomes, patient testimonials, discounts, “free consultation”. Key pages cannot be deleted, and the address of a published page is locked, so fixing a typo cannot break links. He received an owner’s manual in English (69 pages) and Italian (71 pages), plus video walkthroughs.

For a US practice, the list of warnings comes from your own ethics code and board: “guaranteed”, “cure”, client quotes, claims about results. You decide the list; the editor reminds you of it every time you publish.
A therapist website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Assistants can only describe a practice whose facts they can read. The build takes care of that: pages delivered as text by the server, not assembled by scripts after loading; structured data for the practitioner, the practice, the conditions, therapies and services, and the Q&A; and explicit robots.txt rules saying which AI crawlers may read the site. Giuseppe’s new pages already appear in ChatGPT answers, and he found me by asking ChatGPT himself.

children.text: A site serving two markets that never meet

Logistics companies have an unusual problem: the website has two entirely separate audiences, and both are scarce. Clients with cargo to move, and drivers to move it. Most sites in this field are built for the first and treat the second as an afterthought in the footer — which, in an industry where finding drivers is as hard as finding contracts, wastes half of what the site could do. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.

On the client side, the recurring failure is the enquiry itself. Transport pricing depends on a specific set of facts: route, cargo type, weight, dimensions, dates, any special handling. A generic contact form gathers none of them, so
every enquiry begins with an exchange of emails establishing what a properly structured form would have asked once

. For some services the same inputs can produce an indicative figure immediately — I've built parameter-based calculators where a few selections return a price on the spot, and the principle transfers directly.

The second client-side gap is segmentation. Domestic haulage, international freight, refrigerated transport, oversized loads and hazardous goods aren't variations of one service — they're separate businesses with separate clients searching separate terms. A page called "our services" competes for none of them, while a page about oversized transport can rank for exactly the client who needs it.
Then there's what happens after the contract. Once cargo is moving, clients want to know where it is, and without any way to check, that question arrives by phone. A status lookup solves it cheaply —

And back to drivers. They search for work like everyone else, and they compare employers on concrete things: routes, equipment, how pay is structured, how often they're home. A recruitment section written for them, in the languages they actually speak, competes for attention in a market where every operator is short-handed.

matters here for a reason it doesn't elsewhere — the language your clients read and the language your drivers read may have nothing to do with each other.

children.text: The question every visitor is already asking

Travel agencies operate under a condition that most businesses don't: their customers can, in principle, do the job themselves. Flights and accommodation are a browser tab away, and everyone knows it. So every visitor arrives with an unspoken question — what does going through you actually add — and the site either answers it or loses to the alternative by default. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.

The answers exist, but they have to be made explicit. Knowledge of a destination that isn't in a search result. Itineraries with enough moving parts that assembling them alone is genuinely difficult. Someone accountable when a connection fails or a hotel doesn't match its photographs. Financial protection when a large sum is paid months in advance. None of these are obvious from a page listing tours with prices, and none of them persuade if they're implied rather than stated.

That last one deserves particular attention, because agencies consistently underplay it. Paying a substantial amount now for something that happens in six months is an act of trust that people are right to think about. Registration, guarantees and insurance are precisely what make it reasonable — and most agency websites treat them as compliance text for the footer rather than the argument they actually are.

Then there's where visitors come from. People search for places long before they search for agencies: what a trip somewhere involves, when to go, what it costs, whether it suits a family. An agency that publishes real knowledge about the destinations it works with appears in those searches — at the moment when someone is deciding where to go rather than who to book with. Publishing that knowledge feels like giving something away, and it's the most reliable way this business gets found. It's also increasingly what AI assistants draw on when someone asks for advice on a destination.

a visitor who can't compare on your site will do it somewhere they can

children.text: I do tree service SEO for tree care companies and arborists: search data, pages for removal, trimming, stump grinding and storm work, Google Maps, trust facts and AI answers. Tree work is dangerous, expensive and done on someone’s property, often a few feet from their house. What the customer fears most is not the price but the damage — a limb through the roof, a crew without insurance, a fine for cutting a protected tree. Most of tree service SEO comes down to answering those fears on the pages people find.
Tree service SEO keywords: how homeowners describe a problem tree

Homeowners rarely search in arborist terms. They describe what they see: “tree leaning toward house”, “dead tree removal”, “branches over roof”, “tree roots lifting driveway”, “tree fell on fence”. Next to these sit job searches — “tree removal near me”, “tree trimming service”, “stump grinding” — and cost searches such as “how much to remove a large oak”. Keyword research for a tree company maps all three:
problem pages that explain what a sign means and when it is urgent
job pages for removal, trimming, stump grinding, cabling and land clearing
cost answers inside the job pages, with the factors that move the price
the towns and suburbs your crews reach, with the ones people search by name used on the pages
Tree removal pages: hazardous trees, crane work and removal cost

Removal is the biggest job and the most searched one. A removal page explains how you take a tree down close to a house: climbing and rigging it down in sections, working from a bucket truck, or bringing a crane for the largest trees and tight backyards. It also answers the cost question with the factors you really price by:
height and trunk diameter
how close the tree stands to the house, the neighbor’s property or power lines
access for a bucket truck, crane or chipper
whether stump grinding, log removal and cleanup are included
If you do crane removals, give them their own page. Few companies own the equipment, the searches are fewer and every job is large.
Tree trimming and pruning pages: clearance, deadwood and timing

Trimming is the repeat business of a tree company. Searches run from “tree trimming near me” to “when to trim oak trees” and “how much to prune a large maple”. A trimming page says what you remove and why — deadwood, crossing branches, limbs over the roof, clearance for driveways and trucks — and gives the timing rules customers ask about. Where oak wilt is present, pruning oaks during the growing season is discouraged, and many species are best pruned while dormant. Topping, which many homeowners still ask for, deserves a short, polite explanation of why you offer crown reduction instead. Pages like this show the customer that your crew knows trees, not only saws.
Stump grinding and land clearing pages for tree service companies

Stump grinding is searched on its own — “stump grinding near me”, “stump removal cost” — often by people who cut the tree themselves or whose last contractor left the stump behind. The job is small, fills gaps in the schedule and is usually quoted per stump or by diameter. Land and lot clearing is the opposite: few searches, mostly from builders and owners of rural lots, and large jobs. Both deserve a page, each with photos of the machine and the finished ground.
Emergency tree service SEO: storm damage and fallen trees

After a thunderstorm, an ice storm or a hurricane, searches like “tree fell on house”, “emergency tree removal” and “storm tree cleanup” jump in the affected towns. The calls go to companies whose emergency page already ranks and whose phone gets answered. An emergency page for a tree service states:
what you do first — make the site safe, take the weight off the roof, clear the driveway
your real hours: around the clock, or same-day callbacks
how emergency work is priced compared with scheduled work
that homeowner’s insurance often covers removal when a tree damages a structure, and that the customer should check their own policy
If you do not take night calls, say so on the page and in the Google profile. A customer who knows you will call back at seven waits; one who hears nothing calls the next number.
ISA certified arborists, insurance and permits: trust facts on a tree service website
Before letting a crew climb above their roof, customers check. Tree service websites that rank and convert put the checkable facts in plain text:
ISA Certified Arborist credentials with the certificate number, which customers can verify with the International Society of Arboriculture, and TCIA membership or accreditation if you have it
liability and workers’ compensation insurance, with certificates sent on request

a permits page: many cities and counties require a permit to remove trees above a certain trunk size, protected species or trees in historic districts, and HOAs add their own rules — explain in general terms how you help and link to the official city page
photos of your own crew, trucks and equipment instead of stock images
These are also the facts AI assistants look for when they decide which company to name.
Local SEO for tree service companies: Google Maps without a storefront
Most tree companies work from a yard that customers never visit, so the Google Business Profile is a service-area profile with the address hidden. Local tree service marketing on the map depends on:
“Tree service” as the primary category, with secondary categories only for work you really do
a service area made of the towns your crews reach in a working day
photos from jobs — the tree before, the rigging, the clean lawn after — added through the year
reviews that mention the job and the town, requested while the crew is still loading the chipper
The rest of the map work — listings, review replies, fake competitors — is on the
local SEO services
page.
Tree service leads vs SEO: shared leads, job size and the work you want

“Tree service leads” is searched more often than “tree service SEO”, and many companies buy them from Angi, Thumbtack, HomeAdvisor or through Google Local Services Ads. With bought tree leads, the bigger problem is often the mix rather than the price: many are small trims and price checks sent to several companies, while your climbers and crane wait for a large removal. SEO lets you pick the work. Pages for crane removals, hazardous trees and land clearing bring the jobs your equipment was bought for, and the calls are not shared with anyone.
Many tree companies keep Local Services Ads for steady volume and use SEO to move the mix toward larger jobs over a season or two.
Tree service advertising ideas that feed your search results
Some of the best tree service advertising happens offline, and it works harder when search backs it up:
truck wraps, yard signs and door hangers on neighboring houses during a job — people then search your company name, and that search should show your site, your profile and your reviews
short videos of removals and crane lifts on YouTube, embedded on the matching job page
referral partners — roofers, fence builders, property managers — linking to your site
a mention on a local news site or a city page after storm cleanup work
Each of these adds searches for your name and links to your site, and both help the map and the website rank.
Seasonality in tree service SEO: storms, dormant pruning and winter removals

Tree work does not peak only in spring. Storm seasons — hurricanes from June to November on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, summer thunderstorms, ice storms in the North — bring emergency peaks. Winter suits removals and dormant pruning: no leaves, frozen ground that protects lawns, crews with free days. A tree company’s content plan follows its own region: storm pages checked and updated before the storm season, a winter tree removal page published in the fall, pruning-time pages before the dormant season starts.
Tree service SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Homeowners now type tree questions straight into ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews: “is my tree dead or dormant”, “who pays when a neighbor’s tree falls on my fence”, “how much does it cost to remove a 60-foot pine”. Some answers end with a few company names. Being one of them is the job of generative engine optimization (GEO), also called answer engine optimization (AEO), and for a tree service it rests on:
answers to tree-health and responsibility questions written by your arborist, with a name and credential under them
cost factors and typical ranges from your own jobs, in plain text
certifications, insurance and service area stated the same way on the site, the profile and listings
structured data marking the business as a tree service, with its services and area
I record what assistants say about your company at the start and again after a few months; the method is on the

page.

children.text: I design and build vacation rental websites for owners and property managers who want more direct bookings and less dependence on Airbnb and Vrbo. Design and build come from one person at one price. A direct-booking site has a harder job than a platform listing: the guest does not know you, has no platform guarantee to lean on and must decide to pay a stranger. Every page is laid out to make that first direct booking feel safe and the second one routine.
Why build a vacation rental website: direct bookings, lower platform fees and your own guests

Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking.com bring guests and charge for it, through service fees, commission or both, on every stay. They also keep the relationship: next year the same guest searches the platform again and may book the listing next door. Your own site changes that:
a direct booking carries no platform commission, only your payment provider’s fee and your booking software
with the guest’s consent you keep their email, so you can invite them back next season or offer an off-season rate
repeat guests, their friends and people who found you on Google can book without a middleman

For most owners a direct site sits next to the platforms rather than replacing them, and takes a growing share of returning and referred guests. Platforms have rules about sharing links and contact details with guests who booked through them, so check each platform’s terms before mentioning your site in messages.
Vacation rental website builders or a custom site: which to choose

The quickest way to create your own vacation rental website is the builder that comes with your property-management software. Guesty, Hostfully, Lodgify, OwnerRez and similar tools offer vacation rental website templates tied to their calendars and payments, and when people look for the best vacation rental website builder they usually mean one of these, or a general builder with a booking plugin.
A builder suits an owner with one or two properties who wants a working booking page this month. Its limits appear as the business grows:
the site lives inside the software subscription, so changing PMS usually means losing the website
the layout of property pages, search and area guides is fixed by the template
control over speed, structured data and search setup is limited
every owner on the same builder starts from the same few designs

A custom site is yours: domain, content and code stay with you whichever booking software you use, and the booking widget is placed where it converts best. It costs more at the start and pays off for managers with several properties, for owners who want direct bookings to be a real share of revenue and for anyone who has outgrown a template.
Vacation rental website design: property pages with photos, amenities, house rules and prices
The booking is decided on the property page, so vacation rental website design starts there. Each property page answers, in this order:
what and where: “Three-bedroom sea-view apartment, five minutes’ walk to the beach”
a gallery that walks through the place room by room, full screen on tap, with bedrooms and bathrooms labeled
sleeping arrangements as text: bedrooms, beds, sofa beds, cots
amenities grouped as guests check them: kitchen, workspace, parking, air conditioning, pool, pets
house rules, check-in and check-out times and how keys or codes are handed over
the calendar and the total for the chosen dates, with cleaning fees and taxes shown before the last step

Fees that appear only at checkout are a common reason guests abandon a direct booking. Where your city or region requires a registration or license number on listings, it goes on each property page as well.
Booking widget and availability calendar from your PMS or channel manager

A direct site must never double-book a property that is also on Airbnb and Vrbo. That is why the booking part normally comes from your property-management system or channel manager, which already keeps the platform calendars in sync. Most such tools offer a booking widget, a hosted booking page or an API for websites; which applies, and how far it can be styled, depends on the tool and your plan, and I check it before design starts.

The design then puts the widget where the decision happens: dates and guests beside the gallery, a fixed “Check availability” button on phones and a confirmation page saying what happens next. Without a PMS, the site can start with an inquiry form and a synced calendar and move to instant booking later.
Multi-property vacation rental websites: portfolio search for property managers
Managers with ten or fifty homes need a site that works like a small travel catalog:
search by dates, guests and area on the home page, showing only properties free on those dates
filters guests actually use: bedrooms, pets allowed, pool, sea view, parking, step-free access
area pages grouping the properties in each town or resort
a page for homeowners, if you also want to sign new properties to manage
Photos, descriptions, amenities and rates come from the PMS where it allows, so the team updates one place, not two.
Trust for a first direct booking: reviews, secure payment, deposits and cancellation
On a platform the guest trusts the platform. On your site they have to trust you, and they look for proof before entering a card number:
reviews imported through your PMS where it supports that, or quoted from Airbnb, Vrbo and Google with source and date — never invented or edited
who you are: a photo of the owner or team, a real address, a phone number or WhatsApp
payment through a known payment provider, clearly part of your booking software
the cancellation policy in plain words next to the price, not only in the terms
the deposit and damage policy: a refundable security deposit, a card hold, a damage waiver or insurance, and when money is returned
Which deposit and damage options are available depends on your booking software, payment provider and local rules; the design makes the one you choose visible before the guest pays.
Local area guides on a vacation rental website

Guests choose a rental by the place around it as much as by the property. Guides written by the owner — the bakery that opens at seven, the beach that stays quiet in August, where to park for the trail, what to do on a rainy day — help guests decide, give past guests a reason to return to the site and give search engines and AI assistants real local text. Each guide links to the nearby properties. Check-in instructions, Wi-Fi details and house manuals can sit in a private section for booked guests.
Bed and breakfast website design and B&B website builders
A bed and breakfast sells something different from a whole-home rental: rooms in a house where the hosts live, breakfast and the hosts themselves. Bed and breakfast website design reflects that:
the hosts on or near the first screen, with a few lines in their own words
breakfast described as it is: what is served, when, and which dietary needs you cater for
a page per room, booked by room rather than by whole property
what guests should know before arriving: quiet hours, check-in window, children and pets

Bed and breakfast website builders and bed and breakfast website templates, often bundled with room-based booking systems, fit a B&B with two or three rooms. A larger guest house with a restaurant or events is closer to a small hotel;
hotel website design
covers that case.
Vacation rental SEO: being found in Google Vacation Rentals and search

Google shows vacation rentals in its own listings, with prices and availability. Properties get there through connectivity partners — usually channel managers and property-management systems that send Google your rates and availability — under eligibility rules Google sets. The website’s role is to be the official site those listings point to and the place where the guest completes the booking.

Ordinary vacation rental SEO does the rest: a page per property and per area with a clear title, VacationRental and LodgingBusiness structured data, fast pages and a Google Business Profile where your type of rental qualifies. “Apartments in [town] with parking” is a realistic target for a small site; “vacation rentals in [country]” usually is not. Ongoing search work for lodging businesses is described on the
hotel SEO
page.
A vacation rental website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Travelers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews for places to stay: “a dog-friendly cabin by a lake for six”, “an old-town apartment with a balcony and parking”. Assistants recommend what they can read and check. Bedrooms, beds, amenities, pet rules, distances and prices written as text, with structured data matching your platform listings, give them something to repeat; details locked inside a booking widget or a photo give them nothing.
Getting your properties into those answers is ongoing work, described on the
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.

Brief. You send the properties, photos, your PMS or channel manager, house rules and the questions guests ask most.

Launch. Redirects from any old site, structured data, analytics and a test booking before going live.

How much it costs to build a vacation rental website
Design is part of building the site, and the price covers both.
A simple vacation rental or B&B website for one or a few properties, with your booking widget: 700–1,400 €.
A vacation rental website for a portfolio of properties, with search, property and area pages, booking widget and search setup: from 2,000 €.
Booking software subscriptions and payment fees are paid to their providers and are not part of the price. Send your listing links and I will prepare a fixed quote; full price ranges are on the

Booking software and payment fees are paid separately to their providers. After a look at your listings I give a fixed quote.

children.text: I do veterinary SEO for independent clinics and animal hospitals myself — the clinic website, the Google Business Profile and the search data behind them — so the person who finds the problems is the one who fixes them. SEO for veterinarians is judged by booked appointments: the new puppy owner who books a vaccination series, the cat owner who chooses you for a dental, the call at 11 p.m. about a dog that ate chocolate.
Veterinary SEO for emergency searches: “emergency vet near me” and 24/7 care
A large share of veterinary searches is made in fear, on a phone, often at night. The phrases are short:
“emergency vet near me”, “24 hour vet”, “vet open now”
“dog ate chocolate”, “cat not eating”, “dog hit by car”
“after hours vet” with the name of a town

These searches show the map first, and Google checks the opening hours in your profile against the time of the search. If you are an emergency hospital, the website needs one page that says so in the first line, shows the phone number as a button, gives the address with a directions link and tells the owner what to do on the way. If you are not open at night, the page says who you refer to after hours. That is honest, and it still keeps your clinic in the owner’s mind for the follow-up visit.
Routine care pages in SEO for veterinarians: vaccinations, spay/neuter, dental and wellness plans
Planned care is searched calmly, and the owner compares two or three clinics. Each service with its own demand needs its own page:
Vaccination pages for puppies, kittens and adult pets
Owners search for “puppy shots”, “kitten vaccination schedule” and “rabies vaccine near me”. The page lists which vaccines you give, at what age the visits fall, and how to book the series.
Spay and neuter pages
Questions here are about age, recovery and cost. The page explains what happens on the day, how long the pet stays, what aftercare looks like and what the price includes.
Pet dental care pages
“Dog teeth cleaning cost” and “cat dental” are common searches. The page describes anesthesia, dental X-rays and extractions in plain words, without promising outcomes.
Wellness plan pages
If you sell monthly wellness plans, a page per plan with what is included and the monthly price turns a comparison search into a sign-up.
Species pages in veterinary SEO: dogs, cats and exotic pets

“Cat friendly vet”, “rabbit vet near me”, “avian vet” and “reptile vet” are searches that general pages do not answer. Many owners of rabbits, birds, reptiles or small mammals drive past three clinics to reach one that sees their animal. If your team treats exotics, a page for each group you see — with the vet who handles them and the services offered — is often the fastest way to rank, because few local competitors have one. A cat-only waiting area or a fear-free approach is worth a page too, since owners search for it.
Local SEO for veterinarians: Google Business Profile, categories and the map

For most clinics the map brings more calls than the website. The profile needs a primary category of “Veterinarian” or “Animal hospital”, whichever describes you better, with hours that are kept up to date, holiday hours included. Add the services you offer, real photos of the clinic and team, and an appointment link that goes to your booking page rather than the home page. Clinics with several locations get one profile per location, each linked to its own page on the site. Name, address and phone must be the same on the site, the profile and directories.
Pet owner reviews in SEO for veterinary clinics

Pet owners read reviews closely, and reviews also move a clinic up the map. A steady routine works best: the client gets a text with a direct review link after the visit, every review gets a reply within days, and replies never confirm medical details about the pet. Negative reviews after a lost patient are part of veterinary work; a calm, private follow-up does more than an argument in public. Bought reviews and asking only happy clients break Google’s rules, so neither is used.
Online booking and reminders in veterinary SEO: PetDesk, Vetstoria and the clinic site

Many clinics already use an online booking or client communication tool such as PetDesk or Vetstoria, connected to their practice-management software. For SEO it matters where booking sits: a link from the profile, a button on every care page and a widget that does not slow the page. Reminders for vaccines and annual checks bring clients back without search, so the website’s job is to win the first visit. I also set up tracking so organic search appears as its own source of bookings.
Pet health articles and YMYL: content reviewed by a veterinarian

Articles about symptoms, toxic foods, medication or post-surgery care touch the health and safety of animals, and Google’s quality guidelines hold this kind of content to a higher standard. Pages of this type should:
name the veterinarian who wrote or reviewed them, with their degree and a link to their profile on your team page
show the date of the last review and be checked again when advice changes
tell the owner to call the clinic, not treat the pet from the article

This is not medical advice on the website’s part; it is a clear route from a worried search to your phone. A small library of reviewed answers to the questions your front desk hears every day is often the best content a clinic can publish.
SEO for independent veterinary practices competing with VCA, Banfield and other corporate groups

Corporate groups such as VCA or Banfield have strong brands, hundreds of location pages and budgets to match. An independent practice wins on what a template location page cannot show: the names and faces of its vets, how long they have served the town, the species and services they really handle, and reviews that mention them by name. Detailed care pages, a real team page and a well-kept profile let a single clinic outrank a chain location for its own neighborhood.
Veterinary SEO and AI search: visibility in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Pet owners now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews “which vet near me treats rabbits” or “is it an emergency if my dog is vomiting” before they open any website. Getting a clinic into those answers is called generative engine optimization (GEO) or answer engine optimization (AEO). For a veterinary practice it means:
services, species, hours, emergency policy and the vets’ credentials written as plain text an assistant can quote

children.text: A website used at the worst moment of someone's week

Veterinary websites are visited under conditions that don't apply to most businesses. A significant share of visits happen when someone is frightened about an animal, often late in the evening, on a phone, with no patience for navigation. That single fact should shape the entire structure: whether you're open right now, the phone number and how to reach you belong in the first thing a visitor sees, not behind a menu. The same goes for
booking the visit
— it should be one tap away, not a phone call during business hours.

The rest of the site serves a calmer visitor, and there the structure differs from human healthcare in a specific way. Owners don't search by treatment first — they search by animal. A person with a rabbit or a parrot looks for a clinic that treats rabbits or parrots, because plenty don't, and a clinic that hasn't said so simply isn't in that search. Species and specialisation pages catch searches that a general services page cannot. Getting found for those searches is
ongoing SEO work
, not a one-time setup.

Price is unavoidable here in a way many clinics wish it weren't. Veterinary care is paid for directly, often unexpectedly, and owners search for specific procedures alongside their cost. A clinic that gives a range for common procedures does two things at once: it appears in those searches, and
it stops fielding calls that were only ever about price

Then there's preventive care, which is where the long-term value sits. Vaccination schedules, what a young animal needs and when, routine checks by age — this content reaches owners before anything is wrong. That's both the moment a relationship with a clinic begins and, increasingly, the kind of question people put to an AI assistant rather than a search box, which makes clear structured content on your own site worth more than it used to be.

One part deserves particular care rather than optimisation. Every clinic offers services around the end of an animal's life, and those pages need a different register entirely — quiet, factual, without marketing language. Handling that well says something about a practice that no amount of copy about compassion can. This is what

children.text: I design veterinary websites for clinics and animal hospitals and build them myself, so design and build come from one person at one price. Veterinary website design is about what a pet owner sees and does in the first seconds — sometimes calmly booking a puppy’s first shots, sometimes holding a phone in one hand and a bleeding dog in the other. Every page is laid out so that each of those owners finds their action without reading what is meant for the other.
Veterinary website design for two paths: the emergency and the routine visit

The same site is opened by two very different people. One has a pet that ate something toxic, was hit by a car or cannot breathe properly. This person scans for a phone number, whether you are open now and how to get there. The other wants a vaccination, a spay appointment or a dental check and is comparing clinics on the team, the prices and how the place looks.
The design keeps the two paths apart:
the emergency path is one clearly marked button — “Emergency? Call now” — that leads to the phone, the address with directions and two or three things to do on the way
if you do not see emergencies, or not at night, the same place says where to go instead and when you open
the routine path is a calmer “Book an appointment” button that leads to booking, never to the emergency page
the two buttons look different, so nobody has to think which one is theirs
Mobile veterinary website design: what the first screen shows on a phone
Most owners open a clinic site on a phone. The first screen carries four things and nothing else:
what you are and where: “Veterinary clinic for dogs, cats and exotics in [your town]”
today’s opening hours and whether you are open now
the emergency button and the booking button
one real photo of your team or clinic

Sliders, slogans and welcome letters move further down or go. The call and booking buttons stay fixed at the bottom of the phone screen on every page, within reach of the thumb. On a desktop the phone number and hours sit in the top right of the header, where people look for them.
Warm but clear veterinary website designs: color, type and accessibility

Veterinary website designs often lean on paw prints, cartoon animals and pastel colors. Warmth is right for a place people trust with a family member, but it must not get in the way of reading. The design aims for warm and clear at once:
a calm palette with one strong color kept only for the emergency button
body text at 16 pixels or larger, short headings and one idea per paragraph
contrast between text and background that meets the WCAG accessibility guidelines, since many clients are older owners
form fields with visible labels, large tap targets and alt text on every photo
decoration kept to the edges: a paw icon in a corner does no harm, a paw pattern behind text does
Your logo and clinic colors carry the brand; the emergency color is chosen for visibility first.
Real team and pet photos in veterinary website design, with owner consent

A stock photo of a smiling model holding a golden retriever is recognized at once and says nothing about your clinic. Owners want to see the vets and nurses who will handle their animal, the waiting room, the consulting rooms and real patients. Those photos also help a nervous owner recognize the person who comes out to the waiting room.

Patient photos need the owner’s permission. A short consent line on the intake form, or a simple form at the desk, covers it; the pet’s name is shown only if the owner agrees. Surgery and injury photos stay off the public pages. Phone photos in daylight are enough; I give your team a short shot list: each vet and nurse, the building from the street, the rooms, and a few calm patients.
Species sections in veterinary website design: dogs, cats and exotic pets
A rabbit owner and a cat owner look for different signs that a clinic is right for them. Species sections let each one go straight to their animal:
a clear “Dogs · Cats · Exotics” choice near the top of the home page, as text, with simple icons
a page for each species with the services you offer for it and the vet who leads that work
for cats, a note on a separate waiting area or a calmer approach if you have one
for exotics, the list of animals you really see — rabbits, birds, reptiles, small mammals — so owners do not need to call to ask
Where online booking, pharmacy and food ordering go in a veterinary website design

Most clinics use an online booking or client communication tool, such as PetDesk or Vetstoria, and many offer an online pharmacy or prescription food ordering through a partner. These help only if owners see them when they need them:
booking as the second button in the fixed bar on phones and at the end of every routine care page
never on the emergency page, where it would suggest that a poisoned dog can wait for a slot
pharmacy and food ordering in the header menu and on the page for existing clients, not on the first screen for new ones
each external tool styled to match the site as far as it allows, with a line saying where the owner is going
How the site is structured, connected to your practice-management and booking software, hosted and kept fast is covered on the
veterinary clinic website
page.
Pricing transparency on veterinary websites: exam fees, vaccines and wellness plans

Cost is one of the main reasons owners delay a visit. A clinic does not need to publish its full fee schedule, but a page or a section that shows the exam fee, the price of a vaccination visit, a range for spay and neuter, and the monthly price of each wellness plan answers the first question before the phone rings. Where a price depends on weight or tests, say what it depends on. If an emergency exam has a separate fee, it belongs on the emergency page, stated calmly.
What the best veterinary websites have in common
Lists of the best veterinary websites mix large hospital groups with single clinics. The decisions that make the good ones work fit any practice:
one sentence on the first screen saying what the clinic is and where
an emergency path and a booking path that never get mixed up
real photos of the team and patients, and a page for each vet
a page for each main service and each species
hours, address and prices that can be read, not guessed
a site that reads as easily on an older phone as on a new one
Veterinary website design templates vs custom design

A veterinary website design template, free or paid, looks good in the demo: perfect photos of puppies, invented reviews, a neat services grid. Collections of pet clinic website templates show many of them. With a real clinic’s content the gaps appear — no separate emergency path, one page for all services, nothing for species, a contact form instead of booking. Free veterinary website design offers from builders work the same way: the design is free, the decisions are left to you.

A template is a fair start for a small new practice. A custom design is worth it when you see emergencies, treat several species, run more than one location or want new clients from search. Moving off a template later usually means designing from the beginning.
Choosing a veterinary website design company

Veterinary website design companies range from vendors that bundle a website with their booking or communication product, to agencies that build vet sites from one template, to single designers and developers like me. Questions to ask any of them:
Who owns the website, the domain and the content if we stop working together?
Can we change the layout of the emergency and booking paths, or only the colors?
Will the site use our photos and our vets, or the vendor’s stock library?
Who updates opening hours and prices, and how fast?

My process: you send services, hours, species and photos; I design the first screen, an emergency page and a routine care page on a phone screen; we agree them; the rest of the site follows the same system and is built by me. If you already have a site and want a new design without losing your Google positions, the

process keeps addresses and redirects in place.
A veterinary website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

More owners ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to suggest a vet nearby or to say whether a symptom is urgent. Assistants work from text, not pictures. A design that keeps hours, species, prices and the vets’ credentials inside images hides them; the same facts set as real text, with structured data for the clinic, its services and its vets, can be read and repeated.
