children.text: Why websites in Cyprus so often fail to bring enquiries

Most Cyprus business sites are built as brochures: a homepage, an «about us», a services page listing everything in one block, and a contact form. They look finished and they rank for the company name, which is the one query where the company would be found anyway. Nothing on them answers the question a buyer actually types, so nothing on them can be found by a buyer who does not yet know the company exists.

The second reason is language. A Cyprus business often serves three audiences at once — local Greek-speaking customers, English-speaking expats and residents, and Russian-speaking buyers and business owners — and a site built in one language with a translation plugin bolted on serves none of them properly. Search engines treat a half-translated site as a weaker version of itself, and a buyer who lands on a page in the wrong language leaves.

The third is speed and structure, which nobody notices until a competitor outranks them. A site on a page builder with twelve plugins loads slowly on the phone, where almost all of these sites are actually opened.
Web design in Limassol, Paphos, Larnaca and Nicosia

I work with companies across the island and remotely, which in practice is how most of this work happens anyway: the files, the content and the review all travel over the internet, and nobody has to drive to Limassol for a meeting about a heading. What differs between the cities is not the build but the audience.
Limassol — the largest concentration of international companies, shipping, professional services and Russian-speaking business; sites here almost always need English and Russian, often Greek too;
Paphos — tourism, property and a large expat population; English first, with Russian and German worth measuring before adding;
Larnaca — logistics, trades and local services, where the buyer is closer to home and the local-search side matters more than the language count;
Nicosia — government, finance, law and B2B, where the site is read by people checking whether the company is credible before they call.
Which languages a site actually gets is a question I answer with data rather than by habit: there is no point paying for a Greek version if nobody searches your service in Greek.
Website design in Cyprus: what goes into a business site
a page per service rather than one page listing all of them, because a buyer searches for one service, not for your catalogue;
structure planned around what people search, so each page has a query it can realistically be found by;
the languages your buyers use, as separate pages with their own addresses rather than a switcher that translates on the fly;
forms that reach you where you actually read messages, including WhatsApp, which in Cyprus is often the real channel;
speed on a phone, measured on the templates that carry the business, not on the homepage;
a content management system you can edit without calling a developer, because prices and services change.
Custom and bespoke web development in Cyprus: when a standard site is not enough

Some businesses here need more than pages. A property agency needs listings that filter by city, type and price, and that stay findable one by one. A law firm needs practice-area pages that read differently for a local client and for a foreign one. A hotel needs availability and a booking path. A school or clinic needs accounts and records.
That is custom development, and it is where most of my work sits: listings, filters, user accounts, and data arriving from a system the client already runs. The technical side of it is
Next.js development
, and when the data has to come from somewhere else it is
CMS integration and API work
Website redesign in Cyprus without losing the rankings

If a site already brings some traffic, a redesign is the moment that traffic is most often destroyed. What protects it is unglamorous: a map of every existing address, a redirect for every address that changes, the structured data and the page speed carried over rather than rebuilt, and the old pages' text kept where it was earning. A redesign that skips this costs months of rankings, and rebuilding them costs more than the redesign did.

A site is not finished at launch; it is finished when somebody is responsible for it. Maintenance means updates and backups, fixing what breaks, and making the small changes a business needs every month — a new service, a new price, a new team member. Without it, a WordPress site becomes a security problem within a year and a custom site becomes impossible to change because nobody remembers how it works.

These are separate pages because they are separate jobs, not because it looks thorough. The questions a client asks before booking are different in each, and a site that answers the wrong set loses the booking while looking fine.
What every beauty website needs, whatever the format
a page per treatment with the price or a «from» price and how long it takes;
booking that lands in the system the front desk already watches, not a second one;
the people: who performs the work, with a photograph and a direct booking link;
your own photographs of the rooms and the work, not stock images;
speed on a phone, because that is where these sites are opened;
prices as text rather than as a photographed price list, or search and AI assistants cannot read them.
That list is short and it is most of the value. The differences below are what the format pages are for.
What actually differs between the formats
Multi-service salon

The hardest part is the treatment list: twenty or thirty items, several specialists, and a client who wants one of them. The structure has to let somebody arrive on «lash lift» and book it without passing through a general services page.
Hair studio and barbershop

The client books a person and a result they have seen. The portfolio has to be organised by what was done — balayage on dark hair, grey coverage, a specific fade — and tied to the stylist who did it, not presented as one undifferentiated gallery.
Day spa

Here the unit sold is often a package or a voucher rather than a single treatment, and a slot is frequently booked for two people. Both change what the booking has to support, and vouchers mean the site needs a way to sell and redeem them.
Aesthetic clinic

This is the format with rules. Pages have to state who performs the procedure and with what qualification, what the contraindications are and what the recovery looks like — and they must not promise a result. Advertising law in several markets limits what a clinic may claim, and a page written like a salon page is a liability rather than an asset.
Tattoo studio

Portfolio by style and by artist, because nobody books «a tattoo» — they book a style from a person. And a deposit, because no-shows cost a full session, which makes the deposit flow part of the site rather than a detail.
What a beauty website costs and what moves the price

A single-service landing page runs €700–1,400. A full website with treatment pages, prices, team profiles and online booking starts at €2,000. A redesign that keeps the existing rankings starts at €1,000. What moves the price: the number of treatment pages, whether booking has to integrate with an existing system, how many specialists get their own page, and how many languages. Design is included, never a separate line. The full list is on the
pricing page
How long a beauty website takes to build

A landing page takes two to three weeks, a full site three to six. What stretches it is the material rather than the code: photographs, the treatment list with prices and durations, and who on your side signs off on the text.

Some of it is administrative and boring: invoicing that fits Polish requirements, the payment providers customers here expect to see at checkout, the practical details of running a project with a company registered in this country. None of it is difficult, and all of it is friction when it's unfamiliar. This is what

contentBlocks.title: What I build

children.text: Booking is an operations decision, not a form
The distance between wanting an appointment and having one is where most bookings are lost.
Every step in between — finding the number, calling during working hours, waiting for a reply, agreeing a time
across several messages — removes a share of the people who were ready a moment earlier.

Online booking compresses that distance, but only if it's built as part of the site rather than attached to it. Embedded widgets from booking platforms are the common shortcut, and they carry three costs that surface later: they slow the page, they look and behave like a different product, and many of them insert themselves between you and your client — taking a commission and treating the client as theirs rather than yours. That's a reasonable trade for a business starting out, and a poor one for a business with an established client base.

The mechanics that matter are unglamorous. Availability has to reflect reality, which means syncing with whatever system your team actually works in rather than maintaining a second calendar. Confirmations and reminders have to be automatic, because reminders are the cheapest measure against no-shows there is. And where a booking should carry commitment, a deposit changes behaviour — people who have paid something turn up far more reliably. I've implemented Stripe payments on a client's site for exactly that purpose.
There's also a quieter question: what happens to the data. A booking form collects personal details, and
in some fields it touches health information
. Where that data goes, how long it stays and who can reach it are decisions worth making deliberately rather than inheriting from a plugin's defaults. This is what
website development
looks like when the structure comes first.

children.text: I build websites for contractors from start to finish — structure, design, development and launch — and the site is yours when it is done. A contractor website is not a brochure: it is where homeowners and property managers decide whether to call you, so it is built around calls and estimate requests, and around the way your office actually handles them.
What a website for contractors needs to bring calls and estimate requests

Most contractor websites have a home page, an “about us”, a list of services on one page and a contact form. That is enough to exist, not enough to be found or chosen. A contractor website that brings work has:
a page for each service — the jobs you want more of, not everything you have ever done
a page for each town or area you cover, with projects from there
projects with before-and-after photos, the job and the town
an estimate form that asks what you need to price the job and takes photos
licence, insurance, warranty and reviews shown as text
click-to-call and a request button on every page
How these pages look and lead a visitor to a call is covered on the
contractor website design
page.
General contractor websites: many services, one clear structure

A general contractor sells additions, remodels, basements, roofing and repairs to different people at different budgets. Put on one page, those services compete with each other and none of them is found. On a general contractor website every service gets its own page with scope, timing, a price range where you can give one and projects of that type, and each page leads to the same estimate request.
If you also build commercial projects or work for developers, those get their own section, so a homeowner looking for a kitchen remodel is not shown a warehouse.
Estimate requests that reach your office and your scheduling tool

The estimate form is built in short steps: type of job, address or postcode, timing, budget range, photos. Requests arrive by email with everything in one place, or go straight to where your office already works:
a CRM or shared inbox
a field-service or scheduling tool such as Jobber or Housecall Pro, through its own request form or booking link
a Google Sheet, if that is how your office keeps track
Calls from the website are tracked separately from calls from your Google profile, so you can see which one brings work.
Contractor website builder or a custom-built website

Website builders for contractors — general ones like Wix and Squarespace, or the site that comes with a field-service platform — put a page online quickly for a monthly fee. For a one-person business with one service in one town, that can be a fine start.
The limits show as soon as the business grows:
one services page instead of a page per service and area
a gallery instead of project pages that can be found in search
a slow site once it is full of job photos
a monthly fee for as long as the site exists, and a site you cannot take with you when you leave the platform
A custom-built website costs once, is shaped around how you sell, and the code, content and domain are yours.

Speed, hosting and maintenance of a contractor website

Customers look at a contractor’s site on a phone, often on mobile data. Pages are built to appear in under 2.5 seconds — the threshold Google uses for a good page — even with dozens of job photos, because images are compressed on upload, served in modern formats and loaded only when they come into view.
The site runs on fast hosting with SSL, automatic backups and spam protection on the forms. There is no monthly retainer: when something needs changing, you pay for the work done.
A contractor website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Homeowners increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews to recommend a contractor nearby. Assistants can only recommend what they can read and check. The site is built so the facts about your business are machine-readable from day one:

children.text: I build websites for electricians and electrical contractors, from the page plan to launch, and hand over a site that belongs to you. An electrician’s website has a narrow job: turn a search for a specific piece of work — a charger, a panel, a dead circuit — into a call or a request your office can schedule without phoning the customer back three times.
What electrician websites need: a structure built around jobs and calls

A typical electrician site is a home page, a list of services and a contact form. It exists, but it cannot be found for “EV charger installation” in your town, and it gives the office nothing to work with. The structure I build has:
one page for each job you want more of, each with its own request button
one page for each town or county you serve
a separate emergency page with the on-call number
a commercial section, if you do commercial work
license, insurance and service area stored once and shown on every page
a careers page, if you are hiring apprentices or journeymen
Service pages on a website for electricians: one page per job

The jobs electricians are asked for change with what people buy. An electric car brings an EV charger install and often a panel or service upgrade. A heat pump, a hot tub or a workshop brings a new circuit. Storm season brings standby generators and transfer switches. Older houses bring rewiring and inspections for buyers. Each of these gets a page built from the same template: what the job includes, what decides the price, whether a permit is needed, how long it takes and what you need from the customer.
The template is set up in the admin panel, so your office can add a new service page — smart home wiring, lighting design, surge protection — by filling in fields, without a developer.
Service-area pages for the towns and counties an electrician covers

An electrician’s map position is limited by distance, but the website can rank in each town you work in. Every area page lists the jobs done there, the response time for emergencies, the local permit office or utility where it matters and reviews from that town. The pages pull recent jobs automatically, so they stay current without anyone rewriting them. Pages that only swap the town name are not built — Google filters them out.
Request forms with panel photos, linked to ServiceTitan, Jobber or Housecall Pro
Half of an electrical estimate can be done from photos. The form asks, step by step, for:
the type of job and the address
a photo of the main panel with the door open, and of the label
for a charger: the car, where it will park and the distance to the panel
how soon the work is needed

Requests then go where your office already works. ServiceTitan, Jobber and Housecall Pro each offer online booking or request forms that can be placed on the site; where an API connection is possible, the website form sends the job straight into the tool. Otherwise the request arrives by email with the photos attached. Calls from the site are tracked on their own number, apart from calls from the Google profile.
Emergency electrician call button and after-hours routing

The emergency call button on every page dials the on-call phone, not the office line that goes to voicemail at five. After hours, the request form can send a text to whoever is on call, and the page says what happens next: who calls back, how fast and what the after-hours fee is. If you do not take night calls, the site says so clearly and offers a morning slot instead.
Electrical company website: commercial projects, capabilities and hiring

An electrical contracting company with commercial work sells to general contractors, developers and facility managers. They check a website after they hear your name, and they look for different things than a homeowner:
project pages by sector — retail fit-outs, offices, multifamily, light industrial — with the scope your crews handled
capabilities: design-build, service work, low voltage, lighting retrofits, maintenance contracts
license classes, insurance and safety practices, with documents available on request
a contact path for bids that is separate from the residential request form

A careers page with open positions for apprentices and journeymen, the license levels you hire for and a short application form sits in the same section. Electrical companies compete for licensed staff as well as for contracts, and a candidate checks the website just as a general contractor does.
Electrician website builder or a custom-built website

An electrician website builder — Wix, Squarespace, an AI site generator or the website that comes with your field-service software — gets a page live quickly, paid monthly. For a one-person shop that works one town and lives on referrals, that is enough to be found by name.
The limits show when you want more work from search:
templates with one services page, not a page per job and per town
forms that cannot take photos or send them to your scheduling tool
slow pages once you add job photos
a site that stays on the platform when you leave it, and a fee for as long as it exists
A custom-built site is paid once, follows the way your shop sells and schedules, and the code, content and domain are yours.
Speed, hosting and ownership of an electrician website

Your customers often open the site on a phone in a dark basement next to the panel, on a weak signal. Pages are built to load in under 2.5 seconds — Google’s threshold for a good page — by compressing photos on upload, serving them in modern formats and loading them only when needed.

Hosting is fast, with SSL, daily backups and spam filtering on forms. The domain is registered in your name, and you get admin access from day one. No retainer is required; later changes are billed per task.
An electrician website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

People now ask ChatGPT or Google’s AI Overviews whether a charger needs a permit, why breakers trip and which electrician nearby does panel upgrades. An assistant only names a business it can verify, so the build puts these facts where machines find them:
services, areas, license number and insurance as text, not inside images
structured data for the electrician business, each service and each area
short answers to cost, permit and safety questions on every job page
the same name, address and phone as in the Google profile and directories
Getting into those answers is ongoing work, described on the

page. Ranking in Google and the map for your jobs is covered on the

children.text: I build websites for plumbers and plumbing companies: a site for your own business that rings your phone when a pipe bursts and fills the rest of the week with water heater swaps, drain jobs and repipes. I plan, design, build and launch it, connected to the software you dispatch from, and the site is yours when it is done. This page is about how the site is built; how it looks to a customer standing in water is on the
plumbing website design
page.
What a website for plumbers has to handle: emergencies today, planned jobs next month

A plumbing business gets two kinds of work through its website, and they behave differently. Emergency calls — a burst pipe, a backed-up toilet, no hot water before work — come from someone who will phone the first plumber who looks available and close. Planned jobs — a new water heater, a whole-house repipe, a sewer line replacement — come from someone who reads, compares two or three companies and wants an idea of the price before calling.
A website for plumbers is built for both at once:
a short, fast path from any page to a phone call for emergencies
a page for every service you sell, with enough detail for the person who is comparing
a page for every town or suburb you send vans to
online booking for jobs that can wait a day, linked to the software your office already uses
The emergency path on plumbing websites: burst pipe and no-hot-water pages

Emergency searches are short: “emergency plumber”, “burst pipe”, “water heater leaking”, “sewer backup”. Each of these gets its own page that tells the visitor what to do in the next five minutes — where the main shut-off valve usually is, when to turn off the water heater, what not to flush — and then gives the number. Someone who has just stopped the water with your page’s help is very likely to call you.
Behind those pages the build takes care of the details that decide whether the call reaches a person:
the phone number is a tap-to-call link on every page, written the same way as in your Google Business Profile
after-hours calls go to the on-call plumber or an answering service, and the site says plainly which hours are covered
opening hours, including 24/7 if you offer it, are in structured data, so Google shows them correctly
website visitors see a tracking number, so you know how many emergency calls the site brings, while Google keeps seeing your main number
Plumbing service pages: drain cleaning, water heaters, sewer lines, repiping, leak detection
A single “Services” page with fifteen bullet points cannot be found for any of them. On plumbing websites that bring steady work, each service you want more of has its own page:
Drain cleaning — clogs, hydro jetting, camera inspection
Water heaters — repair, replacement, tankless installation, the brands you service and how fast you can swap a failed unit
Sewer line — camera inspection, repair, trenchless replacement where you offer it
Repiping — galvanised or polybutylene pipes, how long a whole-house repipe takes, whether the family can stay at home
Leak detection — slab leaks and hidden leaks behind walls, found without opening the whole floor

Each page answers the questions your dispatcher hears every day, shows jobs of that type and ends in the same two actions: call or book. Commercial work — restaurants, property managers, backflow testing — gets its own section, so a homeowner with a dripping tap does not land on a grease trap page.
Service-area pages for plumbers: one page for each town your vans reach

People search “plumber” plus a town or suburb, and Google prefers a page about that place. A service-area page is not the same text with the town name swapped — that gets ignored. Each one carries something real about the area: the typical housing and its pipes (older homes with cast-iron drains, new builds with PEX), jobs done there, how quickly a van usually gets there, hard water if it shapes your water heater work, and the permits or inspections the city or county asks for.
Area pages are generated from one template and a short entry per town, so when you hire another plumber and start covering a new suburb, adding it takes minutes, not a new project.
Online booking on a plumbing website through ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber

Most plumbing companies already run their jobs in field-service software. ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro and Jobber each offer an online booking tool or request form that can sit on your website, so a booked job lands on the dispatch board rather than in someone’s inbox. The build connects it properly:
the booking widget loads only on the pages that need it, so it does not slow the whole site
where the tool allows it, the service the visitor came from is passed into the booking, so the dispatcher sees “water heater replacement” rather than “general enquiry”
each completed booking is recorded as a conversion in analytics and Google Ads
without any of these tools, requests arrive by email or in a shared Google Sheet
Emergencies are kept out of online booking. A burst pipe should never be offered a slot two days away, so emergency pages lead to the phone only.
Flat-rate prices, price ranges and financing on a plumbing website

Customers want to know whether a job costs a hundred or a few thousand before they call. Plumbers who work on flat-rate pricing can show a starting price per job; others can show ranges — drain clearing, water heater replacement, whole-house repipe — with what pushes the price up. Even a range filters out calls that would never turn into jobs.

For larger jobs, a financing page explains the monthly payment option you offer through your financing partner and links to its application. Maintenance plans — a yearly water heater flush, a drain check, priority service — get a page of their own: they bring repeat work.
Speed of a plumbing website on a phone and mobile data

Emergency visitors open your site on a phone, sometimes in a basement with one bar of signal. Pages are built to appear in under 2.5 seconds — the threshold Google uses for a good page load — and the phone number and call link are in the first part of the page to load, before photos and scripts. Chat, review and booking widgets are loaded only when the visitor scrolls or taps.
Hosting includes SSL, daily backups and spam filtering on forms. There is no monthly retainer; changes after launch are paid as work done.
Plumbing website builders and platform sites or a website you own

Plumbing website builders — general ones, and the sites bundled with marketing platforms and field-service software — put a page online in a day for a monthly fee. For a solo plumber in one town who gets most work by word of mouth, that is often enough.
The problems appear when the business grows:
the template has one services page and no real way to add a page per service and per town
the content sits inside someone else’s account, and leaving the platform usually means starting again
pages slow down as the platform adds its own scripts
the monthly fee continues for as long as the site exists
A website you own is paid for once, grows with the business and moves with you to any host.

Brief. You send the services you want more of, the towns you cover, your hours, your software and the questions your dispatcher answers most.
Structure. I propose the list of pages — emergency, services, areas, prices, financing — and the path from each one to a call or a booking.
Design and build. Pages are designed on a phone first, then built and filled with your content.
Connections. Booking, forms, call tracking, analytics and your Google Business Profile are connected and tested with real calls and bookings.
Launch and hand-over. You get access to everything and a short guide to adding jobs and changing prices.

If you already have a website, every old address is mapped to its new page and redirected before launch, and the titles and structured data that already rank are carried over. The process is described on the

What the best plumbing websites have in common
Lists of the best plumbing websites usually pick sites by looks. Seen from the build side, the ones that bring steady work share a few plain decisions:
a separate page for each emergency, each service and each area, not one long list
a phone link that works on every page and loads first
booking connected to the dispatch software, not to an inbox nobody checks at weekends
prices or price ranges wherever the business can give them
a site the owner controls, so it can change when the business changes
A plumbing website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

People now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews things like “who can fix a slab leak near me” or “how much does a tankless water heater cost to install”. An assistant can only recommend or quote what it can read and check, so the site is built to hand it clear facts:
services, service areas, hours, license number and insurance written as text, not only inside images or badges
structured data for the plumbing business, each service and the areas it serves
answers to cost and how-to questions on the service pages, in plain sentences
the same name, address and phone as in your Google Business Profile and the directories you are listed in
Getting into those answers is ongoing work, described on the

page.

contentBlocks.title: What the migration includes

children.text: When a migration is worth doing — and what makes it safe

Most businesses don't migrate because they want to. They migrate because the current platform has stopped allowing something: the site can't be made faster, a needed feature only exists as a workaround, the language versions don't work properly, or every small change requires going around the system rather than through it. At that point staying costs more than moving.

The hesitation is almost always the same, and it's justified: the fear of losing rankings. That fear is well founded, because a badly executed migration does exactly that — and the damage is neither gradual nor self-correcting.
A client of mine had a redesign pushed straight to production without checks
addresses changed with no redirects, language versions ended up swapped, structured data disappeared
. Traffic started falling within two days and hadn't recovered a month later. Diagnosis and repair took two weeks, and the recovery took roughly another month after that.
What makes the difference isn't the platform chosen. It's whether the migration treats
the old site's search equity

as an asset to be transferred rather than a side effect that will hopefully survive. Concretely: a baseline recorded before anything moves, an address structure either preserved or mapped completely, metadata and structured data carried over deliberately, language versions rebuilt with correct routing, and the whole thing assembled on a staging environment before anyone sees it.
Done that way, a migration is unremarkable — which is the point.
I moved a Warsaw workshop
from an ageing platform to a custom-built WordPress theme:
the address structure stayed intact, the markup came across, the four language versions kept working
, and
mobile performance went from around 50 to 92
. The visible result was a faster, better site. The invisible result was that nothing was lost in the process, which is what the work was actually for. The same discipline applies when
a startup outgrows its first platform
Already migrated and traffic dropped afterwards?
See traffic drop recovery instead — this page is for a planned move, not a repair.
If the platform is staying and the site only needs to look and convert better,
that is a redesign
rather than a migration.

Bilingual psychotherapist website in Milan and Monza
— 468 blog posts moved off WordPress with every old URL still working.

children.text: That's the risk the whole process is designed around. Positions typically wobble for one to two weeks after any migration while search engines re-crawl, which is normal. A lasting drop is a sign of something specific going wrong — missing redirects, lost markup, broken locale routing — and those are exactly the things planned for in advance rather than discovered afterwards.

items.question: Will we lose our search rankings?

children.text: Usually yes, and it's the safest option. Where the old structure genuinely has to change, every old address is mapped to a specific new one, with nothing left pointing at the homepage or nowhere at all.

items.question: Can we keep our current addresses?

children.text: Yes, though builders rarely export cleanly — the markup is proprietary, some content is locked into blocks, and metadata often doesn't come across. In practice this means part of the migration is a rebuild. That's worth knowing before starting, because it affects both cost and timeline.

items.question: Our site is on a website builder. Can it be moved?

children.text: They're rebuilt with correct routing and markup on the new platform. This is the part of a migration that breaks most often and is hardest to spot afterwards, so it's checked explicitly rather than assumed to have worked.

items.question: What happens to our language versions?

children.text: It depends on the size of the site and how much has to be rebuilt rather than transferred. The assessment stage gives a realistic timeline — and includes an honest answer about whether migrating is worth doing at all, since sometimes the better move is fixing what you have.

children.text: I do winery SEO: the work that puts your tasting room, events and wines in front of people planning a day in wine country — in Google results, on Maps and in AI answers. A winery visit is usually planned ahead: a weekend away, a birthday, a bachelorette party, a client outing. The search starts days or weeks before anyone parks by your tasting room. I work alone and build websites myself, so whoever spots a slow page or broken markup on your site is also the one who repairs it.
Winery SEO keywords: how wine tourists search before a trip
Few people search for a winery by name until someone has told them about it. Before I write anything I collect search data for your region and your experiences, and the phrases fall into four groups:
region — “wineries in Paso Robles”, “best Finger Lakes wineries for groups”, “wine tasting day trip from Austin”
experience — “winery with food”, “dog-friendly winery”, “private tasting”, “vineyard tour and tasting”
events and venues — “vineyard wedding venue”, “winery live music this weekend”, “harvest festival”
the wine itself — “[your winery] pinot noir”, “where to buy [label]”, “[region] wines to try”

Region searches bring people who have not chosen a winery yet; experience and event searches bring people close to booking; wine searches bring people who already know you. The data shows where competition in your region is weakest, and that is where the work starts.
Tasting room SEO: experience pages that turn searches into reservations

Many winery sites put every tasting on one “Visit” page with a reservation widget. That page cannot rank for a private cave tour and a picnic tasting at the same time, and the widget alone tells search engines almost nothing. Each experience you sell gets its own page that states:
what is poured and how many wines, how long it lasts and the price per person
food, seating — indoors, on the terrace, among the vines — and group size limits
reservation policy, walk-ins, cancellation and minimum age
kids, dogs, accessibility and the walk from parking to the tasting room

These are the details people check before they book. A page that answers them gets the reservation; a page that leaves visitors guessing sends them to the next winery on the list. Group and corporate tastings deserve a page of their own: planners search with other words and book larger tables.
Wine tourism SEO: region, itinerary and getting-here pages

Wine tourists plan by region first. They search how to spend a day in a valley, where to stay and how to get between wineries without driving. A winery that answers those questions on its own site meets them before they have a shortlist. Useful pages: a one-day itinerary that includes your tasting room and the neighbors you are happy to recommend, directions from the nearest city and airport, ride and shuttle options, and the best months to visit. The aim is a page a visitor bookmarks, not a block of keywords around your name.
Estates with guest rooms or a cottage also compete in lodging searches, which follow their own rules; that side is covered on the
hotel SEO
page.
Google Maps for wineries: Business Profile, tasting room hours and reviews
For “wineries near me” and “wine tasting near me” the map decides most visits, and travelers often check it from the car. A winery profile needs:
“Winery” as the primary category, with secondary categories only for what you really run — a wine bar, a restaurant, an event venue
tasting room hours including seasonal and holiday changes, so nobody drives out to a closed gate
a reservation link that opens your booking page, and attributes such as outdoor seating or dogs allowed
new photos every few weeks: the tasting room, the vines through the seasons, events — not only bottles
a review request after each visit that asks guests to mention the experience they booked
If your tasting room is in town and the vineyard is elsewhere, each place that receives visitors needs its own accurate listing. The full routine for map listings is described on the
local SEO services
page.
Winery event SEO: weddings, concerts, harvest and release parties

Events bring people who would never search for a tasting. Each recurring event gets a permanent page — harvest party, summer concert series, release weekend — updated with new dates every year instead of a new page each time. A page that has gathered links and visits over several seasons ranks far better than one created three weeks before the date. Event structured data gives Google the date, place and ticket link.

Weddings and private events are a separate market with long research. Couples and planners search “vineyard wedding venue” with your region and compare capacity, season, rain plans, catering rules, nearby lodging and price ranges. A venue page that answers those questions and shows real weddings at your estate brings inquiries far larger than any tasting reservation.
Wine club pages in winery SEO: reaching people ready to join

Many people join a wine club at the tasting bar, but many go home and search first: “[winery] wine club”, “best wine clubs in [region]”, “is a wine club worth it”. If your club page is a sign-up form without text, review sites and comparison articles answer those questions instead of you. A club page that ranks states the tiers, bottles per shipment and how often, member discounts and tasting privileges, pickup parties and how to pause or cancel. Member-only pages stay out of search; the public page carries the facts.
Wine and vintage pages in winery SEO: your labels and where to buy them

After a glass at a restaurant or a bottle at a friend’s house, people search the wine’s name. A page for each current wine — varietal, vintage, vineyard, tasting notes, food pairing, awards with year and competition, price — catches that search. When a vintage sells out, its page stays up, marked sold out with a link to the next release, instead of turning into a 404 that throws away what it had earned. Where you cannot ship, the page names the stores and restaurants that pour the wine.
Alcohol advertising rules, shipping limits and age checks in winery SEO

Wine content follows rules that most local businesses never face. Advertising standards, health wording, direct shipping and age requirements differ by state and by country, and they change. SEO pages describe wines, places and experiences rather than drinking, avoid health claims and say plainly where you ship. If the site uses an age gate, search engines and AI assistants still have to reach the text behind it. Check the rules that apply to you with your compliance adviser; this is general information, not legal advice.
Seasonal winery SEO: harvest, holidays and the quiet months

Visits follow a calendar: spring openings, summer weekends, harvest in late summer and fall, holiday gift buying and a quiet winter in most regions. A page needs weeks to rank, so harvest and holiday pages go live a couple of months ahead. The quiet months are for rewriting experience pages, adding new photos and reworking the club page before the spring rush.
Winery SEO in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Travelers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews questions such as “which wineries near Napa take groups of twelve”, “dog-friendly wineries in the Willamette Valley” or “where can I do a cave tour with food pairing”. Assistants build those answers from pages they can read and check against other sources. The industry calls this work GEO, generative engine optimization, or AEO, answer engine optimization. On a winery site the work is concrete:
experiences, prices, group limits and policies on dogs and kids written as plain sentences, not only inside a booking widget
structured data for the winery, its tasting room, events and wines
the same name, address and hours on Google, Yelp, TripAdvisor, your reservation platform and regional wine trail sites
answers to common visitor questions on your own pages, signed by the winemaker or the owner
I save what assistants say about your winery at the start and compare it later with what they say after the changes, including which neighbors they suggest. More on the method:
AI SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Reservation platforms, wine trails and winery marketing agencies: where SEO fits

Reservation platforms such as Tock, Resy or Commerce7 have discovery pages of their own, regional wine associations list member wineries, and tour companies sell your tasting as part of a day trip. They all bring visitors, and they all keep part of the relationship. Your own site and profile are where a guest comes straight to you and can join your list. Winery marketing agencies often bundle SEO with social media, email and ads. Whoever you hire, ask whether reports show reservations, club sign-ups and event inquiries rather than rankings alone, and keep the website, domain and Google profile in your name.

children.text: Winery website design, as I do it, runs from the page plan to launch in one pair of hands: the visual design, tasting reservations, wine club and shop are drawn and coded by me for one agreed price. A winery site serves three visitors at once — the traveler checking whether the tasting room is open on Saturday, the club member changing a shipment and the couple looking for a venue — and each of them is usually on a phone.
Winery website first screen: tasting room hours, location and a reservation button
Drone footage over the vineyard looks good in a pitch and costs visitors their patience on a weak signal in the countryside. The first screen answers practical questions:
who you are and where — “Family winery and tasting room in the Russian River Valley”
today’s tasting room hours and whether walk-ins are welcome
a Reserve a tasting button and a Directions button
the next event, in one line
On phones, Reserve and Directions stay fixed at the bottom of the screen on every page. A video, if you have one, plays further down and only when the visitor scrolls to it.
Tasting reservations on a winery website: Tock, Resy, Commerce7 or a request form

Most wineries already take reservations in a system — Tock, Resy, Commerce7 or the booking module of their wine platform. The website does not replace it; it presents each experience clearly and hands the guest over with the right one selected. Depending on what your system allows:
a button per experience that opens the booking flow preset to that tasting
an embedded widget that loads only when tapped, so the page stays fast
a request form for large groups, limo parties and corporate tastings that need a call first

Experience cards share one layout — wines poured, duration, price per person, food, seating, minimum age, dogs — so a guest comparing a standard flight with a library tasting sees the differences at a glance. Deposits and cancellation terms appear before booking starts, not on the last step.
Wine club pages on a winery website: tiers, sign-up and member accounts

A wine club is often a winery’s steadiest income, and its page should work like a product page. Tiers sit side by side in a table: bottles per release, reds only or mixed, shipping or pickup, member discounts, complimentary tastings. A Join button leads into your wine platform’s club sign-up, and existing members get a visible link to log in, change their address, skip a shipment or choose their wines. Tasting room staff often sign members up on a tablet at the bar; the same page, built to work well on that tablet, saves them a separate tool.
Online wine shop on a winery website: selling where shipping is legal

Selling wine online is regulated: direct-to-consumer shipping is allowed in some states and countries, restricted or banned in others, and usually needs licenses and tax registration. Check the rules for your winery and each destination before the shop goes live. The design follows what you are allowed to do:
a shop connected to your wine platform, which checks the address, age and taxes at checkout
the list of states or countries you ship to, shown before the visitor fills a cart
order online and pick up at the winery, where shipping is not possible
a where-to-buy page with stores and restaurants, if you sell only through distributors
Wine pages share one template: label photo, varietal, vintage, vineyard, tasting notes, pairing, awards, price and the right button — buy, reserve a tasting or find a store.
Age gate on a winery website: when it is needed and how it should work

Some markets, platforms and payment providers expect alcohol sites to ask visitors to confirm their age; elsewhere it is your own policy. Where you use one, keep it light: one question or a date of birth, remembered for the visit, styled like the rest of the site rather than a grey pop-up. I build it as a layer over pages that already exist in the HTML, so the first visit stays quick and the content stays readable for crawlers. Age checks at checkout and at pickup belong to your shop and your staff, not to the entry screen.
Winery events, weddings and venue inquiry pages

An events calendar with filters — concerts, dinners, releases, harvest — shows upcoming dates and links each one to tickets in your system. Past events move to an archive with photos, which shows newcomers what an evening at your winery looks like. Weddings and private events get their own section: each space with its capacity, a gallery of real weddings at the estate, catering and vendor rules, the season and an inquiry form that asks for the date, guest count and budget range, so your events coordinator can reply with something useful the first time.
Wineries with a kitchen or a restaurant will find menus and dining reservations covered on the
restaurant website design
page.
A multilingual winery website for international wine tourists

In regions that draw visitors from abroad, a second or third language brings guests that an English-only site loses. Each version has its own address, translated experience and wine pages, and a language switcher that opens the same page in the other language, not the home page. Prices and hours are entered once in the CMS and stay the same in every version. Tasting notes need a translator who knows wine; machine translation turns “grippy tannins” into nonsense. The Cyprus real-estate platform in my portfolio runs in five languages, including Hebrew, which is written right to left.
How I plan and build language versions is on the
multilingual website development
page.
Winery photography and web design: vines, cellar and people

A winery sells a place and a mood, so photography carries more of the site than text. Plan one shoot across a season if you can: the tasting room set and empty, guests at the bar, the winemaker in the cellar, the vines in spring and at harvest, food pairings, the event lawn at dusk. Stock vineyard photos are recognized at once and make every winery look alike.

The design around the photos stays calm: a short palette taken from your labels, a heading typeface that matches the label, plenty of space and one accent color kept for reservation buttons. The premium site I built for a Warsaw renovation and investment company works the same way — large photographs, restrained type, few colors and the contact button always in reach. Images are served in modern formats and sized for each screen, so a gallery of forty harvest photos still opens quickly.
A winery website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

Ask ChatGPT or an AI Overview for a winery in the valley with picnic tastings, or one whose club holds pickup parties, and the reply is assembled from text an assistant was able to read. The build keeps experiences, prices, hours, policies, wines and club tiers in plain HTML rather than inside images, PDFs or third-party widgets, adds structured data for the winery, its events and its wines, and matches the details on your Google profile. On the site I built for Giuseppe, a Milan psychotherapist, robots.txt sets explicit rules for AI crawlers and structured data describes his practice; ChatGPT already quotes his new pages.
Staying in those answers is ongoing work, explained under

Best winery websites: templates, wine-platform themes or a custom design

Lists of the best winery websites mostly showcase hero videos and big type. The parts that earn reservations are less photogenic: experiences that are easy to compare, a reservation two taps away, a club page that explains itself and a shop that knows where it can ship. A Wix or Squarespace template, or a theme supplied by your wine platform, is a fair start for a small tasting room with one experience. A custom design pays off once you run several experiences, a tiered club, events and weddings, a second language, and want search traffic to grow.

ScanM2, which produces 3D laser scans and BIM models, had two leadless years on a no-code builder. I moved the same design to WordPress; organic traffic is now 29 times higher and inquiries come in weekly. When a winery site moves, rankings survive if each old URL points to its new one — the process is on the

page.

A full winery site with experience pages, reservation integration, wine club, shop connection, events and weddings, age gate and language versions: from 2,000 €.

What an AI SEO consultant does
The job has four parts, and a consultant should be able to do all of them, not only the first:
measure where you stand: what Google and the assistants say about you now, for the questions your buyers actually ask
find why: unclear facts on your site, a name the assistant confuses with another company, sources it trusts that say nothing about you
fix it: pages, structured data, technical issues, listings and mentions — in the code and on the sites where they live
measure again with the same questions, so the result is a comparison rather than a screenshot
The full list of work is on the

page. This page is about who does it and how working with me looks.
AI SEO consultant or agency: what changes for you

An agency gives you a team: an account manager, an SEO specialist, a content writer, sometimes a developer, and handovers between them. An independent consultant gives you one person. In practice that changes three things:
speed — fixes reach the site in days, because the person who finds a problem can change the code
context — nothing gets lost between the audit, the implementation and the report
price — you pay for the work, not for the structure around it
The limits are real too: one person has a fixed capacity, and I do not run paid ads or social media. If you need those, an agency is the better choice, and AI SEO can still be done separately.
Experience behind the work of an AI SEO expert

I have worked in search for 15 years: first as a copywriter, then in SEO, then as a developer, because audits kept failing for lack of someone to apply them. Today I build with Next.js, React, Sanity and WordPress, and do SEO for companies in Europe, the UK, the US, Cyprus and Israel, in English, Polish and Russian.

children.text: I provide AI SEO services: SEO work that gets a business found in Google and named, with the right facts, when buyers ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini or Google’s AI Overviews instead of searching. These are two channels that reward different things — Google ranks pages, assistants quote sources they trust — so the work covers both and measures each separately.
What AI SEO services include: Google rankings and AI answers, measured separately
A buyer who asks an assistant “which accounting firm in Warsaw works with startups” gets two or three names and usually contacts one of them. Whether yours is among them depends on three things:
whether the assistant can tell your business apart from others with a similar name
whether it can find pages that state clearly what you do, for whom and where
whether other sites it trusts — listings, reviews, articles, directories — say the same about you
whether those facts agree with each other, so the assistant is sure it is talking about you

AI SEO services work on all of these, and regular SEO stays part of the job: Google’s AI Overviews draw on pages that already rank, while ChatGPT and Perplexity lean more on video, professional networks, forums and established publishers. Effort on one channel does not carry over to the other by itself, so it is split between them on purpose.
What is AI SEO, and what it is not

“AI SEO” is used for two different things. One is SEO for AI search: making a business visible and correctly described in AI answers. The other is SEO done with AI tools: content generators, “AI humanizers”, automated link building. These services are the first. I use AI tools where they save time — clustering keywords, checking pages at scale — but I do not sell mass-generated content: it rarely ranks, and assistants have little reason to quote a page that says what a thousand other pages say.
How AI assistants decide which businesses to name
Assistants answer from sources they can read and cross-check. In an analysis of
141 AI answers to “who should I hire” questions

, two things mattered more than how good a page was: whether the assistant could tell the business apart from its namesakes, and whether the business said what it does in plain declarative sentences — the one answer that explained its choice quoted exactly such a sentence. The sources the assistants cited were also different from what ranks in Google.
That is why AI SEO starts with what is written, not with tricks: an assistant cannot recommend a company for “startups” if the word appears nowhere it can read.
AI SEO optimization of the website: facts, structure, crawlability
On the site itself, AI SEO optimization covers:
the facts that set you apart — services, markets, clients, prices where you can give them — written as plain, checkable statements
one page per question buyers ask, answered in the first lines, so it can be quoted
structured data that repeats what the visible page says, not more and not less
content reachable without running scripts, because many AI crawlers do not run them
This part can be bought as a separate project:
AI search optimization
Off-site AI SEO: mentions, listings and reviews assistants trust

Assistants rarely trust a company’s own description alone. They look for the same facts on other sites: business profiles, industry directories, review platforms, articles and comparisons. Off-site AI SEO finds which of those sources the assistants in your market actually use, makes sure your details there are complete and identical, and earns mentions where you are missing. No paid “AI citations” or fake reviews: they are easy to detect and break the rules of the platforms that host them.
Wrong information about your business in AI answers

Sometimes the problem is not being invisible but being described wrongly: an old address, a service you stopped, a competitor’s price. The fix is to find the source the assistant took it from and correct it there. How that works is on the

page.
How AI SEO results are measured

AI answers change from one run to the next, so a single screenshot proves nothing. Measurement uses a fixed set of questions your buyers ask, run across assistants and languages on a schedule, and records whether you are named, how you are described and which sources are cited. Next to it: Google rankings, AI Overview citations and the enquiries that come from them.

GEO, AEO and LLM SEO: what the names mean

The same field goes by several names. Generative engine optimization (GEO) is about being named in answers that assistants write. Answer engine optimization (AEO) is about your wording being the one quoted for a specific question — in an answer box, an AI Overview or a chatbot. LLM SEO and ChatGPT SEO are informal names for the same work. In practice they overlap, and AI SEO services cover all of them.

children.text: Why AI brand monitoring is a slow measurement and should be sold as one

The uncomfortable part first: this measures something that moves slowly. The first three months produce a baseline and very little else, because the natural variation between runs is large enough to swallow any real change over a shorter period.

I'd rather say that before you subscribe than explain it in month two. Anyone promising visible movement sooner is selling optimism, and optimism is easy to sell in a field where the client can't easily verify the claim.
What actually changes month to month

Corrections landing. A source you fixed gets recrawled and the wrong claim disappears from one platform, then another a few weeks later. That's the most satisfying thing monitoring catches, and it's also the thing that would otherwise go unnoticed.
New errors appearing. Something wasn't there last month and is now — usually because a new source appeared or an old one resurfaced. Caught early, it's one page to fix; caught late, it's been copied.
The competitive set shifting. Who else gets named alongside you, and whether that list is changing. It's often the earliest signal that someone in your market started publishing seriously.
What I won't put in the report
Sentiment scores. At the volumes a single company can measure by hand, sentiment scoring is noise dressed as rigour.
Share-of-voice percentages. Same problem, plus they invite comparison against benchmarks nobody can verify.

Screenshots of flattering answers. Anyone can find one by running enough prompts. Presenting one as evidence undermines the credibility of the numbers that are real — which is the whole point of keeping a log.
Who this isn't for

If nothing has been fixed yet, monitoring measures a stable situation and tells you it's stable. Do the audit, fix what's fixable, then start measuring. Buying monitoring first is paying to watch a number that isn't moving because nothing has been done to move it.

contentBlocks.title: What the AI visibility audit includes

children.text: Why an AI visibility audit is a measurement, not a screenshot

Almost everyone's first encounter with this is the same: someone types the company name into ChatGPT, reads the answer, and either relaxes or panics. Both reactions are premature, because a single answer isn't evidence of anything.

Assistant answers vary between runs. Ask the same question twice in one afternoon and the companies named may differ, the description may shift, the sources may change. That variation is a property of the systems, not a fault. It also means one check produces an impression, and impressions are a poor basis for spending money.

An audit is the same question asked in a controlled way — a fixed set, a clean session, every platform separately, every language separately — and recorded so that next month's run can be compared against it. That comparison is the whole value. Without it you have anecdotes.
What an AI visibility audit usually finds
Three patterns recur.
You're not named at all.
In which case the problem is visibility, not accuracy, and the work is different: stating your facts unambiguously, structured data, confirmation from independent sources.
You're named and described incorrectly.
Outdated prices, services you dropped, the wrong geography. This is the correctable kind, provided the source is retrievable.
You're described correctly, in the language of your category.

The most common and the least noticed: nothing is wrong, but nothing distinguishes you either, because everything distinguishing was written as imagery rather than as fact, and imagery doesn't survive summarisation.
What an AI visibility audit can't do

It can't guarantee that any answer will change. Where a claim comes from a live page, correcting that page usually works, on a timeline measured in weeks. Where a claim comes from the model's training data, source corrections don't reach it at all until that model is retrained — on the platform's schedule, not yours.

The audit's job is to tell you which of those you're dealing with, before you spend anything on fixing it. That distinction is the single most useful thing in the report, and it's the reason the audit comes before the work rather than instead of it.

contentBlocks.title: What answer engine optimization covers

children.text: AEO vs SEO vs GEO: three terms, three different jobs

The three labels are sold interchangeably and they are not the same work. SEO gets a link ranked so a person clicks it. Answer engine optimization gets your wording lifted into the answer itself — Google's answer box and AI Overview, an assistant's reply, a voice result — whether or not a click follows. Generative engine optimization is about being named as a provider when someone asks who to hire, which is a recommendation rather than an answer to a factual question.

The honest way to tell them apart is what each one measures. SEO counts positions and clicks. AEO counts the questions your page appears in as the answer. GEO counts how often you are named among the two or three companies an assistant suggests. A site can do well at one and badly at the other two, which is why a single number for AI visibility says almost nothing.

Most businesses need parts of all three, and the order matters more than the labels. Everything about visibility and accuracy across AI assistants, including which of those services applies to you, is set out on
the page about AI SEO and GEO optimization
When all three are needed as one ongoing piece of work, that is what the
AI SEO services
page describes.
A longer comparison — with Google's own guidance, click studies and one question tested in three engines — is in
SEO vs GEO vs AEO: how they really differ
What AEO is, how Google and AI tools choose one answer, and how to do it step by step is explained in
what is answer engine optimization
What answer engine optimization changes on a page
An example from this site, because it is the clearest kind.
The Polish SEO audit page

carried the heading "Ile kosztuje audyt SEO?" — how much does an SEO audit cost — and contained no price anywhere on it. The figure lived on the pricing page instead. Ranking was never the problem: the page could not be the answer to the question it asked, because it did not hold one.

The fix is unglamorous, and it is most of what AEO actually is. The question is restated as a heading in the words people use. The answer follows in the next sentence, with a number and the date it was true. The caveats and the detail come after it, not before. The same figure appears in the structured data, so the markup repeats the page rather than paraphrasing it. Then the paragraph can be quoted — by a featured snippet, by an AI Overview, by an assistant reading the page.
What this is not: adding a frequently asked questions block to the bottom of every page. Questions nobody asks, answered in text nobody reads, change nothing except the size of the page.
When AEO is not the work you need
If assistants describe your company incorrectly — old prices, services you dropped, a capability credited to a competitor — that is accuracy work, and the fix is
correcting the source they read
, not reformatting your pages. If you do not yet know what is said about you, the measurement comes first:
an AI visibility audit
answers that for a defined set of prompts instead of a single screenshot.
If the site cannot be read without executing JavaScript, or its facts are not stated as claims anything can check, then
preparing the website for AI search

comes before any question mapping. Answer formatting on a page a fetcher never finishes reading is worth nothing. And if the answers are already right and the real question is whether they hold, that is
AI brand monitoring
, which is a subscription rather than a project.
AEO is the layer above all of those: which questions you intend to own, and whether your wording is the version that gets quoted.

children.text: Why CMS & API integration matters
Without integrations, your website becomes an island — isolated from your CRM, analytics, and payment tools.
With proper integration, your business becomes faster, leaner, and more data-driven.

Most websites today use at least 3–5 connected services: CMS, CRM, payment, analytics, automation. When they communicate via APIs, your entire digital workflow becomes a single system — not a mess of disconnected apps.

I specialize in building these connections. You get a clean, efficient architecture that’s easy to maintain, scale, and secure. Whether you’re running a marketing site, e-commerce platform, or SaaS dashboard — I make sure everything runs smoothly in the background.

All projects are handled officially — with contract, invoice, and transparent terms.
You work directly with me, no agencies or middle layers — just efficient communication and reliable results.
How It Works
Discovery & Briefing
— we discuss your goals, existing setup, and desired automation.
Architecture Planning
— I design the data flow between CMS, CRM, and APIs.
Integration & Development
— I connect services securely and test authentication.
Testing & Optimization
— full QA for data accuracy and performance.
Deployment & Support
— I launch integrations and stay available for assistance.
This process ensures everything is reliable, measurable, and future-proof.
When a no-code connector is enough — and when it is not

Zapier, Make and tools like them solve a real problem, and for many businesses they are the correct answer. If a form needs to create a CRM record and send a notification, and that happens thirty times a month, a no-code connector does it in an afternoon and costs less than any custom work would.

They stop being the cheap option in three situations. Volume: pricing is per task, so a flow that fires thousands of times a month quietly becomes a subscription larger than the integration would have cost once. Logic: anything requiring conditional branching, reshaping of data, deduplication or a lookup against your own database turns into a long chain of steps that nobody except its author can read. And data: if customer records must not leave your own infrastructure, routing them through a third-party automation platform should be a deliberate decision rather than a default.

The rule I use is simple. If a flow is simple, low-volume and stable, use the connector and spend the money elsewhere. Custom API work earns its cost when the flow is central to how the business actually runs — that is the reasoning behind
automating page production
on this site, where the volume made the case obvious.
What makes an integration keep working after launch

Most integrations do not break loudly. A token expires, a provider retires an API version, a webhook stops being delivered — and nothing on the site looks wrong. Leads simply stop arriving in the CRM, and somebody notices a week later, if at all.

Which is why "does it work?" is the wrong question to accept an integration on. The useful ones are these. What happens to a submission if the CRM is unreachable at that moment — is it queued and retried, or lost? Who is notified when a call fails, and how? Are credentials stored where they can be rotated without a redeploy? Is there a log showing what was sent and what came back, so a failure can be diagnosed rather than guessed at?

An integration with answers to those questions survives an API change. One without them works perfectly until the day it doesn't, and the cost of that day is counted in lost enquiries, not in developer hours.

children.text: I provide conversion rate optimization services as the same person who builds and repairs websites, so the analysis ends in changes to your site’s code, not in a slide deck for someone else to implement. CRO means getting more of the visitors you already have to do what the site exists for: call, send an inquiry, book or buy. Most sites lose those visitors in a few predictable places — a first screen that does not say what is sold, a form that breaks on a phone, a delivery cost revealed at the last step, a contact button nobody finds. Finding them takes measurement. Fixing them takes a developer.
Website conversion rate optimization services: what the work includes
The mix depends on the site, but the work usually covers these parts:
analytics and event setup: GA4 events for form sends, calls, WhatsApp clicks, bookings and purchases, so a conversion is counted the same way before and after every change
funnel analysis: which pages people land on, where they leave, and how phones differ from desktops
session recordings and heatmaps, used to see where people hesitate, tap on things that are not links or stop scrolling
first screens: what you sell, for whom, where, at what price level, and one clear next step
forms: only the fields you need, the right keyboard on a phone, errors shown next to the field and a confirmation that says what happens next
speed: slow templates, heavy images and third-party scripts fixed at the source
trust elements: real photos, reviews, prices or price ranges, terms, and who is behind the business
calls to action and contact paths: call, WhatsApp, form and booking buttons placed where the decision is made and sized for a thumb
Every check above is done on a phone first, where layout, form and speed problems show up before anywhere else.
Conversion rate optimization companies vs a conversion rate specialist who writes the code

Conversion rate optimization companies usually work in two steps: a strategist finds problems and writes recommendations, and your developer or another agency implements them weeks later. That model fits large stores with a product team, a testing program and enough traffic for several experiments a month.

Most businesses looking for CRO help are in a different position: one website, one developer or none, and a list of known problems that has waited for months. As a conversion rate specialist who also builds sites in
WordPress
and
Next.js

, I change the template, the form or the checkout step myself, test it on real devices and measure it. The person who found the problem is the person who fixes it, so nothing gets lost in a ticket queue.
CRO audit: what I check and what you receive

A CRO audit is the usual start. I need read access to Google Analytics 4 and Search Console, and your definition of a good lead or a good order. Then I go through the site the way visitors do: from the pages they actually land on, on a phone, filling in and sending every form.

You receive a written list of problems, each with a screenshot or a short recording, why it costs you inquiries or sales, and the effort to fix it. The list is sorted by expected effect against effort, so the first items are cheap fixes on the pages with the most traffic. If tracking is missing or wrong, fixing it comes first: without it, nothing that follows can be measured. You can carry out the fixes with your own developer or have me do them.
A/B testing in CRO: when your traffic is enough and when it is not

An A/B test shows two versions of a page to two groups of visitors and compares the results. It is the cleanest way to measure a change, but it needs volume: each version has to collect enough conversions to tell a real difference from chance. A busy store can get a usable answer about a product page within weeks. A service site with a few dozen inquiries a month would wait many months for one test.
When A/B tests are worth running
pages with high traffic and frequent conversions: product pages, checkout steps, landing pages behind a large ad budget
questions where the outcome is uncertain, such as how prices are presented or the order of checkout steps
Before-and-after measurement for smaller sites

For most small and medium sites I use careful before-and-after measurement instead: a fixed baseline period, changes released in dated groups and annotated in analytics, conversion rates compared by channel and device, and the same period of the previous year where the business is seasonal. It is less precise than a test, so I use it for clear problems — a broken form does not need an experiment — and keep testing for the questions that remain open.
CRO for lead-generation websites: from the first visit to a qualified inquiry

On a lead-generation site the conversion is an inquiry, and its quality matters as much as the count. A form that collects ten vague messages is worse than one that collects four with a budget and a deadline. The work focuses on:
service pages that answer what a buyer asks before contacting anyone: scope, process, price range, timelines and examples of work
a quote form that asks for exactly what you need to reply with a price
a thank-you page that says when and how you will answer
tracking that separates spam and job applications from real inquiries

ScanM2, a 3D laser scanning and BIM company, had received no leads for two years from its no-code website. After I rebuilt it on WordPress, keeping its design, it gets inquiries every week. That change came from search and conversion work together.
CRO for local service businesses: calls, WhatsApp and forms

For a workshop, a clinic or a repair service, most conversions happen on a phone, and many of them are not forms at all: people call, write on WhatsApp or tap for directions. Conversion work for local services means:
call, WhatsApp and directions buttons on every page, fixed to the bottom of the screen on phones
a WhatsApp link that opens with a prefilled message naming the service the visitor was reading about
every tap on the phone number, WhatsApp button or map counted as a conversion, so you see which pages bring contacts
opening hours, service area and price ranges visible without long scrolling
The Warsaw auto repair shop and the tyre-storage service in my portfolio are built this way. Getting found on the map in the first place is a separate job, covered by
local SEO services
Ecommerce conversion rate optimization services: product page, cart and checkout
In a store the path is longer, and every step can leak buyers:
product page: photos that show the product in use, the price, delivery cost and time before the cart, availability, sizes and returns in plain words
cart: quantities and options editable in place, the full cost visible, no forced account
checkout: guest checkout, the payment methods buyers expect in their country, working autofill and clear error messages
after the purchase: a confirmation page and email that answer “when will it arrive?”

The Landi Room course page is a compact example of a page built to sell: one offer, Stripe Checkout and a protected video link delivered automatically after payment. It sold more than 100 courses from its first Google Ads campaign. For product and category pages that need organic traffic, see
ecommerce SEO services
CRO and SEO together: traffic that does not convert vs conversions without traffic

A website can fail in two opposite ways. It can rank and get visits that leave without contacting you — a conversion problem that more traffic will not solve. Or it can turn its few visitors into customers well while almost nobody finds it — a visibility problem that CRO will not solve. Most sites have some of both, so I look at both numbers before deciding where your budget goes first.

Conversion changes must not cost rankings: the headings, text and internal links a page ranks with are kept or moved on purpose, not deleted for a cleaner layout. The search side of the work is on the
SEO optimization and strategy
page.
CRO for visitors who come from ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews

Visitors who arrive from ChatGPT, Perplexity or a link in Google AI Overviews rarely see your homepage. The assistant sends them to the page it quoted: a service page, a price list, a blog post from two years ago. They come with part of their question already answered and a specific reason to click. So every page that can be cited has to work as a first page: who you are, what you offer, the price level and the next step, without assuming the visitor has seen anything else on the site.

In analytics I separate this traffic — ChatGPT adds utm_source=chatgpt.com to its links, and other assistants show up as referrers — so you can compare how these visitors convert against search and ads. Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan whose site I rebuilt, found me through ChatGPT. Getting cited at all is the work described on
AI-ready SEO and GEO optimization
; which sources assistants rely on when they recommend a business is in my
study of 141 AI answers
How conversion rate optimization results are measured
Before any change, we agree what a conversion is for you — a sent form, a call, a WhatsApp chat, a paid order — and I record a baseline. After each group of changes the report shows:
conversion rate by channel and device, against the baseline and, where it matters, the same period last year
the number and quality of leads or orders, not only the rate
what changed on the site and when, so every rise or drop can be traced to a date
Results are reported as measured numbers, including changes that made no difference, rather than as a percentage promised before anyone has seen your data.

One-off fixes — a form, a checkout step, a first screen or the speed of key templates: 250–700 € per task.
Monthly CRO work — analysis, changes in the code, tests where traffic allows and a monthly report: from 800 € per month.

Tracking setup so conversions are counted correctly, analysis of where visitors leave, and changes to the site: first screens, forms, checkout, speed, trust elements and contact buttons. With me the changes are made in the code, not only recommended.
