children.text: Why wrong information in ChatGPT is fixed at the source, not with the platform

The instinct on finding that ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google's AI Overviews describe your company incorrectly is to contact someone about it. That instinct is why most of this effort goes nowhere. No channel exists through which a business corrects its own record with an AI assistant, and the feedback buttons that do exist are a signal rather than an edit.

What changes an answer is changing what the assistant reads. When it searches the web, it retrieves pages and summarises them — so the wrong claim exists somewhere public, and fixing that source changes the claim on the next crawl. Not because a request was processed, but because the input changed.
Wikipedia, Wikidata and the knowledge graph: where entity facts actually live

Assistants do not assemble a company from scratch on every question. They lean on structured entity sources: Wikipedia and Wikidata, business registries, industry directories and the profiles that feed a search engine's knowledge graph. When those are stale, empty or contradictory, the answer inherits the problem — and no amount of editing your own website reaches it.

So the work covers the entity as well as the site: the Wikidata item and whether it exists at all, the directory listings carrying your details, the profiles that rank for your own name, and the structured data on your pages that tells a machine what kind of organisation this is and what it sells. Where several people or companies share your name, disambiguation is the whole job — an assistant that cannot tell which one you are will name someone it can.
The step that makes an AI correction hold

One corrected page against six stale ones loses. That's why corrections revert: the source gets fixed, the answer improves for a fortnight, and then the older material reasserts itself because it's still there and still says otherwise.

Making the correct fact the consistent version everywhere — your site, your profiles, your listings, your Wikidata item, every directory carrying your details — is the step that makes a correction hold. It's also the least interesting part of the job, which is presumably why it gets skipped.
The honest limit: what can't be corrected in ChatGPT or any AI answer

Some claims can't be reached. If the wrong information comes from the model's training data rather than a retrieved page, source corrections don't touch it, and it persists until that model is retrained — on the platform's schedule, not yours, and possibly months away.
These are identifiable: ask the same question with search enabled and disabled. If the answer is right when the assistant searches and wrong when it doesn't, the error is in the model.

The workaround isn't a fix but it works: make the correct version dominant enough in retrievable sources that search-grounded answers stay right regardless of what the model remembers. Since a growing share of answers involve search, that covers most of the practical exposure — and I'd rather explain that than sell you a campaign against something no campaign reaches.
What this AI correction service doesn't cover

Not the assistant's opinion of you, only its facts. If an answer says something accurate that you'd rather it didn't, that's a different problem and mostly not a technical one. The method here corrects wrong claims; it doesn't suppress true ones, and I don't take that work.

children.text: Where ecommerce SEO earns: category pages, not the homepage

People who already know your shop type its name. Everyone else types the thing they want to buy, and that phrasing matches a category or a filtered view of one — not the homepage and not the blog. In most catalogues those pages are the weakest part of the site: a grid of products with no text, a title generated from the category name, and a URL that changes as soon as anything is filtered.

So the work starts there. Each category worth ranking gets a title that matches how people actually phrase the need, a short piece of text that answers the question a buyer has at that moment — sizing, compatibility, what to choose between two options — and internal links pointing at it from whatever content already attracts attention.

The blog is not the point of this work, but it is not decoration either: its job is to bring links and attention to the pages that carry the products. A guide that ranks and links to nothing is a hobby.
Faceted navigation and duplicates: the two things that break a catalogue

Ten filters on one category produce more URL combinations than the catalogue has products. A crawler will happily spend weeks on colour-plus-size-plus-sort-order variations, and the pages you wanted crawled wait behind them. The fix is not one setting: it is a written rule for which filters create indexable pages because there is real search demand behind them, which are blocked from crawling, which canonical back to the clean category, and how pagination and sort orders behave.

The second problem is the same product living at several addresses because it belongs to several categories. Each copy splits the signals of the others. One canonical address per item, everything else pointing at it.

The third — the one that quietly costs the most — is what happens when something stops being sold. A page that 404s loses every link and every ranking it earned. A page that stays live with no stock and no alternative wastes the visit. Each discontinued item needs a decision: keep it with alternatives shown, redirect it to the category above it, or return 410 and let it go. That decision belongs to a rule, not to the platform's default behaviour.

Template work is where a large catalogue gets cheap, and it is the first thing I look at.

Timing, honestly: technical fixes show up within weeks of being crawled again. Category rankings move over three to six months, and seasonal categories move on their season's schedule regardless of when the work was done. children.text: How to tell which of the four services you need
Start with the audit if you don't know

Almost everyone's first move is to type their company name into ChatGPT and read what comes back. That produces an impression, not a measurement — answers vary between runs, so a single check proves nothing either way.
The audit is the same question asked in a controlled way

, recorded so that next month's run can be compared against it. It's also the only one of the four that tells you which of the other three you actually need. If you're unsure, it's the cheapest way to stop guessing.
The distinction that decides everything
An error can live in one of two places, and only one of them is reachable.
In a retrievable source
— an outdated directory listing, an old press item, a competitor's comparison page. The assistant searched, found it, repeated it. Fix the source and the claim changes on the next crawl.
In the model's training data
— no live source exists. That version of your company persists until the model is retrained, on the platform's schedule, and source corrections don't reach it.
Knowing which you're dealing with is what stops months being spent on something that was never going to respond. It's established in the audit, before
any correction work is quoted
What none of this promises
Nobody can guarantee what an assistant will say. Answers vary between runs, get reassembled over time, and depend on phrasing, language and whether the assistant searched at all.
No fixed timeline for corrections either: source changes take effect after a recrawl, usually weeks, and training-data claims may not change at all this quarter.
And this doesn't replace search work. AI visibility rests on the same technical foundation as search — if your pages aren't indexed or load badly, there's nothing here to build on.

contentBlocks.title: What international SEO work involves

children.text: Why several markets are a different job from one market repeated
The assumption behind most multi-market projects is that the work multiplies: what was done for one country gets done again for the next, at roughly the same cost each time.
Part of that is true and part of it is the reason these projects overrun.
What genuinely transfers is the technical layer.
The structure, the routing, the markup, the measurement setup

— build them once properly and every additional market costs a fraction. That's the real economy of scale here, and it's why the structure decision made at the start determines the cost of everything after it.

What never transfers is the query research and the content. Each language phrases commercial intent its own way, and no amount of care in translation produces the phrasings people actually type. Every market is a fresh start on that side, every time.
So the honest shape is: technical work once, market work per market. A supplier promising that entering the second country costs a tenth of the first is describing only the half that scales.
Why hreflang matters more than it sounds like it should
The most common structural failure, and it's invisible without looking.

Search engines encountering several versions of the same page have to decide whether they're duplicates competing for one position or alternatives serving different audiences. Hreflang is how they're told. Get it wrong and the versions are treated as duplicates: the signal splits between them, and both rank worse than a single version would have.

The failures are specific and findable. Missing return references, so version A points at B but B doesn't point back. Codes that don't match the actual content. Versions that reference pages which no longer exist. A default version declared for nobody or for everybody.
None of this shows in analytics as a problem. It shows as underperformance without a cause, which is why it survives for years on sites that are otherwise well run.
I've seen the sharper version of this too:
a site rebuilt with AI assistance where the language versions were wired to the wrong locales
. Traffic fell within two days, and the two weeks it took to resolve were almost entirely diagnosis.
Choosing markets is the part that saves the most money
Before any of the technical work, there's a question most projects skip: which markets are actually worth entering at your budget.

They are not equal. A market where established competitors have held the commercial terms for a decade has a realistic ceiling that a new entrant can't reach in a year. A smaller market with thin competition may return more for a fraction of the effort. And some markets you're already reaching adequately through an existing language version, in which case building separately duplicates what you have.

That assessment is cheap relative to what it prevents. An audit that establishes there's no reachable target in your largest intended market costs a few hundred euros; discovering it after a year of retainer costs the year.

Sequence matters too. Entering three markets simultaneously means three sets of everything for a partial presence in each. Entering one properly and letting it fund the next produces something you can build on — and the technical work, done once, makes the second market genuinely cheaper.
Measurement is where multi-market work usually fails
Not in the execution — in the reporting.

Combined organic traffic across five markets is a number that cannot be acted on. A rise in one market masks a decline in another. Branded searches in the home market swamp non-branded growth abroad. And because the aggregate keeps moving, nobody notices that one of the five has been flat since the start.
What the reporting has to separate: non-branded clicks per country, positions on a query list built per language, and — increasingly —
presence in AI assistant answers per language
, since that moves independently of search positions and a blended number hides it completely.

This has to be set up from the first month. Once several markets have been reported together for a year, the historical data can't be separated retrospectively, and the question of which market ever worked becomes unanswerable.

Worth saying plainly rather than in small print.
If you're entering one market, this isn't the service.
The work is that market's specifics — how buyers there search, what they check, which competitors hold what — and there are pages on this site for individual markets that cover exactly that.

This service is for the machinery: structure that carries several languages, the decision of which markets and in what order, and reporting that keeps them apart. It's the layer underneath the country work rather than a substitute for it.
Most companies working across borders need both, and the order is usually structure first — because entering a second market on a foundation built for one is where the rebuild costs appear.

children.text: I provide LLM SEO services: work that makes a business visible and correctly described in the answers of large language models — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google’s AI answers. LLM SEO is not one optimisation applied to all of them: each model knows different things and reads different sources, so the work and the measurement are done per model.
What LLM SEO is: training data and live search
A language model can know about your business in two ways:
from training data — what was published about you before the model was trained, often months ago; this is what the model “remembers” without searching
from live retrieval — what it finds when it searches the web while answering; this is current, and this is where most buying questions are answered
LLM SEO works on both: being described consistently in the places that end up in training data, and being findable and quotable when a model searches today.
A longer guide — where each model searches the web, why most AI crawlers ignore JavaScript, and one question tested in four assistants — is in
LLM SEO: how to optimize your website for ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity
Why ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude cite different sources
In my analysis of
141 AI answers to buying questions
, the assistants read almost different webs:
Perplexity cited 16.7 sources per answer, mostly companies’ own websites — work on your site shows up there first
Google AI Mode cited 3.7 per answer, a tight selection close to what ranks in Google
ChatGPT cited 1.6 per answer and only about one company website per answer — work that gets you named there is mostly outside your site
That is why one “AI optimisation” package averages three different problems. LLM SEO decides which models matter for your buyers and works on each. For ChatGPT alone, see
ChatGPT SEO services
Entity clarity: one business, one description, everywhere

Models build an answer by joining facts from several sources. If your company name is shared with others, or your description differs from site to site, the model either skips you or mixes you up with someone else. In my study this mattered more than how good a page was. LLM SEO makes the entity unambiguous: one name, one description of what you do, for whom and where, the same on your site, in structured data, in listings and on professional networks.
Content that survives summarising

A model does not quote your page; it compresses it. Marketing phrases disappear, and what is left is whatever was stated as a plain fact. So the key pages state the facts that set you apart — services, markets, clients, prices where possible — in short declarative sentences, with one question answered per page. That copy survives summarising and is what a model can repeat without distorting.
AI crawlers and llms.txt

Each vendor uses its own crawlers, and many sites block them by accident through a security plugin, a CDN rule or a copied robots.txt. I check what your server actually lets through and set it per vendor:
OpenAI: OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT search, GPTBot for training — they can be set separately
Perplexity, Anthropic (Claude) and others have their own crawlers for search and training
Google-Extended controls whether your content is used for Gemini models; it does not affect Google Search

An llms.txt file — a short Markdown summary of the site for language models — is a proposed convention. No major assistant has confirmed it uses it, so I add it as a cheap extra, not as a strategy. This site has one.

You see the result per model, because a gain in Perplexity says nothing about ChatGPT.

contentBlocks.title: What local SEO work involves

children.text: Why local search is decided above your website rather than on it

For a business with an address, the search result that matters usually isn't a link to your site. It's the map block — three businesses, their ratings, their distance, a phone number and a route, all resolved before anyone scrolls far enough to see a website at all.

That changes where the work happens. Conventional SEO improves how a page ranks. Local work improves whether you appear in a panel that draws on your company profile, your reviews, your consistency across the web and your proximity to whoever is searching — with your website as one input among several rather than the main event.
Which is why a business can have a good site, rank respectably for its category, and still lose almost every nearby customer to a competitor whose profile is simply better maintained.
The three things local ranking actually weighs
Simplified but accurate enough to plan around.
Relevance

— how well what you've declared matches what someone searched. This is category selection, service descriptions and the specifics on your profile and site. It's the part most businesses under-fill: a category chosen carelessly at registration quietly excludes you from searches you should appear in.
Distance
— how far you are from the person searching, or from the area they named.
Nobody controls this.

It's the reason no honest supplier can promise a place in the map's top three: a search from the other side of the city may not show you at all regardless of what's been optimised, and a competitor two streets closer will beat you on that query while losing on another.
Prominence
— how well known and well regarded you are, assembled from reviews, mentions, links, directory presence and general web footprint. This is the slowest to move and the most durable once moved.
Work can improve two of the three. Being told plainly which is which is worth more than a promise that ignores the one that can't be moved.
The consistency problem, which is boring and decisive

Your business details exist in more places than you'd expect: your site, your company profile, industry directories, mapping services, listings you've never registered for that were populated automatically.

When those disagree — a suite number in one, absent in another, an old phone number somewhere, a name from before the rebrand — the systems assembling local results have to decide which version to trust. Uncertainty produces caution, and caution means being shown less often.

Fixing this isn't clever work. It's finding every place your details appear and making them identical. It takes hours rather than months, it's the least interesting thing on this page, and it's frequently the change that produces the clearest improvement.
Reviews, and the part suppliers usually skip

In local search, reviews are read before the website and sometimes instead of it. A business with a handful loses to one with dozens, and the gap compounds because the more visible business collects more.

What actually works is unglamorous: asking consistently at the point where a customer is most satisfied, making it take seconds rather than minutes, and responding to everything — including the negative ones.

What doesn't work, and what I won't set up: filtering who gets asked so only happy customers are invited, generating reviews, or threatening reviewers. All three are against platform rules, all three are detectable, and all three produce a worse reputational story than the reviews they were meant to prevent. For a business selling trust locally, that trade is never worth it.
And where the reviews are poor because the service has a real problem, no amount of profile work fixes that. I'd rather say so during the audit than take a retainer to paper over it.
Location pages: when they're legitimate and when they're doorways
The temptation with a service area is obvious — a page per district, each targeting a local query.

The line is whether the page has something specific to say. A page about working in a particular area that names local conditions, describes real jobs done there and answers questions specific to that place is a real page. Fifteen pages generated by swapping the place name are doorway pages, and search engines name them explicitly as a violation. The penalty applies to the site, not to the pages.

Practical rule: if the page can be produced from another one by find-and-replace, it shouldn't exist. Most businesses need far fewer location pages than they think, and are better served by one strong page that lists the areas honestly.
What this work looks like on a site that also sells elsewhere
Worth separating, because the two get confused.
Local work targets people near you searching for something nearby.
If your customers are in another country and find you by category rather than by proximity
, this isn't the service you need — the market-specific pages elsewhere on this site are.

Many businesses need both: a clinic serving its own city and also attracting patients from abroad, a workshop serving local drivers and also selling parts nationally. Those are two different projects sharing a technical foundation, and it's worth being deliberate about which one is being paid for at any given time.
I built a four-language site
for a Warsaw workshop where exactly that split applied
— local customers arriving through the map, others arriving through search in their own language. The technical work served both; the targeting didn't, and it shouldn't have.
Recovering from a sudden traffic drop is a different, separate service —
see traffic drop recovery
if that's what's happening rather than a lack of local visibility.
For owners who run a small business themselves, the
local SEO for small business
page walks through the Google Business Profile, reviews and local listings step by step.
Law firms have their own rules for Google profiles, reviews and directories; they are covered on the
local SEO for lawyers
page.
Local SEO and AI search: getting your business named in Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT (GEO, AEO)

Nearby customers now ask an assistant the way they would ask a neighbor: “Which dentist near Mokotów takes emergency patients on a Saturday?”, “Who can fix a leaking boiler today in Wola?” GEO and AEO, said simply, give AI models enough reliable local facts about your business to name it in that one-paragraph answer. For a business with an address, that means:
Opening hours, services, price ranges, parking, payment options and the languages your staff speak, written on the site and not only on the profile.
A LocalBusiness subtype that fits your trade, such as Dentist, AutoRepair or Plumber, with address, geo coordinates, opening hours and areaServed matching the visible page.

The same details on Google Business Profile, Bing Places and Apple Business Connect, plus the one or two directories your trade relies on; the last two profiles are the ones owners most easily forget to claim.
Answers to what people phone in about, such as whether booking is needed, how long a job takes and whether you come to their district, on the service pages themselves.

Before and after the work I check whether ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews mention your business, and how, when asked what a customer a few streets away would ask; as with the map, nobody can guarantee a place in those answers.

contentBlocks.title: What I build

children.text: Multilingual is a technical problem, not a linguistic one

Most businesses approach a multilingual website as a translation task: take the content, get it translated, publish it under a language switcher. The translation part usually goes fine. The site then underperforms anyway, and the reason is almost never the words.
What decides the outcome is how search engines are told which version belongs to which audience. That's
the hreflang and canonical setup

, and it's easy to get subtly wrong — the versions end up read as duplicates of one another, the ranking signal splits, and each version performs worse than a single-language site would have. This is the most common failure mode, and it's invisible: nothing looks broken, the traffic simply never arrives. Getting found in AI-generated answers depends on the same clean structure — I've seen a client get
found through ChatGPT
for exactly that reason.

The second decision is structural. Markets don't phrase things identically, and a literal translation targets phrases nobody in that country types into a search box. Keyword research has to be done per language, and page structure has to follow it. Sometimes that means a market needs a page the original language doesn't have at all.

The third is fragility. Locale routing breaks easily during redesigns and migrations — versions get swapped, redirects go missing, hreflang keeps pointing at old addresses. I've had to repair exactly this for a client
whose language versions were swapped during an AI-assisted redesign
: traffic fell within two days and took over a month to recover after the fixes.
Done properly, the payoff is straightforward.
A real estate catalogue I built

runs in four languages, brings over 1,500 organic visits a month with no ad spend, and its buyers come from more than twenty countries — because each version was built to work in its own market rather than to mirror the original. The same logic applies to
hotels with international guests
and
logistics companies
whose clients and drivers are in different countries.
A recent one:
a residency-by-investment guide covering five jurisdictions
, built in three languages on native URLs per language.

children.text: I offer Next.js development services as an independent developer based in Warsaw: I design and build websites on Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Sanity as the headless CMS where your team edits content. It is the stack my own site runs on and the one I choose for most new projects. You work with one person who writes the code, sets up the SEO and is still reachable after launch.
What Next.js is used for: the websites I build with it

Next.js is a React framework that renders pages on the server or builds them in advance, so a visitor and a search engine receive finished HTML instead of an empty shell that JavaScript fills in later. It powers web apps and dashboards too, but my work with it is websites that have to be found, read and acted on:
marketing sites for service businesses, with a page for every service and a clear way to get in touch from each one
multilingual sites where every language has its own translated URLs
content-heavy sites with a blog, guides or hundreds of articles that editors add every week
personal-brand sites for consultants, therapists, artists and other specialists
landing pages that sell a course, a consultation or a booking with online payment
Why a Next.js website loads fast: static generation and image optimization

The speed comes from how pages are delivered. Most pages of a marketing site are generated once — at build time or right after an editor publishes a change — and served from a CDN close to the visitor. Nothing is assembled on each request, so there is no database query or theme rendering between the click and the page.
incremental static regeneration rebuilds a page in the background after an edit, so content stays current and nobody waits for it
the Next.js image component serves every photo in a modern format at the size the screen actually needs
fonts are self-hosted and load without shifting the layout
only the JavaScript a page needs reaches the browser; static sections stay plain HTML

The DJ and producer site I built on Next.js 14 loads in under one second; it replaced slow pages from a website builder. Speed is not an extra line in the quote — it comes from the stack and from keeping the code lean.
SEO in a Next.js website: metadata, sitemaps, hreflang and structured data in code
In Next.js, SEO lives in the code instead of in a stack of plugins that may conflict after an update. I set it up once, so editors cannot break it by accident:
titles, descriptions and Open Graph images generated for every page from CMS fields, with fallbacks when a field is empty
an XML sitemap built from the content itself, so a page appears in it the moment it is published
hreflang links between language versions and a canonical URL on every page
JSON-LD structured data for the organization or person, services, articles, FAQs and breadcrumbs, matching what is visible on the page
readable URLs, 301 redirects managed in one file and real 404 responses for missing pages
Deeper work on large sites — crawl analysis, index coverage, Core Web Vitals across thousands of URLs — is described on the
technical SEO services
page.
Headless CMS website with Next.js and Sanity: editors change content, not the layout

A headless CMS keeps content separate from design. In Sanity your team fills in structured fields — a heading, a price, a list of benefits, a set of FAQs — and the Next.js site decides how they look. Pasting text from a Word document or uploading an oversized photo does not break the page.
content types are modeled on your site: a service, a case study, an article, a team member, each with only the fields it needs
a live preview shows the page before it goes public
images are cropped around a focal point you choose, for every screen size
translations are linked documents, so it is visible which pages still miss a language

Sanity is my default for Next.js and Sanity builds because its editing studio is code in the same repository and evolves with the site. Other headless CMS options and connections to the systems you already use are covered on the
CMS integration and API work
page.
Multilingual Next.js websites with translated URLs

My own site runs in English, Polish and Russian; the retail analytics consultant’s site I built has 153 pages in the same three languages; the psychotherapist’s site in Milan runs in Italian and English. In each of them every language has its own URL structure with translated slugs, hreflang tags and a language switcher that leads to the same page in the other language rather than to the home page. Texts are written for each market, not passed through a machine translator. The method in full is on the
multilingual website development
page.
Integrations in a Next.js website: forms, CRM and Stripe payments
Next.js runs server code next to the pages, so a website can collect leads and take payments without a separate backend to host and patch:
forms that send leads to email, WhatsApp or a CRM, with spam protection and analytics events
Stripe Checkout for courses, consultations or deposits
access to paid content delivered after a successful payment
data from external APIs — availability, prices, a listing feed — cached so pages stay fast

For Landi Room, a beauty salon in Warsaw, I built a landing page for an online course on Next.js and Sanity with Stripe Checkout: after paying, the buyer receives a protected link to the video. The first Google Ads campaign to that page brought more than 100 course sales.
Migration from WordPress to Next.js with 301 redirects

Many Next.js projects start as a WordPress site that has become slow or painful to update. The content and the rankings have to survive the move. For Giuseppe, a psychotherapist in Milan, I rebuilt the site on Next.js 16 and Sanity: 468 blog posts migrated, every old URL redirected with a 301 to its new address, structured data added and explicit rules for AI crawlers written. From start to handover it took 44 working days.
Steps of a WordPress to Next.js migration
Export posts, pages, images and SEO fields, and convert them into structured CMS content.
Map every old URL to a new one, including categories, tags and media attachment pages.
Carry over titles and descriptions, then test all redirects on a preview before launch.
After launch, watch Search Console for 404 errors and indexing changes for several weeks.
Moves from other platforms follow the same order, described on the
website platform migration
page.
Next.js or WordPress: when Next.js is overkill

Next.js does not suit every project. WordPress is the better choice when you rely on a large set of ready plugins, when your team already knows its admin panel, or when a small site will never grow beyond a few pages and needs to launch cheaply. I build on both, and the case from the WordPress side is on the
WordPress development services
page.
A Next.js website that ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews can read

AI assistants and their crawlers read HTML, and many of them do not run JavaScript. A site that assembles its text in the browser can look almost empty to them. A Next.js site rendered on the server or at build time hands over the full text of each page in the first response.
server-rendered HTML with real headings, lists and tables that a crawler parses without executing scripts
structured data that names the business, its services and the authors of its articles
robots.txt rules written explicitly for GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended, so you decide which bots may read and which may use content for training
an llms.txt file with a short map of the site where it is useful
Giuseppe found me through ChatGPT, and new pages of his rebuilt site already show up in ChatGPT answers. Getting mentioned in AI answers is ongoing work beyond the build; it is described on the
AI-ready SEO and GEO optimization
page.
Hire a Next.js developer instead of a Next.js development company

A Next.js development company assigns a project manager, a designer and frontend and backend developers. For a website that is often more people than the work needs. I do the design, the code, the CMS setup, the SEO and the launch myself, and you talk to me directly. I have worked in internet marketing since 2010 — first as a copywriter, then in SEO, then in development — so the site is planned around search demand and content, not only around components.
Brief and structure: pages, languages, integrations and content types, with a fixed price.
Design: the home page and one inner page agreed first, on a phone and on a desktop.
Build: Next.js, Sanity, SEO and analytics, with work in progress on a preview URL.
Content and launch: content entered or migrated, redirects tested, domain connected.
Handover: a short CMS guide, the repository and all accounts in your name.

Hosting usually goes on Vercel, the platform from the company behind Next.js, which builds a preview for every change; other Node.js hosting works as well. Updates and small changes after launch are covered on the

children.text: Why AI search readiness is a different job from accuracy work
Two problems get sold under one heading, and they need separating before anything is quoted.
Accuracy
is what assistants say about you when they name you — outdated prices, services you dropped, a capability credited to a competitor. That's correction work, and it's covered by two other services.
Visibility

is whether you get named at all. That's this one, and no amount of correcting fixes it: you can have entirely accurate information nobody ever retrieves, because nothing in it is stated in a form a machine can confidently repeat.
The audit tells you which of the two you have
. If you appear in two answers out of twenty, the problem is here.
What assistants actually do with your copy
They don't quote, they compress. Everything they return is a restatement, and restatement selects: it keeps what can be stated compactly and corroborated elsewhere, and discards what can't.

That's why brand language disappears. "Helping ambitious businesses unlock their potential" can't be restated usefully, so it either drops out or gets replaced by the generic description of your category — which is the opposite of positioning. What survives is anything checkable: who you serve, where, in which languages, what you technically do, what you don't.
None of this means abandoning how you sound to human readers. It means making sure the checkable version exists alongside it, because that's the version that travels.
Where this overlaps with technical SEO — and where it doesn't

Honestly: part of this work is technical SEO. Structured data, semantic structure, content reachable without scripts, sensible loading — all of it helps search engines too, and if you've had serious technical SEO done recently, some of this is already in place.

The difference is what it's aimed at. Technical SEO targets a ranking position; this targets being repeatable in an answer. A page can rank perfectly well and still be summarised into something generic, because ranking rewards relevance while summarisation rewards specificity you can verify.
If you want the ranking work and the AI side as one ongoing job, see
AI SEO services
I'll tell you during the audit which parts you already have, rather than re-selling work someone else did.
What AI search optimization cannot guarantee

Nobody can guarantee that an assistant will name you. Answers vary between runs, get reassembled over time, and depend on phrasing, language and whether the assistant searched at all. What can be done is removing the reasons not to name you: ambiguity, unreachable content, contradictory markup, and claims stated in a form nothing can repeat.
That shifts probability. It doesn't buy certainty, and anyone selling certainty here is selling something they don't control.
This is one of four services under
AI-Ready SEO & GEO
, the broader work of making a business legible and accurate to AI search.

robots.txt, sitemaps, and canonical tags

Why SEO Strategy Matters Now
Search behavior is evolving faster than ever. AI-driven search platforms such as Google SGE, ChatGPT Search, and Perplexity AI are transforming the way people discover information online.
Websites optimized for GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) are already gaining extra exposure — appearing directly in AI-generated search results, not just traditional SERPs.
That’s why SEO today is no longer optional or static. It’s a living system that requires strategy, adaptability, and a clear understanding of how search is changing.
When you invest in SEO strategy now, you’re building a structure that continues to grow — while competitors chase the algorithm of yesterday.
Real Optimization Examples
Practical improvements often start small — but add up fast:
fixing crawl issues and sitemap hierarchy,
optimizing metadata and intent alignment,
refining internal links and canonical logic,
setting structured data for articles, FAQs, or services,
and ensuring your site passes Core Web Vitals on all devices.
These optimizations combine to make your website AI-readable, Google-friendly, and human-centered.
Future SEO — AI and GEO
I prepare every project for the future of search. With Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), your content becomes understandable for AI models that power Google’s SGE and ChatGPT-like engines.

This means your brand can show up inside AI-generated responses — not only in traditional search results. It’s the next evolution of visibility — and I help you get there now, while others are still adapting.

children.text: I am an SEO consultant: an independent specialist who finds out why a website gets less search traffic than it should, fixes the causes in the site itself and measures what changed. I work alone and remotely from Warsaw, for businesses in Europe, the UK, the US, Cyprus and Israel — so the person who reviews your site is the same person who edits its templates and sends you the report.
What an SEO consultant does: audit, fixes in the code, measurement
SEO consultant services are often sold as advice. Advice alone rarely moves a site, because the recommendations wait in someone’s backlog for months. My work has three stages, and I do all three:

Audit. I crawl the site, read Search Console and analytics, compare your pages with the ones Google ranks for your searches and write down what blocks you: indexing problems, thin or duplicate pages, slow templates, weak internal linking, titles that do not match what people type.
Fixes. I make the changes myself — in WordPress, in Next.js and React code, in a headless CMS — or give your developer tickets precise enough to apply without a meeting.
Measurement. Before the first change I record a baseline: clicks, queries and the pages that bring enquiries. Every report compares against it, so you see what the work did and what it did not.
The full list of SEO work — technical fixes, content plans, links, international SEO — is on the
SEO optimization and strategy
page. This page is about hiring the person who does it.
SEO consulting formats: a consultation, an audit, monthly work or a second opinion
Not every business needs a retainer. I work in four formats, and the free first call is where we pick one:
One-off SEO consultation — a call about a specific question: a planned redesign, a sudden traffic drop, a choice between two site structures. You get a written summary of what we agreed.
SEO audit — a written review of the whole site with priorities and a plan, from 250 €. What it covers is described on the
SEO audit
page.
Monthly work — I keep fixing, writing page briefs, building internal links and reporting, from 800 € per month.
A second opinion for an in-house team — I review what your marketer, developer or agency plans to do before money goes into it, and say what I would change and why.
SEO consultant vs SEO agency vs in-house specialist vs marketplace freelancer
Many buyers search for an “SEO consultant agency” because they are not sure which of the two they need. There are four common options, and each fits a different situation:

SEO agency — a team with an account manager, writers and often ads and social media under one contract. Good when you need many channels at once; the price includes the structure, and the specialist on your account can change.
In-house SEO specialist — a full-time employee who knows your product deeply. Worth it when SEO fills a full week, every week; for most small and mid-size sites it does not.
Freelancer from a marketplace — quick to hire and cheap per task. Fine for a defined job such as fixing broken links; risky for strategy, because nobody checks the decisions.
Independent SEO consultant — one experienced person who plans the work and does it. You get senior SEO skills and the speed of someone who can change the live site the same day.

My focus is organic search: Google and AI answers. If you also buy ads or post on social media, I work alongside the people who manage them — shared data on landing pages, search terms and conversions helps both sides.

contentBlocks.title: What promoting a Polish clinic to German patients involves

children.text: Why a foreign patient asks questions a local patient never asks

A clinic wanting to receive patients from Germany usually starts by translating the site. That step is necessary and entirely insufficient, because a foreign patient differs from a local one not in language but in situation.

A local patient compares clinics. A patient in Germany is planning an undertaking: how many times they will travel and at what intervals, how long each stay lasts, how far it is from the border or the airport, where they will stay, what happens if dates move, and above all what happens once they are home again.

None of those questions appear on a site built for local patients, because local patients don't ask them. A translated site therefore answers half of what a foreign patient needs, and loses to the clinic that wrote the other half.
The query research has to be built in German, not translated
This is the part that transfers between markets not at all.

Patients describe their situations using the terms current in their own system and everyday speech. Procedure names, the way costs are discussed, how waiting and scheduling are referred to — all of it has local equivalents that don't emerge from translating a Polish keyword list.
The failure is silent: the site ranks for descriptive phrasings nobody types
while the queries actually being made go elsewhere. Nothing shows in analytics, because missing queries leave nothing to count.
"And afterwards?" is the question that decides
A patient committing to treatment abroad isn't thinking about the day of the procedure. They're thinking about the weeks after it, when they will be in another country.

Who answers the phone if something is worrying. Whether the arrangements cover situations needing attention later. How contact works at a distance. What happens if another visit becomes necessary, and on what terms.

This is the most common quiet reason for withdrawing and the least described area on clinic websites. The answer doesn't have to be impressive; it has to exist. A clinic that wrote it looks prepared to receive foreign patients rather than merely willing not to refuse them.
Language versions have to be markets, not copies

A frequent technical failure: the German version exists but without correct hreflang, or with incomplete return references. Search engines then treat both versions as duplicates competing for one position, the signal splits, and both perform worse than a single version would have.
Nothing shows in analytics as a fault — only underperformance without a cause. Worth checking before adding any content.
The advertising rules here are doubled

Medical advertising is restricted in Poland, and material addressed to a patient in Germany may fall under German rules as well. The two are different, and in cross-border communication the question of which applies stops being theoretical.
That's a question for your clinic's lawyer rather than for whoever builds the site, and it's worth asking before the content is written rather than after. I am neither a lawyer nor a physician.
Practically it means content describing process, organisation and conditions rather than promising outcomes. That content sits within both frameworks and is exactly what the patient is looking for.

Separately: this page doesn't compare healthcare systems or claim where anything is cheaper or better. The patient does that comparison themselves; the job is to make sure they find you while doing it.
AI assistants answer in the language of the question

A patient looking for treatment abroad increasingly describes their situation to an assistant and asks where to go. The assistant answers in the language of the question, drawing on sources in that language.
A clinic well described in Polish can be entirely absent from German answers — and won't learn that from any report which doesn't measure it separately.
What gets repeated is checkable fact: where the clinic is, which procedures it handles
, which languages it works in, how a stay is organised. Promotional language gets discarded and replaced by the generic description of the category.
What the work covers

Query research built in German. Content about travel, scheduling and how the process spreads over time. An answer to what happens after returning home. A multilingual structure with correct hreflang. Visibility in German AI answers, measured separately. And reporting split by market, so the question of whether the German version paid for itself has an answer.

What comes from your side: what foreign patients ask before travelling, how you organise the stay and contact afterwards, and what you don't take on. That's what the query research and the content are built from.

children.text: Why a Swiss premium maker's audience is almost entirely abroad
The domestic market for a Swiss watchmaker, jeweller or premium workshop
is a rounding error against the international one. That isn't a limitation — it's the defining fact of the category, and it decides what the website has to be.

The buyer is in Germany, the Gulf, the United States, East Asia. They are searching in their own language, comparing against alternatives they can see, and — because the sum is significant and the object is bought unseen — verifying before they commit. Every part of that differs from selling to someone standing in front of the display case.

Which means the three Swiss language regions, which matter enormously for most businesses here, matter comparatively little for this one. The relevant languages are wherever the demand is, and establishing that from data rather than from geography is the first useful step.
The most common problem is that resellers outrank the maker

Before any category-level ambition, there's usually a more immediate loss: someone searching for your brand, a model name or a reference number finds retailers, marketplaces and secondary-market listings above your own site.

That's a buyer who was already looking for you specifically, arriving somewhere else — often somewhere that sells the same object with a margin attached, sometimes somewhere selling something that isn't yours at all.

Reclaiming those searches is usually the fastest meaningful result available in this category. It requires the maker's own pages to be structured, complete and unambiguous about models, references and collections — which sounds obvious and is frequently not the case, because maker sites are built as brand statements rather than as answers to specific searches.
Authenticity is the content nobody publishes

A buyer about to spend a significant sum on an object they have not held searches for reassurance, and the searches are specific: how to verify a serial number, what the certificate should say, what's included with an original, how to tell a piece with replaced parts, whether a particular seller is authorised.
They almost never find the maker's own answer. They find forums, collector communities and, occasionally, competitors explaining it better.

Publishing this is straightforward, uncomfortable for some makers because it acknowledges the grey market exists, and among the highest-value content available in the category. It matches searches with clear purchase intent, it establishes the maker as the authority on their own product, and
it's exactly the material an AI assistant will draw on when asked how to verify a piece
Craft has to be stated in facts to survive being repeated
The standard text in this category is heritage, tradition, precision, passion, generations of expertise. None of it is untrue and none of it does any work.

A search engine can't match it to a query. An assistant summarising your brand can't restate it usefully, so it substitutes the generic description of the category — and a maker with two hundred years of history is described in the same words as one founded last year.

What survives is specific: where the work is done, how many people do it, how long a piece takes, which components are made in-house, what the finishing involves, what the guarantee covers. Facts of that kind can be repeated by a machine and checked by a buyer, which is the same requirement from two directions.
Product data is the technical half

Materials, movement or mechanism, dimensions, collection, reference number, edition size. When these live in prose or in photographs, the page doesn't match the search — a buyer looking for a specific reference or a specific case size types it, and finds retailers who put it in a structured field.

For makers with a catalogue, there's an additional consideration: every product page multiplies across language versions, and a structure that handles that poorly produces near-duplicates competing with each other rather than covering markets.
The origin question, handled carefully

Designations of Swiss origin are legally defined, with conditions on what may be described how. What your specific business is entitled to claim is a question for your lawyer, and one worth confirming rather than assuming — the phrasing on a website is exactly the kind of thing that gets examined.

The practical approach is precision: describe what's actually true about where and how the object is made, in enough detail that it needs no shorthand. Specificity is more persuasive than a claimed designation anyway, and it carries no risk.

children.text: Why a Swiss car business is an export business whether it means to be or not
Switzerland is a small market surrounded by large ones
. For most categories that's a constraint; for the car trade it's the defining condition.

Vehicles move across these borders constantly — sold to buyers in Germany, Italy, France and further east, brought in, exported again, moved for a specification that isn't available locally. A dealer or exporter based here is trading internationally by default, and the buyer on the other end is searching in their own language for something specific.

That changes what the website is for. A Swiss-language site aimed at Swiss buyers serves the smallest part of the addressable market. The German-language buyer searching for a specific model, the Italian buyer comparing prices across the border, the buyer who needs to know whether the paperwork will work in their country — none of them are reached by a site that assumed a local audience.
The three-language problem inside the country, before you even leave it
Switzerland has German-, French- and Italian-speaking regions that search differently, in different languages, with different competitors.

Most car business sites here pick one — usually whichever the owner speaks — and lose the other two without noticing. That's a decision made by default rather than deliberately, and it halves the domestic market before the foreign one is even considered.

The practical question isn't whether to be multilingual. It's which languages actually send you buyers, in what proportion, and which one leads. That answer differs by region, by vehicle segment and by whether you're selling locally or exporting, and it's worth establishing from data rather than assumption.
What a foreign buyer researches before making contact
Worth knowing because it's content that almost no competitor has.

Whether the vehicle's specification matches what's registrable in their country. What the export paperwork involves and who handles it. What customs will cost. Whether the technical inspection in their country will pass a vehicle certified here. How payment and transport work across a border. What happens if something is wrong on arrival.

A buyer spending a significant sum on a vehicle they haven't seen, in a country they're not in, reads all of this carefully — and usually finds it nowhere. The site that answers it is the one that gets the enquiry, and this is the single clearest content opportunity in the category.
Listings are the part most sites get technically wrong
Vehicle pages are search pages, and most of them aren't built as such.

Model, year, engine, transmission, equipment level, mileage and condition are what buyers type. When those exist as free text in a description or, worse, only in photographs, the page doesn't match the query. Structured data makes them machine-readable, which matters for search and
matters more for AI assistants
— which increasingly answer "find me a 2019 model with this specification in Switzerland" directly.

There's also a structural point specific to listings sites: every vehicle page multiplies across your language versions. A structure that handles that badly produces thousands of near-duplicate pages competing with each other, which is worse than having fewer languages done properly.
The platform question

Most car businesses here get much of their visibility from listing platforms, and that arrangement is reasonable — platforms bring buyers who would never have found the dealer directly, and the commission pays for that.

What's worth reclaiming is the share of buyers who already know your name and use the platform out of habit. Those enquiries cost a percentage for nothing, and they're the ones a properly found site captures.
This isn't an argument for leaving the platforms. It's an argument for not being invisible without them.
What the work covers
Multilingual structure that carries every language a car business needs

without the versions competing. Listings built so a specification typed in another country matches the page describing it. Structured data that search engines and AI assistants can repeat. And the cross-border content — paperwork, customs, inspection, registration — that answers what a foreign buyer researches before making contact.

children.text: Why the domestic platforms leave the export buyer underserved
Germany has the strongest used-vehicle marketplaces in Europe

, and for a German buyer they work extremely well: enormous inventory, precise filtering, established trust. A dealer competing with them for German search traffic is fighting a losing battle and should not bother.
The picture changes entirely when the buyer is not German.

A buyer in Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, the Baltics or further east searches in their own language, using their own vocabulary for models and specifications, and asks questions the platforms were never built to answer. They get filtered listings and a price. They do not get an explanation of what exporting the vehicle involves, what paperwork changes hands, what customs will cost them at home, or what happens if something is wrong on arrival.
That is the gap. Not a gap in inventory or price, where the platforms are unbeatable, but a gap in language and explanation, where almost no dealer has written anything at all.
The buyer's language is not a translation of yours
The common approach is to run the German site through translation and consider the market served. It isn't, for a specific reason.

Vehicle searches are highly idiomatic. Models are referred to by different shorthand in different markets. Equipment levels and specification terms have local names. The words buyers use for condition, mileage bands and service history differ. A translated German keyword list produces pages targeting the descriptive version of a query rather than the version people actually type.

Building the list in the buyer's language is the difference between appearing for terms with volume and appearing for terms with none. It's also the part that never transfers between markets — the technical work does, the query research doesn't.
The export explanation is content that barely exists

Ask a foreign buyer what they need to know before committing to a vehicle in Germany, and the list is consistent: how deregistration works, which documents they receive and when, whether transit plates are arranged and by whom, what customs will cost in their country, whether the specification will pass registration at home, how payment is handled across a border, and what recourse exists if the car isn't as described.
These are practical, answerable questions. Almost no dealer answers them publicly, and the buyers looking for answers find forums, intermediaries and occasionally competitors who did write it down.

Publishing this is the single clearest content opportunity in the category. It matches searches with unambiguous purchase intent, it establishes the dealer as the source rather than the middleman, and
it's exactly the material an AI assistant will draw on when a buyer describes their situation
and asks how the process works.
Vehicle pages have to be readable by a machine

A buyer searching for a specific model, year, engine or equipment level types that specification. If those details live in a free-text description or in photographs, the page doesn't match — and the platform listing, which stores them in structured fields, does.

Structured product data on vehicle pages is what closes that gap. It matters for search and increasingly more for AI assistants, which answer specification questions directly and can only work with what they can parse.
For dealers with large inventories there's a second consideration:
every vehicle page multiplies across language versions
. A structure that handles that badly produces thousands of near-duplicate pages competing with each other, which costs more than the extra languages gain.
One channel is a business risk, not just a marketing one

A dealer whose entire visibility comes from one marketplace has no position of their own. Fees change, ranking rules change, terms change — and none of that is negotiable from a position of total dependence.

This isn't an argument for leaving the platforms; they bring buyers who would never have found the dealer directly, and the fee for those is fair. It's an argument for owning the segment that the platforms don't serve, which happens to be the same segment with the highest margins and the least competition.

Most vehicle markets sell to the person who will drive the car

That single fact reorganises everything the site has to do.

A driver wants to know how the car feels and what it costs. A dealer wants to know whether it can be sold where they operate: whether the specification registers there, what the documentation looks like, how shipping is arranged, what happens if the inspection at arrival disagrees with the description, and whether the supplier will still be reachable in three months.
Those are business questions, and a site written in consumer language answers none of them.
The specification question decides the deal

In a market that re-exports, the decisive variable is compatibility. Regional build, drive side, climate and emissions configuration — a vehicle that cannot be registered in the buyer's country is worthless to them regardless of price or condition.

So the buyer's first question, before price, is whether this particular vehicle works where they are. And in most listings that answer simply isn't there: the specification exists in the seller's shorthand, in photographs, or not at all.
Publishing it clearly — what each vehicle is built to,
in terms a buyer can check against their own requirements

— is the single highest-value change available in this category. It matches searches with unambiguous intent, it removes the enquiry that exists only to ask this question, and it filters out buyers who would have withdrawn anyway.

Requirements differ by country and change over time, which is precisely why the site should state what the vehicle is rather than what it is permitted to be somewhere. The first is a fact you control; the second is a moving target you don't.
Selling to a dealer is not selling to a driver

The buyer running a resale business evaluates on different axes: consistency of supply, terms at volume, how inspection and documentation are handled, shipping arrangements and timelines, and what recourse exists if something is wrong on arrival.

They also evaluate the supplier, not just the vehicle. A dealer committing to a shipment is entering a relationship, and everything on the site that establishes the exporter as a stable, contactable, documented business does more work than any description of the car.
This is content most exporters have never written, because the business grew through brokers and personal contact where none of it needed writing down.
The broker channel doesn't scale, and search is what does
Trade here runs substantially through intermediaries and messaging. That works well and there's no argument for abandoning it — relationships in this business are genuinely valuable.
The limitation is structural: a buyer you haven't met cannot find you through a channel built on people you already know. The broker network reaches its own edges and stops.
Search reaches past them

. A dealer in another country, searching for a specific configuration in their own language, finds whoever wrote for them — and almost nobody has. That's not a replacement for the existing channel; it's the part of the market the existing channel structurally cannot touch.
Buyers arrive from markets that don't search in English
Vehicles from here go to Central Asia, the CIS, Africa and South Asia. Those buyers search in their own languages, using their own vocabulary for models, configurations and condition.

An English-only site serves the portion of that demand that searches in English, which is smaller than it appears — professional buyers often read English adequately and still search in their first language, because that's how they think about specifications.
Which languages are worth building is a data question rather than a guess, and usually the answer is two or three markets rather than all of them.

children.text: Why one client a quarter changes what search work should look like
Most search advice assumes traffic is the goal
: more visitors, better conversion, more business. For a professional firm in Switzerland that logic inverts almost completely.

An engagement here can be worth more than a year of search work. Which means the useful question is not how many people arrive but whether the specific few who matter can find you — and whether what they find holds up when they check it, which they will, thoroughly.

That reframes everything. A query with forty searches a month is not a weak query in this context; it may be the strongest one on the list. Volume thresholds imported from consumer categories discard precisely the terms worth having, and a supplier who dismisses a market as too small is applying arithmetic from somewhere else.
Being findable requires saying what you actually do
The most common problem in this category isn't technical. It's that the site could describe any firm in the sector.

Strategy, expertise, tailored solutions, trusted advisor, decades of combined experience. None of it is false, and none of it matches a query. Someone looking for a specialist in a specific regulatory question, a particular industry, a defined kind of transaction types that specificity — and finds firms who wrote it down.

The uncomfortable part is that stating a specialisation means declining the work outside it, at least in what the site says. Many firms won't, and stay invisible as a result. The ones that do get found by exactly the clients they wanted.
This is also what AI assistants can repeat

. A machine summarising your firm can restate "advises on cross-border structuring for manufacturing groups"; it cannot usefully restate "trusted strategic partner", so it substitutes the generic description of your category — and you appear as an unremarkable example of it.
The three language regions, and when English overrides them

German-, French- and Italian-speaking Switzerland behave as separate markets with separate competitors and separate search behaviour. A firm in Zurich serving Romandy in German only is not serving it.

But there's a case specific to this category: when the clientele is international — foreign companies with Swiss operations, cross-border transactions, international families — English may carry more of the commercial intent than any domestic language. That happens often enough here to be worth establishing from data rather than assuming the domestic default.
Which of the four leads is a business question that determines the whole structure, and it's the first thing worth settling.
What a prospect verifies before making contact
This category is checked more thoroughly than almost any other, because the buyer is often a professional themselves.

Named individuals rather than a firm-level "our team". Actual credentials, stated plainly and verifiable. Regulatory standing and memberships. Engagements described specifically enough to be believed, within whatever confidentiality allows. And consistency: the same details in every professional directory, association listing and profile carrying your name, because a discrepancy in a category built on precision reads badly.
None of this is expensive. What's expensive is not knowing the evaluation happens before the first email, and that a prospect who finds a gap usually just stops.
Professional advertising rules are a constraint, not an obstacle

Regulated professions in Switzerland operate under restrictions on how services can be presented — what may be claimed, how results may be described, what constitutes acceptable promotion. Which rules apply to your practice is a question for your professional body rather than for a supplier, and worth confirming rather than assuming.

What this means practically is that the work adapts. Content that demonstrates expertise rather than asserting outcomes, specificity about capability rather than claims about results, and structure that makes a firm findable without saying anything a regulator would object to.
That constraint is workable, and firms that treat it as a reason not to be findable at all are leaving the position to competitors who found the line.
What the work covers
Query research at the level this category actually searches

— narrow, specific, low-volume and high-value. Specialisation written as checkable claims that both a reader and a machine can repeat. Language decisions made from data. The verification layer: structured data, consistency across professional directories, and the facts a prospect checks. And measurement specific enough that single-figure results are readable.
What comes from your side is the specialisation itself — which work you want more of, which you'd rather decline, and what genuinely distinguishes the practice. That shapes everything after it.
If a business runs the same kind of search work across more than one country market, that broader, multi-market version is covered separately in international and multilingual SEO.

Prospects increasingly brief an assistant the way they would brief a trusted colleague. The CFO of a German group asks “Which Zurich firm advises mid-sized manufacturers on transfer pricing for their Swiss subsidiaries?”, and a founder moving to Zug asks “Which advisers in Zug help a foreign entrepreneur set up a holding company, and do they work in English?”
Put simply, GEO decides whether a model counts your firm among the sources it draws on, and AEO whether one of your own sentences becomes the reply it gives.
Practice areas, industries served, languages of advice and the partners’ names with their qualifications, written on the pages themselves rather than locked in a PDF brochure.

Identical firm details on Google Business Profile, Bing Places, LinkedIn and your professional association’s member listing: the same name, address and practice areas in each.

children.text: Why organic search carries more weight in this category than in most
Advertising for intimate apparel runs into platform restrictions.

What exactly is permitted varies by platform, by market and by how a product is presented, and the rules change — so any specific claim about them dates quickly, and it's worth confirming the current position for your own products rather than relying on what was true last year.

The commercial consequence is stable regardless of the detail: a manufacturer in this category cannot simply buy its way to visibility the way one in an unrestricted category can. Paid reach is available but constrained, and every constraint on paid channels raises the relative value of organic position.
Most manufacturers here have not acted on that. Which means the search results for sourcing terms are, in many sub-categories, noticeably less contested than the size of the industry would suggest.
The buyer is not the wearer, and searches nothing like them
This is the distinction that decides the whole strategy.

Consumer search in this category is about product: style, fit, occasion, brand. Sourcing search is about capability: who can manufacture to a specification, at what minimum, with which certifications, in which country, with what lead time.
The two vocabularies barely overlap.
A manufacturer whose site is written in consumer language

is competing in the wrong auction — against brands and retailers with far larger budgets — while the sourcing searches, which are fewer, less contested and worth vastly more per visitor, go to whoever wrote for them.
Establishing which sourcing terms your buyers actually use is the first work, and it typically produces a list that looks small and converts unusually well.
Size conversion is the visibility opportunity hiding in plain sight

Sizing in this category is not standardised across markets, and the differences are not a simple offset. Buyers, retailers and distributors look up conversions constantly — it's one of the most searched practical questions in the industry.
Almost no manufacturer publishes a good answer. Retailers do, marketplaces do, and forums do it badly.

A manufacturer with a correct, well-structured conversion resource — genuinely useful, covering the systems its export markets use — earns visibility in a category where paid reach is limited, positions itself as the technical authority in its own product, and provides material that AI assistants will draw on when asked. It's the clearest content opportunity here and it costs nothing but accuracy.
Trade fairs are twice a year; search is every day
The traditional channel in this industry is the fair: a concentrated few days where buyers and manufacturers meet.

Fairs work, and nothing here argues otherwise. But between them, buyers still have specifications to source, suppliers to replace and ranges to plan — and what they do in that time is search. A manufacturer visible only at the fair is discoverable four days a year.
The practical framing is that search doesn't replace the fair; it covers the fifty weeks the fair doesn't.
Sourcing questions are increasingly asked of assistants
Worth noting because it's recent and because this category is unusually exposed to it.

A buyer looking for a supplier now often starts by describing the requirement to an AI assistant — a category, a quantity, a certification, a region — and receiving a shortlist of two or three names. What puts a manufacturer in that list is not advertising, which is restricted here anyway,
but being described unambiguously and corroborated by sources outside its own site
That's measurable, it moves independently of search positions, and in a category with constrained paid channels it's one of the few places a manufacturer can gain ground quickly.

children.text: Why the buying process is where the search demand actually is
An agency selling to foreign buyers usually builds its site as a catalogue
, on the reasonable assumption that people looking for property want to see property.
They do — eventually. What happens first, and takes far longer, is working out whether buying is feasible at all.

A buyer considering a purchase in another country spends months on questions that have nothing to do with any specific apartment: what the total cost is beyond the asking price, what the sequence of steps looks like, which documents are needed and when, who is involved, what happens between agreement and completion, what ongoing costs follow ownership, and what the situation is for someone who isn't resident.

Every one of those is a search. Most of them are answered by forums, expat communities, law firms and occasionally a competitor who wrote it down — and by the time the buyer starts looking at properties, their understanding, their expectations and often their shortlist of who to contact have already formed elsewhere.
The agency that answers those questions meets the buyer at the start of the process rather than at the end of it. That's the whole strategic point of this page.
Competing with the portals on property searches is the expensive way to lose
Searches for apartments in a specific town or region are held by the large property portals, which have inventory, authority and years of accumulated signal that an individual agency cannot match.
This isn't a defeatist observation, it's a targeting one. Those searches are the most obvious and the least reachable, and budget spent pursuing them buys impressions rather than enquiries.

What is reachable sits beside them: the process questions the portals have no reason to answer thoroughly, the area-specific explanations that require local knowledge rather than inventory, and the situational queries that come from a buyer's circumstances rather than from a property type.
Those searches are fewer, far less contested, and produce enquiries from people who have already decided to buy.
Three audiences, and you probably don't serve all three

Local Spanish buyers, foreign residents already living in the country, and buyers researching from abroad are not variations of one audience. They search in different languages, at different stages, with different questions and different anxieties.

A remote buyer needs the process explained and needs to trust an agency they will meet, at most, once before committing. A resident foreigner already understands the country and is comparing areas and prices. A local buyer needs neither and is comparing on entirely different axes.

Most agencies sell primarily to one or two of these and build a site that vaguely addresses all three. Establishing which you actually sell to — from your own enquiry history rather than from ambition — is the first work, because it determines the languages, the content and the entire structure.
The regulatory questions belong on the site, stated carefully

Costs, taxes, documentation requirements and the rules affecting non-resident buyers differ by region and change over time. That variation is exactly why buyers search for them so persistently, and exactly why so few agencies publish anything.

The workable approach is to explain the shape of the process and the categories of cost while making clear that specifics depend on the region, the property and the buyer's circumstances, and that professional confirmation is needed. That's honest, it's genuinely useful, and it captures the search without asserting anything that could become wrong.
An agency that publishes nothing because the details vary leaves the entire demand to sources with less accountability.
Assistants now answer the process questions too
A buyer working out how to purchase abroad increasingly asks an AI assistant rather than searching. They describe their situation and ask what the process involves and who they should approach.
What gets repeated in those answers is anything stated as a checkable fact

— where an agency operates, which buyer nationalities it works with, which languages it handles, what it does and doesn't cover. What gets discarded is brochure language, which is replaced by the generic description of an estate agency.
The practical consequence is that the same content which captures process searches also determines whether an assistant can name you. It's one piece of work serving two channels.

, over 1,500 organic visits a month with no advertising budget, and nearly all of those buyers deciding remotely before ever visiting.
