contentBlocks.title: What search work for a UAE real estate agency involves

children.text: Why selling before completion changes what the buyer searches for
In most property markets the buyer looks at something that exists
. Here, a large share of transactions concern something that doesn't yet — and that single difference reorganises the entire search demand.

A buyer choosing a finished apartment asks about the apartment: layout, view, condition, price, neighbourhood. A buyer committing before completion asks about time and process: what the stages are, what they pay and when, what they receive at each point, what happens if the schedule moves, what completion involves, and what their position is throughout.

Those are the searches that dominate this category, and they are answered almost nowhere by the agencies themselves. Buyers find forums, communities of previous purchasers, and occasionally competitors who wrote something — and their understanding of how the whole thing works forms there, months before they contact anyone.
An agency that publishes clear answers meets the buyer during that period rather than after it.
The evaluation is partly about who is building

When a purchase precedes the building, the buyer is assessing an organisation as much as an object. Their questions reflect that: who is delivering this, what have they delivered before, what does their record look like, what should I check.

Most agencies avoid this territory entirely, which is understandable — it involves discussing third parties. But avoiding it means the buyer forms their view somewhere with less accountability, and arrives either wrongly reassured or wrongly alarmed.

The workable version is factual and general: what a buyer should look at, what kinds of information exist and where, what questions to ask. That's genuinely useful, it captures a large volume of anxious searching, and it positions the agency as the source rather than the interested party.
Regulatory questions belong on the site, stated with unusual care

Rules on purchasing before completion, the mechanisms protecting buyer funds, registration procedures and foreign ownership arrangements are regulated, they differ by emirate and project type, and they change.

That variation is exactly why buyers search so persistently — and exactly why the answers must be framed carefully. The site should explain the shape of the process and the categories of question a buyer needs answered, while stating plainly that specifics depend on the project and require confirmation from the appropriate authority or professional.

What does not belong anywhere on such a page: claims about returns, characterisations of property as an investment, or assurances about safety and reliability. Those are financial statements, they are regulated, and they turn a useful page into a liability.
Buyers arrive from dozens of countries at once

This is the structural difference from almost every other property market. Demand here does not come primarily from one or two neighbouring countries; it arrives simultaneously from South Asia, the CIS, Europe, Africa and East Asia.
Every one of those buyers searches in their own language, describes property types with their own vocabulary, and brings different assumptions about how buying works where they come from.

That has two consequences. The obvious one is that language versions matter more here than in a market with concentrated demand. The less obvious one is that you cannot serve all of them — and the useful work begins with establishing, from your own enquiry history, which four or five markets actually produce buyers, rather than which twenty are theoretically present.
The catalogue multiplies, and the structure has to survive it

With a property catalogue and several language versions, every listing exists many times over. Handled badly, that produces thousands of near-duplicate pages competing with each other, diluting the site rather than covering markets.
Handled properly, the language versions are structural and the listings inherit them, so adding a market is a content decision rather than a rebuild.
This is the technical half of the work and it's worth settling before any content is written, because retrofitting it is where the cost appears.
Assistants answer these questions now too
A buyer working out how purchasing here functions increasingly asks an AI assistant, describes their situation and receives both an explanation and a shortlist of who to approach.
What gets repeated in those answers is anything stated as a checkable fact

: where the agency operates, which buyer nationalities it works with, which languages it handles, what it does and doesn't do. Promotional phrasing gets discarded and replaced by the generic description of an estate agency — which is the opposite of positioning.
So the same content that captures the process searches also determines whether an assistant names you. One piece of work, two channels.

I've built for buyers deciding remotely before ever visiting: a four-language property catalogue drawing buyers from more than twenty countries, over 1,500 organic visits a month with no advertising budget. Different market, the same behaviour.
What the work covers

Content built around stages, timing and process rather than the catalogue. Query research per buying market rather than translated. A structure that carries the catalogue across languages without duplication. Material that helps buyers evaluate what they're committing to, stated factually and within the limits above. Facts an assistant can repeat. And reporting split by buyer country, because an aggregate figure across dozens of markets is unusable.

What comes from your side is the market knowledge — which countries your buyers actually come from, what they ask before committing, which projects and areas you know properly, and where deals fall apart. That shapes the query research, and it can't be produced from outside the agency.
If a business runs the same kind of search work across more than one country market, that broader, multi-market version is covered separately in international and multilingual SEO.
Real estate SEO in the UAE for AI search: off-plan buyers’ questions answered by ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Buyers abroad bring their off-plan questions to an assistant months before they call an agent. A buyer in Germany asks “How do off-plan payment plans in Dubai work, and which agency explains the escrow arrangement in German?”, and a family in the UK asks “Which Abu Dhabi agency handles the handover inspection for owners who live abroad?”
Generative engine optimization means being part of the material an assistant reads before it writes; answer engine optimization means being the paragraph it actually returns.
Stated facts: the emirates and communities you cover, off-plan or ready stock, your working languages, the stages you accompany and when you refer the buyer to a lawyer or the relevant authority.
RealEstateAgent markup for the agency, listing data per unit with type, size, expected handover quarter and price, and hreflang for every buyer-language version.
The same agency name, address and registration details on Bayut, Property Finder, Google Business Profile and Bing Places.
Answers to stage, payment-timing and handover questions in each buyer language, with no statements about returns or yields.

contentBlocks.title: What Shopify SEO services cover

children.text: What Shopify SEO has to work around

Shopify takes a set of decisions out of your hands, and most Shopify SEO work is about the consequences. The URL structure is fixed: products live under /products/, collections under /collections/, the blog under /blogs/. You cannot flatten those, so the work is to make every internal link, the sitemap and the canonical agree on one address per item — which they do not do by default, because a product linked from inside a collection is served at a second address with the collection in the path.

The theme is the second constraint. All collections share one template and all products share another, so anything written once appears everywhere unless the template is taught to read per-page values. That is a one-off piece of theme work, after which every collection can carry its own title and its own intro without a developer being involved again.

The third is apps. Every app that adds a review widget, an upsell, a pop-up or a currency switcher adds scripts to the same page, and the cost lands on the product template where the buying happens. Auditing that is unglamorous and it is usually where the largest speed win on a Shopify store sits.
Shopify SEO and ordinary ecommerce SEO: what is different

The strategy is the same as for any online store: collection pages are the landing pages, one address per product, a policy for items that stop being sold, markup that matches the visible page. The differences are all in how a fix is applied.

On a custom store a developer changes the routing. On Shopify the routing is fixed and the fix is in the links, the canonicals and the sitemap. On a custom store structured data is written once in the template. On Shopify it is often emitted twice — by the theme and again by a review app — with two different prices, and the work is removing one of them rather than adding anything.
What carries over unchanged is the thinking about categories, filters and dead products, which is described on
the ecommerce SEO services page
. This page is about the platform's own limits.

Theme work is quoted separately from monthly SEO, because it is a one-off: once the collection template reads per-page titles and intros and the duplicate markup is gone, it stays fixed. I can apply it in the theme myself or write it up for whoever maintains it and check the result afterwards.
What I will not do is install another SEO app and call that the work. Most of them add a settings panel over the same theme files, plus more scripts on the page that is already too heavy.

Most sites do not need another list of problems. The SEO audit is the diagnosis: it says what is wrong, in what order it matters and what it will cost. Technical SEO is the treatment: the same problems, fixed in the code and confirmed in Search Console.
If you already have an audit from someone else, I can work from it. If you do not, the audit comes first, and the fixing starts from its priorities rather than from a guess.
Who does the work

The same person who writes the code. That is the difference between a recommendation and a change: no ticket queue, no translation from SEO language into developer language, no fix that never ships because it was nobody's job.
The stack I work in daily is Next.js, React, TypeScript and Sanity, with WordPress where it is the right call. Everything is documented, so your own developer can keep it running afterwards.

An assistant can only quote what its crawler could fetch and read. When a facilities manager asks ChatGPT which firms in Kraków service industrial air conditioning, or a parent asks Perplexity which language schools nearby run evening courses for teenagers, the answer is assembled from pages that loaded cleanly for a bot. Organization, LocalBusiness or ProfessionalService markup generated from the same source as the visible text, and robots.txt rules that admit OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and Googlebot deliberately.
One version of the facts across canonicals, the sitemap, Google Business Profile and Bing Webmaster Tools, with IndexNow notifying Bing when a page changes.
Direct answers near the top of the page as plain text, not inside tabs or accordions that fetch their content on click.

contentBlocks.title: What traffic drop recovery involves

children.text: Why the date the traffic dropped is the whole diagnosis

Almost every conversation about a traffic drop starts with theories. The developer suspects the SEO work, whoever does the SEO suspects the last deployment, and someone mentions an algorithm update they read about. All of it is guessing, and all of it is unnecessary, because the answer is usually visible in ten minutes.
Search Console shows the day the decline started. Not the month — the day. And that single fact does most of the diagnostic work, because causes have signatures.

A drop that begins on the day of a deployment is a deployment problem. A drop that begins two to three weeks after a site launch is usually a crawl problem — the search engine took that long to notice the pages had changed. A drop that appears over several days across every page equally, with nothing having changed on the site, is external. A drop confined to one section is confined to whatever happened to that section.
Working from the date backwards is faster and more honest than working from theories forwards. It's also the reason this work can be quoted at all: without a date, the scope is anyone's guess.
What actually breaks, in order of how often
Redirects after a rebuild.
By a wide margin the most common

. New URLs, old ones returning nothing, and every accumulated signal pointing at addresses that no longer exist. Entirely fixable, usually within days, and the recovery follows once the pages are recrawled.

I've seen this cost a construction company most of its search traffic after a redesign that changed every URL without a redirect map. Two weeks to diagnose, about a month to recover — and the diagnosis was slower than the fix, which is typical.
Indexation quietly turning off.
A noindex left on after staging, a robots directive blocking a section, a canonical tag pointing everything at one page. Fast to find, faster to fix, and invisible unless someone checks.
Migration losses.
Platform, domain or hosting changes go wrong in specific ways
: lost redirects, changed URL patterns, pages that render differently to a crawler than to a browser.
One case I worked on involved
a site rebuilt with AI assistance where the language versions were wired to the wrong locales
. Traffic fell within two days. Diagnosis and repair took two weeks — again, most of that was finding it.
Content and structure changes.
Pages merged, text shortened, headings rewritten during a redesign. Slower to show up and slower to reverse than the technical causes.
External change.
No site change, broad decline,
competitors moving in the same period
. This is where the work stops being repair and starts being strategy.
The part where a supplier should tell you no
Not every drop is recoverable, and the honest position is worth stating before anyone signs anything.

If an algorithm update reweighted what your category rewards, the traffic you had was earned under rules that no longer apply. Recovery there isn't repair; it's rebuilding under different conditions, and it takes as long as building did.
If a competitor genuinely improved — better content, better site, more authority — then nothing on your side is broken. You were passed. That's a strategy conversation, not a fix.
If demand moved, the queries that used to bring traffic bring less to everyone. Your position may be unchanged.

I'd rather establish which of these applies during a diagnosis that costs a few hundred euros than discover it after a year of retainer. And where the answer is "this part isn't coming back", you'll hear that phrase rather than a plan.
Why diagnosis is quoted separately from the fix
Because the fix can't be quoted until the cause is known, and any supplier who quotes both together before looking is pricing a guess.

Redirect repair after a rebuild is a known quantity — days of work, predictable outcome. Recovering from a content change is weeks. Rebuilding after an algorithmic reweighting is months and isn't guaranteed. Those are three different projects with three different prices, and which one you have is exactly what the diagnosis establishes.

The diagnosis is also useful on its own. Several clients have taken the report and had their existing developer implement it, which is a reasonable outcome and one I'd rather have than a padded engagement.
What recovery actually looks like when it works

Not a straight line. Fixed redirects are recrawled over days or weeks depending on the size of the site and how often it's crawled, and positions return unevenly — some pages recover in days, others take a month.

Expect the shape rather than a date: an initial partial return as the most-crawled pages are reprocessed, then a slower tail. Anyone offering a specific date for full recovery is describing something they don't control.

And full recovery isn't always the outcome even when the cause was technical. Signals accumulate over time, and an interruption long enough for competitors to take the positions can leave a permanent gap. That's a reason to act quickly rather than a reason not to act.
If the traffic was never really there to begin with, that's a different problem —
local SEO
is what addresses ongoing visibility rather than a one-off drop.
Not sure which situation is yours? A
technical SEO audit
looks at why a site has no traffic at all — this service is specifically for traffic that was there and then wasn't.

contentBlocks.title: What a website performance audit covers

children.text: What a website performance audit actually measures

A score out of 100 is not a diagnosis. The audit measures what a visitor waits for, on the pages that matter to the business rather than on the homepage: how long until the main content appears, how long until a tap does something, and whether the layout jumps while they are reading. Then it explains which piece of the page is responsible for each of those numbers.

Two things make this different from running a free test yourself. The first is that a test gives you a symptom and the audit gives you the cause — «the largest element takes 4.1 seconds» becomes «the hero image is a 2.4 MB PNG served at full size and the font blocks rendering until it loads». The second is prioritisation: of the twenty things a test flags, usually three carry almost all the delay, and the rest are noise that costs more to fix than it returns.
Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP and CLS, and which one is costing you
LCP — how long until the main thing appears

Usually an image, a heading or a hero block. The common causes are an oversized image, a font that blocks rendering, a slow first byte from the server, and a page that renders in the browser instead of arriving ready. This is the metric most often responsible when a page «feels» slow.
INP — how long until a tap does something

Replaced the old FID in 2024 and is harsher: it measures every interaction, not just the first. Heavy JavaScript on the main thread is the usual cause — analytics, chat widgets, sliders, and page-builder scripts that keep running after the page looks finished.
CLS — how much the layout jumps while being read

Caused by images without dimensions, ads and embeds inserted after load, and fonts that swap and reflow the text. Cheap to fix and often ignored, because it annoys visitors without showing up in any report the owner reads.
What these three mean in practice, and what to check first when a site simply feels slow, is in the article
why is my website slow
Website code audit: what the code review finds that a speed test cannot

A speed test sees the finished page. A code audit sees how it was built, which is where the fixable problems live: components re-rendering on every scroll, data fetched on the client that could arrive with the page, images not run through any pipeline, a bundle shipping libraries used on one screen to every screen, and third-party scripts loaded in the head because that is where the instructions said to put them.

It also finds what is cheap to leave alone. Not every inefficiency is worth paying to fix, and an audit that returns a list of forty items without saying which three matter has given you homework rather than an answer.
JavaScript and rendering: why a fast server still gives a slow page

A site can respond in 80 milliseconds and still take four seconds to become usable, because the server sent a nearly empty document and the browser had to download, parse and execute JavaScript before anything appeared. That pattern is normal in single-page applications and in WordPress sites carrying a page builder plus a dozen plugins.

The fix is architectural rather than cosmetic: render on the server what can be rendered on the server, send to the browser only what the browser needs, and load the rest when it is actually required. On Next.js that is
Next.js development
, and when a site is too tangled to fix in place it is cheaper to
rebuild it keeping the rankings
than to keep paying for patches.
Performance audit or SEO audit — which one you need
They answer different questions, and buying the wrong one wastes the money rather than half of it.
the pages load slowly, the site works and is found — a performance and code audit;
the pages load fine and the site is not found — an SEO audit;
traffic dropped after a redesign or a migration — an SEO audit first, because the cause is usually addresses and redirects rather than speed;
Google says «poor» in Search Console but the site feels fast — a performance audit, because the field data disagrees with your laptop.
What the search-side audit covers is on the
SEO audit page
. Speed does affect rankings, but it is a tie-breaker between pages that are otherwise equal — it will not rank a page that answers nothing.

The audit is €250 and you get a document, not a dashboard screenshot: measured numbers for the templates that matter, the cause behind each number, a fix list ordered by milliseconds gained against hours spent, and what I would not touch. If the site turns out to be too tangled to fix in place, a rebuild that keeps the existing rankings starts at €1,000, and I will say which of the two is cheaper for you. The full list is on the

The report takes three working days. Implementation depends on what is found and is quoted after the audit rather than before it — anyone quoting the fix before measuring is guessing. Field data in Search Console moves on a 28-day rolling window, so Core Web Vitals there change about a month after the fixes ship, not the same week.

Send the address, say what the complaint is — slow on phones, Search Console reporting «poor», visitors leaving within seconds — and tell me what the site is built on if you know. When an SEO audit is the right first step
An SEO audit is especially useful if:
your website doesn’t generate leads or enquiries
organic traffic from Google is stagnant or declining
SEO was done in the past without clear outcomes
you’re planning to invest in SEO or a new website
you want to understand what to prioritise first — and what can wait
An audit removes guesswork and allows you to make decisions based on data.
What I analyse during an SEO audit
This is not an automated tool report. It’s a manual, business-focused analysis aimed at real issues and real growth. The audit typically covers:
Technical SEO
website speed and performance
technical errors and indexing issues
site structure and internal navigation
Core Web Vitals and mobile usability

What you get after a website SEO audit
After the audit, you receive clear, actionable insights, not generic advice:
a precise diagnosis of key issues
a prioritised action list (what first, what later)
recommendations tailored to your business
an honest assessment of whether SEO makes sense for your case
The audit does not require further cooperation.
What an SEO audit can tell you — and what it cannot

An audit answers a narrow set of questions precisely: why the pages you already have are not ranking, which of them have potential and which are dead weight, what is technically blocking indexation, and what a realistic order of work looks like. Those answers are worth having before money goes into content or links, because most wasted SEO budget is spent doing correct work on the wrong pages.

What an audit cannot do is predict positions. Anyone who attaches a ranking forecast to a diagnostic is selling certainty that does not exist — search results depend on what competitors do next, and that is not knowable in advance. An audit also cannot substitute for the work itself: it produces a prioritised list, not a finished site.

The honest framing is that an audit buys you a decision, not a result. If the conclusion is that search is the wrong channel for your business, that is a useful outcome — it saves the months and the budget that would have gone into finding out slowly.
How to tell a real SEO audit from an automated tool report

A tool report is generated in seconds and lists every deviation from a generic checklist, sorted by the tool's own severity scale. It will tell you that eighty images lack alt text and that a heading is out of order. Neither fact explains why the site does not bring enquiries.

A real audit starts from the business question and works backwards. It looks at which queries your buyers actually use, which of your pages compete with each other for the same query, what competitors rank for and why, and which two or three changes would move the most. The output is ordered by impact on your situation, not by a scanner's severity colour.
The practical test: if the document could have been produced without knowing what you sell and to whom, it is a tool report with a cover page.

children.text: Why Australian buyers check your service area before anything else

In most English-speaking markets a buyer assumes a supplier serves them until something suggests otherwise. In Australia the assumption runs the other way, and it's worth understanding why, because it isn't hostility.

Offshore delivery is routine here. A great deal of professional and technical work is bought from suppliers elsewhere, and that arrangement is normal, accepted and often preferred. What follows from its normality is that buyers have learned to check: whether a supplier actually works with Australian clients, what that looks like in practice, and what happens when something needs attention.

The mistake is treating that check as scepticism to be overcome. It's a routine question, and the cost of leaving it unanswered isn't an objection you get to handle — it's a buyer who moves on to a page that answered it.
What answering it looks like on a page
Concretely, and none of it is difficult:

A stated service area, in the copy and in structured data, so both a reader and a machine can see it. Pricing that acknowledges the market. Contact conventions in the local format. Some indication of how work with buyers here actually runs — because "we serve Australia" answers less than a description of what serving Australia involves.
What matters is that the answer exists on the page rather than in a reply to a first email, because the buyer who needed it usually doesn't send one.
Population concentration changes the targeting question
An unusual feature of this market, and the inverse of the American situation.
In the United States the country is too fragmented to target nationally, and narrowing is compulsory.

In Australia most of the population sits in a small number of metropolitan areas, which means national and metro-level targeting nearly coincide — reach the major metros and you have reached most of the market.

The practical consequence is that for regionally delivered services, city-level intent is where the reachable queries are, and a country-wide aim tends to rank for nothing in particular. For nationally delivered services the concentration works in your favour: a smaller set of geographic targets covers a larger share of the market than the same effort would elsewhere.
Australian English is its own thing

Not a footnote. Terminology, spelling and phrasing here diverge from both British and American usage, and the divergences land in commercially relevant places — the words buyers actually type when looking for a service.

A keyword list built for the UK misses. A list built for the US misses differently. Both produce pages targeting terms with less volume than the ones being searched, and both read to a local as having been written somewhere else — which loops back to the service-area question the page was supposed to answer.
The competitive field is mature
This is a developed digital market with established domestic players who have held the obvious commercial terms for years.
That's the same situation as Britain, and the same conclusion applies
: the reachable positions are narrower and more specific than the head terms a newcomer aims at first.
Where that leaves a realistic ceiling too low to justify the budget, that's worth establishing for the price of an audit rather than a year of retainer. It happens, and I'd rather say so early.
Assistant answers about this market draw on a smaller pool

English-language AI answers are the most contested there are. But a question asked specifically about Australia — naming the country, referencing local conditions, asking about suppliers serving this market —
works from a much narrower set of sources than a general English query does

That's where a company entering deliberately has room. Clear facts, outside corroboration and explicit statements about serving this market count for more here than the general English picture would suggest, and it moves independently of search positions.
Measured separately, with a fixed set of Australia-context prompts run monthly, because a blended English-language number hides it entirely.
What gets checked before anything ships

The part that's hard to advertise and easy to verify. Every language version is opened and read rather than assumed to work because the first one did. Layouts are checked in each script the site actually carries, on mobile conditions rather than on a fast connection at a desk. Structured data is validated against what the page actually says instead of being copied from a template. Every claim on the page is one that can be checked, because a claim that can't be is a liability the first time someone tries.
None of that is remarkable individually. What makes the difference is that it's done every time rather than when there's room in the schedule.
AI SEO for the Australian market: visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews (GEO, AEO)

Australian buyers increasingly put the service-area question to an assistant: “Which software studios in Europe work with Sydney clients and overlap with AEST hours?”, “Is there a European lab equipment supplier that ships to Brisbane and quotes in AUD including GST?” In plain words, GEO and AEO make a company easy for an AI model to describe correctly when the question names Australia, instead of hoping a generic English page stretches that far. What an assistant needs to find:
Facts on the page itself: the states or cities you deliver to, prices in AUD with GST treatment stated, support hours in AEST or AWST.
Organization or ProfessionalService markup whose areaServed lists Australia and your metros, plus an en-AU hreflang version if the site also serves other English-speaking markets.
The same company name, contacts and service description on Google Business Profile, LinkedIn and the review platforms Australians look at, such as Trustpilot, or Clutch for agencies.
Direct answers in Australian English to what buyers here want settled first: who they will deal with, when they can reach you, how invoicing works.

I start by putting Australia-specific buyer questions to Perplexity, ChatGPT and Google’s AI Overviews and keeping what they say about you; after the changes go live I ask again, so the difference is visible rather than assumed.

children.text: Why "the Baltics" is a label rather than a market

The three countries are grouped constantly — in trade statistics, in regional sales roles, in the way companies plan expansion. Commercially the grouping makes some sense. For search work it makes almost none.

Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian are not variations of one another. Lithuanian and Latvian are related to each other; Estonian is unrelated to both. Nothing transfers between them: not a keyword list, not a page, not a phrase. Whatever you build for one country you build again for the next, and the only things that carry across are the technical layer and the site structure.

The competitive sets are also largely separate. A company dominating results in Vilnius is often absent in Riga, and vice versa. So "we're in the Baltics" describes a commercial intention rather than a search position — you're in one of them, or in each individually, and the difference matters when the reporting arrives.
Which is why sequence beats simultaneity here
Faced with three small markets, the instinct is to enter them together and treat the region as a single project. In markets of this size that's usually the more expensive path.

Opening all three at once means three keyword sets, three sets of content, three sets of local signals and three reporting streams — for markets where the realistic outcome in each is measured in modest numbers. What that produces is a shallow presence in three places rather than a real one anywhere.

The alternative is to choose one, do it properly, and let it fund the next. Which one comes first depends on where your buyers actually are, which language capability you already have, and where the competition is thinnest — a question the audit answers rather than a preference.

The technical work carries over entirely, which is what makes sequencing cheap. The second country costs the query research, the content and the local signals; the structure, the markup and the measurement setup are already built.

One factor here has no equivalent elsewhere on this list, and it's worth stating precisely and narrowly.

In Latvia and Estonia, a share of the population uses Russian day to day, and a share of commercial search happens in Russian alongside the state language. Whether that segment matters to your business depends entirely on your category, your customers and where in each country they are.

That's a question for data rather than assumption, in either direction. Deciding from the outside that the segment is irrelevant leaves buyers unreached; deciding that it's the whole market gets the emphasis wrong. What the audit does is show which languages your specific buyers actually search in, per country, and the answer varies by category more than most people expect.

children.text: Why English fluency doesn't mean English search in the Netherlands

Almost everyone you deal with here will speak English well enough that the language never comes up. Meetings happen in English, emails happen in English, and it is entirely possible to run a commercial relationship with a Dutch company without a word of Dutch being needed.

From that, companies draw a reasonable conclusion and lose the market on it. Speaking a language and searching in it are different behaviours. A buyer types their query in the language they think in, and for the overwhelming majority of commercial intent here, that's Dutch. Your English site may be perfectly readable to them — but readability only matters after they've found you, and they were never going to.

This is the quiet version of missing a market. Nothing fails visibly. There's no language barrier to hit, no competitor obviously outranking you, no signal that anything is wrong. There's simply a set of searches happening every day that your site isn't part of.
Where English does still work here
Not everywhere is Dutch-first, and pretending otherwise would be as wrong as the assumption it corrects.

International B2B frequently runs in English, particularly where the buyer is themselves part of an international organisation. Technology sectors often do. Categories serving the large expatriate population in and around Amsterdam do, sometimes exclusively. In those segments an English site isn't a shortcut — it's the correct choice.

Which side of that line your category sits on isn't a guess. It's visible in what actually gets searched, and establishing it is the first thing the work does — because building Dutch content for a segment that searches in English is the same waste as the reverse, just less common.
Directness as a market characteristic, not a style preference
The second thing that separates this market: buyers here are unusually intolerant of vagueness, and it shows up in search behaviour and conversion alike.

Prices are the clearest example. A page that talks around cost and invites an enquiry is read as evasion rather than as flexibility, and the buyer moves to a competitor who published a figure. This is not a market where withholding price creates a conversation.

Beyond price: claims without numbers land poorly, capability described in adjectives lands poorly, and stated limitations land unexpectedly well. A supplier who says plainly what they don't do reads as more credible than one who implies they do everything — which is true everywhere, and unusually decisive here.

The practical consequence for the work is that content built for this market is shorter, more concrete and more numerical than content built for markets that reward warmth. That's a structural difference, not a matter of taste.
The Dutch AI answer layer is smaller than the English one
Dutch-language sources are a fraction of the English-language pool
, and assistants can only assemble answers from what exists.

That works in favour of a company entering deliberately. In English an assistant chooses between a great many well-described competitors; in Dutch there is considerably less to choose between, which means clear facts, consistent details and corroboration from outside your own site count for proportionally more.

The mistake is assuming visibility in English carries over. It doesn't — an assistant answering a Dutch question draws on Dutch sources, and a company invisible in those is simply absent regardless of how well it does elsewhere. This has to be measured separately, with a fixed set of Dutch prompts run monthly, because a blended number across languages hides exactly this gap.

Every claim on the page is one that can be checked, because a claim that can't be is a liability the first time someone tries.

children.text: Why one French version reaches several markets, and what that changes
Every other market on this list is entered on its own terms.
Work done for Germany serves Germany. Work done for the Netherlands serves the Netherlands. French is the exception, and it's worth understanding precisely, because it's easy to overstate.
A French-language site built for France is comprehensible and usable to buyers in Belgium,

What it isn't is a finished job in four other countries. Vocabulary differs — some commercial terms are simply different words in Belgium or Quebec. Conventions differ. Competitors differ entirely. And search engines localise results, so ranking in France does not automatically produce visibility in Brussels or Geneva.

a French version is built once and adapted several times, and adaptation is a fraction of the cost of a new language

Northern European markets tolerate English-only sites for a range of B2B categories. France tolerates it less, and the difference is measurable in search rather than a matter of national character.

Commercial intent here is expressed in French with high consistency. A buyer comparing suppliers types a French query, receives French results, and forms a shortlist from them. An English-only site isn't outranked in that process; it isn't in it. The domestic field is more developed than newcomers expect

This is an assessment rather than a promise, and it comes before the work. If your category's realistic ceiling is low at your budget, that's worth knowing for the price of an audit rather than the price of a year.

That isn't a style preference imported from anywhere. It shows up in behaviour: shorter time to bounce on thin pages, more pages read before an enquiry, more detailed first messages when one arrives. Content depth is a competitive position in this market rather than an indulgence.

children.text: Why you don't need to be in Germany to sell to Germany
This is the part that separates this work from building a site for a company registered somewhere.

A search engine doesn't ask where a supplier is incorporated. It asks whether the page answers the query, in the language of the query, from a site it can crawl and trust. A company in Warsaw, Lisbon or Tbilisi can rank for German commercial terms, and plenty do — what stops most of them isn't location, it's that they entered the market by translating a page rather than building for it.
Which is why this is a separate service from website development. You may already have a perfectly good site. What it doesn't have is a reason to appear when a buyer in Hamburg searches in German.
What actually stops companies entering German search
Translated keyword lists.

The most common and the most expensive. German forms compound nouns where English uses phrases, and the compound is what gets typed. A list translated from English targets the descriptive version nobody searches, and the site ranks for terms with no volume while missing the ones with all of it.
One page trying to serve several markets.
Hreflang exists precisely because search engines otherwise treat language versions as competing duplicates. Without it,
the German page and the English page split the signal instead of covering two markets
Assuming AI answers follow search rankings.
They don't, and they behave differently by language. An assistant asked a German question draws on German sources, so a company visible in English search
can be entirely absent from German AI answers
. This is measurable and needs measuring separately — a single blended number across languages hides exactly the gap that matters.
What German buyers check before they contact anyone
Worth knowing whether or not you sell here already, because it changes what the pages have to contain.

Company details, stated fully and in the place they're expected. Prices, or at least a range — silence reads as evasion rather than as flexibility. Concrete evidence of delivered work rather than adjectives. And consistency: the same facts wherever they look, because a discrepancy between your site and a directory listing is read as carelessness.
None of this is unique to Germany, but the threshold is higher, and buyers are more likely to leave without asking rather than write and find out.
How you'll know whether it's working
The market is easy to enter badly and hard to evaluate honestly, so the measurement matters as much as the work.

Non-branded clicks from Germany, reported separately from everything else. Traffic from people who already knew your name isn't evidence that a new market opened — it's evidence that your existing customers exist.
Positions on an agreed list of German queries, chosen before work starts rather than selected afterwards from whichever ones improved.
Presence in German-language AI answers, measured with a fixed set of prompts run monthly. This moves independently of search positions and needs its own number.
And a plain statement each period of what was done and what didn't work. In this kind of work some hypotheses fail, and a report where everything went to plan every month is a report worth doubting.

I've built and optimised for markets where the audience arrives from elsewhere and decides in its own language — a four-language property catalogue drawing buyers from more than twenty countries is the clearest example.
Same mechanics, different language.
What gets checked before anything ships

The part that's hard to advertise and easy to verify. Every language version is opened and read rather than assumed to work because the first one did. Layouts are checked in each script the site actually carries, on mobile conditions rather than on a fast connection at a desk. Structured data is validated against what the page actually says instead of being copied from a template. Every claim on the page is one that can be checked, because a claim that can't be is a liability the first time someone tries.
None of that is remarkable individually. What makes the difference is that it's done every time rather than when there's room in the schedule.
Selling to buyers outside Germany, specifically in the car trade?
See SEO for car exporters and dealers in Germany.
AI SEO for the German market: GEO and AEO for German-language ChatGPT answers and Google AI Overviews

A German buyer asks the assistant in German, and narrowly: a purchasing manager in Stuttgart asking which supplier of CNC-milled parts delivers within two weeks, or a practice owner in Cologne asking which booking software keeps patient data on EU servers. GEO and AEO cover what it takes for an AI model to find your company in German-language sources, trust the details and repeat them. That depends on four things:
Company facts in German as text: legal name, address, VAT ID and a full Impressum, delivery times, payment terms, and certifications such as ISO 9001 where you hold them.
Organization markup with the same legal details, Product or Service markup for what you sell, and hreflang marking the German version as de-DE, or plain de if Austria and Switzerland are in scope.
Matching entries in the B2B directories German buyers use, such as Wer liefert was, Europages and Kompass, and on Google Business Profile, down to the spelling of the company name.
Answers in German to procurement questions: minimum order, lead times, warranty, whether a German-speaking contact is available.

Before the work starts I ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, in German, what your buyers would ask and save how each describes you; once the changes are indexed, I ask word for word again and compare.

children.text: Why Ireland gets lost inside British search results

Most markets are missed because of a language you don't speak or a competitor you can't displace. Ireland is missed for a stranger reason: it shares a language and a border region with a market roughly fifteen times its size, and search results reflect that.

Irish buyers routinely encounter UK sites in their results. UK companies rank in Ireland partly by weight of history and domain authority rather than by targeting it. And a company entering Ireland finds itself competing not with Irish incumbents but with British ones who never intended to be there.
That produces a specific strategic question, and it's the first one worth answering:
is Ireland a separate market for your category, or is it adequately served by content aimed at the UK?

Both answers are legitimate and the difference is expensive. If UK-targeted content already reaches your Irish buyers acceptably, building separately duplicates effort for a fraction of a market you already have. If the two behave as distinct markets — which is common wherever local specifics, regulation, or currency matter to the buyer — treating Ireland as spillover leaves it permanently underserved.
This is what an audit settles before any budget is committed, and it's the reason this page exists separately from the UK one.
If your buyers are actually British, use the other page
Worth saying plainly rather than at the bottom in small print.

If your Irish traffic is incidental, your buyers are overwhelmingly in Britain, and Ireland shows up as a rounding error in your analytics, then the work you need is UK-market work and this page is the wrong service. That's a common situation and I'd rather identify it in the first conversation.

What makes Ireland worth treating separately is usually one of: a category where Irish regulation or standards differ; euro pricing being materially easier for the buyer than sterling; a physical or service presence in Ireland; or a competitive picture where Irish suppliers, not British ones, are who you're actually up against.
The one English-speaking market inside the EU
The other side of Ireland's position, and the reason it's structurally interesting for companies already operating in the union.

English-language content, euro pricing, EU invoicing, the same data-protection framework on both sides of the arrangement, and no customs or currency conversion in the commercial relationship. For a company registered elsewhere in the EU that wants to sell in English, this is the least complicated market available — considerably simpler than the UK, where the currency, the regulatory divergence and the paperwork all add friction that Ireland doesn't.

There's a practical detail worth knowing: the .ie domain has historically asked registrants to demonstrate a connection to Ireland, and the rules have changed over time. If a local domain matters to your plan, check the current requirements rather than assuming — it isn't like registering most country domains.
What separates an Irish page from a British one
The signals are small individually and decisive together, because search engines distinguish these markets more carefully than most companies bother to.

Currency is the loudest: prices in sterling on a page aimed at Ireland do the same damage as prices in dollars would. Contact formats and addresses in the local convention. Terminology where it diverges — the two Englishes are not identical in commercially relevant places, and the differences are the sort a keyword tool surfaces and an assumption misses. Service area stated in structured data rather than implied. And references, where content mentions context at all, that belong to this market rather than the neighbouring one.
None of this is difficult. It's just skipped by companies who treated "English-speaking" as equivalent to "already covered".

The English-language AI answer layer is the most developed and most contested there is.

But questions asked in an Irish context — naming the country, referencing local specifics, asking about suppliers serving Ireland — draw on a much smaller pool of sources, because far less has been written specifically about this market than about the English-speaking world generally.

The practical consequence is that being clearly described as serving Ireland, with facts a machine can repeat and corroboration outside your own site, counts for more here than the general English picture would suggest. children.text: Why a market this size is less contested in search than it should be
The usual relationship between market size and search competition is straightforward: bigger market, more competitors, harder to place. Italy is the clearest exception on this list.

The country has one of the highest densities of small and medium businesses in Europe, and digital investment among them has historically lagged behind comparable markets. The consequence is visible in search results: in a number of B2B and service categories, the companies that dominate the actual market have a weak or dated web presence, and the results pages are noticeably less contested than the market's size would predict.

That produces a specific opportunity — one where being competently built and properly targeted is enough to place, without needing the budget that the same position would require in Germany or Britain.

Two honest qualifications. First, this varies enormously by category: some sectors here are as competitive as anywhere, and assuming otherwise wastes money. Second, it's changing. Digital investment among Italian businesses has been rising, and the window where competence alone is sufficient narrows every year. Neither of these makes the opportunity less real; both make it worth checking now rather than assuming it'll still be there.
Which means the audit answers a different question here

On most markets the audit asks whether you can reach a realistic target. Here it asks something more interesting: whether the competition in your category is as strong as its market position suggests.

The answer is often no. A well-known local company with a site built years ago and never structured for search is a strong competitor commercially and a weak one in results. That's a gap a newcomer can occupy, and it's visible in an afternoon of looking rather than after a quarter of spending.
Where the answer is yes — where the category is genuinely contested — I'd rather say so and narrow the target than sell you the version of this page that only mentions the opportunity.
English does less work here than in Northern Europe
Worth stating plainly because it's the assumption that costs the most.

English proficiency in Italy is lower than in the Netherlands or Scandinavia, and commercial search behaviour reflects that: buyers type Italian queries and evaluate Italian results. The exceptions exist — international B2B, technology sectors, businesses whose buyers are part of multinational organisations — but they're narrower than in Northern European markets.
For most categories, entering this market means entering it in Italian. An English site can be excellent and still be absent from the process by which buyers here build a shortlist.
The country isn't uniform, and for regional services that matters

Economic activity, sector concentration and buying behaviour differ substantially between northern Italy, the centre and the south. For a business selling nationally, that's context. For anything sold or delivered regionally, it's a targeting decision: concentrating where your buyers actually are produces results that a country-wide aim doesn't.

This isn't the American situation, where the national tier is unreachable and narrowing is compulsory. Italy can be entered as a country. But where a business serves a region, treating the country as one audience dilutes the work for no gain.

children.text: Why low search volume isn't a reason to skip the Swiss market

Most markets are evaluated by asking how many people search for what you do. Applied to Switzerland, that question produces numbers that look like a rejection, and a good deal of business gets written off on the strength of them.

The arithmetic is different here, and it's worth doing properly. The population is under nine million, split across three main language regions, so a term that returns tens of thousands of monthly searches in Germany may return a few dozen here. That's not evidence of an empty market — it's what a market of this size looks like in a keyword tool.

What the tool doesn't show is the value on the other side. Deal sizes in Switzerland are among the highest in Europe across most categories. A handful of enquiries a year from search can outperform a channel producing a hundred times the traffic somewhere cheaper, and for many businesses selling here it does.

Which means the question isn't "is there volume". It's "what is one client worth, and how many of them are realistically reachable". Those are different questions with different answers, and only the second one is useful.
Three language regions behaving as three markets
The other structural fact, and the one most campaigns handle badly.

German-speaking Switzerland is by far the largest, French-speaking the second, Italian-speaking the smallest. They search in different languages, see different competitors, and have measurably different behaviour. A campaign aimed at "Switzerland" as a whole tends to serve whichever region the site's existing language happens to match, and quietly miss the others.

The practical implication is that entering all three at once is rarely the right first move. It triples the query research, the content and the local signals, in exchange for a partial presence in each. Choosing one — usually the largest, sometimes whichever matches your existing capability — and doing it properly produces a result you can build on.
There's also a carry-over worth knowing:
German-language work for Switzerland transfers substantially to Germany and Austria
if you look at those markets later. The structural and technical parts serve all three; only the query research and the local signals are country-specific.
What Swiss buyers verify before making contact
This market checks. Not unusually so by its own standards, but noticeably compared to markets where a buyer will simply write and ask.

Prices, or at least a range — vagueness reads as evasion, and this is not a market that assumes it will be given a fair number. Verifiable credentials rather than claims. Specifics about delivered work rather than adjectives about quality. A stated service area, ideally in structured data as well as in the copy. And consistency across every source carrying your details, because a discrepancy is read as carelessness rather than as an oversight.
None of this is expensive to get right. What's expensive is not knowing that the evaluation happens before the first email, and that a buyer who finds something missing usually just stops.
The AI answer layer is unusually reachable here
A small language market has a small pool of sources, and assistants can only draw on what exists.

In English-language queries an assistant is choosing between a great many well-described companies. In Swiss-market queries — particularly in French and Italian — there is far less to choose between, which means clear description, consistent facts and outside corroboration count for proportionally more.
This is one of the few structural advantages available to a company entering a small market rather than a large one, and it's recent enough that most competitors haven't acted on it.
It needs measuring separately from search positions, with a fixed set of prompts run monthly, because it moves independently and a blended number hides it.
What gets checked before anything ships

The part that's hard to advertise and easy to verify. Every language version is opened and read rather than assumed to work because the first one did. Layouts are checked in each script the site actually carries, on mobile conditions rather than on a fast connection at a desk. Structured data is validated against what the page actually says instead of being copied from a template. Every claim on the page is one that can be checked, because a claim that can't be is a liability the first time someone tries.
None of that is remarkable individually. What makes the difference is that it's done every time rather than when there's room in the schedule.

children.text: Why the absence of a language barrier makes this market harder, not easier
Every other market on this site has an obvious obstacle.
Germany needs German.

The Gulf needs Arabic or a deliberate decision not to serve it. Portugal needs a choice between three audiences. Britain appears to need nothing — you already have an English site, so the market seems open.

That impression is the problem. The absence of a barrier means no one is filtered out, which means everyone is competing, which makes this the most contested English-language market there is. A site that reaches Britain by default reaches it in the company of everyone else reaching it by default, and none of them place.
What "written in English" doesn't cover

Search engines localise heavily. The same query typed in London and in Chicago returns substantially different results, and a page that reads as being from somewhere else is at a disadvantage before its content is considered.

The specifics are unglamorous and they add up. Terminology diverges — the same service is called something else here, and the other name is what gets typed. Spelling diverges, and while search engines handle much of that, the copy still reads as foreign to a person. Formats diverge: dates, phone numbers, addresses, units. Currency is the loudest of them — prices in the wrong currency tell a buyer the page wasn't written for them, whatever the words say.
None of this is difficult. It's just never done by companies who assume their English site is already a UK site.
Where you can realistically place, and where you can't
This is the part most suppliers avoid saying, and it's the most useful thing on the page.

In a market where established competitors have spent years on the main commercial terms, some positions are not available to a new entrant in any reasonable timeframe. Pursuing them anyway is how a year of budget disappears with a report full of impressions and no clicks.

What is available: specific, narrower queries where intent is clearer and competition thinner; the terms your particular specialisation earns rather than the category head terms; and increasingly, AI answers, where the competitive picture is younger and being clearly described matters more than domain age.

Which of those apply to you is an assessment, not a promise, and it comes before the work. If the honest answer is that this market isn't worth entering at your budget, that's worth finding out for the price of an audit rather than the price of a year.
The AI answer layer is furthest ahead here
English-language assistants have more sources, more usage and more competition than any other language.
For a company entering Britain, that's the double-edged part of the market.

The opportunity: assistant answers name two or three companies, and the criteria aren't the same as search rankings. Being clearly described, consistently corroborated and unambiguous about what you do can put you in an answer that your search position wouldn't earn.
The risk: your competitors are already there, and the answers already have a shape. Changing what an assistant says is slower than changing a page, and it depends on sources you don't fully control.
Either way it needs measuring separately from search. A company can be visible in one and absent from the other, and a single blended number hides exactly that.

Not a UK-registered company. Search engines rank pages, not registrations. A local entity may matter for other reasons — payment methods, certain regulated sectors, what buyers expect in specific categories — but it isn't what determines whether you appear in British results.
Not a local address either, though the absence of any UK-specific signal is worth addressing in other ways.
What it does require is deciding to enter this market rather than assuming you're already in it.

children.text: Why targeting "the United States" is the mistake, not the goal
Every other market on this site can be entered as a whole.
Germany is a country you can address.
Britain is a country you can address.
The United States is not — it's a set of overlapping markets that happen to share a language and a currency, and the search results reflect that far more than most companies expect.

A supplier in Munich competes with suppliers in Munich. A supplier in Denver competes with suppliers in Denver, and separately with national companies serving Denver remotely, and separately again with whoever holds the generic national term. Which of those three fights you're in changes everything about what the work looks like — and the default assumption, that you're entering "the US market", puts you in the one you can't win.
Narrowing is the strategy, not a compromise
The instinct is to see narrowing as settling for less. In this market it's the opposite: it's the only version of the plan that produces anything.
Narrowing happens along three axes, usually in combination.
By vertical
— the same service sold specifically to one industry, where the buyer's language is more precise and the competitors fewer.
By geography
— a set of metros rather than a country, which for regionally delivered services is often the whole strategy.
By service
— one narrow thing done conspicuously well rather than a general offering that competes with everyone.
The choice isn't arbitrary and it isn't mine to make for you. It comes out of looking at where competition is thin enough that a realistic budget can place, which is what an audit is for.
I'd rather establish that first than take a year's retainer to find out the target was unreachable.
What this market checks before it checks your website
Something structural about American buying behaviour, and it changes what the work has to include.

Reviews carry more weight here than in any other market on this site. Buyers read them before the site, sometimes instead of the site, and an absence of them anywhere reads as absence of history. This isn't something a website can solve on its own, and I'd rather say that than sell site work as the answer to a review problem.

Then: named people rather than a team page of stock photographs. A physical address. Credentials that can be checked. Specific descriptions of delivered work rather than adjectives about quality. Consistency of all of it across every profile carrying your details, because a discrepancy is read as carelessness rather than as an oversight.
None of this is exotic. It's just checked earlier and more thoroughly here.
Accessibility, and why it comes up in this market specifically

Website accessibility litigation is a recurring feature of the American market in a way it simply isn't elsewhere. Cases are filed regularly, and the pattern is well enough established that most agencies working with US clients treat accessibility as a build requirement rather than an enhancement.

Whether any of it applies to your business is a question for a lawyer, and I'd genuinely recommend asking one rather than taking a supplier's word for it. I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice.

What I can tell you is the same thing that's true of the European requirements: building a site to accessibility standards during development costs very little, and retrofitting it costs a great deal. Given where the risk sits in this particular market, that arithmetic is worth knowing before the site exists rather than after.
Where a new entrant actually has an advantage
Mostly this page has been about what makes this market hard. One thing makes it easier, and it's recent.
AI assistant answers name two or three companies, and the criteria aren't the same as search rankings.

Domain age matters less. What matters is whether your facts are stated unambiguously, corroborated by sources outside your own site, and specific enough that a machine can repeat them without hedging.

That's a younger competitive field than search, and in the market where assistant usage is heaviest, it's the place where a company without fifteen years of history can be named alongside companies that have it.
It needs measuring separately — a fixed set of prompts run monthly — because it moves independently of positions and a blended number hides it.
What gets checked before anything ships

The part that's hard to advertise and easy to verify. Every language version is opened and read rather than assumed to work because the first one did. Layouts are checked in each script the site actually carries, on mobile conditions rather than on a fast connection at a desk. Structured data is validated against what the page actually says instead of being copied from a template. Every claim on the page is one that can be checked, because a claim that can't be is a liability the first time someone tries.
None of that is remarkable individually. What makes the difference is that it's done every time rather than when there's room in the schedule.
AI search for the US market: getting named in Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Perplexity (GEO, AEO)

In the US, the narrowing described above often happens inside the buyer’s question: “Which commercial cleaning companies serve the Denver metro and carry liability insurance?”, “Which HIPAA-compliant scheduling tools cost under $200 a month?” The plain-English version of GEO and AEO: make your company the clear, unambiguous answer an AI model can repeat to that kind of question. An assistant can only do that if it reads:
Facts spelled out on the page: the metros or states you serve, starting prices in dollars, licenses and insurance where your trade requires them, and the names of the people doing the work.
LocalBusiness or Organization markup with areaServed per metro, Person markup for named staff, and sameAs links pointing at your review profiles.

One version of your details on Google Business Profile, Yelp, the Better Business Bureau and Apple Business Connect, and for B2B services on Clutch or G2, where an assistant can find outside confirmation of what your site says.
Direct answers in American English to what buyers ask before they call: cost ranges, turnaround, contract length, whether you work in their state.

Ahead of any changes, I run your buyers’ questions metro by metro through ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews and record which companies get named; after launch, the identical questions show whether yours has joined that list.

children.text: Why most websites in Montenegro were never really built
This is a small market, and most sites in it were made rather than built.

The difference matters. A site that was made exists: it loads, it has the company name on it, someone was paid for it. A site that was built has a structure decided before the first page, language versions that were planned rather than bolted on, and functionality chosen because the business needs it rather than because the template included it.

Most sites here are the first kind, and it isn't anyone's fault — they were produced by whoever was available, usually between other work, for a business that needed something online by a date. That produces a site. It doesn't produce something that can be extended, handed to another developer, or relied on when the business changes.

What that means practically: the bar for being noticeably better here is lower than in a larger market. Not because standards are lower, but because so little of what exists was built with any intention at all.
The season decides the schedule, not the other way round
Something that separates this market from most: timing isn't a preference here, it's a constraint.

The year concentrates into a few months, and everything the site is for — bookings, enquiries, comparisons — happens inside them. A site that goes live in July has missed the year it was built for, even if it's excellent.

Search work makes this sharper. New pages need weeks to be crawled and months to accumulate any position at all, so the search side of a summer season is decided in winter. Practically: if the site matters for this season, the conversation happens before spring. If we're already past that, the honest plan is to build for next season properly rather than rush something that arrives too late to help.
I say this before quoting rather than after, because half of what makes a website work in this market is arriving in time to be used.
What I cover and what I don't
I work in English and Russian.
I don't write or optimise in Montenegrin or Serbian
— that needs a native writer, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Whether this matters depends entirely on who you sell to. If your customers are visitors, relocated residents, or buyers abroad, English and Russian are the languages they search in, and that describes a large share of businesses here. If your customers are primarily local, you need someone who writes the local language, and the honest answer is that I'm not that supplier — though the structure I build will accept a local-language version later without being rebuilt for it.
Buyers who decide before they arrive

The pattern this market shares with the property and relocation markets I've built for elsewhere: a substantial share of buyers are researching from another country, months before they're anywhere near the business.
Someone choosing an apartment, a service provider or a place to relocate reads far more carefully than someone walking past. They compare several options across borders, in a language they chose, and
increasingly they start by asking an AI assistant rather than a search engine
— which means the site is often summarised into three sentences before a person opens it.
A property catalogue I built for that behaviour
runs in four languages and draws buyers from more than twenty countries, almost all of them deciding remotely. Different country, same mechanics.
What gets checked before anything ships

The part that's hard to advertise and easy to verify. Every language version is opened and read rather than assumed to work because the first one did. Layouts are checked in each script the site actually carries, on mobile conditions rather than on a fast connection at a desk. Structured data is validated against what the page actually says instead of being copied from a template. Every claim on the page is one that can be checked, because a claim that can't be is a liability the first time someone tries.
None of that is remarkable individually. What makes the difference is that it's done every time rather than when there's room in the schedule.

children.text: What being inside the EU changes about a website in Portugal
Most of what makes a website work is the same everywhere. The part that isn't, here, is regulatory — and it cuts in two directions at once.

The first direction is practical and in your favour. A supplier registered elsewhere in the EU is, from your accountant's perspective, the least complicated kind there is: intra-EU invoicing, no customs, no currency conversion, the same VAT framework, and the same data-protection rules applying to both sides of the arrangement. That isn't a selling point so much as an absence of friction, which is easy to overlook until you've dealt with the alternative.
The second direction is the one most sites here haven't looked at.
The compliance most local sites quietly fail
Three things, in ascending order of how often they're ignored.
Consent that doesn't consent.

A banner that says cookies are being used while the tracking scripts have already loaded is not a consent mechanism; it's a decoration that documents the problem. Common enough to be unremarkable, and it's the easiest of the three to fix.
A privacy policy describing a different website.
Generated from a template, listing services the site doesn't use and omitting the ones it does. It reads as compliance and functions as evidence of its absence.
Accessibility.

European requirements that came into force in 2025 apply to a range of consumer-facing services, and a good deal of what they ask for — proper contrast, keyboard navigation, real alt text, sensible heading structure — is invisible to a sighted mouse user and therefore never noticed. Whether your specific business falls under them is a question for a lawyer, not for me, and I'd suggest asking one. What I can say is that building a site to meet them costs very little during development and a great deal afterwards.
I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice. What I do is build so that the technical side isn't the thing standing between you and compliance.
Three audiences, not one
The other structural thing about this market: a business here is usually visible to three different groups who search differently.

Portuguese-speaking residents, who search in Portuguese and expect local specifics. English-speaking residents and visitors, a very large group here, who search in English and often have no Portuguese at all. And buyers abroad — property, relocation, longer stays — who research months ahead in whatever language they use at home.

Which of the three matters most is a business question, not a technical one, and it's the first thing we'd establish. What isn't optional is deciding it deliberately rather than defaulting to whichever language happened to be convenient.

I work in English and Russian.

children.text: Why the language question in Spain has more than one right answer
In most countries a website's language is not a decision. There's a national language, possibly English alongside it for international audiences, and that's the whole conversation.

Spain works differently, and the difference is structural rather than cosmetic. Alongside Spanish, several regions have co-official languages with their own audiences, institutions and everyday use. A business in Barcelona, Valencia, Bilbao or Santiago faces a question that a business in Madrid simply doesn't — and the answer isn't the same for a restaurant serving its own neighbourhood as it is for a firm selling to clients across the country.

Add a third factor: on the coasts and islands, a large foreign-resident and visiting population searches in English, German, French or Russian, and for many businesses there they represent more revenue than local customers do.
So the honest position is that there isn't one correct configuration. There's a decision, and it belongs to the business rather than to whoever builds the site.
Why defaulting is the expensive version

What happens in practice is that the decision gets made accidentally. The site is built in whichever language was convenient — often whichever the developer worked in — and the others are postponed until later.
Later is where the cost sits. A site built for one language and then extended to two isn't a translation project;
it's an architectural change

, because language versions affect routing, URL structure, canonical relationships, content modelling and the entire administrative side of adding a page. Doing it at the start is close to free. Doing it eighteen months in usually means rebuilding.

The practical advice is the same regardless of which languages you land on: decide the full list now, even if you launch with one of them. Building the structure to accept a second and third language costs almost nothing when nothing exists yet.
Who your buyers actually are, which isn't always who you'd assume
Worth establishing before the language question, because it answers it.

A business in a Spanish city serving that city has one profile. A business on the Costa del Sol or in the Balearics may find that most of its enquiries come from people who don't live there yet — buyers researching property, relocation, services and schools from another country, months in advance. A business selling professional services nationally has a third profile again.
Each of those reads a website differently. Local customers check for local specifics and immediacy. Foreign buyers researching remotely read far more carefully, compare across borders, and
increasingly ask an AI assistant before they open a single site
— which means the facts on your pages get summarised before a person ever sees your design.
I've built for that last pattern directly

Different country, same behaviour.

Spanish, Catalan, Galician and Basque content is not part of what I deliver.
